en: First Chapter. Homage to the Supreme Deity, whose self is unconquered by the three qualities (guṇas), who is omnipresent in the form of yoga, and who is the cause of the cessation of saṃsāra. 1.1
Salutation to the wise Mahādeva, the twenty-sixth principle, the primordial matter (pradhāna), who expands within and is the cause of maintenance, destruction, and creation.
In the great field of Prajāpati, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Kālindī,
at Prayāga— the supreme, most meritorious place, the path to the world of Brahmā.
The sages, firm in their vows and with their impurities destroyed by austerity,
having performed their daily rites on the day of the full moon, set out for the purpose of bathing at the sacred fords.
Not seeing the Sūta, who was devoted to truth and a knower of the Purāṇas,
they approached him after bathing in that great holy place in order to pay their respects.
Seeing the charioteer approaching, the sages, with joyful hearts,
prepared a seat and a place for him to rest as was appropriate for him.
Having bowed down to all those bulls among sages, the charioteer,
endowed with every virtue, took the seat that had been offered to him.
In former times, O virtuous one, while he was seated at the Brahma-sacrifice of the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest, the sages who had perfected themselves through austerity questioned him.
The narrative of the Mahābhārata and the supreme Purāṇa have been told by you;
therefore, you appear to us as the son of Satyavatī himself.
He knows the supreme meaning of all scriptures, is devoted to truth and righteousness, and is constantly intent on honoring the twice-born; therefore, it is fitting for you to question him.
We ask you about the birth of the wise Kārttikeya— that which is distinguished among the Purāṇas as being like the Bhārata narrative.
For all these sages are solely devoted to your worship,
their minds filled with eager longing to serve the son of Skanda.
Thus addressed then by those perfected, eminent sages, Sūta spoke these words, expressive of the true state of affairs, to all the munis.
Listen, all you sages, to the birth of Kārttikeya,
his devotion to Brahmanas, his majesty, and his valor which surpasses that of the thirty gods.
When the great-souled Śuka had departed for the supreme abode out of a desire for liberation,
Vyāsa, tormented by grief for his son, beheld Tryambaka.
Upon seeing the Great Lord, Vyāsa,
the son of Satyavatī, became free from all affliction as he wandered through the worlds at that time.
Then, on the peak of Meru, he beheld the first-born son of Brahmā,
Sanatkumāra, the granter of boons, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
He stood in a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun, possessing a brilliance like fire,
surrounded by high-souled sages who were perfected in yoga and devoted to asceticism.
It was surrounded by those who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who were endowed with the knowledge of all religious traditions,
and who had attained complete learning, so that it resembled the four-faced Brahmā himself.
Having seen that great-souled sage Vyāsa standing there,
he paid homage with supreme devotion, as if to the Grandfather himself.
Then the son of Brahmā, having embraced the highly effulgent Vyāsa who had arrived, spoke these auspicious words with supreme affection.
"By good fortune, O knower of dharma, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, you have attained freedom from sorrow; ask whatever you wish, and I shall speak."
O Brahmins, having heard the words of his son, that bull among sages spoke these words to Brahmā, which had long resided in his heart.
How was the birth of the wise Kumāra Kārttikeya? For what purpose and from whence did it come? Indeed, I wish to know this.

How was he the son of Rudra, and how was he the son of Agni and Gaṅgā? Furthermore, how was he the son of Umā, and how again the son of Svāhā? And how was he the son of Suparṇī, of the Mothers, and of the Kṛttikās? || 1.25 ||
Who was he that arose in the beginning, what were his austerities, and what was his prowess?
For this is a delusion of all beings; tell it to me exactly as it happened.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned, that radiant and most excellent son of Brahmā,
the omniscient one, related everything to Vyāsa, who performs his deeds without weariness.
Listen to that, O sinless ones, as it is being recounted by me according to its true nature.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 1.1.
The Second Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
I take refuge in the Lord Īśāna, the omniscient and unconquered.
To Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Lord of the entire universe.
Whose power is unimpeded and whose sovereignty is universal—his lordship and pervasiveness are said to be the results of his own actions. (2.2)
Having bowed down to that divine Soma, being self-restrained and pure,
I shall relate the auspicious account of the birth of Skanda for one who desires to know the ancient narrative.
The descent of the body of the god Rudra, the Supreme Self;
his consecration by Prajāpati, and likewise the severing of his head. 2.4.
The vision of those belonging to the six families and the dismissal of the assembly; the origin of Naimiṣa and the conclusion of the sacrificial session.
In that [section] there is the arrival of Brahmā, as well as the practice of austerity,
the appearance of Śarva, and the manifestation of the Goddess.
The truth regarding the dispute, as well as the curse of Dakṣa, and how Menā was born, and how the Goddess’s svayaṃvara took place. 2.7.
The granting of boons by the gods, the [birth] of the wise Vasiṣṭha,
and the origin of Parāśara and the high-souled Vyāsa.
The occurrence of the conflict between Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika,
the desolation of Vārāṇasī, and the description of the greatness of that sacred field.
In this [chapter], there is the presence of Rudra here, as well as the grace of Nandin;
furthermore, there is the sight of the Gaṇas and their description in its entirety.
The utterance of Kālī, as well as the performance of penance,
the narrative of Somanandin, and likewise the granting of the boon.
The state of being Gaurī, the obtaining of a son, and the very birth of the Goddess;
the motherhood of spirits by Kauśikī, as well as the lions who serve as her chariot-warriors.
The abode of Gaurī on the Vindhya mountains, the meeting of the Vindhya range with the sun, the majesty of Agastya, and the slaying of Sunda and Nisunda. 2.13.
The departure of Nisumbha and Sumbha, as well as the slaying of Mahiṣa;
the consecration by the Kauśikī river and also the granting of boons.
The birth of Andhaka, the binding of the Earth,
and likewise the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The binding of Bali, the agreement with the Goddess, the departure of the gods, and the office of Agni as messenger; || 2.16 ||
The granting of boons by the gods and the dismissal of Śukra;
likewise, the birth of his son and the appearance of Andhaka to the queen. || 2.17 ||
The assault by the Daityas led by Śailādi, the hundredfold forms of the Goddess, the granting of boons to Āryā, and the hymn of praise (stava) to Śailādi. 2.18.
The arrival of the god, the narration of what had occurred, the account of the devoted wife, and the service rendered to the preceptor. (2.19)
The narrative of Pañcacūḍā and the invincibility of her splendor;
the arrival of the messenger, their conversation, and then his departure. (2.20)
The conversation with the Asura Andhaka, the arrival at Mount Mandara,
the arrival of the Gaṇas, and likewise the hearing of their enumeration.
Then there was the subjugation of Andhaka through a great battle,
as well as the gift of half his body and the taking of Aśoka’s son.
The origin of Bhasmasoma, as well as his dwelling in the cremation ground;
the reason for Rudra's blue throat, and likewise the description of his sanctuary.
The birth of Kubera, the wise king of the yakṣas;
the subduing of the lords of serpents; and the felling of Śikhara.
And the subjugation of the three worlds together with Śakra, the granting of the army of the gods, and the consecration as commander-in-chief. || 2.25 ||
The arrival of Nārada, who had been sent by Tāraka;
the fierce slaughter of Tāraka; and the expedition to Bhadravaṭa.
The slaying of Mahiṣa, the destruction of Krauñca,
the extraction of the Śakti spear, and the auspicious killing of Tāraka.

The origin of the fear between the gods and the asuras, the battle of the three cities, the conflict with Prahlāda, and the narrative of the ungrateful— these, along with the great majesty of the brahmins, are proclaimed in detail. 2.28.
Having understood this correctly, one should become an attendant to the prince;
being strong and endowed with intelligence, he obtains a son who is highly esteemed. || 2.29 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 2.2 ||
The Third Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to this divine narrative, which destroys all sins.
Listen to this wonderful narrative, rich in meaning and consistent with the Vedas, which I shall relate;
by hearing it, even a person of sinful deeds may attain the supreme goal. (3.1)
One should never relate this story to an atheist, one who lacks faith, a rogue, or a man who is prone to finding fault. (3.2)
O Great Brahmā, this should be told to a son, to a disciple who is righteous and free from malice, or to one who is devoted to the gods,
as well as to one who is devoted to Kumāra and possesses faith. (3.3)
In the beginning, Brahmā, the overseer of creatures, was produced within this cosmic egg;
enveloped by darkness, he did not know his father, Brahmā, due to ignorance. (3.4)
Knowing "I am alone," he gazed upon all the worlds;
yet, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, he saw no other there.
And when Brahmā was addressed as "Son, son" by the wise Śarva, he bowed down with palms joined in reverence and sought refuge in him alone. (3.6)
Having bestowed upon Brahmā the power of creation accompanied by knowledge, as well as sovereignty over the worlds and the power of disappearance, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, [vanished]. || 3.7 ||
Thus, O Vyāsa, this eternal Upaniṣad has been declared by me, hearing which yogins attain Maheśvara through meditation. 3.8.
To him who in the beginning created Brahmā as his son and who bestowed knowledge upon him—to those wise ones who perceive Him dwelling within themselves belongs eternal peace, and not to others. 3.9.
Seeing his father endowed with supreme radiance, that Vyāsa, desiring a son for the sake of progeny, performed intense austerity. (3.10)
In a very short time, his father was fully gratified by that great-souled one who was endowed with such vast yogic austerity.
He came into his sight, and the Giver of Boons said to him, "I am here.
Bowing down and placing his joined palms to his head, he offered praise. (3.12)
Salutation to the Supreme God, the creator even of the gods;
salutation to the Ordainer of the world-systems, the Lord of Brahmā. 3.13.
To the one who is endowed with power and devoid of incapacity, who is infinite, immeasurable, and beyond the scope of the senses. (3.14)
To the all-pervading one, who was pervaded in the past, the sustainer, the impeller,
the one who has brought about consciousness, and the maker of the arrangement of the principles.
For the sake of granting peace to those possessing qualities who have urged him as their primary leader,
for the sake of bestowing vision upon all, and indeed for his own manifestation, || 3.16 ||
And to the grasper of objects, to the performer of restraint,
and likewise to the mind, the senses, and the very act of restraint therein.
To the creator of the qualities of beings and likewise the giver of power,
to the maker of the cosmic egg and of me, to the inconceivable one who is unborn,
O immeasurable Father, being ever pleased with us, grant us the Śakvarī hymn. 3.18.
O Vyāsa, as he was thus offering praise, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, being pleased, spoke himself to his son Brahmā, who was likewise prostrate before him. (3.19)
"Since this subtle [reality] has been known by you, O child of great splendor, therefore you shall attain renown in the worlds by the name 'Brahman'. (3.20)
And because I have been called "Father" by you, O best among the wise, therefore your status as "Grandfather" (Pitāmaha) shall attain renown in the world. (3.21)
"Because you have performed such fierce and most difficult austerity for the sake of progeny, I grant you the status of Prajāpati, O self-restrained one. (3.22)
Having spoken thus, that Lord of the Gods created women in embodied form—
those eight primary natures (prakṛtis) along with the specific objects and the senses;
and all those states of being approached the God in their own forms.
Then the Lord, the husband, endowed with his own splendor, said to them:
"Complete this consecration today; do not delay."
Taking each their own divine and inconceivable disposition, the exceedingly radiant Prajāpati was consecrated [as king]. (3.25)
In that regard, having thus seen the subtle with the divine eye, the yogis who know the reality of yoga sing this ancient [hymn] concerning the three qualities (guṇas). 3.26.
O Lord, Rudra is indeed the creator of all beings and of you as well;
together with us, you are the one who sets the world in motion. (3.27)
That god, being fully satisfied and possessing supreme sovereignty,
consecrated his first-born son Brahmā in the office of Prajāpati.
Having respectfully composed this work called the *Tattva*, which is endowed with various paths and yogas, the Lord of Beings—

who, ever abiding in the minds of all, knows both the auspicious and the inauspicious— I bow with devotion to that God, the Master of the Pramathas, and constantly seek refuge in Him who is subtler than the subtlest. (3.30)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 3.3.
The Fourth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having then obtained the status of Prajāpati, he proceeded to create progeny.
And those creatures being created did not increase for him. || 4.1 ||
While performing that creation, the Grandfather, being devoid of power, then began once more to practice austerities for the sake of creation. (4.2)
Knowing his asceticism to be for the sake of creation, the Lord of the Three Worlds,
having pervaded the universe with his splendor, approached him;
the Creator, the Lord of the World, revealed the entire universe within his own body.
Having come in person, Hara, the Lord of Gods and Master of the great elements,
pervading as it were the entire universe with his supreme splendor,
Śambhu said to the Grandfather, "O child, ask for a boon."
Brahmā, for the purpose of creating the world, mentally declared, "You are my son.
Knowing that intention of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, the giver of boons himself, reflected, "This one is deluded," and spoke thus. (4.5)
"Since you desire a son from your father who has returned, therefore,
by my command, your son shall be an embodiment of myself."
And he, my leader of the Gaṇas, shall become your son;
Rudra, having assumed a physical form, O fool, will humble you.
He possesses sovereignty over all branches of knowledge and over all forms of yoga;
he holds the lordship of strength and the mastery of employing divine weapons.
All these things given by me shall immediately attend upon him in every way:
the bow Pināka, the trident, the sword, and even the battle-axe.
A water-pot, a staff, the Pāśupata weapon,
the thunderbolt of universal destruction, and the wheel of reabsorption—
endowed with all such powers, your son shall thus come to be.
When that great-souled one had spoken thus and vanished,
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, desiring sons, then performed a sacrifice.
While offering oblations, joined with the sacrificial ladle and accompanied by the ritual striking,
he wiped his forehead with his hand holding the fuel-stick.
For that splendor of Maheśvara, which had been deposited in Brahmā and transmitted, was impelled by the God of gods and fell into the consumer of oblations (the sacrificial fire). 4.14.
At that moment, having remembered that supreme boon, Maheśa dispatched Rudra as a leader of his attendants (gaṇapa), and he then became Sadyojāta immediately.
And that moisture-born fire, having first been joined with the flames and become red, then suddenly turned blue once again. || 4.16 ||
Because he cried out "Nīlalohita," that lord became so named;
three-eyed and ten-armed, the glorious one stood as if overshadowing Brahmā.
Having praised that omnipresent god, the imperishable Nīlalohita, with names beginning with Śarva and with forms such as water and the rest, Brahmā [proceeded].
Having first known the creator of all, who is established in the great elements,
that Lord then created other various kinds of beings in the world.
He too, having established himself in yoga and endowed with sovereign power,
entered all the worlds and sustained them at all times.
From him, moreover, the auspicious sons of Brahmā, such as Dakṣa, Dharma, and the others, created all beings, teeming with gods and humans. (4.21)
Then, after a long time had passed through many kalpas,
as he repeatedly sustained living beings through his yoga, this present kalpa arrived.
When the economy was established, when the release of rain had begun,
and when the subjects had increased in prosperity, he performed a sacrifice at Prayāga.
These sages of strict vows belong to the six lineages of Brahmā: the Marīcis, the Atris, the Vasiṣṭhas, and likewise the Kratus. (4.24)
The Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, their sins burnt away by ascetic penance,
approached Brahmā together during an interval between rites and spoke.
"O Blessed One, we are enveloped by a great darkness;
exhausted and disputing with one another, we do not perceive that which is supreme. (4.26)
"O Lord, this doubt has long resided within our hearts;
for you alone know the supreme cause according to its true nature. (4.27)
What is the supreme among all beings, and what is the strongest in every respect? By whom is the universe presided over? Who is eternal, and who is everlasting? (4.28)
Who is the creator of all beings and the impeller of primordial nature? Who is that high-minded one who directs us in all our undertakings? (4.29)
To whom are all beings subject? Who is the ordainer of all?
How indeed may we behold him? Tell us all this in its entirety. (4.30)
Thus addressed, Brahmā then spoke in the presence of all—
the gods, the sages, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the rākṣasas.
Those who were the leaders of the yakṣas and asuras,
and those others belonging to the birds and piśācas who were in their vicinity,
rose up with palms joined in reverence and uttered the words "Rudra" three times with a protracted tone. || 4.32 ||
He can be seen through austerity alone and by no other means;
he is the creator of all beings, powerful, and the universe is composed of him.
All beings are subject to his will, and by him this world is sustained.
Then all those lords of the world paid homage to the Great-Souled One.
The sages said:
"O God, what is that great austerity by which that Lord may be seen?
Tell us that, O Lord of Gods, and grant us your boon."
The Grandfather said:
"Perform a great sacrificial session (sattra), free from the defects of speech and mind;
and I shall tell you the place in which you shall perform it. (4.36)
Then, having created that mind-made wheel, he said to them:
"This wheel has been hurled by me; follow it without delay. (4.37)
"Wherever its rim should break, that place shall be auspicious for asceticism.
Then he released that discus, and they followed after it.
As he was traveling swiftly, the place where his wheel-rim shattered became known by the name Naimiṣa; it is meritorious and honored everywhere.
It was worshipped by gods, humans, and siddhas; by fierce rākṣasas and divine serpents;
by yakṣas along with hosts of gandharvas and piśācas; by all the apsarases and by the sons of Diti. (4.40)

He was praised by self-controlled Brahmins endowed with tranquility and yoga, by all the lords of the earth who visit sacred fords, and by Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the Pitṛs. (4.41)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 4.4.
The Fifth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Having reached that Naimiṣa forest, the sages of blazing splendor—
They performed a great divine sacrificial session lasting for a thousand years.
All of them were single-minded, free from the sense of "mine," and devoid of egoism;
they constantly meditated upon the Lord of Lords, together with their wives, sons, and sacred fires.
All of them, being devoted to that, intent on that, joined with that, and taking refuge in that, perform all their actions while having gone to him alone with their minds. (5.3)
Perceiving their state of mind, the illustrious and auspicious Mātariśvan—
the great ascetic who moves through all living beings and impels all creatures— appeared in embodied form before those performers of the sacrificial session.
Having seen and honored that imperishable Mātariśvan as he sat upon his holy seat, the sages of rigid vows questioned him regarding the entire origin of the world as well as its dissolution. (5.5)
And the entire duration of their stay, the lineages, the ages and the intermediate periods (manvantaras), the complete genealogical histories, and likewise the divine measures of time— 5.6.
The origin and dissolution of the eight classes of divine beings, as well as the entire creation of the ancestors and the measurement of Brahmā’s lifespan. (5.7)

The entire course of the moon and the sun, as well as the movement of the stars and planets; the station of all the lords, and the laws of the continents in their entirety; the establishment of the castes and stages of life, and the performance of sacrifices. (5.8)
The Lord related all of this in its entirety, as well as their divine thousand-year period of practice following that departure. (5.9)
Then she appeared in a divine form, with the Sāman as her voice, the quarters of space as her gaze,
the Yajus as her sense of smell, the Atharvaśiras as her head, and the Śabda-veda as her auspicious tongue.
Logic is her ear, etymology her skin; she moves upon the feet of the Ṛgveda verses;
Time is her arm, the rain-giving clouds her hand, and she bears the days as her fingers. (5.11)

With her limbs as the divisions of time such as *kalās*, with her fingers as the months, she was divine and shared in the nature of the cosmic cycles (*kalpa*); she was skilled in the arts and possessed lofty breasts.
With prosody as her waist-cloth and Mīmāṃsā as her navel, she has the Purāṇas for her broad hips and the Dharmaśāstras for her desires. 5.13.
Her feet were the stages of life (āśrama), her knees the social classes (varṇa), her ankles the sacrifices (yajña), and her toes the fruits [of action].
Her body was the worlds and the Vedas, adorned with the beautiful hairs that were the Vedic meters (chāndasa). || 5.14 ||
Clad in the garments of faith and virtuous conduct, proclaiming the teachings of yoga, she emerged from the center of the altar and proceeded with a supreme stream of water. (5.15)
At its conclusion, having plunged into the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), they were united with Vāyu;
they asked him, "Who indeed is this [woman]? to the god Vāyu of great intelligence. (5.16)
That one of great splendor spoke to the sages who were permeated by righteousness:
"You are all pure through your asceticism, and you have performed a great act of dharma. (5.17)
Since this meritorious river has come here from the world of Brahmā, she is named Sarasvatī, the ornament of the world of Brahmā. (5.18)
First, she came to this world of mortals for the sake of your success;
there exists no woman more meritorious than she in all the three worlds. (5.19)
Vāyu said: In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history, the conversation between Brahmā and Sacrifice itself in the past. 5.21.
In ancient times, having performed sacrifices with blazing splendor, the divine Brahmā created all beings, both stationary and moving. (5.22)
Having seen him, the radiant god, endowed with supreme splendor,
gazed upon his own worlds with his four lotus-like faces.
Having seen again and again the gods and others, as well as humans and others, the high-minded one thought:
"In this world, there is no other equal to me, nor any superior. (5.24)
For I am indeed the creator of all beings; no other whatsoever exists.
There is nowhere anyone equal to me as a ruler and a maker of the world. (5.26)
While he was thinking thus, the high-minded Sacrifice arrived;
and that radiant being said to him, "O great-minded one, do not think so!
For this delusion of yours will lead to your destruction. (5.27)
Such a thing is not fitting for you today, who are established in courage and born of your own nature;
for you alone are the creator and there is no other, yet even so, this act brings you no glory.
"For I am indeed the creator of all beings and likewise of the world;
yet I do not experience delusion, unlike you, O God, who boast in this manner. (5.29)
Then Brahmā said to him: "O Lord, you are not the sustainer;
for I alone am the supporter and the nourisher of all beings. All beings were created by me; it is you who are utterly deluded in this matter. (5.30)
Then the Veda, supremely radiant and deeply agitated, arrived there;
and the Lord Veda said to those two, "It is not so. (5.31)
"I am the foremost, O illustrious ones; I never speak an untruth. Listen to who is the creator of all beings, and of you two as well. (5.32)
The Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, Rudra, the omnipresent Master, by whom I was given to you and by whom you were made the Lord of Creatures. (5.33)
This sacrifice, its origin, and the cosmic egg wherein it is established—all this has indeed been produced from Him; there is no other creator for us anywhere. (5.34)
To him who spoke thus, the divine Brahmā addressed this Vedic utterance:
"I am the leader and likewise the creator of all the Vedas. (5.35)
"By my grace, you are indeed the Veda and this sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
You two are deluded, or else unrighteousness has been committed by you. Perform an expiation, and then you shall be released from that sin. (5.36)
When he had spoken thus, a great sound arose; and a vast circle, shaped like the orb of the sun, was seen high above in the sky by that great noise. (5.37)
Having fallen from that state and reached the surface of the earth, he arrived at a grove of the Himalayas resounded with the songs of various birds;
after remaining in the sky for a long time, he indeed became one who dwells upon the ground. (5.38)
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, having gazed toward all the quarters with his four lotus-like faces, did not see him stationed in the sky.
He created a blazing fifth face situated upon his head;
with that, he beheld him stationed in the sky, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns,
having the form of the solar disc, roaring, and terrible to behold.
Seeing that fifth head of his, which was born of wrath, great and resembling the fire of universal destruction, it grew in size as if to devour him. (5.41)
Then that [fire], increasing and resembling the mouth of the submarine mare, blazing and accompanied by sound, was that very god with his radiant orb. || 5.42 ||
With the nail of the thumb of his left hand,
as if in mere disdain, he swiftly severed that great and terrible fifth head of Brahmā.
Then, his head severed by the blazing [discus], afflicted by intense suffering and tormented by heat,
he fell down, his mind bewildered and utterly deprived of the practice of yoga.
Then, like one who has awakened from sleep, the great ascetic regained his composure and praised Mahādeva, who stood within the sacrificial circle, with a piteous voice.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one; indeed, salutations to the hundred-eyed one.
Salutations to the one with the wide-open mouth; indeed, salutations to the hundred-faced one.
Salutations to the one with a thousand faces, indeed salutations to the one who is all faces;
salutations to the one with a thousand feet, indeed salutations to the one who is all feet.
Salutations to the thousand-handed one, and salutations to him whose hands are everywhere;
salutations to the creator of all, and salutations to you, the witness of all. 5.48.
Salutations to the one whose color is like the sun, and salutations to the one who performs the cutting off of the head;
likewise, salutations to the creator of creation and dissolution, and to the creator of maintenance.
Salutations to the one with a thousand lingas and to the one with a thousand feet;
salutations indeed to the one whose linga is the dissolution and to the one whose linga is water.
To Him who moves within, who is all-pervading, and who impels primordial nature;
to Him who pervades all beings and who impels the Puruṣa. (5.51)

To Śarva, who brings about the excellence of the senses and their objects, who ordains all things accordingly, who exists in the past and the future, and who is eternally endowed with the quality of purity.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone are the creator of the worlds, as well as their sustainer and bestower;
it behoves you to show favor to one who has come for refuge and is self-restrained. 5.53
As he was thus praising him with perfect and supreme devotion,
the Lord of the gods then granted him divine vision.
Then, with that eye, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
beheld a mass of splendor within a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun.
Then, from the midst of that [assembly], they heard a great voice—
deep, sweet, and well-composed, endowed with auspicious characteristics—
which had previously been uttered by the god, saying, "O son, O son! (5.56).
"Since this son of dark-blue and red hue was born from your perspiration,
and since I previously spoke thus to you when I was seeking a son," (5.57)
"That leader of my host who is yours shall become an embodiment of me;
having attained supreme knowledge, O fool, he will instruct you. (5.58)
This accomplishment of its fruit—the severing of your head—has been brought about by me alone; therefore, be at peace now.
"And it is he, O great-minded one, who shall cut off the head of that very sacrifice which has strayed onto a wrong path for some other reason.
I am pleased by this hymn; what shall I give to you, O sinless one? (5.60)
Vāyu said:
Then that blessed one, being delighted, bowed with auspicious words and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that Lord who was both visible and invisible. (5.61)
"O Blessed One, the sight of you does not cause me any pain at all;
rather, I desire that you always bear this head upon yours, so that I might remember even this severing of my head, O Lord. (5.62)
Furthermore, I desire that you yourself restrain me from unrighteous deeds;
and thus, with this purpose in view, may I behold you at your ease. (5.63)
Having heard the request of Brahmā, the Lord of the World said:
"He who is known as your son is none other than Nīlalohita, my own form;
he shall sever the head of the sacrifice and he shall carry away your head. (5.64)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods vanished on that very spot.
When Mahādeva had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
together with the sacrifice and the Vedas, returned to his own world.
Vāyu said:
That mortal who should hear this secret, which is equal in meaning to the Vedas, shall, upon the dissolution of the body, attain union with Brahman. 5.66.
Whoever constantly recites this in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This divine narrative is not to be told to those who are not sons, disciples, or yogis; nor should it be told to one who lacks understanding, nor to the deceitful, nor to the arrogant. 5.68.
One should always recite this great, divine ordinance against unrighteousness in an assembly of Brahmins and physicians.
Such a man gains an opportunity here in this world, and upon the dissolution of the body, he shall enter the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 5.5 ||
The Sixth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed god, the one with matted hair, who is blue and red, [spoke].
By the command of the Supreme Lord, he seized the head of Brahmā.
Taking that blazing head and assuming a deformed appearance,
he set out for alms, employing the play of yoga.
Then, O twice-born ones, he went to the abode of the gods for the sake of alms;
yet no one gave that lord a fitting alms. (6.3)
He went by way of the gateway to the house of the high-souled Viṣṇu;
he stood at his door, uttering the auspicious word for alms. (6.4)
Having beheld that vulva with his eye of yoga, Viṣṇu split open the head from the forehead and caused a stream of blood to fall;
and it fell then, spreading out for fifty yojanas.
O best of Brahmins, although she flowed for many years with that stream, not even half of the skull of the Grandfather was filled.
Then the God, smiling, spoke these auspicious words to him: (6.6)
A maiden is given in marriage but once; fire is kindled but once;
kings speak [their solemn word] but once; and alms are bestowed but once. (6.7)
"I am pleased with this fitting gift of yours, O giver of honor!
Choose a boon—blessings upon you—for I am indeed the granter of boons to you today. (6.8)
Viṣṇu said:
"This alone is a praiseworthy boon, that I behold the lord of the gods, the divine Śaṅkara, the fierce Śarva with matted hair. (6.9)
Then, seeing the shadow upon the nectar situated in the skull-cup,
the god created a radiant man, powerful and resembling Viṣṇu.
They said to him: "You are indeed inexhaustible and truly free from old age and death;
you are without rival in battles, the unsurpassed friend of Viṣṇu, and the glorious performer of the gods' work. Dwell together with him. (6.11)
Since your birth was from women (nārī) who were born from the body of Viṣṇu,
you shall therefore be known by the name Nara, and you will be dear to him.
Vāyu said:
Having then comforted him and entrusted that man to Viṣṇu himself,
the Lord went to the abode of Brahmā, and those two entered his house.
Whoever, having obtained this human birth here, should either hear or recite this [work],
shall be endowed with supreme renown and be glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 6.6 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
Vāyu said:
Having reached the world of Brahmā, the Blessed One, the protector of all worlds, [remained there].
Saying, "Alms! Alms! he stood at the gate.
Seeing him with his deformed appearance and adorned with a skull in his hand, Brahmā,
through great yogic power, recognized him and praised the Lord of the World.
Then the God, being pleased with him, spoke: "I am the giver of boons;
choose, without distraction, whatever boon resides in your heart. (7.3)
Brahmā said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, I desire this mark to be made by you, O Lord of the world, by which this world may be marked. (7.4)
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One, the best among speakers, uttered "Om," the Brahman consisting of all the Vedas. (7.5)
By the mere utterance of Śambhu, this goddess of speech, possessing a divine form, issued forth from his mouth and stood there, bowing humbly. (7.6)
Then the God spoke to her with a voice that seemed to restore her to life:
"Since you have emerged from my speech as an imperishable being, you shall therefore become, O Goddess, the presiding deity of all knowledge. (7.7)
"Since this Sarasvatī has taken refuge in my mouth, therefore you shall attain fame in the world by the name 'Sarasvatī'. (7.8)
Having purified this world with your excellent waters, O one of radiant splendor, you shall again deliver all the worlds; of this there is no doubt. (7.9)
And those gods, together with the Grandfather (Brahmā), will grant you a share of the sacrifice;
you shall become the most sacred of all rivers—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having been granted permission by Śaṅkara,
that radiant lady created the meritorious Brahma-lake, which is exceedingly purifying in the world of Brahmā.

It was completely filled with the nectar of water, adorned with golden lotuses, crowded with flocks of various birds, and its waters agitated by fish; having emerged from there once more, it purified this world. (7.12)
Taking that skull of immeasurable power,
Mahādeva reached this world and established himself in an excellent region.
There, the Lord of the gods, the Master, established that great, divine skull with its blazing radiance at the forefront of his hosts.

Then, seeing that [bow] set up, all the hosts of the Great-souled One raised a tremendous roar, making the ten directions resound; it was like the agitated ocean or a thunderbolt, by which the very sky seemed to shatter. (7.15)
At that terrible sound, the Asura known as Hālāhala, a thorn to the gods,
approached that place.
Intolerant, blinded by rage, evil-minded, and a destroyer of sacrifices, he had received a boon from Brahmā and was invulnerable to all living beings;
Mahiṣa was surrounded by hundreds of Asuras who had assumed concealed forms. (7.17)
Beholding that buffalo, the thorn in the side of the gods, charging forward in a rage, the leader of the Gaṇas addressed all the attendants of the wielder of the Pināka bow: || 7.18 ||
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, this wicked Daitya, a thorn to the gods of the three worlds, is approaching swiftly; therefore, you must slay him. (7.19)
Then all those leaders of the Gaṇas, filled with rage, pierced the approaching enemy of the gods with their spears and deprived him of his life.
When he was slain, the god then gazed upon all the quarters;
from them there emerged Piśācas with gaping mouths and mighty Piśācīs,
who approached the Lord of Gods and reported this to him.
Having been fully provided for and assigned duties by them,
they then returned to that very dwelling place ordained by the gods.
Because those Mothers of the Skulls (Kapālamātaraḥ) devoured the buffalo by repeatedly dividing it up, they were thus designated as such by the wise God.
Because the skull was placed in that place by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
it is therefore celebrated throughout the three worlds as Mahākapāla.
When the skull had been established, it then became as described;
that place became known as Śivataḍāga, which liberates one from all sins.
Then Brahmā, having arrived there surrounded by hosts of deities,
addressed Kapardin and took possession of that place.
This field will extend for half a yojana on all sides;
it will undoubtedly become a field of perfection for the Great-souled One.
For the wise know that *śma* denotes evil and *śāna* denotes destruction; because it is purified through meditation and observances, it is designated as *śmaśāna*.
It is the secret, most beloved, and unsurpassed [abode] of the God beyond gods. (7.28)
In this way, a man shall abandon all his sins there;
having fasted for three nights and worshipped the bull-bannered god, he will obtain that fruit which belongs to the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (7.29)
And that man who shall there renounce his dear life-breaths will attain equality with the gods of the Guhyaka hosts.
Then, having established there two auspicious images of the God—
the great-bodied Śūleśvara and the beautiful sanctuary of Rudra— [he departed].
By merely approaching that place, one effects the destruction of sin and attains the world of Rudra; thus spoke the Grandfather.
And where the Lord of the World cut off his head, that region became by name Kaśmīra, a land most meritorious at all times. (7.33)
Then the Lord, together with his attendants, having assumed a transformed appearance,
vanished from the sight of all the gods.
And when the Lord of the Gods had departed, he then endowed the imperishable site of Kapāla with the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords.
Even today, O best of Brahmins, that great divine lake is seen there;
it is known as Mahākapāla, and the worlds there are considered imperishable.
This auspicious, divine [teaching], which destroys unrighteousness, yields great fruit, and is honored by Indra along with the gods and asuras;
it is the exposition of Mahākapāla, beneficial for penetrating the worlds of the Lord of the Gods and beyond. (7.37)

He who always recites or hears this hymn, which is praised by those whose wealth is austerity and by hosts of Siddhas, and which possesses a circle of twice-born kings equal to those dwelling in heaven, goes to the third heaven, highly honored.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 7.7 ||
The eighth chapter.
Vāyu said:
Thus is this Blessed One, who follows after the world of Brahmā.
For the sake of your success in dharma, he emerged from the center of the altar.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, when their thousand-year sacrificial session had concluded and the Sarasvatī had begun to flow, the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived there. 8.2.
Brahmā said:
"Perform sacrifice once more to the Lord, the God, with another sacrificial session;
when an obstacle shall arise for you, then your austerity will become stainless. (8.3)
Having overcome that very obstacle and having performed radiant austerity, you shall attain the great yoga; then, being fully disciplined, you will behold Śaṅkara.
Having said, "So be it," when he had departed, those men of great vows, being diligent, then performed many sacrifices of various forms. (8.5)
Having made this entire earth devoid of Soma, O twice-born ones, they then desired to bring King Soma back and consecrate him. (8.6)
Then, after he had been offered hospitality, Soma was seized by the invisible and evil-minded Svarbhānu; consequently, they became sorrowful. (8.7)
Having gone there, all those sages dwelling in the village of Kalāpa brought King Purūravas and consecrated him.
And those illustrious ones said to him, "O Lord, our Soma has indeed been carried away by someone;
therefore, may you bring it back here quickly, without delay. (8.9)
Having been addressed thus, the lord searched for him but did not find him;
then, afflicted by fear, he bowed to the brahmins and spoke. (8.10)
"Exerting the utmost effort, I have searched for Soma;
yet I do not know by whom he has been taken, nor where, O Lord. (8.11)
To him who spoke thus, all the sages of rigid vows, enraged and highly incensed, said to the high-minded son of Ilā: 8.12.
Why have we, afflicted by fear, made you our king? For you are not capable of destroying that fear of ours, even in an instant. (8.13)
With your soul excessively attached to sense-objects, you do not perceive him through yoga;
therefore, by persisting in hostility toward the twice-born, you shall meet with death.
For we ourselves shall bring King Durvinda here by our own ascetic power, O Indra among kings; behold our supreme strength! (8.15)
Then all those sages, whose sins had been burnt away by austerity, praised Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas, with their desired words. 8.16.
Then, as they were offering praise, Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas,
appeared in bodily form before their sight and spoke these words to those twice-born ones.
"I am pleased, my children; what shall I do for you today? I am here as a giver of boons to you. Speak, and that shall be accomplished right here, without a doubt. (8.18)
The sages said:
"O Goddess, our Soma has been stolen by some very wicked-souled being.
Bring him back; salutations be unto you! This is our supreme boon. (8.19)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus and having reflected, she beheld with her divine eye and, transforming herself into a female hawk, quickly went toward the Asura Svarbhānu. 8.20.
While the Asuras were distracted, she took the Soma and returned;
having arrived, she said to those ṛṣis, "Let this Soma be pressed. (8.21)
Having reached him and obtained the great fruit of their sacrifice, those twice-born sages thought, "Our asceticism has become stainless. (8.22)
Then Brahmā himself, having arrived there along with the gods, serpents, and others, spoke to those sages: "Perform your austerities; do not delay."
Having gone together with Brahmā to Maināka, the best of mountains, they,
along with all the hosts of gods, performed austerities with concentrated minds.
After a long time, for those whose selves had been refined through austerity, there arose an engagement with yoga; they then became joined with the subtle.
Those sages, together with the gods, being united with Brahmā,
fixed their minds upon Maheśvara and remained as motionless as stones.
Then Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, blue-and-red in hue,
arrived at that place in a celestial chariot possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Knowing that his state was transformed by that supreme reality,
he, whose voice resounded like a cloud and whose sound was like a hundred kettledrums, spoke to him.
"O gods, including Brahmā, together with Viṣṇu, the ṛṣis, and the cāraṇas!
I grant you divine vision; behold me as you desire. (8.29)
Sanatkumāra said: Then they all beheld a celestial chariot, possessing the brilliance of ten thousand suns, resembling Mount Meru, and adorned with various jewels.
In its center stood a massive, blazing mass of fire,
encircled by garlands of flames and adorned with radiant rays.
With a face made terrifying by its fangs, eyes like blazing fire, matted locks tawny as the three sacrificial fires, and a girdle bound with serpents; (8.32)
He had polished earrings, and his great hand was grasping a trident;
he carried the Pināka bow, held a staff in his hand, and bore a mallet and a thunderbolt in his palms.
He held a thousand sword-blades and possessed a discus; his phallus was turned upward, and he held a rosary of beads.
He was difficult for those of unrefined souls to behold, adorned with garlands and ornaments fashioned from the moon, the sun, and the planets.
All those gods beheld him with their divine vision—him, upon seeing whom death could never again occur even for a mortal. (8.35)

Through their asceticism, the sages— whose vision was granted by the Lord of the Sky (Viśvabhuj)— bowed with joy to Bhava, who is as stainless as the moon, while he was engaged in his yoga of withdrawal along with the gods.
Having perceived that the Great Lord of Asuras was like Death himself, and having reflected in their minds upon his unbearable nature,
they— having set aside all thought of self-interest— bow down along with the gods, praising the Source of the World.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 8.8 ||
The Ninth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen the Lord of the gods, all those deities, including Brahmā, [beheld him].
Having prostrated before the one whose vehicle is the bull, they praised him with desired words. || 9.1 ||
The Grandfather said: Salutations to Śiva, to Soma, the remover of the fear of devotees;
salutations to him who holds a trident-tip in his hand and who carries a water-pot. 9.2.
To the one who wields the staff, to the blue-throated one, to the one with formidable fangs,
to the one whose eyes blaze like the three sacrificial fires, to the three-eyed one, and to Hara.
Salutations indeed to the wielder of the Pināka bow; let there be salutations to the bearer of the thunderbolt, to him who has a serpent as his sacred thread and who is adorned with earrings. 9.4.
Salutations to the wielder of the discus and to the wearer of the tiger skin;
likewise to him who has the black antelope skin as his upper garment and the serpent as his girdle.
And to Rudra, the giver of boons, who likewise created Sarasvatī,
who wears garlands of the moon, sun, and stars, and who holds a rosary in his hand.
Salutations indeed to the one with a thousand garlands of flames, to the upward-pointing Liṅga;
salutations to the dweller of the mountains and to the one who took away my head in the past. 9.7.

Salutations to the destroyer of Hālāhala poison, to the bearer of the excellent skull-bowl, to the one who rides upon the best of celestial chariots, to my very own progenitor, to the giver of boons, to the most eminent one, and to the lover of the cremation ground. 9.8.
Salutations to the creator of man and salutations always to the sustainer; salutations to the author of origins and dissolutions, and to the helper of all.
O Lord of the ṛṣis and the gods, sovereign of all beings, be auspicious and gentle, O Lord of Devas; be favorable to us, you who are compassionate toward your devotees. 9.10
Sanatkumāra said: While Brahmā was thus offering praise, that God of gods, the protector of the worlds,
being pleased, spoke to those gods and sages who were strengthened by their ascetic penance.
"I am well-pleased with this perfect austerity of yours, O seers and deities!
Choose a boon; I shall grant it. Having reflected well, let it be spoken. (9.12)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O best of Brahmins, having beheld them all— satisfied and strengthened by their asceticism— Brahmā spoke these words merely by his glance.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us,
then become auspicious, gentle, and visible to us."
He is always easy to deal with and likewise ever-contented in mind;
in all matters he is always beneficial, wholesome, and auspicious.
"O God, bestower of thousands of boons, let him be given to us, together with the Goddess, his son, and the hosts of gods. 9.16.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, that blessed one, the best of gods and knower of all yoga, emitted his own great and divine splendor. 9.17.
From half of his own splendor, the Blessed One, who assumes all forms, emitted a meteor from his mouth; he said to it, "Become a woman. (9.18)
Pervading the sky, the heavens, and the earth with her majesty, she stood firm;
and like a blazing lightning flash, she approached the Lord of the Gods.
The Lord, smiling, said to that lotus-eyed goddess:
"O Goddess of pure smiles, propitiate Brahmā, the granter of boons."
Having promised "So be it," she began to perform austerities.
And Rudra said to those sages, "Listen, O best of the fruit-bearers, you whose wealth is asceticism, to what I say regarding the reward for pleasing me. (9.21)
"Immortal, free from old age, healthy, and devoid of rebirth;
endowed with austerity, you shall dwell right here, devoted to me. (9.22)
And this very hermitage on Svarṇaśṛṅga, the best of mountains, shall undoubtedly become a meritorious and holy place. 9.23.
Since I became gold on Maināka, the most excellent of mountains, and since I created the goddess Svarṇākṣī, that place is therefore known as Svarṇākṣa. (9.24)
"O Ṛṣis of the six clans, you whose wealth is asceticism, by my command you shall dwell here at Svarṇākṣa;
indeed, that sacred field extending for a yojana all around is undoubtedly pure. (9.25)
It was frequented by gods and gandharvas and served by hosts of apsaras;
it was filled with lions, elephants, and śarabhas, and teeming with tigers, bears, and deer;
it was crowded with many birds and thick with creepers, trees, and shrubs. (9.26)
A celibate student who observes the rules, who has conquered anger and subdued his senses,
having fasted for three nights and offered a sacrificial oblation (caru),
shall dwell in the world of Brahmā even if he dies anywhere at all. || 9.27 ||
Whoever, even if possessed by desire, should likewise behold the bull-bannered god there,
he too shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows through my grace;
and having died here with self-restraint, he shall wander with me.
"As long as the worlds endure, and as long as this mountain Maināka remains,
so long shall you, O gods, move about together with me through my grace."
Having thus spoken to those sages and looked upon them with a gentle eye,
he vanished right there while everyone was looking on.
Sanatkumāra said:
That mortal who should hear this, or cause the twice-born to hear it, shall also attain that fruit and move about free from death. (9.31)
Victorious is the bearer of the clouds, the time of destruction for all beings, the remover of afflictions for ascetics established in tranquility, self-restraint, and discipline;
he who removes birth and death for those striving in righteousness, endowed with manifold powers, moving through the sky and treading upon the earth. (9.32)

The destroyer of the city of Madana, who casts down eyes and teeth, free from fear and dejection, the wise perceiver of all beings, constantly proclaiming himself as Cekitāna, the ornament of hands and feet, the all-seeing God of gods. 9.33.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa. 9.9.
The Tenth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
That goddess, addressed by Tryambaka, performed penance for a very long time.
At times she was without food, and again she ate but a single leaf; furthermore, she subsisted on air, and once more she lived on water alone. (10.1)
Knowing her to be intensely radiant as she was engaged in the practice of asceticism, Brahmā said:
"Speak, O Goddess; I am pleased. What may I do for you? (10.2)
She said to the three-eyed god, her husband, who possessed the luster of the moon: "O God, having obtained you as my lord, may I wander happily through all the worlds; salutations to you. (10.3)
Brahmā said: "Indeed, it is not by that very body with which supreme austerity is performed that this Supreme Lord, the Master Śambhu, is attained. (10.4)
Therefore, through this yoga, you shall become the daughter of Dakṣa, the Lord of Progeny, in this world; having been born as his daughter, you will obtain Rudra as your husband.
Then, having heard those words, that high-minded goddess,
the daughter of Dakṣa and a supreme yoginī, was born through her yogic power under the name Satī.
Dakṣa gave that blameless woman as a wife to Tryambaka at the word of Brahmā; upon her he begot his mind-born sons.
There were many thousands of Rudras of immeasurable splendor, equal in strength to himself, radiant, and free from old age and death.
Seeing them being created, Brahmā forbade him:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, do not create subjects who are exempt from death. (10.9)
"Create other offspring, may you be blessed, who are endowed with death. Because he replied, "I am standing firm," he was therefore known as Sthāṇu. || 10.10 ||
The God said:
"O Brahman, I shall by no means create progeny joined with death.
I stand here today at your word; I am not to be spoken to by you again. (10.11)
But these high-souled and mighty beings who have been created from my mind—
all of them shall indeed wander with me as performers of sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, after some time had passed, Dakṣa, on account of the curse,
invited his other sons-in-law along with their wives and honored them in his home.
Filled with wrath, he did not invite Satī to be present with Tryambaka;
but Satī, having understood all that had occurred, went to her father and spoke to him. (10.14)
"I am the eldest and the most excellent, O observer of noble vows;
it does not behove you to honor these women along with their husbands while passing me by. (10.15)
Then, overcome by anger, his senses impaired by that wrath,
Dakṣa looked at him and spoke as if burning him with his very eyes.
Ascetics rich in penance enter my home accompanied by their wives;
therefore, I always consider them to be most excellent, and for that reason, I honor them.
Therefore, whatever I do for you today, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
accept that honor, O daughter, or go wherever you please.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, her face blazing with anger and being exceedingly provoked, that auspicious lady did not accept the unwelcome and inferior worship, and she spoke this to him: (10.20)
"Since you offer me this unwelcome worship—which is praiseworthy, faultless, and excellent—you reproach me, O father. (10.21)
Therefore, I shall abandon this body of mine; here is your daughter.
What is the use to me now of this inauspicious life, since she has been treated with such disrespect?
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having mentally offered salutations to the Three-eyed Lord,
she who is the source of speech spoke these words with great intensity.
"May I be born again in a body by my own will;
and being thus born there, undeluded, virtuous, and true, may I become the lawful wife of the wise Tryambaka himself. (10.24)
Then that virtuous woman, having suddenly performed the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā), indeed consumed her own body with the fire arising from within herself. || 10.25 ||
Having learned that the goddess had become thus, the highly illustrious Tryambaka,
skilled in speech, approached Dakṣa and spoke these words.

"Because you have censured me while praising these others separately— these sons-in-law together with their wives— you shall, in the Vaivasvata interval, be born again as my very own sons-in-law at your sacrifice. (10.27)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Dakṣa, with a truly grieving heart, spoke to him:
"If my own daughter was indeed spoken of by me, or even abandoned again,"
"What have you done here, O Lord? I am always her master. || 10.29 ||
"Since you have cursed me, therefore, O Śaṅkara, you too shall dwell eternally in the world of mortals (bhūrloka) and never in the heavenly world (svarloka). || 10.30 ||
And having given you a share in their sacrifices, O Mahādeva of great splendor, all the twice-born shall everywhere touch water.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that three-eyed god, laughing, spoke to him:
"The world of the earth (bhūrloka) is said to be the root of all the worlds. (10.32)
I alone sustain him out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
for when the earthly realm (bhūrloka) is supported, all the worlds remain eternal.
Therefore, I abide here perpetually, and not by your command. || 10.33 ||
Having given portions to others, those twice-born ones who wish to give to me touch water for the sake of purification and then offer a portion to me; having given,
they touch water again for the further increase of dharma.
For just as pure people carry away the withered garlands of the gods, and those desiring to touch what is impure cast them aside and then touch water, so it is here. (10.35)
When the bulls among Brahmins, desiring to give portions of water to the gods and others in this manner, touch the waters, what cause for lamentation is there? 10.36.
But you, scorched by my curse, lowest of men and perverted in mind, shall produce a son upon your own daughter. (10.37)
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus cursed Dakṣa, the Lord, the Master of the World,
possessed of great splendor, ceased speaking and departed as he had come.

We perpetually bow here before Him whose eyes are like the moon, the sun, and fire; whose face resembles the moon and whose eyes are like lotus petals; who is borne by a bull; and who is an immeasurable flood of virtues, carrying the moon upon His head. 10.39.
He who, being firm in his vows, hears this account of Dakṣa’s curse and the bodiless state of the Goddess, or causes it to be heard by Brahmins,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Rudra. (10.40)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 10.10 ||
The Eleventh Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Once, Kaśyapa, the best among bipeds, arrived at his own home.
Himavat asked this question: "What indeed brings renown in the world? (11.1)
O Sage, tell me that by which the worlds may become inexhaustible, supreme renown may be attained, and likewise, one may be worthy of worship among the virtuous. (11.2)
Kaśyapa said:
"O mighty-armed one, all this is obtained through offspring;
it is by means of offspring that my fame, as well as that of Brahmā and the sages, has been established. (11.3)
"Do you not see, O Lord of Mountains, why you ask me this? I shall relate to you that which was seen by me long ago, O Mountain. (11.4)
As I was traveling toward Vārāṇasī, I beheld in the sky a celestial chariot standing aloft—resounding, divine, incomparable, and beyond reproach. || 11.5 ||
Beneath it, in the place of a pit, I heard a cry of distress;
having recognized those [beings] through my ascetic power, I remained there, hidden from view. (11.6)
Then, O Lord of Mountains, a brahmin arrived there— one who was observant of vows,
pure, whose soul was purified by ablutions at sacred fords, and established in supreme austerity.
Then, as that twice-born man was proceeding along, pursued by a tiger,
he entered that region where the mountain had its chasm.
Then that distressed twice-born man saw the sages hanging from a clump of *vīraṇa* grass in a pit; afflicted with grief, he questioned them.
"Who are you, O sinless ones, hanging head-downwards from this clump of vīraṇa grass?
Why are you suffering, and by what means will your liberation come to pass? (11.10)
The ancestors said: "We—your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are suffering because of your evil deeds, you who have performed no meritorious acts. (11.11)
"O illustrious one, this is hell, situated in the form of a pit;
you are a clump of vīraṇa grass, and we are hanging from you. (11.12)
O Brahmin, as long as you live, so long shall we remain;
but when you die, we, being of sinful mind, shall go to hell.
"If you, having entered into marriage, shall procreate a son of superior virtue, by that means we may each be released one by one. (11.14)
"Neither by any other austerity, my son, nor by the fruit of visiting sacred fords, can this be achieved;
therefore, O one of great intelligence, do that which will deliver your ancestors from fear. (11.15)
Having promised "So be it" and having propitiated the bull-bannered god,
he raised his ancestors from the pit and made them leaders of his hosts.
And he himself, beloved of Rudra and known by the name Sukeśa,
became a highly esteemed and powerful leader of Rudra’s hosts.
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, having performed severe austerities, procreate a most virtuous offspring; through that, you shall attain glory.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the sage, the lord of mountains remained steadfast in his observance and performed intense penance, by which Brahmā was indeed gratified. 11.19.
Then Brahmā, the bestower of boons, having approached him, spoke:
"Speak, O mountain of noble vows; I am pleased with this austerity of yours. (11.20)
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son adorned with all virtues;
if you are pleased with us, O Lord, grant me this boon. (11.21)
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Mountains, a daughter of excellent complexion shall be born to you, by whose power you will attain abundant fame everywhere. (11.22)
Worshipped by all the gods and surrounded by ten million holy fords,
you shall be purifying and meritorious in every respect even for the gods;
and she, O auspicious one, shall be your elder sister, while the others shall follow after her.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then vanished right there;
and in due time, that lord of mountains begot [a son] upon Menā.
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā.

Ekaparṇā took refuge in a banyan tree, while Ekapāṭalā took refuge in a trumpet-flower tree; but Aparṇā, having no shelter at all, performed austerities for a hundred thousand years that were difficult even for gods and dānavas to practice.
Saikarṇā subsisted on food from a single leaf;
likewise, Ekapāṭalā provided her sustenance with a single pāṭala flower.
When each full thousand had passed, they both took food;
but Aparṇā remained without food, and her mother addressed her, restraining her with the words "No, do not," distressed by maternal affection. (11.27)
Thus addressed by her mother at that time, the goddess who had performed difficult deeds became renowned in the worlds by that very name, honored by the gods.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, belongs to these three maidens;
it was obtained by their ascetic power and shall endure as long as the earth exists.
All three of them were embodiments of asceticism, endowed with the power of yoga;
all were highly fortunate, and all possessed eternal youth.
They are indeed the mothers of the world and practitioners of celibacy;
they always sustain the worlds through their own ascetic power.
Umā was the most excellent and the most distinguished among them, a woman of supreme complexion;
endowed with the power of great yoga, she attended upon Mahādeva.
Dattaka and Uśanas were her sons, that delighter of the Bhrigus;
and Asita begot a son, Devala, by Ekaparṇā.
Among those maidens, the third, Ekapāṭalā,
attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśalāka;
and his two sons, Śaṅkha and Likhita, are remembered as being not born from a womb.
But as for Umā, that woman of excellent complexion whom I have described to you—
then, perceiving the entire three worlds to be filled with smoke due to her ascetic practice, Brahmā spoke these words: ||| 11.35 ||
Brahmā said:
O Goddess, O most beautiful one, why do you torment the worlds with penance?
This entire universe was created by you; do not destroy it once it has been made. 11.36.
For you indeed sustain all these worlds by your own splendor;
speak, O Mother of the World, what do you desire? Be gracious unto us.
The Goddess said:
"O Grandfather, you already know the purpose for which I am performing this penance; why then do you ask me about it? (11.38)
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, O sustainer of the worlds, he for whose sake you weary yourself with penance will himself come here and choose you as his bride. (11.39)
He is the supreme lord of all the gods, the sovereign of the lords of all the worlds;
we, together with the gods, are subject to his will and speak as his servants.
That god of gods, the Lord of the Supreme Lord, the protector of the world, will himself come into your presence;
he possesses a noble form, yet his appearance is transformed, for he has no form identical to that of anyone else.

Maheśvara, the dweller in the world of the mountains, the lord of the moving and the unmoving, the first and immeasurable one—though without the moon, his face was like the moon; he stood here in this foremost form, terrifying to behold.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 11.11 ||
The Twelfth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the blessed Lord Brahmā spoke to her in a melodious voice.
O Goddess, he by whom you were created in his mind, and he who was chosen by you—he, the Lord of Gods, shall be your husband; do not perform penance.
Then, having circumambulated the daughter of Mount Vyāsa, Brahmā vanished from her sight, and she too ceased [her speech]. || 12.2 ||
Having said, "So be it," that queen went to the gate of her own hermitage and stood there, leaning against an aśoka tree that grew right there.
Then Hara, the moon-marked one who removes the suffering of the gods, arrived,
having assumed a deformed appearance— short in stature and with arms like those of a charioteer.
Having become one with a crooked nose, hunchbacked, with tawny hair at the ends, and with a distorted face, he said, "O Goddess, I choose you as my bride. (12.5)
Then Umā, perfected in yoga, knowing that Śaṅkara had arrived,
was purified within by her state of being and desired to perform the ritual acts.
Having brought water for the guest-offering and likewise the honey-mixture, the Brahmin’s beloved wife honored him; then, once the Brahmin was seated at his ease, she spoke to him. (12.7)
The goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I am not my own mistress; my father and likewise Araṇī exist.
They alone have the power over my giving, for I am a maiden, O bull among the twice-born. (12.8)
"Go and beg my father, the imperishable lord of mountains;
O Brahmin, if he gives me to you, that will be pleasing to me."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, the powerful one who had likewise assumed that transformed form, spoke to that king of mountains: "O king of mountains, give Umā to me."
Recognizing him as the imperishable Rudra in his transformed form, he became afraid of the curse and, with a troubled mind, spoke these words: || 12.11 ||
"O Blessed One, I do not hold the Brāhmaṇas, the deities of the earth, in contempt;
however, O one of great asceticism, hear that which was my previous desire. (12.12)
"A svayaṃvara for my daughter shall take place, honored by the brahmins;
whoever she herself chooses there, he shall become her husband. (12.13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the mountain, the high-minded Lord whose banner bears the bull approached the Goddess and spoke this: 12.14.
"O Goddess, it has been heard that you have been commanded by your father to hold a svayaṃvara;
O sinless one, he whom you choose there shall indeed be your husband."
Therefore, I take my leave; I shall depart, for you are difficult to find, O lovely-faced one!
Having rejected one so handsome, how could you choose someone like me?
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having been addressed by him there, she contemplated what he had uttered—the disposition placed within her by Rudra as well as the grace of his mind. (12.17)
Having approached the Lord of Gods, he said: "Let your mind not be otherwise;
I shall choose you as my bridegroom, and no other being whatsoever."
Or perhaps you have some doubt concerning me in any way, O Brahmin;
here and now, O illustrious one, I grant you the fulfillment of your heart's desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Taking a cluster of flowers that was situated there,
the Goddess placed it upon the shoulder of Śambhu and said, "You are chosen by me."
Then that Blessed Lord, thus entreated by the goddess,
spoke to Aśoka as if reviving him with his voice.
"Since I have been covered by you with this cluster of beautiful flowers, therefore, abandoned by old age, you shall become immortal. (12.22)
He can assume any form at will, he is the flower of desire, he goes wherever he wishes, and he is dear to me; he is rich with the flowers of all ornaments and possesses the fruits of all trees.
"You shall be the consumer of all foods and the flow of nectar itself;
you shall possess all fragrances and become a steadfast favorite of the Goddess.
You will wander through all the worlds free from fear and perfectly at peace."
And whoever, seeking merit, shall visit this hermitage renowned as Citrakūṭa, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
and wherever he may die, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And whoever here, disciplined by observances, should completely renounce his life-breaths, he, endowed with the power of the Goddess’s asceticism, shall become a great lord of the Gaṇas.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus and having taken leave of the daughter of Himavat, the divine Lord, the creator of the world and protector of all beings, vanished from sight. 12.27.
When that Blessed One of immeasurable soul had departed, the queen also remained standing there with her face turned upward,
and then sat down upon the stone.
When that great archer, the lord of creatures, had departed, she,
looking up toward him, appeared then dejected like a night bereft of the moon.
Then Śailajā heard the sound of a distressed child near the hermitage by a lake filled with water.
Then Śiva himself, the God of gods, having assumed the form of a child for the sake of sport, became seized by a crocodile in the middle of the lake.
Then, employing his yogic power— the cause of the manifestation of the phenomenal world—
he assumed that form in the middle of the lake and spoke thus:
"May someone come here to save me, whose mind has been seized by a crocodile!"
"Alas, what misery! Though still but a child, with my desires for wealth yet unfulfilled, I shall meet my death in the mouth of this wicked crocodile. (12.33)
Though seized by the crocodile and tormented by pain, I do not grieve for my own body as much as I grieve for my father and my ascetic mother.
Hearing that I have met my death in the jaws of a crocodile, those two who love their son and have but one child will surely give up their lives in their great anxiety. (12.35)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard that cry of the distressed Brahmin, the beautiful goddess rose up and ran to the place where that twice-born man stood. 12.36.
That moon-faced woman saw the boy of beautiful form,
trembling as he stood there being swallowed by a crocodile.
That illustrious and excellent crocodile, seeing that the goddess had approached,
seized her and quickly went into the very middle of the lake.
As he was being dragged away, that radiant youth let out a cry of distress;
then the queen, afflicted with grief upon seeing her son, spoke, she who was devoted to great vows.
O King of Grāhas, O Great Being, O one with great tusks and fearsome prowess, release this child who is indeed your only son; do so quickly!
The crocodile said:
"O Goddess, he who first comes to me on the sixth day—that has been ordained as my food from of old by the creators of the world. (12.41)
"O illustrious daughter of the mountain king, on this sixth day, this very man has surely been ordained for me by Brahmā; I shall not release him by any means whatsoever."
The Goddess said:
"O King of Grāhas, release this child by virtue of the supreme austerity I performed on the peak of Himavat; homage be unto you. (12.43)
The crocodile said:
"O Goddess, daughter of the king of mountains, do not let your ascetic merit go to waste;
even the King of the Gods himself is not able to release him."
By the gratified Lord Śarva, the fierce wielder of the trident,
immortality, invincibility, and inexhaustible strength were granted to me.
Furthermore, the release from his own capture and his imperishable knowledge were granted by him;
therefore, I tell you that he shall not attain liberation.
Or else, O goddess of auspicious countenance, you have great compassion for this child;
therefore, do as I say, and he shall thereafter attain liberation.
The goddess said:
"O lord of crocodiles, speak quickly that which is not censured by the virtuous;
that has been done, there is no doubt here, for Brahmins are certainly worthy of my respect. (12.48)
The crocodile said:
"Whatever ascetic merit you have acquired, even if it be very small, give all of that to me; then you shall obtain liberation. (12.49)
The goddess said:
"O great crocodile, whatever merit I have earned since my birth—all that I give to you; release the child before me. (12.50)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the crocodile, empowered by that asceticism, blazed forth;
he became as difficult to look upon as the sun at midday. || 12.51 ||
With a satisfied soul, he spoke thus to the Goddess, the sustainer of the world:
"O Goddess of great vows, why have you done this without deliberation?
For the acquisition of ascetic merit is difficult, and its abandonment is not praised. (12.52)
"Accept this asceticism and this boy, O lady of pure smiles;
I am pleased with your devotion to the brahmins, and therefore I grant you a boon. (12.53)
Thus addressed by the crocodile, that woman of great vows replied:
"O great crocodile, having reflected well, the liberation of the boy has been accomplished.
There is no austerity superior to that of the Brahmins; in my view, the Brahmins are the highest. (12.54)
"O Lord of Nagas, you know that once I have given something, I do not take it back;
for no man, O Naga, would ever reclaim what has been given away. (12.55)
"This has been given by me to you; indeed, I shall not take it back.
Let this remain with you alone, and let this boy be set free. (12.56)
Having been addressed thus, he then praised her, released the child, and paid homage to the goddess who shone with the brilliance of the sun; then he vanished right there.
Then the boy, though released by the crocodile on the shore of the lake,
vanished right there like a mass of wealth obtained in a dream.
Then, perceiving her ascetic merit to be exhausted, the goddess, daughter of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains,
began once more to perform penance, applying herself with great effort.
O Vyāsa, knowing that she desired to perform further ascetic penance, Śaṅkara himself spoke these words: "Do not perform penance. 12.60.
"O Goddess of great vows, this ascetic merit was given by you to me;
by that very act, it shall become inexhaustible for you in a thousandfold way. || 12.61 ||
Having thus obtained this supreme and inexhaustible boon from her asceticism, the goddess remained there,
filled with joy and looking forward to the svayaṃvara.
Indeed, that man who always recites this account of Śambhu’s conduct while in the state of a child shall, upon the dissolution of the body, become purified and a Gaṇa equal to Kumāra. 12.63.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 12.12.
The thirteenth chapter of the End-of-Eon [text].
Sanatkumāra said:
On the vast expanse of the Himalayas, crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots,
the svayaṃvara of the Mountain’s Daughter took place in due course.
Then that Himavat, the king of mountains, skilled in meditation,
understood that his daughter had been consecrated with mantras by the God of gods.
Although he already knew [the truth], the Great Mountain, desiring to perform the proper formalities,
then proclaimed the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of the Goddess throughout all the worlds.
"May my daughter choose the Supreme Lord in the presence of the gods, dānavas, siddhas, and all those who dwell in the worlds. (13.4)
"Only that is well-done, praiseworthy, and conducive to my prosperity"—
having reflected thus, the lord of mountains placed Maheśvara in his heart.
In the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, that best of mountain lords,
having made the region filled with jewels for the Goddess, caused a svayaṃvara to be held.
Then, O Vyāsa, as soon as this proclamation had been made regarding the svayaṃvara of the daughter of Mahīdhra,
the gods and all other inhabitants of the world arrived, having assumed celestial attire.
Seated upon a full-blown lotus throne, surrounded by immeasurable perfected ones and yogins,
the Grandfather arrived there at the request of that king of mountains.
Bearing a thousand eyes and possessing a noble form adorned with divine ornaments and garlands,
that king of the gods mounted Airāvata, the foremost of all lordly elephants, who created a flowing stream from his trickling ichor;
then that sovereign of all the immortals, wielding his thunderbolt, arrived at the front of the deities.
Possessing a divine form exceeding in brilliance and majesty, the Sun-god, illuminating all directions,
arrived swiftly with great speed, having mounted a golden celestial chariot with fluttering banners.

Wearing earrings blazing with the brilliance of jewels, Kaśyapa’s son, the Brahmin, arrived in a celestial chariot resembling the splendor of fire and the sun; he was Āditya, who bears the name Bhaga.
With a stout body and graceful movements of his limbs, possessing a majesty equal to his splendor, strength, and authority,
Kṛtānta arrived with speed, mounted upon a fearsome buffalo and wielding his staff.
With limbs as massive as the height of a great mountain, wearing a beautiful garment adorned with gold and other jewels,
Vāyu, the sustainer of the entire world, arrived having mounted his celestial chariot.
Scorching all the lords of the gods and asuras, and having entered into the fire with his own superior splendor,
Agni approached into the midst of the lords of the gods and stood forth blazing, wearing a magnificent form.
With his slender body illuminated by various jewels,
that lord of all masters of wealth, the king of kings, having mounted a supreme celestial chariot that traverses the world, approached in haste.
Gladdening all the lords of the gods and asuras with his beauty and his attire,
the moon, of lovely form, arrived having mounted a celestial chariot of variegated appearance made of blazing great jewels.
With a dark-limbed frame, wearing most variegated attire and bound with fragrant garlands of every kind,
