that wielder of the mace has arrived swiftly, mounted upon Tārkṣya, who is like unto a mountain.
Likewise, the two Aśvins, the preeminent physicians of the gods, having swiftly ascended a single celestial chariot,
arrived at the assembly of the gods— those two heroes, enchanting and clad in brilliant, beautiful attire.
The noble-souled Śeṣa, possessing the brilliance of a blazing sun, bore a thousand hoods flashing with the color of fire;
accompanied by other great serpents, he ascended the celestial chariot and approached.
Having assumed an attire suitable for his station, he approached before the host of gods— the sons of Diti, those great asuras whose splendor was equal to that of fire, the sun, Indra, and the wind.
And that Gandharva king, of beautiful form, moving through the divine air and traveling in a celestial chariot,
arrived there at the command of Śakra, accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.

And other gods, lords of the triple heaven, each assuming their own beautiful attire, arrived having mounted the backs of celestial chariots, as did the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and kiṃnaras. (13.22)
There, in the midst of the lords of the gods, the husband of Śacī— his form marked by the superior authority of a king—
fell into a delusion caused by the power of his commands and sovereignty, and exerted himself in vain with excessive effort.
She is the cause of the three worlds and the mother of the universe, including the gods and asuras;
she is the wife of Śambhu, the abiding Puruṣa, and is celebrated in the Purāṇas as the supreme Prakṛti.
Out of Dakṣa’s anger, that consort of the Supreme Lord went to the home of Himavat for the sake of her purpose. (13.24)
Thus, because they did not know her, delusion entered them from the Supreme;
therefore, being utterly bewildered, they came seeking boons, for they had been rendered so by the Lord.
Then, with the Apsarases dancing and the throngs of Gandharvas singing sweetly,
the assembly of gods, asuras, and other denizens of the triple heaven stood there in various forms and attire.
Standing upon the roof of the celestial chariot, which was variegated with jewels and gold, her body fanned by waving yak-tail whisks,
the queen set forth with haste, holding a fragrant garland of flowers from every season.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods,
Śakra and the other deities arrived, having come to the svayaṃvara.
Out of a desire to test the Goddess, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu suddenly became a young boy with five tufts of hair and lay down upon her lap.
Then, suddenly, through her yogic concentration, the queen recognized that the five-crested infant was standing there; filled with joy, she rejoiced.
Then she, whose resolve was pure and who had obtained the true fruit of her desire,
remained as if in a state of bliss, keeping him alone within her heart.
Then, seeing the infant resting in the lap of the goddess, the gods consulted among themselves, "Who is this? and, being greatly afflicted, they became enraged. (13.32)
Raising his arm, the slayer of Vṛtra fashioned the thunderbolt;
that arm of his remained poised exactly as it had been raised.
Paralyzed by Śambhu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a child,
he was unable to hurl his thunderbolt nor even to move his arm.
Then the powerful god Āditya, the son of Kaśyapa, named Bhaga,
being deluded, raised up a flaming club and desired to hurl it;
the Blessed One likewise paralyzed his arm as well at that time.
Shaking his head, Viṣṇu looked at him with anger;
the god then brought about baldness upon that head as well. (13.36)
Pūṣan, his teeth grinding against each other, glared at Śarva in his delusion;
yet as soon as he was beheld by Śambhu, his own teeth fell out.
The Lord paralyzed the staff of Yama, the heat of Agni, the radiance of the Moon,
the strength of Vāyu, and likewise the strength, energy, and yogic power of all the other inhabitants of heaven within him.
Then, while those gods remained thus filled with resentment,
Brahmā, deeply agitated, applied himself with reverence to meditation and perceived the Lord of the Gods of gods seated upon the lap of Umā.
Having recognized the Supreme Lord, the Grandfather (Brahmā) rose quickly and with reverence prostrated at the feet of Śambhu,
praising him with ancient Sāman chants and sacred, secret names.
O God, you are the unborn, the immortal, the creator, the destroyer, the all-pervading, and the supreme;
you are Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Tattva—the imperishable Brahman that is to be meditated upon.
He is the nectar, the Supreme Self, the Lord, the Great Cause;
He is the Creator of Brahmā, the Maker of primordial nature, the All-Creator, the Supreme Lord. (13.42)
And this goddess Prakṛti is always the cause of your creation;
having assumed the form of a wife, she has come as the cause of the world.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the World, and constant salutations to the Goddess as well;
by your grace and by your command, O Lord of Gods, the subjects [have been created] by me. || 13.44 ||
These gods and others who were created are now deluded and bewildered by your yoga;
show them favor so that they may become as they were before.
Then, having thus petitioned the Supreme Lord, the highly effulgent Brahmā spoke these words to all those gods who had been paralyzed: ||| 13.46 ||
"You are all deluded, O deities; you do not recognize this Śaṅkara, the God of gods who has arrived here, the very cause of my own origin. (13.47)
This is Rudra, Mahādeva, Śarva, Bhīma, and the one with matted hair;
he is Ugra, Īśāna, the Self, the Unborn, and Śaṃkara himself. (13.48)
The god of gods, the supreme abode, the Lord, Paśupati, the Master;
the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the cause of the world’s maintenance.
"Go quickly for refuge, O lords of the immortals, together with me alone, to the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable. (13.50)
Then all those inhabitants of heaven, being thus paralyzed,
bowed mentally to Śarva with a heart purified by devotion.
Then Maheśvara, the God of gods, became gracious toward them;
he immediately restored the bodies of the deities as they had been before.
Then, while all the gods were thus engaged in their efforts to ward him off,
the Lord of the Gods assumed a most wonderful three-eyed form;
before whose splendor those very gods sought refuge with the All-pervading One for protection.
To them, the supreme Lord of Gods granted a supreme eye, endowed with the power to behold his own form; they then beheld the Lord.
Having seen the Supreme Lord bearing the third eye,
all those lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, quickly bowed down.
Then the goddess, rejoicing in the presence of the inhabitants of heaven,
placed a garland of flowers at the feet of that one of immeasurable splendor.
Having cried out "Excellent! Excellent!", those deities again paid homage to the Lord together with the Goddess, bowing their heads until they touched the surface of the earth.
Then, O Vyāsa, in the meantime, the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke these words to the great mountain Himavat.

For today you are indeed praiseworthy, worthy of worship, and venerable to us all, since this great alliance with Śarva has been formed for you. Let the marriage be performed quickly; why do you remain further delayed?
Then, having bowed down to that god, Himavat replied:
"O God, you alone are the cause by which this Śarva has come to me."
This sudden grace has arisen, and you alone are indeed its cause;
therefore, O Grandfather, ordain the marriage in whatever manner and with whatever form it shall be.

Then, having heard these words from the king of mountains, the Grandfather said to the god, "O Lord, let the marriage be performed. To him, Śaṅkara, the protector of the world, replied, "As you wish."
And at that very moment, O Vyāsa, a city fashioned by Brahmā for the wedding of Maheśvara appeared,
adorned with various jewels.
Precious gems, variegated jewels, gold, and pearls,
having approached in embodied form, adorned that most excellent city.
The ground was variegated with emeralds and adorned with golden pillars;
it featured radiant crystal walls from which pearl necklaces hung down.
In that beautiful city of Śiva, which had been constructed for the purpose of the wedding,
the high-souled Maheśvara, the God of gods, shone resplendently.
There, the moon and the sun shone equally like two great jewels;
and the wind, wafting a delightful fragrance from the offspring of Surabhi,
blew with a pleasant touch, inspiring devotion toward the Lord.
There were the four oceans, the supreme gods headed by Śakra,
the celestial rivers, the great rivers, as well as the Siddhas and the Munis.
All the Gandharvas and Apsarases, Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
Guhyakas, other sky-dwellers, Kinnaras, and the celestial Cāraṇas— 69.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū—
the singers of the Sāmaveda— then arrived at that city, bringing jewels and musical instruments.
There, the sages, whose wealth was their asceticism, with joyful minds, recited in their entirety the sacred wedding mantras sung in the Vedas. (13.71)
All the mothers of the world and all the daughters of the gods,
in their entirety, sing with joy at the wedding of the Supreme Lord.
There, the six seasons, bringing various fragrances and pleasures,
stood present in embodied form as the wedding procession of Śaṅkara.
The peacocks, delighted by the deep thundering of the masses of dark clouds,
were crying out their cries and dancing on all sides.
It was illuminated by the clear streaks of flickering, tawny lightning,
and adorned with cranes that were yellowish-white like water-lilies.

With fresh *śilīndhra* mushrooms and *kandala* sprouts just born, with lovely young shoots emerging from the creepers and trees, and resounded by swarms of frogs languid with passion, awakened by the affectionate embrace of auspicious rain-showers; (76)
Even for passionate women whose minds are firmly resolved and whose hearts are uplifted by pride toward their beloveds,
the enchanting cries of peacocks in an instant cause the collapse of their self-possession.
Likewise, she was brilliantly adorned on all sides by the great Indra’s bow, which shone with its beautiful form radiant in three colors, curved like the crescent of the moon,
and positioned near a mass of clouds.
With breezes made fragrant by contact with various flowers and exceedingly cool due to their mingling with dense waters,
it stirred the beautiful tresses of the celestial nymphs with its enchanting gusts.
With the orb of the moon veiled by thundering clouds, and with beautiful dūrvā grass sprouting from the sprinkling of fresh rainwater,
she was gazed upon with longing and respect by the wives of travelers, who sighed like smoke.
Rich with the sound of swans and anklets, with uplifted breasts,
her girdle like a flickering streak of lightning, and her eyes clearly like lotuses.
With swans terrified by the roar of masses of dark clouds, with the tips of its lotuses bent by the falling streams of pure water,
and with the beauty of all its limbs fashioned from the pollen of fragrant flowers, the rainy season arrived for the prosperity of the mountain’s daughter’s wedding.
Freed from her garment of clouds, with breasts emerging from the calyxes of lotuses,
resounding with the anklets of swans, she filled all the quarters of space with her loveliness.
Her broad hips were like a wide sandy bank, her girdle was the warbling of cranes, and she was enchanting with eyes as expansive as full-blown blue lotuses. (13.84)
Her lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit, she smiled with teeth like kunda flowers, and she was adorned by a line of body hair as dark as a young śyāmā creeper.
With her excellent necklace of moonbeams gliding across her lofty chest,
she delighted the hearts of all the inhabitants of heaven.
She spoke with a sweet voice, sung forth by a multitude of bees;
she was graced by beautiful earrings that resembled clusters of swaying white water-lilies.
She held fingers made of sprouts arising from the tips of red Aśoka branches,
and she was beautifully adorned with garments consisting of heaps of those flowers.
Her feet were like the tips of red lotuses, her rows of nails like jasmine flowers,
her thighs as beautiful as plantain trunks, and her face like the moon.
Touching the gods with her fingertips— the vanguard winds mingled with the filaments of lotuses— the delightful autumn arrived like a beloved woman, out of love.
Having cast off their garments of dark clouds, with faces like the orb of the full moon,
and drenching the mountain crags with exceedingly cool waters,
the two seasons of Śiśira and Hemanta arrived, possessing surpassing splendor.
When those two seasons arrived, that Himavat, the best of mountains,
quickly shone like silver, raining down a powder of frost.
By that dense and deep shower of snow,
the Himālaya mountain then shone like the ocean Kṣīroda.
In the snowy regions, Himavat destroyed the trees that were hospitable to virtuous beings,
like a wicked man who, having suddenly achieved his purpose, destroys those who had served him well.
With its peaks covered by layers of frost,
that mountain shone like a lord of the earth with large, white parasols.
White, vast, glorious, and auspicious,
the lofty mountain peaks shone like palatial mansions.
In the caves of that lord of mountains, which were exceedingly crowded with flocks of variegated deer,
streams of frost, white as the rays of the moon, fell down like streams of cow’s milk.
Breezes, their bodies laden with heaps of many flower-pollen and rendered cool by contact with droplets of frost, blew gently,
causing the extremely fine garments of the lords of the hosts of immortals to flutter slightly.
The spring season, having shaken off the defects of harsh winds and cold and bearing ear-ornaments of blossoming mango sprouts,
quickly arrived at the Himalayas for the sake of serving the Daughter of the Mountain.
When he had reached that mountain for the purpose of serving at the wedding of the Mountain’s Daughter,
the trees, shrubs, and thickets all around manifested themselves adorned with floral crests.
Fragrant, auspicious, and very cool breezes blew repeatedly, their bodies laden with the pollen from the tips of various flowers; they increased the passion of the gods and the celestial nymphs.
And likewise, the lotus-pools filled with clear water, endowed with the buds of lotuses and water-lilies,
became most beautiful, like women whose breasts have just begun to emerge.
Due to the nature of the season and the arising of passion, as the branches blossomed,
the male cuckoos, with their wings tucked in, warbled most melodiously— a sound that was enchanting to the hearts of the celestial nymphs.

The foremost among the divine elephants, filled with joy, drank from the waters of the lake which were neither too hot nor too cold, turned brownish by the pollen of lotus filaments, and made resonant by the calls of pairs of ruddy geese.
The priyaṅgu trees and the mango trees, and the mango trees and the priyaṅgu trees as well,
shone as if threatening one another with their clusters of blossoms.
Upon the peaks white as snow, clusters of flowers shone like elders who had assembled for a specific purpose.
There, flowering aśoka creepers clinging to the śāla trees shone like beloved women with their bodies entwined around the necks of their lovers.
With clusters of flowers on their creepers being sung over by flocks of bees, the *mālatī* vines appeared as if they were conversing with one another. (13.109)
The waters were made dark blue by blue lotuses, white by white ones with their stalks and stems,
and intensely red by red ones whose petals were half-bitten by intoxicated bees.
In some lakes with vast waters, golden lotus groves grew everywhere; in others, they were made of emerald; and in some, the stalks of the lotus forests were of beryl. || 13.111 ||
There were beautiful ponds there, adorned with lotuses and water-lilies,
resounding with the cries of various birds, and featuring rows of golden steps.
O Sage, the peaks of that mountain, covered with dense and beautifully blossomed *karṇikāra* trees, shone as if they were made of gold.
All the quarters became pale-red with pāṭala trees that had slightly blossomed, their forms trembling in the wind.
The blue *aśoka* trees, resembling the peaks of mountains of black collyrium,
grew upon the mountain in full bloom as if in mutual rivalry.
And forests of *kiṃśuka* trees, resounding with the cries of *cīruvāka* birds,
were found on all the ridges of the mountain.
Then the splendor of that Himalaya was like that of Tamāla thickets,
appearing as if masses of dark clouds were nestled within its recesses.
Then the Himalaya mountain shone exceedingly with its lofty campaka trees, which possessed vast branches and abundant blossoms, and with the warbling of intoxicated male cuckoos.
Having heard from all sides the cries of cuckoos sweet with the passion of the season, and finding the sun’s heat intense while its reservoirs were mostly warm with water,
the summer arrived at the Himalayas for the purpose of serving the Goddess’s wedding.
And he, too, adorned the peaks of the Snowy Mountain on all sides with many trees and clusters of blossoms.
And during that season, delightful winds blew there,
carrying the fragrance of the *pāṭala*, the expansive *kadamba*, and the *arjuna* flowers.
The ponds, filled with masses of blossoming lotuses whose forms were reddened by filaments,
resounded on their banks with flocks of ruddy geese.
Likewise, the kuravaka trees as well, their forms pale with blossoms,
appeared upon all the peaks, frequented by swarms of bees.
And on the broad slopes of the mountains, Bakula trees shed lovely blossoms in every direction.

Thus, O hero among sages, the six seasons— whose trees were variegated with blossoms and whose regions were delightful with the songs of various birds— approached for the sake of the prosperity of the Himavat’s daughter’s wedding.
Then, when the assembly of all beings had thus gathered and was filled with hundreds of various musical instruments, my father Brahmā himself appeared.
Having adorned Śailaputrī with a wealth of fitting ornaments, the Sustainer of the World himself took her and led her into the city. (13.128)
Then Brahmā once again addressed the omnipresent Lord:
"Standing in the position of preceptor, I shall offer oblations into the fire;
if you grant me permission, this ritual procedure may be performed. || 13.129 ||
To that god, Śaṅkara, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, said:
"O Lord of the gods, whatever is desired, do that according to your wish;
O Brahmā, O pervasive Lord of the world, I shall carry out every word of yours. (13.130)
Then, with a joyful heart, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bowed down and joined the hands of the God and the Goddess in the yogic gesture.
Having himself prepared the fire, he stood with palms joined in reverence before it,
as the great mantras, celebrated in the Vedas, appeared there in embodied form.
Having offered oblations according to the prescribed rite with clarified butter and that very nectar,
he caused the god Agni to circumambulate him three times.
Having released his joined palms and accompanied by all the deities and all his mind-born sons, with a heart full of joy,
he bowed to the bull-bannered god when the time for the wedding ceremony had arrived.
O Vyāsa, by means of yoga alone, that supreme marriage between Umā and the Supreme Lord took place,
which the gods do not know anywhere.
Thus has this entire auspicious account of the self-choice marriage and the most wonderful wedding of the god been related to you as you listened.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named [so-and-so], in the Skanda Purāṇa. 13.13.
The fourteenth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, when the marriage of Bhava, of immeasurable splendor, had taken place...
Having attained incomparable joy, the gods, together with Pitāmaha, prostrated themselves before Maheśvara and praised him with pleasing words. 14.1.
Salutations to the mountain-liṅga, salutations indeed to the Lord of the Mountain;
salutations to him who possesses the speed of the wind, to the multiformed, and to the unconquered.
Homage to the destroyer of afflictions and the bestower of the abundance of auspiciousness;
homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin, the husband of Ambikā. 14.3.
Salutations to the one whose form is the wind, salutations indeed to the one of a hundred forms;
salutations to the one whose form is Bhairava, and to the one with deformed eyes.
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one and to the thousand-footed;
salutations to the secret of the Vedas and to the limb of the Vedas—salutations again and again.
Salutations again and again to the one who paralyzed the arm of Śakra, to the sprout of the Vedas, to the sovereign of the moving and the unmoving, and to the bringer of peace.
Salutations to the one whose linga rests in the waters, whose linga is as vast as the end of an eon;
salutations to the one who wears a garland of skulls, who bears a wreath of severed heads.
Homage to the one who holds a skull in his hand, to the fanged one, to the mace-bearer;
homage to the one who carries the three worlds, and to the one whose chariot is the seven worlds.
Salutations to the one who holds a skull-topped staff in his hand and who removes the afflictions of the Pramathas;
salutations to the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and who took away the dark hair [of Śiva].
Salutations to the one who caused the fall of Bhaga’s eyes, who took away the teeth of Pūṣan, and who bears the Pināka bow, the trident, the sword, the scimitar, and the mallet.
Salutations to Suvarṇaretas, who wears serpent-earrings; to Vāḍvali, the destroyer of yoga, and the teacher of yogins.

Salutation to the one whose eyes are the moon and the sun, and to the one who has an eye on his forehead; salutation to the one who delights in the cremation ground and to the one who grants boons from the cremation ground.
Homage to the Lord of the gods, to Tryambaka, homage again and again;
to him who laughs like a hundred thunderbolts, who is devoted to Brahman, and who is unconquered.
Salutations always to the virtuous householder, to the one with matted hair, and to the celibate student;
salutations to the shaven-headed and to the half-shaven-headed; salutations to the Lord of Creatures.
Salutations to him who is being heated within the waters, who bestows the sovereign power of yoga, who is peaceful and self-controlled, and who brings about both dissolution and creation.
Homage to the one who bestows favor and homage again and again to the one who maintains [the world];
homage to Rudra, to Vasu, to Āditya, and homage to the Aśvins. 14.17
Homage to the Father, and likewise to the Sādhya and the Viśvedevas;
homage to Śarva, to Sarva, to Ugra, and to the Giver of Boons.
Homage to Bhīma, the leader of the army; homage to the Lord of creatures!
Homage indeed to the pure one, who licks repeatedly, and to him who is newly born! 14.19
Salutations to Mahādeva, the wondrous, and to Citraratha;
to the primordial principle, the object of knowledge, the effect, and the instrument.
Salutations be unto you, O Puruṣa, and salutations to the one who fulfills the desires of Puruṣa;
salutations to the one who brings about the qualities of the Pradhāna through its union with Puruṣa.
To the initiator of primordial nature and of the person in every respect,
to the witness of what has been done and what has not been done, and to the bestower of the connection with the fruit.
Salutations everywhere to the Knower of Time, to the Ordainer of rules;
salutations to the creator of inequality and to the giver of the activity of the qualities.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Creator of all beings!
O Lord, be gentle, auspicious, and pleasant to behold for us, for you are indeed the Moon.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, while being praised by all the gods, that blessed Lord, the Master of the Universe and the Consort of Umā, spoke these words to the immortals.
"O gods, I am pleasant to behold and gentle; I am here for you, O blameless ones.
Ask for whatever boon you desire, and I shall grant it; speak, O sinless ones! (14.26)
Then all those gods, including Brahmā, bowed down and said:
"O Blessed One, let this boon remain in your very hand;
when the time for action comes, you shall grant us our desired boon. (14.27)
Having said "So be it" to them and dismissed the gods, Hara then entered his abode together with the Pramathas and the worlds.
But he who sings this wonderful festival of Hara in the presence of deities and brahmins, shall, upon the dissolution of the body, become like the peerless Gaṇeśa and be happy. (14.29)
Sanatkumāra said:
O son of Parāśara, whoever should hear or recite this hymn of praise, he shall go to the heavenly world and be honored by the gods like the king of the immortals. (14.30)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 14.14 ||
The fifteenth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Lord had entered the palace and was well-seated upon an excellent throne,
Standing outside, that cruel Manmatha became intent on piercing the God.
Him, who was joined with improper conduct, evil-minded, the lowest of his lineage, tormenting all the worlds, and devoid of compassion toward all— (15.2)
He saw him who had come with Rati in the form of a peacock, a creator of obstacles for the sages along with their observances and vows. (15.3)
Then, O Vyāsa, he looked with his third eye at the Lord of the Gods, who was intent on piercing him as an assailant, with a look full of contempt. (15.4)
Then the fire born from his eye, possessing thousands of garlands of flames,
enveloped the husband of Rati and consumed him along with his retinue.
Burning with pain and afflicted by grief, he cried out in a discordant voice;
and seeking to propitiate that god, he fell upon the surface of the earth. (15.6)
Swiftly, that Manmatha, whose limbs were enveloped by fire and who torments the world,
fell down and was reduced to ashes in an instant.
But his wife, deeply distressed, lamented piteously;
afflicted by grief, she, full of compassion, implored both the god and the goddess.
And having heard her lamentation, those two gods, whose very nature is compassion, looked upon the sorrowful woman, comforted her, and spoke to her. (15.9)
"He is certainly burnt, O blessed lady; his rebirth here is not expected.
Even though he is bodiless, he will perform all your tasks for you in due time."
But when Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva, O auspicious one, then this son of his shall be your husband; he will become yours.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained that boon, she— the beautiful-faced wife of Kāma—
departed for her desired destination, filled with joy and free from fatigue.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus consumed Kāma, whose mind was deluded, Śaṅkara spoke to the daughter of Himavat with devotion toward that best of sages.
"The preeminent brahmin named Vasiṣṭha, holding me in his heart, is performing austerities;
O lady of great vows, I shall go there to grant him a boon."
Having spoken thus to the goddess with devotion and affection,
the omnipresent Lord then went toward the vicinity of the ascetic sage Vasiṣṭha.
Then [he beheld] Vasiṣṭha, the best among the excellent sages, the most eminent of those who practice austerities, a tiger among ṛṣis, performing supreme penance.
When a full thousand years had passed, the Blessed One, approaching him who was like a blazing fire, said: "Tell me, what shall I give you?
O twice-born one, I grant you divine vision; behold me together with my retinue."
Having seen that Lord Īśāna, he bowed his head to the Master, placed his joined palms upon his head, and praised him with a joyful countenance. || 15.18 ||
Vasiṣṭha said: Salutations to the golden liṅga; salutations indeed to the Vedic liṅga. Salutations to the thousand-fold liṅga; salutations indeed to the fire-liṅga. (15.19)
Salutation to the ancient liṅga; salutation indeed to the liṅga of the Vedas.
Salutation to the liṅga of the wind; salutation indeed to the liṅga of Brahman. 15.20
Salutations to the Liṅga of the three worlds; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of burning. Salutations to the Liṅga of the mountain; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of stability.
Homage to the secret liṅga, whose liṅga rises above the seven continents;
homage to the liṅga of all objects, whose limbs are the liṅgas of all worlds. 15.22
Homage be to the one whose mark is unmanifest; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is intellect.
Homage to the one whose mark is the ego-principle; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is the elements. 15.23
Salutations to the one whose mark is the senses; salutations to the one whose mark is the subtle elements;
salutations to the one whose mark is the Puruṣa; and indeed salutations to the one whose mark is the states of being.
Homage to the one whose mark is all objects, and indeed homage to the one whose mark is darkness;
homage to the one whose mark is passion and the upper realm, and indeed homage to the one whose mark is goodness.
Homage to the sky-linga, and indeed homage to the fire-linga;
homage to the wind-upward-linga, and indeed homage to the sound-linga. 15.26
Homage to the one whose mark is the praise of the *Ṛgveda*; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is the *Yajurveda*.
Homage to you whose mark is the *Atharvaveda*; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is the *Sāmaveda*. (15.27)
Homage to you whose emblem is the constituent parts of sacrifice; indeed, homage to you whose emblem is sacrifice itself.
Homage to you of infinite emblems, whose emblem is followed by the gods.
Grant us supreme yoga, as well as offspring equal to yourself;
O God, grant us imperishable Brahman and supreme tranquility, O All-pervading Lord;
grant the immortality of our lineage and an inexhaustible mind devoted to dharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, being thus praised by Vasiṣṭha of immeasurable soul, the Blessed One was gratified;
and being gratified, he then spoke this to him. (15.30)
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you; I shall grant you all that is in your heart, as well as the supreme, subtle, imperishable yoga that fulfills every desire. (15.31)
"And I shall grant you a divine grandson, equal to yourself and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga, O best of sages; he shall indeed shine forth for you. (15.32)
Self-restraint, tranquility, as well as fame, contentment, and freedom from anger shall be yours eternally, and you shall possess immortality in every respect.

"O Brahmin, [grant me] invincibility, invulnerability, and eternal imperishability; may my lineage remain unbroken and may I have undecaying devotion to dharma. Speak of other boons as well; I shall grant them, O best of sages."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Blessed One, O best of gods, all that is yet to come is known to you.
For it may not turn out exactly as you, O Lord, consider it to be. (15.35)
Thus, there is no doubt in this matter regarding what has been ordained by me;
therefore, your imperishable son shall again bestow his grace upon you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the god Kapardin Nīlalohita then vanished in an instant while that brahmin-sage was looking on. (15.38)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 15.15 ||
Chapter Sixteen.
Vyāsa said:
Having obtained those boons, our grandfather, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, [proceeded].
Which son did she give birth to, whose splendor was equal to his own?
Sanatkumāra said:
By that boon from the trident-bearing God of gods,
he begot [a son] upon Arundhatī, who was endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga.
To his eldest son among a hundred sons, named Śakti, who was most devoted to Brahman—
From his very childhood, that high-souled son of Vasiṣṭha possessed a devotion toward the one who has the bull as his banner, directed with a supreme mind.
Once, for the sake of offspring, he propitiated the Lord of Umā;
Mahādeva, being pleased with him, spoke: "I am the giver of boons. (16.4)
Then, having seen that Lord, he spoke these words with a bowed face:
"O God, with what shall I praise you, who are the Lord of the entire world?
O All-pervading One, you sustain all the worlds by yourself through the power of your own law. (16.5)
You alone are the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the agent as well as the action; likewise, you are the producer, the produced, and the very process of production in every respect.
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, I desire that you grant me a son named Ātman, equal to me in virtues; let this boon be granted to me. (16.7)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, the God, the best among speakers, laughing at him who spoke thus, addressed him with words that made all the quarters resound. 16.8.
"O Śakti, I have been requested by you, and he shall be born to you—a bull among sages who will be equal to you and a knower of all the Vedas. (16.9)
And likewise, that which has arisen from the nature of a seed becomes itself the nature of a sprout;
having undergone a transformation, it no longer exists as the nature of a seed. (16.10)
Thus, this self of yours, having come into being as what is designated as "offspring," will no longer exist as that same self once it has undergone a change of state.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to him, the god, laughing and looking upon him, that yogi of exceeding splendor suddenly vanished from sight. (16.12)
When that Great God had departed, your grandfather Śakti, having reflected upon those words, thought, "It is even so. || 16.13 ||
Then, after a very long time had passed, O Śubhavratā,
the one of great wisdom, having been purified by great austerity and possessing a radiance like fire, conceived an excellent embryo in Adṛśyantī. (16.14)
While she was pregnant, King Kalmāṣapāda, his mind carried away by a Rākṣasa, became enraged and devoured the sage. (16.15)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 16.16 ||
The seventeenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Why did that king devour the sage who was endowed with ascetic power?
And for what reason did the king become one whose mind was stolen by the rākṣasa? (17.1)
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a lordly king named Mitrasaha, the sacrificer of Vasiṣṭha;
he was the powerful son of Sudāsa, possessing a splendor equal to that of Indra and Candra. (17.2)
Having approached him, Śakti said: "O King of kings, having been initiated, I shall perform a vow;
during that time, O Indra among kings, I must always consume flesh at night. (17.3)
"Give to me, who have come here, that which is pure, endowed with all virtues, free from any remedy, and given at once in a solitary place. (17.4)
Having been told "So be it" by him, that high-minded one departed;
then, at that moment, the Rākṣasa vanished from the sight of the king.
O best of sages, he did not then command the cook for his sake.
Then, when that day had passed, O dear one, the self-restrained lord of men, remembering [the prince], summoned the cook and spoke to him like one afflicted: (17.6)
Saudāsa said: "O Amṛtāvasu, I have promised the wise son of my preceptor that tomorrow morning I shall provide him with flesh prepared as his meal for the night."
Therefore, act accordingly with haste, so that our time does not pass us by.
Thus addressed, the cook Amṛtavarus then replied:
"O King, O bull among men, you did not tell us beforehand;
at present, there is not even a small amount of meat remaining that could be desired. (17.8)
Because the flesh itself was so small, because there were so many who ate it,
and because of the giving away of what was immeasurable, nothing at all remained.
The king said:
"I know your utility for all purposes, and I know your incorruptibility;
I know that the meat required is small, and this task is of such a nature."
"Let meat be sought quickly; you shall obtain it wherever you deem fit."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, Amṛtāvasu applied himself with great effort;
yet, while searching thoroughly for flesh, he did not find any at all.
When he did not obtain any meat, he went to the great king at night and spoke these meaningful words to the lord of men: (17.12)
"O King, there is no meat at all in this city that is ever pure;
searching for it, I am exhausted. Command me, what shall I do for you? (17.13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by the cook at that time, O lord of men, the king said nothing to that cook and remained silent. (17.14)
Immediately after that, a Rākṣasa named Rudhira, impelled by Viśvāmitra, entered the body of the king.

Then, possessed by that evil-minded Rākṣasa and drenched in blood, the highly resplendent one spoke softly into the ear of the cook: 17.16. "Go, and having brought whatever meat you can find—even human, or at least that of a donkey or a camel—you must prepare it all. || 17.17 ||
"What will he understand of refined speech (*saṃskṛta*) from you at night? Prepare it quickly, making it flavorful and fragrant. (17.18)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by him, O Vyāsa, he then took the human flesh of a certain man who had offended the king and had been cast out after death. (17.19)
Then, at the hour of midnight, they beheld that best of sages, possessing a radiance like the form of the sun and a brilliance equal to a hundred fires.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, water for the guest-offering, and an excellent, foremost seat, he served him food.
Having touched that food which had been brought, the great ascetic became enraged;
and in his anger, as if burning him up, he spoke to the king.
Śakti said:
"O lowest of kings, the feeding of Brahmins is not fit for Rākṣasas;
it is not given by one who knows the sacred law, yet you treat me with contempt. (17.23)
"Since you wish to give this Rākṣasa as food for me, therefore, by that very act, you shall become a man-eater. (17.24)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, the radiant king then reflected upon those words;
with his eyes reddened by anger and his mind possessed by a Rākṣasa, he spoke. (17.25)
"O twice-born one, since you have said to me, 'Become a man-eater,' therefore I shall devour you along with your brothers."
Having eaten for the sake of purification, I shall thereafter be freed from the curse;
then, having restrained the collection of my senses, I will practice pure austerity.
Permitted by your father, I shall dwell in heaven as long as I desire.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 17.17 ||
The eighteenth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king, having renounced his own kingdom together with his wife, [departed].
He entered the forest; there dwelt a man-eater of great strength. || 18.1 ||
He first devoured the great sage Śakti there, and then the hundred brothers of that very Vasiṣṭha, while he was looking on. (18.2)
Then, having witnessed the terrible slaughter of his sons, the powerful Vasiṣṭha, son of Brahmā, did not direct his anger toward Kauśika;
rather, he was utterly overwhelmed by the great grief for his sons. (18.3)
Having tied a great stone to his neck, that powerful son of Brahmā threw himself into the river; out of fear, it split into a hundred channels,
and thus the sages of rigid vows call it the Śatadrū.
Having bound him again with firm nooses, the self-controlled one released him into another river;
in that river he became "Vipāśa," and from that she became known as the Vipāśā.
Then, having reached the forest, fasting and with his senses subdued, he remained there subsisting on air alone, causing his own body to waste away. (18.6)
Then he suddenly heard the melodious sound of the Vedas being recited by someone there, and he immediately fell into deep meditation.
Then his wife, whose every limb was beautiful, with full and elevated breasts,
and with a dejected face and downcast eyes, approached him standing before Śakti.
He said to her, "From where do you come, and whose sound is this that is heard?
Then, weeping, she spoke with a piteous voice to her father-in-law. (18.9)
Adṛśyantī said:
"O Guru, from the very moment you departed from the hermitage due to grief for your son, I have been devoted to the Blessed One, remaining invisible. (18.10)
O Lord, this is the sound of your son studying while still within your womb; do not set your mind on sorrow. (18.11)
Sanatkumāra said:
"Now, my child, I have hope for my life," he said;
then, establishing himself in patience and fortitude, the sage departed for his hermitage. (18.12)
While going to that hermitage, he saw King Saudāsa on the road,
his limbs smeared with fat and blood and his eyes red.
The sage paralyzed with mantras the demon as he rushed forward with speed;
then, from his body, there emerged an exceedingly terrible rākṣasa.
And he said to him: "O evil-souled one, I would burn you along with your kinsmen!
But what use is it to me that you are burned? Go, you are released, O wicked-minded one! (18.15)
Then that released Rākṣasa, a doer of cruel deeds, dejected in spirit and terrified, bowed his head and went into the presence of Kuśika. || 18.16 ||
When the night-stalker had departed, the king, bowing his head to the sage, sought to propitiate him;
and he then spoke these meaningful words.
O Indra among kings, there is indeed no fault on your part for being possessed by a Rākṣasa;
your sons were slain by Fate, and the Rākṣasa was merely the instrument in that matter.
"Rule the kingdom, O Indra among kings, which was inherited from your father and grandfather, O Lord!
Tell me, O bull among men, what dear thing shall I do for you today? (18.19)
The king said: "O Blessed One, O Acyuta, I desire a son begotten by you upon this queen, one of great being; therefore, do that which is pleasing to me. (18.20)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," to his wife, that observer of great vows, being at peace, begot a son named Śoṇaka. (18.21)
Then, having consecrated his own son Śoṇaka upon the throne,
he quickly departed for the forest with his wife, intent on ascetic practice.
In the course of time, a powerful son was born to Vasiṣṭha by Śakti;
through Adṛśyantī, a son named Parāśara was born.
Then the wise one regarded Vasiṣṭha as his very father;
he repeatedly addressed the preceptor of his father, saying, "Father! Father! (18.24).
Then, having learned at one time that his father Śuci had been devoured by a Rākṣasa, he performed a sacrifice for the destruction of Rākṣasas through ascetic penance and mantras.
There, that one of great splendor offered fifty crores of Rākṣasas of cruel deeds into the fire; then he quickly approached Brahmā.
Having approached and paid homage to Sūta, the Lord, together with Vasiṣṭha,
the sages, and the deities, spoke these words to Parāśara.
Brahmā said:
"This eighth station is indeed the foremost among the gods, being of such a nature. (18.28)
Parāśara said:
Together with the gods, I shall consume all the worlds with fires;
having burnt them, I shall spread forth other worlds there—of this there is no doubt. (18.29)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, which were so full of pride, the divine Grandfather spoke these words to him in a gentle voice, consoling him. (18.30)
The Grandfather said:
"O high-minded one, what you have done is exactly as you say; there is no doubt about it.
All of this must be forgiven by you out of a desire to do what is pleasing to us. (18.31)
"Those by whom my father, O highly fortunate one, was devoured along with his brothers—they themselves must be offered as oblations into the fire while Viśvāmitra looks on.
May there be well-being for all others everywhere, including the gods together with the Rākṣasas. (18.32)
"O illustrious one, my son, you must restrain Vasiṣṭha. || 18.33 ||
All the gods, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down to that great sage;
and all those seers likewise then praised him with words of hymn.
Then, while Viśvāmitra looked on, he of great splendor honored their words and spoke these things in a melodious voice.
Whosoever among these— whether a brahmin or even a kṣatriya— who, being evil-minded,
takes the side of the rākṣasas, shall provide the remedy.
Enraged even at him here, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
I shall destroy him by the force of my penance and cast him into a blazing fire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
having recognized that power of his, worshipped Parāśara.
When those evil-minded Rākṣasas had been sacrificed,
he then withdrew the sacrificial session with the permission of Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who, having become pure, causes this to be heard by the twice-born at the time of a śrāddha or during a rite for the gods, him the rākṣasas do not harm. (18.40)

Having heard this account of Parāśara, which arises from undaunted birth and is produced by the performance of pure speech and action, a brahmin who is born of a lineage established in spiritual perfection does not enter a demonic womb. 18.41
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 18.18 ||
The nineteenth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"In this manner, O Vyāsa, your father performed the Rākṣasa-sacrifice."
And having completed it, he again performed radiant ascetic penance.
Vasiṣṭha, the imperishable one, having approached him who was radiant as the sun through his ascetic power, spoke these meaningful words to him who was filled with joy.
Vasiṣṭha said: Desiring sons, the ancestors indeed performed most difficult austerities and produced a son endowed with ascetic power and knowledge. (19.3)
"The one who is possessed of knowledge and endowed with ascetic power will provide for our progeny and ensure their destiny"— thus do those learned in the Vedas know.
O Lord, you are endowed with asceticism, possessed of knowledge, and graced with fame;
yet, though the best among those who have sons, you are deprived of offspring.
Therefore, O best of those who observe vows, go to freedom from debt toward your ancestors by quickly procreating a son, whether one who excels you or one who is your equal. (19.6)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha of immeasurable soul,
that radiant one reached Mount Maināka and performed a most difficult penance.
After a long time, to him who had been purified by ascetic penance, the Lord of Umā granted a boon; and he chose a virtuous son as his reward.
Having obtained the boon, he returned and made a request for the sake of a son:
"Grant me a perfectly pure field where my son might be born. (19.9)
In his agitation, he then beheld Kālī, the daughter of the king of the Dāśas, who had attained the status of his own daughter and possessed a divine form. || 19.10 ||
Born from the womb of a fish, she was formerly a consumer of the seed of Vasu;
she was Adrikā, the most excellent of Apsarases, auspicious and composed of the splendor of Brahman.
Having granted a boon to her, that great ascetic begot you upon her—
you, the source of all austerities and the promoter of the Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Your son was Śuka as well, the best among those who know yoga;
he had four sons and one daughter of slender waist.
Vyāsa said: How did the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha arise, and how was it again removed? I wish to know this. 19.14.
Sanatkumāra said: While Parāśara was still in the womb and the son of Gādhi had attained the status of a brahmin, both of them had their hermitages on the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra. (19.15)
There, recollecting his enmity, the wise Viśvāmitra,
while Vasiṣṭha looked on, slew a hundred sons in a fit of rage.

The sage also said: "In that matter, let the powerful Viśvāmitra take Vasiṣ�ṭha, who is bathing here, and having swept him away with a great current, bring him to me, O Sarasvatī, at a secluded spot on the great river. (19.17)
Having been addressed thus, she went to Vasiṣṭha and spoke to him in her distress;
and that which Gādheya had said, he in turn told to the great river.
"Do so, O illustrious lady; lead me wherever you desire, lest that cruel son of Gādhi cast upon you an inescapable curse. (19.19)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, as the sun reached its meridian, that auspicious river, while Gādheya was offering oblations into the fire, swiftly carried Vasiṣṭha away by her current.
Seeing that best of sages carried away by the current, O Vyāsa, he said:
"Since you have carried me away with such speed through this deception, therefore, by this act, you shall become a river of bloody water. (19.21)
Cursed by Viśvāmitra, that river which bestows happiness upon the world flowed with blood,
as well as flesh and fat.
Then, on the occasion of visiting the sacred fords, the sages who had gathered there bestowed their grace upon her, by which her waters became clear.
Then, through the power of his great asceticism and after a long time,
that bull among sages, having recognized the forbearance of Vasiṣṭha, [acted].
The immensely powerful Viśvāmitra abandoned his enmity toward Vasiṣṭha;
thus did those two best of sages relinquish their mutual hostility.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who would constantly hear this, or cause the Brāhmaṇas to hear it, crosses over difficult and impassable obstacles with unwearied manliness. (19.26)

Endowed with the qualities of modesty, manliness, and magnanimity, and possessing a radiant and beautiful appearance, he shall become equal to all the kings of the gods; and he may sport at his own will in the triple heaven.
Thus, O Vyāsa, that enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha came to an end once again for the sake of the welfare of the worlds. (19.28)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 19.19.
Then Viśvāmitra, having gone to the lord of the gods, said:
"O Kauśika, give me your thunderbolt;
I shall slay the ill-behaved Vasiṣṭha, that lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (19.23)
"O Śakra, his sons of evil mind have been slain by me;
yet even after killing them, O Lord of the Gods, there will be no peace for me. (19.24)
Śakra said:
"O Brahmā, O Īśāna, Vasiṣṭha, and you yourself, O best of sages—I hold no distinction between them; indeed, I do not know your true intentions. (19.25)
Enraged there, that son of Gādhi, the delight of the Kālīs, forcibly dislodged Śakra from his body through the power of his ascetic energy.
Having entered that body of the enemy of Vṛtra,
the powerful one stood with his thunderbolt raised, like one seeking a vulnerable point.
While he was offering oblations into that fire, [Indra] split it into seven pieces with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, even as the sages were looking on.
Then the sage himself, having quickly gathered the fragments and reconstituted his own body, spoke these words in anger: || 19.29 ||
Stay, Kauśika! You shall not depart from me now that you have been seen by me;
I know you to be stationed in the sky under a disguise because of Indra’s command. (19.30)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, O descendant of Kālī, that radiant son of Gādhi then stood in the sky in the form of Indra, filled with wrath.
Then the fortunes of the high-souled gods began to perish;
thousands of meteors fell from the sun, which appeared like a headless trunk.
Blood fell from the sky like stones,
inauspicious winds blew, and celestial chariots fell from the heavens. The Vedas of the Brahmins were lost, and likewise, the serpents who travel through the air perished.
Having seen such portents and various omens foreboding the destruction of the world,
the gods together with the sages spoke to that son of Gādhi.
Vasiṣṭha of great splendor and you, O righteous son of Gādhi,
are both immortal, free from old age, and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga.
For there shall be no destruction for you two, nor will you cause destruction,
even while fighting one another in the worlds of the gods.
Just as when two elephants in rut are fighting in the forest, a great destruction of creepers and trees occurs. || 19.37 ||
Thus, through this enmity that has arisen between you two great-souled ones, a calamity for the worlds will clearly come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, let there be for you two friendship with the worlds and the gods along with the sages, and let there be an end to this enmity. (19.39)
Thus addressed by the sages together with the deities, the son of Gādhi,
amazed at that time by their splendor, said to them, "So be it."
Then all the dwellers of heaven spoke thus to Vasiṣṭha as well;
he too, saying "So be it," established a friendship with Ulkā.
From that time forth, indeed, the entire world, both stationary and moving,
rejoiced with happiness and joy, freed from all affliction.
Sanatkumāra said. Chapter Twenty.
Vyāsa said:
O great sage, tell me in its entirety everything that those two lords of the gods, Umā and Hara, did when they were united together. 20.1.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Umā and Hara, both irreproachable, having come together with one another, united a brahmin of the Śālaṅka lineage with a boon. 20.2.
And that son, born not from a womb, having propitiated the Supreme Lord and attained equality with Rudra, shone forth as Mahāgaṇapati.
Vyāsa said: How was Nandin born, and how, having propitiated Śaṅkara, did he attain equality with Śambhu as well as the office of doorkeeper? 20.4
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a virtuous and powerful ṛṣi named Śilāda;
because his livelihood consisted of stones (śilaka), he was called Śilāda.
That twice-born one beheld his ancestors hanging in a pit, their lineages severed, having indeed fallen into a terrible hell. (20.6)
Addressed by them, who were desirous of offspring, he said: "O best of the twice-born, propitiate the imperishable Lord of the World, Mahādeva, for the sake of a son."
As he was performing austerities for a thousand years, Śarva, the wielder of the trident, surrounded by his hosts, spoke to him: "I am the giver of boons."
Having seen that Soma, the Lord of the lords, he bowed at the feet of the All-pervading One and praised the Sovereign of the gods with a voice faltering with joy.
Salutation to the supreme deity, the Great Lord, the Great Soul;
salutation to the creator of all the lords of the gods, to the Lord of Brahmā.
Homage to the destroyer of the body of Kama, the cause of the arising of yoga;
homage to the dweller of the mountains, the creator who is attainable through meditation. 20.11.
Salutations eternally to the Lord of the sages, salutations to the Lord of the gods;
salutations likewise to the Lord of the Vedas and to the Lord of the yogis.
Constant salutation to the Pradhāna, to the Reality known as Amara;
salutation to the granter of boons to devotees, and to the omnipresent one.
Salutations to the creator and the lord, the sovereign source of the transformations of the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements, together with their qualities.
Salutations always to the Lord of the world and to the Creator of the world; eternal salutations to the Lord of primordial nature (prakṛti) and to Him who transcends the Puruṣa.
Homage ever to the one worthy of refuge; homage to him whose limbs are smeared with ashes;
homage to you who hold the fire-tongs in hand; homage to the lord of all splendors.
Salutations always and eternally to the Creator of the three worlds, who abides as the sun, wind, fire, water, moon, ether, and earth.
O Lord, how can there be rest for you who are worthy of praise, since you alone are the cause of this world’s maintenance and destruction? (20.19)
O Lord of Gods, for me who am without refuge and who seeks refuge in you, grant your supreme grace; be a bestower of boons, O Creator of the Universe! 20.20
Sanatkumāra said:

That twice-born man who, being pure and observant of his vows, recites this entire hymn in the morning before the Brahmins—him neither Brahma-rākṣasas, night-stalkers, spirits, nor yakṣas harm, nor do bipeds, serpents, or pūtanās. (20.21)
Then that Blessed Lord, being praised along with Umā, said:
"I am the giver of boons; speak what is in your heart."
When the god had spoken thus, Śilāda then paid him honor;
and with faltering voice, he spoke these words to the Lord of Gods: || 20.23 ||
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, I desire a son equal to myself—one free from death and not born from a womb. (20.24)
Thus addressed, the three-eyed god, being well-pleased, said to him,
"So be it," and vanished right there.
When that great archer had departed, the highly honored sage returned to his own hermitage and then related the matter to the other sages.
Then, O best of sages, having been thus praised by them, and desiring to sacrifice after some time had passed,
he ploughed his own sacrificial ground with a plough.
As that furrow was being drawn,
a youth arose from it, appearing like the fire of universal destruction at the end of an aeon.
Seeing the prince thus arisen and blazing with splendor,
the Rākṣasa recognized him as "this one" and, out of fear, did not approach him.
The prince, having likewise emerged, approached his father of blazing splendor with a dejected soul and cried out, "Father! Father! (20.30).
When, even though addressed as "Father," he did not respond to him, then Vāyu spoke to Śilāda in the sky with a melodious voice: || 20.31 ||
Vāyu said:
"O Śālaṅkāyana, this son of yours who was formerly given by the god Śambhu, being not born from a womb—he is here; rejoice! (20.32)
"O best of the twice-born, since this [child] of yours shall always bring you joy, therefore this son of yours shall be known by the name Nandin. (20.33)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, at the word of Vāyu, he embraced Nandin and,
taking him with him, led that increaser of joy to his own hermitage.
He performed for him the rites of tonsure, initiation, and the others.
And having composed them, he taught the Vedas in their entirety along with their auxiliary branches,
as well as the science of medicine, the science of archery, the science of music, and the science of grammar.
The behavior of elephants, the characteristics of men and women, all the arts and crafts, and the knowledge of omens as well. (20.36)
O Vyāsa, in just five years he studied everything: the medical treatment of the host of spirits, the conduct of the Mothers, and whatever movements there were of all the serpents.
He was skillful, pure, and noble-minded; he spoke kindly and was free from malice.
He was always beloved by all the world, bringing delight to both the mind and the eyes.
Then, in the seventh year from that time, two divine rishis, rich in ascetic merit and possessed of great luster, arrived at the hermitage of Śilāda.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rites, Śilāda, who was of great ascetic merit,
observed that they were seated comfortably on highly honored seats.
The two named Mitra and Varuṇa, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
were cognizant of all beings in the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile.
Permitted by them, he sat down upon an excellent seat;
having sat down, he was pleased and praised them with words that were agreeable to him.
And questioned by them, he replied: "Is your son auspicious and a giver of satisfaction?
Is he devoted to the study of the Vedas? And is there a continuity of dharma?"
I hope that the fool does not show contempt for the elders or for his teachers; I hope he observes his religious observances and bestows satisfaction upon the virtuous. 20.44.
Thus addressed, the radiant Śilāda, who was devoted to his son,
virtuous, and the enhancer of his family lineage, replied appropriately.
Having summoned his son Nandin, who was steadfast and dear to him, he fell with his head at the feet of those two out of joy. (20.46)
Those two gods bestowed upon her a blessing consisting of constancy in righteousness,
a disposition toward service of her elders, and likewise imperishable worlds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Śilāda, perceiving that blessing from the two gods,
dismissed Nandin and, filled with fear, questioned those two best of sages.
Śilāda said:
"O venerable and truthful sages, who know the destiny of all embodied beings, for what purpose have both of you granted long life to my son?"
But those two best of sages did not properly pronounce a blessing.
Mitra and Varuṇa said:
"O dear one, this son of yours is short-lived, though esteemed by all;
therefore, he shall sustain his life for only one more year. (20.50)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, tormented by grief and distressed, he fell upon the earth;
having left the two tigers among sages, he lamented all alone.
Hearing the sound of him lamenting out of grief, his auspicious son Nandi came;
he then beheld his father, who was exceedingly distressed. (20.52)
Nandi said:
"O father, by what sorrow are you so tormented that you weep?
From where has this grief arisen? O sire, I wish to know. (20.53)
Śilāda said: "O son, you shall indeed lose your life within a year.
When the two sages spoke thus, distress then took possession of me. (20.54)
Nandi said:
"It is true, dear one; those divine seers did not speak a falsehood.
Nevertheless, death shall have no power over me; do not grieve. (20.55)
Śilāda said: What is your austerity, what is your knowledge, what is your yoga, and what is your exertion, by which you shall deceive Death who is prepared for you? Tell me. (20.56)
Nandin said:
"O father, I shall not evade death by means of asceticism nor by means of knowledge;
through the grace of Mahādeva alone shall I conquer death, and not otherwise. (20.57)
"I shall behold the god Śaṅkara; then death shall not be mine.
When death is destroyed, I shall dwell with you for a long time in perfect peace. (20.58)
Śilāda said: "In former times, after performing most difficult austerities for a thousand years, Mahādeva was beheld by me, since you were obtained as my son."
But you, having practiced asceticism for only a single year and not yet fully perfected it, how will you behold Mahādeva? This is what I wish to know.
Nandi said:
"O dear one, the Lord is not seen through austerity, nor is He seen through knowledge;
the Supreme Lord is seen through devotion with a purified mind. (20.61)
"O father, once released by you, I shall go and behold the Three-eyed Lord before long; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, release me quickly."
"Yama approached me while I was standing there and did not harm me as you have witnessed; therefore, my dear son, I am departing from here."
Whether standing, lying down, running, or fallen—realizing that death does not wait for anyone, attain tranquility. 20.64
Having descended into the divine water and established myself in a state of pure being,
I shall practice the Raudra chapter and thereafter behold Śaṅkara.
For me, who am engaged in recitation, disciplined, and surrendered to the state of Rudra,
many deaths and times of death shall cause no affliction.
Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving him speaking thus with pure speech,
the great ascetic of undepressed soul released his son from his distress with difficulty.
Having saluted his father’s feet with his head, that man of great renown circumambulated him and set forth with firm resolve.
Having paid homage to all the sages, that noble-minded seer, desiring to see him,
went to Lord Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. 20.20.
The Twenty-First Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Nandin, having departed from there, went to the best of rivers.
She was renowned as Bhuvanā, bringing happiness to all the worlds.
Having entered it, the wise one then took his stand by the lake with one-pointed mind; terrified of death, he then recited the Rudra hymns with full concentration. (21.2)
While he was reciting there with single-minded devotion, by virtue of that prayer,
when one crore had been recited, the god was indeed pleased.
Approaching him, the Blessed Lord Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair, said:
"Nandin, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Choose a boon according to your desire. (21.4)
Bowing down, he spoke to Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him:
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, I wish to recite a second ten million [mantras] of the Blessed Ones.
Having said, "So be it," the God also departed as he had come.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having descended from there once more, with his self thus restrained,
he likewise muttered another ten million [times], meditating solely upon Rudra.
Then, when the second ten-million-year period was completed, the bull-bannered god arrived and said to him, "I am here as a granter of boons."
He said, "O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, by your grace I wish to recite even a third ten million times during this period of time. (21.8)
"So be it," the Blessed One replied once more;
having spoken, the one of great splendor went to his own abode together with the Goddess. || 21.9 ||
Then he recited another ten million mantras dedicated to Rudra;
thereupon, O twice-born one, he became like the sun at the end of an eon.
When three crores of those [years] had passed, O Vyāsa, the god Soma, possessing a flaming luster, approached that place together with his hosts.
Having grasped him with his trunk and lifted him out of the water,
Kālahasta, wiping Nandin with the tip of his hand, spoke to him.
The God said:
"O son of Śilāda, I am the granter of boons to you, gratified by this asceticism.
Well recited by you, O wise one; tell me what is in your heart. (21.13)
Śailādi said: "By your power, O Lord, I shall again chant another ten million [times].
O All-pervading One, if you are pleased with me, O God, I choose this boon. (21.14)
The Blessed One said: "What is the use of your further recitation? I am entirely pleased with you.
Whatever desire you choose, I shall grant it all to you. (21.15)
"Shall it be the state of Brahmā, or the state of Viṣṇu, or the state of Indra, or the state of Vāyu? Become the Āditya, or Rudra? Speak, or what shall I give to you? (21.16)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the God, he bowed his head at the Lord’s feet and praised Him, the destroyer of the cities, the desires, the limbs, the sacrifices, and the mountains.
Nandi said:
Salutations to the God beyond gods, salutations indeed to Mahādeva;
Salutations to the destroyer of the body of Kama, salutations indeed to the blue-throated one.
Homage to the destroyer of Tuṣita and to the burner of the three worlds;
homage to the one with the fierce staff of Time, and indeed homage to the one of terrible punishment.
Homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍa; homage to the thousand-headed one, and to the thousand-handed and thousand-footed one.
To Him whose hands and feet are everywhere, whose eyes, faces,
and ears are everywhere, who stands encompassing all.
Salutations to you who are of golden hue and likewise beyond the senses;
salutations to the one whose emblem is gold, and indeed salutations to the one who is all-emblem.
Salutations to the one whose complexion is like the moon and the sun, the Lord of Yoga, the unconquered;
salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, and to the one who holds the trident and the mallet in his hands.
Salutations indeed to the one armed with a mace and a sword, to the bearer of the battle-axe,
to the chariot-warrior, to the one clad in armor, and to the great archer.
Salutations to the one who holds a trident in his hand and wields a fierce staff;
salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and salutations to the Lord of the Rudras.
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one, salutations indeed to the hundred-eyed one;
salutations to the lord of the Ādityas and to the lord of the Vasus.
Homage to the Lord of the Earth, homage to the Lord of Space;
homage to the Lord of the Heavenly World, homage to the Lord of Umā.
Homage to the Lord of Yoga and the bestower of all yoga;
to the meditator, to him who is being meditated upon, and to him who is praised by those who meditate.
To Death, to the Wielder of the Staff of Time, to the Great-Souled Yama,
to the Lord of the Gods, and to Him of divine constitution.
To Savitṛ, the giver of wealth for sacrifice, the progenitor of heaven,
the dharma of all the gods, who possesses manifold forms.
To the one who is the nectar of immortality, the most excellent, praised by all the gods,
and the severer of the head of Brahmā and of the great-souled Sacrifice.
To the destroyer of Tripura, the fierce one, the remover of all inauspiciousness;
to him whose form consists of half the body of Umā, and who has an eye upon his forehead.
To the destroyer of Mahiṣa and Andhaka, to the creator, the supreme lord,
to the teacher of Brahmā, and to the progenitor of Brahmā.
Salutations indeed to the teacher of Kumāra, to the bestower of boons upon Kumāra, to Halin, to the wielder of the mace, and to the one of great laughter.
To him who holds the noose of death in his hand, who wears Takṣaka as his sacred thread,
whose vehicle is a cloud flashing with lightning, and likewise to him who rides upon a bull.
To the one who dwells in the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, who resides on Mount Meru,
who dwells on Kailāsa, and who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth.
To him who has given half of his own body to Viṣṇu, to him who grants boons to that very Viṣṇu,
to him who is unequaled among all beings, and who is compassionate toward all beings.
To him who has internalized the higher and lower elements, who bestows life upon living beings, who is the mind itself, who is the object of thought, and who is indeed beyond all pride.
Homage to the one who is awakening and the awakened, to the seer and indeed to the eye;
homage to you, the toucher, and likewise to the sense of touch.
Salutations to the Taster and likewise to the Sense of Taste;
salutations to the Smeller and the Smell, and indeed to the Hearer and the Sense of Hearing;
salutations to the Grasper and the Hand, and likewise to the Walker and the Foot.
Homage be to the creator of bliss and homage indeed to bliss itself;
likewise to Speech and to the Speaker, and to the Great-Souled One who consists of those subtle elements.
Salutations to the subtle and the gross being, to Rajas;
salutations always to Tamas, and to the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the unconquered.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world and the lord of creatures;
salutations to Manu, the seven seers, who are performing austerities and are full of fervor.
Salutations to the one devoted to Brahman, to the pure one, and likewise to Durvāsas;
to the artisan, the lord of craftsmen, the wise Viśvakarman.
Salutations likewise to Atri, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras;
and to Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Dakṣa, and Anala.
Salutations to you who are Dharma, to Ruci, and to Vasiṣṭha;
salutations to the Being, the Lord of Beings, and the Lord of Kuṣmāṇḍas.
He stands and he moves, and indeed he sings and even dances;
he is the dew, the unslayable, the ageless, and the immortal.
To the one who is inexhaustible, immutable, and likewise unimpeded;
to the one who cannot be entered by any, who is visible yet possesses an invisible form.

Salutations to you, the subtlest of the subtle, the all-pervading Great Soul! O Blessed One, three-eyed one, salutations to you! O Blessed One, Śiva, salutations to you! O Lord of all worlds, salutations to you! O Creator of the world, salutations to you! 21.49
Neither by sovereignty over the gods, nor again by the state of Brahmā;
neither by being Viṣṇu, O Lord of Gods, nor even by being Indra, O Protector of Beings—
O Īśāna, I desire eternal and imperishable membership in your retinue.
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to see you eternally, together with your attendants, Ambā, and your retinue, in a state of grace; let this boon be granted to me. (21.51)
O Lord, you alone were our refuge in the past; you are the sovereign protector of the distressed, and you alone are our shelter—never do I perceive another.
And for one abandoned by you, swift destruction is certain; there is no doubt in this matter.
I see no other course of action that leads to ultimate well-being.
"Devoted, faithful, intent upon you, and taking refuge in you—accept me always, O God; let this be the boon granted to me. (21.54)
Sanatkumāra said: That man who, having risen in the morning, recites this with an undistracted mind, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become equal to Nandīśvara.
Whoever should constantly hear this or cause it to be heard among the twice-born,
having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
For by hearing this sin-destroying hymn even once,
O Vyāsa, wherever one may die, one shall not fall into an evil state of existence.

For one who, having constantly studied this foremost hymn, always worships the God with self-restraint—what need has he for various sacrifices, gifts, pilgrimages, or likewise for well-performed austerities? (21.58)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 21.21 ||
The twenty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord of the Gods of gods [spoke to him] who was endowed with supreme devotion.
With eyes full of tears, wretched, he bowed his head at [his father's] feet.
Taking hold of her with his two very gentle hands, the Moon, the dispeller of supreme suffering,
raised her up and wiped away her eyes which were filled with tears.
Then the Lord, his soul gratified, gazing upon all the leaders of the Gaṇas together with the Goddess, spoke to him as if nourishing him with his very words. (22.3)
The god said:
"O sinless one, I know your devotion to me, and I know your distress.
O son of Śilāda, listen now to the future outcome of all this. 22.4
Immortal, abandoned by old age, eternally free from suffering,
inexhaustible and indeed immutable— such shall he be, together with his father and his circle of friends.
He shall be my beloved Gaṇapa, possessing my own vigor and my own prowess; he shall always be dear to me and always remain by my side.
Endowed with the power of great yoga, he shall indeed become like my very own form.
I grant you this island, possessed of supernatural power, with the Ocean of Milk as its source of nectar; I provide you a dwelling there, where you shall always take delight.
Then, having removed from himself a garland made of lotuses,
the one of great splendor fastened that divine-looking wreath upon Nandin.
With that garland fastened around his neck,
the glorious Nandin shone like a second Śaṅkara, possessing three eyes and ten arms.
Then the Blessed Lord Hara, taking him by the hand, said:
"Tell me, what supreme boon shall I grant you today?"
And this hermitage, thoroughly sanctified by your asceticism,
shall become my secret retreat, renowned as Japyeśvara.
For a league in every direction, the field will be divine, surrounded by hosts of gods,
crowded with siddhas and cāraṇas, and frequented by throngs of apsarases;
it will become a supreme and secret field of spiritual attainment— of this there is no doubt.
Whatever a person performs here by deed, thought, or speech—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—all that shall come to pass; therefore, let all of it be auspicious.
The mental recitation shall indeed be equal to that of the Rudras;
wherever mortals die, they shall go to your world.
Then, taking the water dripping from his matted locks, which was as pure as a pearl necklace,
the great ascetic said, "Become a river," and released it.
Then that great river flowed forth— divine in its waters, meritorious, auspicious with its jewel-like water,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, graced by ruddy geese,
and endowed with groves of lotuses and water-lilies.
Assuming the form of a woman, with palms joined in reverence and head bowed,
she whose eyes possessed the luster of lotus and water-lily petals stood before Mahādeva.
Then the god spoke to that river who had presented herself before him:
"O goddess of auspicious countenance, since you have issued from the water of the matted locks (jaṭodaka), therefore you shall be known by the name Jaṭodā, O best of rivers. (22.18)
Whoever, being pure and with a restrained mind, performs a bath in you,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and be glorified in the world of Rudra.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Mahādeva, having declared to the Goddess, "This is your son," caused Nandīśvara, who was exceedingly radiant, to bow at her feet.
Having smelled his head and stroking him with both hands, the goddess,
gazing at the god, drenched him out of maternal love with the three streams of milk from her breasts, white as conch shells.
"Those three streams of hers flow like a river;
therefore, she is the river Trisrotasī, the holy one," said Hara to her then.
Seeing the river with its three streams, Vṛṣa was filled with supreme joy;
he bellowed, and from that sound another river came into being.
Since that great river began with the roar of the bull,
the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva) spoke to her as Dhitkirikā.
The god bound upon him his own wonderful crown made of Jāmbūnada gold, most marvelous, as well as two earrings born of nectar.
Seeing him thus honored in the sky, the cloud Prabhākara— the vehicle of the gods— rained down, accompanied by thunder and streaked with lightning.
When he had been consecrated, two streams then began to flow profusely;
because one river issued forth from his golden [body], Mahādeva named it Svarṇodakā (Golden Water). || 22.27 ||
Because a holy river flowed forth from that second auspicious crown made of Jāmbūnada gold, they called it the Jambū River.
This place, situated near Japyeśvara, is named Pañcanada;
the fruit of these [five rivers] has been explained by the Great-souled One at Jaṭodā. || 22.29 ||
Having gone to that divine Pañcanada and to that Lord Japyeśvara,
and having fasted for three nights, bathed, and worshipped the wielder of the trident (Śūlin), [one attains the goal].
Having gratified the Brahmins, a man who dies anywhere shall become an attendant of Nandīśvara, with his abode in the Ocean of Milk.
But he who gives up his life-breaths, so difficult to abandon, at Japyeśvara—
whether by means of a formal vow or otherwise— he shall become a Gaṇapati unto me.
Constantly equal to Nandīśvara, eternal, perpetual, imperishable, and undecaying, he never departs from my side; he is beloved and highly esteemed by me.
Any man who, having come to Japyeshvara and Panchanada, casts off his body there,
shall always be my most excellent attendant (gaṇapa), equal to you, and forever possessed of beauty and a physical form.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 22.22 ||
The twenty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
The Blessed One, the Lord of the gods of gods, Hara, the master of all beings—
Vāgīśa said to the goddess Umā, the daughter of the king of mountains: || 23.1 ||
"O Goddess, I shall consecrate the god Nandīśvara, the lord of beings; I shall summon the Gaṇas. Or what do you think, O imperishable one? (23.2)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, my eldest son Nandin deserves all this—the sovereignty over the seven worlds as well as that of the lords of the Gaṇas. (23.3)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
facing the east, performed the invocation of the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Then, O great sage, listen as I describe how thousands of lords of all the worlds, the leaders of the Gaṇas, arrived there filled with joy.
Then [he appeared] with formidable fangs, his face adorned with a frown,
white as a conch shell, a pearl necklace, or water, possessing tusks, wearing a garland, and having three eyes.
With a thousand matted locks rising from his head, hair like flames, and massive jaws,
he had eyes like glowing embers and wore a girdle made of serpents.
He had a tongue like lightning and a massive body, with his penis pointing upward;
