he wore a serpent as a sacred thread and likewise carried an axe.
With a girdle of muñja grass bound by serpents and bracelets likewise made of snakes,
emitting loud bursts of laughter resembling the crash of thunderbolts,
the leader of the hosts known as Diṇḍi was seen.
He was surrounded by ten crores of those like himself—
leaders of the hosts, lords of the gods, yogins of blazing splendor.
Then another appeared, with great hair and a massive body, urinating upwards;
he had three eyes, resembled a hundred fires, and roared like the falling of a thunderbolt. || 23.11 ||
Dancing and singing, performing various and manifold dramatic acts,
with blazing fangs and a great laugh, he was broad-shouldered and wielded the Pināka bow.
Together with twice ten million high-souled hosts of diverse forms, he was seen all at once.
O Vyāsa, that leader of the Gaṇas named Aṣāḍhi arrived there, possessing the faces of a lion, an elephant, and a crane, and having the countenances of a leopard and a tiger.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then another arrived, O Vyāsa, possessing the splendor of the sun at the end of a Yuga,
with arms a hundred yojanas long, naked, and with his organ turned upward.
He was exceedingly tall and possessed an oversized penis; his eyebrows hung down, his nose was thick, his mouth was round, his eyes were large, and his face was knit with a frown.
It was five yojanas in width and likewise in length;
it bore four fangs in its mouth, as white as a conch shell or the moon.
With five tongues and ears reaching upward, a noose in his hand, and swift as thought,
he was seen surrounded by a hundred crores of his own like-minded followers.
Renowned as Bhārabhūti and endowed with the power of great yoga,
that leader of the Gaṇas approached the presence of the God of gods.
Then [he saw the Lord], shining like a kunda flower, the moon, or a conch shell, resembling a mass of snow or water,
with the luster of a lotus stalk or crystal, and draped in a waist-cloth of ashes.
And he seized Aśanīhāsa, who had three feet, was clothed in rags,
possessed a hundred bellies, three heads, three eyes, and hair that stood upright.
His hair was crowned with garlands of flames, he wore a tiger skin as his garment,
possessed the speed of the wind, let out a great laugh, and had a girdle bound with serpents.
Afflicted by a mahoraga, with spike-like ears and an erect penis,
using ashes as a weapon, possessing great fangs and a large jaw.
He beheld that heroic leader of the hosts, renowned as Jvara, the Great Gaṇapati, who was surrounded by hundreds of millions of attendants.
Then another appeared, gentle in form, his limbs smeared with ashes,
holding a trident in his hand, naked, and endowed with the power of great yoga.
Wearing many disguises and devoted to the yoga of meditation, the lord known as Somavarṇa arrived when summoned by the God, surrounded by hundreds of crores of such leaders of the Gaṇas. || 23.26 ||
Then another appeared, massive in body, trident-bearing, and possessed of great strength;
resembling the fire at the end of an eon, he was steadfast, with a firm reputation and power.
Candramauli, Mahākeśa, Caturbāhu, and Vilohita—these were the great-bodied ones with three eyes, holding tridents in their hands, and accompanied by many-legged beings. || 23.28 ||
Accompanied by a hundred crores,
Rudra— the destroyer of all asuras— appeared there along with his great attendants, like a pillar.
Then another appeared, pure, with short feet and belly,
wielding a spear, possessing a thousand arms and feet, a thousand eyes, and great majesty.
He had formidable fangs, wore black serpents as garments,
possessed three eyes, bore the moon as a crest-ornament, and was adorned with a garland around his neck.
Known as Ugrasena, surrounded by a hundred crores of followers,
he, the lord himself, having been summoned, came into the presence of the god.
Then another [being] approached the god who bears the crescent moon—
the four-faced, immensely radiant Lord with twenty-four eyes.
He had a thousand arms, a mouth of flames, great eyes, and an upward-pointing penis; he had formidable teeth, spike-like ears, and large claws.
The sword-handed one of great splendor, the hundred-footed, the hundred-bellied,
the lightning-haired, the excessive-laughter, and likewise the one who moves in both directions.
Known as Ajaikapāda, he was surrounded by a hundred crores [of followers];
rich with golden rocks and trees, he was like a mountain shrouded in clouds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then another leader of the Gaṇas, O Vyāsa, arrived—one of great strength, glorious, with faces on all sides, and possessing hands and feet everywhere. (23.37)
With short arms, thighs, and feet, and bearing a beautiful thunderbolt,
he was surrounded by eight hundred million attendants equal to himself;
known as Nikumbha, he possessed a hundred feet, bellies, and faces.
Then another of great strength arrived, Vidyutkeśa, who wore a garland of moons; terrible, he came laughing and shaking [the earth].

Wielding a staff, with a great countenance and the luster of a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, he was surrounded by hundreds of millions of attendants; he was supreme and the scorcher of his enemies.
Then another one of great asceticism, surrounded by a host of ten million followers,
arrived wearing a garland of sunbeams.
He, named Sūryāpyāyana, was the supreme favorite of the god;
armed with a bow, he was of great energy, renowned, and possessed of immense splendor.
Likewise, there was another named Sarpamāla and Cakrābharaṇa;
the highly energetic Cakrāyudha had short feet and a protruding waist.
Renowned in the world by the name Grahāpyāyana,
he was pursued as he fled, surrounded by six hundred million astrologers.
The mighty Śaṅkukarṇa advanced with ten million attendants;
Nandika also with ten, and Piṅgākṣa with eight;
Vināyaka with sixty-four, and the one renowned by the name Kuṣmāṇḍa.
Hiraṇyavarṇa with six, Ekapāda likewise, Dhūmrakeśa with twelve, and Patākī with ten. || 23.46 ||
Sahasraghaṇṭa was surrounded by eighteen thousand, Tapa by five thousand,
Sahasraśīrṣa by six thousand, and Bhava was encompassed by hundreds of millions.
Varas approached with ten [elephants], Kumbhakarṇa likewise with eight;
Viṣvaksena with a thousand, and Annada indeed with a hundred.
Āveśanī is likewise surrounded by eight, and Pravartana by seven;
Mahārava is surrounded by a thousand crores of attendants.
Caturmukha with twelve arms, Bāhūpahāraka, Mahākāla with a hundred arms, and likewise the Gaṇa Agniśikhara.
Ādityamūrdhā with ten million, and likewise Dhanāvaha; Saṃnāma with one hundred, and Kukkuṭa with eight.
Kunda with fifteen [crores], and another, Saṃkoṭaka; Amoghabhūti with ten million, and likewise two Meghabhūtikas.
Ekapāda consists of one [syllable], while the other group, Saptaśiras, consists of sixty;
Mahābala consists of nine, as does the well-known Apasmāra. || 23.53 ||
Nīla, the lord of the gods, as well as Pūrṇabhadra and Nirṛti,
approached together with seventy crores.
Surrounded by twenty billion followers,
the Ītis, endowed with the power of great yoga, arrived there.
The Bhūtas with ten billion, the Pramathas with three billion,
Vīrabhadra with sixty-four thousand, and the exceedingly powerful Vṛṣabha.
Megha, surrounded by ninety followers including Saudāminīmāla, arrived;
as did Prabhākara with twenty, and the very powerful Viṭpati. || 23.57 ||
Girika, Meghanāda, Udara, Maṇi, the divine-souled Kāṣṭhakarṇa, and the renowned Bilvarūpa. || 23.58 ||
Śatamanyu, as well as the heroic Pañcākṣa, Tālaketu, Ṣaṇḍa, Kāpālī, and Gajanāśana. || 23.59 ||
Saṃvartaka, as well as Caitra, Trailokyadahana, Lokāntaka, Dīptātman, and Hemakuṇḍala; || 23.60 ||
Mṛtyu, Yama, Kāla, and Viṣahara; Śatamāya, Mahāmāya, and likewise Sarvatrāśaraṇa; the famous Ekaśṛṅgin, and he who is Bhṛṅgiriṭi. (23.61)
These and other leaders of the hosts, who are secret and possessed of great strength,
all arrived there filled with joy, skilled in fighting with various weapons.
Singing, running, and dancing, those of great strength likewise made the sounds of their mouths and cymbals resound.
Some were mounted on chariots, elephants, and horses; others had monkeys or birds as their mounts, while still others rode upon tigers, lions, cats, serpents, and even winged creatures.
With kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums; with cymbals, ānakas, and gomukhas; and with various musical instruments, including paṭahas and single-headed drums.
With the resounding blasts of kettledrums and jharjharas, with āḍambaras and ḍiṇḍimas,
with maḍḍukas, flutes, lutes, and even with vivṛṣas and tuṇavas.
To the assembly of the gods came the great yogis, accompanied by the sounding of drums, cymbals, lutes, tortoise-shells, and small drums.
To Viśvakarman, the subduer of enemies, the Lord of All, the single-syllabled and imperishable, they—
resplendent like the likeness of the thousand-eyed Indra— bowed down deeply and uttered loud cries of praise.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 23.23 ||
By means of the Puṣpaka aerial chariot as well as by a rutting elephant.
Having thus covered the sky, the Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as others by the tens of millions, ascended various celestial chariots there.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those lords of the Gaṇas, all of great being and masters of the lords of the gods, having bowed down to the God and the Goddess, spoke these words: 24.1.
O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, Lord of Ambikā, the God of gods!
For what purpose have we been summoned? Command us; it shall be done.
"Shall we dry up the oceans, or shall we strike down Yama along with his servants?
Shall we slay Death, or let the Lotus-born one not exist today? (24.3)
"Having bound Indra together with the gods, including Viṣṇu and Vāyu, we shall bring them here;
or else, being greatly enraged, we shall bring the Daityas along with the Dānavas."
"Whose terrible calamity shall we bring about today by your command?
Or whose festival, O Lord, filled with the fulfillment of all desires, shall we provide today? (24.5)
To all those who were speaking thus and bowing down, Bhava, the Lord of the Gaṇas, affectionate toward his devotees, spoke after first honoring them.
The god said:
Listen to that for which you, who are devoted to the welfare of the world, have been summoned here;
having heard it, being self-restrained, perform it without hesitation. (24.7)
"This Nandīśvara is our son, the Lord of all lords; he is your beloved leader and your composed commander-in-chief. (24.8)
Therefore, all of you, being in full agreement, should at my request consecrate this great lord of yoga as your commander-in-chief and husband.
"From this day forward, this auspicious Nandīśvara shall be your beloved, respected, and authoritative lord and commander-in-chief among the immortals."
Sanatkumāra said:
When this had been spoken by the Blessed One, all those leaders of the Gaṇas,
having deliberated and agreed, saying "So be it," then brought together the necessary materials.
Then they brought for him a divine, beautiful seat made of Jāmbūnada gold, which was as radiant as Mount Meru and enchanting to the mind.
It was made of gold, possessing the luster of beautiful refined gold,
hung with strings of pearls, and illuminated by precious gems.
Having constructed a pavilion facing all directions, adorned with pillars made of lapis lazuli, covered with networks of tinkling bells, and furnished with beautiful jewels,
they then prepared an excellent and auspicious seat in its center.
Before him they prepared a blue footstool, radiant with diamonds,
for the purpose of placing his feet; and two jars,
filled with the finest water and their mouths covered with lotuses, were placed at his sides.
Having established the fire in front and a bull at his side,
he then placed Surabhi with her calf on his right side.
And there was a beautiful parasol with a hundred ribs, made of pure Jāmbūnada gold,
resplendent with a back as white as a conch shell, a pearl necklace, or water.
A beautiful fan, white as the moon and with a golden handle;
and a garland of lotuses frequented by swarms of bees.
There the leaders of the hosts brought golden *nandyāvarta* designs,
as well as two fish from the abode of Varuṇa, representing the lunar mansions Punarvasu and Puṣya.
The golden svastika, the vardhamāna, and the śrīvatsa;
the kīcaka bamboos and the highly honored maiden.
These two elephants, Airāvata and Supratīka, are honored;
likewise, the divine banner is honored, as is the conch shell with the luster of the moon.
And a thousand golden jars of great luster, as well as a thousand silver ones and likewise earthen ones.
Then he gave a thousand divine copper vessels with the brilliance of fire,
a pair of garments made of tree-bark, and fine, stainless cloth.
A golden crown, well-crafted by Viśvakarman,
two stainless divine earrings, and the thunderbolt, that supreme weapon.
The great divine sword Paṭṭiśa, the trident, and the thunderbolt,
as well as a thread made of Jāmbūnada gold and a pair of armlets.

And the leaders of the hosts, esteemed by the gods, calmly brought from all sides a necklace with its surface variegated by gems, as well as yellow pigment and gold ornaments, sacred darbha grass, divine fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and incense.
Then the quarters of the sky, the oceans, Varuṇa the lord of wealth,
Yama, Agni, and the Vasus, as well as the Moon and the Sun along with the planets, [all came].
All the stars in the form of Tārās, as well as the constellations (nakṣatras) and Dhruva;
the Rudras, the Rākṣasas, and the Yakṣas; the two Aśvins, and the Daityas and Dānavas.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as Nārada and Parvata;
the Earth and the oceans, the regions and the mountains likewise. (24.30)
The trees, the creepers, and the mighty medicinal herbs,
as well as all the rivers and all the animals from every quarter, gathered together.
The mothers of the world, as well as the earth and heaven,
the elements, primordial nature (prakṛti), and all the senses in their entirety.
All sacred fords and various kinds of gifts,
as well as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and even the Atharva-Āṅgirasa, [are contained therein].
Sacrifices, rituals, offerings, and likewise observances;
all the Vedic meters, as well as the Piśācas and divine progenitors;
Brahmā, the sages, and Viṣṇu along with his attendants—[all these were present]. (24.34)
When they had all arrived, the Blessed One, whose banner bears the bull,
commanded the Grandfather to perform the rites for every necessary task.
Having prepared each individual pitcher there, provided with all medicinal herbs, filled with water, and covered with a lotus upon its mouth; || 24.36 ||
And likewise Jayā and Vijayā, Siṃhī and Vyāghrī,
as well as Suvarcalā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Punarnavā.
Kumārī, Candrakāntā, and Mṛtasañjīvanī, as well as Ādityavarcasī, Amṛtā, and Śrīniketanā. (24.38)
Likewise, O Vyāsa, those lords of the Gaṇas then cast medicinal herbs into all those earthen vessels, including Kumudvatī.
The Blessed One established all the various sacred fords (tīrthas) and all the gifts (dānas) within all those golden [images].
And within the silver jars were the mantras and the Vedic meters,
as well as various other sacrifices, both those performed for specific desires and others.
In all the Audumbara regions, the Blessed One likewise deposited the rivers, the oceans, the ascetic penances, and the religious observances.
Having filled each jar there and consecrated them with mantras,
the Lord wrapped them with thread and presented them to the gods.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, took one jar for himself;
he gave one to Viṣṇu and one to the wise Indra;
likewise, the Grandfather gave others to the Gaṇapas and to the ṛṣis.
Then, having seated him upon that throne and honored him, the high-minded Brahmā himself performed the consecration.
Then Viṣṇu, Śakra, the ṛṣis together with the immortals,
and all those lords of the hosts, consecrated Nandin.
He himself gave him a pair of celestial garments and likewise celestial perfumes;
he also gave him armlets, earrings, a crown, and a necklace, as well as a sharp-edged spear, a trident, a thunderbolt, and a lightning bolt.
The Lord of the Gods took up the parasol, and Vāyu the fan;
the sages, led by the Grandfather, offered hymns of praise.
Viṣṇu said:
Salutations to the King of Kuṣmāṇḍas, whose hand is raised with a thunderbolt;
to the grandson of Śālaṅkāyana, who has arisen from the path of the plow.
Salutations to the son of Śilāda, to the one who performs the recitation of the Rudra-hymns,
to the devotee of Rudra, to the god who reclines within the waters.
Salutations to the Lord of the hosts, salutations to the Lord of beings,
to the divine son of Umā who bears the paṭṭiśa weapon.
Homage to the one with terrifying fangs and the eye on his forehead;
to the one who crushes, the most excellent, and the one offered to Īśāna.
Salutations to the guardian of the gate, the hero, the lord of great renown;
salutations to him who wears a preeminent garland and whose abode is the Ocean of Milk.
To the great lord of the hosts, the great master of yoga,
to Diṇḍi and Muṇḍa, to Caṇḍa, and to the one devoted to the single syllable.
To the one who is imperishable, the nectar of immortality, the ageless, and the deathless;
to the Lord of Creatures, and likewise to the conqueror of Death.
Homage to him who possesses the speed of the wind, to the omniscient and the unconquered,
to him who has many heads and many feet.
O god who wears a crown and earrings, whose arms are like great iron clubs—protect all the gods and the hosts; O god, let there be homage to you!
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus praised him, O Vyāsa, the god then, becoming composed and with palms joined in reverence, uttered the word "Victory! to that high-souled one.
Then the hosts said, "Victory!", then the gods, then the asuras,
then all beings, as well as Brahmā and Śakra.
Then [they sounded] conchs and kettledrums, as well as paṭahas and āḍambaras, flutes and cymbals, and likewise kṛkavās and cow-horns.
The leaders of the hosts, filled with joy and delight, sounded dindimas, flutes, and mṛdaṅga drums on every side.
Sanatkumāra said: That mortal who constantly recites this hymn composed by the gods for Nandīśvara shall go to my world.
Having uttered "Homage to Nandīśvara," whoever should perform this rite while dreaming will have no fear whatsoever from the kings of the Kuṣmāṇḍas.
O Vyāsa, wherever this most highly honored hymn is constantly established,
there is never any fear from the planets.
Those mortals who constantly bow down to Nandīśvara, their senses ever serene and their being purified,
become beloved and most excellent attendants of the God of gods together with the Daughter of the Mountain.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 24.24 ||
Chapter Twenty-Five.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Bhava, the lord of the gods, [beheld] the deities who had arrived there.
Having honored the Maruts, the Lord of the existent and non-existent spoke regarding the matter of the maiden.
The Lord, together with Śakra and the Grandfather, addressed by name those Maruts who possess great speed, great being, and great power. (25.2)
"O you of great strength, you ought to give me that daughter of yours, Suyaśas— fortunate and of divine form— as my daughter-in-law, she who possesses beautiful eyebrows."
The Maruts said: "O Lord of the three worlds, you are the sovereign power over us, over her, and indeed over the entire universe; it does not behove you to make a request. (25.4)
By you alone must these be given and by you received; you are our unsurpassed refuge.
Do not distress us with the request for the dwellings of others.
The illustrious Kaśyapa is our father, and Marīci is our grandfather;
Brahmā is the grandfather of our grandfather, and you are his grandfather as well.
As such, you are our great-grandfather; it does not behove you to treat us as strangers.
Thus addressed by the Maruts, the best of gods,
the Lord of the Gods immediately brought Suyaśā, the daughter of the Maruts.

The Grandfather of the worlds himself was the Hotṛ priest there; Kaśyapa was the Brahman, and Atri likewise sang the Sāman. The two gods Atharvan and Aṅgiras also performed the office of the Brahman priest. (25.8)
Nārada and Parvata, the singer Citrasena, Viśvāvasu and Ruci, as well as Hāhā and Hūhū.
Likewise, Śāliśiras, the renowned Gaṇḍamaṇḍaka, Īti, Indravāha, Yajñavāha, and Dakṣiṇa—
these and other Gandharvas with sweet voices sang. || 25.10 ||
Urvashi, Rambha, Ghritachi, Purvachitti,
Tilottama, Vishvachi, and other auspicious Apsarases,
all highly fortunate, danced a dance most enchanting to the gods.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, such was the incomparable and blameless marriage of that wise Nandin, the chief of the Gaṇas. 25.12.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony, the high-minded Nandin went and paid homage at the feet of the God, the Goddess, and Brahmā;
and the lord of the world, endowed with supreme splendor, also paid homage to Śilāda.
The god said:
"Choose a boon, my son, and this dear daughter-in-law of yours as well;
O child, I grant you a boon together with her, whatever you desire."
Nandin said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, let my devotion to you be firm;
and may you, together with Ambā and the lords of the Gaṇas, always remain well-disposed toward me. (25.15)
O God, O Lord, granter of desires, you ought to unite this father of mine, my progenitor, with your gracious favor.
The God said:
O wise one, I, the Lord of the Ganas, together with Pārvatī, am always well-pleased with you, Nandīśa; now hear these words of mine. 25.17.
He is desired by all, most excellent, endowed with supreme sovereignty,
a great yogi, a mighty archer, and possessed of great strength and prowess.
Be forever invincible and a conqueror, worthy of worship and a worshipper;
wherever I am, there you shall be, and wherever you are, there I shall also be.
And I shall give him Mount Vaibhrāja, which moves at will, is made entirely of gold, filled with divine palaces, and crowded with people;
by means of it, he shall travel through all the worlds as he desires.
And his place shall be on Śrīparvata, where he will be highly honored.
Furthermore, that righteous person who gives up their life at that Bhrigu shall become a leader of the Gaṇas in Vaibhrāja, moving according to his own will.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the highly blessed goddess granted a boon to the son of the mountain;
he said, "May my devotion to you always remain unfailing. (25.23)
Then the daughter of Marut, urged by both of them, replied to them: "Choose indeed a boon according to your desire. || 25.24 ||

"O lords of gods, grantors of thousands of boons, I desire this boon from you both: may my devotion remain fixed upon you and likewise upon my husband; and may my supreme mind be ever constant in righteousness. (25.25)
Sanatkumāra said: Then those two gods, being delighted, spoke thus to that daughter-in-law of excellent complexion: "O lady of pure smiles, it shall be for you exactly as this has been. (25.26)
Then all the Gaṇas, desiring to do what was pleasing to the gods, approached him;
those great beings granted him a boon, and he, who possessed a golden luster, chose it.
My devotion to you and my sovereignty are likewise esteemed;
all of you are under my control, and I am dear to you, and you are dear to me.
The Gaṇas said:
"You are the thinker and the one who approves; you are the goal and the means of arrival. You are the lord of us all, and the sovereign even of the gods. (25.29)
You are the most excellent of the Kuṣmāṇḍas, you are the one of great strength among the Rudras,
and likewise the gatekeeper of the calamities as well as of the Pramathas.
You are indeed considered by us to be of great strength, a great yogi, and our commander;
you are the being, the leader of beings, the guide, and the one who leads beyond.
You are the sovereign of the planets and likewise the wielder of the fierce rod of punishment;
you are the foremost warrior, the slayer of enemies, the hero, and the lord of heaven.
You are indeed possessed of great majesty, the abode of the Milky Ocean,
the sanctuary of the Lord of Recitation (Japyeśvara), and one who is manifested by the Lord of Recitation.
O creator of all beings, granter of boons, worshipped by the givers of boons;
O Lord, Master of Beings, be a granter of boons to us as well. 25.34.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by all the lords of the Gaṇas, the omnipresent Lord Nandīśvara spoke to them as they bowed down: "Tell me, what shall I do for you? (25.35)
Thus addressed, all those leaders of the hosts, who were possessed of great strength and knew the divine nature [of the Lord], spoke to him in the presence of the God of gods.
"You have been made the leader of our host by Lord Śambhu, and you have been consecrated by us as our guide and bestower of dharma. (25.37)
Therefore, being auspicious and gentle, and possessing virtues even amidst those who lack them,
be endowed with patience, purity, and self-restraint, and always do what is pleasing to us.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, he then bowed to all with great reverence;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he then praised the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Nandi said:
Salutations to you all, O beings; salutations likewise to the yogis. Salutations also to those without abodes, and salutations to the lords of yogis.
Salutations to those who move at will and salutations indeed to the fierce ones;
salutations again and again to the Deaths, to the Yamās, and to the Kālas.
Homage to those with golden garlands and to all who possess the nature of phenomena;
homage to you, both to those who are slayers and likewise to those who are not to be slain.
Homage to those clothed in bark and to those clothed in skins;
homage to those with white garments and garlands, and to those with variegated garlands—salutations again and again!

Salutations again and again to those who are running, to those who are rushing, and to those who have set forth; salutations again and again to the sages who are singing and to those who are reciting prayers.
Homage to those in the form of cats, and likewise to crows and cranes;
homage to those in the form of deities, and similarly to the winds.
Homage to the fires and likewise to the waters, and also to the Varunas;
homage to those who have the form of the Lord of Wealth, and indeed to those of every form.
Salutations to those with bellies for mouths and to those with mouths on every side;
salutations to those of dwarfish form and to those of beautiful forms.
Salutations again and again to you who nourish the gods, asuras, and humans;
salutations to you all beings, and salutations to you from every side, O auspicious ones!
Homage be to you, O planets, and likewise homage to you, O liberations;
homage be to you, O auspicious ones, and likewise to you, O inauspicious ones.
May these leaders of the hosts be gentle and auspicious toward me.

Thus praised with auspicious words, may the Gaṇapatis of great strength, the destroyers of the enemies of the gods, grant me incomparable happiness; may they, the bestowers of bliss, grant me strength, heroism, and steadfastness in battle.

May the lords of the gods grant me imperishable austerity, an incomparable state, as well as fame, the highest position, and abundance of eternal righteousness; and may they likewise grant me all that is desired by my mind, as well as unsurpassed prosperity.
Sanatkumāra said: He who constantly studies these two hymns of praise to the lords of the hosts of Nandins is liberated from all sins, as if by the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice.
By reciting prayers during the evening twilight, one abandons the sin committed during the day;
by reciting them during the morning twilight, one likewise casts off all that was done throughout the night.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those leaders of the Gaṇas, having been thus praised by that wise one,
bowed down to the bull-bannered Lord and departed as they were dismissed.

Then the gods and all the worlds departed; thereafter, the high-minded Lord himself, having created the abode of Nandīśvara and bestowed it upon him, went together with the Goddess to his own eternal realm, as he had desired.
Whoever reads or causes others to hear this account of Nandin’s birth, as well as his granting of boons, his consecration, and his marriage—
that Brāhmaṇa, upon death, attains the same world as Nandīśvara.

But whoever, with a disciplined mind and full of devotion toward Bhava, should recite this entire [work] while bowing down, even he, having departed for the next world, shall become like Nandi, a follower of mine. (25.59)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 25.25 ||
Chapter Twenty-Six.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, Nandīśvara was born as an attendant.
He was consecrated to the office of general of the God of Gods.
Vyāsa said:
Then the Blessed One, the granter of desires, was seated there together with the Goddess.
What did Mahādeva do then? This I wish to know. 26.2.
Sanatkumāra said: On a peak of the Himavat, the Blessed Lord Śarva, desiring to please the Goddess,
repeatedly produced laughter through his variously shaped attendants.
And the one who has the crescent moon as his forehead mark delighted and sported with the goddess,
together with those auspicious ones of great majesty, who were omniscient and capable of assuming any form at will.
Then the goddess Parameśvarī approached her mother,
who was seated upon a bright, golden throne that was most highly honored.
Then, seeing the goddess Satī arrived in her beautiful form,
he offered the blameless lady a seat of great value.
And as she sat there, Menā, the beloved wife of Himavat, said to her:
"O daughter of auspicious eyes, it has been a long time since your arrival today;
for you play together with your husband using the toys of the poor."
Those who were once poor and likewise without refuge—
both of them now sport in this manner, O auspicious lady, just as your husband does.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by her mother, she became somewhat dejected in mind;
filled with great indignation, she said nothing at all to her. (26.9)
Having been dismissed by her mother, she then went and spoke to the God:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, I will not dwell here on this mountain;
O Lord of the world, O you of great splendor, choose another abode for me."
The god said: "O Goddess, though you were constantly urged by me for the sake of a dwelling, O Sovereign Lady, you never once chose to take up residence elsewhere."
"Now, O beautiful lady, why do you yourself seek to dwell elsewhere? Tell me that, O goddess of pure smiles. (26.12)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, today I went to the home of my high-souled father;
and there, in a secluded place, I beheld my mother, the creator of the worlds. (26.13)
Having honored me with a seat and other offerings, she spoke to me thus:
"O Umā, O auspicious one, your husband always plays with the toys of the poor;
for the play of the gods is not of such a kind. (26.14)
O Mahādeva, O Bull-bannered One, that you indeed take delight with various auspicious attendants is truly disagreeable to me and my mother.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord, the Master, laughing, spoke to the Goddess in order to make her laugh: "It is even so; there is no doubt. Why then did anger arise in you? (26.16)
Clad in a hide or indeed naked, dwelling in cremation grounds,
homeless in the forests and in mountain caves,
I wander surrounded by naked hosts, O lotus-eyed one.
"Do not be angry, O Goddess; your mother spoke the truth to you. For there is no kinsman equal to a mother for living beings, O beautiful one. (26.18)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the foremost of gods, I have no concern whatsoever with my kinsmen.
O Mahādeva, act in such a way that we may dwell elsewhere. (26.19)
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the Goddess, the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign and Master,
spoke to the leader of the Gaṇas standing at his side, the renowned one named Nikumbha.
"O Nikumbha, lord of the Gaṇas, go to the auspicious Vārāṇasī and make it empty by means of stratagem alone, O mighty-armed one, and not by force."
There dwells the powerful King Divodāsa, who is righteous, devoted to me, a great yogi, and possessed of great strength. (26.22)
Therefore, you should act in such a way that you do not offend him;
for it is through his offense alone that Vārāṇasī would become desolate.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, the radiant Nikumbha, the best of the Gaṇas, bowed with joined palms and a joyful countenance, and spoke to the God. || 26.24 ||
"I shall do so, O Lord of Gods, that indeed that lord of men shall become a transgressor, you shall be satisfied, and Vārāṇasī itself shall become empty; of this there is no doubt. (26.25)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus and bowing his head to Hara, that lord Nikumbha departed for the holy city of Vārāṇasī, which is renowned throughout the worlds.
There, that Gaṇa granted an audience in a dream to Maṇḍūkākṣa the barber and then revealed his own true form to him.
Nikumbha said:
"O Maṇḍūkākṣa, I am Nikumbha, the leader of the Gaṇas and the destroyer of grief. I have come here to bestow grace upon you; do exactly what I tell you. (26.28)
"Establish my abode at the gateway of Divodāsa’s palace, and install there an auspicious image that resembles my own form. (26.29)
I shall grant you wealth, as well as sons and good fortune; moreover, I shall grant you universal popularity and, finally, the highest state.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Nikumbha, the barber then went to King Divodāsa—who was like Indra or Vaivasvata—and spoke to him. (26.31)
The barber said:
"O Master, I shall fashion a Gaṇapālaya at your house door;
I will install Gaṇeśa there, and you ought to grant me permission for this. (26.32)
"So be it," he replied; and having received permission, he then constructed a dwelling there and installed an image exactly as he had seen it.
The great-souled one performed a magnificent and beautiful worship for Gaṇeśa, and he accepted it.
By that ritual act, the Lord bestowed upon him whatever wealth he desired,
as well as cattle, sons, and good fortune.
But having observed that incomparable prosperity of the barber,
the world, desiring to please him, indeed offered him honor.

Some undertook journeys, while others observed fasts; likewise, some performed fire-sacrifices and recitations, others offered worship seeking boons; and still others presented offerings, while others engaged in song and dance.
To them who had thus approached him, the highly illustrious Nikumbha granted all the desires that each of them wished for.
O Vyāsa, having thus recognized him as the granter of desires, King Divodāsa then spoke to his queen once, out of a longing for a son.
"O Goddess, he grants all desires to those who seek them;
you too should propitiate this Lord of the Gaṇas for the sake of offspring."
Having been addressed thus, that beautiful woman then went and approached Gaṇeśa, and said: "O Blessed One, O God, O Lord, I am childless."
"I shall observe a fast for the propitiation of you, O God;
I will not eat until a boon has been granted to me by you, O Lord. (26.42)
"And when a son is born, O Lord of Herds, I shall give ten times ten hundreds of milch-cows to the twice-born on your account."
Likewise, with a thousand jars of curd, of clarified butter,
of milk, and of the five products of the cow, I shall perform your ceremonial bath.
"When a son is born to you, I shall undoubtedly feed a hundred thousand well-honored brahmins before him. (26.45)
The king will grant you many villages as well as female slaves;
O Lord, he will always perform sacrifices and offer you worship.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to him, O Vyāsa, she remained established in her observance;
fasting, she then performed a great worship for him. (26.47)
To her who was standing thus, that god, the lord of the Gaṇas, said:
"Arise; you have no son; do not indulge in vain grief."
Thus, though she was repeatedly exhorted by that high-souled Gaṇeśa Nikumbha, she desisted from her vow.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the queen herself, O King, that lord of men remained constantly observant of his vows before Gaṇeśa. (26.51)
Nikumbha spoke also to that king who was established in his vow:
"Do not remain here in vain, O King; I will not give you a son. (26.52)
Thus addressed by Nikumbha, that mighty lord of kings,
his eyes red with rage, rose up and spoke to the lord of the Gaṇas.
The king said:
"Whether you are a Gaṇa, a Piśāca, a Bhūta, or even a Rākṣasa, you are ungrateful; of this there is no doubt. You do not deserve worship here. (26.54)
"He was honored by the citizens at my very own house door, and he resides within my kingdom; yet you do not grant me a son. (26.55)
Therefore, you are not worthy of worship; instead, you deserve punishment from me, for you are cruel, arrogant, harsh, and filled with envy.
Then he caused his dwelling to be broken up by the leaders of elephant herds;
he quickly demolished the sacrificial altar and set ablaze the radiant image.
The lord Nikumbha, having achieved his purpose, remained stationed in the sky and spoke to Divodāsa as if burning him with his splendor.
The gods grant whatever desired boon one wishes;
if that was not granted, what cause for anger did you have in that matter? (26.59)
"Since you have destroyed my home, though I am one who has done you no harm,
therefore your city shall remain desolate for a thousand years."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus spoken to the king, the self-possessed Nikumbha,
having made his report to the Lord of the Gods, stood by the side of the Master.
And the king, because of his words which were both true and meaningful,
was overcome with great shame and then returned to his palace.
Then, by that curse, the city of Vārāṇasī quickly became empty, purified, and frequented by deer.
But perceiving that it was empty, the wielder of the Pināka bow, endowed with great splendor, arrived there together with the Goddess, his attendants, and Nandin.
There, the god mentally fashioned a celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, possessing incomparable qualities.
My wisdom does not suffice to describe that in its entirety;
for it can only be said that its qualities are beyond all comparison.
The Lord created a glorious garden that was far superior to those delightful celestial gardens, such as Nandana and others.
In that celestial chariot, endowed with every supernatural power and beyond the reach of words, the goddess— the daughter of the King of Mountains—
rejoiced with eyes like blooming blue lotuses, and she no longer remembered her mother’s words.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The twenty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, while the mountain-born [Pārvatī] and the bull-bannered [Śiva] were seated comfortably there, [the following occurred].
Upon a divine golden seat, adorned with various jewels.
Then the goddess, the daughter of Acala, seated comfortably during the night,
the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, spoke to her husband, the lord of all the worlds.
O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, adorned with the crescent moon as your ornament,
O Lord, bestower of honor, tell this to me which I ask of you.
O Lord of Gods, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, what fruit do those obtain who perform any act for you with a specific result in mind? (27.4)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Umā, the trident-bearing god whose banner is the bull, the God of gods, being composed, spoke of all that is auspicious and inauspicious. (27.5)
Vyāsa said: When the imperishable Lord, that deity of great asceticism, was asked out of affection by the Goddess, what did he, being well-pleased, then relate?
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, in former times I too questioned the lord Nandīśvara;
O Brahmin, I shall relate to you exactly what he told me. 27.7.
I, being undistracted, questioned the highly fortunate Gaṇeśāna, who possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, the immensely radiant Nandīśvara.
O best of the Gaṇas, tell me exactly as it happened that which was previously spoken by Īśa to the Goddess; for my curiosity is indeed great. (27.9)
Nandīśvara said:
Listen, O great sage, as I shall declare to you that which was spoken of old by the God of gods to Pārvatī for your benefit. 27.10.
The God said:
Listen, O lady of virtuous vows, to that which you ask me;
for the benefit of my devotees, O Goddess, I shall answer what you have asked. 27.11.
O goddess, O blameless one, for whoever shall build a bright palace for me,
I grant him an imperishable home in the city of Śiva, as vast as Arjuna.
And whoever shall establish my linga according to the prescribed injunctions as described,
he shall always move together with me, endowed with the eightfold supernatural powers.
To whoever shall give me even a single tuṭi of gold, or even much more,
I shall grant an excellent dwelling upon the peak of the Himavat.
"To whoever would give me cows or gold with a joyful heart for my pleasure, to him I shall grant worlds endowed with all desires. (27.15)
Whoever should give a bull, whether white or even blue,
shall deliver twenty-one generations of both his lineages across [the ocean of rebirth].
Or even he who would give me land the size of two cow-hides,
having reached my city, rejoices together with the lords of the Gaṇas.
Whoever should give me the fruit of their own merit previously acquired,
that person obtains infinite fruit and rejoices in heaven.
He who performs my Anuyāna procession on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with a chariot yoked to bulls rejoices in my world.
"O slender-waisted one, he who thinks in his mind, 'I shall worship Hara,' yet is unable to do so because he lacks the necessary materials, [is not at fault]. (27.21)
Purified by that faith and liberated from all sins, he attains my world upon the dissolution of the body; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having bathed, always approaches me at the morning twilight,
becomes a powerful yakṣa, a friend of the king of the yakṣas.
Sweeping is worth five hundred, and plastering is worth a thousand;
perfumes are worth ten thousand, and worship is said to be infinite.
There should be one hundred and eight applications of oil for anointing, three hundred for the ritual bathing,
five hundred portions of scented water, and likewise five hundred of the five products of the cow.
"O Goddess, I forgive him here even for his many offenses;
this secret sprinkling with ashes, which leads to infinity, is what I desire."
Ten thousand units of agaru, six thousand of sandalwood,
and fourteen thousand of kālāgaru are prescribed for incense.
Unbroken grains of rice and barley, two hundred measures of śāli rice, and guggulu resin for endless [offerings], well-perfumed with clarified butter, are prescribed.
O Goddess, he who burns two thousand palas of mahiṣākṣa for a full year shall become equal to Nandin unto me.
One who gives an incalculable vessel of ghee gains eternal reward both in this world and after death;
he gratifies all the ancestors and rejoices in a celestial chariot.
And he who gives an umbrella likewise shines with splendor in heaven.
O blameless one, on both the thirteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight, he who observes a fast and worships me with devotion and offerings— to him,
O Goddess, being well-pleased, I shall grant my own eternal realm.
"Whoever worships me always with devotion using red and yellow garments as well as various kinds of flowers, him I regard as my own son."
And to that mortal who, remaining steadfast, maintains a lamp for a single night,
I grant the fruit of all sacrifices as well as prosperity itself.
All the worlds, including both the ignorant and the learned, are deluded by me alone;
blinded by passion and thickened by darkness, they do not perceive me.
Those who are meditative, ever-disciplined, devoted to the true Dharma,
one-pointed in mind, and self-controlled— they behold me at all times.
Those who are my devotees and are always proficient in Sāṃkhya and Yoga perceive everything within me, and by means of yoga, they perceive me everywhere.
Having transcended the three worlds as well as the world of Brahmā,
they go to my own realm, having pierced through the darkness that is so difficult to pierce.
I cannot be seen even by hosts of sages endowed with ascetic power;
O Goddess, only the wise who are meditative and eternally disciplined behold me.
"O fair-hipped one, whatever sacred fords and abodes of deities exist in the worlds, they are always present at my feet. (27.42)
With his mind perpetually surrendered to me and thus permeated by my nature,
he is liberated from all sins through my very power alone.
O Goddess, whatever way a man may live, if he should always remember me, that doer shall never at any time be joined with impurity.
Even if he is a person of evil nature in every respect, whoever constantly worships me with a mind fixed on knowledge shall become equal to my own self.
And whoever always worships me with the sixfold yoga shall quickly enter into me; there is no doubt about this.
Even one who delights in the company of the wicked, who is born of a low womb, and who is always possessed of sinful deeds— even such a person,
O Goddess, whose mind is fixed on me and who offers himself to me, goes to an inconceivable state.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, the auspicious goddess again addressed her husband, the lord of vows.
Worshipped with hundreds of offerings, she asked about the fruit connected with her vow.
O Lord of the three worlds, O Maheśvara, tell me what the fruit of vows is—whether it be small or great—and what kind of vow it must be. (28.2)
The god said:
O auspicious and blameless lady, listen to what kind of vow has been prescribed, whether it yields great fruit or even small fruit. (28.3)
Pure on both the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnights,
for one year he remained without food, peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered his senses.
Whatever fruit belongs to those who perform the Sattrayajña sacrifices and who speak the truth and approach their wives in season—
that very fruit he obtains, and he does not see Yama.

He who has taken refuge in me, yet remains on his bed or seat amidst women, addicted to pleasure and devoted to sensual delights—he burns constantly from the tips of his nails to the very marrow. (28.6)
My devotee, endowed with austerity, attains Me alone, O Goddess;
his worlds are imperishable, even if he has been a great evildoer.
O Goddess, that man who always eats from an earthen vessel on the sacred festival days (parvan) obtains the fruit of a three-night fast in a single day and night.
He who, for a full year, eats daily without weariness after having offered [the food] to the ancestors and the gods, shall become the sole ruler upon the earth.
O Goddess, that man who, being self-restrained, does not eat on these days—the ninth, the eighth, the full moon, and the thirteenth—for an entire year; || 28.10 ||
O blameless one, he attains lordship over the Gaṇas without rival;
he becomes beloved by all beings and assumes a divine form. (28.11)
One should offer a śrīvatsa mark made with flour and an auspicious golden fruit;
one should scatter black sesame seeds there, as well as rice and unbroken grains (akṣata),
along with various kinds of fruits of diverse shapes, as available, endowed with flavor.
He indeed rejoices in heaven for sixty-two thousand years,
assuming a divine form, glorious, and always in the company of the deities.
Whoever should give me their own image made of gold,
well-prepared with all kinds of perfumes, juices, and resinous exudations.
On the sides, one should indeed offer yellow orpiment, black agallochum, realgar,
and sandalwood, each worshipped in its respective order.
O Goddess Mattakāśinī, hear from me the fruit of his merit:
he shall be liberated from all diseases and indeed become free from all blemish. (28.17)
Having enjoyed great happiness in heaven for eight hundred million years,
he is born as a happy man in this world and attains me alone.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a woman, whoever should give this Ratnāvalī, shall attain supreme happiness like mine in my world.
Furthermore, by offering white mustard seeds for the purpose of the *argha* oblation, whether in rites for the gods or for the ancestors,
one shall satisfy even the ancestors for thirty thousand years.
He attains the form of all the ṛṣis and all the gods in its fullness;
for a manvantara, he is honored by the daughters of the cowherds in Goloka.
All the gods, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the sages, indeed provide their presence for the arghya offering; know that it has issued forth from them.
This is a supreme secret, O Goddess; he who knows it is a man of great austerity.
By its power, he shall become wealthy and pleasing to behold, endowed with wisdom, beauty, and virtue, for ten million years.
If anyone, rising three times a day, should constantly bathe me with milk,
I shall forgive even a thousand offenses of his.
And whoever should behold that bathing ceremony is liberated from all sins;
he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand recitations of the Mānasa hymn.
He who, being pure, performs the ritual bathing with milk for one year,
attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and constant favor.
The man who, with an undistracted mind, performs an anointing for me with clarified butter,
shall obtain the fruit of two thousand recitations performed mentally.
That best of men shall become worthy of being approached by the gods,
and he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand pieces of gold.
To him who performs the sweeping while observing the vow for a full year,
I grant a beautiful world that is eternal, firm, and auspicious;
O Goddess, even when all worlds perish, there is no destruction for him.
O Goddess, he who, firm in his vows, performs the worship of my linga,
rejoices in heaven for a hundred thousand divine years.
Śaṅkara smells the fragrance of four kinds of flowers:
the arka, the karavīra, the bilva, and the buka.
O Goddess, it is said that for every flower, a gold niṣka is [the value]. 28.31.
Whatever fruit is said to be obtained by giving a thousand arka flowers, that same fruit is indeed obtained by giving a single karavīra flower. (28.32)
Whatever fruit may result from giving a thousand *karavīra* flowers,
that same fruit is said to result from giving a single *padma* flower.
Whatever fruit is obtained from giving a thousand lotuses to me,
that same fruit one obtains by giving a beautiful leaf of the *bilva* tree.
Whatever fruit is traditionally said to be obtained by giving a thousand bilva leaves to me,
one obtains that same fruit by giving a single bukā flower to me.
Whatever fruit is obtained from giving a thousand *buka* flowers to me,
one obtains that same fruit by giving a single *dhuttūraka* flower.
For whoever shall constantly bear my floral remains upon his head—
even a man who is impure, who has violated the bounds of propriety, and who is filled with sin— (he shall attain the highest state).
Self-willed, likewise unapplied, and excluded from the religious observances, he shall fall into a terrible hell and be reborn in the womb of an animal. (28.38)
O observer of great vows, if one who is a celibate student, having become pure, should wear my remains after worship, I shall swiftly destroy his sin. 28.39.
He who, being pure, offers a garland of lamps to me during the month of Kārttika, and at the conclusion of the lamp-offering gratifies the Brāhmaṇas,
attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and shines like the sun. (28.40)
One should offer black sesame seeds together with white mustard seeds;
O Goddess, he who always places these upon my head shall be equal to Nandin unto me.
For those which are called white mustard seeds, as well as those black sesame seeds—all of them consist of you, O Goddess; this secret has been declared by me. (28.42)
The host named Citra rejoices with me;
even when the universal dissolution has arrived and the destruction of the three worlds occurs, he abandons all sufferings and attains me alone. (28.43)
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, I am not as satisfied by being worshipped through an image as I am exceedingly pleased when the *liṅga* is worshipped, O Pārvatī. (28.44)
Whether one is attached to all the senses or joined with all sins, O Goddess, he who worships my Liṅga here goes to heaven. (28.45)
Having abandoned all evils, free from the pairs of opposites, with his sins burnt away,
eating my remnants and offering salutations to me, he attains to me alone.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lady again asked her husband, the Lord of all the worlds: "O God, with what, when your face is blossoming, are you pleased? (28.47)
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all worlds, with a smiling face, spoke these words out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The God said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the truth as it is, by which all living beings in the three worlds who are my devotees, O fair-faced one, attain an auspicious state. (28.49)
Whatever is that supreme secret, all of that resides within you;
for whoever knows it in its true essence is completely liberated from the cycle of existence.
A man should not disclose this secret; rather, rising in the morning with palms joined in reverence, he should always proclaim your name as "the All-enduring One."
And from that recitation, one shall utterly burn away all evil;
having attained fame and renown, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whoever should constantly offer all kinds of garlands upon all the images,
according to the ritual and with the mantra, his meritorious fruit shall be great.
The mantra: "Salutation always to the omnipresent Lord of gods, who consists of all the gods, and to the Blessed One, the secret of secrets. (28.54)
To Soma, the lord of beings, to Bhāvana and to Bhava;
to the one who is all secrets, Svāhā! And to the one whose nature is the secret of the gods.
The mantra consisting of all secrets: *svāhā* to Soma indeed, and *svāhā* to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, and *svāhā* to the powerful god! 28.56.
Whoever should constantly offer flowers with this mantra,
by him a thousand recitations of the mental [mantra] will have been performed.
Then, on the new moon day, being well-composed, he offers his joined palms fully filled with black sesame seeds and mustard seeds, O Pārvatī,
having worshipped according to the rule and as they are available.
And let him speak these words: "O Sūrya" and "mine.
Released from all sins, that man shall go to the heavenly world. (28.59)
And having worshipped me, O Goddess, if one does not satisfy the brahmins, he does not obtain that fruit; indeed, I am not pleased with him. (28.60)
Having honored the twice-born and me, whoever shall proclaim my names on the fourteenth and the eighth days of both fortnights— that person,
O Goddess, shall behold me and shall not go to a base womb.
"O Vāmadeva, O Sudeva, O Hara, O Gupta;
O Lord of Umā, O Blue-throated One, O Peaceful One, O Śrīkaṇṭha, O Lord of the Cow! (28.62)
One should proclaim the secret names: Śarva, Bhīma, Paśupati, Śaṅkara, Ugra, Bhava, and likewise Mahādeva;
by doing so, one is liberated from all sins and is honored by the gods in heaven.
Whoever should explain or read even one of these,
having pierced through the path of the body, attains me alone—
this which has been proclaimed by me with every prostration. (28.64)
O my beloved, he who constantly burns guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter and milk on the new moon day— this is my secret—
he attains the imperishable state by my grace; of this there is no doubt.
And, O Goddess, whoever shall offer to me this supreme secret—
a vessel made of Arka leaves filled with ghee together with honey—
having presented it according to the rules and with devotion, is liberated from all sins.
And, O highly fortunate one, whoever should proclaim these names of mine—even if he dwells in a cremation ground, naked, sleeping on ashes, and firm in his vows—[he shall attain success]. (28.67)
Vāmadeva, the profoundly peaceful, he whose phallus is motionless, the three-eyed,
who delights in the left, the auspicious one, the multiformed, the ender of the ender.
He is the ancient one, invoked by many, the death of death, and the conqueror of the senses;
he is without senses and beyond the senses, abiding in the hearts of all beings.
He is the wheel of saṃsāra, the soul of yoga, the bearer of the skull, and indeed Diṇḍi;
he is Mahādeva, Mahādeva, and Mahādeva.
One who possesses self-restraint should either recite this or listen to it constantly;
upon the dissolution of the body, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas with a mind absorbed in yoga.
Sanatkumāra said: A devoted person should never recite this meritorious [text] to one who is inauspicious, nor to a sinner, nor to a liar, nor ever to one who is devoid of devotion.
It brings wealth, fame, and long life; it increases peace and is auspicious;
it is pure, sanctifying, and the supreme blessing among all blessings.
It should not be heard by everyone, nor should it be given to anyone at all.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Worship of Īśvara," in the Skanda Purāṇa. Chapter Twenty-nine.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus reached their home in Vārāṇasī in due time, what did the two gods, the parents of the world, do thereafter? (29.1)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Blessed Lord spoke to the Goddess, the daughter of Himavat: "O Goddess, let us visit the garden, if it pleases you. (29.2)
The Goddess said:
"So be it, O Lord of Gods, just as you have spoken, O Bull-bannered One;
for I must not go anywhere beyond the garden, O Hara. (29.3)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, the Bull-bannered Lord, together with the Goddess, wandered everywhere in Vārāṇasī out of a desire to see the divine gardens. 29.4.
In that eastern quarter, the god who wields the Pināka bow showed the goddess a garden adorned with various flowers.
It was crowded with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, and *priyaṅgu* trees,
as well as mangoes, along with *bilva*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *nyagrodha*, and *udumbara* trees.
And with fragrant flowers— jasmine, kesara, and ketakī—
as well as lovely, sweet-smelling blossoms frequented by swarms of bees,
the forest was everywhere endowed with splendor, resembling the Vaibhrāja grove.
Having reached that garden, the Lord of the World said to the Queen:
"O beautiful goddess, formerly while I was staying in this place..."
Above, as the cows dwelling in Goloka drank their milk with great speed along with their self-born calves, froth fell upon his head.
Then I beheld those cows standing by the side of Soma;
as they were gazed upon there by me,
those cows then became of many colors, scorched by his splendor and severely afflicted.
"O Goddess, these cows were formerly born of a uniform tawny color;
they did not possess various colors when they were first observed by me. (29.11)
O Daughter of the Mountain, having recognized their capacity to provide refuge, Soma came and took shelter with me alone; accompanied by the cows, he has not abandoned them.
Then, by those cows who were thus afflicted, Brahmā spoke to me:
"O Lord of Gods, worshipped by all the deities, show favor so that Surabhi may not perish instantly through your splendor. (29.13)
Then, O Goddess, I myself established myself in this very place;
I am known as Goprekṣaka, praised by all the deities.
Having gone to Goprekṣeśvara, having seen it and worshipped it,
a person does not meet with misfortune and is liberated from all taints.

Then, while I was pleased with Surabhi, those cows, being scorched, approached this lake and fell into it; having become cooled, they shone forth at that time. From that moment on, it has been called the Kapilāhrada.
"In this matter as well, O Goddess, I myself, known as Vṛṣadhvaja, have established my presence; let him be seen standing here."
Having bathed at this Kapilāhrada-tīrtha with a one-pointed mind and having beheld this Vṛṣadhvaja, a man shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having worshipped me here, even after death one attains residence in the same world;
moreover, upon the dissolution of the body, one obtains the status of a Gaṇa, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
In this very place, moreover, all those cows were milked by Brahmā himself for the sake of the peace of all the worlds; he drew from them the nectar of milk.
From their milk was born this enchanting lake, known as Bhadradoha, a holy and auspicious divine forest. || 29.21 ||
"O Goddess, I have been propitiated in this place by all the gods;
go, O Mistress, to peace. Thereupon, he became Upaśāntaśiva.
Having become established here, I remain in this place; even the sight of me is meritorious. A mortal who beholds me with a disciplined mind shall attain the heavenly world. (29.23)
"Here I was brought and established by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
and having been taken from Brahmā, I was established here once again by Viṣṇu. (29.24)
Then Viṣṇu was addressed by Brahmā, whose mind was filled with agitation:
"Why have you installed this linga which was brought here by me? (29.25)
Viṣṇu spoke again to Brahmā, whose face was filled with anger:
"In former times, my devotion toward the god Rudra was exceedingly great. (29.26)
"By me he has been established; therefore, by that name he shall belong to you. Thus, he shall be known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
Since I am seated here, even upon seeing this Lord of Gods, a man shall go to my world. || 29.27 ||
Furthermore, O auspicious one, Brahmā then installed this linga of mine according to the prescribed rites, endowed with supreme devotion;
I myself am established here as Svarlīneśvara.
Dissolved within myself, who am the supreme cause, the Pradhāna;
therefore, this secret field of mine is remembered as "Svarlīna" (dissolved in its own). 29.29.
Having abandoned the vital breaths here, a man is not born again anywhere;
that is his infinite goal, and it is likewise remembered as the goal of yogins.
In this very place as well, a powerful and arrogant Daitya, a thorn to the gods, was slain by me after I had assumed the form of a tiger. (29.31)
Therefore, he is renowned as Vyāghreśvara; I am always established here.
Having seen this Amareśvara, one does not go to an evil state again.

O auspicious one, those two Daityas, Utpala and Vidala, who were created by Brahmā in the past as arrogant beings to be slain by women, have been killed here by you with a contemptuous kick of the ball;
this mark remains as his sign.
"In the beginning, I came here and remained with the lords of the Gaṇas;
therefore, this is my preeminent station, and its sight is meritorious. (29.34)
Having seen this linga of mine, which is situated at the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna, a mortal no longer grieves; perfected, he is liberated from birth and death.
Indeed, lingas have been established on all sides by all the deities;
having seen them, a mortal who is self-restrained shall become a member of the Gaṇas upon the dissolution of the body.

"Now, because I have come here in person and remained where I am, and because it has not been abandoned by me, this sacred field of Vārāṇasī shall henceforth become the bestower of liberation; therefore, it is called Avimukta. (29.37)
Whatever person shall behold me here as Avimukteśvara,
his destination shall be that of the Gaṇas, wherever he may die;
but having surrendered his vital breaths right here, he shall go to the highest liberation.
Formerly, your father Himavat, the king of mountains,
having recognized this place as dear to me, personally installed this linga.
Behold this place known as Śaileśvara, which stands here;
having seen it, O Goddess, a person shall not follow the path of misfortune. (29.40)
And this river Vārāṇasī is holy, a liberator from sin;
having adorned this sacred field, it has joined with the Jāhnavī.
At this confluence, the supreme Liṅga was established by Brahmā;
let it be seen in the world as renowned by the name Saṃgameśvara. 29.42.
For that pure person who, having bathed at the confluence of the two divine rivers, worships Saṅgameśāna—whence can there be any fear of rebirth for him? (29.43)
This is another vast field, the supreme abode of yogins,
wherein I myself am established, having become manifest; I am renowned as Madhyameśvara by all the gods and asuras.
This is indeed the abode of the perfected ones who observe my vows,
of yogis seeking liberation whose selves have conquered birth and death; having seen this Lord of Madhyama, one does not grieve over rebirth.
And this liṅga has been installed by your son Śukra;
it is named Śukreśvara and is worshipped by all the Siddhas and immortals.
Upon seeing this, a human being would immediately be liberated from all sins;
and having died, that man would not undergo rebirth in the cycle of existence.
Formerly, the Asuras, those thorns of the gods,
having assumed the form of jackals and having obtained a boon from Brahmā, were apprehensive of being killed by a vulture.

O Daughter of the Himavat, because I have slain Jambukeśa, I have become renowned in the world and am worshipped by gods and asuras. By beholding even this Lord of Gods, one shall obtain all desires. (29.49)
Indeed, these were established by the planets, with Venus at their head;
behold these meritorious lingas which grant all desires.
Thus, O Pārvatī, these meritorious abodes of mine within your sacred field have been described to you; now hear this other secret.
This field is proclaimed to extend one krośa in each of the four directions;
know, O lady of beautiful limbs, that it bestows immortality at the time of death for a distance of one yojana.
By beholding [the deity] established at the site of Mahālayagiri and at Kedāra, one attains the status of a Gaṇa; in this sacred field (kṣetra), liberation is attained. || 29.53 ||
Since that liberation is supreme even compared to the station of the Lord of Ganas,
therefore, O auspicious lady, this field known as Avimukta is remembered as the most meritorious, surpassing even Mahālaya and the Middle Kedāra.
In the central region of Kedāra is the place called Mahālaya;
among all my meritorious sites in the world of mortals, this is indeed the most excellent.
Since the worlds were created from this place, this field is auspicious;
because it was never abandoned by me at any time, it therefore became known as Avimukta (the Unreleased).
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga here,
a human being is immediately liberated from sin and released from the bonds of Paśu.
Śaileśa, Saṅgameśa, Svarlīna, Madhyameśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, Goprekṣa, and the one whose banner bears the bull. || 29.58 ||
Having beheld Upaśāntaśiva, who dwells in the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna,
as well as the renowned Śukreśvara, Vyāghreśa, and Jambukeśvara,
a mortal is not born again in this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva gazed upon all the directions;
and when the God of gods, Maheśvara, had finished looking and remained still, [the others did likewise].
Suddenly that entire region became as if ablaze,
with the roar of lightning and thunder, like ten million suns risen at once.
Filled on one side with splendors like those of fire and the sun,
there then appeared the Siddhas of the Pāśupata order, white-hued from their smearing of ashes.
The great-souled lords of yogis, likewise those who observe the sacrificial vows,
and those whose emblems are unmanifest, blazing with the splendor of Śiva-yoga—
many of them approached suddenly and paid homage to Maheśvara.
Having gazed once more upon the Lord of Gods and having fully practiced the yoga of meditation,
they stood with their souls absorbed, as if merging into the Lord.
While they remained thus, that Lord of Umā, the God of gods,
having contemplated his supreme form, became the sovereign Puruṣa.
As the Lord of the World stood there assuming that supreme form,
the Daughter of the Mountain King, her hair standing on end with awe, was unable to behold his body.
Then, having realized that she had been created by him, that Prakṛti, established in her own nature,
assumed the form of Prakṛti through yoga and became the Supreme Self;
thus she was able to behold the body of that Puruṣa, the Supreme Soul.
Then, having brought about the dissolution of the person, all those yogins, whose seeds of worldly existence were burnt away, entered into his heart.
Then, having bestowed grace upon all those perfected ones, the foremost of ascetics,
he again assumed his auspicious body abiding in the form of Nīlalohita.
Seeing him, Śailajā, her hair standing on end with joy, went before his feet and, offering praise, asked: "O Blessed One, who are these? (29.71)
Then the best of gods spoke to that goddess, the daughter of the mountain king:
"By those most excellent twice-born ones who, having taken refuge in my vow, practice yoga here with devotion, [liberation shall be attained] in a single birth. (29.72)
By the power of this sacred field and through my sincere devotion,
I indeed bestow such grace as always grants liberation.
Therefore, this great field of mine is frequented by Brahmā and the other gods,
by the foremost of Brahmins who possess the sacred scriptures, and by perfected ascetics.
Furthermore, O Goddess, on the eighth and the fourteenth days of every month, during both fortnights, at Vārāṇasī, my own abode— 29.75.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, and especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, on all meritorious festival days (parvan), at the equinoxes, and at the solstices; 29.76.
All sacred fords on earth are present in Vārāṇasī,
as well as the holy Gaṅgā flowing northward, which issued from my crest.
O lady of beautiful countenance, listen to those auspicious rivers that flow from your father, the king of mountains, Himavat, and which all approach and honor him from every direction. 29.78.
Kurukṣetra with its hundreds of sacred fords, as well as Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and Prayāga together with Pṛthūdaka—these are present here. (29.79)
The Sandhyā, the Saptarca, all the rivers and lakes,
the seven seas, and all the divine tirthas in their entirety shall come here to the Bhāgīrathī, which flows toward Kāśī, on every auspicious occasion.
O daughter of the Mountain, both me, Avimukteśvara, who am stationed in Kāśī,
and all the meritorious shrines on earth that belong to me,
always enter [this place] upon arriving at every sacred festival (parvan). (29.81)
The liṅga that is at Kedāra, the liṅga that is at Mahālaya, that which is situated at Madhyameśvara, and likewise Paśupatīśvara—[these are the four]. || 29.82 ||
Śaṅkukarṇeśvara and likewise both Gokarṇas,
as well as Drimicaṇḍeśvara and Bhadreśvara.
[He visited] Sthāneśvara, Ekāmra, Kāleśvara, Ajeśvara,
Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, and likewise [the deity] situated at Kārohaṇa.
And whatever other meritorious places exist for me upon the earth,
all of them without exception enter me within the city of Kāśī.
This secret has been proclaimed for all meritorious festival days;
by means of it, even a dying creature attains here the immortal state.
O auspicious lady, by merely seeing me after I have bathed in the Gaṅgā, one obtains a reward equal to the fruits of hundreds of thousands of desired sacrifices;
one attains this instantly—what indeed could be greater than this? (29.87)
"O Goddess, among all the foremost of sacred sites on heaven, on earth, and even upon the mountains, know for certain that there is nothing superior to this in its entirety. (29.88)
This supreme place is eternally frequented by Brahmā, Arka, Vaiśvānara, Śakra, Candra, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Vāyu, together with the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Siddhas. 29.89.
"O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, this place of mine is always secret; this field is exceedingly meritorious.
For those ascetics who have awakened to reality declare that it indeed bestows the fruit of liberation and perfect accomplishment. (29.90)
Those virtuous men who always dwell with devotion in this field— this most secret and holy field of mine, so vast, filled with various trees and creepers, and adorned by the Jāhnavī. || 29.92 ||
Having reached the Bhāgīrathī here in Vārāṇasī, my abode,
one obtains the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess, there is nothing more meritorious than this, nothing more secret than this anywhere,
nothing more auspicious than this, and nothing dearer to me than this.

Having reached this field of mine, frequented by gods and Siddhas, a mortal shall become renowned among all the Suras and Asuras through the power of his meritorious deeds; and upon death, he shall go to that supreme state.
The thirtieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, by what means did Piṅgala attain the status of being a Gaṇa?
And the one of great splendor attained the state of being an eater of food in Vārāṇasī.
"How did Kṣetrapāla come into being, and how did he attain the state of being beloved?
O son of Brahmā, I wish to hear this explained by you. (30.2)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, how that Piṅgala obtained the status of Gaṇeśa, the role of the provider of food for the worlds, and the city of Vārāṇasī as his abode. 30.3.
The illustrious and powerful yakṣa Pūrṇabhadra had a son known as Harikeśa, who was devoted to Brahman and righteous.
From his very birth, he possessed unsurpassed devotion to Śarva;
he was intent upon his blessing, intent upon his salutation, devoted to him, and having him as his supreme goal.
Whether sitting or lying down, walking or standing, eating or even drinking, he meditated only upon Rudra. (30.6)
To him whose mind was thus disciplined, his father Pūrṇabhadra said:
"I do not consider you my son, you who are ill-born and act otherwise. (30.7)
"Indeed, such conduct does not belong to those born of the Yakṣa lineage.
Alas, you Guhyakas are by nature cruel-minded;
you are flesh-eaters, eaters of raw food, and violent by habit, my son. (30.8)
"Do not act thus; such is not the livelihood seen for the high-souled ones.
That very mode of life which was created by the Self-born One is what is praised. (30.9)
Harikeśa said:
This mode of life, created by the Self-born One, is indeed wicked, unpraiseworthy, and always censured by the virtuous; it should be abandoned, were it not for our own [circumstances].
Therefore, householders should not perform the duties belonging to other stages of life (āśramas).
Having abandoned the human state through various actions,
let them not seek divinity, but rather the very birth as humans.
If their action is ordained as being dependent upon the attainment of that [state], then behold, my own action is likewise ordained; there is no doubt in this matter.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by his son, the powerful Pūrṇabhadra spoke: "Depart quickly; go wherever you please. (30.13)
Then, having departed and abandoned his household relations and kinsmen,
he reached Vārāṇasī and performed most difficult austerities.
Becoming like a pillar, with unblinking eyes, resembling dry wood or a stone,
he remained motionless, having completely restrained the collection of his senses.
Then, as he thus remained incessantly intent upon that and seeking its blessing,
one thousand divine years passed away.
O Vyāsa, he was overrun by an anthill, being devoured by ants with mouths like diamond needles,
and likewise pierced by them.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, with a radiance like that of the *kunda* flower, a conch shell, or the moon, he became entirely a mere skeleton; and the god thought of him thus.
In the meantime, the Goddess addressed Śaṅkara:
"I desire to see this very garden once again at all times. (30.19)
Indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear of the majesty of this sacred field,
since it is so dear to you and because its fruit is supreme.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Lord of the World, the God,
began to explain everything that had been asked according to the proper order.
And Śaṅkara, the lord of the gods, went forth together with Pārvatī;
the god who wields the Pināka bow showed the garden to the goddess.
It was beautified by various kinds of flowering shrubs in full bloom, charming with its bowing clusters of climbing vines,
and surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees laden with blossoms, as well as by thorny *ketaka* trees covered in flowers.
It was densely covered on all sides with fragrant tamāla thickets and bakula trees in full bloom,
as well as forests of aśoka and puṃnāga trees, beautifully blossomed and filled with swarms of bees amidst their gathered flowers.
In some places it resounded with birds smeared with the pollen of full-blown lotuses, uttering sweet and melodious cries;
and with the calls of cranes and swans, and the charming songs of intoxicated gallinules.
In some places it resounded with the cries of ruddy geese, in others it was filled with flocks of water-fowl;
in some places it echoed with the calls of ducks, and in others it was made tumultuous by swarms of intoxicated bees.
It was frequented by female bees intoxicated with honey and adorned with beautiful, fragrant flowers;
in some places it was hidden by well-flowered mango trees and by tilaka trees entwined with creepers.

It was frequented by Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas who sang melodiously; it was attended by throngs of Apsarases who danced incessantly; it was served by various kinds of joyful birds and resounded with the cries of intoxicated Hārītaka flocks.

In some places it was graced by lakes and ponds filled with various kinds of blossoming and beautiful lotuses, where herds of deer had gathered here and there, their minds agitated and cowed by the roar of the king of beasts.
In some places it was dark with dense *nicula* thickets and delightful with blue-throated peacocks;

in some places the creepers were beautiful where they had been bitten by elephants, and in others lovely trees were embraced by climbing vines; in some places it was frequented by the wives of the *kiṃpuruṣas*, moving about languidly in their playful grace.
It was illuminated by numerous celestial temples of the gods, which were adorned with peaks as beautiful as the cooing of pigeons, reaching to the clouds, white and lovely in form,
and possessing smiles in the form of scattered clusters of flowers.
The royal road was graced by reservoirs of water provided with canopies of thousands of blooming blue lotuses and agallochum;
it was filled with birds perched upon shrubs and branches, which were interlaced with various colorful patterns of flowers fallen from the pathways.

With its clear and expansive waters, where lotuses are stirred by the flight of swans, and where certain regions are frequented by deer; it is graced by Aśoka trees whose lofty tips have their branch-ends bent down by the weight of clusters of blue blossoms.
In some places, with flowers scattered and strewn upon the ground,
siddhas were nestled within bowers of flowering atimuktaka creepers,
while the tips of their feet were tossed by the wind carrying heaps of blossoms.
The surface of the ground was strewn with lovely tilakas white as a network of moonbeams, some resembling powdered collyrium, some like coral, and some with the luster of gold. 30.41.

The *puṃnāga* trees resound with the cries of hundreds of birds; the red *aśoka* trees are bent low under the weight of their clusters of blossoms; the vicinity is delightful, with breezes that dispel fatigue; and upon the blooming lotuses, bees sport. (30.42)
