Then the Lord of the World, the sustainer of all the worlds, spoke to the Goddess:
"O Lord, the garden has been shown, endowed with supreme beauty."
But you ought to speak here once more of all the qualities of that field.
Even having heard of the greatness of this field, Avimukta, at that time, I am not yet satiated; therefore, speak further to me.
The God said:
This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine;
it is at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings. (30.46)
In this place, O Goddess, the perfected ones (siddhas) always abide, having taken refuge in my vow;
constantly assuming various outward forms, they desire my world,
practicing the supreme yoga with disciplined minds and conquered senses.
It was crowded with various trees, frequented by diverse birds,
and adorned with lakes rich in lotuses and water-lilies.
In this auspicious place, which is always frequented by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas, a permanent residence pleases me; hear now for what purpose this is so.
With his mind fixed on me, my devotee, and having surrendered all his actions to me,
attains liberation here in this world in a way that he could never attain anywhere else.
This is my divine city, great and more secret than the secret;
Brahmā and others, as well as the perfected ones (siddhas) seeking liberation, know it.
Therefore, this field is dear to me, and here I find my delight.
Because it has not been abandoned by me, nor will it ever be abandoned, this field of mine is therefore known as Avimukta (the Unabandoned). || 30.52 ||
Since liberation is not attained by bathing or by frequenting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara,
that [place] by which it is attained here is therefore superior to them. || 30.53 ||
Liberation may occur either at Prayāga or here, through my acceptance;
for this very place is remembered as even greater than Prayāga, the foremost of sacred sites.
Jaigīṣavya, that man of great austerity who has attained supreme perfection,
[did so] through the majesty of this sacred field and through his devotion to me with a sincere heart.
The cave of Jaigīṣavya is the most excellent, desired as the abode of yogins.
Meditating upon me there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes forth intensely;
one attains the supreme state of absolute liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (30.56)
Liberation, which is difficult to attain anywhere else at any time, is achieved here by sages whose outward signs are unmanifest and who know all philosophical systems. (30.57)
And to them I grant unsurpassed mastery in yoga,
as well as union with my own self and the desired state.
That great yakṣa Kubera, having dedicated all his actions in that manner,
attained the status of a Gaṇeśa, O Goddess, through the service of this sacred field.
And he who shall become Saṃvarta— he too, through devotion to me alone,
O Goddess, having propitiated me right here, shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
The son of Parāśara, the yogi, the seer Vyāsa of great asceticism,
the speaker of dharma and the future establisher of the Vedic order—
he too, O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages shall take delight in this sacred field.
Brahmā together with the celestial sages, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Divākara,
Śakra the king of the gods, and whatever other inhabitants of heaven there may be—
all these high-souled ones wait upon me here, O lady of excellent vows. (30.62)
And other yogins and perfected ones, in hidden forms under the great vow,
having become single-minded, always worship me here.
And by my grace, Alarka shall obtain this city;
and he, having restored it as before, shall cause it to be filled with the four castes.
Having enjoyed this prosperous land, crowded with people, for a very long time, the king,
having surrendered all his life-breaths to me, shall attain me alone.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful limbs, even those who dwell in this sacred field—
whether householders or ascetics— who are my devotees and intent upon me,
shall attain through my grace liberation that is otherwise most difficult to reach.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense-objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma,
if he dies in this field, shall not enter into saṃsāra again.
But those wise ones who are free from possessiveness, established in being, with senses conquered,
observant of vows, and without worldly undertakings— they are everywhere absorbed in me.
Having attained the dissolution of the body, O lady of excellent vows, those wise ones who are free from attachment have indeed gone to the supreme liberation through my grace.
That supreme liberation which a yogi might attain by practicing through thousands of other births, he attains right here, even before death.
O Goddess, this great fruit of this sacred field, Avimukta, has been described by me to you in brief as the supreme secret. 30.71.
"Therefore, O Sovereign Lady, there is no field more secret than this;
those who know yoga and the masters of yoga on earth understand this."
This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme auspiciousness;
this alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the supreme state.
"O Goddess, Vārāṇasī is known as the essence of the three worlds; it is my constant and most beloved," thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The thirtieth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord [created] gardens as well as abodes for himself.
Having thus spoken to the daughter of Himavat, he then moved on once more.
Then he saw that brahmin Jaigīṣavya,
the son of Śataśalāka, whose wealth was his austerity, performing supreme penance.
Having installed the linga of the God of gods, he worshipped it constantly;
lying upon ashes and smeared with ashes, he gratified it with dances and songs. || 30a.3 ||
Purified by recitation, by the sounds of the *vṛṣa* chant, and by austerity, he was pure;
and as he was thus engaged, endowed with supreme devotion— || 30a.4 ||
The Blessed One, approaching suddenly, spoke these words:
"O Jaigīṣavya of great intelligence, behold me with your divine eye. (30a.5)
"I am pleased; I am the giver of boons. Speak what is in your heart.
Thus addressed by the God, he beheld the three-eyed Soma, and bowing his head at the deity's feet, he spoke with supreme joy.

Jaigīṣavya said: Salutations to the one who has accomplished all aims; salutations indeed to the one perfected through yoga. Salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand, and whose abode is the Himavat mountains.
Homage to him who possesses the speed of the wind, who is always to be meditated upon by those engaged in meditation;
homage to Soma, to Hema, and to the wearer of the golden garland.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and homage to him whose senses are tranquil;
to the one who provides assistance in yoga, and to the one who brings about immediate peace.
Homage indeed to the remover of death, and homage to the remover of sorrow;
homage to the bestower of accomplishment, and to the one who grants the accomplishments of the Siddhas.
Homage to the sustainer of all worlds and the lord of all worlds;
homage to the one of fivefold color and the dispeller of saṃsāra.
Homage to him who has transcended saṃsāra and who is the supreme shore beyond the shoreless;
homage indeed to him who is himself the mantra and the mind, and who is truly difficult to comprehend.
Salutations to the Knower of Time and its Parts, who is both possessed of all parts and devoid of parts.
Homage to the one who perfumes reality; homage to the Lord of Pretas.
Homage to the one free from anger, homage to the lord of anger;
homage to weariness, to the weary one, and to the remover of weariness.
Homage to the knower of the essence of knowledge, to the wise one who removes ignorance,
to him who is devoted to austerity and intent upon sovereign power.
Homage to him who is followed by wisdom, who turns back ignorance;
homage to him whose power is all-encompassing, whose mind conforms to all states of being.
Salutations to the one whose path is self-restraint and tranquility, who removes the messengers of death;
salutations to the Lord of Śailādi and to the protector of the hosts of Śailādi.
Homage to the secret of yoga, homage again and again to the giver of yoga!
O Blessed One, O Lord, grant me all my desires with your whole being.
Sanatkumāra said:
Being thus praised with supreme devotion,
he was pleased and, being further gratified, spoke this to him.
The God of Gods said:
He is undecaying and immortal, entirely free from all sorrow;
he is a great yogin of great prowess, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
And by the power of this secret field of mine, which is eternal,
you shall attain the supreme and great eightfold sovereignty in yoga.
O best of the twice-born, you shall become a renowned teacher of yoga;
and whoever worships this Linga fashioned by you with regular discipline [shall likewise attain success].
Having traversed the seven wombs, he shall attain the state of a Lord of Yoga;
O Jaigīṣavya, whatever twice-born man enters this cave and applies himself to yoga [shall do so].
For seven nights, with his mind disciplined, he is liberated from all sins;
after one month, he shall know his former birth and what was studied in a previous life.
By a single night of pure conduct, one delivers one's ancestors;
by three nights, one may deliver even those who have passed away seven generations back.
What more than this shall I give to you today, Jaigīṣavya?
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, this is the desire residing in my mind;
therefore, I desire nothing other than that which is superior to the imperishable yoga."
May you possess constant devotion to Soma, the lord of the Gaṇas,
as well as freedom from pride, forbearance, tranquility, and self-restraint.
Nor would I cause you defeat, nor would I show contempt for your splendor;
O God of great luster, I always desire these boons from you.
The God of gods said:
"These shall be yours, as well as invincibility by yogins;
and whenever you desire, my very appearance shall be before you."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, the son of Parāśara, together with me,
Sananda, and his own retinue, [set out] out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
While the Yakṣa king was performing penance with Maheśvara held in his heart,
the Lord of Gods then went before him to grant a boon.
Then, he beheld the son of Visravas, who had three feet and short arms, thighs, and feet, performing severe austerities.
Having seen him, O Vyāsa, the god then spoke to Kubera, who was blazing with splendor,
purified by asceticism, and reduced to mere skin and bone.
The God of Gods said: "O son of Viśravas, I grant you divine vision. O being of great power, behold Soma and me with your divine eye. (30a.34)
Then, having beheld the Lord of Gods accompanied by Ambā and preceded by Nandin, he prostrated himself; being utterly exhausted, he was unable to rise up properly.
Observing him to be weak and unable to rise, the Lord said, "Arise;
may it be well with you; let your ancient strength return to you. (30a.36)
Then, rising up on his knees, Kubera remained there,
gazing at the goddess with a sidelong glance from his eye.
This is that daughter of the mountain, revered by all the worlds,
the mother of these three worlds, endowed with the power of great yoga.
"Oh, the power of her asceticism! Oh, her radiance! Oh, her strength!
She who has become the wife of the Lord of all the worlds. (30a.39)
Sanatkumāra said:
Observing him whose mind was thus disposed and looking toward Pārvatī,
the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, understood his intent and became enraged.
Enraged, she burned the brilliantly shining left eye of Kubera,
like a flame of fire consuming a parched thicket.
Furthermore, Śubhānanā, whose source was asceticism, set her mind upon the destruction of Kubera; then Hara spoke to her.
"Do not be angry, O Goddess, with this ascetic Yakṣa who is your devotee;
he is illustrious and righteous, and is especially devoted to you."
"O auspicious one, O Great Goddess, he gazed upon you out of curiosity; please show favor to this child of the Giver of Wealth."
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, he looks at me repeatedly out of immodesty;
why does he, standing before me, O God, fail to recognize my virtues? (30a.45)
He who, out of delusion, would attempt to leap over those whose splendors are immeasurable,
would perish with his strength diminished, like a moth that has flown into a fire.
Sanatkumāra said: Having beheld that daughter of the mountain king, the consort of Śaṅkara, thus enraged with her eyes copper-red from anger, he spoke these words to her in a sweet and gentle manner.
I speak to you, O highly blessed one, the source of the world: do not be angry.
By you the entire world was created; you are primordial nature, O Sovereign of the Gods.
"Since he is your son, O Goddess, you ought not to be angry;
especially as he gazes upon his mother, O beautiful one. (30a.49)
"There is no fault on his part, nor is his mind deluded regarding you. Therefore, O Lord of Gods, show favor to Kubera, who has sought refuge in you and bows before you, according to his desire."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the God of gods, that daughter of the mountain king showed favor to him;
being pleased, she spoke this to him.
The Goddess said:
"O sinless Kubera, that transgression of yours has been forgiven by me.
I am pleased; do not again thus overstep the bounds of your splendor."
"As for this eye of yours which I have burnt while you were looking on, let it remain exactly as it is—tawny and radiant. (30a.53)
Marked by this [mark] in the world, you will undoubtedly become renowned everywhere by the name Ekākṣipiṅgala and honored by all. (30a.54)
This conduct of yours, as well as this austerity, shall be imperishable and eternal;
and through my grace, you shall possess supreme good fortune.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess of auspicious countenance then became silent;
thereafter, the Blessed One said to Kubera, "I am the giver of boons."
Then, having been thus addressed by the god, Kubera, with a joyful mind,
praised the god and the goddess, bowing with his head and palms joined in reverence.
Kubera said:
Salutations to the one who holds a spear in his hand and wears an excellent crown;
salutations to the bearer of bracelets and the bearer of the mirror.
Salutations to the one whose every limb is hair; salutations again and again to the one with long hair.
Salutations to the wearer of a girdle; and salutations to the wearer of a sacred grass belt.
Salutations to her who possesses variegated crests; salutations to the wearer of tawny matted locks;
salutations to the embodiment of knowledge; salutations to the sovereign lord of all beings.
Homage to her who bears the name Tārā; homage indeed to her whose chest is like a lion’s.
Homage to her who bears the foremost of jewels; homage to her whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon.
Salutation indeed to Prakṛti, and salutation be to Puruṣa;
salutation indeed to Buddhi, and salutation truly to Ahaṃkāra.
Homage be to Delight and to Bliss, homage again and again;
homage to the Act, to the Action, to the Beginning, and to the Completion.
Homage to the sacrifice, to the mantra, and to the sacrificial fee; homage to the Ṛc, homage to the Sāman and to the Yajus, to the meters, and homage to the hymn of praise. 30a.64.
Homage to the foremost and to the one worthy of sacrifice, homage to Svāhā and to the oblation;
homage to Lakṣmī and to Śrī, and homage to Dharma, the creator.

Salutations to desire and to delight, salutations to him who is dispassionate toward worldly prosperity; salutations to accomplishment, as well as to nourishment, contentment, and patience—salutations again and again.
Salutations to Svadhā, to Kavya, and salutations again to Havya;
salutations to Vedyā, to Vidyā, and salutations to Śarva and Bhakti.
Salutation to Time, to Death, who exists for dissolution and for origination, for maintenance and for wandering in saṃsāra, and for liberation and for final release.
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O God, Lord of the world, together with the Goddess!
O Lord of the past and the future, grant me that which resides in my heart.
Sanatkumāra said: "Whether he be a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or indeed a Kṣatriya, whoever— having risen at dawn— constantly recites this hymn while muttering it [in prayer]," (30a.70).
The Lord of Wealth, being pleased with him, bestows great wealth;
and the blessed Soma, being pleased, grants him his desired goal.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by Kubera, the Lord of the World said, "I am a granter of boons; speak, O son of Viśravas. (30a.72)
Kubera said:
"O Blessed One, may I always receive your grace and possess eternal devotion toward you;
and may I behold you, O Lord—let this be my boon. (30a.73)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having granted all of that with the words "So be it," the Lord Śiva then bestowed upon him eternal friendship with himself.
The God of gods said:
"Take this palanquin yoked with men, which is free from attachment;
O Lord of the worlds, having mounted it, you shall travel through the worlds as you desire."
And take this very divine thunderbolt, characterized by its irresistible nature;
let this weapon be yours, which shall be unbearable to your enemies.
And I shall grant you a weapon;
it shall be known by your name as the Kaubera, which bewilders all embodied beings.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that god, with a gratified soul, bound upon his head his own faultless garland, which possessed a splendor like that of the sun.
The Lord of Umā, being delighted, indeed fastened a beautiful garland of blossoming lotuses around his neck.
Having granted him a full vision of himself and the status of Lord of Wealth,
the blessed Soma then departed for another desired region.
Sanatkumāra said: He who, being composed, should constantly hear or cause others to hear this entire account of Kubera’s boon-granting to Brahmins, [attains the highest state]. || 30a.81 ||
That man who dies is born endowed with wealth, possessed of beauty, accompanied by sons and grandsons, and gifted with noble lineage, knowledge, and strength.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the illustrious goddess, together with Śambhu,
reflected upon the five-crested, auspicious Apsarases who were performing penance.
Lean-limbed, full of devotion, and with their sins burnt away by ascetic penance, they,
their hearts moved by compassion, addressed these words to the God.

"O Lord, I grant these excellent women, who are performing penance, whatever boon they desire; it behoves you to grant me permission for this. Having heard her petition, the Blessed One spoke as follows: || 30a.85 ||
The God of gods said:
"Do so, O illustrious lady, to grant the desired favor to your devotees;
for these are the Vedic Apsarases known as the Pañcacūḍās."
"Having placed you in their hearts, they suffer; O bestower of boons, let a boon be granted to them.
Then, thus urged by the God of gods, Pañcacūḍā approached and spoke these words.
"I am pleased, O Apsarases; behold me directly, you of pure smiles! I shall grant you your desired boons, whatever resides in your hearts."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by Pārvatī, those auspicious Vedic Apsarases, beholding the Goddess, bowed their heads at her feet and prostrated themselves before her. (30a.89)
With eyes filled with tears and dejected, they steadied themselves by their own effort;
placing their joined palms upon their heads, they praised him together in unison.
The Apsarases said: Salutations to Siddhi, salutations to Tuṣṭi; salutations to Kriyā, salutations to Buddhi; salutations to Kīrti, salutations to Satya, and likewise to Ulkā and Iṣṭi. (30a.91)
Salutations to the auspicious Earth, to Śrī, to Lakṣmī; salutations again and again!
Salutations to Sudhā, to Svāhā, to Svadhā, and to Diti! || 30a.92 ||
Homage be to you, O lightning; salutations again and again to Saudāmanī!
Homage and salutations to Sāvitrī, to Gāyatrī, and to the Mother of the Vedas!
Salutation to the Daughter of the Mountain, to Intelligence, and salutation to Memory;
salutation to the Dweller of the Mountains, and repeated salutations to Rudrāṇī.
Salutations to Prakṛti and to Jyotsnā, salutations to Ṛddhi;
salutations to Śobhā and Dīpti, and to the rays of the sun and the planets.
Salutation to Gatyā and Gatī, to Indrāṇī and Muktī;
salutation to Niyatī and Sarit, and to Gaṅgā and Sūti. || 30a.96 ||
Salutations to Hetu and Prīti, and salutations to Karaṇavṛtti;
salutations to Saṃtati and Irā, and salutations to Vṛtti.
Salutations again and again to Vāruṇī, to Śaraṇyā, to Śānti, and to Kānti;
salutations be to you, Kauśikī, and salutations again and again to Kātyāyanī.
Salutations to Saṃnati and salutations again and again to Mahimā;
let there be salutation to you, Aṇimā, and salutations again and again to Laghimā.
I worship you and offer salutations to Śitibāhu and Sṛpti;
let there be salutation to you, Saṃjñā; and salutation to Gīr and Smṛti.
Salutations be unto Sarasvatī; salutations to the tongue and to vision.
Salutations to the slayer of Mahiṣa, and likewise to Śumbha and Niśumbha.

Salutations to her who has a lion-chariot and to the wielder of the trident; salutations again and again. Salutations to the bearer of the mallet and to the one clad in armor; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the wearer of earrings, salutations to the upholder of the world;
salutations to the bearer of the bow and salutations again and again to the wielder of the sword.
Salutation to Picchadhvajinī and to Dhāriṇī and to Paṭṭiśa;
let there be salutation to Bhūtamātṛ and repeated salutations to Skandamātṛ.
To the mother of Viśākha and Śākha, and indeed to Naigameśa;
to the progenitor of all the gods, and to the deity of the forest.
And salutations always to the Noble One; salutations again and again to Śikhaṇḍinī.
Salutations to Nīlaśikhaṇḍinī; salutations again and again to Dīrghaveṇī.
Homage be to the slender-waisted goddess and to Wealth;
homage to Fortitude, homage to Purity, and repeated homage to Fame.
Salutations again and again to her who bestows good fortune upon women and to Dhāriṇī; salutations again and again to Rākā, Anumati, and Sinīvālī.
Salutations to Action, to Faith, and to Intelligence; salutations again and again. Salutations be to Retention and to Discernment; salutations again and again. (30a.109)
Homage be to you for the sake of exclusion; homage to the primordial source of the *vaṣaṭ* call!
Homage to meditative absorption, and likewise to longing and to consciousness! (30a.110)
Homage be to you, Vedanā; homage, repeated homage, to Bṛhadukthī. Homage to Prabhā, to Śuddhā, and homage to Śuci.
Salutations again and again to the consort of Tryambaka and to Vidyā;
salutations again and again to Dīkṣā, to Dakṣiṇā, and to Jvālā. || 30a.112 ||
Salutations again and again to Bhavānī, for the activity of the senses, for the cessation of karmas, and for the revelation of all the Vedas.
Salutations to Durgā, the savior from distress, the sustainer of all embodied beings;
salutations to you, O goddess of all deities; salutations to you, O source of the worlds.
Homage to Śānti, homage to Kānti, and homage to the wife of Hara;
homage be to Aditi, to Dānavī, and repeated homage to Vitānā.
Salutations to Śivā and to Kartrī; salutations again and again to Prabhāvā;
salutations to Mṛkaṇḍvī, to Mārdavāhū, and likewise to Surabhī.
Salutations again and again to Vinatā, to Lakṣmī, and to Surasā;
salutations to you, O Śitikaṇṭhinī, salutations to you always from every side. Being well-disposed toward us, grant us everything that resides within our hearts.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The man or woman who, with a concentrated mind, recites this daily, shall abandon all sin committed during the nights, without exception. (30a.118)
O Vyāsa, he who, being pure and always restrained, recites this while lying down, shall abandon whatever was committed during the day; and when dead, he shall go to a happy state.
And whoever should hear this constantly, or should always cause the twice-born to hear it, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become beloved of Pañcacūḍā.
And that mortal who, while reciting this, should give up his life-breaths so difficult to relinquish,
shall ascend a celestial chariot resplendent like the sun and frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
That man who, being observant of the rules on the lunar day, honors [it] with supreme devotion, shall be liberated from all sins and rejoice for ten million years.

Having worshipped the Goddess, he who recites [this mantra] is liberated from all sins. Merely by reciting it with austerity, when his body is cast off, that devotee becomes an attendant of the Goddess and is glorified in a meritorious world. (30a.123)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by them, the goddess Pañcacūḍā stood in the presence of the God and, with a joyful face, spoke these words.
"Listen, all you Apsarases, to the great fruit of this asceticism,
and also to the fact that you, O beautiful ones, have sought refuge in me with supreme devotion."
By my command, you shall be free from old age and sorrow, with minds eternally joyful, and beloved by all the world.
Speak without hesitation whatever else resides in your hearts;
I shall grant it all to you. Do not delay, O you who are so deeply distressed.
The Pañcacūḍās said:
"O Goddess, it is known to you that all women exist for the sake of men's purposes;
they are our clients as long as the task is not completed."
And once their task is completed, they become as if strangers to us.
Therefore, O Goddess, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us,
O Great Goddess, let all men be under the control of all women.
The Goddess said:
"From this day forward, in all the worlds, men shall always be under the control of all women everywhere, and they shall indeed carry out every task for them."
In the beginning and at the end, let them give gold, cattle, women, and all objects of enjoyment from all [the quarters], remaining entirely submissive in every way.
Even if they commit many various offenses, they will remain dear; moreover, there shall never be any sin.
Having fallen under the sway of women, they will commit improper acts even toward their mother, father, brothers, friends, and even their sons. (30a.133)
Even though they perceive falsehoods, faults, and even deformities,
those men do not run away from them, for their senses have been deluded by my boon.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that wife of the God of gods, the daughter of Himavat, of auspicious countenance, took a garland and began to whirl it about. (30.135)
Laughing, the imperishable lady said to her beloved, "Become a man," as those parts of the rope being whirled about that had been shattered upon the ground [were restored].
Those lotus-eyed women became flowers; he said to them, "In former times you were free from old age and decay. (30a.137)
All of them cause delusion to the world and bind the hearts of men;
having entered the three worlds through their glances, touches, and amorous sports. (30a.138)
You shall bring men under the power of women,
and all men shall always be devoted to you.
And by my power, the conduct of all women shall become auspicious, for the sake of men’s attainment of sexual enjoyment and for the sake of women’s own pleasure. (30a.140)
The auspicious rites and bodily refinements, both divine and human,
assumed many forms and entered into all the women.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus created those goddesses and then dismissed them,
he said to the Apsarases, "Tell me, what more shall I do for you?"
With their minds satisfied, they said, "O Vyāsa, may we indeed become the necessary [provisions] for gods, humans, and even for Rākṣasas.
Then the goddess said to them, "In this world, you shall be so. (30a.143)
Then the Lord Parameśvara, together with the Goddess, Nandin,
and all his attendants, the powerful master, entered his own abode.
Falling upon the eyes of Bhaga, the remover of the pride of the Daityas, a mass of frost to the lotuses of the gods, the extinguisher of the fire of the sacrifice of Kama,
traveling upon the bull of the clouds, the ender of all suffering, whose banner is the bull in battle— the Moon-crested Lord departed.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to Jaigīṣavya, Dhana, and Pañcadūḍha," in the *Vārāṇasī-avalokana* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, by what means did Piṅgala attain the status of being a Gaṇa?
And the one of great splendor attained the state of a consumer of food in Vārāṇasī.
"How did Kṣetrapāla come into being, and how did he attain the state of being beloved?
O son of Brahmā, I wish to hear this explained by you."
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa, how that Piṅgala obtained the status of Gaṇeśa,
the role of provider of food for the worlds, and the station of Vārāṇasī.
The illustrious son of Pūrṇabhadra was a powerful Yakṣa known as Harikeśa; he was devoted to Brahman and righteous.
From his very birth, he possessed unsurpassed devotion toward Bhava;
he was intent upon him, offered salutations to him, was established in him, and had him as his supreme goal.
Whether sitting or lying down, walking or standing,
while eating or even drinking, he meditated only upon Rudra.
To him whose mind was thus disciplined, his father Pūrṇabhadra said:
"I do not consider you my son, you who were born ill-fated and act otherwise."
For this is not the conduct of those born into the Yakṣa lineage;
alas, you Guhyakas are indeed cruel-hearted by nature!

"O son, do not act thus; for those who eat raw flesh, those who eat anything whatsoever, and those whose nature is violence—such a livelihood was never seen among the high-souled ones. That very livelihood which was ordained by the Self-existent One (Svayambhū) is what is praised."
Harikeśa said:
"Even though it was created by the Self-Existent One, this livelihood is unpraiseworthy and always censured by the virtuous;
yet it must not be abandoned if it is our only means of subsistence."
Therefore, householders should not perform the duties belonging to other stages of life;
indeed, they should abandon their human state through various such actions.
May they not lose their divinity nor their human birth;
yet, if the karma ordained for them is bound to lead to that attainment,
then behold, my own karma is likewise ordained— of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by his son, the powerful Pūrṇabhadra said, "Depart quickly; go wherever you please."
Then, having departed and abandoned his household relatives and kinsmen,
he reached Vārāṇasī and performed a very difficult penance.
Having completely restrained the collection of his senses, he stood motionless, like a pillar, unblinking, resembling dry wood or stone.
Then, as he remained thus incessantly devoted to that and seeking its blessing,
one thousand divine years passed away.
O Vyāsa, he was overrun by an anthill, being devoured by ants with mouths like diamond needles,
and pierced in the very same way.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, and possessing the luster of a kunda flower, a conch shell, or the moon, he became entirely reduced to bone; and the god thought thus.
In the meantime, the Goddess addressed Śaṅkara:
"I wish to see this very garden again at all times. (30b.19)
Indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear of the majesty of this sacred field,
since it is dear to you and because its fruit is supreme.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Lord of the World, the God,
began to relate everything that had been asked according to the proper order.
And Śaṅkara, the lord of the gods, went forth together with Pārvatī;
the god who wields the Pināka bow showed the garden to the goddess.
It was beautified by various kinds of flowering shrubs in full bloom, lovely and bent down by the spreading of creepers;
it was surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees with burgeoning flowers, and by *ketaka* trees covered in thorns and in full flower.
It was densely covered everywhere with fragrant tamāla thickets and bakula trees in full bloom,
as well as forests of aśoka and puṃnāga trees in splendid flower, their clusters of blossoms swarming with swarms of bees.
In some places it resounded with birds smeared with the pollen of full-blown lotuses, uttering sweet and melodious cries;
and with cranes, swans, and water-fowl, as well as the charming calls of intoxicated gallinules.
In some places it resounded with the cries of ruddy geese; in some places it was joined by flocks of *kādamba* birds;
in some places it was made resonant by the calls of *kāraṇḍava* ducks; and in some places it was filled with swarms of intoxicated bees.
It was frequented by female bees intoxicated with honey and adorned with beautiful, fragrant flowers;
in some places it was hidden by well-flowered mango trees and by tilaka trees entwined with creepers.

It was frequented by Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas who sang melodiously; it was attended by throngs of Apsarases who danced incessantly; it was served by various kinds of joyful birds and resounded with the cries of intoxicated Hārītaka flocks.

In some places it was graced by lakes and ponds filled with various kinds of blossoming and beautiful lotuses, while in other places it was adorned by herds of deer who had gathered in groups, their minds agitated and bowed by the roar of the king of beasts.
Delightful with blue-throated peacocks hidden in the dense *nicula* thickets, charming with the songs of flocks of birds intoxicated with passion,
and filled with intoxicated bees clinging to the branches of flowering trees.
Its branches, whose extremities were adorned with the beauty of fresh young shoots.
In some places, the lovely creepers were bitten by elephants; in others, beautiful trees were embraced by climbing vines;
and in other spots, it was frequented by the wives of the kinnaras, who moved with the languid grace of amorous play.

It was illuminated by numerous celestial temples of the gods, which were adorned with many beautiful peaks that scraped the clouds and were lovely with the cooing of pigeons; they possessed white and enchanting forms, and their secluded smiles were the clusters of flowers strewn about them.
The royal road was graced by reservoirs of water covered with canopies of thousands of blooming blue and white lotuses;
it was lined with shrubs and branches, and filled with birds whose variegated plumage resembled the scattered flowers along the pathways.
It was illuminated by lovely *aśoka* trees with lofty tops, whose branch tips were bent down by the weight of clusters of blue flowers,
producing pleasure for the ear through the songs of swarms of intoxicated bees;
at night, it attained a state of oneness with the blossoming *tilaka* trees, which shared the radiance of the moon.
Where the tips of the darbha grass shoots had been grazed by herds of deer who were sleeping, waking, standing, and moving within the shadows.
Its vast waters were pure, with lotuses stirred by the wind from the wings of swans;
its shores were filled with dancing peacocks amidst groves of blossoming plantain trees;
and in some places, patches of earth were colored by the moon-like feathers of peacocks fallen there.
In every region, there were flocks of intoxicated hārīta birds, hidden away and joyfully sporting.
In some places its regions were frequented by deer, in others it was covered with various heaps of flowers,
and in yet other places it was graced by joyful kinnara maidens.
[He saw] a grove of trees [filled] with intoxicated women singing most sweetly.
In some places, the trees were surrounded by the dwellings of sages, where flowers were strewn upon them from above;
in other places, they were vast and laden with fruit from the very roots.
It was filled with tall jackfruit trees.
It was delightful with the sound of golden anklets from the wives of the Siddhas dwelling in bowers of flowering Atimuktaka creepers,
and bees were clinging to the lovely clusters of blossoms on the Priyaṅgu trees.
The *kadamba* flowers, copper-hued and variegated by swarms of bees.
Where the tips of the trees were shaken by the wind carrying heaps of flowers,
where thickets of bamboo were shattered at their base by the gods,
and where herds of frightened does had fled into the interior of the shrubs.
Bestower of freedom from rebirth upon embodied beings who possess discernment.
With lovely tilaka trees white as a network of moonbeams,
with aśoka trees resembling vermilion, saffron, and safflower,
and with karṇikāra trees equal to refined gold;
It was covered with heaps of flowers by its very broad branches.
In some places the ground was strewn with flowers resembling powdered collyrium, in some places like coral, and in other places like gold.
With hundreds of birds warbling among the *puṃnāga* trees, bent low under the weight of clusters of red *aśoka* blossoms,
its borders delightful, its breezes dispelling fatigue, and with bees sporting among the full-blown lotuses— (30b.42)
Then the Lord of the World, the sustainer of all the universe,
together with the daughter of the snowy-peaked mountain and his beloved lords of the Gaṇas,
[reached] that place abounding in various vast trees and filled with intoxicated, joyful cuckoos.
He showed the queen an exceedingly beautiful grove.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the garden has been shown to me, endowed with supreme beauty;
however, you ought to speak here once more concerning all the hosts of the sacred field."
Having heard of the greatness of this field, Avimukta, at that time, I am indeed not yet satiated; therefore, speak further to me.
The God of gods said:
"This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine;
it is for all living beings at all times the cause of liberation."
In this place, O Goddess, the perfected ones (siddhas) always abide by my vow;
constantly assuming various outward marks, they ever desire my world.
With disciplined minds and conquered senses, they practice the supreme yoga in that place filled with various trees and creepers and frequented by diverse birds.
It was beautifully adorned with lakes abounding in lotuses and water-lilies,
and was a auspicious place constantly frequented by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas.
I am pleased with my dwelling here; hear now the reason for this:
he who has me as his mind, who is devoted to me, and who has offered all his actions to me.
Just as one attains liberation here [in this world], it is not so anywhere else;
for those who are intent on recitation and meditation, and whose minds are devoted to knowledge.
And for those men in Vārāṇasī who are struck by darkness and delusion,
Maheśvara himself [comes] at the very moment of their departure from this world.
He bestows the saving Brahman by which one becomes absorbed in That;
such is my divine city, great and more secret than the secret.
Brahmā and the others, as well as the perfected ones (siddhas) who seek liberation, know this;
therefore, this field is dear to me, because here my delight lies.
"Because it has not been abandoned by me, nor will it ever be abandoned, this is my field; therefore, it is known as 'Avimukta' (the Unreleased)."
For liberation is not attained merely by bathing or by frequenting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara.
Since liberation is attained here by this means, it is therefore superior;
whether one attains mokṣa at Prayāga or here, it is through my acceptance [of them].
This very place is remembered as even greater than Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords;
it is here that Jaigīṣavya, the man of great asceticism, attained supreme perfection.
Due to the majesty of this sacred field and my own heartfelt devotion,
the cave of Jaigīṣavya is held to be the most beloved abode of yogins.
For me, meditating there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes intensely;
I attain the supreme state of liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Here, the great ascetic Mārkaṇḍeya attained supreme perfection,
and likewise the Bālakhilyas achieved success in this most difficult-to-attain sacred field.
In this most rare field, there dwell the perfected ones of the lineages of Atri and Bhṛgu—
sages whose outward signs are unmanifest, yet who are knowers of all established doctrines.
In this place liberation is attained, which is difficult to find anywhere else at any time;
and to them I bestow unsurpassed mastery over yoga.
That great-souled Kubera, having dedicated all his actions to him, desired union with the Self as well as that very station.
Indeed, by the mere cultivation of that field, he attained the status of Lord of Wealth.
O Goddess, having worshipped me right here, the yogi Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, the seer of great asceticism, shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
He shall be my devotee and a promoter of the Vedic tradition;
O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages will also take delight in this sacred field.
Brahmā also, together with the sages, as well as Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Divākara, Śakra the king of the gods, and other inhabitants of heaven.
The high-souled ones worship the Lord of All here, O lady of virtuous vows;
having become single-minded, they always worship me alone.
And by my grace, Ālarka shall regain this city;
having restored it as before, he shall once more be filled with the four social orders.
Having enjoyed that prosperous land filled with people for a very long time, he,
having surrendered all his life-breaths to me, will attain me alone.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful limbs, even those dwelling in the sacred field— whether householders or renunciants— who are my devotees and intent upon me, [shall attain liberation].
By my grace, even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in dharma shall attain liberation, which is otherwise most difficult to reach.
Even one who dies here in this field shall not enter saṃsāra again—
those wise ones who are free from the sense of "mine," perfected, and have conquered their senses.
Established in their vows and remaining steadfast, they have been meditated upon by me on all sides;
having attained the dissolution of the body, these wise ones are freed from rebirth.
O you of excellent vows, when I am propitiated, they shall attain supreme liberation;
whereas one who practices yoga for thousands of future births might eventually reach it,
here in this very life, upon death, he attains supreme liberation.

I am not one who slays a Brahmin, a cow, or violates the teacher’s bed, nor one who lives by theft; rather, I am one whose own conduct is restrained and whose grief is liberated from the firm bonds of worldly existence.
The world is approaching my city, Vārāṇasī.
O Goddess, this great fruit of this sacred field, Avimukta, has been described by me to you in brief as the supreme secret.
O Sovereign Goddess, there is no secret more supreme than this, which has been established;
those on earth who know yoga and are devoted to yoga understand this.
This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme auspiciousness;
this alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the supreme state.
But Vārāṇasī, O daughter of the mountain king, is my delightful city, the very essence of the three worlds,
where even those who have committed various evil deeds, once they have arrived, [are purified].
Through the destruction of evil, those free from passion attain liberation by means of sacred revelation.
If any man should somehow come to the city of Vārāṇasī,
one should employ such means that he would not depart from there again.
If one desires a fruitful birth, who else would seek such fruitless [ends]?
If one desires the supreme state, one should cast off the body in the city of Kāśī.
O Goddess, this is known as my most beloved sacred field (*kṣetra*), filled with various trees and shrubs and blossoming with flowers at will;
embodied beings who die here attain the supreme state.
There is no doubt that this very state is called liberation, even Śivatā itself. || 30b.84 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vārāṇasī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Sanatkumāra said:
At that very time, O Vyāsa, Dakṣa Prajāpati—
That king, the son of Pracetas, performed the horse sacrifice.
There, the carrier of oblations, impelled by mantras, then conveyed the sacrificial portions for all the hosts of gods from every side.
The goddess, daughter of the mountain king, beheld him as he was carrying [the child],
recollecting that enmity which had been the cause of the curse.
And Girijā spoke to him, awakening the Ancient One with words that were sweet, coherent, and endowed with reason. (32.4)
"O God, you are the goal and the refuge of all the gods;
O lord of all the gods, how can the sacrifice proceed without you? (32.5)
"O Bhava, this Agni carries the sacrificial portions for the gods; he is not yours, O Maheśāna. What is the reason for this, O you of exceeding luster? (32.6)
"O Lord, this matter cannot be accomplished through conciliation without recourse to valor;
for this king, the son of Pracetas, is both foolish and arrogant. (32.7)
Remembering his former enmity, he will certainly not give it up unless he is commanded;
moreover, O Lord, a boon was granted to Dadhīca by you at that time.
That moment has now arrived; let it be acted upon for that purpose.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having been addressed thus, the blessed Lord whose banner bears the bull then spoke with a smile to the Goddess, your mother, O lady of pure smiles. (32.9)
"O lady of beautiful hips, O auspicious goddess, in a former birth you were the daughter of Prajāpati; it is because of your knowledge of my inner state that you speak thus to me. (32.10)
"For no one in this world desires suffering for their father, O beautiful lady.
Thus was she addressed at that time by the divine Vyāsa of pure soul.
Then the large-eyed goddess, with a frown upon her brow,
pressed the tip of her nose with her hand out of anger, though she possessed a pure smile.

As that nose was being crushed, a woman of exceeding splendor was born, with a frowning face, four tusks, and three eyes; she wore leather finger-guards and arm-guards, and had a girdle fastened around her waist. 13.
Equipped with a sword, a bow, and quivers, bearing banners,
she had ten faces, ten arms, a slender waist, and was dark as the night.
"Having full breasts, broad hips, thighs like an elephant's trunk, and imperishable beauty—the goddess of auspicious countenance called that goddess 'Bhadrakālī'. (32.15)
Then she said to the god: "O Lord, this [army] has been created by me;
you too create another host worthy of it. Let there be salutation to me. (32.16)
Then the god beheld his own radiant shoulder;
from it was born a divine being who seemed as if he were burning up the three worlds.
With his face adorned by a frown, wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors,
clad in armor, equipped with quivers, arrows, a sword, and a bow.
Three-eyed and four-armed, with a body as firm as a thunderbolt, that youth was created;
bowing down, he became the lord of the Gaṇas named Hari.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke to the God of gods who was with Umā:
"Command me, O Lord of the Suras; O All-pervading One, tell me what must be done by me."
Then the Blessed One said to that Hari, the leader of the Gaṇas: "Go and destroy the sacrifice of this son of Pracetas."
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, perform this task quickly together with Bhadrakālī.
Then that blessed god [commanded] the Gaṇas, who could assume forms at will.
The wise one created from his own limbs hosts bearing various forms;
he touched his arm perfectly, and from that were born those of great strength.
Then, O Lord, there were ninety-one crores [of attendants];
the Blessed One spoke to them: "O sinless ones, destroy the sacrifice! || 32.24 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Then, surrounded by that great army, the two of them proceeded amidst the roars of the ocean and the sounds of thundering clouds.
The god also, together with Pārvatī, stood near the hermitage of Raibhya and witnessed that act of the lords of the Gaṇas which destroyed the sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The trees belonging to Kanakhala are situated near Gaṅgādvāra;
and there is the mountain Suvarṇaśṛṅga, which resembles Mount Meru."
At that time, Dakṣa’s sacrifice took place in that region;
and the formidable army of Gaṇeśvara arrived, led by Kālī.
Having reached him, all those illustrious ones, possessing the radiance of blazing fire,
then spoke to that sacrificer, as well as to the ṛtviks, the sages, and the gods.
"For we are all attendants of Śarva, the Supreme Soul;
having arrived here desiring [something], grant us the portions we wish for."
"Whether by asceticism, by the right to a share in the sacrifice, by strength, by self-restraint,
by sovereignty, or by yoga— whichever it may be— you were formerly [the foremost] among you."
For all that belongs to us as well; we too are partakers of a share.
And if the gods are our masters, it is by that very fact that they have become entitled to a portion.
In sovereignty, both power and ascetic merit are the causes; there is no doubt about this.
Both of these belong to us alone, and therefore sovereignty is our rightful choice.
Now, O best of divine sages, if this is the command of anyone:
"The portion must be given to you, but not to us," then let it be so declared.
"Tell me who makes it known, for from that we shall learn.
Thus addressed by Hari, all those led by the gods [replied]. (32.35)
"O lords of the hosts, the mantras are the authority for you regarding the share," they said.
The mantras also said to the gods, "You are those whose minds are struck by darkness."
Since you did not worship Maheśvara for the sake of the first portion,
and since they did not grant the portions even when addressed with mantras, [the gods were overcome].
Then those mantras departed from there to the eternal world of Brahmā;
thereafter, Śakra and all the other gods spoke to the lords of the hosts.
Having abandoned [them]—[we shall] slay all of you who have come here to battle by means of our prowess. 32.39.
Having heard those words of theirs spoken with pride, Hari, the conqueror of enemies, laughed and addressed all of them with these powerful words: ||| 32.40 ||
"Mantras have not been made authoritative by you who are arrogant in your strength;
therefore, because you have acted with violence, I shall today destroy your boasts."
Together with the officiating priests, their sacrificial portions, and the sacrifice itself—
those who incite these, I shall destroy them all.
Having spoken thus, the radiant and powerful Haribhadra and the enraged Bhadrakālī both rushed toward the gods.
And the leaders of the hosts, filled with rage, uprooted the sacrificial posts and hurled them;
the leaders of the hosts likewise threw the charioteer, the Hotṛ priest, and the horse.
Seizing them all in their anger, they threw them into the current of the Gaṅgā;
and having bound the sacrificer with a noose, they led him away at their pleasure.
Some destroyed the altar, others the kusha grass, others the sacrificial ladles, and still others the cups; some threw them about, while others set the halls on fire.
Haribhadra, too, resplendent in spirit and undaunted in soul, paralyzed the upraised arm of Śakra as well as those of the other denizens of heaven. (32.47)
With an angry countenance, he struck out with the tip of his bow and felled the eyes of Bhaga and the teeth of Pūṣan while they looked on.
And that terrible discus of Viṣṇu, possessing the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon, he—whose soul was undaunted—stunned; it remained in his hand and did not waver.
And having struck down the Tuṣita gods, who were likewise intent and eager for battle,
with the Vāyavya weapon, he cast them to the earth.
And that blameless god, by means of his excellent weapon of delusion, utterly bewildered all the other gods who stood ready for battle.
And whatever kings had come there desiring to see him,
he brought them all by force to his own home through the power of his weapons.
Seeing that the sacrificial hall had its jars shattered, its sacrificial posts and archways broken,
and its great halls set ablaze, the sacrifice fled away.
Then, as he was running toward the sky in the form of a deer,
Hari fixed an arrow to his bow and rendered him headless.
Taking up another arrow, the powerful Vīrabhadra pursued Yajña,
who was fleeing in the form of a deer;
he rushed toward him as he approached the two [sages] who were bound, seeking to attain the state of a star.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Vyāsa, having been thus humiliated by the Gaṇas as well as by Kāla and by the divine Hari, they all came to him for refuge."
Then Hari, together with Kālī, spoke to all those gods, sages, and world-protectors who had sought refuge: "Go to the imperishable Soma;
propitiate the Lord of the Gods, and then there will be peace for you."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by Hari, those gods, though filled with indignation, sorrow, and grief, went forth with focused minds to propitiate him. (32.58)
Then, not very far from there, those high-souled ones, with their minds fixed upon him, beheld the Lord together with Sāmba and his attendants.
Having seen him, they bowed down and, placing Brahmā at their head, praised that one of blazing splendor with loud voices using words worthy of sacrificial offerings.
The gods said:
Salutations to you, O slayer of the enemies of the gods, O destroyer of the sacrifices of the asuras!
O great sacrifice, O being of great essence, O you who are praised by hundreds of great rituals! 32.61
Salutations to the destroyer of sacrifices and the giver of the entire essence of the Vedas;
to Viṣṇu, who manifested as Śipiviṣṭa and struck down Narasiṃha.
To the one who dwells on Mount Mandara, the giver of all auspicious things,
the one whose vehicle is a great celestial chariot, and the one who creates obstacles for the seasons.
To him who internalizes the mantras, to him who performs the mantra-vows,
to the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth, and to the remover of the shattered eye.
Salutations indeed to the one who paralyzes Śakra and the discus of Viṣṇu;
salutations to the leader of sacrifice and to the one who brings about the origin of sacrifice.
Salutations to you who have attained the granting of boons, to the progenitor of Brahmā,
to you who wear a tiger skin and are clothed in black antelope hide.
Salutations likewise to the father of men, who wears the most excellent garland,
and to the progenitor of Viṣṇu, Jaya and Vijaya.
Salutations to the destroyer of wrath and to the progenitor of Vīrabhadra;
salutations to joy and to anger, and salutations to the creator of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Homage to Devānutāpa and to Mṛgabāṇārpaṇa!
Homage to you, O Blessed Lord, O God; homage to you, O Blessed Śiva!
Salutations to you, Lord of all worlds; salutations to you, Creator of the world!
By you this entire universe was created—the sacrifice, the gods, and the slayer of the sacrifice.
Be gracious; do not be angry with us; do not bring about our destruction.
Sanatkumāra said:
For one who, having risen early in the morning, recites this daily with self-restraint, no forms of obstacles shall ever arise for him. (32.71)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, the Lord of Gods—the soul of all and the creator of all—then spoke these words with a smile to those who stood praising him. (32.72)
The God of Gods said:
"I am not angry; you are always exceedingly dear to me.
For if I were angry, your life would cease to exist in a mere moment."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord, desiring the welfare of the gods, then caused all those deities to enter by means of his yogic power (yogamāyā). 32.74.
In order to cause amazement by his power within his own body,
those [beings] then entered the body of the high-souled Lord Mahādeva.
Seeing the wondrous world composed of the seven realms,
they all, filled with fear, wandered through all those worlds.
There they beheld the five-eyed Gaṇapa, the Hero, assembled;
by him indeed all those tigers among the gods were uplifted and freed from weariness.
Projected by that very moment, they departed for another world;
those highly fortunate ones beheld a city resplendent like the sun.
It was enclosed by a very large wall made of crystal,
and adorned with various beautiful peaks that were variegated and radiant with jewels and gold.
Then, in the midst of that place, those best of gods beheld another auspicious city, seven koṭis of yojanas in extent on all sides.
It was covered by a divine wall of silver, radiant as the moon;
in its center stood another city, rising upwards and extending sixty million [yojanas] in width.
It was well-enclosed by a rampart made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold;
in its center, moreover, was another [city] measuring five koṭis in extent.
O best of sages, in the midst of that city, which was surrounded by a wall made of sapphire stones, those gods beheld him.
It was four million yojanas in extent, equal in its breadth and length,
and completely surrounded by a wall made of beryl stones.
In the center of that city was a beautiful area extending for three million yojanas,
completely surrounded by a wall variegated with all kinds of jewels.
Among them, the people were entirely free from all suffering;
they were endowed with pure lineage and all possessed perpetual youth.
Free from hunger and thirst, devoid of disease and sorrow,
they are immortal, abandoned by old age, and always joyful in mind.
They were adorned with various long ponds and reservoirs,
and with diverse, wonderful trees that always bore flowers and fruit.
There, other auspicious trees produce all kinds of food;
others produce ornaments, and still others produce all types of garments.
Others [brought] all kinds of flowers and indeed all kinds of fruits;
others likewise [brought] all manner of objects, as well as auspicious honey not produced by bees.
O Vyāsa, there are other trees of great splendor that always exude milk;
they all yield cow's milk.
The entire ground is made of jewels, auspicious and strewn with golden sand; here the waters spring forth from the earth, as do the mountain cascades.
Among them there was neither anger nor greed, nor strife, nor hatred, nor envy;
there was no delusion, nor arrogance, nor any other faults.
In its center was another auspicious city, two koṭis in extent,
adorned with a rampart made entirely of ruby.
Having passed through such cities as these, the gods then [reached a place] extending for ten million yojanas on all sides and surrounded by fire.
Those supreme gods beheld a great, divine, and infinite city that was without gates, difficult to look upon, and resembling the fire of universal destruction.
Having seen them, they went toward the city filled with both wonder and fear.
To those lords of the gods, O Vyāsa, whose faces were pale with terror and who were trembling, the five-eyed leader of the hosts said: "O gods, let there be no fear for you. 97.
This is that very great and terrible city, enveloped by a fearsome fire;
it is what you, O high-souled ones, must behold, for whose sake you have come here.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, that mighty five-faced one, with his spear blazing like fire,
created a gateway while the hosts of gods looked on.
Having entered, those high-souled gods, accompanied by the five senses,
beheld that great city, which was divine and filled with lions.
Of those who were like Mount Meru and Mandara, possessing claws and fangs,
terrible, fire-colored, enraged, and exceedingly radiant.
Then one among them, a powerful lion with a long, hanging mane, having broken his bonds, pursued [the elephant] in a great rage.
At the terrifying roar of that lion, all the inhabitants of heaven,
with dejected faces, went for refuge to Pañcākṣa.
Pañcākṣa said:
"O gods, you must not fear; I shall indeed show the Lord to you now.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, they suddenly beheld Śarva together with Umā;
yet that city was no longer there, O Vyāsa, nor was the lion, nor anything else at all.
Trembling with fear, they approached the Lord for refuge;
then that Blessed One, who is a source of refuge, spoke to them while smiling.
Addressing all the gods who were trembling with fear, the Lord of the Gods said:
"Indeed, you have seen my wrathful forms in the shape of lions, which are terrifying."
By one of them, that fierce one, you have all been threatened:
"If I should ever release all of you out of anger... (32.107)
"There is no doubt that in a moment you shall all cease to exist;
for this goddess, the daughter of the mountain, is angry with you.
Propitiate her indeed, O gods, for I am not angry with you."
Sanatkumāra said: When the Lord had spoken thus, the goddess, her copper-colored eyes wide with wrath, created from her mouth a terrible goddess who increased the fear [of her enemies].
With a face made terrible by fangs, possessing many feet, hands, and fingers,
she bore a bow, an axe, a sword, a fierce discus, a trident, and arrows.
Possessing a splendor like that of a thousand blazing suns and having a universal form,
her body measured ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Overwhelmed by her and being struck down on all sides, those gods were unable to stand before her, like herds of deer before a tiger. || 32.112 ||
Then those gods, their minds distressed by the fear of Kālakarṇī,
entered the heap of ashes lying at the side of the god out of fear.
Seeing those gods, their limbs smeared with ashes, having entered the heap of ash seeking refuge, the Goddess forbade the [other] Goddess.
The Goddess said:
O Kālakarṇī, turn back! Do not slay these best of gods;
they have become devotees of Paśupati, their forms smeared with ashes. (32.115)
This Pāśupata vow was proclaimed by Paśupati in ancient times;
bathing with the purifying ash is the highest of all baths.
"These foremost of gods are under the Lord's control and are worthy of his favor;
since they have entered the ashes, do not destroy them."
For these fierce animals have now been reduced to ashes by their entry;
they have all become leaders of the Gaṇas, O Īśvarī, and must not be slain by you.
Death has no power over those whose minds are dedicated to Śaṅkara;
for by me this entire vow, which fulfills all desires, has been performed.
Thus addressed by the goddess, Kālakarṇī, who had assumed a terrifying form,
turned back from the gods and abandoned the anger that had arisen.
But seeing that Kālakarṇī had turned back, those gods then praised the daughter of Himavat, as their most terrible fear was pacified.
The gods said:
[We praise] Umā, the beloved chief queen of Hara, the wife of Mahādeva, the Mother (Ambikā) of Tryambaka,
the single-syllabled Speech, the destroyer of the worlds, [the consort] of the God of gods.
His auspicious consort Jayā, white as a conch, a kunda flower, the moon, or a pearl necklace, with fierce fangs,
difficult to behold in battle, possessing inconceivable and terrible vision and wide eyes,
clad in yellow silk garments, bearing a great trident, bells, banners, and flags, and fond of divine perfumes, clarified butter, and incense.
She held a staff of Time, a sword, and a shield in her hands; she carried vessels filled with fat, blood, entrails, and marrow;
she wore a beautiful golden band upon the southern quarter;
her eyes were like the fire at the end of an eon; and she let out loud, boisterous laughter.

We take refuge in the divine Kānasī (Kāṣṭhī), who acts according to her will, who is uninjured by the weapons of the bodiless god of love, who is a renowned river of heroic armies, who dwells eternally on Mount Mandara, and who resides in heaven.

She who shatters the Asuras and Mahiṣa like firewood, the destroyer of Sundubhi and the slayer of Sunda; she who is the death of Niśumbha, who emits the splendor of the moon, sun, and fire, the bestower of desired objects,
the remover of the affliction of grief and suffering, the singular desire, the non-terrible one, the dense one, and the end-maker of even Antaka (Death) himself.
[He gave] the power of the sage Jamadagnya,
as well as the queen of kings Urjā, Manojñā, Karālā, Kṣapā, Daṇḍanīti, Sthitisiddhi, and the beloved, auspicious Kālarātri.
[She is] Aparṇā, the refuge, dwelling on the king of mountains, ever-present in the Ocean of Milk, auspicious;
she has great tinkling bells, her hair is disheveled and upward-pointing, and she possesses the luster of a blazing fire or the hue of twilight clouds;
she wears leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, is three-eyed, wears a garland of matted locks and red lotuses, and is free from all thorns of affliction.

I always take refuge in that one Goddess, who possesses eyes like firebrands without charcoal, who wears a garland bound with a golden chain, whose long braid is beautifully braided, who is endowed with glory and fame, who bears a variegated banner adorned with peacock feathers, who is the essence of sovereignty, and who bestows peace.

She has armlets fashioned from a hundred serpents; she is intoxicated by the life-force of great dānavas; her body and hair are rough with the ashes of funeral pyres; she has massive knees and a protruding belly; she wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and half of her face, eyes, feet, and hands are adorned with serpents;
she wears a great girdle and various garlands hanging down like fruit; and she is fond of dancing to the fierce sounding of great clouds and musical instruments.

A fortitude that delights in song, laughter, idle chatter, and pleasure; one that is devoid of recitation, fire-offerings, and fasting, yet characterized by non-departure, non-exile, and constant abiding; one whose essence is known through great yoga and follows the path of fierce reality; and one whose fierce sound is bound like a bowstring and bell, possessing a violently fierce roar like the crashing of a great thunderbolt from a massive cloud into the ocean.

I take refuge in the primordial goddess Pārvatī, the supreme sovereign of all sciences, who is the goal and whose nature consists of self-restraint, observances, and self-control; she who is the ritual action for those initiated and the initiation itself; the wife of Virūpākṣa, who dwells in half the body of Hara; the goddess born from the torch-like mouth [of Brahmā].
And [he saw] the auspicious daughter of the lords of the mountains, the beloved of the Pitṛs, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
she who occupies half the body of Bhava, who caused the fall of the teeth of the Sun, who paralyzed the hand of the chief of the gods with her grasp,
who plucked out the hair of Viṣṇu, who is borne by a vehicle yoked to a great lion, the most terrifying one, who strikes fear into all.
One should meditate upon the Mother, the fire-drill for Skanda, Candra, and Aruṇa, the foremost mother of Gajavaktra,

the birth-fire-drill of Viśākha, the producer of Nandin and Naigameṣa, the primordial fire-drill of the entire world, the venerable Mother, the Yoginī who bestows steadfastness upon those who meditate on her.

She who is inaccessible even to gods, brahmins, and those skilled in Mahāyoga and logic; she who is the abode of distinguished, beloved, and refined excellence; she who is the source of the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satya, which shine with majesty;
she who is the cause of the senses, the creator of ego and the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the impetus for the manifestation of darkness (tamas), goodness (sattva), and passion (rajas).
We take refuge in the supreme activity of Maheśa, as well as his power and consciousness, which are inconceivable to all who possess knowledge;
we take refuge in the goddess Umā, our mother. O Mother, being pleased, grant happiness to us.
We meditate with a single-minded consciousness upon the auspicious consort of Mahādeva who is to be contemplated;

and whatever terrible thing has been done by you, as well as what was done by us previously throughout thousands of millions of births, and what we shall do or are doing now— all that, in this very manner, you must grant.
May all our goals be fulfilled according to our desires, as well as health, vigor, prosperity, the abundance of knowledge and discernment,
as well as retention, reasoning, deliberation, refutation, fortitude, the realization of meaning, spiritual progress,
and likewise constancy in dharma— these, and whatever other qualities there may be besides these.
O Goddess, enjoy all these today; salutations to you! (123–144)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by the gods with joyful hearts, and through the grace of Tryambaka, the Goddess, being well-pleased, spoke this to the gods.
The Goddess said:
"Go all of you, free from fever; I am pleased with you, there is no doubt.
Do not act thus again, O gods, lest destruction come upon you. (32.146)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that god, the blue-and-red one with matted hair, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, smilingly restored all the deities to their natural state.
And the Lord of the Gods said to them: "Go, free from anxiety;
for when the sacrifice is to be performed, then indeed this [task] shall belong to you."
Along with his head, the son of Diti was joined together by means of this mantra.
Then the god gave him the Atharvan hymn and the eternal mantra that effects the joining; and he spoke these words in a melodious voice.
The God of gods said:
"O best of gods, let this sacrifice attain equality with the constellations;
and let even this god Hara become a follower of the deer."
Bhadrakālī, Hari, and these hosts of great strength—
all of you shall forever be auspicious and immortal, O gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, all those gods, together with Brahmā, bowed their heads in prostration and spoke these words to Śarva: 32.152.
O Lord, O God, Master of the Suras, let this best of sacrifices belong to you alone; O Imperishable One, it is being performed for your hundredfold honor.
"In all sacrifices, we give you every portion.
Thus addressed by all the gods, the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the Suras, [spoke].
He assumed a supreme, auspicious form composed of all the gods;
then those gods beheld their own selves within Maheśvara.
Upon their heads, arms, thighs, and feet, as well as on their bellies, hands, and stomachs,
there sat great-souled sages whose wealth was their asceticism.
Having assumed that form at that time, Śaṅkara spoke to the gods:
"You are all high-souled beings, born from my own body."
"And behold your own bodies as being composed of me.
Then, O Vyāsa, those deities perceived the entire world as consisting of Rudra.
Not seeing even themselves, their minds were filled with wonder;
thus did the Lord of the Gods display his own power to them.
He said to the tigers among the gods: "Indeed, these manifestations have been seen;
whichever form one worships, endowed with supreme devotion," || 32.160 ||
"O gods, assuming that form, I myself accept the worship;
I have no need for the sacrificial portions, for those portions belong to you, O gods.
I grant them all today; go now, all of you, free from anxiety."
The gods said:
"O God, this supreme truth has been shown to us by you;
the mortal who shall know it thus will attain the imperishable worlds. (32.162)
And this place, O Blessed One, which is known as Bhadreśvara, shall become the most excellent in the world, the most meritorious of all meritorious sites. (32.163)
The eternal Rudra-field extends for a yojana on all sides;
O God, the deer there shall become your beloved attendant.
O destroyer of sacrifices, whoever recites this daily, having risen at dawn,
or causes it to be heard by Brahmins, is liberated from all sins.
And having bathed in this Bhadrakarṇahrada, whoever should worship Hara,
and having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), the pure one should feed the Brahmins.
That man, liberated from all evil, wherever he may die,
rejoices in the midst of Apsarases like another god in heaven.
And where it was said by you, O Lord, while standing there, "O Blessed One, O Master:
by your grace, let this unborn one become the meritorious Harabhadraka. (32.168)
O Slayer of Sacrificial Demons, O God, may the merit that belongs to one who has properly performed the horse-sacrifice accrue here to the man who constantly worships you.
And whoever among the best of men shall here give up his life,
he shall become a member of Haribhadra’s host, possessed of great strength.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," the blessed Lord Śarva, accompanied by Soma and surrounded by hundreds of his attendants, went to Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves.
The gods, together with the king, remained at that place as they pleased;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu followed behind the gods.
Having traveled a short distance together with both of them, the Lord, not very far from that place, said: "Stop, O Viṣṇu of great strength!"
Then that best of men, having bowed at the feet of Hara, stood leaning upon a mango tree; he became straight once more.
Because Hari remained in that place, having taken hold of a mango tree while gazing at the Lord of Gods, therefore that place became known as such. || 32.175 ||
The prosperous sacred field of Viṣṇu known as Kubjāmraka is meritorious; by visiting it for a distance of one nivartana, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having gone not very far from there, the god Bhūva said to the Grandfather,
"O Vyāsa, turn back," and he entered the sky.
When that god had departed into the sky, Brahmā, with palms joined and face upturned,
circumambulated him clockwise, bowed down, and then departed from that place.
Because Hara was circumambulated there by him while performing that meritorious deed, a whirlpool was produced from his own body.
Therefore, that beautiful region is renowned as Brahmāvarta;
a person who bathes there obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) here and likewise fed the twice-born,
one shall then cast off one's life-breaths and attain the world of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, having approached together with the gods led by Viṣṇu,
performed the glorification of Paśupati at Bhadreśvara.
Having installed that exceedingly radiant *liṅga* there and performed worship,
he bathed in the Bhadrakarṇahrada lake and went to heaven together with the gods.
As he was departing, Dakṣa then said this to Brahmā:
"O Lord, what must be done by me? Tell that to me as I ask. (32.184)
The Grandfather said:
"Propitiate the great archer Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair;
then you shall attain the completion of the sacrifice and the imperishable worlds."
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having been thus addressed in truth by the god Brahmā,
he then fashioned a linga at Kanakhala and worshipped Rudra.
When a hundred divine years of Prajāpati had been completed,
Mahādeva, laughing, spoke to the Daughter of the Mountain upon the summit of the mountain.
O Goddess, the son of Pracetas stands engaged in ascetic penance, self-restrained;
behold him, O Mistress, established with a mind fixed upon me. 32.188.
Then the Great Queen saw him standing there subsisting on air alone,
worshipping Maheśvara at the Linga with supreme devotion.
O Vyāsa, the goddess, her hands joined in reverence, spoke with joy to her husband, the god who is worshipped by all the deities and the lord of all gods.
The Goddess said:
"This man is mean, evil-minded, stubborn, arrogant, and wicked;
yet, by good fortune, he has been humbled by you and has come to you alone for refuge. (32.191)
Therefore, O Maheśvara, you ought to forgive this wicked-natured one who has sought refuge in you; for his sake, I propitiate you, your devotee.
The God of gods said:
"O Goddess, you yourself bestow upon him whatever boons he desires, according to his pleasure. Permitted by me, O fair-browed one, you alone shall grant him his boon."
Sanatkumāra said: Then those two lords of the gods of gods, joined together and surrounded by their own hosts, spoke: "Behold, O Dakṣa; we are both pleased [to see you] with our divine eye. (32.194)
O highly fortunate son of Pracetas, you two are granters of boons and possessors of great ascetic power.
"For the sake of pacifying the curse, I grant you this desired boon:
may you obtain the fruit of that sacrifice which was destroyed by my attendants."
"O illustrious one, become my Gaṇeśa, capable of assuming any form at will;
you shall be imperishable, immortal, and free from suffering and grief, O highly fortunate one, and you shall remain ever by my side. (32.197)
The Goddess said:
Listen further; what else might Maheśvara grant?
For he, when entreated by you, would surely bestow even a most difficult boon.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed in this way by that daughter of Himavat, the high-minded Dakṣa, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and spoke as follows. 32.199.
Dakṣa said:

We, together with our wives, have sought refuge in that god who holds the Pināka bow, the sole deity who brings about the birth and destruction of the three worlds, whom the foolish do not know as the Unspoken One, and who removes the inauspiciousness of his devotees. (32.200)
"Because of our ignorance, our lack of devotion, and the delusion of pride, we did not indeed offer worship along with the daughter of the Mountain;
to that Lord of the Gods who, being provoked to anger, gave me a curse—together with his wife, we have come for refuge to that deity. (32.201)

We, together with our wives, have come for refuge to that god who is the creator of the hosts of gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas; of the siddhas, the sons of Diti, the lords of the dānavas, and the ṛṣis; and of all beings, including beasts, deer, birds, and reptiles. (32.202)

We have come for refuge to that God, together with his wife, who out of anger created the great Gaṇeśvara, the lord of lords, as well as Siṃhendrahari of immeasurable power and form, and his wife endowed with all-encompassing virtues and majesty.

We, along with our wife, have come for refuge to that god who conquered the gods—those protected by Varuṇa, Savitṛ, and Gopā; accompanied by Brahmā, the hundred sacrifices, Viṣṇu, and Vāyu; led by Indra, and possessing great weapons like Samuṇi. 32.204.
Whatever impurity or evil has been done toward you, whether through ignorance or indeed through the defects of passion, hatred, and delusion—
all that, may Śarva, the Great Soul and Lord of All, forgive me today along with my wife, by virtue of his magnanimous nature.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having thus praised the Lord of Gods with eyes clouded by tears,
he stretched out his arms and fell to the ground with his whole body.
Then the powerful god himself, together with the goddess, raised up Dakṣa, who had sought refuge and whose eyes were clouded with tears, O illustrious one.
Her tears fell upon the ground there in the form of drops;
having coalesced, O best of Brahmins, they became a river.
Then the god spoke to that river of auspicious characteristics:
"O goddess, since you have issued forth from the tear-drop of Arjuna... (32.209)
Therefore, O auspicious one of great fame, you shall be known by the name Arjunā; reaching each successive stage of life, you will carry [the burdens] along.
Moreover, one who bathes in you shall obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice;
and having died on this bank of yours, whether by religious observance or otherwise, [one attains the highest state].
Furthermore, he shall not undergo rebirth as a human nor fall into an evil destiny,
provided that he fasts for three nights, prepares the sacrificial porridge (caru), and offers it.
Having bathed, you should feed a Brahmin;
