he too will go to the world of cows, O one of great splendor, and shall not fall from there.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus created the river and bestowed his grace,
the Lord of the Gods consoled him and then spoke to King Dakṣa.
The God of gods said:
"Therefore, let that fear of yours be gone; become my beloved Gaṇeśa.
Speak again, O virtuous one, what desired boon shall I grant you?"
Sanatkumāra said: Then Dakṣa, having bowed down with auspicious words, spoke once more, repeatedly taking heart and looking at him again and again. (32.216)
Dakṣa said:
"If you are pleased with me, O God, let this place be yours, O Imperishable One—sacred and meritorious. Let this be my boon, O Śiva. (32.217)
The God of gods said:
"These two daughters of a sage, having undertaken difficult austerities, have subsisted on ears of grain for a full year by means of that wicked man. (32.218)
"Since you two, O highly fortunate ones, and Dakṣa have remained here, this place shall therefore become my abode known as Kanakhala. || 32.219 ||
And there is a great and meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha), resembling the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
here there are no sinners, nor the afflicted, nor atheists, nor those possessed by pride.
They shall indeed always be able to depart, but never to remain;
and one who dies here shall not undergo rebirth again by my power.
Having approached this place, bathed, and likewise prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru),
one whose soul is liberated from all sins is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Then he appointed Haribhadra there as his minister for the assembly,
and out of affection, he gave him Kālī as a wife, who was preeminent in all virtues.
And he bestowed excellent, vast, and divine boons, as well as the island of Ghṛtoda, upon the many groups of Bāhuja kings.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, that sacrifice of Dakṣa was indeed destroyed by Śambhu;
and how the head of the sacrifice was severed has been related to you.
Vyāsa said:
That terrible, divine [weapon] born from the mouth of the Goddess, which causes fear even to the gods—where has it gone, or how did it come to be? This I desire to know.
Sanatkumāra said: When the Blessed Lady was praised by the best of the gods who were prostrate before her, then that Ambikā said to him, "Speak; what may I do for you? (32.227)
Then Brahmā, having bowed with great reverence to the Great Goddess, said: "O Sovereign of the Gods, let her become my daughter."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," Umā gave her daughter to that goddess;
and he too, having said, "You are Death," appointed her to a terrible task. (32.229)
The goddess who sustains all living beings is auspicious in the taking away of life;
she too was appointed by Brahmā himself to perform that task,
with her arms raised, along with the lords of the gods, ever-exerting herself for you and me.
Whoever [hears] this unsurpassed account of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the installation of Bhadreśvara, and the very grace bestowed upon Dakṣa— 32.231.
Whether one recites it, hears it, or causes even the twice-born to hear it,
that person, liberated from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.

I have approached Śaṃkara for refuge for the sake of my well-being— he who cast down his eye at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, who is the fire of the city of Madana, whose limbs are radiant with the crescent moon, who is the preceptor of the gods and the time of the sacrifice, and the sovereign protector of the seven worlds.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 32.32 ||
The thirty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
O best of sages, as to how the bull carried the god—
Having paid homage to the one whose banner is the bull, I shall fully declare that to you.
Even before this, the Great Being, accompanied by Dharma as his sacrificial assistant,
performed vast and exceedingly difficult austerities in Nyāsa.
Having reached the Himavat mountain,
they subsisted on air alone for thirteen thousand years.
Thereafter, they subsisted on human food and became eaters of herbs;
then, before long, the god of great splendor appeared to them together with his hosts.
Hara granted his vision to all of them, who were identical in form;
they beheld those many Maheśvaras, indeed possessing similar splendor.
They thought to themselves, "Who indeed could be their lord?
Then, having observed them and consulted together, they remembered [the matter] again and again.
In their midst was Maheśvara, the storehouse of splendors;
Menā and Himavat, having bowed with great reverence to that god Bhava standing between them, and placing their joined palms to their heads, those two of immeasurable luster offered him praise. (33.7)
The Dharmayajñas said:
"Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, who is clothed in the directions, whose nature is nectar, who dwells at the crossroads, and who delights in the crossroads. (33.8)
To the god who has four manifestations, who has three eyes, and who is Bhava;
to the one with four faces, the pure one, who moves within the lattice-work.
To the one who bestows grace upon Indra, to the one who effects grace upon Brahmā,
to the god whose liṅga is erect, to the one who intoxicates and yet is free from intoxication.
Homage to the one of golden hue and likewise to the sun-eyed;
homage indeed to the one with pure hair and to the long-tongued.
Salutations to you who have many feet; salutations again and again to you who have but one eye. Salutations to the one with a thousand bells; indeed, salutations to the one with a thousand eyes.
Salutations indeed to the wielder of the Pināka bow and to the one who bears the banner; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the thousand-headed one and to Saṃvarta; salutations again and again.
Salutations ever to the one worthy of praise; salutations again and again to the slayer of enemies.
Salutations to Bhava, to the one who is to be, and to the creator; salutations again and again.
Salutations always to the Excellent One, and likewise to the Giver of Boons;
salutations always to Gokarṇa, and salutations to the Lord of Sovereignty.
Homage be to Viṣvaksena; homage again and again to Prabhāsa. Homage be to you, the giver of food; homage be to you, the giver of life.
Homage indeed to the one who sets [the wheel] in motion, homage to the one adorned with a garland of lotuses;
homage to the great chariot-warrior, and repeated homage to the Terrifier.
Salutations indeed to the four-faced one, salutations to Mahādeva;
let there be salutation to Brahmā, both to the immovable and to the moving.
Homage be to you who take the form of a woman, to the fortunate one; homage, homage!
Homage be to you, O Middle One; likewise, homage to you from every side.
Salutations! You are the one who permits and the thinker, the instigator of all beings;
O Lord of the World, grant the desires we both seek.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who constantly praises [the Lord] with this [hymn], endowed with self-restraint, shall be fulfilled in all his desires and attain his desired goal. (33.21)
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord restored all those Gaṇas to their natural state— Nandin, the Goddess, and even himself as well.
And he said to them, "I am pleased; let the desired boon be accepted."
The two gods said:
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then even when we have entered into other births, may we always carry you, O Lord of Suras. (33.23)
"And this secret place has been intensely cultivated by us through austerity;
by your grace alone, O Lord of the Gods, may it become meritorious."
The God of gods said:
"This is my supreme secret, an excellent place that shall come into being; indeed, within the distance of a five-arrow-shot, a deer shall become a leader of my hosts."
"Since the state of being 'I am in the middle' has been honored by you two and remains established there,
therefore let this be renowned by the name 'Madhyama' (the Middle)."
Having attained another birth, you two, honored and exceedingly powerful,
shall sustain the worlds by becoming my vehicles.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having thus addressed those two best of gods, the Lord departed for Mount Mandara, which has golden caves, together with his hosts of attendants.
Then, after a long time had passed since the departure of the gods with their hosts,
the auspicious Surabhi propitiated Rudra during this Manvantara.
O Vyāsa, Bhava was gratified by her asceticism for a thousand years; he appeared before her and said, "I am the granter of boons."
She chose an incomparable son, the best among all living beings,
as well as other sons of great being who were worthy of sacrifice and like the foremost of the gods.
Likewise, he gave his daughters and other most beautiful female supporters of the world;
then the god bestowed everything and vanished from sight.
When that Great God had departed,
Surabhi gave birth to a son, a bull of blazing splendor, the first-born among all beings.
Likewise, the world-sustainer Gā gave birth to the eleven auspicious Rudras, who were younger than Vṛṣabha,
as well as those seven daughters.
Having performed his daily rites every morning, that bull among men would always approach his father, his mother, and likewise his grandfather.

Having paid homage to that vast, radiant forest frequented by elephants from the four quarters and inhabited by hosts of Siddhas— therein indeed dwells she who was born from the nectar of immortality.
Divine, with the nectar-like sap of *dūrvā* grass, it heals those who are cut or burned;
once, while wandering in that forest, he was satiated yet afflicted by thirst. (33.37)
The king of bulls, the son of Surabhi, went to drink from the ocean;
having plunged into the great waters of the ocean, he then became a massive consumer.
Opening his mouth wide, he drank the water of the ocean along with its fish and timiṅgila whales; yet he did not reach satiety.
While he was drinking, fourteen thousand lords of the Daityas, all equipped with swords and arrows and holding bows in their hands, stood ready for battle.
Resembling Śakra, like the fire of Yama and Kāla,
the great beings, sons of Maya, rushed with speed toward Vṛṣabha.
That one of great strength drank up those enraged Daityas, who were armed with swords, mallets, and lances, along with the waters of the ocean itself.
Seeing them already drunk and those being made to drink, all the inhabitants of the ocean were suddenly terrified and cried out in distress.
Then the blessed ocean, being drunk up and deeply distressed,
approached the Mare’s Mouth and sought refuge with Saṃvarta.
And that exceedingly powerful Anala, having granted him safety, approached Vṛṣa with great agitation and spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
Saṃvarta said:
"This auspicious abode of the Daityas is the refuge of all beings;
you, O valiant one, ought not to deprive it of its waters."
Vṛṣabha said:
"O Agni, it did not occur to my mind to dry up the ocean entirely.
Since you are its counselor, I shall indeed do so today."
Whatever pride and arrogance you have, whatever strength and whatever manliness—show that to me, O Lord of Sacrifice; I shall drink it right before you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the lord of bulls began,
out of impetuosity, to drink up the ocean dwelling at the Mare’s Mouth until it was entirely exhausted.
Anala said:
"You are no match for me in power, nor do I have any enmity toward you. However, I shall indeed accomplish that task for which I am bound; so shall I do."
"You shall not drink; I will protect the ocean in my presence.
I shall restrain you, O boastful son of Surabhi! (33.51)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the illustrious and immensely radiant Fire-god, having leaped up, seized him by the throat with his strength; yet he did not move from that spot.
Except for the Dānavas, that water which he had drunk was vomited up;
indeed, they were all consumed by the fire within his belly.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the fire Saṃvartaka, having released Kakudmin who had been restrained, said, "Go, O lord of bulls; I do not kill you."
I am indeed capable of burning you, but you are incapable of killing me;
nevertheless, I do not roar, for what is the use of boasting for those who are truly powerful?
Sanatkumāra said:
Having dismissed the bull, Agni quickly went to his own abode;
the bull also departed, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow. (33.56)
Thus, that spirited bull, the son of Surabhi,
his soul overwhelmed by the pain of this humiliation, departed while reflecting in this manner.
"I am weak, while the fire is powerful, by which I have been thus humiliated;
yet, having become the lord of my life, I have not been deprived of my vital breaths."
All my strength and likewise my roaring have become futile,
like a rain-cloud in the sky that has been deprived of its water.
Today I shall renounce my life, firm in my vow and intent upon it,
so that such a humiliation of my honor may never happen to me again.
For one who is weak, evil-minded, and held captive by an enemy, I consider death to be superior to life; what is the use of living?
Sanatkumāra said:
While the bull was thus reflecting, he heard an auspicious voice from the sky:
"O son of Surabhi, you need not fear; do exactly what I tell you. (33.62)
Seek refuge in Rudra, the lord of all gods, who is more powerful than all;
through him, O lord of the gods, you shall conquer the Fire-god.
He is undoubtedly the creator of all beings, beginning with Brahmā;
O Bull, he will dispel all this suffering of yours.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard this from the great-souled Sādhya,
the one of great splendor reached the Himavat mountain and performed extensive austerities.
When a thousand years had passed for him who was devoted to that and intent upon its blessing,
the Blessed Lord, the Master of all beings, together with Ambā and his attendants, spoke.
The God of gods said:
"O highly fortunate son of Surabhi, my dear child, I am pleased with you. Ask for the boons you desire; I shall grant them to you, even if they be very many."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having beheld the Lord together with Ambā and his attendants,
he bowed his head at the feet of the Master, with palms joined in reverence and well-composed in mind.
Gazing at him again and again and bowing down repeatedly, he said:
"O Lord of the World, I truly desire inexhaustible ascetic power."
O Lord, you possess supreme strength and likewise inexhaustible mastery over yoga;
yet I, your own vehicle, have been thus insulted by Agni.
O Lord of Gods, O Imperishable One, I desire to see the fire of universal destruction, which dwells within the mouth of the submarine mare, subdued by you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus and having granted those boons, the son of Satyavatī,
having likewise rubbed his left side, created a single Rudra.
Wearing a crown and a garland, three-eyed, adorned with earrings and armlets,
broad-chested, clad in armor, holding a bow in his hand, possessed of great strength,
wearing leather finger-guards on his arms, and bearing a sword and divine weapons— (he saw him).
He said to him, "Go to Rudra, who dwells in the submarine fire; having bound Saṃvartakānala, bring him here while he is quivering with rage."
Sanatkumāra said: Having bowed at the feet of that Soma, the leader of the Gaṇas went swiftly to the ocean and beheld the consumer of oblations (Agni).
Having waged a powerful, most terrible, and hair-raising battle,
he bound Saṃvartaka and brought him before the presence of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
"O best of speakers, what was that battle like between the lord of the birds and the fire? I wish to know this; please tell me. (33.77)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone to the fire Saṃvartaka, that leader of the Gaṇas, his eyes red with anger, then spoke these meaningful words: 33.78.
Sanatkumāra said: Having gone to the fire Saṃvartaka, that leader of the Gaṇas, his eyes red with anger, then spoke these meaningful words:
Ganapati said: "The Lord of the entire world, the God adorned with the crescent moon, commands you, O Agni: propitiate this bull."
"Tell him, along with your circle of friends, 'I am bowing before you';
abide by his command and do whatever must be done. (33.80)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed and having heard those words of the God of gods, Anala, greatly delighted, spoke these meaningful words. (33.81)
Anala said:
"I am always to be employed by that very God of gods and his constant follower;
yet, having appointed me here, he will never engage me elsewhere."
"Go and speak to the three-eyed Lord in my name:
'If he speaks to me again, then I shall do accordingly.'"
Gaṇeśvara said:
"Alas, those who are wise yet are excluded from strength and knowledge, when addressed in this manner, behave exactly as you describe me. (33.84)
The word of those who are powerful and those who possess authority carries weight only once;
moreover, he alone is the best of messengers who succeeds in accomplishing his purpose.
Thus, I, a powerful messenger, have been dispatched here by that mighty creator of the world, the wielder of the Pināka bow, for the sake of accomplishing all purposes.
"If you do not carry out my word, then today indeed,
having bound you with great nooses while you struggle, I shall lead you into the presence of the Sustainer of Heaven."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, that radiant one, his eyes blazing with the fire of anger, rushed toward the leader of the Gaṇas and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (33.88).
As it was rushing forward with speed, that powerful master of weapons struck it with the Parjanya weapon;
and it blazed up with great force.
Then, as he approached blazing and overwhelmed with rage,
he struck him in the middle of the chest with a great thunderbolt weapon.
Then, struck by that weapon, even though he was full of vigor,
the lord of fire stood for a moment stunned and agitated, like a smokeless flame.
Then, overcome with rage, the leader of the Gaṇas bound that flickering great fire within his two hands by means of a noose of Rudra.
And indeed, seeing him fallen, bound by that excellent snare,
his sons and circles of friends, with various weapons in their hands, [rushed forward].
Then, enraged, they rushed toward Gaṇapa by the hundreds and thousands;
but having defeated them as well, that Gaṇapa [confronted] the fire-god Hutāśana.
He quickly brought him before Hara, like a sacrificial animal at a ritual;
and Mahādeva, beholding him who was brought forth and whose food was the ocean, [spoke].
He said to the bull, "Tell me, what should be done for him?
Beholding that wretched one, the great bull [looked upon] him with a dejected mind.
Bowing his head at the feet with palms joined in reverence, he spoke this:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Great Sovereign of all the worlds! (33.97)
O Lord, Master of the existent and the non-existent, this majesty of yours has been witnessed;
for even this wretched and powerless one, O You of great power, has been seen by me.
"O best of gods, let him be released; he is already slain, there is no doubt.
For all his sons have been killed, as have all his friends in every way. (33.99)
"O Lord, the slaughter of this wretched one is not desired by me; let him be released.
These were the words spoken by the bull to Maheśa.
Having heard this, he was pleased and, smiling,
then released that fire and that Rudra who is free from old age, sorrow, birth, and death.
Having made him the lord of the Gaṇeśvaras, the Sovereign gave him a continent renowned by the name Manoramaṇa, which possessed great prosperity.
O Vyāsa, it was divine, moving at will, adorned with palaces made of bright Jāmbūnada gold and endowed with everything that fulfills every desire.

At that time, all the gods, led by Brahmā, approached the God of gods and spoke these words according to the truth: tasmin kāle tadā devyāḥ sarve brahmapuraḥsarāḥ | devadevaṃ samāgamya vākyam ūcuryathārthavat || 33.104 ||
"O Blessed One, O Slayer of the Enemies of the Gods, this bull is the best of deities;
for it was formerly occupied by you, and now that mighty one fills the air with its roar."
O Lord, protector of beings, out of pride he has brought the entire three worlds into distress,
and with his speed, he has filled all directions with his celestial chariots.
Making the gods tremble with his roar, he moved through the sky;
having now obtained boons, he will surely treat us in the same manner once again.
O God, let that means be ordained so that he does not act [thus].
You are our goal, O Lord of Gods, and our refuge, O Protector of Beings;
you are the protector in every way for those who are constantly overwhelmed by fear, O Lord. (33.108)
The God of gods said: "I shall ordain for you all such that no fear shall arise and all the worlds may forever remain in well-being. (33.109)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Vyāsa, the god of gods of great splendor,
by virtue of his granting of a boon, created Gaṇeśa, who wore beautiful earrings.
With a mouth gaped as far as his ears, he was massive in body and possessed of great strength;
his arms were like mighty iron clubs, and his frame was firm with a constitution as hard as adamant.
He had great tusks and a broad chest, wielding a massive sword and bow;
his three eyes were like glowing coals, and he was radiant in his armor.
He bore two quivers for the purpose of providing inexhaustible arrows, was clothed in a hide,
and carried a shaft in one hand and a bow in the other.
Adorned with planets and stars, illuminated by lightning and the sun,
it shone like the radiant peak of Mount Meru with the sky as its upper garment.
Having clearly addressed him as "Prabhākara," the Blessed One spoke these words to Prabhākara in the presence of all the gods.
O Guṇākara, you have been commanded by Prabhākara;
endowed with supreme sovereignty, restrain Vṛṣavega.
"Jyotsnā shall be your wife, and you, commanded by me, shall become ageless and immortal as my great Gaṇapati."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all the deities, together with Brahmā, bowed down to him and departed for their own abodes; and the god too shone forth, mounted upon his bull.
The bull of Dharma is said to be his face, sacrifice his hips;
the moon and sun are his two eyes, and Brahmā rests upon his head.
Varuṇa is on his tongue, and Vāyu himself moves within;
Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Śakra are established in his feet.
The remaining divine calves and thighs were likewise supported;
the Rudras occupied the ears, the nose, the neck, the lips, and the jaw. (33.121)
His weapons were his hooves, and the discus and thunderbolt were on his two horns;
Mitra himself was in his anus, and all gifts were in his tail.
All his bones became mountains, and his excrement became auspicious prosperity;
his urine, O Vyāsa, became divine, purifying nectar.
All the sages became her body hairs, and all the constellations everywhere became her limbs;
O Vyāsa, the auspicious planets became her beautiful joints.
The sacrifices, Vedic rituals, mantras, hymns, and their fruits became his flesh; the rivers and oceans became his blood. (33.125)
The seven worlds were indeed the mouth of that one of incomparable splendor;
the Marīcis were his slayer, and the medicinal herbs were his marrow.
Animals that have become mantras, as well as sinews, creepers, climbing plants, trees, shrubs, and likewise other auspicious forest trees. || 33.127 ||
The Nāgas were his channels (nāḍīs), and the Vasus were the accumulation of his semen;
the two Aśvin deities are remembered as his stomachs for undigested and digested food respectively.
The clouds were her skin, and the garlands of lightning—there too were the yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases. (33.129)
From them were born the veins and arteries, as well as intoxication and pride;
and from them also arose human mothers and various kinds of living beings.
The pores of that great-souled bull were [the abodes of the gods].
Thus the blessed Lord, endowed with supreme sovereignty,
the Great God Saurabheya, became composed of all the gods.
Whoever hears or recites this entire great account of the birth and deeds of Saurabheya according to their true nature— 33.132.
Constantly pure and undepressed in spirit, one is liberated from all sins;
and at the time of death, whether at the appointed hour or otherwise, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
This should never be given to a deceitful person, nor even be heard by one; likewise, it should not be given to an atheist, a wicked person, or one who performs evil deeds.
This secret, eternal [teaching] should be given and heard by a son, a disciple, one who is righteous, high-souled, and pure. || 33.135 ||
May that Maheśa, who by his power over the world and the Vedas— by that Sarvārthasiddha of great strength—
causes the ocean of clouds to roar, be forever well-disposed toward you.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Origin of the Bull," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 33.33 ||
The thirty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus did the blessed Vyāsa, the protector of the gods, release the cloud.
He became one whose vehicle was a bull, just as I have described to you.
Vyāsa said:
How did the blessed goddess Kṛṣṇā attain a fair complexion? What was the cause of that as well? This I wish to know. 34.2.
Sanatkumāra said: Seated on the plateau of Mount Mandara, Umā and the Destroyer of Kāma then took delight together with the Pramathas, who assumed various forms.
Then, while the god was sporting there, he addressed that illustrious lady as "Kṛṣṇā" in the course of conversation; the high-minded woman was enraged.
Mahādeva, of great splendor, embraced her as she was angry and,
remaining unperturbed, spoke sweet words repeatedly to soothe her.
The God of gods said:
"O God, O sinless one, O imperishable creator of the universe, do not give way to anger;
this was uttered by me as a joke when I addressed you as 'Kṛṣṇa'. (34.6)
"From this day forward, O fair-faced one, I shall not speak to you with such words; abandon your anger," said the wielder of the Pināka bow to her.
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Blessed Lord [spoke] again to Sukeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas.
He made Vyāsa a Brāhmaṇa devoted to austerity and truth.
Vyāsa said:
How did that Brāhmaṇa formerly attain the state of Gaṇeśa?
By what austerity was the Lord pleased, such that he granted him the status of Gaṇeśa? 35.2.
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a brahmin born in the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, truthful in speech and pure, who was devoted to pilgrimages and dedicated to fasting. (35.3)
Once, while staying in a foreign land, he saw on the path in the forest a terrible tiger standing there, its mouth wide open, with claws and fangs as its weapons.
Having seen him, that brahmin then quickly abandoned the path and entered a vast,
terrible forest devoid of living beings.
There he saw men leaning against a clump of vīraṇa grass in front of him,
hanging down and crying out in great distress.
Seeing those twice-born ones hanging there with their heads downward, he asked, "Who are you? and they spoke this to him: || 35.7 ||
The ancestors said:
"We are all your ancestors, hanging head-downwards in this hell;
we hang upon you, O Vīraṇa, because of your own fault, O evil-minded one! (35.8)
"Human beings desire sons with the thought, 'These will deliver us from hell'; yet you, instead, will cause us to fall into suffering."
The Brahmin said:
"Whatever ascetic merit has been acquired by me through visiting sacred fords,
as well as whatever auspicious deed has been performed by me since birth— "
Therefore, O ancestors, lift yourselves up from this pit.
The ancestors said: "We cannot be raised up from this pit by means of asceticism, nor by sacrifices, nor otherwise than as we say; do for us that which we command. (35.11)
"Procreate a son endowed with virtues and joined with ascetic power;
then we may be released from this pit, if you so deem fit. (35.12)
The Brahmin said:
"I am one whose vital energy is drawn upward; this is the vow I have undertaken. I shall not take a wife, and I shall indeed deliver my ancestors. (35.13)
Then, having thus abandoned them and being overwhelmed by great sorrow, he went to Rudra for refuge; thereafter, the Pitṛs vanished.
When his ancestors had thus vanished, the twice-born one then subsisted on air alone;
becoming like wood, clods of earth, or stones, he remained there without breathing.
Fixing his mind on Rudra, steady and well-composed,
he stood in the open air, muttering the Rudra hymns with his heart.
When his month was then complete, there arose a great wind and rain,
which crushed all living beings, unbearable and accompanied by a terrifying sound.
During that great year, he experienced neither suffering nor defeat; rather, he remained perfectly steadfast.
Then, when the seventh month had arrived, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, assuming his divine form, spoke to that best of the twice-born.
"I am pleased with you; may it be well with you, O observer of noble vows, by virtue of this asceticism.
Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever resides in your mind. (35.20)
Then Sukeśa, seeing Nārāyaṇa approach, said: "I do not desire a boon from you, O Śaṅkara. (35.21)
Viṣṇu said:
"Enough of this persistence regarding Hara, O brahmin-sage!
He cannot be seen even by the gods, much less by mortals. (35.22)
Sukeśa said:
"Whether I am capable of being seen by you or not—what is the use of these deliberations? Whether I am a bad grasp or a good grasp, nevertheless, I am the master of myself. (35.23)
O Lord of the Wheel, from Śaṅkara alone I desire a boon, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; I do not desire one from you, nor from anyone else under any circumstances.
"O sirs, because you all, being composed in mind, worship and praise that god, he is therefore called the most excellent."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having understood his resolve, the blessed Lord Hara was satisfied;
casting off the form of Viṣṇu, he resumed his own form.
And he said to him, "O best of brahmins, become my imperishable attendant (gaṇapa), immortal, freed from old age, and devoid of all suffering. (35.27)
Endowed with sovereign power, my beloved attendant shall dwell upon this divine mountain named Trikūṭa, which was created by me.
"I give you this golden chariot that moves at will, for whose sake, my son, you have endeavored to please me. (35.29)
And all these ancestors here, O sinless one, have been delivered from the terrible hell by you, their excellent son; they now stand before you, O Gaṇeśa.
They shall become your servants, eternally freed from suffering;
these lords of the Gaṇas shall remain ever obedient to your will.
"You shall be renowned by the name Sukeśa,
and you shall always move about endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers."

Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen his ancestors along with their circle of friends delivered from hell and endowed once more with the status of a lord of the Gaṇas, which is worthy of worship— 35.33.
With a joyful mind, bowing his head with palms joined in reverence, he whose face was beaming with delight and who was skilled in speech then addressed Maheśvara.
Sukeśa said: "O Blessed One, the status of a Gaṇapati and sovereignty have been obtained; likewise immortality, as well as the boon of inexhaustibility and freedom from old age. (35.35)
These ancestors have been delivered, and these leaders of my hosts have been appointed;
moreover, this mountain that moves at will has been obtained by me through your grace.
O Mahādeva, O bestower of desires, I desire that you—Soma, the supreme lord—be forever exceedingly gracious and truly beautiful to behold. 35.37.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Sukeśa, the Blessed One spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, all this shall come to pass."
"Taking refuge on this mountain together with these most excellent and noble ones, go, my child, to your desired destination, and protect both the gods and the brahmins. (35.39)
Then, having dismissed that Sukeśa as the leader of his host,
the god Soma vanished from the sight of all who were looking on.
Sukeśa also, on that mountain in the city resembling heaven,
diligently questioned his ancestors regarding the true nature of the hells.
Vyāsa said:
For what purpose, O Brāhmaṇa, did the leader of the Gaṇas question those ancestors, and how did the ancestors there respond to that wise one? (35.42)
O dear one, I wish to hear from you this matter exactly as it is, whether in detail or in brief—beneficial and bringing about all happiness. (35.43)
Sūta said:

Thus addressed, the lord who is the son of Surasṛj and the maker of celestial chariots, having lost his purpose, spoke these words that increase the world of the gods and destroy all previously performed merit. (35.44)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Sukeśa," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 35.35 ||
The thirty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
On that peak of Trikūṭa, in the city fashioned by the gods, [he dwelt].
He was seated in a divine golden celestial chariot crowded with women.
Having then summoned all the ancestors and honored them according to the prescribed rites, he saw them seated comfortably and spoke these words. (36.2)
Sukeśa said: "O gods, by your splendor all this sovereignty is such as it is; it was brought about by you, whereby I have been made a partaker of happiness. (36.3)
The ancestors said:
"Do not speak such a falsehood, my son; let there be no unrighteousness for you here.
By our grace, O son, there shall never be any loss of sovereignty for you. (36.4)
But we, being driven into a most dreadful and terrible hell,
have attained through your asceticism and prowess a happiness that is very difficult to obtain.
Just as we have been delivered from hell by you, our excellent son, so do we see no other way; for you are blessed, truly our son.
"Today we might have been cooked for many thousands of years in a terrible hell,
you who were so ill-behaved, had you not been our kinsman."
"O son, many living beings who are unrestrained, extremely fierce, of wicked conduct, and devoid of austerity, go there. (36.8)
Sukeśa said:
"O ancestors, never before have I spoken falsely, nor do I speak it now; for by the power of you all, my sovereignty was exactly as yours is. (36.9)
Listen to me as I speak correctly; do not disregard my words. O fathers, I do not hold the deities in contempt—who indeed would hold them in contempt? (36.10)
The ancestors perform deeds that are esteemed by the virtuous on this earth; they also constantly pray: "May we have abundant offspring. (36.11)
Those who are righteous, grateful, and devoted to virtuous deeds will constantly deliver us from our state in the pit of hell.
Because they perform those duties and do not fall away from their own dharma,
that dharma, when properly practiced, produces auspicious offspring.
They were righteous, generous, grateful, and established on the path of the virtuous;
they were devoted to their fathers and everywhere intent on the salvation of their ancestors.
Thus, by you all, through righteousness and supreme meditative concentration, I have been produced, endowed with ascetic power, entirely for your sake.
Having propitiated the god, he has once again delivered his ancestors from hell;
such is your power, as well as the fruit of your well-performed asceticism.
O you of great wisdom, what falsehood is there here in my words? And this is the auspicious Vedic tradition, O best among the knowers of the Vedas. (36.17)
If you consider yourself to be the authority, thinking "I have created this," then [know that] you are produced from limb after limb; you are born from the heart.
"You are indeed my very self, named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! For I have arisen from your limbs and from your heart. (36.19)
"Since I have thus delivered myself and you as well,
therefore may you all consider yourselves as being in a state of meditative concentration."
For it is by one's own action that one is delivered from that terrible hell;
no other person of evil mind is delivered by the action of another. Indeed, for all living beings, the ripening of the fruit is ordained by their own action alone.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those very ancestors, addressed thus by that high-souled one, spoke these words with joy and eyes brimming with tears. (36.22)
The ancestors said:
"Who else but you would speak thus, unless he were approved by the Lord?
These words of yours are fitting for a righteous and high-souled one. (36.23)
O son, how could anyone who is not such as you be properly united with all the desired objects by the Lord of all gods, the one whose banner bears the bull, just as you have been?
You are the Ordainer, for you are our kinsman; you are our progenitor, O Great-minded One! You alone are our father, and we are your sons—of this there is no doubt. (36.25)
In this regard, O high-minded one, we shall satisfy you with an ancient account as it is sung in the Śruti and the Smṛti; you ought to consider it for us.
The Pitṛs said: "Indeed, the sons were created by Brahmā with the words, 'O gods, worship me.
They then worshipped their own selves; at that, Brahmā became enraged with them. (36.27)
And he spoke to them in his agitation, "You shall lose your senses.
Having been thus cursed by Brahmā, all those inhabitants of heaven assembled together.
Joined with suffering and grief, they were wretched;
yet, beholding him so serene, they then praised him, bowing their heads and speaking thus.
"O Lord, our consciousness has been lost; grant it back to us, O Master. And forgive us, O Lord of Gods, for that which we have done out of ignorance. (36.30)
Then, having been addressed in this manner by those gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke these words with compassion to the prostrate deities:
36.31. Then, having been addressed in this manner by those gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke these words with compassion to the prostrate deities.
Brahmā said:
"O beings of great courage, perform penance according to the prescribed rules;
then you shall cast off all the sin born of transgression."
The gods said: "O Lord, O Creator of all, O Protector of the world, that very designation by which we might know those expiations is not known to us. (36.33)
Brahmā said:
"Ask your own sons; from them you shall obtain what is beneficial. Furthermore, O knowers of dharma, do not lose your composure again."
The Pitṛs said:
Then those tigers among the gods questioned their own sons regarding expiations,
duties, and the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and in full detail.
Then those auspicious sons, being self-restrained, related all that had been done by Yātātahya through his supreme meditative concentration.
Then, having regained their senses and likewise attained their desire,
they addressed their sons with affection, filled with joy.
The gods said:
"O sons, you are not our sons; rather, we are the sons born of you, by whom eternal knowledge has been bestowed upon us whose consciousness was lost. (36.38)
When they had spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there;
and that one of great glory spoke these words to all those gods.
Brahmā said:
"The gods do not speak untruth; truth abides among the gods.
For all of you have been called 'sons,' and 'fathers'—that indeed is no falsehood. (36.40)
Therefore, your fatherhood toward your sons shall be eternal and imperishable;
of this there is no doubt, for you are all truly sons in every respect.
For secrets are never told to one who is not a disciple; both son and disciple share the same purpose, and therefore you are all my sons in every respect.
Fathers cross over by means of their sons, and those sons in turn cause them to cross;
having caused them to cross, they attain the state of being fathers through that very deed.
And you have likewise been delivered from hell by your sons through their ignorance;
therefore, these indeed are your fathers and you are all their sons in every respect.
Because he protects, he is called "father" (pitā), or else because he procreates, he is called "father.
Since both of these qualities exist in you toward your sons, you are therefore considered fathers.
Then they [addressed] Brahmā—
[the rest of the verse follows].
The Pitṛs, free from distress, invited them with their desired boons. || 36.47 ||
Then the Pitṛs chose first the sacrifice for themselves, [declaring]:
"He who should worship the gods without having sacrificed to us would not obtain the fruit thereof. (36.48)
And being overcome by sin, he was greatly— [the rest of the verse is missing].
Then they all departed together with Brahmā, returning by the same way they had come.
The ancestors said:
"O son, just as we, who were deprived of consciousness in hell, have been rescued by you and restored once more to our senses and preeminence. (36.51)
Therefore, you are my father, worthy of worship, whom I follow as a great [disciple].
— the most excellent one, having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to his ancestors. (36.53)
Thus it is exactly as you have said; your auspicious words are not false, for it has been declared that you are all fathers to one another.
"O lords of the Gaṇas, grant me yet another boon!
For by this [boon], O best of the twice-born, my desired question has indeed been answered. (36.55)
The Pitṛs said:
O Supreme Lord, there is nothing unknown to you;
yet you wish to explain the truth here for our sake as a standard of authority. (36.56)
"Speak what you know we possess;
for we shall tell that to you—whether it be heard or experienced—according to our ability and exactly as it is.
Sukeśa said:
"You have all been tormented in a terrible and most dreadful hell;
therefore, you are undoubtedly knowers of the scriptures regarding all the hells."
I wish to hear all of that—their essential nature, their application, the distinction of time, and the sequence; for my curiosity is indeed great. (36.59)

How many are those hells, and what is their extent? What are their foundations, what is their appearance, and who is cast into them? And how indeed do they become so deeply afflicted by suffering? (36.60)
And how does a living being suffer, and likewise, how is he rebuked?
After what length of time is he released from hell? Once released, by what means does he arise, and how does he transmigrate again? (36.62)
"O you of great wisdom, tell me all this in its entirety, in detail, and exactly as it is; for my curiosity is supreme."

They call this the foremost yoga, directed toward the one who is the preeminent lord of Upendra, Pitāmaha, and Īśvara, who has realized the treasury of the true nature of reality, and who is liberated from the yoga marked by evil. 36.64.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Great Fortune of Sukeśa," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 36.35 ||
The thirty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those ancestors [considered] the establishment of their son with respect to him.
Those imperishable ones spoke of him who was known as Suśarman.
The ancestors said: "O son, this is your father Suśarman, world-renowned;
he will relate to you in truth that which was recounted by you. (37.2)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O brahmin-sage, the high-minded Suśarman, having taken leave of him, spoke these words to Sukeśa, that being of great courage and foremost among the Gaṇas.
Suśarman said: "O Sukeśa, we have not ourselves fallen directly into the ocean of hell; yet, with our hearts dependent upon you, we shall fall without you. (37.4)
But we, fearing those torments, contemplate day and night:
what are those most terrible hells like, so dreadful to hear of? (37.5)
Therefore, O Lord of the Lords of the Gaṇas, we shall speak according to our wisdom and as we have heard it; listen to me regarding those hells that have been proclaimed.
Difficult to approach, extremely impassable, and terrifying to all living beings,
the first hell there is renowned as Yamalācala.
The second is named Śālmala; the third is Kālasūtraka;
the fourth is Kumbhīpāka; and another is Asipatravana.
Likewise, Vaitaraṇī is the sixth, and Ayodhana is the seventh;
the eighth is Padma, and Mahāpadma is the next.
Raurava is the tenth, and Mahāraurava as well;
the twelfth is named Tamas, and likewise Tamastamataras.
These are the great hells, and likewise others that are "elevations" (ucchrayas);
for each elevation, eight hells are indeed proclaimed. O Lord, in these elevations there is torment interspersed with intervals of rest.
But in the others there is no rest; for this is declared to be the distinction. || 37.12 ||
For those men, there is indeed constant suffering due to their sinful deeds;
the sequence of their [suffering] through the division and exhaustion of that sin will now be declared.
But it is not possible here to state the measure of Gaṇeśa one by one;
because of the omnipresence of his activity, one perceives its end only through its exhaustion. || 37.14 ||
Everyone who has fallen into hell does not see its end;
those whose sins have been exhausted do see it—listen to me, O Imperishable One, as to how that is so.
Having fallen into a terrible hell due to his own evil deeds,
he proceeds most piteously, driven along until he reaches a certain direction.
Having traveled quickly along that road extending for many yojanas, and having reached many others, he turns back without finding its end. || 37.17 ||
Turning back from there once more, he proceeds senseless, driven along;
having gone again toward another direction, he likewise turns back.
Thus, having gone in all directions and not finding an end, he wanders there in misery;
no one whatsoever exists here [to help him].
But at the end of the torment, and then again at the end of the sin,
he perceives once more that which is limited and entirely circumscribed.
One is liberated from that [suffering] by means of the great gate;
for in this way, all hells are indeed infinite, inexhaustible, and imperishable.
No calculation in terms of *yojanas* can be made for them;
rather, it is by the time that a living being falls again, afflicted with suffering. (37.22)
Listen, O Lord, O sinless one, as I describe how this occurs:
having committed sinful deeds, the evil-minded man, at the end of their exhaustion... (37.23)
Then, afflicted by disease and mental anguish, he abandons his own bodies;
thereafter, driven by suffering, he is bound with great nooses by the messengers of Yama.
O Lord, one of deformed appearance is led along a rugged path,
being pierced here and there by thorns made of iron.
Being smeared on all sides with mud made of hair, marrow, and bones,
he falls again and again into uneven pits and is broken.
In some places he is overwhelmed by a great rain of stones;
there, his head, knees, feet, arms, and thighs are shattered.
He is dragged by the messengers of Yama, and again he is pulled over thorny trees; he is stretched out, split apart, and bound fast with creepers.
Thus, O Lord, being led helplessly along various paths that cause suffering, one falls under the power of afflictions and reaches the abode of Yama.
Then, without reaching Yama, he approaches Citragupta from afar by Yama’s command and is made to hear of the karma that he has performed.
Then Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Sūrya—these are the witnesses who declare there what living beings have done or left undone. (37.31)
Thus addressed, scrutinized, and urged by Citragupta,
he is cast into hell in a state of agony, with his feet upward and his head downward.
With iron clubs, arrows with exceedingly sharp points, battle-axes, slings, mallets, swords, and long spears; || 37.33 ||
With iron bars, saws, thunderbolts, chisels, plows, stones,
wedges, pestles, and indeed with alkaline paste.
Being struck day and night by blazing, terrible weapons and even by a rain of fire, he cried out piteously and excessively.
For a thousand years he attains an inauspicious hell;
having fallen there, he remains exceedingly miserable as he is tormented.
For ten million years, without ceasing, he falls into the depths of hell;
and even when released from the great hells, he takes refuge in other places of torment.
Touched by the cool breeze, he finds happiness there;
having attained that respite, he then forgets his torment.
When the dream was withdrawn for a moment, he was dragged away by the Rākṣasa;
and as he was being dragged by him, he was once again afflicted by pain and grief.
Lamenting piteously and excessively in many ways, he remained there; then that Rākṣasa dragged him back once more toward the place of torment.
It indeed torments that conscious being without respite;
there, for a thousand years, he is indeed tormented once again.
Indeed, he remains for exactly as long as it takes to pass through one terrible height;
thus, having undergone eight such heights by means of his sinful deed.
In saṃsāra, those lowest of men who go to those terrible hells become creatures such as worms and insects.
I shall describe them to you, my son, in brief;
first is the hell called Yamalācala which was mentioned by me.
There, men destined for the Great Hell go;
there are two mountains teeming with great creatures, lions, and tigers.
It was crowded with śarabhas and elephants, teeming with many serpents,
and filled with birds of various forms and men with uplifted weapons.
They were joined by leafless trees with needle-like thorns of diamond;
the single space between them was indeed level and covered with needles.
They were likewise covered on all sides by upward-pointing, adamantine-beaked, and impenetrable [thorns],
as well as by other terrible men with weapons in their hands.
They were surrounded on all sides by an iron wall,
and even in the sky above, they were covered by an iron net.
Those men who violate another's wife against her will, as well as those who defile a maiden, go there. (37.50)
One who steals a deposit, likewise one who steals meat, one who steals liquids, and also one who defames others; || 37.51 ||
Those who destroy the collection of the senses, those who falsely assume the marks of an ascetic,
those who kill deer and beasts of prey, and those who eat meat from the back [of animals].
Those who eat meat in vain and those who commit acts of violence—
these lowest of men, O son, go to the mountain of Yama.
And among those born as twins, that lowest of men who,
being impure in soul, does not perform the rite of atonement, shall himself encounter that [consequence].
Overwhelmed by those men as they rushed at him according to their instructions,
and being cut by their weapons, he took refuge in that mountain.
There he is devoured by enraged tigers, śarabhas, hyenas, serpents, cats, birds, and creatures with iron beaks.
And if, while being devoured by them, he climbs a tree,
there he is pierced by their sharp thorns and by birds.
But if he desires to go to his mountain cleft or cave,
even there he will turn back, scorched by fire and afflicted by suffering.
If, however, he encounters a terrible chasm between those two,
there the man's feet are pierced by needles with sharp points.
And seeing him divided and indeed incapable of retreating, those two immovable ones would quickly unite and crush him excessively. (37.60)
Being crushed by the two immovable pillars as if by a machine like sugarcane,
he experiences that torment while crying out piteously.
Furthermore, for that which has been eaten, torn apart, devoured by birds,
or burned, a new body is born once again.
Thus, being driven along for many years in great suffering,
he reaches the gate and, having emerged, is cast down upon the heights.

Whoever should repeatedly hear of this Mount Yamalācala, which possesses fierce velocity and is joined with the performance of manifold sinful deeds, shall not go to that place of terrible sin, for its speed is exceedingly swift.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Yamalācala," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
The thirty-eighth chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe once more the Śālmalī hell.
There, men who have committed very grave evil deeds go to their end.
O Lord of the Preeminent, there are many thousands of śālmalī trees;
they are all lofty, terrible, and extend for many yojanas.
They possessed great branches, great leaves, and were covered with large thorns;
they were completely surrounded by a massive enclosure wall made of iron.
Above, they were all completely covered by a great net,
and many men with wrathful faces stood there.
Holding vajras, staffs, and stones, and bearing swords and mallets,
their hands were grasping various other kinds of weapons.
Those most cruel beings violently torment the creatures who are helpless;
and there too, they are cut by Rākṣasas of wicked deeds.
Afflicted by sensation and deeply distressed, he flees in all directions;
wherever he goes, there he is struck down. (38.7)
And the Rākṣasas, having surrounded him on all sides in pits,
being exceedingly cruel, hacked him with weapons of various forms.
Proclaiming the evil deeds committed in the past by that wicked-souled one,
they were indeed censuring that fallen man of evil conduct wherever he might be.
Then, rising up with his limbs mangled and pursued by the Rākṣasas,
he reaches another region filled with needles and thorns.
There, being pierced again by fierce needles and iron thorns,
he cries out from his suffering and falls down, overwhelmed with extreme agony.
Even there, having encountered him, Rākṣasas with various weapons in their hands rushed at him, just as enemies attack an enemy.
If, rising up from that with speed, he climbs a tree,
there he is pierced and even cut by those sharp thorns.
With his ears, eyes, nose, and lips torn away by birds of various forms with iron beaks, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
There, they are pierced in all their limbs with fierce needles;
thus do those suffering there undergo torments of many kinds.
Listen as I describe those of evil conduct who fall [into hell]:
the arsonist, the poisoner, and he who approaches a woman of low caste. (38.16)
He who emits semen in a male, a poisoner, a seller of meat, one who travels by sea, a wicked-souled person, and he who eats delicacies alone—[these are excluded]. (38.17)

He who does not honor a guest, he who observes false vows, the Brahmin who abandons sacred study, the one who goes naked, and he who enters [the assembly] improperly—[these are those whom one should avoid]. 38.18.
One who rings a bell, a village priest, a teacher of Śūdras, as well as a usurer, a greedy man, and one who sells the Veda; 38.19.
These evildoers go to the place known as Kūṭaśālmalī;
having emerged from there after two crores of years, they indeed return once again.

Having been cast down upon the height, they rest there for a short time and are then cast again into that hell until their sin is exhausted. O Sage, this same rule is recorded for the other hells as well.

He who, though possessed of a curious mind, listens with self-restraint to this account of the intense suffering found on that mountain so difficult for the virtuous to traverse, shall certainly not go to the Śālmalī hell.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kūṭaśālmalī," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the hell known as Kālasūtraka.
It was well-enclosed on all sides by a great and lofty wall.
And likewise, even the sky was completely covered by a net of iron;
as it was with one, so were all the hells completely covered.
Those who are highly elevated should also be known; I shall not describe them again.
There, those lowest of men, haters of the world, go to their end. (39.3)
He who abducts a woman, or likewise one who sells cows, and he who reviles dharma, himself, and the brahmins. || 39.4 ||
Furthermore, he who deceitfully denies his teachers' scriptures, and he who reviles his teacher, as well as his father and mother; (39.5)
He who reviles his father-in-law, his elder brother, or likewise other elders, and also treats them with contempt— 39.6.
O twice-born one, he who destroys the hermitages and all secret doctrines, and he who takes what has not been given, shall indeed go there. (39.7)
Having fallen there into that terrible hell, those evil-minded ones,
the lowest of men, remain for a full three crores of years;
crying out at the command of Death, they wander about deprived of their senses.
Having repeatedly measured out their evil deeds with a great black thread,
they violently sever the limbs of the creatures with weapons that have blunt points.
By those servants, who are tireless day and night, [the being] is led without rest;
then, when the time is fulfilled, the creature undergoes the states of existence.
Having rested there, that creature is then cast again into hell until all the evil he committed has been exhausted without remainder. (39.11)

Whoever should hear this sūtra on the doer of many evils, this sūtra on the difficult deeds of the world, shall not go to that hell of fierce suffering, that Kālasūtra hell of the realm of Yama. 39.12
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Kālasūtra," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. || 39.39 ||
The fortieth chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter I shall describe the most terrifying Kumbhīpāka.
For at that time, it was indeed terrifying even for the listeners whose minds were undisciplined. || 40.1 ||
There were many iron cauldrons resembling mountains of collyrium,
filled with oil, glowing like fire, and most difficult to endure.
Binding those evildoers again and again as they cry out most terrifyingly, the mighty and fierce Rākṣasas hurl them into those heated [cauldrons]. (40.3)
And there, O Lord, living beings are cooked for four million years; learn from me as I describe those who are so punished. 40.4.
The one who bakes bricks, as well as the one who bakes pots—he who destroys those two, he who sets fire to houses, and he who is a burner of dwellings; (all these go to hell). 40.5.
Whether in the forest, in a threshing floor, or in a cow-pen, he is one who destroys food and drink;
he is an obstacle-maker at meals, a destroyer of sacrifices, and a burner of sacrifices.
He who commits fraudulent acts, as well as one who gives false testimony, one who falsely piles the sacrificial fire, and likewise one who falsely maintains the sacred fire; 40.7.
He who provides false wages, he who is a defamer of the elders, and that lowest of men who steals the tools of artisans—(these are the ones who fall). || 40.8 ||
Thus they pass their time there, finding rest only for a further period of rising;
having reached that state, they fall again into hell until its destruction.

Indeed, that person who hears this ripening of the end of many misdeeds, the ripening of karma, shall not go to that hell of wicked-souled ripening, where the jars of suffering are brought to maturity. (40.10)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Kumbhīpāka," in the section on the description of hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 40.40.
The forty-first chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe once more the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana).
Hell is the suffering of the evildoer, which strikes fear into all living beings.
There, trees known as "sword-leaved" (asipatra) are difficult to approach;
they are numerous, with very large branches, dense, and exceedingly tall.
Their leaves were terrible, sharp, and like swords;
they were superior to those made of iron, for they were not indeed made of iron.
O Mahāmati, those [leaves] are distinguished by their sharpness for cutting;
they are covered with such leaves and likewise possess thorns.
There, living beings bound by their evil deeds were being slaughtered by the rākṣasas with swords and clubs, as well as with various other great weapons.
Being scorched by the fire, they flee toward those trees;
and as soon as he perceives them approaching, their leaves fall away.
Great and sharp [weapons] indeed cut them down;
with their heads and necks severed, they depart from that place.
Having gone there, they are repeatedly obstructed by Rākṣasas and by trees difficult to approach;
for five tens of millions of years, they remain there in great suffering.
Then, released from those [tortures], they indeed enter the *ucchrayas*;
having rested there, they all once again enter the *ucchrayas* in hell. (41.9)
Those sinful men who go to that terrible hell are cast down helpless and deluded until their evil karma has reached its exhaustion.
I shall fully declare those [sins] to you; listen attentively, O twice-born one.
That evil-minded man who destroys a tree that has been treated like a son— || 41.11 ||
The evil-minded man sells it either in a grove or in a village;
likewise, he may have the tree grown in a hermitage or along a road. (41.12)
Whether at a pond, or likewise in a garden, in temples of the gods,
or in a house, at a water-station, or on the bank of a river, or at a crossroads.
Whether grown here or there, the evil-minded man who destroys trees,
shrubs, creepers, bushes, or even grasses— (41.14)
For that fool who destroys [a tree] for the sake of its shade, flowers, or fruit, or for the sake of performing his own work, meets with that very same fate.
And he who plucks the roots, flowers, and fruits for his own sake, out of a desire for personal gratification and not for the sake of the gods or the ancestors; || 41.16 ||
He who should block a river, he who should fill up wells,
or that lowest of men who should cut down a tree for the sake of its leaves or bark,
or who should destroy that tree— he incurs the same [sin]. (41.17)
And whoever harasses creatures that have come near his shadow,
or frightens those who have approached his own dwelling, or even drives them away— 41.18.
They all fall into that great, elevated hell;
and having emerged from there, those auspicious ones return once more to the cycle of worldly existence.
He who, with an unwearied mind, should hear of this hell named Asipatravana—a place of misery for evildoers—shall not enter it, for he is a man of meritorious deeds who has realized the self. (41.20)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Forest of Sword-Leaves," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 41.41.
The forty-second chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter [I shall describe] the river Vaitaraṇī, which destroys all sins.
Listen attentively, my son, to that which brings fear from evil deeds.
O son, the auspicious river Vaitaraṇī has its banks cut away by sharp-edged tools;
it is filled with hair, bones, and blood, and possesses a most caustic liquid.
By *ullumpakas*, *gardabhas*, *makaras*, and even *kacchapas*;
by *śiśumārās*, *nakras*, *tantukas*, and even *rākṣasas* as well. (42.3)
It was crowded with flesh-eaters of massive bodies and great tusks,
and it was completely covered by those sword-leafed trees growing upon its banks.
Covered by long moss as if by a canopy,
its shore was bordered by a formidable forest teeming with śarabhas and bears.
Crowded with tigers and leopards, and teeming with lions, elephants, and donkeys,
there those of evil deeds were tormented by those tigers and other beasts.
Then those miserable ones are cast into that most terrible river;
having fallen there, O child, they are entangled by fibers and moss.
Bound by nets and covered by canopies, they are devoured by those fish and other creatures;
being scorched by the salt water, they cry out in their misery. (42.8)
They remain there for sixty million years until the exhaustion of their evil karma;
once released from that, they are indeed cast down again and again into the heights of the hells.
Having found rest there, they are all cast down again into the Ucchraya hell,
helpless and deluded, until their sin has reached its end.
Having crossed over these elevated realms, he enters into cyclic existence;
having crossed over the very depths, he again enters into various hells. Indeed, for a duration of one *koṭi* of time, [the suffering] increases further and further.
But for each and every one of all those elevations, O son, the duration increases by a thousand years respectively; this is the summary.
But those of wicked mind who go to that terrible hell—listen to them as they are correctly described by me, O sinless one. 42.13.
He who curses the river, he who treats her with contempt, he who enters her while naked, and he who has sexual intercourse with her; || 42.14 ||
He who spits, or voids urine or excrement, or carries away water belonging to fields, gardens, or inhabited places; 42.15.
A man who destroys the embankment of waters, one who breaches a pond, as well as one who defiles lotus-pools; 42.16.
Whether she be wicked or innocent, whoever defiles a woman, or that evil-minded man who steals or destroys a lotus pond; 42.17.
Those lowest of men who bring fear to a caravan or to any living being—all of them go to a terrible hell. (42.18)

He who, being self-restrained, constantly hears this [hymn] which destroys impurity and wards off uncleanness, shall not go to the impassable river Vaitaraṇī, which must be crossed through meditation.
This is the forty-second chapter, titled "Vaitaraṇī," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. || 42.42 ||
The forty-third chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the hell that destroys sin.
It was known as Ayodhana, which struck fear into all living beings.
There, those terrible men who resemble Yama, the servants of Yama—
possessing great strength and great courage, and all likewise masters of yoga— [await you].
Just as blacksmiths, having firmly gripped with tongs a lump of iron heated by fire, place it upon a solid block of iron; || 43.3 ||
Likewise, there too, living beings are struck by other heavy clubs and are slaughtered by terrible Rākṣasas who threaten them most cruelly. (43.4)
Thus, for seven times ten million years, they have passed through by their own karma;
likewise, in those elevations, they undergo terrible torments.
I shall now fully describe those men who go to that great hell of high elevation— those irreproachable lowest of men.
One might strike one's father, mother, or even a venerable person with the foot; or likewise, one might strike any other woman with the hand, a whip, or similar implements. (43.7)

Likewise, he who would step over one who has gone forth as a renunciant, or even over a sacred fire; or he who, for the sake of wealth, should bring a child to death; [he too shall go to hell]. (43.8)
Whether it be a woman, a man, a eunuch, or any other person, that lowest of men who seeks to deceive his own brothers over some matter of wealth; 43.9.

Whether it be a father, a mother, a sister, a husband who deceives his own wife, or sons who deceive their parents— the destiny that awaits them is said to be the same as that of the wife who deceives her husband or her sons. (43.10)
And for that evil-minded person who defiles the images of the gods, sacred fords,
and divine sciences and scriptures— that is said to be his destination.

He who constantly hears this [account] of the cause for the conjunction with many evils, which brings perpetual unhappiness and universal tearing apart—being self-restrained, he does not go to that terrifying hell, difficult to traverse, like a descent into a battle. 43.12.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Battle," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. || 43.43 ||
The forty-fourth chapter. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the lotus-array (padmavyūha), which is very difficult to penetrate.
It is unattainable for those of good deeds, yet it brings terror to those of evil deeds.
There, the fire named Tāpana blazes as if being fanned;
living beings are scorched there and become the color of fire.
All [the pillars] resemble lotus petals as they are being heated here and there;
in the center of that [hall], a great iron pillar stands firm.
They go there and conceal him; that fire is also exceedingly terrible.
Thus, they are driven incessantly through those horrific heights.
Listen to me as I describe those men who go to that state free from attachment:
he who would approach the wife of his guru, or he who would steal the property of his guru. (44.5)
He who consumes or repeatedly destroys the property of the gods, or who seizes the property of a Brahmin and even forcibly retains it; 44.6.
He who steals the property of a child, he who misappropriates the wealth of a woman, he who abandons those who are impotent, and he who kills one who has come for refuge; || 44.7 ||
He who covets another's wealth, he who misappropriates the property of the gods,
he who eats all things indiscriminately, and he who sells water— [these are the ones who fall].
One who sells Soma, one who extinguishes the sacred fire, one who strikes with fire, and one who strikes with poison; || 44.9 ||
And that man who, in battle, should slay with a parasol one who is unarmed, or likewise one who is begging, or even one who is seated; || 44.10 ||
Those who turn their faces away, those who are entangled with another, and those who argue with one another—all these men, being of unrefined intellect, go there. (44.11)

He who, being self-restrained, constantly hears this account of the abode of Death—a dwelling place of manifold sufferings—shall not go to that hell of fierce grief, which is like Death itself, the abode of eternal time. (44.12)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Padma," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. || 44.44 ||
The forty-fifth chapter. Suśarman said:
Beyond that is another hell, Mahāpadma, which causes the hair to stand on end.
Where those terrible servants of Yama, who resemble Yama himself, reside.
Those pitiless doers of evil, with blunted weapons, repeatedly cut off the flesh of living beings and give it back to them. (45.2)
Having devoured their own flesh, those doers of evil deeds become like lotus petals and are scorched in fire day and night.
And when the iron has been liquefied by a terrible fire,
the cruel servants of Yama force it back into the mouth.
Likewise, women and men made of iron, possessing a radiance equal to fire,
come together and embrace one another as they run hither and thither.
And there were many trees there, well-flowered and laden with fruit;
afflicted by suffering, they took refuge in them, and they too rained fire upon them.
And when those many other stones there come into contact with them,
they then burn those men intensely, glowing like the color of fire.
Thus has this great hell, Mahāpadma, been fully described;
as well as the man who steals gold and the man who violates his mother.
He who approaches his mother or his son, he who defiles the Vedas or violates his vow of celibacy, he who is envious, he who is ill-behaved, and he who is a worshiper of the śramaṇas. || 45.9 ||
That outcaste who might speak the Veda, or even listen to it, or who, being evil-minded, would seize it or show contempt for Brahmins; (45.10)
One should not listen to or recite the secret doctrines for Brahmins or those pertaining to other stages of life (āśramas) in a place where one is not authorized. (45.11)
Likewise, that twice-born man who provides food to wicked śramaṇas, nirgranthas, and ājīvakas, falls into hell. (45.12)
He who, being of evil conduct, speaks ill of Yoga, or of the ancestors, or of the grandfathers, or of the lords of Yoga, or even of the dharma of Yoga— (45.13)

The Vedas, the castes, the stages of life, and the sacrifices—all these belong to that [state]; the rogue who delights in censuring them, the atheist, and the rationalist—all such people fall into it.
Everything I have spoken is the truth; this is so, without a doubt. || 45.14 ||
Thus they pass their time there, bound by the fruits of their own karma;
then, connected by what remains, they are born among the species of insects.

If a wise and intelligent person, free from greed, delusion, and sorrow, should constantly reflect upon this and hear it, his soul impelled by divine destiny shall go to heaven itself and never descend therefrom again. 45.16.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, named "Mahāpadma," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. || 45.45 ||
The forty-sixth chapter.
Hereafter I shall describe again the Raurava hell, where those living beings, bound by their own karma, remain helpless. 46.1.
Afflicted by suffering and grief, they go at last to the great hells;
because the sound "ru" is uttered there, it is heard from that place. (46.2)
Because it is filled again and again with the cries of the *bhīma* (terrible) creatures, it is called Raurava;
being entirely full of cow-dung, it blazes and is exceedingly dreadful. (46.3)
In its center stands a pillar made of iron, possessing the luster of molten gold;
a creature sinking deeply into it is helplessly burned upon entering.
Uttering cries of distress, he fell down unconscious;
then, with great effort, he raised himself up by his own power.
Having reached yet another spot, he should enter it in the same manner;
then, if he leaps up from that and takes refuge in a pillar, || 46.6 ||
He is burned by that even more intensely; having been cast out, he enters again.
Thus he is tormented there for many years, suffering great misery.
Then, having been released, he attains higher elevations once more;
for men who drink liquor yet teach the Dharma go to that place. (46.8)
The slayer of a father, the slayer of a mother, the slayer of a brother, and likewise the slayer of a teacher;
those who delight in contentious speech and those who revile them [the aforementioned]. 46.9.
A cow-killer, a tamer of living beings who is exceedingly cruel, a throat-cutter, a fraudulent measurer, and one who imitates the actions [of others]—[these are those who fall]. (46.10)

The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who marries before his elder, one who delights in the cremation ground, one who has sexual union with the son of a remarried woman, and he in whose house lives a paramour—
these men all go to the Raurava hell.
Whoever should hear this account of the Raurava hell, most terrifying for evildoers,
being self-restrained and disciplined, shall certainly not go to Atiraurava or even to Raurava, even in thought.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Raurava," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 46.46.
The forty-seventh chapter. Suśarman said:
Listen to me regarding another great hell, Mahāraurava, which is a place of torment for the wicked.
Where there are streams and water and ponds, O son.
There were pits filled with cow-dung and others glowing like gold, as well as trenches filled with fire;
there were many pillars made of iron and trees covered in sharp thorns.
There, Rākṣasas of various forms, bearing sharp weapons and missiles,
have bound that creature with much evil.
Falling with a distorted form and crying out again and again,
he quickly fell there, his head split open by the rākṣasas.
He is cooked most cruelly in a fire-colored pit of cow-dung;
then, distressed by that burning, he suffers supreme agony. (47.5)
For the sake of allaying the burning sensation, he immerses himself in a pond;
there, afflicted by a twofold agony caused by the heated alkaline water, he suffers. (47.6)
Rising up in haste, he climbs either a tree or a pillar;
there he is pierced by those sharp thorns as if they were made of iron.
Indeed, in the trench of fire, the potato (or the sinner) cries out piteously in many ways;
thus, being driven along, he goes on, afflicted by thirst and lamenting much.
He resorts to that stream to drink, but it then carries water as hot as fire;
thus, afflicted by fainting, he would die.
And when his torments are complete, the creature is released from that great terror;
he is then subjected to extreme cruelty among the elevations (ucchrayas).
There goes the king-killer, the one who insults the wife of a king, he who,
having given hope, does not fulfill it, and he who defiles sacred fords.
A thief, a slanderer, one who lives off women, and a doer of evil; one who obstructs a gift to the fire, to a cow, or to a Brāhmaṇa. (47.12)
That lowest of men who sells his own wife or his offspring, or who steals the sacred fires, the ritual vessels, or anything whatsoever belonging to yogins; 47.13.
Or he who favors thieves, as well as those men who are appointed over Brahmins and those appointed over the administration of dharma. (47.14)
He who possesses a tawny cow, a Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire, one who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice in vain, and one who serves food at the daily rites—[these four are equal]. (47.15)
The man who contemplates the slaughter of princes, as well as famine, the ruin of the kingdom, the loss of his wife, and the loss of his wealth— (47.16)
And whoever should cause the destruction of a country or perform acts of sorcery—
all of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
Whoever should hear this constantly will certainly abide with a mind fixed on the Dharma; he shall not go to that terrifying Raurava hell, nor to the fierce Ugraraurava. (47.18)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Mahāraurava," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 47.44.
The forty-eighth chapter. Suśarman said:
There is another terrible hell, most fearsome, named Tamas.
There, as soon as he has flown down, he is struck by the rākṣasas.
With swords, mallets, and the points of spikes; with clubs, pestles, and battle-axes; with terrifying iron bars, chisels, thunderbolts, spears, and hatchets.
Struck by others in various ways who are enraged and utterly merciless,
he faints and, seized by darkness, falls into that hell.
With his body destroyed and his form stupefied by darkness, bound by a continuous succession of suffering, he undergoes intense torment.
Because that living being, seized by darkness and lacking any consolation, undergoes most terrible torment, for that reason it is called "darkness" (tamas). 48.5.
The wicked-minded one experiences there all those various kinds of torments that have been proclaimed, as a result of his own evil deeds.
Even when one has reached the end of the cycle of rebirth and crossed over by means of one's own karma,
a living being, bound by the fetters of karma, is made to rise up once again.
The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of an embryo, the drinker of liquor, and that lowest of men who [pollutes] the watering place of cows when they are thirsty—[these four are equal]. (48.8)
He who, blinded by delusion, creates obstacles and reviles [the guest] after having invited him;
he who constantly hates brahmins and he who insults a petitioner—[these are the ones who suffer]. (48.9)
He who steals the scriptures, the man remembered as a cow-killer, the follower of Kapila, one of vain views, and the defiler of the purpose of Vedic dharma; || 48.10 ||
Those who revile Brahmins, those who corrupt the meaning of the Vedas and the Dharma, and those atheists who consider themselves gods—these indeed go to that [place]. 48.11.
He who, with senses ever vigilant, should hear this [work] composed of darkness, shall never go to that hell composed of darkness which brings grief to cruel beings. (48.12)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Tamas," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 48.41.
The forty-ninth chapter.
Suśarman said:
Listen further to that most terrible hell, even more profound than darkness.
Where there is no light at all, vision does not function.
As soon as he falls there, the man is rendered unconscious by the demons of deformed appearance; therefore, it is called tamas. (49.2)
