There, that fool, having fallen, is intensely burned by fire;
then, rising up again with speed, he is sightless and unconscious.
He is indeed cut and torn apart by Rākṣasas of cruel deeds;
thus afflicted, he likewise flees from that place to another region.
There too, restrained by them, he is killed like a sacrificial animal;
then once more, unconscious, he is thrown into wells and inaccessible places.
Sinking into the fire-ash pit, he is born there without making a sound;
thus, having experienced many such tortures, he remains deeply afflicted by suffering.
Having reached the end of hell, he is cast down upon the elevations;
so too is one who causes abortions or who is greedy for sovereignty. (49.7)
Right here, this unworthy servant, intent on the king's slaughter, is one who, being no teacher himself, undertakes the work of teachers. (49.8)
He who would destroy the sciences of the treatises and medicines along with their antidotes for diseases, and he who praises the Dānavas.
And that preceptor who, out of hatred, does not provide instruction,
goes to a terrible, difficult-to-cross hell filled with darkness.
Having fully judged the ungrateful person, all those denizens of hell,
together with the servants of Yama, bow down to Yama and speak.
"O Blessed One, we are not capable of destroying this evil;
please show us favor, O Lord, and look for another means here. (49.12)
Thus addressed, the Blessed Yama, lord of the pretas,
then questioned those most excellent sages who were skilled in the meaning of all dharmas.
"Venerable sirs, how can there be atonement for this ungrateful and evil-minded man for his most terrible sinful deed? (49.14)
Then all those sages, having beheld Yama, the best among the upholders of dharma, with their far-reaching vision, spoke these words.

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for the breaker of vows, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
Then that blessed Lord, the excellent son of Mārtaṇḍa, gave his command to the denizens of hell: "All of you, [bring] this man! (49.17)
"You shall purify yourselves; go, for it is taught that his destination is not one.
Then, at his word, those hell-beings [addressed] the evildoer.
All these extremely cruel beings torment [the sinner] in succession;
[so too do] he who steals the food provided by his master and he who steals the ancestral offerings due to his father.
Therefore, he who, having received the sacred knowledge, does not bestow the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), [is at fault]. || 49.20 ||

He who does not follow one who has been nourished, he who causes such a person to be slain, he who speaks of the fault of what was done, and he who does not fulfill his own desire—[these are the four]. (49.21)

He who does not remember what has been done for him, who defiles the stages of life (āśramas), and likewise fails to support his draft animals, those who have sought refuge with him, and those who have rendered him assistance; || 49.22 ||
Likewise, he who speaks jesting words to his servants who are devoted to their duties and act for his benefit, as well as to his wife and his laborers; ||| 49.23 ||
Manu declared that all those who say, "Nothing was given, nothing was offered in sacrifice to him," are ungrateful, along with the ṛṣis. (49.24)
The ungrateful, the deceitful, the atheist, and the one whose doubts have been severed—all these who have been mentioned by me fall into these [states]. 49.25.
The progenitor, the one who performs the initiation, the one who imparts knowledge,
the protector from fear, and the giver of food— these five are remembered as fathers.
One who speaks of their faults, who is envious, and likewise one who is intent on malice—one should utterly abandon those lowest of men. (49.27)
A treacherous friend, wicked-souled, whose secret faults are made public, and he who does not return a kindness nor act kindly toward one who has previously rendered him assistance; (49.28)
All these men are wicked; they are all devoted to what is unwholesome. Bound by their sinful deeds, they fall into the hells.
All these whom I have described go to the great hells; so too do those other men who commit evil deeds and undergo the process of rebirth.
Whoever should hear or recite this terrible account of darkness,
unrighteousness shall turn away from them, and they shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Darkness Beyond Darkness," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. 49.39.
Fifty-first Chapter.
Hereafter I shall explain the revolution of worldly existence (saṃsāra), how those who have indeed crossed over from hell transmigrate in brief. 50.1.
Those who were described by me as being in the first hell due to their watery deeds,
however, are born in the wombs of worms because of the remainder of their karma.
Having returned to birth in the womb of worms for hundreds of thousands of years,
they are then born again as monkeys and then as hyenas.
When they are subsequently born among cattle, then, after a hundred births remaining there, they are liberated from that state. (50.4)
They are born among human beings; of this there is no doubt.
There, they commit no further sin whatsoever.
Then they indeed obtain a pure birth once again;
they shall never again encounter the terrible cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
But in the second [birth], they were declared by me to be liberated from their remaining karma;
yet they are born among worms and insects for six hundred thousand times.
Likewise, they go again for a hundred times ten thousand;
they are born from the womb of a fish for that very same duration, of this there is no doubt.
Then they become tigers and bears, and from that state they attain the condition of cattle;
then they are reborn among humans, but as contemptible beings due to their own past actions.
But as for those whom I have described in the third [chapter] as doers of evil deeds,
they are released from that karma, though still enveloped by its remainder.
They are born as worms and insects for six hundred thousand times, and likewise for ten thousand other births, and for exactly that same number of times they become birds.
Then there were lions, serpents, cattle, and subsequently humans;
and those who were described by me as the fourth group, the doers of evil deeds.
All of them, however, are born with their karma remaining in the wombs of worms—
eight hundred thousand and another sixteen thousand times over.
For from those wombs they are born again as deer;
and when released from their state as deer, they are born once more as donkeys.
Then the goats and the gavayas, and thereafter the cows, and those who were mentioned by me as being in the fifth [state], they too [attain] human status through the remainder of their karma.
Indeed, they are born among worms and insects for ten million lifetimes,
and likewise for that same duration among elephants, camels, and horses.
Then, having attained the state of a cow, they obtain human birth,
being liberated from the sixth [debt] by means of their remaining karma.
Indeed, by doubling the number of births, they are born among worms and insects; then for ten million births they become lice, then fish, and then pigs.
Having attained the state of a buffalo thereafter, one is born as a human from the state of a cow;
in the human state, one is born wretched and indeed afflicted by disease.
Released from the seventh [state], he is born among worms and insects;
for exactly three ten-million-fold periods, he attains the state of a tree.
From that he becomes a creeper, from that a shrub, and from that an elephant is born;
having attained the state of a cow, he is thereafter born as a human being.
Released from the eighth [birth], yet bound by the remainder of his karma,
he is born among worms and insects for two hundred million and twice that many [lives].
Thereafter, by way of medicinal herbs, among shrubs and kuśa grass;
then, released from the state of a cow, he is born as a contemptible man. (50.23)
Even after emerging from the ninth hell, being bound by the remainder of his karma,
he is born among worms and insects for five crores of years, and thereafter as a bird.
Then he indeed becomes a fish for that long, then likewise a reptile;
then for that same duration he becomes a dog, and thereafter he becomes a kinnara.
Released from the state of being a kiṃnara, he is then born among cattle;
thereafter, released from the womb of a cow, he is born among human beings.
Having transcended even ten crores of births as a worm due to the remainder of his karma, he was thereafter born as a monkey. (50.27)
For that long he was a monkey here, for that long a cock, for that long a crow, and likewise a jīvañjīvaka bird.
He is born as a tree, a child, a cat, and an ant;
thereafter, having been born among cattle, he is born among human beings.
Released from Mahāraurava, he remains in great misery for seventy million births;
born among worms and insects, he then attains the state of a fish.
Then he becomes a dog, a donkey, a crane, and a parrot;
after that he becomes a cow, and then a eunuch among humans. (50.31)
Released from those dark hells, the creature, still deeply afflicted by suffering, undergoes eighty million births as a worm in excrement.
Then he is born again as a dog, and repeatedly as a cakravāka crane;
thereafter, having attained the state of a frog, he is born among beasts and birds.
He is born as a kinnara, and also as a leopard and a śarabha;
thereafter, having attained the state of a cow, he reaches human status.
Released from the Tamonaraka hell, he is indeed born among worms and insects for ninety million births due to the remainder of his very same karma.
From that he becomes a crow, and after that a vulture;
then he becomes an eater of vomit, and thereafter again a bird, an owl.
Furthermore, he becomes a tree and a shrub, and then indeed a wild animal; thereafter he becomes a cow and a human, and then he perishes while remaining in the womb.
Being born again and again for a hundred thousand years,
he is born repeatedly as one afflicted by disease and full of loathsomeness.
But he who, having experienced all these hells, is born here again,
undergoes the entirety of transmigratory existence within all wombs.
If, after the lapse of time, he should ever attain human status,
even there he repeatedly enters a contemptible womb.
Unwelcome to all beings, suffering and likewise afflicted by disease,
he assumes a deformed appearance through his own past actions, being thus tormented.
He was a hater of gods and Brahmins, excluded from all vows,
devoid of all dharma, and bereft of virtuous conduct.
One who offers no salutation, is of immoral conduct, reviles the Vedas,
does not frequent sacred fords or temples, and is devoid of the utterances *svadhā* and *svasti*,
becomes unworthy of praise among people by his own karma. (50.43)
Suśarman said:
"O son, all this has been told to you in its entirety and in brief—the true nature of the hells and the distinctions between their stages, according to my understanding. (50.44)

Sanatkumāra said: He who, being disciplined, should always listen to this on every sacred festival day (parvan), or should properly cause the twice-born to hear it, is liberated from all sins. (50.45)
It brings merit, fame, long life, and heaven; it accomplishes all goals.
It should be heard and constantly recited by one who desires prosperity. (50.46)

But this [work], which brings about all goals and happiness, which is eternal, of great power, bestowing a happy rebirth, and auspicious—having studied it, a Brahmin with a concentrated mind should always retain it; for it is certain and equal to the Vedas. 50.47.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Course of Saṃsāra," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 50.50 ||
The fifty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, Sukeśa, having then heard [this] from his father like one deeply distressed, [proceeded].
Distressed, he then reflected upon that destiny of living beings.
His soul overwhelmed by anxiety and struck down by sorrow, his mind bewildered, he did not perceive the means for the liberation of living beings. (51.2)
But when he, having fallen into deep thought, did not speak to those ancestors, then all those ancestors spoke thus to Sukeśa: || 51.3 ||
The ancestors said:
"Why do you worry so excessively? O sinless one, from what cause does this anxiety come to you?
O son, since you are a lord, this [sorrow] is not ordained for you. (51.4)
Sukeśa said:
Having heard what you have described regarding the suffering of living beings born of their own actions, I reflect upon how there might be a means for their liberation. (51.5)
The ancestors said:
"O son, disregarding decay, there is no liberation for them; for it is held that in this world, the exhaustion of one's own performed karma occurs only through its experience. (51.6)
And the experience [of suffering] in hell is inevitably ordained for living beings;
nor can those denizens of hell be removed without the exhaustion of their karma. (51.7)
Indeed, a wise person should not undertake those goals which are impossible to achieve;
for just as one who attempts to cross the ocean meets with death, so does he who pursues the unattainable.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, that radiant one, his heart overwhelmed by longing for them, bowed down and said, "Do not treat me with contempt, for I am indeed your son. (51.9)
What power do I have to forcibly deliver those beings to auspiciousness?
It is the grace of Mahādeva that will deliver them from their miserable states.
Just as you have crossed over, so too shall all those creatures dwelling in hell, though they are bewildered, cross over; of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that high-souled leader of the Gaṇas, having taken leave of them,
entered the waters of the ocean and remained within the depths of the sea.
The pure-souled one, motionless and well-composed, recited the Rudra hymns; as that great-souled one was thus engaged in yoga while chanting, || 51.13 ||
O Vyāsa, the entire triple world was scorched by his ascetic power;
thereupon all the gods then spoke to the Grandfather.
"What is this, Blessed One? We are all tormented and rendered helpless.
Whose power of asceticism is this? Whose yoga is such as this? (51.15)
"O tiger among gods, who is this that performs such severe penance, as long as he does not burn [us] and as long as he does not become enraged? (51.16)
"O Lord, fulfill all his desires for as long as he lives.
Thus addressed by those gods, the Blessed One, the best of deities, [consented].
He said, "Let there be no fear for you; this is no one who is not esteemed.
He is that very leader of the hosts (Gaṇanāyaka), the high-souled one of the God of gods."
Seated within the waters at the edge of the ocean, the practitioner of yoga mutters the Rudra hymns;
yet, O mighty ones, his intention toward the worlds is not malicious.
He intends to rescue these denizens of hell from their infernal state;
therefore, if you so desire, go and pay homage to Rudra. (51.20)
"We request that a desired boon be granted to this god.
"So be it," they all replied, having come together with Brahmā. (51.21)
Having gone to Mount Mandara unperturbed and being ushered in by Nandin,
they beheld the Lord Īśāna and, having praised the All-pervading One, spoke as follows.
The blessed Sukeśa, your beloved leader of the Gaṇas,
having shown compassion for living beings, performs difficult austerities.
O Lord of the World, fulfill their desire;
having heard their petition, Bhava, the God of gods, then [acted].
Accompanied by Brahmā and others, he then approached Sukeśa;
the ocean and other sages of celebrated vows were also there.
Taking up the water for honor by the hundreds, they bowed to Śaṅkara who had arrived;
then the God of gods spoke these words to him, the foremost of the Gaṇapas.
Vyāsa spoke sweetly, bringing pleasure to the mind and ear:
"Child, arise, O Sukeśa; ask for whatever you desire. (51.27)
"I shall grant all of that to you, for you are indeed like Nandin to me.
Then Sukeśa, having risen and offered praise to the bull-bannered god, [departed].
Having prostrated, he again requested his previously desired wish:
"O God, men who have committed evil deeds go to the hells. (51.29)
O Lord, my heart is tormented with grief for them;
O Master of the World, how may they all be liberated? (51.30)
"Act accordingly for me this very day; this is the boon I have requested.
O Lord, as for those men who are currently being cast into the hells," || 51.31 ||
"O Lord of the Gods, I entreat you for their sake that they may be liberated.
Then the God, granting what was requested, spoke these words: || 51.32 ||
"Let it be so for you, my child; the men in the hells are released.
And by this [act] of yours, as well as by Kāṇḍarūya, you have become beloved. (51.33)
"Be entirely free from anxiety, endowed with supreme sovereignty.
Then all those denizens of hell ascended their celestial chariots.
Then, having approached the God of gods, they bowed down to Sukeśa;
and the Lord spoke again to Sukeśa, the leader of the hosts.
For he who delivers even some living beings from calamities,
having become their father in dharma, does not behold saṃsāra again.
For even that righteous being who, with his mind alone, always desires to liberate creatures from their afflictions,
is himself liberated from all sufferings.
And he who, having acquired merit for himself, bestows it upon living beings for their happiness, he too is completely liberated from all sufferings. (51.38)
Endowed with supreme yoga and sovereignty, you are dedicated to the deliverance of living beings; who else on earth is equal to you? (51.39)
Sukeśa said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace all this shall come to pass for me.
But from where would I have the power, O God? It was by you alone, O Lord, that this was brought about. (51.40)
Yet there is another task to be done, which is in my heart;
I am your servant and slave—there is nothing surprising in this for me. (51.41)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, that blessed Lord, having dismissed the leader of the Gaṇas,
went to Mount Mandara, surrounded by all the immortals.
Even the gods, having beheld from all sides the hell-beings situated in their celestial chariots, and seeing that the suffering of the world had been stilled, departed as they had come. (51.43)
Whoever should hear or recite this "Extraction from Hell" shall never despair, even when encountering suffering.
Having heard this entire ritual procedure of Yoga, even a man who is sinful by nature or utterly merciless shall never again encounter the terrifying refuge of evil.

However, he who approaches this [teaching] here constantly endowed with purity, and being firmly devoted to Śaṅkara, recites it in an assembly of gods, Brahmins, and physicians—[attains the highest state]. (51.45)
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation from Hell," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 51.51 ||
Fifty-second Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Furthermore, which doers of auspicious deeds do not go to that hell?
O Brahmin, even those who delight in evil deeds—this is what I wish to know.
Likewise, what is the most excellent and auspicious destiny for women? By what ripening of karma does this come to pass? This I wish to know. (52.2)
Sanatkumāra said:
O giver of honor, hear from me about those men who, though devoted even to sinful deeds, do not go to that hell of extreme suffering. 52.3.
One who maintains the sacred fires does not go to hell, nor does one who wears the triple thread, nor one who observes the cow-vow,
nor he who has performed the horse-sacrifice, nor he who has bestowed a thousand cows.

Nor [is there merit for] that twice-born man who is constant in private Vedic recitation, nor for one who mutters the Rudra hymns, nor for one who delivers Brāhmaṇas from calamities ending even in death. (52.5)
A man who is devoted to this duty should attend upon a Brahmin who is diseased, distressed, helpless, and oppressed by suffering. || 52.6 ||
He who provides a dwelling for a Brahmin who is destitute yet endowed with Vedic study, by means of household requisites, does not behold hell.
Likewise, he who, with a disciplined mind, protects a cow that has sunk down, fallen, and is deprived of strength, does not go to that [hell]. || 52.8 ||
And he who would constantly worship Maheśa with supreme devotion, with a state of being, and with meditative concentration—he likewise does not go there. (52.9)
But for others, transmigration certainly occurs; there is no doubt about this. Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas do not go there. || 52.10 ||
O Vyāsa, they were devoted to the six duties, established in their own dharma,
endowed with austerity and purity, compassionate, and firm in their vows.
Those twice-born ones who have desisted from accepting gifts and are devoted to the Lord, and those Kṣatriyas who are constantly intent upon the protection of their subjects; || 52.12 ||
Those who give up their lives in battle do not go to hell;
nor do the Vaiśyas who are devoted to their livelihood and established in justice and righteousness. (52.13)
Those whose livelihood is uninterrupted and who worship the gods and Brahmins do not see hell; they are proclaimed to be destined for heaven.
Those devotees of the three castes who are free from pride, and especially those Śūdras who constantly serve the Brāhmaṇas; || 52.15 ||
They do not perceive hell nor the happy realms; having died, they go to auspiciousness among men of all four castes through their inner disposition.
Those devotees who have dedicated all their actions and states to Śarva, who are constant and ever-vowed to Him, do not go to hell; they attain the supreme goal.
Those who, having constructed a temple, worship the God of gods,
they indeed deliver their ancestors from hell as well.
Those by whom lotus ponds, reservoirs, and lakes were excavated, and those by whom groves of trees were planted—even they do not go there. (52.19)
Those who constantly provide protection for the twice-born and for others who are suffering likewise do not go there. (52.20)
Those who are ever free from anger, who constantly worship the gods and the Brahmins,
and who are always devoted to giving— they do not go to a downward state.
Those who are devoted to speaking the truth, who avoid harmful undertakings, and who are engaged in the practice of their own duty— such people do not see hell.
Therefore, one who is devoted to the worship of the Liṅga is liberated from everything;
indeed, he who is pure and always meditative or recites the names of the Gaṇas [is likewise freed]. || 52.23 ||
But the yogi, even while performing acts as small as mustard seeds, is not defiled;
for women, the husband is always their supreme deity. (52.24)
Therefore, those who reflect upon the Dharma perceive nothing else superior to that which one gives or offers as an oblation through action, mind, or speech.
A woman who abandons her husband does not enjoy the fruit thereof; rather, she who is devoted to the service of her husband through the actions of mind, speech, and body [reaps the reward]. 52.26.
Even when her husband has died, she who does not desire another man even in her mind,
and who performs whatever merit there is for her husband and offers it all to him—
that woman does not go to any of the hells, even in thought. (52.27)
She does not at all encounter the entire terrors of saṃsāra;
but for others, O observer of noble vows, there is no doubt regarding hell.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus shown favor to Sukeśa, the Lord who has the bull as his vehicle departed for the hermitage of Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
He showed favor to that brahmin Kāṣṭhakūṭa, whose wealth was his asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, what was the asceticism of that high-souled Brāhmaṇa, and in how much time did he obtain a boon from Maheśvara? 52.30
Whose son was he, whose grandson was he, and what was the name of that most excellent being?
O Blessed One, I desire this auspicious account to be told by you in detail. (52.31)
Sanatkumāra said:
In the lineage of Gautama, there was a lordly Brahmin named Kṛṣṇa;
his son was the renowned Bhūmanyu by name. (52.32)
He had a wife named Sukhṛt, a daughter of Atri, who was renowned by the name Yaśas.
Once, after having performed his marriage, that Gautama named Bhūmanyu—
Enveloped by old age, he found no son through her;
afflicted by sorrow, that man, skilled in speech, spoke these words to his wife.
"Through a son, they desire the worlds and indeed become free from debt;
yet I have reached old age and no son is seen by me.
Therefore, O auspicious one, being permitted by me, you should [obtain] some kinsman of my own lineage."
"Enter [the womb], O son; I entreat you with palms joined and body bowed."
Suyaśā said:
"O sinless one, I have not heard this from you, nor has it been spoken by you in such a manner;
for how could one like me even contemplate this in her mind? (52.37)
Born into the lineage of the Atris, I have entered the family of Gautama;
how could one such as I commit this act, which is censured by the virtuous? (52.38)
One should seek wealth, lives, and pleasures through austerity; one should seek sons, family, and lineages through austerity. O great sage, practice austerity! 52.39.
For by means of austerity Śakti obtained that son Parāśara, and the great sage Cyavana obtained Aurva through his own austerity. (52.40)
And Vasiṣṭha begot Indrapramati upon Kapiñjalī, while Śilāda likewise produced his son Nandin through ascetic penance.
In the same way, may you also perform penance with perfect concentration;
you shall obtain an excellent son endowed with the power of great yoga.
"For in the past, upon seeing me, Atri himself, the son of Brahmā, said:
'This woman shall become the mother of a virtuous son'; that shall not prove false."
"Whatever ascetic merit I have acquired through your grace, O Lord, endowed with that and with my own, worship Rudra. (52.44)
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, that radiant one, filled with supreme shame and permitted by her in this manner, went for refuge to Rudra. (52.45)
Having arrived at the Narmadā quickly and filled with joy,
he sat down upon its bank and remained there for years subsisting only on air.
But that brahmin did not at all achieve his purpose by that deed;
thereupon, becoming even more distressed, he remained steadfast in the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, after one year, the powerful Lord said to him:
"O Brahmin, why do you afflict yourself in this way? You have no son anywhere."
"This sacrifice of yours is in vain, for you have no son, O sinless one.
Thus addressed, he became despondent and lost all hope of obtaining a son.
He reflected upon death rather than returning to his own home;
gathering wood and taking fire, he was deeply distressed. (52.50)
Lamenting, afflicted by manifold sorrows, he desired to burn himself;
and Rudra, perceiving that most difficult resolve of his, [acted]. (52.51)
"O son! O son!"—thus an invisible voice spoke deeply:
"A son shall be born to you; go now, and do not act with such rashness. (52.52)
"And that son of yours shall be known by the name Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
Then, with a joyful heart, the brahmin of great asceticism went and [conceived] in his wife.
He begot a son, the great sage Kāṣṭhakūṭa;
then, with the passage of time, the thought occurred to him regarding that which is conditioned.
"This father of mine is unable to teach me due to his old age;
therefore, having taken leave of my father, I shall go for the sake of the Vedas."
Having gone there, that illustrious brahmin, having properly bowed his head to his mother and father, spoke these words: || 52.56 ||
"I was born of you two for the sake of dharma, not out of desire;
and he shall likewise be the deliverer of us both and of our ancestors. (52.57)
And our lineage shall continue without interruption, of this there is no doubt;
we shall both attain the desired worlds by means of a worthy son in every way.
"I am your son, born as you both desired, so that we two might be free from debt to our ancestors;
yet I am unskilled in the duties of dharma and excluded from the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti. (52.59)
"Because of the ignorance of the doer, the ancestors were made miserable by that deed;
and you yourself shall remain submerged in hell for a long time like a wicked man. (52.60)
"Because of your old age, you will not be capable of teaching day after day;
and due to affection for your son and because of your duties, you will not retain [the knowledge] properly. (52.61)
Moreover, this mother of mine will never consent to my being properly governed by you, thinking, "This one is her only son."
"Therefore, it is my resolve that I shall seek out another preceptor who is constantly devoted to asceticism, utterly merciless, and endowed with wisdom. (52.63)
Nor do I determine that there is no one among you two who would constantly perform service at my feet; thinking thus, [I have come]. (52.64)
And it was not that I did not declare this to you both; whatever thought I have formed, whether auspicious or even inauspicious, you two are my supreme refuge. (52.65)
When they had been addressed thus by their high-souled son,
the parents stood for a moment with eyes filled with tears,
and then, having smelled his head, embraced him, and wiped him out of affection for their beloved son, they spoke as follows.
Bhūmanyu said:
"O son, service to the ancestors is of two kinds, which is in accordance with dharma;
it must be performed with diligent effort by a high-souled son. (52.67)

Service to one's elders in this world and the gift of dharma in the next—by these the ancestors cross over and obtain imperishable desires. Of these, we do not desire that which pertains to this world as much as that which is beneficial for the life hereafter. (52.68)
Therefore, perform those actions which bear fruit in the world beyond;
go and study both the Śruti and the Smṛti of those who have performed virtuous deeds.
Suyaśā said:
"O son, act in such a way that this father of yours, who has realized the self, may speak as he does;
act so that Lord Bhava may become the granter of boons to you."
O Mahāmati, you were carried in my womb with great suffering;
likewise, you were obtained through many hardships for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Your father, having abandoned his life-breaths—which are exceedingly difficult to give up—through fierce asceticism, obtained you from Mahādeva; therefore, act in a manner worthy of him.
"O son, act in such a way that we both may become like Tuṣṭi and Jīva, who were reunited with their own life-breath. (52.73)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, permitted by them and having had his head smelled [as a blessing], he, being self-realized, circumambulated them and departed. (52.74)
Dismissed by those two, he then went toward Cyavana,
like a sacrificial oblation offered by the Rig and Yajur Vedas proceeding toward Varuna.
Having approached him, he was made successful by that [sage] who was pleased,
just as a mantra preceded by ritual recitation becomes effective when it attains its allotted portion from the gods.
Then, when his son had departed, the father met his end;
thereafter, Kāṣṭhakūṭa returned, having acquired learning and being very righteous.
He saw his mother, dejected like a lotus pond without water, like a night bereft of the moon, or like royal fortune deprived of its command;
weeping with eyes full of tears, lamenting, and deeply distressed. (52.78)

But Kāṣṭhakūṭa, seeing her overwhelmed with grief, spoke these words to her, just as Śakra spoke to Jayantī when Paulomī had been lost: 52.79. But Kāṣṭhakūṭa, seeing her overwhelmed with grief, spoke this, just as Śakra spoke to Jayantī when Paulomī had been lost.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"I have already heard this, and the funeral rites have indeed been performed.
Do not set your mind on grief; this is the eternal dharma. (52.80)
He was a refuge for the gods, the sages, and the high-souled yogis;
how much more so for mortals? O mother, do not grieve for that one whose wealth is asceticism.
"Indeed, I have been created as a self by that very Self through its own splendor;
behold me, O Gāyatrī, your son, who has accomplished his purpose."
All the Vedas have been studied by me, along with their limbs (Aṅgas) and sub-limbs (Upāṅgas), in full detail;
likewise, all the Upavedas and the entire science of the inner self (Adhyātma) as well.
Whatever is to be known by men, all that is indeed knowledge;
likewise, everything that is to be heard has been heard, and the yogis have also been worshipped.
Rejoicing with great intensity and filled with joy,
protect me, O Great Being, as Gāyatrī always protects the sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those truthful words of that high-souled one, his mother, weeping with even greater sorrow, spoke to him. (52.86)
Suyaśas said: "O son, this is not a source of grief to me that he is considered dead;
for this is ordained for all living beings who are subject to mortality. (52.87)
And that high-souled one, endowed with ascetic power, has accomplished his purpose;
indeed, there is nothing here for us to grieve for him.
"O son, I grieve for myself, who have been deprived of him;
I did not die following him because I was longing for your return. (52.89)
Neither wealth, nor enjoyments, nor kinsmen, nor sons,
nor even relatives remain there for women where the husband stands.
If there is a husband, then everything exists; without a husband, nothing exists at all. Indeed, everything brings suffering to those women who have no husband or son. (52.91)
And this is my further sorrow, that today I do not rejoice with you as I did before;
I am not thrilled like Śrī with Viṣṇu upon the birth of a son.
"For many times he said to me, 'Kāṣṭhakūṭa will come here;
once he has acquired learning, I shall choose a beautiful daughter-in-law for him. (52.93)
"This daughter of the merchant Kāśyapa is exceedingly virtuous;
I shall ask for that woman of noble vows from Kāṣṭhakūṭa."
Then I shall see that son of firm vows together with his wife;
indeed, having seen him accompanied by his wife, I shall bring back the sacred fires.
"When shall I, gratified by the marriage of my son, perform with both mind and speech many auspicious rites for my wife? (52.96)
Thus, for him who possessed his heart's desire, who was like a father to his son, and who loved his son dearly, this thought did not occur: "My son is burning me. (52.97)
Indeed, you were previously told by me while going into his presence: "May we both see you alive," but it did not happen so. (52.98)
"Today my heart, though made of the essence of diamond, does not shatter,
even though I see you here, O son, once again without him, as if I were unfaithful."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, like a highly renowned female osprey deprived of her mate, she,
afflicted by great sorrow, lamented and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Having burned her— who was afflicted by grief, fallen, lifeless, and unconscious— with fire, Kāṣṭhakūṭa lamented, deeply distressed.
"Alas, father! For me, who am of evil intellect and ignorant of righteousness—" || 52.102 ||
"Where have you gone? You do not speak with me today, even though you were accompanied by your wife. Did you not joyfully direct me, saying, 'Go and study'? (52.103)
"Thus have I come today after completing my studies; why do you not address me?
Surely you have obtained this through your asceticism and supreme meditative concentration. (52.104)
"I am indeed the son of Rudra, the God of gods; why do you not speak to me?
O sinless one, what harm have I done to you and your wife, my father? (52.105)
"Since you have come with my mother and do not greet me warmly at all—alas, I am ruined by this one wicked son of mine, this evil-souled one! (52.106)
"I consider this world to be without a king, since he does not slay me, a killer of my father.
Thus did Vyāsa lament, along with many other sages.
Once he had been established and consoled, that man of great asceticism performed no water-libation rites;
instead, he made this vow in the midst of the sages: || 52.108 ||
Having performed this difficult rite for all beings with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"From this day forward, I shall not take another breath under any circumstances."
The vital airs residing within my body shall never move again;
free from blinking or opening my eyes, with one foot planted and arms raised upward,
I shall become like wood, a clod of earth, or a stone— of this there is no doubt.
"As long as I do not behold Rudra, and likewise my father together with his wife, so long shall this vow of mine remain."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, while being watched by those sages, that great ascetic remained right there, constantly meditating upon Maheśvara.
O Vyāsa, although the god Śaṅkara remained thus pleased by his devotion to his father, on the eighth day he spoke to him himself.
The God of gods said:
"O sinless Kāṣṭhakūṭa, I grant you divine vision.
Behold me with full confidence, for I am invisible even to yogins. (52.114)
"Speak, my son, whatever boon is held in your heart;
I shall grant it to you, there is no doubt. Having reflected well, tell me."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen the Lord of Gods appearing like the rising sun,
he fell at his feet in joy and spoke these words in a melodious voice.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"O Blessed One, my mother and father have been joined with death by Time;
O Lord, I desire this boon that both of them may live. (52.117)
The God of gods said:
"Both of them have fallen into a terrible hell, tormented by death;
they cannot be brought back to life again. Choose something else from me."
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"O Lord, I do not desire any other boon under any circumstances;
this undertaking is for the sake of my father, so please grant it. Salutations to you. (52.119)
The God of Gods said: "If the body of one who has died still exists, it is indeed possible to unite it with life this very day; however, this is not possible for one who has been cremated."
They have no body, nor likewise any other instrument;
as your father is in respect of his body, so are you.
Grant this body to them, and then they shall both become living beings.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"There is indeed nothing to be done by those two; yet, if it be thought that something must be done, the rising of Dhruva is seen even without a body. (52.122)
"Moreover, O Lord, I have no pleasure in this body without those two;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, take my body if you so deem it right."
"This has arisen from his very limbs, limb by limb;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, grant me this, for I have no need for him. (52.124)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord, the best of sages, smiling with a pleased soul and desiring to unite him with auspiciousness, replied thus.
The God of gods said:
"O son, best among those who follow the path of dharma, this test has been conducted upon you.
I am thoroughly pleased by this devotion to your father; listen to my words. (52.126)
Inexhaustible and imperishable, free from old age and death,
and endowed with sovereign power— you, my beloved, shall become the leader of my hosts.
Known as Kāṣṭhakūṭa, endowed with the power of all yogas,
you shall travel in a celestial chariot created by me that moves according to your will.
And all these sages, ascetics in this hermitage,
shall become your attendants and lords of the Gaṇas.
They shall be indeed inexhaustible and immutable, endowed with the power of great yoga, and equal in sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
And this father of yours, O son Bhūmanyu, together with his wife,
has arrived, having become your very own attendant and being equal to you.
And I bestow upon you the divine white mountain, adorned with celestial chariots,
moving at will, and resembling heaven itself, as your dwelling place.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, having bestowed his grace upon that powerful one, went back to Mandara, while he [the other] returned to his desired place. 52.133.
While the queen, engaged in asceticism, remained upon the mountain peak of her father,
the god performed all this that has indeed been described.
The man who hears this account of the deeds of the God of gods,
or causes it to be heard by the twice-born, shall not fall into an evil state.
Constantly studying this, pure and with a restrained mind,
one attains the dissolution of the body and goes to the world of Rudra.
He who recites this supreme means of attaining proximity to Rudra, which destroys many evils and accomplishes the success of one's hosts, shall not experience a miserable rebirth when he dies.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Great Fortune of Kāṣṭhakūṭa," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 52.52 ||
The fifty-third chapter.
Vyāsa said:
She is indeed the goddess, the blessed one, the daughter of Himavat, the imperishable.
For how long did he practice that most difficult austerity?
And how did she, the kindler of hundreds of boons, obtain that boon?
O best of the twice-born, I wish for all this to be told.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen; after some time had passed, the Goddess performed a most difficult penance, becoming self-restrained with palms joined in reverence and thus concentrating her mind. (53.3)
Fixing her gaze and her mind upon the sun,
she stood with unblinking eyes, as if bound to a tree by wooden pegs.
Gazing at the sun with her face turned upward, she remained standing on one foot with her arms raised, holding her breath. (53.5)
For a thousand divine years, she remained motionless like a stone;
accompanied by a tiger, Rudrāṇī was devoted to austerity and observed auspicious vows.
Neither did she suffer from exhaustion, nor was there any loss of strength;
for that queen remained as steadfast in her asceticism as before.
By the power of her asceticism, the entire world, including all things stationary and moving, remained as if struck by non-existence and overwhelmed by distress. (53.8)
The sun was not overly bright, nor did the moon shine; the stars became obscured by darkness, and the Siddhas did not travel through the sky. 53.9.
Their celestial garlands withered and their aerial chariots fell;
even in heaven they found no happiness, and a sense of longing arose within them.
All the quarters of space and the entire triple world are smoking;
the movement of the Vidyādharas is broken, and their weapons are blazing.
Deer, tigers, lions, cats, owls, mice,
serpents, and mongooses were also wandering together in one place.
Then all the gods, having assembled together, said to one another:
"This reversal seen in these three worlds cannot be without cause."
There must be a great cause here; this cannot be without a cause.
Therefore, being unaware of this total reversal, we have come to this state.
"What shall we do, remaining thus agitated? Let us go into the presence of Brahmā.
Having said this, all those gods, led by Bṛhaspati, [set out].
Having gone to the palace of Vairāja, they paid homage to Brahmā;
duly honored by Brahmā, they sat down according to their rank.
When questioned by him regarding the cause of their arrival, those afflicted by grief at heart said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, the true nature of the world is as if directly perceived by you."
"O Lord, tell us why this world has become so perverted today.
Having heard those words of the terrified ones, he who knows all yogas [replied].
He spoke these words, which were sweet, gentle, and profound:
"This divine lady, the daughter of Himavat, Rudrāṇī, the sustainer of the world, practices asceticism with a disciplined soul, established in unwavering yoga. (53.19)
Indeed, by means of her meditative absorption (samādhi), one thousand divine years have passed for her,
as well as two hundred years and another hundred autumns.
O gods, this is the power of the asceticism performed by her through yoga, by which the worlds have fallen into a state of reversal. (53.21)
The gods said:
"If, by her power, this great fear of portents has arisen, and she will burn the worlds even more than this, then restrain her. (53.22)
For that queen, endowed with ascetic power, will become even more radiant at night;
she would undoubtedly burn up these worlds along with us. (53.23)
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world and even at our word,
act in such a way that the virtuous and beautiful lady may turn back.
The Grandfather said:
"So be it; go, O sinless ones, and be at peace.
By means of this desired boon, I shall establish Rudrāṇī."
Then, after the gods had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
[ascended] a bright golden celestial chariot crowded with hundreds of altars.
It was bound with networks of small bells, illuminated by strings of pearls,
and featured pillars made of sapphire as well as lattices of gold.
It was surrounded on all sides by bells of manifold forms,
and illuminated by diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, great blue gems, and other jewels.
It was covered with suitable spires marked with crystal,
and that entire structure was made of metal, fashioned by the God himself.
For that [body] consists of the five elements and is situated in its natural state;
yet it is bound by the web of sound-phenomena, like the clear sound of a bell perceived by the auditory faculty.
That celestial chariot, possessing great radiance, was adorned with eight strings of pearls, encircled by sixteen small bells, and featured twenty altars.
It was adorned with divine jeweled floors possessing fifty thousand auspicious marks,
and it was furnished with many seats located throughout the various worlds.
Brahmā ascended that celestial chariot together with his sages,
as well as with the Vedas, the mantras, and all the Śāstras.
In its center was a divine, firm seat consisting of a golden lotus;
there sat comfortably Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
Beside him were Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, both of great luster;
the Ṛgveda was to his right, and the Yajurveda was to his west.
To the north was the Sāmaveda, and likewise, in front, the Atharvaveda;
there also were expiations, duties, observances, and austerities.
Various kinds of gifts, sacrifices, and likewise well-performed rites; the seven sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), as well as all the worlds in every respect. || 53.37 ||
The mountains and rivers, as well as the mothers of the world, the guardians of the world, the lords of creatures, Dakṣa, and likewise Dharma; 53.38.
Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Marīci, Aṅgiras, and the highly illustrious Ruci.
R̥bhu, Sanātana, and Virāja of great asceticism,
as well as the Pitṛs and the Devas— all these are the progeny of Brahmā.
Earth, wind, space, water, and likewise light;
these, as they have been enumerated, as well as the oceans and the directions. (53.41)
The sciences and the instruments of dharma stood before him,
as did the staff of Brahmā, the rod of punishment, and the golden water-pot.
A water-pot was at both his sides,
a splendid sacred thread was [around him], and likewise the syllable Om was before him.
The rosary, yoga, and the muttered prayer stood before him;
Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, Vauṣaṭ, and Agni were at his sides.
The restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), as well as many means of accomplishment—
all these [factors] of dharma then became his attendants.
Compassion, pity, generosity, and faith, together with modesty—
all these attendants of the sages are the sacrificial fees that attend the side of the sacrifice.
Then all the gods whatsoever who dwell in the world of Brahmā quickly ascended and took their positions on every side.
When they had thus all ascended that celestial chariot and were seated comfortably, Brahmā exhorted them.
Impelled by him, who was the foremost of those skilled in yoga and the possessor of a supreme great celestial chariot that travels everywhere,
he went with a power that follows the mind, just as the mind moves by the will of the Creator of All.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Departure of Brahmā," in the *Devīvarapradāna* section of the *Skandapurāṇa*.
The fifty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, by means of that celestial chariot, the four-faced creator of all went forth.
The wise one went to Mount Mandara, which possessed caves and boulders of various colors.
Having reached that vast, incomparable, and exceedingly radiant place,
which was pleasing to the sight from afar, he looked upon those seated in the assembly hall and spoke as follows.
Behold this auspicious abode of Rudra, invisible even to the doers of good deeds,
possessing a splendor like the form of the sun, and visible even to the gods.
Having entered this, the sacrificial glory of the gods does not depart;
there is constant victory in battles, and even very great righteousness. (54.4)
This was created by him himself through his mind, he of incomparable splendor;
for indeed, there exists no other dwelling in this egg that is equal to it.
Having entered this, the righteous-souled one does not experience suffering again;
nor does he undergo rebirth, for he has attained eternal sovereignty.
This is indefinable even for yogins constantly engaged in yoga; how then could anyone else, however great, describe it? (54.7)
Struck by the wind with fury, this [cloud] of our celestial chariot increases in size like the peak of Mount Vindhya together with its mountain mass.
This [being] stands obstructing the path of our celestial chariot,
both above, across, and below, by the splendor of the God of gods.
Having created this blinding darkness, that cloud itself, becoming a living being,
advanced against him with thundering noise, wearing a garland and holding a raised thunderbolt in its hand.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
having steadied that foremost of celestial chariots, stood there with palms joined in reverence.
And then all those sages, remaining well-restrained in their celestial chariots, praised the god Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair.
They illuminated the entire world, both the stationary and the moving;
then that cloud, having released its rain, returned to its own place.
All the quarters became stainless and a great light shone intensely;
and perceiving him engaged in silent recitation, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull appeared.
To Nandin, who was standing at the gateway, the Lord of the Gods said this:
"This Brahmā has arrived here in his celestial chariot to see me."
"Tell me for what purpose you have come here; I already know it.
Do that and depart quickly, for the time for it has now arrived."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by Rudra, Nandin, the leader of the Pramathas,
while remaining at the gate, spoke these words to Brahmā who was seated in his celestial chariot.
Nandi said:
"The Blessed One knows for what purpose you have come;
perform that task quickly, for the time for it has now arrived."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having offered salutations mentally to Śambhu and having performed a circumambulation, he departed for Mount Mandara.
Having bypassed the entire Mandara mountain, that high-minded one proceeded through the middle of Śākadvīpa and arrived at Jambūdvīpa.
Being gazed upon by the gods and by sages of restrained vows, he approached Himavat, the best of mountains, and spoke this: || 54.21 ||
This lofty, radiant peak of Himavat stands there;
from afar it is perceived as resembling the sun at the end of a cosmic age.
Here, the mountain-born goddess, the sustainer of the world, performs ascetic penance while protecting the entire universe as a mother protects her own biological son.
"Oh, how meritorious and fortunate indeed must this peak be in every respect, since the Destroyer of Desire will unite it with a bridegroom for the sake of the Mountain's Daughter! (54.24)
Behold the power of the penance of the goddess Su-carita, by which,
having seen this peak, we no longer behold rebirth.
Even as he was speaking thus, the four-faced god arrived at the gateway of Śikhara by means of his celestial chariot, accompanied by all the sages.
Then the attendants of Rudra, with weapons raised in their hands, rushed toward him, threatening him and crying out, "Stay! Stay! (54.27).
Brahmā, with palms joined and a disciplined mind, spoke to them in gentle words preceded by consolation, praising them all.
Brahmā said:
"All of you are high-souled and endowed with sovereign power; indeed, you are imperishable, immortal, and likewise unassailable."
Endowed with the power of great yoga, you are invincible by anyone in battle;
O supreme lords, who could surpass you, even Śakra himself?
"By the command of the God of gods, I have come here from Mount Mandara;
please grant me permission to bestow a boon upon the Goddess. (54.31)
The lords of the Gaṇas said:
"The high-minded God himself shall be the giver of the desired boons to the Goddess;
for the Goddess should not even mentally think of a boon from anyone else. (54.32)
The Lord Maheśvara is capable of bestowing grace upon the entire world;
he bestows grace upon you as well—how much more so, then, upon the Goddess, the mistress of the world?
The Grandfather said:
"The high-minded Mahādeva is incapable of granting a boon;
he who should think thus of the God would never [attain his goal] in any way. (54.34)
It is said that the goddess Pārvatī does not wish to receive desired boons from the presence of the Blessed One;
therefore, the god Śiva has sent me here.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those lords, with disciplined minds, beheld the Great Lord (Maheśvara) and the Guardian of the World (Lokapa), who had granted them permission. 54.36.
O great sage, having understood the matter, all those appointed lords of the hosts spoke again there to Brahmā, the cause of the world.
"O Grandfather, we have learned that you were sent by the God of gods;
O Lord, enter now into Pārvatī with the desire to grant her a boon."
Then, having quickly descended from the celestial chariot, the Grandfather alighted upon that mountain peak,
which was variegated with various minerals.
Then that king of mountains, possessing streams of precious minerals and consisting of a vast mass of great rocks,
shone forth like the divine mountain of sunrise when the sun has emerged from it, stainless and radiant.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Brahmā," in the *Devīvarapradāna* section of the *Skandapurāṇa*.
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the daughter of the Mountain saw him approaching suddenly.
He was surrounded on all sides by those highly fortunate sages.
Like the sun at midday, the source of all splendors, he was radiant with rays of light;
Rudrāṇī honored him as he approached with offerings of water for his feet, water for washing his feet, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka). (55.2)
Brahmā said:
Having become the mother of the world and having likewise sustained the universe, why do you now desire to burn the world here once more with your ascetic power? 55.3
Having created this world, do not destroy it by practicing asceticism;
having understood this, sustain this world, O Goddess—salutations to you!
O sinless goddess, bestower of boons, this world and I were created by Rudra from you in the past; do not destroy us after having brought us into being. (55.5)
O Rudrāṇī, by your ascetic power, the entire world, both mobile and immobile,
suffers as if it were a lotus uprooted from the water at the midday of summer.
"Or what is it in your heart, O Goddess, even if it be very difficult to accomplish?
Choose a boon; I shall grant you all of them, O daughter of Himavat. (55.7)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O four-faced God, if you are the granter of boons to me, then this devotee of mine, who is devoted and always dear to me, O Master. (55.8)
"First, seize this tiger; then you shall grant me a boon.
Today, it has indeed remained standing before me for a thousand years."
"O Lord of the World, grant a boon to this Nimiṣa who meditates with his ears fixed;
for I myself do not yet seek a boon. (55.10)
The Grandfather said:
"This wicked-souled beast has come here to devour you;
his mind is not pure, O Goddess, for he is cruel and evil-minded."
Behold this evil-minded one; his mind has no regard for your welfare.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard those words, Rudrāṇī, the creator of the worlds,
beheld with her divine eye that act of rashness committed out of ignorance.
Previously devoted to no other, yet defiled by the fault of her birth,
the daughter of Himavat then spoke after having come to understand the matter.
"O Blessed One, who indeed in the worlds, while existing in the state of an animal, remained motionless with ears and eyes fixed, even for a single divine day without food? (55.14)
Why would he, who possesses such great majesty, remain for a thousand years? He has not been born among the animals. || 55.15 ||
"Whether this one be evil-minded or not, let him be of great strength;
'he is to be favored by me'—let this boon indeed be granted to him. (55.16)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, the four-faced Grandfather,
spoke these words to the Goddess while the sages were listening.
Even outcasts may attain perfection here through association with the noble;
just as this man, though a doer of cruel deeds, shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
Therefore, noble ones should always be served even by one who has constantly committed evil;
for a man who stays near those who are sinless quickly attains perfection.
"O blameless one, this sinful man of wicked intent is worthy of your favor;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, grant him whatever boon pleases you."
The Goddess said:
"I am immortal, free from old age, inexhaustible, and likewise immutable;
I am endowed with the power of great yoga and possessed of great sovereignty."
And let this Lord of the Gaṇas be my beloved, if you so desire.
The Grandfather said:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours. All this shall come to pass.
Do you know the minister of Brahmadatta, that wretched Brahmin? || 55.22 ||
"Even in the past, he possessed devotion to you; yet, having fallen into the state of a tiger due to a curse, this Yakṣa formerly became the gatekeeper for Pāñcāla."
"Since such joy as this has been produced by you and me for his sake,
he shall therefore become famous by the name Somanandī."
Whoever should recite this in times of distress, in wildernesses, and in moments of fear—for him no fear arises from tigers, lions, or leopards. (55.25)
Speak also, O Īśānī, whatever is your cherished desire;
by my command as the Supreme Lord, I shall grant it all to you.
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, O Lotus-born, I desire a divine complexion with the luster of gold, and may I become renowned in the world as Gaurī. (55.27)
The Grandfather said:
"So be it, O Mother of the World, O you whose wealth is asceticism!
Choose another boon; may prosperity be yours, O Goddess, for I grant you a boon."
"Great indeed is this asceticism performed by you for the welfare of the world;
yet no suitable husband has been found for it, therefore let another be sought. (55.29)
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son who shall be the foremost among all upholders of dharma, possessed of great strength and great energy, and honored by all the worlds. (55.30)
The Grandfather said:
"O Goddess, a son shall be born to you, endowed with the power of great yoga,
unconquerable by all beings, and possessed of the eight qualities of sovereign power."
He who is the conqueror and likewise the teacher, is ageless and indeed unslayable;
he is forever incapable of being seized, the most excellent of all living beings.
He was always strong, moreover, fortunate, a knower of dharma, and a lover of dharma;
he was a protector of the gods and brahmins, learned, and indeed all-knowing.
He has six faces and twelve arms, and likewise holds a spear in his hand;
he is devoted to Brahman, a refuge for all, and the slayer of the hosts of those who hate the gods.
"Born not from a womb, possessed of great splendor, and indeed the bringer of happiness to the worlds," he said this slowly, and then he became silent.
Sanatkumāra said: Having granted those boons and having performed a circumambulation, the Lord of the Gods then ascended that celestial chariot and departed for his own world.
When he had departed, Rudrāṇī also, preceded by Somanandin and stationed in the sky,
shone like Śacī with Jayanta—
just so did Rudrāṇī appear, preceded by Somanandin. (55.38)
Whosoever, being wise and free from sloth, recites this every morning, for him Somanandin, the bestower of boons, and Hara, the son of Soma, shall indeed cause no fear. 55.39.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Somanandi and the Goddess," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 55.55 ||
The fifty-sixth chapter. Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, that which was previously described by you in the account of the hells—"
Having committed an evil deed, men indeed go to hell.
All those who have performed good deeds become endowed with the happiness of heaven;
whereas Brāhmaṇas, having committed evil deeds, go to a miserable state of suffering. (56.2)
How do they again attain the great fruit of heavenly happiness?
Or, having entered many wombs among the mixed castes, how do they once more become doers of good deeds and reach an auspicious destination? (56.3)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to this ancient account as it was heard among the Daśārṇas concerning the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of seven disciples of a twice-born man. (56.4)
There was a famous Brahmin named Suparvan, a descendant of Kuśika, who was pure, righteous, generous, wise, and honored by the learned brahmins. (56.5)
He indeed had seven disciples who were dull-witted; they were devoted to the service of their teacher. Learn their names from me.
Ātreya named Kaṇḍara, Upamanyu and Dāmana, Śāṇḍilya, Hāla, Gārgya, and likewise Vidala. (56.7)
Śauśira Gautama, Daṇḍakīla Kāśyapa,
Vidarbha, and Hārīta— these seven are renowned.
Then the preceptor, possessed of great ascetic power, said this to those brahmins:
"Having gone from here before long, [you shall find] Surūpī, who has been given as a sacrificial fee."
"Go quickly and bring [the fire] from the city of Māhiṣmatī for the sake of the oblation.
Thus addressed by him, those men set out from Māhiṣmatī without delay.
Returning from the land of Mṛttikāvatī after taking cattle,
they found themselves amidst a famine brought about by a drought.
Overcome by hunger, they all became eaters of anything whatsoever;
when the seventh day had arrived, being without food, they were deeply distressed.
They addressed this village, saying, "Let us eat; why do you sit idle?
Among them was one named Kaṇḍhara, born of the lineage of Atri.
He said to them: "Do not eat this cow of our preceptor;
for even death on account of the preceptor is praiseworthy for us, O simple ones. (56.14)
"Let us not go to our destruction, consumed by the anger of our preceptor!
But when they, being tormented by hunger, did not at all accept those words, || 56.15 ||
Then he spoke these meaningful words to them once more:
"O Brahmins, rich in asceticism, if it has been resolved by you that she is to be eaten, do not consume her in vain;
let us consecrate her for the sake of the ancestors."
O auspicious ones, let there not be a loss for us here through these two faults.
"In this way, we would be joined with a very small fault in every respect.
Having been addressed thus, they properly took to heart his words. (56.18)
Undistracted, they sprinkled that beautiful woman for the sake of the ancestors;
then, O great sage, having prepared her according to the rules, they offered her up.
Then, having offered oblations into the fire and each having partaken [of the meal],
they brought a single calf, tied by its neck, to their preceptor.
Then, seeing that calf, the brahmin asked the cow;
they, being heartless, replied, "A tiger killed her on the road."
Then, having heard their words and suspecting those evil-minded ones,
the great ascetic beheld with his divine eye that she had been devoured by them.
Then that righteous one, his eyes red with rage as if burning them up, spoke;
yet, seeing his child, he was deeply pained by compassion.
"She was indeed eaten by you, yet you did not tell me the truth;
therefore, because of that deed, your fate shall be miserable. (56.24)
Pleased by those disciples, that Brāhmaṇa of great splendor spoke these words again to them all out of compassion: || 56.25 ||
"What I have spoken is the truth; it shall not be false.
But as for those whom you have served, they shall determine what is auspicious. (56.26)
"You must not remain near me now under any circumstances.
Having seen this young calf, I might burn you; therefore, depart."
Then they all, together, having lost their senses and being bewildered,
were joined with Time (death) while reflecting upon the words of their preceptor.
O Vyāsa, that auspicious river named Daśārṇā has sacred waters;
on its bank is a divine, celebrated, and most radiant forest.
There, a brave and powerful hunter named Kṣupaka lived;
he had sons of great strength born to him by Citakā.
Citrakā gave birth to seven highly esteemed sons;
they all became hunters and were indeed known as the Caitakas.
Carrying their bows, they roam about, slaying deer and birds, as well as lions, tigers, elephants, boars, and all other creatures in every direction. (56.32)
Hear from me their names as they were when they were hunters:
Kāṇḍāra was named Arjunaka, and Damana became Siṃhaka. (56.33)
Hāla, Vyāghraka, Vidala, and likewise Śarabha;
Śaiśira, Himavat, Hastika, and Daṇḍakīlaka. (56.34)
Vidarbha and Vajraka—these indeed are their names;
one among them wanders alone in the terrible forest as a flesh-eater. (56.35)
All those fierce beings, destroyers of other creatures, had entered into that wicked womb;
wandering about at times, they likewise slaughtered deer.
Having reached the hermitage of their preceptor by virtue of their well-performed deeds,
all those deer there became agitated with fear.
Observing the frightened deer, that brahmin of great asceticism looked in all directions and saw hunters approaching. (56.38)
Recognizing that his own disciples had fallen into a state of madness due to their meditation,
he, overcome with compassion and desiring their welfare, spoke to them.
Formerly, I was served with devotion by you Brahmins;
by that deed, I am now [afflicted] by the curse incurred from the killing of a cow.

"You have attained this state of being hunters here, which is indeed contemptible and characterized by a predatory livelihood; moreover, that cow was eaten by you for the sake of a rite for the ancestors, not out of mere violence."
Therefore, having fallen from this state, you shall be endowed with the memory of your former births;
having become deer at Kālañjara, you shall then become cakravāka birds once again.
Then, having again become swans on the island in Lake Mānasa,
they were born once more as human beings, endowed with consciousness in birth after birth.
"Endowed with yoga, great-souled, and unwearied through my grace,
you shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Brahmā."
Having heard this, their former memory then arose; the thought occurred to them at that time, "This is our preceptor. (56.45)
Then, loathing the karma they had performed in their previous birth,
they turned to the right and departed toward Daśārṇa.
Having reached the bank of the Daśārṇā and consulted with one another,
remembering their former births, they resolved upon death itself.
Then, among those who had reached a firm decision, the twice-born man who was Kāṇḍarī, the hunter named Arjunaka, spoke these words: || 56.48 ||
"Sirs, that which was previously spoken by me has not been done by you;
now that it has arrived, do not disregard my word."
"I shall proclaim what is for your highest good; listen and act accordingly, so that we may be liberated from this birth and not lose our memory. (56.50)
Fathers desire sons for the sake of their own prosperity and for their deliverance;
and we have been begotten by that high-souled hunter. (56.51)
And we, who were raised by our mother and likewise by our father with such great effort—how can we desire death without having taken leave of them? (56.52)
If you think that, having taken leave of them and being dismissed by them, we shall unite ourselves with what is better—this is for your supreme benefit. (56.53)
If they do not dismiss us,
we shall remain intent on serving them until, in the course of time, they both have died.
Then, having perfected ourselves and being entirely free from debt, we shall go to the meritorious destination; this is our supreme good.
Saying "So be it," they all accepted his words;
reflecting upon his birth in the city, they returned to their very homes.
Then, seeing that they had arrived, their father and mother Citrakā were filled with supreme joy and spoke these words to them: || 56.57 ||
"O sons, you have returned home today after a very long time.
Today we two were utterly deluded; why was this delay made? (56.58)
Citrā said:
"O dear sons, your father is overcome with hunger today; yet out of affection for you, he does not eat this cooked meat, nor does he drink this wine. (56.59)
Sanatkumāra said:

Those others as well, all of whom were of sinful birth, feeling loathing for their own kind, spoke these auspicious words to Kṣupa and Citakā: 60.60. "Those others as well, all of whom were of sinful birth, feeling loathing for their own kind, spoke these auspicious words to Kṣupa and Citakā."
"Sirs, eat without hindrance for the sake of nourishment and peace as well;
we do not eat here today, for we shall eat tomorrow—of this there is no doubt. (56.61)
Then, due to their advanced age, they were no longer able to endure hunger;
yet they took their food and became very well-satisfied.
Then, perceiving that the two were pleased, they all bowed their heads and spoke these words with effort and in unison: || 56.63 ||
"O parents, we are utterly weary of this birth;
we wish to renounce it, and you ought to grant us your permission. (56.64)
Having heard those words of theirs, the father,
his eyes clouded with tears, embraced all his sons and spoke this to them.
"O sons, in former times I was a brahmin of celebrated vows, a highly esteemed friend of the royal sage Divodāsa. (56.66)
Once, in a delightful forest, he was intensely engaged with his bow.
Addressing him as one who was worthy, I said this: "O King, you do not know the bow;
not knowing it, why do you undergo this useless hardship? (56.68)
The king said to the brahmins: "Knowledge of the mantras is prescribed for the invitation and the feeding; the twice-born are indeed skilled in speech. (56.69)
Laughing, I said to him: "Bring me my bow. (56.70)
"Until I have shot the arrow at the target where you tell me it is.
Thus addressed, he then handed over to me the bow together with the arrow. (56.71)
He said: "Then, aiming at the target, I discharged an arrow;
standing there was a brahmin, a wanderer among deer, firm in his vows. (56.72)
Pierced by him, that radiant youth died instantly;
seeing him dead, I was dismissed by that king. (56.73)
Out of fear of the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin, he questioned his father;
[the father] replied, "There is no fear for you; how could there be the sin of killing a Brahmin for you? (56.74)
Having passed through hundreds of other births, this was seen by the Self-Existent One;
therefore, with supreme devotion, I am intent upon the service of my father.
Having lived for many years together with this wife, my father eventually met his end in the course of time. (56.76)
And I remained right there with this very woman, O sinless ones;
then, after a long time, I was struck down by a cow.
"And this fair-eyed woman, having descended from the fire-altar, wept for me, saying,
'He has been killed by a cow' and 'by the killing of a deer.'"
"O sons, because of my sin, I have fallen from the status of a Brahmin at birth and was born as a hunter;
thus, O sons, I have been born through a thousand births that were exceedingly terrible. (56.79)
"O sons, it is indeed because of that devotion to my father and through his perfect propitiation that my memory has not failed me, and knowledge also proceeds within me. (56.80)
"I know that all you brahmins have indeed fallen because of your actions regarding the cow, and likewise that you have lost your senses due to the curse of your preceptor. (56.81)
Afterwards, by his command, all those sons of great strength indeed regained their composure and likewise recovered their senses this very day.
For this mother of yours knows you well; she is virtuous and ever devoted to her husband.
Do what I tell you today, for it is pleasing to me.
Then you shall all, being unwearied, attain what is most excellent; you shall be free from disease and sorrow, and you shall not lose your consciousness.
"O sons, this is undoubtedly my final birth among humans;
having died from here, I must go to the auspicious abode of Brahmā. (56.85)
Therefore, wait for me for some time without weariness;
when I have ascended to heaven, you shall do what is beneficial—do not grieve.
Sons must certainly serve their mother and father when they are in great distress;
there is no duty more powerful than this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, filled with wonder, their grief vanished and free from envy,
they waited upon him for as long as it took for those two to give up their lives.
Having properly performed the funeral rites for those two who had passed away,
they [performed] the fast unto death according to the prescribed rule in the great river Daśārṇā.
Then those seven hunters, having failed to achieve their purpose regarding themselves,
were born once more on Mount Kālañjara as seven deer.
Remembering their former birth there through their fall from the wind-god's realm,
they then perfected themselves and were reborn among the ruddy geese.
Learn from me those names which they bear in their state as deer:
Dīrghajīva, Anādhṛṣṭa, Vāyuvega, and Abhikampana. (56.92)
Śrīpārśva, Śaṅkhapāda, and Somalakṣya as the seventh—remembering their former births and feeling mutual respect for one another, [they lived together]. (56.93)
Together, they suddenly gave up their lives by leaping from the mountain;
those seven were likewise reborn among hunters and wild animals. (56.94)
Having been born again after their previous birth, they then became birds in Śaradvīpa;
thus that auspicious lake among the Kāmpilyas became renowned as Śaradvīpa.
There too, seven cakravāka birds were born as brothers:
Maruddeva, Śikhaṇḍin, Rathanemisvara, Śikhin, Jīva, Vṛkṣa, and Dhvaja—thus they are remembered. (56.96)
Once, while they were reborn there,
the immensely radiant King Aṇuha of Kāmpilya himself came to that region.
Having reached that lake, he rejoiced together with his women in great delight,
like an immortal god who has attained the Mandākinī and is accompanied by Apsarases.
Seeing him playing there with the god Marut,
that cakravāka bird indeed felt a longing for those sensory pleasures.
"If I were indeed his son, I would surely obtain the kingdom;
then I would obtain these objects of sense, of this there is no doubt. (56.100)
Knowing that thought of his, the second one,
known by the name Cakra and called Śikhaṇḍin, then spoke to him while laughing.
"You have contemplated the status of a prince and even kingship;
in that regard, I would be your domestic priest, for this is my own desire as well. (56.102)
Having learned of their deliberation from those two, Rathanemisvara then thought: "O Lord, may I be your minister there. (56.103)
Sanatkumāra said: While those three were thus reflecting, the other Cakravāka birds then became enraged and spoke these words to them. || 56.104 ||
That which was conceived by you, who seek sense-objects, is inconceivable;
therefore, being liberated from this, you shall obtain your heart's desire.
Having cursed them and observed that they were dejected in mind,
he again reflected upon his status as a prince and his sovereignty.
Out of compassion, they spoke these words to him whose mind was lost, employing many qualities of consolation, as if they themselves were suffering. (56.107)
"O Lord, by your power we have crossed over this hardship;
for you are our provider of wisdom and are considered by us to be a bridge. (56.108)
For if you were not to speak, the cow would have been offered to the ancestors;
we would not have served our fathers, and consequently, there would have been no common understanding.
Through your power, this manifestation of our mastery over yoga has occurred;
therefore, we shall speak again of what is for your ultimate welfare—listen to us.
O lord of men, you will remain with a heart attached to worldly things as long as you,
accompanied by your followers, do not hear our words which are true;
but once you have attained the knowledge of yoga, you shall reach the auspicious goal.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those great birds, together and with disciplined minds,
completely relinquished their state as birds and entered another womb.
Then all those fowlers and the deer named Cakra, consumed by the sage’s anger, were born again in human bodies; those three alone became lords of yoga in that kingdom.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Curse of Kauśika," in the Narrative of the Seven Hunters within the Skanda Purāṇa.
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Furthermore, those four teachers are birds who act according to their own will.
The daughter of the high-souled Yāyāvara, a brahmin, was born.
When they were born, that brahmin of great asceticism, through his own merit,
effortlessly provided for their livelihood, guided by their good fortune.
Having fulfilled their Vedic vows and having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
they devoted themselves exclusively to yoga, being established in it and intent upon it as their supreme goal.
The other three Vyāsas as well, impelled by their own past actions, attained that very birth which had been previously envisioned by them. (57.4)
For the first was born from Aṇuha, known as Brahmadatta;
Aṇuha had one son, and the second was the son of his priest. (57.5)
Then, the third [son] was born to the minister; thus those three were his offspring.
Those three high-souled ones grew like the three sacrificial fires, or like the three worlds, or like the three oceans. (57.6)
When they had acquired their learning and were proficient in their own duties,
their fathers, with joyful minds, assigned them their respective tasks.
Aṇuha bestowed the abundant kingdom upon Brahmadatta;
then, accompanied by Kīrtimatī, he departed for the forest.
But the family priest Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having established his son in his own duties, departed for Pañcāla, he who was firm in his vows. || 57.9 ||
The minister Sudhanvan, however, having established his son Brahmadhanvan—the steadfast one—in his own office, departed together with his wife. (57.10)
When they had departed for their own worlds, the powerful Brahmadatta ruled the kingdom together with the Pañcālas and Brahmadhanvan.
While thus governing the kingdom, performing sacrifices, and enjoying pleasures,
those virtuous ones then passed many years in happiness.
Then, after a long time, he dwelt happily in his home with his wife and his circle of friends, like Kubera in the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then he, the knower of all sounds, observed an ant acting according to its own will, making a nest within another ant.
But he, having reflected through his knowledge even regarding such a birth as that of a worm,
O sinless one, uttered a laugh that was both manifest and like a sound.
