Seeing that smile of his, his lotus-eyed wife became angry and said: "What is this? Why have you perceived such a transformation in me today? (57.16)
The king, having embraced her who was dearer to him than his own life, sought to appease that fair-faced woman; yet she did not become appeased with him.
When she was not satisfied even though much that was true was being said,
he then propitiated Viṣṇu for the sake of winning her favor.
Having gone to the Sālavana grove with the Pañcāla prince,
that great man, preceded by Brahmadhanvan, proceeded on a magnificent chariot.
Thereupon, on the seventh day, having been dismissed by Viṣṇu,
that tiger among men went to his own excellent city, Kāmpilya.
At that very time, four auspicious brahmins, endowed with great yogic power, spoke thus to one another: || 57.21 ||
"We have achieved our purpose; what further task remains for us to stay here in the human world?
Let us go to our own Brahman-source and be liberated from this great fear. (57.22)
Those three of ours who share our vows are indeed sinking;
we shall awaken them so that they do not meet with defeat.
Then all those twice-born ones, having bowed down to their father, said:
"O father, we are masters of yoga; indeed, we have attained perfection through our own actions."
We take our leave; we shall go to our own source created by Brahmā.
Having abandoned these human bodies, depart; salutations to you.
The father said:
"Fathers desire sons, thinking, 'They will deliver us from fear';
yet that fear is difficult to overcome both in this world and in the next, O sons. (57.26)
Bound by debt and not having released your own pledge, how can you go away—may it be well with you? Do you not perceive this as unrighteousness? (57.27)
The Sūtas said:
"O dear one, we are masters of yoga; we shall describe to you the worlds that are free from affliction."
"O father, how could we, as your sons, not enable you to attain the status of a Brahmin?
Listen, for we shall likewise provide you with wealth even in this world. (57.29)
"Take this letter and show it to Brahmadatta;
while the king is reading it, he will provide for your livelihood. (57.30)
Sanatkumāra said: Then their father, that bull among sages, being aware of their power, considered all that to be exactly so and approved them once again.
Then, having assumed their postures, those ascetics departed with disciplined minds;
and your father, of exceeding splendor, beheld them as they had become like luminous lights.
Taking that letter and reflecting upon his sons,
he went quickly to Kāmpilya, desiring to see the best of kings.
And that king, having come from the Sāl forest, entered the city;
and from afar, a brahmin presented that letter to him.
Having observed those auspicious omens, the lord of men,
saying "Bring the letter," remained seated upon that chariot.
Standing then at the city gate in his great chariot,
he held the Brahma-bow and a parasol, his face fanned by the feathers of a peacock.
Then, taking the letter, he read it with composure;
and upon that letter there were two verses that bestowed auspiciousness. (57.37)
Those who, though afflicted by the slaughter of a cow due to a curse pronounced by their guru,
became grateful through devotion to their father, have all attained an auspicious outcome.
The seven hunters were reborn as deer in Daśārṇa;
on Mount Kālañjara they became cakravāka birds; and in Lake Mānasa they became swans.
They too were born in Kurukṣetra as Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
they have set out upon a long journey—why do you despair? (57.40)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those two verses, the three of them were as if they had drunk poison;
then, falling into a swoon, they regained consciousness and entered the city.
Having entered the city and their own home, they remained untiring;
reflecting thus and so on, they set their minds upon the forest.
And that highly fortunate wife, having approached the lord of men together with his circle of friends, spoke these words to the king with great joy.
"Since you, though being a lord of yoga, were entirely attached to sensual enjoyments, I then aroused my wrath against you for the sake of awakening you. (57.44)
I know you to be an expert in the cries of birds, and I likewise know you to be a bird;
therefore, O King, knowing this, I have risen to awaken you. (57.45)
Therefore, having consecrated this son of theirs in the kingdom today, you should endow their father, this imperishable Brahmin, with wealth.
"Tomorrow we shall go to the forest, O King; do not let the time pass.
Having performed all those duties together with his wife, the king remained devoted to his vow. (57.47)
He departed toward the forest and ascended to heaven by means of yoga;
and when he had gone, Pañcāla also performed very difficult austerities.
And having broken his fast,
the great-souled Brahmadhanvan, firm in his vows, attained the state of a Yakṣa in due course of time.
Through ascetic penance, he beheld the goddess, the daughter of Himavat;
seeing her, the giver of boons, Brahmadhanvan then spoke to that auspicious lady.
I desire the power to assume any form at will and your devotion forever; and for me when I have fallen into great distress, I desire deliverance from it by you alone. (57.51)
Having said, "So be it," she then departed for her desired destination;
meanwhile, the evil-minded Brahmadhanvan became intoxicated with passion.
Having previously been righteous, he was oppressed by unrighteousness;
he then began to violate maidens and the wives of sages on every side.
Having gone there in the form of her husband, he was infatuated by desire;
yet no one recognized him as he conducted himself in such a manner, even among those closest to him.
Now there was one known as Āla, a great ascetic who lived among the deer;
his wife was named Sudharmā, who was truly beautiful.
For the gods, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas declare of her: "This passionate woman is peerless in beauty compared to all others in the three worlds. (57.56)
And he did not perceive any opportunity while she was with her husband;
he could not discern at what time their separation from her husband might occur.
Having heard that she was so beautiful and virtuous, Brahmadhanvan,
longing for separation from his wife, assumed the form of a tiger.
And having assumed a very large, deformed, and terrifying form at that time, O Vyāsa, that fool terrified the wild animals with his appearance. (57.59)
Then, O Lord, that herd of deer, terrified by the fear of the tiger,
became invisible as it fled with the speed of thought or the wind.
Then Hāla also went along with the deer, seeking to save his life;
and that beautiful Brāhmaṇī Sudharmā likewise fled out of fear of the tiger.
And because of her feminine nature, she did not follow the herd of deer that had fallen;
seeing her alone, the evil-minded Brahmadhanvan [seized her]. (57.62)
Casting off his tiger form,
he addressed her with gentle words full of consolation, as she was tormented by fear.
"Do not fear; let there be no dread for you, O blessed one. I am your husband, O slender-waisted lady. That king of beasts has gone; take heart, my beloved."
Having comforted him, she of great renown beheld his form, which resembled that of her husband;
and she thought in her heart: "He whom I saw with those deer has been seen [by me]."
Seeking to save his life, he fled; from where has he come back again?
This wicked Indra, ever vigilant, constantly assails me.
"Since he has come here desiring love, why should he not be one who seeks an inner purpose?
Therefore, I shall see clearly with my divine eye. || 57.67 ||
Sanatkumāra said: In that interval, Brahmadhanvan then took her by the hand and, being delighted, spoke this to her: "What are you thinking in your heart? (57.68)
"You do not embrace me today, even though I have emerged from the jaws of death.
Surely I am your beloved husband; do not be angry, O woman of excellent complexion. (57.69)
Then, out of wickedness, he smelled her on the cheek;
and that evil-souled one, having embraced her, pressed his limbs against her limbs.
He loosened her waist-knot and forcibly drank from her lower lip;
and that beautiful woman recognized him as wicked by that deed.
Sudharmā said:
"O fool, you are not my husband; you are Śakra, there is no doubt about this.
O wicked-minded one, I am no longer within the range of Madana. (57.72)
Thus addressed by her, he who was entirely cast off fell upon the surface of the earth and assumed his own form.
Then, her eyes copper-red with anger as if she were about to consume him with her gaze, she looked at his face and spoke these words: (57.74)
Many wives of sages have been seduced by you with your wicked mind;
yet no other woman like me has ever been won by you before.
Now behold this difficult-to-attain fruit of that deed previously committed by you, received from my presence.
In whatever form you have here terrified the deer by force, in that very same form you shall wander for many years. (57.77)
Furthermore, you will be unable to kill any human being at any time;
and when the sixth mealtime arrives, you shall obtain a deer as food.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having addressed that cruel man, the high-minded woman of auspicious conduct went toward those very deer, and then she no longer saw her husband. (57.79)
He too, tormented by grief and thinking that she had been killed, saw her while still lamenting; having embraced her, he spoke these words: (57.80)
"By good fortune you have arrived, having escaped from the jaws of death. I hope, O beautiful one, that you were not seen by that king of beasts."
Sudharma said:
"That lion was not a beast of prey; he was some being capable of assuming any form at will. He approached me for my sake and was consumed by me like a moth. (57.82)
By my curse, that evil-minded one has assumed the nature of a tiger,

Mahiṣa, the best among speakers and skilled in the meaning of speech, spoke these profound and significant words.
It is known to you all how your ancestors,
those tigers among the Dānavas who were solely devoted to valor, were slain by the gods.
Therefore, O best of Dānavas, enough of this way of life that is like that of moths falling into fire;
let us make peace with the gods and conduct our affairs through our own proper duties.
O Dānavas, how do you, whose power has failed, desire success through war with the gods who are superior to you and free from vulnerabilities or calamities? (60.118)

For those endowed with an excellence of qualities, when there is an increase in the power of mantras, enthusiasm, and majesty, and upon the attainment of the proper place and time, [the vehicle proceeds]. || 60.119 ||
Now, if you think that success for yourselves can be achieved by traveling together—armed, prepared, and united with the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas in battle—(then consider this). || 60.120 ||
The Rākṣasas, who were weak and terrified, took refuge with the very deities from whom they had received the remnants of the oblations in the fire by the son of Śakti.
The Yakṣas and the best of the Asuras are always dependent upon Kubera;
and he, in turn, being diligent, carries out the work of the foremost of the gods.
Except for those who are more powerful than the enemies of the Daityas in the worlds,
O best of Asuras, there is no state of duality because of their non-existence.
When the Dānava Mahiṣa had spoken these words, clear and meaningful, in the assembly— "I am well"— the great Asura Druma replied.
How can the gods— who were previously undefeated by us when we were weak, yet are now victorious and endowed with power— be reconciled with us?
Having quickly prepared our mountain and water fortresses,
and being constantly intent on victory, let us remain in a state of waiting after having declared war.
Constantly destroying sacrifices, vows, and observances,
they sought to annihilate the system of castes and stages of life throughout this world on all sides.
Then, when the path of righteous conduct has been severed by the destruction of the world,
and having perceived that the gods have been diminished, we shall advance against them clad in armor.
Then they all approved his words,
just as living beings whose death is imminent accept unwholesome food.
Having resolved upon the destruction of the world,
the enemies of the gods rose up like oceans overflowing their bounds, agitated by the winds at the time of universal dissolution.

Then his younger brother Nisunda, dark as a rain-cloud, with a body full, round, and elevated, with arms like iron bars and large, red, long eyes— blue as a water-carrier cloud and terrifying to his enemies— remained at his seat without losing his composure. (60.132)
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 60.60 ||
The sixty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, for the destruction of the worlds, he set forth against the leaders of the Dānavas.
An army crowded with rutting elephants and thick with chariots and horses.
Then that army of Dānavas scattered in every direction,
like the waters of the ocean tossed by the wind at the time of universal dissolution.
Some slaughtered brahmins; some ground the vaiśyas to powder;
others devoured the kṣatriyas, and others ate the śūdras. (61.3)
The enemies of Mura devoured, licked, swallowed, and shattered on all sides the food, the sacrificial offerings, and the sacrificial posts at the sacrifices.
Resounding with the sound of the study of the Vedas well-recited, where the groves of trees were cherished by the foremost of sages,
where there were abundant stores of bark garments, deerskins, and darbha grass, and where there were mountain torrents of cool water flowing in inexhaustible abundance.

Others, having spread out, destroyed the hermitages, which were filled with wild rice and *gavedhuka* grass near their borders, where deer, bears, and monkeys slept in confidence, and which were crowded with the spreading smoke of sacrificial fires.
Some asuras, whose splendor was like that of aged serpents,
seized the matted locks of the sages and tore them out, washing them with the water of sacred fords.
Having cast them down, some asuras trampled them upon the earth with their feet,
like blazing fires for the destruction of the sages themselves.
Some destroyers of the Dānavas touched the heads of the sages’ wives with their three palms,
purifying them with holy waters.
Then, perceiving their own impending rise and knowing that the army was scattered for the destruction of the world, they summoned it from all sides and set out on their expedition.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and at a victorious moment,
they struck the war-drums and performed rites that bring victory.
Having brought forth powerful, rutting, and noble elephants equipped for battle,
the Asuras properly honored them and bound their armor according to the prescribed ritual.
They fastened mechanical devices filled with iron arrows on both sides of the seat,
and bamboos filled with spears positioned crosswise.
They fastened tomaras, kaṇapas, spikes, spears, discs, and axes,
and they secured the appointed attendants at the middle seat and on both sides.
Prepare the supreme weapons and well-maintained quivers,
filled with sharp-pointed, stone-tipped arrows feathered with vulture plumes.
They fastened iron neck-chains, which were without goads and possessed the luster of the crescent moon,
white in color, upon the necks of the horses between their two frontal globes.
The elephant-riders fastened auspicious garlands of razor-edged arrows, made of gold,
upon the frontal globes of the elephants.
And the Dānavas raised up long, variegated Vaijayantī banners, clearly marked with their own insignia,
for the elephant division.
The bells of the preeminent elephants rang out with a great sound,
as did the very long yak-tail whisks, beautiful as the shoulders of swans.
And for each one, four female elephants of beautiful appearance,
capable of warding off enemy elephants, were stationed in front by the Daityas.
They made the horses, clad in armor and protected by iron mail, precede the young princes who were mounted upon them— young men themselves, well-trained and skilled in the use of weapons.
They were armored, clad in mail, and bearing polished swords; they were followed by foot-soldiers marching in front of them and by archers following behind.
Then other Daitya warriors, armored and equipped with iron mail,
mounted horses that were bathed and clad in yellow trappings, having girded their swords.
Then some [servants] yoked the chariots with well-trained, bathed, and consecrated young horses that were swift as the wind.
Then some mounted chariots adorned with gold, equipped with weapons and banners, and resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells.
Having heard that plan thus devised, Sunda, the tiger among Dānavas, who is honored by armies, set forth after performing the auspicious rites.
It was easy to drive, possessed beautiful poles and excellent wheels, was made of the finest gold,
and was adorned with various wonderful jewels in the form of floral patterns and figures of animals and birds.
Then, having mounted a divine chariot adorned with banners and flags, drawn by horses swift as thought and yoked with great joy, [he departed].
Clad in armor and with his sword girded, with white chowries being waved about him,
he was being praised on all sides by charioteers, panegyrists, and bards.
Mounting his war-elephant, whose temples were dark with rutting-ichor and upon which bees clung, Nishunda quickly departed for the battle.
And other Dānavas, skilled in battle and well-armored, set forth from there with great joy on chariots, horses, and elephants.
Placing the great asura Tārakākṣa at the head of the army,
accompanied by many brave chariot-warriors, elephants, horses, and infantry.
Having quickly stationed the great asura Mahiṣa, who is intoxicated with strength, at the rear with his fourfold army for protection, [he departed].
Having stationed Meghasvana and Mahāsvana on both flanks—
those two slayers of enemies who were protected by a vast army— the two Dānavas [remained there].
In the midst were Sunda, Nisunda, Maya, Śambhu, Khara, and Mura—
mighty heroes, fully armed, who could repel the enemy forces.
The best of the Dānavas set forth with great resolve toward heaven,
like the clouds of the dissolution age driven by the wind.
Knowing of their arrival, Śatakratu, together with the inhabitants of the heavenly world, withdrew and quickly departed for Janasthāna.
Then, having ascended the peak of Meru, all those enemies of the gods together established their army in the Nandana grove.
Then, having provided protection for the army on all sides, the lords of the Daityas took up their respective well-ordered and spacious quarters.
Then, having been granted permission by the foremost of the Dānavas,
all those Dānavas removed their armor and all their equipment.
The soldiers, having quickly removed the weapons of the rutting elephants, slowly cast off their armor as they mounted the young female elephants.
Then the Dānava soldiers removed their armor, cast off their breastplates, and laid aside their various body-protectors.
Some Dānava soldiers bound the elephants— whose temples were free of rut, who had bathed and drunk, and whose fatigue had vanished— to the wish-fulfilling trees.
Some powerful nāgas, with bees clinging to them from their rutting ichor, broke down the wish-fulfilling trees, while the birds— terrified, intoxicated, and bewildered— fled in all directions.
Some powerful elephants, dark with rut,
rubbed their temples against the rows of bees clustered upon the blossoms of the Kalpa trees.
Some elephants, intoxicated, plunged into the river Mandākinī,
whose banks were rendered tawny at their edges by the filaments of golden lotuses.

The horse-grooms bound the horses, which were freed from their sets of battle armor, whose minds were serene, whose bodies were rubbed down, who had drunk their fill of water, and whose exhaustion was removed. (61.47)
Then the Asuras brought from the Kalpa trees fine garments, variegated and most excellent garlands, fruits, and honey.
Some Dānavas, their bodies reddened by that pollen, went joyfully to the river Mandākinī and broke the golden lotuses there.
Some soldiers brought heaps of mandāra flowers;
others brought many sweet fruits.
Having stayed there for one night and beaten their drums, the Dānavas,
prepared according to that very same method, set out for Amarāvatī.
Then, by the sound of trumpets, the trumpeting of elephants,
and the lion-roars of the Daityas, Amarāvatī itself seemed to tremble.
Then, beholding the city empty, those best of Dānavas, greatly rejoiced and shouting with a terrifying sound, spoke thus: || 61.53 ||
Victorious is the lion among the lords of the Daityas, Sunda, the enemy of the gods;
thereafter, victorious is he whose long eyes have lovely reddish corners.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 61.61 ||
The sixty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having conquered the two lords of the Daityas, those two endowed with prowess ascended to heaven.
Together with the Daityas, they went to the Vindhya, that mountain of lofty crags.
Having duly honored the Daityas and dispatched the two brothers,
they then took their pleasure at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, where the slopes were covered with blossoming trees.
Then Brahmā, having learned of the defeat of the gods by the two Daityas,
reflected with a one-pointed mind upon the proper means for their destruction.
Taking up every single sesame seed from the jewels,
he created a woman of beautiful appearance, with limbs that inspired desire and a lovely voice.
The Grandfather gave her the name Tilottamā;
she then shone as the very model for even the most divine women.
Her face was exceedingly full, her eyes surpassed the blue lotus,
her speech was sweeter than the cry of a swan, and her gait excelled that of a rutting elephant.
Seeing Lakṣmī, she became bashful and covered her face with a lotus; and the deities of the grove trembled at the sight of the beautiful-limbed woman’s body.
Having brought her forth, the Creator then spoke to Indra, the subduer of Pāka:
"Previously, Madana was consumed by Śambhu with the fire of his eye. (62.8)
Let us all go to the side of the wielder of the Pināka bow so that he may arise;
having propitiated him, we shall then act so that Madana may come to life once more.
Then those enemies of the Asuras, together with Brahmā and her,
went to the peak of Mount Vindhya where the blessed Lord Hara resides.
Not seeing Śarva there, all those best of gods were consumed by grief;
with their minds entirely surrendered to Śiva, they all uttered the sacred syllable Om.
Then, in the midst of those dwellers of heaven, a Liṅga rose up,
perfectly compact and firmly joined, like a mass of radiant energies.
Then, from that [fire], a loud voice with clear syllables resounded:
"This wicked one, a thorn to the people of the ascetics, has been consumed by me. (62.13)
"For your sake I shall release her; she will perform this task for you.
Let this woman circumambulate me from all sides."
Thus addressed by Maheśa, she performed a circumambulation,
placing her hands joined in reverence upon her head, as delicate as a red lotus.
Then, from that previous form,
there emerged a face with three eyes, with bright lips, of immeasurable splendor and radiant beauty.
Then, a radiance issuing from the moon-like face of the wielder of the Pināka bow,
brilliant as the autumnal sun, quickly entered that woman.
Then that woman of lovely appearance bowed to the southern form;
thereupon, the radiant face of the preceptor of the gods emerged from it.
With a terrifying roar like that of a cloud heavy with rain,
he shone with formidable fangs and eyes with glowing red corners.
Then, a splendor exceeding the sun issued from his right mouth and,
being beheld by all the gods, entered the most excellent of women.
She then immediately bowed before his western form;
from it, there emerged a face with three unsurpassed eyes. (62.21)
Then, a radiant splendor issued forth from the moon-like face of the enemy of Madana and swiftly entered that very same most excellent woman.
Having approached the northern image, she bowed with palms joined in reverence;
from its face there issued a full and very gracious smile.
Then, issuing forth from him, a radiance with the brilliance of the sun and blazing fire quickly entered that very woman of excellent complexion.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, four faces of the God of Gods issued forth toward the cardinal directions; they did not [remain] because of their astonishment at his form.
Because the Lord of the Gods had previously consumed the fire residing within himself and thereby rendered Madana powerless, he showed favor to that most excellent of women.
And there Śiva spoke these words to all the gods:
"Since she has circumambulated me and you all in a clockwise circle... (62.27)
"Therefore, O best of gods, you have established this place for me;
on Mount Vindhya, it shall be known by the name Maṇḍaleśvara."
Whoever performs this circumambulation of the Lord of the Maṇḍala,
by him the earth with its seven islands has been circumambulated;
for I, the bestower of boons, shall always maintain my presence here.
Having beheld Īśāna, the Lord of the Maṇḍala, a man who is self-restrained shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attain my world.
Crowded with many perfected beings (siddhas) and frequented by kinnaras and uragas,
my beloved [abode] shall always be attended by you all.
"And this Tilottamā, for whose sake you, O best of gods,
have created her with undistracted minds— she shall accomplish that task for you."
Having seen her, those two Daityas, deluded and tormented by passion,
will go to their destruction at each other's hands, and she herself shall likewise perish.
Ageless and immortal, the most excellent of all Apsarases and auspicious,
she shall always be worthy of worship and reverence here in this place.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Maheśa had spoken thus, the gods, their hearts well-pleased,
then dispatched that woman for the purpose of slaying the two Daityas.
And Brahmā, whose vehicle is the lotus, gave her as companions Wrath,
Pride, all the Seasons, Envy, and Arrogance.
Then the one of immeasurable splendor, having dispatched those deities— Kāla, Mṛtyu, Moha, and Viṣāda— as well as Tilottamā, [departed].
All those gods, the bulls among the deities, indeed gathered themselves together, asking, "Who is coming here today? Who? Which one? (62.38)
Then, after bowing again to that Supreme Lord who stood in their midst—
since he remained positioned in the center while the gods were being ground down— [they spoke].
From that time on, he became known there as Piṇḍāreśvara;
and by beholding the Lord Īśāna at Piṇḍāreśvara with devotion, a human being [attains his goal]. || 62.40 ||
Freed from all impurity, upon the dissolution of the body, he shall become a member of the Gaṇa; and whatever lingas exist on earth that are four-faced and elongated— 62.41.
For all those visible things come into being once this has been seen;
then all those deities, having performed their task with unwearied diligence, [departed].
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord, they returned to their own abodes;
she too, with her lovely face and sidelong glances, and her full, uplifted breasts, [departed].
Then, as if captivating the minds of the gods with her charms,
she set out toward the southern quarter where those two Dānavas were waiting.
Then, as those two lords of the Daityas were wandering through the delightful foothills of the Vindhya mountains, whose ridges resounded with the songs of birds, they beheld her standing there.
She was clinging to a branch of an Ashoka tree in full bloom, frequented by intoxicated bees;
she wore a variegated silken garment and a girdle set with jewels.
She was singing sweetly, passionately, evenly, melodiously, and without distraction,
perfectly adorned with notes that were high, low, and exceedingly high.
She was like the very personification of the perfection of asceticism, as if she were embodied success itself;
she was like Rati incarnate, and like the splendor of the moon made manifest.
"This is mine alone! This is mine alone!"—saying this, those two foremost of Dānavas rushed toward the goddess and simultaneously seized her by both hands. (62.49)
Then those two best of asuras, their minds possessed by pride, intoxication, anger, and envy, became exceedingly enraged with one another.
Then Antaka, Kāla, and Mṛtyu swiftly entered into those two clubs;
then, seizing their clubs, the two enraged warriors struck one another.
Then, struck there by each of them with a single blow,
they became despondent, their entire bodies mangled, bewildered by the curse of Śiva.
Falling unconscious to the ground like two trees cut at their roots,
they then emerged from there, their minds overcome by passion.
The two souls of those two chief Dānavas, together with Śukra,
then departed from there as the life-breaths of those two evil-minded ones.
The two boys, strong and with beautiful limbs, quickly became [grown].
There, one boy said, "I am Śumbha, the enemy of my foes. (62.55)
Then Niśumbha spoke, saying, "I am one, but there is another who is a child.
Thereupon Vindhya approached those two boys of immeasurable luster. (62.56)
He commanded his wife, "Protect these two children.
Then both those sons of the lord of the Dānavas grew up there.
Just as at the end of the dark fortnight the moon and the ocean [rise] simultaneously,
so too did those two subduers of enemies perceive their birth from the two Dānavas.
They performed most intense penance, subsisting on leaves, water, and air;
propitiated by them through their asceticism, the Lord came there and spoke.
"I am pleased with you both, my sons; what boon shall I grant you?
Those two heroes chose as their boon invincibility and eternal immunity from death.
Having heard that prayer of theirs, the Grandfather replied:
"Death must inevitably come to both of you by some means or another."
"O lords of the Daityas, immortality does not exist for anyone other than the gods.
To Brahmā, who had spoken thus, the two Dānavas requested a boon.
Having both reached a firm conclusion, their hair standing on end with joy, they said:
"O Grandfather, there is that maiden who is the mother of the world; without her [the lineage cannot continue]. (62.63)
"O Lord, may we never again suffer defeat by Death!
Having said, "So be it," both sons of the lord of the Daityas [departed]. (62.64)
The creator of the entire world vanished right there;
then, having desisted from their intense asceticism and performed the auspicious rites, those two— || 62.65 ||
Wearing crowns and fastened armor, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
their limbs smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, they were dressed in yellow silken garments.
Having heard of the boon obtained by Śumbha and Niśumbha from the Grandfather (Brahmā), those two foremost of Dānavas roamed through the delightful plateaus of the Vindhya mountains.
The Dānavas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla arrived, filled with joy:
Śambhu, Maya, Ghana, Keśin, Naraka, Namuci, and Druma.
And other millions of arrogant enemies of the gods who had survived the slaughter,
all those Dānavas together, settled upon the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
In that place strewn with heaps of flowers from various trees, creepers, and shrubs,
there stood archers equipped with swords and adorned with variegated ornaments.
Like clouds in the sky accompanied by Indra’s bow and lightning,
the Dānava Maya then spoke there to those two best of Dānavas.
"O Daityas, the entire three worlds were enjoyed by your two fathers in the past; why then are they not taken back by you two now? (62.72)
Having utterly defeated all the assembled gods at the forefront of battle, those who were indeed the allies of your parents, the enemies of the gods, [were slain]. (62.73)
"These very companions of yours in battle are intoxicated with strength," said Maya, the lord of the Daityas, to the great Asura Śumbha.
Looking at Niśumbha’s face, she then spoke these words:
"O Daityas, the entire world of Bhūrloka is now [under your control] along with you. (62.75)
"Having shared [the spoils] with all the gods, we shall conquer at the front of the battle.
Then that best of asuras himself seized Jambūdvīpa.
The Lord gave Śākadvīpa to his younger brother Niśumbha;
he gave Śālmalidvīpa and Gomeda to the Dānavas.
He gave Krauñcadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa to the Daityas,
and the lord of the Daityas offered Puṣkaradvīpa to Bhārgava.
Having thus quickly divided the entire world of mortals,
he then [appropriated] all sacrifices, offerings with joined palms, prostrations, rituals, and acts of hospitality.
Having snatched it away from the gods, the Daityas and Dānavas seized it;
thereafter, the sacrifice of the high-souled Kaśyapa proceeded.
Then the enemies of the gods arrived and desecrated that sacrifice, saying,
"For now Kaśyapa holds sovereign power over the entire world of mortals."
"In all circumstances, you ought to sacrifice for us in this sacrifice.
Thus addressed by the Daityas, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, then [replied].
Having made the three worlds his own by conquering all the immortals in battle, he spoke these words, profound and meaningful, as if smiling: (62.83)
"Therefore, you Daityas ought to take all the sacrificial portions.
Thus addressed by him at that time, the foremost of the Daityas and Dānavas [acted accordingly].
Having mustered their entire force and performed the rites pertaining to battle,
they— whose conduct was established in what is praiseworthy— set out on auspicious moments, under favorable constellations, and on propitious days.
The Daityas and Dānavas set forth on chariots, elephants, and horses,
positioned properly behind, in front, and on both sides.
Having established their protection, they set out prepared, desiring to conquer the gods;
and Indra, the subduer of Pāka, having learned of the arrival of those enemies, [prepared for battle].
Having carefully prepared all the defensive works within his own city, he remained vigilant while those who were united fought, desiring to conquer heaven.
On auspicious lunar days, asterisms, moments, and astrological configurations,
he duly honored the sages and paid homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Having performed the auspicious rites, he set forth together with all the hosts of gods upon a four-tusked elephant, which resembled a peak of the Himalayas.
Having mounted Airāvata, who was constantly raining down streams of ichor,
[he rode] with a great golden-handled [umbrella] encircled by the rays of jewels.
With a radiant, uplifted parasol being held over him,
he was fanned by whisks as pure as the mass of rays from the autumnal moon.
He was honored by sages with blessings and shouts of victory, while yak-tail whisks with interiors inlaid with clusters of rays from jeweled handles fanned him.
Being praised on all sides by the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards,
he then [proceeded] to a wide, level space, free from trees.
Bṛhaspati formed a lotus-array for the gods,
placing Śatakratu at the pericarp together with the Maruts.
And he placed the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas within the petals;
and Yama, Kāla, Kubera, and Varuṇa within the filaments.
The preceptor fashioned an infinite stalk accompanied by serpents,
as well as other assembled gods, along with the armies of Rākṣasas and Gandharvas.
Furthermore, he arranged a lake all around that lotus;
then, hearing the sound of the Dānavas' musical instruments, the denizens of heaven [prepared for battle].
Delighted, they beat their drums and sounded their cries in great throngs;
hearing those sounds of the denizens of heaven mingled with the noise of musical instruments, [the people rejoiced].
The lords of the Dānavas, being fully prepared, exerted themselves even more intensely;
then those Dānavas beheld the lotus-array (padmavyūha) of the dwellers of heaven.
There, those of immeasurable prowess questioned Bhārgava regarding the breaking of that formation;
thus questioned by the foremost of the Dānavas, he, unperturbed, explained the method for breaking the array.
Having reflected thus, the wise son of Bhṛgu then spoke to the Asuras, who were scattered all around like heaps of snow: 62.102.
"O enemies of the gods, the array of the lords of the gods has been completely destroyed.
Thus were the Daityas addressed by the high-souled Bhārgava.
Having quickly let out a lion's roar and rushed toward them from all sides,
a battle then ensued between the armies of the gods and the dānavas.
Striking one another with various sharp weapons—
horsemen with horsemen, elephants with elephants, and chariots with chariots.
Arrogant foot-soldiers fought with arrogant foot-soldiers in battle;
some were pierced by iron shafts, and others were cut down by battle-axes.
The Vasu warriors fell from both armies alike;
"Cut! Pierce! Strike now! Stay, you fool! Where are you going? they cried. (62.107)
Thus these words, uttered by warriors in battle, rose up clearly—
words stained with fat and blood, and covered with armor and mail.
That battlefield became a mire of slain elephants and horses;
then, the dwellers of heaven were oppressed there by those Dānavas.
Wounded and for the most part slain, they sought refuge with Śakra;
the chief Nāgas went to Ananta, and the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas to Kubera.
When the array of the gods had been broken, the Daityas and Dānavas were overjoyed;
they let out loud lion-roars and struck their musical instruments once again.
Rushing forward and prepared for battle against the subduer of Pāka (Indra),
Śakra then raised up his elephant with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Enraged, he pulverized the host of Daityas and Dānavas;
Pākaśāsana set the army of the Dānavas ablaze on all sides.
Then, like a blazing fire in the heat of summer consuming dry undergrowth,
Śumbha approached and spoke to Śakra in the midst of battle.
"O Śakra, having been seen by me today, you shall not return alive.
Then Brahmā, having arrived, spoke thus to the best of the gods: || 62.115 ||
"O gods, you must not fight the Daityas; the enemies of the gods are not to be slain by you.
You must not fight, you must not fight the Daityas of great power, O gods!"
For these enemies of the gods had previously obtained boons and were therefore unslayable; thus,
upon hearing his words, all the inhabitants of heaven vanished from that battle and quickly departed with their armies and mounts.
Then the Daityas, greatly rejoiced, struck their musical instruments once more;
shouting loudly, those warriors skilled in battle spoke these words.
In the darkness of dust trampled by the hooves of horses, amidst throngs of foot-soldiers terrified by the roar of elephants and chariots,
Śumbhasiṃha— the conqueror of the gods and whose great cry was like that of a rain-cloud— triumphs in battle, free from fear and despondency.

Thereafter, victorious is Niśumbhasiṃha, whose long and thick neck and arms are preeminent, whose broad, beautiful, and elevated chest is well-knit, who has the gait of a lion-king and the roar of a rain-cloud, and who is triumphant in the best of battles. (62.120)
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Victory over Śumbha and Niśumbha," in the Devāsura-saṃgrāma section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-third chapter.
Then, having conquered the gods in battle, the enemies of the gods went together to the Vindhya mountain, where clouds were resting upon its peaks.
Having duly dispatched all those Daityas and Dānavas,
the two of them then took their pleasure together on the Vindhya mountains, in caves where Kinnaras sang.
There, a great asura named Mūka, who was guarding those two,
beheld the goddess upon the peak, blazing as if with splendor.
She was endowed with the marks of merit and adorned with meritorious ornaments;
she had arrived there like the very personification of meritorious deeds.
Then Mūka, his eyes wide with wonder upon seeing the Goddess,
went in his mind to Śumbha, the best of the Dānavas.
Just as she, with all her limbs beautiful, is the foremost among all women,
so too is that Śumbha, the moon among the lords of the Daityas, the foremost among men.
A dark-eyed woman with broad hips would be a fitting wife for him, who has a wide chest and long eyes. (63.7)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he spoke to that slender-waisted woman:
"Who are you, O lady with eyes like those of a frightened and bewildered fawn? (63.8)
"O lady of faultless limbs, who is your father, and who is your mother, O sinless one? For what purpose do you dwell here on this mountain frequented by the Dānavas? (63.9)
Having been addressed thus by Mūka, the Great Yoginī, sovereign of the gods,
perceived in her mind that the time for Śumbha and Niśumbha had arrived.
Preceded by a smile, she who was skilled in speech spoke these words: "Know me to be a human woman, dwelling here upon this mountain. (63.11)
My learned father, the son of Atri, who wandered as a mendicant, has gone to heaven;
leaving me behind while I was still a child, my mother too has followed her husband.
"O Dānava, I was then commanded by my mother after she had bestowed these weapons upon me:
'Dwell on the beautiful Vindhya mountain and always practice yoga.'"
Fulfilling the word of the noble lady, I dwell here in this best of mountains,
which is frequented by lions, tigers, elephants, and deer.
Having heard these words of the goddess, Mūka, his mind filled with joy,
went in haste to see Śumbha, the foremost of the Dānavas.
Then, having approached Śumbha with eyes wide open in joy,
he seemed to announce the sight of an unprecedented jewel through his very appearance.
Seeing him with eyes wide with wonder, Śumbha, whose own eyes were red and long, then said to Mūka: "O Dānava, why are you so pleased?"
Thus addressed by Śumbha, Mūka spoke these words:
"Today I have seen an unprecedented jewel among women upon the peak of the mountain."
No woman so beautiful as she exists among humans, nor even among the gods;
neither among the rākṣasas, nor the yakṣas, nor in the cities of the gandharvas.
"O King, neither among the Nāgas, nor among the Siddhas, nor in the palaces of the lords of the Daityas,
have I ever before seen such a woman of exquisite form."
"Who are you, whose daughter are you, and for what purpose do you dwell here on this mountain?"—thus questioned, she spoke these words to me: "I am indeed the daughter of Atri. (63.21)
"And by my mother's command, I dwell here upon the peak of the Vindhya mountains.
Having thus addressed his master, that Dānava fell silent. (63.22)
Then, in the heart of Śumbha, along with the words of Mūka,
desire found an opening for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Then the lord of the Daityas, his mind agitated by desire, said:
"Go, Mūka, and for my sake entice that slender-waisted woman."
Thus addressed by Śumbha, that Dānava rose up quickly and went to where that goddess had previously been sighted.
Seeing that Dānava standing before her with palms joined in reverence, the goddess then asked Mūka, "For what purpose have you come? (63.26)
Thus questioned by Kauśikī, the Dānava Mūka then replied:
"Noble lady, I am the messenger of Śumbha; I have come into your presence. (63.27)
Then the goddess, having smiled and looked upon him with favor, spoke thus to the messenger who had arrived: "What did that lord of the Asuras say? (63.28)
Thus questioned by the goddess, the mute one then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Noble lady, Śambhu, the lord of the Daityas, chooses you to be his wife."
O deer-eyed one, among all the wives of Śakra, the conqueror of that lion among Dānavas in battle, you are the foremost and his most beloved wife.
Thus addressed by him, the Goddess of the Immortals then laughed and said:
"Behold my own arms; know me as one for whom battle is the bride-price."
"Having conquered me, this Daitya ought indeed to make me his wife;
or else, slain by me, let him go to be the food of crows and jackals. (63.32)
To the goddess who had spoken thus, Mūka said, as if laughing:
"O beautiful lady, what need have you for war with the Dānavas and Daityas through your husband? (63.33)
Even the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, though mounted upon the shoulders of Airāvata, was unable to gaze upon the face of that one when he was enraged in battle.
Having heard those words of his, the goddess spoke as if smiling:
"O lords of the Daityas, even all of you are but blades of grass to me on the front line of battle."
"Go and inform Śumbha, O lowest of Dānavas!
Since you have come here as a messenger, you shall not be harmed by me. (63.36)
Then, having bowed to her, the mute man went to the side of the enemy of the gods;
and being permitted by him, he began to relate [the matter]. (63.37)
O best of Dānavas, that maiden was requested by me for your sake;
she said, "I am one whose bride-price is battle; you must take me away only after conquering me. (63.38)
Furthermore, O King, that woman, filled with pride and wonder, spoke thus: "In my battle, the Daityas are but as blades of grass. (63.39)
Having heard those words spoken by Mūka at that time,
that best of Asuras could not endure them, due to anger, pride, and lust.
Then, having risen, the lord of the Dānavas went to the beautiful assembly hall,
which possessed pillars and balconies made of crystal and was adorned with archways of variegated jewels.
Upon that great, firm, and well-spread golden lion-throne,
the mighty-armed one sat down comfortably, like Varuṇa himself.
Then Niśumbha also sat down upon an excellent throne,
his chest at that time glistening with the mass of rays from his jeweled armlets.
Following those two, the great beings— the Daityas and Dānavas—
entered the delightful cave of the Himalayas, like clouds darkened by rainwater.
Then, when those kings of the Daityas and Dānavas had taken their seats,
Śumbha, with a voice like the rumbling of thick clouds, spoke these words:
My guardian on Mount Vindhya, the Mūka-dānava,
beheld a maiden of beautiful form upon a peak of the Vindhya range.
"O Lord of Daityas, she said, 'I am the bride-price for battle,' and for my sake she was indeed requested by him; furthermore, she spoke these words regarding the grasses."
Having forcibly conquered that proud maiden in battle,
I am resolved to bring her here this very day, even as she struggles and is rendered helpless.
Then, having heard his words, the mighty-armed great asura named Śambhu laughed aloud and said this to the lord of the asuras:
63.49. Then, having heard his words, the mighty-armed great asura named Śambhu laughed aloud and said this to the lord of the asuras:
"O King, all women are by nature inclined toward the left; you ought to win her over by means of conciliation. (63.50)
Then, having heard the words of Śambhu, Maya, the best of the Dānavas,
whose eyes were like freshly blossomed blue lotuses, spoke.
O Lord of the Asuras, what is her form, or what is her activity? And what are the constant implements that remain by her side? (63.52)
When Maya, the lord of the Daityas, who possessed the prowess of an intoxicated elephant, had spoken thus,
the lord of the Daityas then urged Muka, who was standing at his side.
Regarding the question he had asked, Maya, the best among the wise,
though then mute, began to explain it all.
She was always well-established, three-eyed, with a mouth of formidable teeth;
she had eight arms, was dark as a rain-cloud, possessed a beautiful nose, and had a lovely voice.
All her weapons were always kept ready,
along with her excellent armor and various beautiful ornaments.
"Her form surpasses the sun, and her luster exceeds the moon"—having thus spoken in the assembly of the Daityas, Mūka then fell silent. (63.57)
Then, sighing deeply, the great asura Maya,
skilled in speech, spoke these words of auspicious conclusion in the assembly.
Surely a magical spell (kṛtyā) has been conjured by the gods defeated in battle;
it has come to the Vindhya mountain for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Therefore, enough of that for you, O King; there are slender-waisted maidens with long eyes and beautiful limbs in the dwellings of the Daityas and Dānavas.
"O King, having properly acquired those suitable, sweet-sounding instruments, stay constantly within the interior of the palace and sport as you please. (63.61)
When these words had been spoken by Maya in the assembly of the Asuras, the great Asura Śumbha then laughed and spoke these words:
63.62. When this speech had been uttered by Maya in the assembly of the Asuras, the great Asura Śumbha then laughed and spoke thus.
If that maiden was created by the gods under the command of the Dānavas,
then she will not cease her activity until the Dānavas have been swiftly slain.
As long as she has not yet exerted herself against this task,
you ought to seize her quickly and bring her under your control by force.
Then all the best of the Daityas and Dānavas,
impelled by Time, agreed with the words of the king of the Daityas.
Then, having addressed these words to all the lions among the Daityas present in the assembly, the conqueror of the lord of the gods rose up,
trailing his pure white silken garment like a cloud in the rainy season bent low under the weight of fresh water.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the dialogue between Mahat and Ara, in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 63.63 ||
The sixty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having struck the kettledrums and having equipped themselves for battle, those sons of Diti and the Dānavas—
Then they caused the chariots, elephants, and horses to be equipped for battle.
Then the Daityas brought elephants that had taken up water,
with their temples flowing with rutting-ichor, and offered them incense and morsels of food.
Likewise, there were girths and trappings, well-fashioned neck-ornaments, and goads made entirely of iron and adorned with gold and jewels.
Then, the elephant-riders mounted upon their female elephants bound on various kinds of armor according to the prescribed rites.
They properly fastened quivers with their openings facing sideways and upwards,
and they also bound all their weapons upon both [the princes].
Then, on both sides of the three seats, Vaijayantī banners were raised up in their respective places.
The Dānavas, having bathed and drunk, mounted horses whose tails were tied;
they were armed with swords and wore iron mail. || 64.7 ||
Some chariot-warriors mounted their chariots, which were yoked with horses, equipped with weapons and banners, well-prepared, and possessed of excellent axles and poles.
Then Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two brothers and lords of the Dānavas,
those great asuras intoxicated by their own strength, donned their armor and mounted [their chariots].
Two battle-chariots, well-prepared for combat, with bounding horses,
equipped with weapons and banners, and made of gold, stood separately.
Those two broad-chested men went forth, having performed the auspicious rites for victory,
while being praised by Magadhan bards, panegyrists, and heralds who marched before them.
Then, having struck their musical instruments,
the asuras set out in great numbers toward that mountain where the goddess Kauśikī dwells.
Then the banners of the lions among the Dānavas fell as they were about to depart;
and jackals, stationed in the blazing quarter, howled inauspiciously.
Dust, grey as the belly of a pigeon, fell from the sky,
and vultures and crows wheeled above the army.
A wind filled with dust blew against them;
the sky roared harshly and the earth trembled.
Perceiving the signs of defeat, the enemies of the gods approached,
as if helplessly dragged away by Death himself.
Then the lord of the Daityas commanded the guard Mūka:
"Go and say to that slender-waisted woman, 'Pay the toll. (64.17)
Having gone there at his word and having bowed down, he said to Kauśikī: "O Noble Lady, please accept the bride-price being offered by the enemy of the gods. (64.18)
Saying "So be it," she dismissed that Dānava,
and Kauśikī, employing her great yoga, began to increase in size through her yogic power.
Then, from her limbs, there emerged excellent women of terrifying appearance, equipped with weapons and wearing leather finger-guards and arm-guards.
The mighty Vāyasī was surrounded by ten million women with the faces of crows,
and Upakā, of great strength, by as many women with the faces of cuckoos.
The fierce one was surrounded on all sides by goddesses with lion-like faces, and she was protected by formidable ones with tiger-like faces.
And the sinless Jayā, along with the mighty Jayantī,
were surrounded by immeasurable goddesses who had the faces of elephants and peacocks.
Jayamānā was surrounded by those with dog-like faces, while Prabhāvatī, possessed of great strength, was surrounded by those with swan-like faces; and Cakrāhvā had faces like the cakravāka birds.
In the battle against his enemies, Śivā was surrounded by jackal-faced women who were inauspicious to her foes;
Saramā, moreover, was surrounded by dog-faced women and was exceedingly difficult to conquer.
Vijayā was protected on all sides by those with the faces of hawks,
and surrounded by those with the faces of herons— slayers of enemies in battle— who were like Death itself.
Fate was made difficult for enemies to conquer in battle by those with faces like cormorants;
it was made to resound by many thunderbolts with faces like cocks.
Revatī, Vṛṣadaṃśā, Pūtanā, Kaṭapūtanā, Ālambā, Kinnarī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Śakuni, and Mukhamaṇḍikā. || 64.28 ||
Alakṣmī, Adhṛti, Lakṣmī, Potakī, Vānarī, and Spṛhā—
these and other mighty daughters were born of Kauśikī.
She was surrounded on all sides by many women wearing various costumes,
who bore diverse armor and weapons.
He quickly created from the Kauśikī river golden chariots for battle,
yoked with horses swift as thought, equipped with weapons, and bearing raised banners.
Horses with their equipment, elephants intoxicated with rut,
weapons, armor, and various kinds of musical instruments.
And that great yoginī spoke to those goddesses standing before her:
"O goddesses, Śumbha and Niśumbha are two brothers who are thorns to the gods. (64.33)
"Having indeed conquered me in battle at the forefront of the fray,
those two, intoxicated by their strength, have come together with the Daityas and Dānavas to take me away."
I shall slay those two; as for the remaining enemies of the gods who have been struck down, you shall become free from old age, immortal, and possessed of great strength.
Having thus granted them a boon and instructed those goddesses at that time, the illustrious goddess, having resolved upon battle, [departed]. (64.36)
Then that unswerving lady mentally thought of her great chariot;
the daughter of the king of mountains immediately presented to her that very chariot which she had envisioned.
Beholding before her the golden-winged bird, a product of her own merit, who possessed a luster like a blazing fire and was encircled by a garland of rays from his jewels, Kauśikī gazed upon him.
It was equipped with various weapons and armor, and joined by mighty lions, victorious in battle against the enemy forces, whose thick manes were tawny and swaying.

He was resplendent with a preeminent golden banner, exceedingly firm and raised high, its radiance shimmering with the luster of jewels, while its crest was a dancing peacock whose plumage was spread wide.
Vijayā took up the parasol, while Siṃhī became her charioteer;
then Jayantī and Jayā both held chowries for her.
Then, having donned her armor and taken up various weapons,
she ascended the divine chariot after receiving benedictions for victory and auspiciousness.
With a sunshade held aloft above his head, possessing the brilliance of the full moon,
he was being fanned with variegated-handled fly-whisks as white as moonbeams.
Then, having struck their musical instruments, those goddesses sounded various kinds of notes; and the divine women, being well-prepared, became her precursors.
At that sound, the hearts of the Daityas trembled;
the elephants and horses in the army of the Asuras discharged excrement and urine.
The world of mortals seemed to tremble, the oceans were as if agitated,
the lords of mountains shook, and the vault of heaven was filled.
Then that army of deities, adorned with banners and standards,
shone brightly as musical instruments resounded, crowded with white-sheathed swords.
Variegated with rows of cranes, accompanied by Indra’s bow, and possessing a great roar,
it was like the mass of water-bearing clouds in the month of Nabhasya, together with their clusters of lightning.
Then, restraining himself, he proceeded toward the lord of the Daityas with such speed that the host of gods seemed to contract the ten directions.
Then the enemies of the gods beheld the approaching army, with its various lofty banners,
producing terror with its great roar, like a towering mass of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Armies," in the Battle between Śumbha and Niśumbha within the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those deities, enraged, [attacked] the Daityas who were at their forefront.
They struck them with various weapons, and they, in turn, pierced them in the battle.
Then, in that battle, the Daityas, the enemies of the immortals—powerful heroes equipped with various weapons—struck down the goddesses. (65.2)
Horsemen on horseback [attacked] foot-soldiers, and foot-soldiers [attacked] foot-soldiers;
chariot-warriors stationed in their chariots [attacked] those, and elephant-riders [attacked] those mounted on elephants.
Chariots, elephants, and horses [attacked] chariots, elephants, and horses; brave foot-soldiers [attacked] horsemen, and horsemen [attacked] foot-soldiers. (65.4)
The goddesses also, enraged in battle, slaughtered the infantry, cavalry, chariots,
and elephants of the lords of the Dānavas with spears, javelins, and battle-axes.
Having struck down the heroic Dānavas to the ground, they crushed them with their feet;
some even split open the heads of those enemies of the gods with their fists.
Tearing open the chests of those arrogant ones in battle, some of the goddesses drank the blood along with the life-breaths of the enemies of the gods.
Some, rising up with speed, violently hacked weapons into pieces;
others, enraged, struck down the deities with fists as hard as thunderbolts.
Some elephants, their temples darkened by the flow of rut-fluid,
being exceedingly enraged, crushed the chariots of the gods in battle.
Some elephants, with rows of intoxicated bees clinging to their temple-walls and their riders slain, slaughtered both Daityas and gods.
Some, clad in armor and with bright swords whirling in their hands, cut down the host of the gods, while the gods likewise struck down the dānavas.
Some elephant lords, having recognized by scent those elephants that were intoxicated and had their faces mangled,
suddenly struck them upon smelling that odor, even though they were held fast by their mahouts.
The great bows being drawn by the mighty leaders of the Dānava warriors resounded shrilly upon the field of battle,
like cranes in the autumn nights across the sky.

Then that entire Vindhya mountain, its bowers, hollows, and caves filled with the sounds of musical instruments, the slapping of bowstrings, the neighing of elephants and horses, and the rattling of chariot wheels, seemed to tremble.

Having driven back the goddesses of the enemies in battle, the Daitya warriors, their hearts filled with joy, loudly roared and shouted cries as they forcefully repelled the divine forces in the fray.
There, the horses, their bodies slightly drenched with blood, performed repeated gallops back and forth,
like great forests with rising shoots stirred by the wind.
The severed heads of those leading warriors, radiant with various golden ornaments,
lay fallen upon the battlefield by the goddesses like lotuses with their stalks cut off.
With its elephants repelled and fleeing in fear, its horses and warriors struck down by the deities,
and as the lion-like lords of the Daityas turned back to attack, the army became like a swaying swing.

Slain in battle by excellent arrows that pierced their vital organs, the lordly elephants— resembling mountains of black collyrium and adorned with various bells fastened by the goddesses of the enemies of the gods— fell down trumpeting.
Having rushed forward with speed, their forces were struck down in battle and quickly retreated,
like the waters of rivers driven back when they encounter the great ocean at the time of its swelling tide.
In that great assembly, the gods and the Daityas shone forth with their arrows locked against one another,
like clusters of stars in the sky when the light of the sun has set behind the clouds.
Then, having called out their names, the lords of the Dānavas quickly emerged from their own forces, mounted upon their chariots;
enraged and well-prepared, those best of chariot-warriors drew their variegated bows.
The goddesses also, standing upon their chariots, became even more resolute and rushed forward with speed in their anger;
then Death herself, her wrath aroused, advanced against him on a chariot that sounded like a thundercloud and was adorned with gold.
Then Lakṣmī was joined with Druma, Kānti with Maya in the battle, Saramā with Mura,
Caṇḍā with Ghana, Niyati with Khara, and the wrathful Prabhāvatī with Dhundhu.

Those Daityas, their minds eager for battle, approached swiftly with their arms and weapons, accompanied by goddesses; unable to endure [the gods], they were renowned for their pride and well-equipped on their own chariots.
Those of undaunted spirit discharged in battle the finest arrows of the gods— shining with light, with golden shafts, released from bows drawn back to the ear.
Then the goddesses likewise discharged an infinite number of sharp, well-feathered, long-reaching arrows that pierce the vital organs, against those approaching leaders of the Dānava hosts.
Those various excellent arrows, released by one another and interlacing,
shone like the combined splendors of the moon and the sun gathered together at the end of the day on a cloudless full-moon night.

Severed by the deities in battle, the arms of the lords of the Daityas fell from their weapons, like great, thick-bodied serpent-kings whose coils have been cast off and whose tongues have been swallowed. 65.29.
Then, in that battle, the enraged Ṣaṣṭhī discharged showers of arrows at Meghasvana;
the Daitya cut those hundreds of shafts into pieces with his own arrows in the sky as they approached from all sides. || 65.30 ||
Then, seeing his arrows cut down, the Daitya quickly discharged other, lighter shafts;
the Daitya, moreover, repeatedly severed those incoming arrows with volleys of his own.
Having cut down those arrows, the son of Diti again hurled ten gold-feathered shafts at Ṣaṣṭhī;
having quickly warded them off, Ṣaṣṭhī pierced the Daitya with six gold-feathered arrows. (65.32)
Wounded by them, his body smeared with blood and greatly distressed, he spoke but little;
his own charioteer then bore him away from the battle on a chariot adorned with gold.
Kārtasvana loosed arrows with variegated golden shafts at the goddess in battle;
Death, however, cut those shafts down with his own voluted-feathered volleys of arrows before they had even reached her.
Having cut his arrows with his own variegated shafts, he pierced him in the chest with sixty-five;
pierced by them, he quickly shone like a rain-cloud split by the rays of the sun.
And Death swiftly struck his horses with separate arrows having golden shafts;
then, leaping from that chariot whose horses were slain, he seized a shield and a polished, excellent sword.
Enraged, with eyes extremely long and red, he rushed impetuously toward the Goddess;
as he was falling upon her, Death cut that shield into hundreds of pieces with his sharp-pointed showers of arrows. || 65.37 ||
With his shield of hide shattered, the lord of the gods raised a sharp-edged sword and rushed toward Death; at that moment, he appeared like a cloud flashing with lightning over Rohiṇī in the sky.
As he rushed forward in battle like Death itself, Mṛtyu struck him in his vital organs with arrows resembling fierce serpents;
he then swiftly deprived him of his life-breaths.
On the field of battle, Lakṣmī, invincible through her showers of excellent arrows, overwhelmed the tree-like Bāṇa— who possessed the grace of a lordly elephant—
with sharp, straight shafts adorned with beautiful golden feathers, released from a distance reaching to his ears.
Those various straight-flying arrows with beautiful feathers fell upon the limbs of the tree in the battle;
with those diverse shafts clinging to it, that great tree shone as if inhabited by flocks of birds.
Then that steadfast lord of the Kimpuruṣas pierced Lakṣmī with ten well-feathered arrows in her face—
she whose countenance was like the full moon— and struck each of her two arms separately with eight hundred more.
While they were not thinking [of him], he, whose face is excellent, plunged sharp arrows into her mouth;
and he fixed countless other well-feathered shafts with gold-polished nocks into her body.
Then the lord of the Daityas, with a sharp crescent-headed arrow, severed the tip of Lakṣmī’s banner on her chariot;
he quickly pierced her four horses with four arrows and struck her charioteer with an arrow.
Then, taking up an iron shaft (nārāca), Lakṣmī struck the charioteer of that enemy of the gods in battle;
she pierced his horses with various arrows and swiftly cut down the banner of the chariot. || 65.45 ||
Then, deprived of their driver, his horses— tormented by those peerless arrows—
carried him away from the field of battle, as if seeking to preserve their own lives.
Then Maya showered Kāntimaya with hundreds of arrows, and Kāntimaya [showered] him with volleys of sharpened shafts;
like the falling of frost upon darkness, there was no space between the two of them at that time.

In seizing, supporting, and dragging; in standing, advancing, grasping, and exerting force—they both distinguished themselves from one another through their training and skills in the midst of the arena.
Maya cut down those arrows consisting of splendor, and Maya, with his own splendor, [cut down] the shafts discharged by Kānti;
though both were invincible, they found no opening whatsoever against one another. (65.49)
The splendor of Maya’s arrows— straight-flying, with shafts polished with gold— plunged into his horses, his driver, his charioteer, his banner, and indeed into every single limb of his body.

And Maya covered Kānti—along with her chariot, her charioteer, and her beautiful, variegated banner and foremost horses—with sharp arrows, just as a cloud covers a forest glade with showers of rain. (65.51)
Then, enraged in battle, Kānti struck Māya’s charioteer with a principal iron arrow equipped with fine feathers;
at that moment, she also swiftly slew the eight horses of the enemy with eight arrows.
Then Maya, his horses and charioteer slain and himself deprived of his chariot, took up a sword with a sharpened edge;
realizing the power of Kāntī in battle, he abandoned the fight and flew up into the sky like a bird.
On the field of battle, Saramā pierced Mura, the leader of the hosts of Dānavas and Daityas, with sharp arrows;
the Daitya likewise struck Saramā with straight-flying shafts fletched with the feathers of vultures and peacocks.
Then the enraged goddess, with a sharp broad-headed arrow, cut his variegated bow;
he then took up another bow and pierced the four horses of the goddess.
Struck by the arrows of the lord of the Daityas, those horses, overwhelmed and vomiting blood, fell to the ground panting in the battle; all of them together swiftly gave up their lives at once.
Then the goddess Saramā, enraged, raised her sword with its bright edge and,
leaping into the sky, struck the driver and the horses of great size belonging to the asura.
Then Mura, having leapt into the air with speed, his horses and charioteer slain by his wrath, pierced the Goddess in the chest with ten exceedingly sharp arrows resembling fierce serpents. (65.58)
Disregarding those arrows, Saramā then cut through Muru’s bow;
with his bow shattered, that enemy of Indra vanished from the sky, quickly abandoning the battle.
The fierce [goddess] pierced the oncoming cloud with gold-feathered arrows having sharp points in battle;
pierced by them, that lord of the Daityas shone like a dark cloud struck by the rays of the moon.
Disregarding those arrows, Caṇḍā, raining down a mass of shafts like a cloud, rushed toward them;
as he approached, she pierced his excellent chariot-horses with her well-feathered arrows.
The Daitya also cut down the goddess’s banner with its lofty top and slew her horses;
abandoning their chariots and descending to the ground, the two of them took up excellent shields and swords and prepared for battle.
In the midst of the battle, they moved through the circle of the field, their toes barely touching the ground;
moving with such lightness of foot, they traversed various paths without either of them finding an opening against the other.
The *abhipluta*, *uccapluta*, *siṃhapāta*, *nivṛttaka*, *ākrīḍitaka*, *ūrdhvabāhu*, *khagāpayāta*, *abhihatāpayāta*, *niṣaṇṇaka*, *āviddhaśiras*, and *abhighāta* [strokes]. (65.64)
Then, leaping up with speed, Caṇḍā swiftly severed his neck;
with his head cut off, that Daitya fell quickly upon the battlefield chest-first.
With his body smeared with blood, that dense-bodied one then fell lifeless upon the earth;
he shone like a dark cloud in the sky, its vast form suffused by the twilight.
Niryāti pierced Khara in the chest with sharp, gold-feathered arrows provided with excellent wings;
then, as he charged directly toward him in the battle, he cut down his standard with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla).
Pierced by them, that invincible enemy, his body smeared with blood, rushed furiously at the Goddess in battle, desiring to slay her; then, swiftly seizing a heavy mace, he hurled it at the Goddess.

That mace, released by the foremost of the Dānavas—resplendent with various golden ornaments and beautiful bells—swiftly crushed the chariot of Niyati, along with her charioteer and her banner with its lofty top. (65.69)
Leaping swiftly from her own vehicle, Niyati, her eyes rolling and bloodshot with rage,
approached that foremost leader of the Dānava warriors and split his head asunder at the crown with her sword.
With his head split open and streams of blood flowing,
that Dānava shone upon the earth like a mountain whose peak has been shattered by a thunderbolt and from which flows a stream of mineral ores.
Prabhāvatī struck Dhundhu with straight-flying, well-feathered arrows;
the noble lady pierced his chest with ten sharp-pointed shafts that resembled a mass of rain-clouds.
She struck the sixteen horses of the enemy of the gods with sixteen arrows;
having slain his charioteer with one, she cut down his banner with another. (65.73)
Dhundhu hurled a mace, heavy as a thousand *bhāras* and adorned with beautiful golden bells;
as it came flying toward her, Prabhāvatī shattered that weapon released by the lord of the Daityas into hundreds of pieces.
Seizing a massive iron club and leaping from his mount, that Daitya,
dark as a mountain of collyrium, rushed toward the Goddess on the field of battle like Time himself with staff in hand.
As the lord of the Dānavas rushed forward in battle, the goddess struck him with well-feathered arrows;
disregarding all those shafts of the goddess, he approached her at the front of the fray out of rage.

Whirling that iron mace, which was like the rod of Vaivasvata and had been forged with great effort, he—whose arms were as thick as the mace itself—hurled it at his chariot; he struck it down upon the slope of the mountain, just as Indra hurls his thunderbolt.

That iron club, hurled by the Asura, swiftly pulverized the goddess's chariot—along with its horses, charioteer, banner, and golden wheels; yet the goddess herself, by her speed, escaped from that spot.
Seeing her fleeing there at that time, that chief of the Danava warriors seized that very iron club and rushed after her,
like a dark cloud in the sky pursuing the streak of lightning.
Leaping up, she cut his iron club with razor-edged arrows and other excellent divine weapons;
then, raising her fist tightly, the Daitya once more sprang into the sky after her.
The goddess swiftly struck that Dānava in his vital organs with excellent arrows that reached those very spots;
pierced by those well-feathered shafts aimed at his vitals, that chief of the Dānava warriors vanished from sight.

Then, the enemies of the Lord of the Gods, having abandoned the battle as the chief warriors departed with their prowess and manliness shattered, raised a great roar and stood upon the excellent elephants, grasping their weapons.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Goddess," in the Śumbha-Niśumbha conflict of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
The goddesses also, having learned of their efforts, mounted those excellent elephants with great effort.
Pure, with streams of rut flowing, possessing fine tusks, and with excellent bodies, trunks, and ears; || 66.1 ||
With well-formed foreheads, high and rounded frontal globes, beautiful manes, and gracefully curved ears;
with fine tusks, eyes like those of the kalaviṅka bird, broad chests, and straight backbones.
[He saw] war-horses, leaders of their kind, in the prime of youth, well-trained, with powerful forequarters,
equipped with armor and weapons and adorned with variegated bells, with their tall standards and banners raised high.
Adorned with banners and flags, and decorated with various wonderful weapons,
those herds of elephants then appeared like forest groves come together in the woods.
Those Daityas also, stationed upon the head of the elephant, shone as they drew their bows,
which were adorned with rainbows and filled with the sound of thunderbolts, like clouds resting upon mountains.
Those armies, urged on by their elephant-drivers at the place of slaughter,
rushed at one another like masses of clouds driven together by the wind.
Rushing impetuously at the elephants, the elephants struck them in the frontal globes with their tusks— tusks that were dark as ichor from rut, bound with iron rings, and white as stalks of reeds.
Stretching out their trunks toward him, some elephants, white as clouds, sought the scent of his gift;
though prodded by their mahouts with goads, nooses, and words, they remained arrogant with rut.
Sharp razor-headed arrows severed the raised sunshades,
while various colorful banners and diverse standards fell from the elephants as they struck one another.
The warriors fell, groaning aloud as they were pierced in their vital organs by the arrows of the deities;
vomiting blood mixed with foam from their mouths, they still held their strung bows in their hands.

The elephants of the lords of the Daityas fell on all sides, struck through their vital organs by excellent arrows; they collapsed in battle like boulders hurled down by the wind as they were assailed by the goddesses.
Seeing the leaders of the Mātaṅgas fallen lifeless upon the field of battle— resembling the great blue mountains—
some rutting elephants, circling them and lowering their heads, trumpeted with their trunks.
Severed heads adorned with earrings, arms still clutching weapons and smeared with fine sandalwood paste,
fell from the elephants of the Asura leaders in battle, struck by the sharp razor-headed arrows of the goddesses.
The foremost enemies of the gods cried out loudly on all sides as they struck their bows;
the bowstrings quivered as they were drawn, and the elephants, pierced by the released arrows, sank down.
The earth is strewn with falling elephants, pierced by arrows and with their lofty standards and beautiful backs raised high,
driven by the wind like the foothills of mountains together with their palm trees.
The Nāgas struck the elephants in the combat; the Daityas struck the goddesses and the daughters of Diti, while the goddesses struck the Daityas.
There, the Daityas, enraged and full of wrath, rushed forward against the lordly elephants and the tuskers.
With masses of elephants, resembling mountain peaks, fallen on all sides and scorched by weapons,
the ground became impassable for the gods and dānavas during that torrential downpour of missiles.
Seeing their own forces overwhelmed in battle and their elephants slain by the goddesses,
Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two lords of the Daityas, arrived at the field of combat mounted upon their chariots.
Accompanied by vanguard foot-soldiers, cavalry, and elephants, as well as hosts of the enemies of the gods,
they— whose arms were as formidable as iron clubs— stretched their variegated bows and prepared for battle.
Then, perceiving their arrival, the Goddess urged on the lions of her chariot— creatures endowed with swaying, tawny manes— as she drew her bows wide in the battle.
By the very sound of her lute, the goddess brought about the loss of speed in the horses, the deprivation of rut in the great elephants, and the confusion of mind in the enemies of the gods.
Having exerted the utmost effort in battle, all the arrows of the enemies of the gods,
failing to reach the Goddess, fell upon the earth as if proclaiming the defeat of the asuras.
Just as the Sun pervades all things stationary and moving with his rays during the days,
so did the Goddess pervade the forces of the lords of the Daityas on the field of battle with her showers of arrows.
The horses fell down swiftly, deprived of life; the rutting elephants, with ichor flowing from their temples, stumbled;
and all the foremost warriors of the enemies of the gods trembled together in battle, struck by arrows. (66.24)
Just as a blazing fire, kindled by its radiant flames, burns through dry thickets without restraint,
so did Kauśikī consume the armies of the enemies of the gods in battle with her showers of flaming arrows.
Just as at midday the sun makes the shadow of all things stationary and moving very small,
so did the goddess make that army of the enemies reduced to a small remnant in battle.
Then, having summoned the goddess, the two lords of the Dānavas drew their great bows and struck out;
in the arena of battle, they covered Kauśikī with sharp, well-feathered arrows.
With bows drawn, their minds overcome by wrath,
the two long-armed lords of the Daityas, intent upon the gods as their targets, loosed excellent, well-feathered arrows at them in the battle.
Then the lords of the Daityas, disregarding those volleys of arrows which destroy the pride of enemies,
pierced the two Daityas in battle with excellent, well-feathered shafts, gold-tufted and furnished with fine joints.
Disregarding the arrows, the two heroic Daityas seized their maces, which were adorned with brilliant and beautiful bells;
whirling them with extreme effort, they hurled those massive weapons upon the Goddess in the field of battle.
Having cut those [armors] in the sky by the hundreds with well-jointed arrows possessing beautiful golden feathers,
the Goddess severed their variegated armor with other sharp-pointed razor-headed shafts.
He struck down the horses and the charioteers, and cut away the two variegated banners from the chariots;
