furthermore, he pierced the vital organs of the two enemies of the gods with other excellent, gold-feathered arrows.

Then Śumbha and Niśumbha, the lords of the Daityas, casting aside their chariots and tormented by the excellent arrows, seized two superb swords; with those sharp blades appearing dark as sapphire, they leapt into the sky.
Then, in a cloudless sky as blue as a polished sword, the Goddess, having rushed forward with great speed and seized them by their necks,
swiftly crushed those two lords of the sons of Diti while being praised by the foremost of sages, who were free from fear and despondency.
Then, vomiting frothy blood from their mouths, their strength suddenly destroyed and all the joints of their limbs crushed,
those two lions among the Daityas fell upon the surface of the earth with their lives departed and their eyes red at the corners.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the denizens of heaven went to see the Kauśikī river and the Vindhya mountain.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, Marutvan, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins.
Dharma, Aṅgiras, Uśanas, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Kaśyapa,
Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Sanaka, Āttri, and Sanandana.
The Apsarases, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Mahoragas;
the Upavedas, the sacrifices, the Vedas, the sciences, and Sarasvatī.
The oceans, rivers, mountains, and various sacred fords;
the Mothers, the world-protectors, the lunar mansions, Dhruva, and the planets.
Then the radiant deities, their minds filled with joy, spoke to the goddess of great splendor, who sat there with a delighted heart, an enemy of the asuras.
O Goddess, by slaying those two lords of the Dānavas, those beings of great power who were thorns to the three worlds, you have removed the dart of suffering for all people.
"O Goddess, the seers are now offering purifying oblations;
they recite the Vedic hymns aloud and observe their sacred vows. (67.7)
Now this sacrifice, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, is being performed by the brahmins;
and in the leaf-huts, the sages lie down in comfort, full of trust.
O Goddess, the virtuous who have taken refuge in the path of truth dwell free from fear;
yet the path of righteous action, which had been severed, has now appeared once more in the world.
By your grace, the world-protectors bear their heads held high,
and the wind blows pleasantly, mingled with the pollen of flowers.
O Goddess of great yoga, by your grace the rivers carry their waters, which are clear and cool, free from all fatigue.
And now, O daughter of the mountain, the mountains have been reborn,
free from feverish distress, carrying forth cool and sweet water from their cascades.
The serpents now bear their hoods high, marked with the svastika and the wheel;
and the oceans, out of confidence, rest in peace. (67.13)
O Goddess, by your grace, the Apsarases now wander in the sky, which is pure with its virtuous mind, their eyes languid with amorous play. (67.14)
And now, O Goddess, the wives of the Siddhas, full of confidence, frequent the blossoming sandalwood trees upon the peaks of the mountains. (67.15)
By their very nature and from drinking honey, the yakṣas with eyes like red lotuses now roam upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana.
Now, free from fatigue, Śeṣa supports the earth with ease upon his hoods,
which are encircled by the canopy-like radiance of their own jewels.
"You are the mother of the worlds, the bestower of fearlessness upon those who are afraid.
O Goddess, choose your desired boons and be consecrated as Acyutā."
Thus addressed by the gods, the Goddess spoke as if smiling slightly:
"I wish to see my father, who bears the incompletely full moon upon his crest."
"Once my mother, who is so serene and gracious, and the daughter of the mountain,
as well as my two parents, have given their permission, you shall then consecrate me."
Thus addressed, the gods then reflected with unperturbed minds upon Mahādeva,
who was accompanied by his consort and possessed immeasurable splendor and prowess.
Then those gods beheld the god of gods, the lord of Umā,
standing before them like the concentrated mass of all splendors.
Bearing upon his head the weight of matted locks that were brown at their tips,
he carried a blazing fire as if it were a mass of radiant flames.
He performed his ablutions with holy ashes as white as crushed camphor,
appearing like a towering silver mountain crowned with a network of golden creepers.
He eclipsed the splendors of the gods with his own brilliance,
like the sun at midday outshining the flames of lamps.
He bore upon his crown a slender digit of the moon, slightly curved, which, on one side, was encircled by a halo and seemed to distill nectarous water.
He wore a lion’s skin that was curved, radiant, heavy, and grey with the dust of ashes;
it hung down loosely, marked by slight wrinkles.
With his body’s edges streaked by the rays from the jewels on his hoods,
the great lord of serpents spread across his chest with his massive coils.
And he saw Bhavānī standing by his side, blazing with her own splendor,
wearing a red silken garment produced from the Kalpa tree.
She bore upon her head a full-blown mandāra garland, frequented by swarms of intoxicated bees and tawny with a profusion of pollen.
Adorned with excellent, praiseworthy ornaments made of gold, fashioned by celestial artisans, variegated and encircled by the rays of jewels.
She bore upon her neck a large, peerless single-string necklace, beautiful and pure, as stainless as the rays of the autumn moon.
Then all the gods and Kauśikī, with her face bowed down, rose up and,
with contented minds, fell at the lotus-feet of those two.
Then Mahādeva, looking up at Kauśikī, spoke these words:
"O you of great yoga and great splendor, you are invincible to all beings."
"You shall wander through the worlds, unimpeded everywhere;
and all these deities, O blameless one, [shall be yours] through your grace. (67.35)
Out of devotion, human beings shall worship you with offerings and oblations;
and you, O sinless one, shall always be a granter of boons to those who are devoted.
And be consecrated quickly by the gods, O destroyer of asuras;
protect the entire world of mortals, being ever worshipped, O imperishable one.
And having embraced Kauśikī and smelled her head, the illustrious Śarvāṇī, being pleased, said: "By my power, you shall become [great]."
O blameless lady, just as the gods, yakṣas, great serpents, gandharvas, sages, and siddhas worship me, so too shall they worship you.
"Devotees shall worship him everywhere and praise the Imperishable One.
Having thus granted this boon to him, the Daughter of the Mountain and the Bull-bannered Lord [departed].
Then, having been saluted by the gods, the two imperishable ones vanished;
thereafter, the lord Indra gave instructions to the Viśvakarman-s.
"Let a divine assembly hall, like Sudharmā, be constructed here at once.
Thus did Śatakratu command all the seasons to be present there.
Let the ground be quickly and properly adorned with heaps of various flowers,
fragrant with the pollen of the blossoms of shrubs, bushes, creepers, and trees.
May the breezes here blow pleasantly, captivating the minds;
may the clouds drench the plateau of the Vindhya with their holy waters.
Let the peacocks, overjoyed, cry out loudly in every direction;
let them dance all around, displaying their various and wonderful plumage.
All the hosts of apsarases should withdraw their flavors, emotions, and graceful charms;
and the gandharvas should likewise withdraw their sweet-toned lutes.
Let songs be sung everywhere in harmony with the *layatāla* rhythm,
and let the celestial drums (*devadundubhi*) be struck vigorously on all sides.
Quickly struck by rough hands, they produced variegated forms and great sounds,
like rows of bees resting upon lotuses stirred by a gentle breeze.
And let divine showers of flowers fall upon this spot,
and let banners of variegated forms be raised on every side.
Then the immensely radiant Viśvakarman quickly fashioned there various kinds of banners with well-crafted golden staffs.
It had pillars blazing with various jewels and a pedestal of variegated gems;
its archways were made of diamond and crystal, and it was auspicious, fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold.
With stairways of sapphire for its thighs, draped with hanging strings of pearls,
adorned with banners and flags, and resounding with the ringing of bells.
Then the deities beheld her, appearing like the manifest perfection of asceticism, self-restraint, and sacrifice, as if flowers from different seasons gathered together at once.
They were equal in measure, possessed of excellent fragrances, diverse and numerous;
filled with the pollen of flowers, they were pleasant to the touch and sweetly scented.
Winds blew there, repeatedly sounding their bells;
the gods and gandharvas sang, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
Then the sages praised Kauśikī with auspicious hymns;
she was filled with all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, fragrances, and holy waters.
There, auspicious jars made of gold and jewels were brought,
adorned with four lions made of rubies and diamond manes.
It was as if breathing out golden splendor, being carried by its majesty,
with its circular perimeter encrusted by a network of light from all kinds of jewels.
And Viśvakarman prepared a magnificent seat for the Goddess, while she was being praised from all sides with hymns and shouts of "Victory! (67.59).
Then Kauśikī, the daughter of the God of Gods, was seated upon that divine throne by the sages and the deities.
Having had rites for prosperity performed by Brahmins over the well-kindled Jātavedas fire,
they were dressed in two white garments produced from the wish-fulfilling tree.
Her limbs were adorned with strings of pearls, and she was decked with white garlands and unguents;
then the Seven Sages, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Yajña, and Prajāpati [approached].
The Ādityas, Kaśyapa, the Rudras, the world-protectors, the fire-gods,
the earth, the Gaṅgā, the moon, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins.
The oceans, the Vasus, Lakṣmī, Sandhyā, Kīrti, Sarasvatī, the lords of the nāgas, the lords of birds, and various excellent rivers; || 67.64 ||
Taking all the jars, they consecrated Kauśikī with that immensely radiant staff of jewels,
which resembled the orb of the full moon.
Śatakratu himself held the extended umbrella,
while [attendants] fanned him with long chowries having golden handles, as pure as the rays of the moon.
Then the world-protectors, exerting themselves, infused that imperishable [being] with seed;
thereafter, the glorious subduer of Pāka spoke to Kauśikī.
Protect the entire earth, O Goddess; you are my sister, O Eternal One.
Show favor to your devotees, O Sovereign, and destroy the thorns of immortality.
Wander through all the worlds, honored by the hosts of Siddhas.
Having spoken these words to Kauśikī, the King of the Gods, accompanied by the hosts of the thirty [gods] and adorned with shimmering white necklaces of lotus fibers,
then flew up from the Vindhya mountains, scattering dark clouds heavy with water all around in the sky.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or recite it in the assembly of the virtuous,
having attained happiness in this world, goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Consecration of Kauśikī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, those deities who were born from the body of the goddess Kauśikī—
The highly fortunate ones settled them in various regions and cities.
He settled Bahuputrā and Pralambā in Laṅkā;
Lambauṣṭhī, Vṛṣadaṃśā, and Kinnarī in Siṃhala.
At Gokarṇa she is the goddess Revatī; among the Pāṇḍyas she is Mukhamaṇḍikā;
among the Ābhīras she is Aśivā; and on the bank of the Varaṇā she is Śānti.
The goddess Prabhā in Vatsagulma, Lakṣmī on Mount Kolagiri,
Upakā among the Pārasyakas, and Vāyasī among the Yavanas.
And he settled Pracaṇḍā among the Tuṣāras, Lambikā among the Kośalas,
and both Jayā and Vijayā in his own city.
She [established] Prabhāvatī among the Kaliṅgas, Jayantī in the city of the Nāgas (Hastināpura),
the sixth, Saramā, among the Kaśmīras, and [the seventh] in the Malaya mountains.
And Pūtanā in Supīra, Mṛtyu in Pṛṣṭapura, Bāhumāṃsā in Koṭivarṣa, and Kaṭapūtanā in the Pauṇḍras. (68.7)
[He saw] Aspṛṣṭā in Madhyadeśa, Kinnarī among the Barbaras,
Nirāyāsī in Vārāṇasī, and Citraghaṇṭā in Kauśikī.
Mahākālī in Mahākāla, Vānarī among the Śabaras,
and all the remaining deities in the villages and cities.
In mountain strongholds, Kauśikī established her residence;
then, after some time, that one of great asceticism [arrived] at Svarṇākṣa.
There, Viṣṇu, having propitiated the god Śaṅkara, obtained a boon:
the discus named Sudarśana, which was like the end-maker of his enemies.
"There dwells a highly fortunate seer named Śaradvān Gautama;
the goddess then went to his sacrifice, having been invited by him. (68.12)
Having learned of her arrival there, the powerful son of Śumbha,
a Dānava named Mahiṣa, quickly came to that place.
He was well-knit, broad-chested, with a large neck and a beautiful tail;
he had curved horns, broad hooves, and a wide, elevated forehead.
With a mind fixed on enmity, cruel and a being of great power, exceedingly difficult to conquer,
he roared with a mighty sound harsh as the crashing of a thunderbolt.
Resembling the mountain of collyrium, eager for battle and arrogant in his strength,
the son of the lord of the Dānavas stood there, blocking the path of the goddess.
Having perceived his arrival, Vindhyavāsinī, the mistress of yoga,
went swiftly to that place where that lowest of Dānavas was.
Then, having seen that goddess, the Dānava, his eyes reddened with rage, approached her with speed, exerting all his effort.
With his tail erect and the tips of his sharp horns prominent, with a broad chest and hard, upright ears,
he— resembling a dark mountain— rushed with speed toward the goddess, his eyes copper-red like guggulu resin.
Seeing that son of the lord of the Daityas, Mahiṣa, rushing toward her in a rage, Kauśikī—
the slayer of the lords of the Asuras— stood upon the earth with her beautiful, wide, copper-hued eyes filled with wrath.
Approaching the goddess, whose necklace was swaying, the son of the king of the Dānavas— intoxicated by supreme power—
struck her on the chest with his horn, as hard as Indra’s weapon.
Having endured that blow from him at that time, she seized the buffalo by the horn with her trunk;
then, whirling it high in the air in a rage, she threw it down onto the surface of the earth as it gasped for breath.
Seizing the hair of the enemy of Indra and forcibly placing her foot upon his head, she took up her trident and pierced him in the back; she swiftly deprived the Daitya of his life-breaths.
Then, having slain the buffalo of fierce pride, whose horn was as hard as a diamond and who resembled a dark blue cloud,
Kauśikī— being showered from all sides with a rain of various flowers— proceeded to her dwelling on the mountain.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sixty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, knower of all worlds, you who are as exalted as the Grandfather (Brahmā)!
Then the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, having performed extensive austerities, [spoke].
O great sage, having obtained from Brahmā the boon he desired— the restoration of his fair complexion— what else did the brahmin do at the conclusion of his ascetic penance?
And Somanandin and Śārdūla—what auspicious boon did they obtain?
Tell this to me, who am your devotee and bow before you, as I ask. (69.3)
Sanatkumāra said: Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the supreme, eternal Brahman, whom the followers of Sāṃkhya always recite as the twenty-fifth Puruṣa. (69.4)
And the yogins, as well as the twenty-sixth principle and the celestial dwellers beginning with Brahmā, having bowed their heads with supreme devotion to that three-eyed one, [stood there]. (69.5)
O Vyāsa, best among those who know yoga, I shall relate to you in its entirety how the union of Śaṅkara with Gaurī came about; listen. 69.6.
Having performed most difficult austerities on that peak of the Himalayas,
she then became fair-limbed, with a radiance like pure gold.
Then, desiring a vision of Śaṅkara, Śarvāṇī set her mind upon it;
she went to Mount Mandara accompanied by Somanandin. (69.8)
In her husband's abode, the goddess saw Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas, stationed at the foot of the tree, bearing his blazing spear.
Then, seeing Nandīśvara devoted [to her], the Daughter of the Mountain Lord spoke with love: "Come, my child; you have not been seen for a long time. (69.10)
And Nandi, beholding that fair-limbed woman who shone with the luster of gold, was filled with great joy and fell prostrate at her feet. (69.11)
Having prostrated, that wise one then praised the daughter of the mountain:
"Homage to Siddhi, to the Great Goddess; homage to Rati, to Gati. (69.12)
You are action and its cause, you are primordial nature and liberation itself;
you are patience, splendor, contentment, peace, and the supreme auspiciousness.
Dakṣiṇā, Niyati, Mṛtyu, Sandhyā, Vidyut, Ahas, Kṣapā, Pṛthivī, Kauśikī, Śrī, Śarvāṇī, and the beloved of Śarva. (69.14)
Gaṇamātā, Diti, Pavitrā, Vindhyavāsinī, Kṛṣṇā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Īśvarī. || 69.15 ||
"O Goddess, be gracious to me, your devotee who bows before you.
Then the Goddess, seeing Nandin prostrate at her feet, [spoke].
She said, "I am the giver of boons," and he chose an auspicious boon:
"I desire you to be forever pleased with me; this is my supreme boon. (69.17)
Saying "So be it," that large-eyed woman entered;
Nandin went before her, and Somanandin followed behind.
She shone like the crescent moon between two planets;
having beheld her from afar, the God of Gods was filled with joy.
The one of great splendor arrived with eyes wide open in agitation;
the goddess fell at the feet of the wise god of gods.
Then the god, the best of the deities, having gazed upon the goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, who had just arrived, spoke to her again and again.
"By good fortune you have a joyful countenance; by good fortune your asceticism has borne fruit;
and by good fortune you possess this excellent complexion, fair and radiant as gold. (69.22)
"O Goddess, it is most pleasing to us in every way that you have come here;
having fulfilled your vow, from where does this tiger of yours come? (69.23)
Thus addressed by her husband with words tender with affection,
the goddess then related her entire history to the god.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, when you previously addressed me as 'black-complexioned,' my limbs were then overcome with resentment as I desired to attain a fair complexion. (69.25)
Having gone to a peak of the Himalayas, I have undertaken great asceticism;
thinking of you alone, I remain standing on one foot.
On the very day that I undertook asceticism there,
this tiger Somanandin appeared before me.
Mahādeva remained there, endowed with supreme devotion;
for a thousand divine years, I remained engaged in ascetic penance.
For that same length of time, he too remained near me,
gazing with his tail, eyes, and mouth motionless, abstaining from food.
At the conclusion of my ascetic penance, Brahmā, the granter of boons, arrived;
O Lord, it was for his sake that I previously requested a boon from him.

Therefore, O Lord Śaṅkara, this immortal one, free from old age and sorrow, has been made my attendant by your side; and at your command, the Grandfather (Brahmā) bestowed this complexion upon me. (69.31)
The God of gods said:
"I am well-pleased with you, O Goddess; choose a boon as you desire.
This king of beasts, Somanandin, is the foremost of my attendants and possesses great strength. (69.32)
"As my Nandīśa is, so shall yours be;
whatever else you say, O beloved, I shall do all that for you."
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I desire to see once again that place where supreme austerity was practiced by you together with me. (69.34)
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord spoke:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, it pleases me to go there, O imperishable one."
Having summoned Nandin and thousands of his attendants, he then went to that beautiful peak of the Himalayas where you had performed your austerities. (69.36)
Accompanied by the goddess, he went to the great mountain Himavat,
together with the gods, vidyādharas, siddhas, gandharvas, and the best of sages.
Being repeatedly saluted and praised from all sides,
the Lord of the Ganas, having mounted the back of Nandin, sported about.
Having come to the Himavat mountain, he arrived at that region;
having reached that peak, which was adorned with beautiful minerals, [he stayed there]. (69.39)
The Lord of the Gaṇas was highly pleased and rejoiced;
then, seeing that the Great One had arrived, the immovable Mountain, bowing with palms joined in reverence, approached Mahādeva.
Having fashioned that sacrificial pit on that most excellent peak,
the wielder of the Pināka bow favored the lord of mountains with a boon.
By my grace, you shall become immortal, freed from old age, devoid of all suffering,
and indeed unbreakable even by the thunderbolt.
"O best of immovable things, you shall be meritorious and a liberator from sin;
you will attain fame in the world by the name Gaurīśikhara. (69.43)
O best of mountains, merely by seeing you from afar as you stand so lofty, people shall be liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme goal. (69.44)
He who, having fasted for three nights with pure vows, ascends you, beholds Gaurī, worships her, and gratifies a Brahmin; || 69.45 ||
Whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever here gives up their life-breaths with self-restraint and a concentrated mind shall go to the world of Gaurī. (69.46)
Having attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, he shall wander together with me;
and Gaurī’s presence shall be with you right here at all times.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to that best of mountains, the three-eyed God of gods,
accompanied by Pārvatī, wandered about there in every direction.
Then, O Vyāsa, the Lord saw a stone adorned with gold and jewels; he said to the Goddess, "Look at this stone. (69.49)
The Goddess said to the Lord of Gods: "Austerity has been performed by me here;
this place is indeed dear to me, as it is to Somanandin. (69.50)
Then Bhava, out of affection, favored that stone, saying:
"He who shall remain pure and fast for three nights upon this [stone] shall be blessed. (69.51)
He shall have performed a penance that is truly heated, and he shall go to your world—that mortal who, being pure, should stand on one foot for an entire day. (69.52)
Having become intent upon the Sun, devoted to you, and having you as his supreme refuge,
he too shall go to your world and become a leader of your hosts.
And he who shall here renounce his life-breaths, which are so difficult to give up, even upon a stone,
having performed fervent penance, shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And whoever should visit this mountain region, the abode of Somanandin, for a day and night, he too shall become equal to Nandi.
Then the Lord, wandering about, questioned Pārvatī once more:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, how did these pools come to be here? (69.56)
Thus questioned, the goddess spoke these words once more:
"O Lord, O Master, when I first came here to perform ascetic penance... (69.57)
At that time, two great streams flowed repeatedly from my breasts;
these became for them two lakes of white water with vast expanses.
O Lord, when I cast off my ornaments in order to perform penance, streams of water flowed swiftly from them at that moment. (69.59)
And by her this second auspicious pool of water was made for me,
when she obtained that supreme golden complexion from Brahmā.
Then, O Lord, a sheath emerged from my body;
from that sheath this third pool was produced.
In this place, O Lord of Gods, having worshipped you according to the prescribed rite,
I have performed the fire-ritual with oblations accompanied by mantras.
"These bark garments from the trees are ready for you;
this bright black antelope skin was previously set aside by me. (69.63)
Then, having heard the words of Pārvatī, the Lord Mahādeva,
filled with supreme affection, replied to the Goddess.
Since your pond, radiant as the moon, was filled by the water from her breasts, these two shall attain supreme fame as the "Breast-Ponds. (69.65)
He who, fasting, bathes here and worships the deities, and having gratified all the ancestors, shall feed the Brahmins; (69.66)
That shall be inexhaustible for him, and he shall indeed become a member of my retinue;
O fair-faced one, this stream which has flowed from your ornament— || 69.67 ||
This shall become renowned by the name Alaṅkāradhārā;
for whatever man bathes in it and satiates his ancestors, [he shall obtain great merit]. (69.68)
That act of faith shall become inexhaustible, and one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
for this great pool of yours, Nīlatoya, possesses auspicious waters.
This place shall attain renown everywhere as Nīlakuṇḍa;
whoever, being observant of the rules, bathes here and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods, [shall obtain great merit].
All that shall become inexhaustible for him, and he is liberated from all sins;
and when that man dies, O Goddess, wherever and in whatever manner it may be.
Having bathed here at Kauśikī, the abode of Vindhyavāsinī, the pure Brāhmaṇa who performs the fire-ritual shall become a Great Gaṇapati. (69.72)
"By him the Agnihotra sacrifice shall have been offered for twelve years.
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Mahādeva rose up.
Then the Lord, taking the bark garments that were upon the trees,
said, "Become a river," and cast them down as if laughing.
At that time, O Vyāsa, those [waters] became a beautiful river of clear water,
adorned with various trees growing on its banks and graced by swans and ruddy geese.
The best of the gods spoke to that great river of holy waters:
"Since you have emerged here from the bark garments, O best of rivers."
Therefore, you shall become the most meritorious place in the world;
having bathed in you, a person is swiftly liberated from all sins.
For him who gratifies the ancestors with a śrāddha, that [offering] shall become inexhaustible;
and he who, being composed, gives a Kapilā cow here to a Brāhmaṇa— || 69.78 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, the merit of giving a thousand cows shall be his,
because you have performed austerities here after ascending to the highest peak.
This place shall become renowned everywhere as Agrāraṇya;
it is auspicious, yielding great fruit, possessing great merit, and bestowing all spiritual accomplishments.
The excellent peak of Gaurīśikhara extends for five yojanas;
having fasted here, bathed, and being endowed with supreme devotion, one becomes pure. (69.81)
Having attained the dissolution of the body, he shines resplendent, seated in a celestial chariot;
for your black antelope skin is of great merit and removes all sins.
For that brahmin who shall behold this, heaven is not difficult to attain;
whatever fruit is found in the Naimiṣa forest and whatever fruit is found at Puṣkara, [he shall obtain it].
O Goddess, upon seeing the black antelope skin, the twice-born man obtains that very same [merit];
and I shall dwell here forever with you, my beloved. (69.84)
"O Goddess, whichever man shall worship us while we are stationed here, he shall become a leader of our host and traverse the entire world. (69.85)
Thus, having thus favored the lord of mountains, Śarva, accompanied by the daughter of the king of mountains and followed by the gods and the Siddhas, returned once more to Mandara, O Lord of Sages.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons at Kośīśilā, Stanakuṇḍa, Ajina, and Gaurīśikhara," in the Devīsamāgama section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having gone again to Mount Mandara together with the daughter of the mountain, the Lord—
O great sage, tell me that which Mahādeva performed.
Sanatkumāra said: Having come to Mount Mandara together with Pārvatī, Hara took his delight in that divine golden abode, adorned with every kind of jewel.
In that most excellent city, which had been fashioned by his mind, there were beautiful staircases crowded together upon surfaces of variegated cloth-like stone slabs.
The Lord of the World was being served by the lords of the Gaṇas, great yogins led by Nandīśvara, as well as by perfected beings and the best of sages.
He dwelt together with the Goddess, being likewise honored by her;
O Vyāsa, as that wise God of gods was thus sporting, || 70.5 ||
Then the thousand-eyed Indra, the moon, and Vāyu arrived;
having come together to the city gate, they saw Nandin standing there.
With palms joined in reverence and desiring to see Śaṅkara, they said: "O Nandin, you ought to act in such a way that we may behold the Lord of Gods. (70.7)
Then Nandin, having arrived and stationed himself at the base of the door,
announced to Śambhu that the three gods had come.
When the God of gods thus commanded, "Enter," O Nandinī,
those three deities then entered into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Having prostrated, they stood together gazing upon the all-pervading Lord who grants boons;
then the Lord of the World spoke to them as they stood with their heads bowed in reverence.
"O gods, what is your business? For what purpose have you come? Speak, O immortals; I shall grant you all whatever you seek. (70.11)
Then the thousand-eyed god spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
"In order to slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, the mighty lord of the asuras."
Although Viṣṇu, the crusher of enemy forces, assumed the terrifying man-lion form and slew that lord of the Daityas, [he did not destroy him completely]. (70.13)
Without ever casting off that form, O Lord, he assumed his own attire;
in that very form, O Lord of Gods, though it was cruel, he acted out of a desire for the world's welfare.
O Śaṅkara, we do not remain here out of fear, having attained liberation;
rather, it is so that Mādhava may abandon that lion-form. (70.15)
"O best of gods, you ought to show us such favor.
Then the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, spoke to Śakra.
O Śakra, just as Viṣṇu will cast off his terrifying lion-form, so shall I do; O Śakra, let the fever of your mind depart.
Then Vāyu addressed the god Śaṅkara:
"You ought to act in such a way that I may no longer be bodiless. (70.18)
Having heard the request of Pavana, the three-eyed god granted him a very great body, by which he became embodied.
O Vyāsa, the high-souled Śaśānka then related what had been requested:
"In former times, I was cursed by Dakṣa, saying, 'You shall have a body afflicted by consumption. (70.20)
"Act so that I may be freed from this consumption; grant me your grace.
Having heard this petition to the Moon, the Lord God spoke these words to him: || 70.21 ||
The one of great splendor spoke this to Śaśin as he bowed before him:
"By performing penance at Prabhāsa, you shall be freed from consumption."
Having thus obtained the boon, all three of those most excellent gods—
Vāyu, Soma, and Sahasrākṣa— returned to their own abodes.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, how was that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu slain by that Narasiṃha, and what was his power?
What was his vigor and what was his austerity? Tell this to me as I ask you.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, there was a wife of Kaśyapa Prajāpati named Diti;
she was the daughter of Dakṣa, and she gave birth to two sons.
Having consecrated Hiraṇyakaśipu as the elder and Hiraṇyākṣa as the younger,
he was formerly anointed by Brahmā as the king of the Daityas.
Then, among the Dānavas, the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti was Indra; and among the gods, the thousand-eyed one was Indra. Thus, this triad of Indras shone forth.
Then, O Vyāsa, while they were thus ruling over the three worlds,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu arose with the desire to seize the kingdom of Śakra.
Resolved to bring the three worlds under his own power, he applied his mind to asceticism;
having gone to the southern region, he took up residence on Śrīparvata.
The immensely powerful king of the Daityas performed great and intense penance;
he offered into the fire oblations of sacrificial wood and cooked rice mixed with his own blood.
With arms raised, without support, his gaze fixed upon the sun by day,
standing on one foot and without blinking, he remained there, firm in his resolve.
The powerful one remained there for two thousand divine years;
by his great ascetic power, the three worlds were thoroughly shaken. (70.32)
Then Brahmā, the best of gods and whose vehicle is the lotus, having approached, respectfully said to the king: "O King, choose a desired boon. (70.33)
Having seen that Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons, the king of the Daityas requested a boon;
O Vyāsa, hear what kind of desired boon he sought.
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, O Lord, let this boon be mine:
may I be immortal, invulnerable, free from old age, and possessed of great strength. (70.35)
Neither by sword nor by missile, neither by night nor by day, neither by the wet nor by the dry, neither by a man nor by a woman. (70.36)
Brahmā spoke to him from within, and he replied to him:
"Therefore, O Lord, whatever death shall come about otherwise than this, that shall be mine. (70.37)
Having said to him, "So be it," Brahmā, the best among the foremost of gods,
the Grandfather, departed quickly for his own city, peaceful and pleased.
Then that Hiraṇyakaśipu, the best of all the asuras and the son of Diti,
having conquered Śakra, himself ruled the kingdom.
Having brought the three worlds under his own control and conquered all the inhabitants of heaven,
Śakra himself became Vāyu, Yama himself,
Dhaneśa, Varuṇa, and Agni; indeed, he himself became everything.
"Bow down to me and worship me; I am Brahmā together with Purandara," that asura said to all the ṛṣis, the siddhas, and the brahmins.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, regarding that which was mentioned by you as Śrīparvata—how indeed did it become Śrīparvata? What is the merit there, and what is the fruit? (70.42)
Sanatkumāra said: "Ah, O you of noble vows, I shall indeed tell you that which you ask me concerning where the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed his great penance."
On that most meritorious mountain, the god of gods, whose banner bears the bull and who possesses great splendor,
took perpetual delight together with the goddess Umā.
While the god was staying there, the goddess, daughter of the mountain king,
[beheld] those great yogis who had attained perfection through austerity and possessed the splendor of fire and the sun.
Having performed a circumambulation of Śambhu with prostrations, O great sage,
he looked repeatedly at them as they were departing and questioned the Lord of the World.
"Who are these perfected gods and lords of yoga who have prostrated before you?
Then the Supreme Lord, the God, laughed and said to her:
Those great-souled ones, perfected in yoga and established in the Pāśupata yoga, who, O Goddess, having propitiated me here, gave up their lives—those best of men [attained success]. (70.48)
These ones, having attained bodies of perfection, wandering at their own will,
shall go to the supreme state, the ultimate goal for the attainment of liberation.
Then, having reflected for a very long time with eyes wide with wonder,
Śarvāṇī spoke these most highly honored words to the God.
"O Lord of Gods, so that I too may attain such perfection as this, I shall exert myself accordingly; O All-pervading One, here I am, having come before you. (70.51)
Then, having assumed the form of Śrī, the most beautiful goddess performed great penance there for a thousand years.
And the god of great splendor granted her a boon equal to theirs:
"O beautiful lady, regarding this entire system of spiritual science (adhyātmatantra) proclaimed by me..."
"You shall become a perfected one (siddhā), a mistress of great yoga, and a knower of the welfare of others;
and this glorious mountain shall bear your name.
Renowned as Śrīparvata, it shall be adorned with manifold forms. (70.54)
For a hundred yojanas all around, you shall be possessed of great merit.
And whatever mortal, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, having come here and bathed, shall worship you and me while pure, he shall go to my world. (70.56)
But he who shall here give up his life on Śrīgirau, the best of mountains,
shall become three-eyed and able to go at will, and attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
And those who, having come here, shall perform circumambulation of the mountain associated with the abode of Śarva,
they shall become my Gaṇas.

Those men who, pure and with the stains of impurity removed, behold me on Śrīgiri—a mountain exceedingly beautiful, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), and variegated with fragrant flowers—they travel through the sky in celestial chariots yoked with birds. (70.59)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Auspicious Best of Mountains," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 70.70 ||
The seventy-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
At that time, while that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was ruling, [the following occurred].
A great deal of time has passed, O Vyāsa, since the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, came into being.
Possessed by great pride, his mind agitated by the intoxication of prosperity, he held all the gods in contempt and paid no heed to dharma.
Overwhelmed by rage, he caused all the gods together, headed by Śakra—even though they had been displaced from their own kingdom—to undergo extreme suffering. (71.3)
Being tormented, they all went to Brahmā for refuge:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Grandfather of great splendor! (71.4)
O sinless one, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, having obtained a boon from you, has seized the entire three worlds and taken away our kingdom, including heaven. (71.5)
Constantly treating us with contempt, he employs this as a means of avenging his enmity;
driven away by him, we have all come here for refuge. (71.6)
"O Lord of Gods, show us favor so that the powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu—our enemy who has abandoned dharma and is a foe to the world—may no longer exist. (71.7)
Thus addressed by the gods at that time, the lotus-vehicled god,
possessed of great wisdom and intent on pleasing the gods, spoke these words.
The ascetic power of that evil-minded king of the Daityas has been exhausted—
that enemy who brought you to such hardship and seized your kingdom.
Therefore, he previously requested from me the supreme state of being invulnerable to all;
and having been deluded by my sign, he spoke of a loophole.
O mighty ones, as soon as the king of the Daityas became senseless upon hearing that interval, at that very moment I attained satisfaction in my mind.
Go now, all of you together, to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; speak to that Acyuta for the purpose of his destruction.
Having assumed the body of Narasiṃha, he will slay the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu by striking him but once; thereafter, you shall attain peace.
"So be it," they all replied, and having prostrated before the Grandfather,
the gods together went with reverence to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Then, having seen the gods standing before him, the immensely radiant Viṣṇu spoke in gentle words, uttering speech that was captivating to the mind.
"Welcome to you all! For what purpose have you come?
You are all venerable to me and my most esteemed friends."
"O denizens of heaven, whatever task is in your minds that must be done by me, tell it to me briefly; I shall perform it quickly and without hesitation."
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the gods, led by Śakra,
spoke with joyful faces, praising Janārdana.
"O Lord, from the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu, the king of the Daityas, a very great fear has arisen for us, and our kingdom in heaven has been seized. (71.19)
O best of gods, that son of Kaśyapa, a knower of Brahman, who has shown contempt toward us, enjoys the entire world. (71.20)
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of all enemies, act in such a way that this Daitya may be slain by you; let this boon be granted to us.
Then Viṣṇu, the best of the gods, having meditated for a long time and having reflected upon a means of slaying him,
spoke to the deities as if refreshing them with his speech.
"So be it, O best of gods; I shall do all according to your word.
Since that lord of the Daityas is possessed of great power, I speak thus to you."
"O you of excellent vows, enter my body as well;
having become composed of all the gods, I shall slay your arrogant enemy."
Then all the gods entered the body of Viṣṇu;
and he too, having become powerful, assumed a terrifying form.
The immensely radiant Viṣṇu, manifesting as Narasiṃha adorned with claws and fangs,
went to the city of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Seeing that garden outside his [the Daitya's] city, filled with flowers of every season, that lion among men stood there greatly amazed. (71.27)
It was adorned on all sides with campaka, aśoka, and jātī flowers, as well as with kadamba and bakula trees, and other fragrant blossoms.
With lakes covered by lotuses and adorned by swans and ruddy geese,
and with trees that grant every desire, the forest was like the Vaibhrāja grove.
But the exceedingly fierce Nṛsiṃha, moving with playful gait, broke it;
like an elephant intoxicated with rut, he agitated the lakes.
Moving here and there in the midst of the forest,
he shone like the towering peak of Meru, the king of mountains, standing firm.
Then the forest guards, filled with rage, approached that Man-lion and tried to restrain him;
but the powerful one struck them down as well. (71.32)
Then those asuras who remained after the slaughter and had taken refuge there went and reported that matter to Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Having heard those words of theirs, the exceedingly powerful king of the Daityas [addressed] Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Namuci, Bāṣkali, and Bali.
Having summoned all the Dānavas, with Vipracitti as their leader, he went quickly and said to them: "Bind the lion and bring him into my presence. (71.35)
"O lords of the Daityas, bring him here; he must not be killed by any means whatsoever.
This lion cub shall be a plaything for my goddess. (71.36)
Having heard this, all the asuras, led by Vipracitti,
went together to the garden and beheld the Man-lion standing there.
Standing at a distance, they hurled nooses, which Mādhava cut asunder;
then he, like a lion, violently put the Dānavas to flight.
Then those Daityas, their companions having been slain, departed dejected in spirit and reported everything to the presence of the king of the Dānavas.
Then the powerful King Hiraṇyakaśipu himself, enraged and fully armored, mounted his chariot and rushed toward Nṛsiṃha in a fury.
That chariot, resembling a mountain and equipped with weapons, was whirled around by the king of lions and swiftly cast down; it was reduced to powder upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Daitya, his chariot shattered, with eyes bloodshot from rage,
uprooted a tree and hurled it with great force at the Man-lion.
Then that tree fell upon the body of the lion king;
like a clod of earth thrown against a stone, it was reduced to powder.
Then, having seized Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lion struck him once with his palm and swiftly deprived him of his life.
Having let out a great lion’s roar, the all-pervading Hari, with his nails made of diamond,
tore open the chest of the Daitya, which was like a massive mountain.
O son of Śakti, when that great Daitya was seized by Viṣṇu’s hand,
those Dānavas who were not slain entered the netherworld (rasātala).
Śakra regained the great sovereignty of heaven, free from all thorns;
and all those dwellers of heaven took possession of their respective kingdoms.
Then, O Vyāsa, the god who bears the trident and has the bull as his banner arrived there, having been entreated by the gods, and spoke to me that which I have related to you.
In order to cause Viṣṇu, the performer of wondrous deeds, to abandon his leonine form,
he then became a śarabha, resembling a peak of the Himavat mountains.
With four hind legs, possessing sharp fangs and great strength,
he approached the presence of Narasiṃha and roared with focused intent.
Then the lion, seeing the śarabha standing before him,
was overcome with great rage and struck him with his paw.
Though struck by that lion, the śarabha was not at all agitated;
then, having struck the śarabha—who possessed a body like a diamond and great strength—[the lion fell]. (71.52)
He himself fell into distress through the touch of that great-souled one;
then Viṣṇu, having meditated for a long time, realized that Śaṅkara had arrived.
Having bowed his head to him, he proceeded to offer praise in this way:
"Salutations to Śarva, to Rudra, to the commander of the army, and to the bestower of refuge. (71.54)
Salutation to the Supreme Deity, to Brahman, and to the Highest;
salutation indeed to Time, who takes the form of Yama, and to the Staff of Death.
Salutations to the one who brings about the end of time, and to the one who seizes time within time;
salutations to the one with the Pināka bow in hand, and to the bearer of the fierce arrow.
Salutation to Caṇḍa, to Vāmadeva, and to the Lord of all Yogins;
salutation to the Sovereign of Knowledge, salutation to the Lord of Brahman.
Homage to you, Kālacakra, the slayer of the foremost of the asuras; homage to you, the wheel of the fire of destruction, who brings an end to the dissolution of the world.
Salutations to the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, whose very self is Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
to the bestower of boons upon me alone, and to the granter of all desires.
Salutations to Śarabha of beautiful form, who is well-clothed in a tiger skin;
to Nandīśvara, the lord of the Gaṇas, the master of the hosts.
Homage to the Lord of the senses, the Master of the mind;
homage to the Lord of primordial matter (pradhāna), homage to the Lord of the gods. 71.61.
Homage be to the Lord of beings; homage to the Lord of the principles (tattvas).
Homage to the Lord of the moving and the unmoving; homage to the Lord of all creatures.
Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds and to the Lord of all worlds;
salutations to the giver of yoga to my mind, and likewise to the giver of sovereign power.
To the giver of invincibility and likewise the giver of that which cannot be uttered [in vain],
O Blessed One, I am established in you, I am rooted in you, and you are my supreme goal;
having sought refuge in you, be gracious to me forever.
Whoever should constantly hear this, pure and with a restrained mind,
shall reach the world of Rudra and become an attendant of the God.
It brings merit, fame, long life, and heaven, and it destroys sin;
its recitation, listening, and constant remembrance are likewise [beneficial]. (71.66)
Sanatkumāra said:
Being thus praised by Viṣṇu,
the Lord of the World spoke these most venerable words to Hṛṣīkeśa.
O Viṣṇu, this meritorious and auspicious boon has indeed been granted to you by me:
the restoration to your own womb of one who was attached to a non-womb.
You, Viṣṇu of great splendor, having always received boons from me,
were born of a lower species by the ocean at the appointed time.
"All that was to be done has been accomplished by you; Hiraṇyakaśipu has been slain.
Come now, go to your own most wonderful and auspicious birth. (71.70)
Then that best of śarabhas stepped upon the lion with his feet and once again joined Keśava with his divine body.
Then, having granted a boon to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of Daityas, he whose banner is the bull said,
"Be established in your true nature," and vanished right there.
Having granted that incomparable boon to Viṣṇu, the Sustainer of the World— being gazed upon by the eyes of the wives of the gods’ city,
bearing a chest resembling the luster of a dark cloud, and holding his trident— departed for his own supreme abode while being honored by the great sages.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Rescue of Narasiṃha by Śarabha," within the account of Hiraṇyakaśipu in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventy-second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, knower of all yoga, I have heard this most excellent narrative.
O best of sages, I wish to hear from you what occurred.
Having then removed that lion-form of Viṣṇu, what else did the wise one whose banner bears the bull do? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Bhava, the god of gods, having brought Viṣṇu— who is his own source—
to Mandara, wandered there together with the Goddess, he of great splendor.
Gliding everywhere, the Lord of Gods graced the lovely forest regions and the mountain cascades.
Knowing that the imperishable Lord Śaṅkara was delighted by the sight of the forest,
the two seasons of autumn and spring arrived there together.
Then all the trees and the lakes on every side suddenly and simultaneously shed various kinds of flowers.
There were enchanting ponds covered with lotuses and water-lilies, frequented by swarms of bees, and inhabited by swans and cranes.
Species rich in fragrance quickly came into bloom along with the campakas;
likewise, the aśokas with their fragrant flowers and the atimuktakas did so as well.
Having seen that supreme forest strewn with flowers of every season, fragrant breezes pleasant with all kinds of scents attended upon the god simultaneously.
Taking the flowers himself, the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World,
with a joyful heart, adorned the Goddess, the daughter of the Himavat mountain.
Then Pārvatī, having bowed to the Lord of Gods, spoke these words out of affection to the Lord of the Gods, who stood beside Nandīśvara and herself.
The imperishable Mother of the entire world spoke these words:
"O you whose banner is the bull, how shall I have a son born of my body? (72.12)
O you who are saluted by all the gods, possessed of your own heroism and majesty,
act accordingly, O Mahādeva, if you hold me dear.
Thus addressed by the goddess, the three-eyed God of gods,
possessed of great splendor, spoke these words out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the goddess.
"Let it be so, O Queen! I shall make this petition of yours fruitful, O Īśānī, so that he may become your son. (72.15)
O beautiful lady, he shall be the foremost among all the lords of the gods, endowed with the power of great yoga, and this entire world shall remain under his control.
"Even before you went forth to perform that penance, this boon was requested by you for the sake of a son; therefore, I must certainly grant it to you."
Having spoken thus, those two gods, the Mountain-born Goddess and the Lord of the World,
the teachers of the universe, then wandered together with Nandīśa.
Beholding all the gardens, they arrived at the Vindhya mountain;
then, having reached the golden, most excellent peak of the Vindhya, they stayed there.
It was filled with caves and caverns, joined by various waterfalls,
and its mountain peaks were made dense by masses of clouds accompanied by lightning.
It was endowed with various trees and rocks, joined with various flowers,
fragrant with the scents of various bees, and auspiciously radiant with gold and jewels.
Having created in its center a city of great supernatural power, made of jewels and gold, divine, and bewildering to both gods and asuras, he established his mind there.
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, the two entered the city together;
then the imperishable Goddess commanded Nandin.
"O child Nandin, O lord of the Gaṇas, you must likewise stand at the gate so that no one may enter here, not even the subtlest breath of air. (72.24)
Having placed that command upon his head, Nandīśa, the lord of the Gaṇas,
stood at the entrance, manifesting an exceedingly unbearable radiance.
Then the two gods, Pārvatī and Bhuvaneśvara, the source of the entire world, remained established in their supreme form through the practice of yoga.
Those two of great splendor remained for a very long time for the sake of obtaining a son;
that [matter], O great sage, cannot be fully described by me, nor even by Brahmā.
That auspicious union which occurred between the Goddess and the trident-bearing God of gods—
He is that Supreme Lord, superior even to Brahmā and to those such as myself.
However, it must certainly be recounted in the scripture exactly as it happened and exactly as it was heard;
therefore, O Vyāsa, I shall speak to you, for you are my beloved disciple.
O great sage, while the two of them remained thus established in the application of yoga,
a divine thousand years passed away.
Then there occurred terrible and terrifying omens;
the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled. (72.31)
Then the rivers went to dryness, the lord of streams was agitated, the sun became lusterless, and a hot wind blew. (72.32)
Terrible meteors fell and the quarters of the sky became most dreadful;
thus did the earth tremble, terrified by these portents, for the sake of a blessing.
He went for refuge to Viṣṇu and, having approached him, reported his distress:
"O Lord, many terrible portents have occurred most intensely. (72.34)
Therefore, being exceedingly distressed, we have today come to you for refuge.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu addressed all the gods with these words: || 72.35 ||
Then all the inhabitants of heaven, led by Bṛhaspati,
having assembled together in one place, engaged in various kinds of discourse.
Then the one of great intelligence, the son of Aṅgiras, spoke these words:
"This is the blessed Śrīkaṇṭha, the god of gods, the three-eyed one."
The one of great splendor was engaged in yoga for the sake of a son with the daughter of Himavat for a thousand divine years, through the power of the Supreme Lord.
Then, for Pārvatī who had spoken thus, there arose terrible portents that struck terror into the world; what more need be reflected upon here? (72.39)
"Let us all go together with devotion to praise the bull-bannered god, so that a son may be born to the goddess from his body, O lords of the gods. (72.40)
The immortals likewise quickly informed the Lord of the Gods;
thereupon Vaivasvata spoke words issued forth from his wrath.
"For what reason are you all so deeply distressed?
For if he is indeed the son of the God of Gods and possesses devotion toward us," (72.42)
"He shall not arise as an enemy; therefore, O gods, we shall forgive him.
But if he should become harsh toward us or an adversary, [we shall deal with him]. (72.43)
"Therefore, O immortals, having bound this cruel boy with the noose of Time, I shall bring him under my control along with Death. (72.44)
If Purandara does not hurl his thunderbolt at his head,
by which that fool will be split in two and shall abandon his life-breaths so difficult to give up.
While he was speaking thus at great length, the righteous Viṣṇu, who knows the supreme truth, spoke these words with eyes bloodshot with anger.
"Ah! O son of the Sun, you speak with such confidence, being under the sway of anger and without understanding the ultimate truth. (72.47)
"The son who shall be born to Śambhu by Girijā will indeed become like some fool, subject to your control. (72.48)
"Is this man another person subject to birth and death, O son of the Sun, who will arise so that he may come under your control? (72.49)
O son of the Sun, even if the time were not yet full, you would not have been able to destroy a mere youth; how much less so the son of the Wielder of the Trident?
O Lord, how could that unsurpassed splendor of the Blessed Śambhu, which is destined to come to pass, be subject to slaughter by you or by Śakra, O All-pervading One? (72.51)
"I speak for your benefit, O gods, if my word is to be carried out:
let us all go together to propitiate that Hara."
"The boon that was granted to us at our self-choice marriage and which remains with Śaṅkara—that very boon, the foremost Pinākin, we shall choose. (72.53)
Just as no son shall be born to the Goddess from her own body,
so Śambhu shall not procreate a son who would be harmful to us.
"We alone, O lords of the gods, are all the elder sons of the omnipresent Śaṅkara; he cannot be seen through austerity, nor can he be known through wisdom. (72.55)
That bull-bannered Lord can be seen through supreme devotion;
come, let us go to where Śaṅkara resides.
"Having established supreme devotion, so that I may behold Śaṅkara, may the god Agni enter into his presence. (72.57)
"O best of gods, [this shall be so] for all the gods through their very consciousness.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, [the gods were filled with joy]. (72.58)
Led by Bṛhaspati, those celestial dwellers, the best of gods, with joyful hearts and satisfied, spoke these words: "Excellent! Excellent! (72.59)
Then, accompanied by Viṣṇu, they went to that supreme peak and addressed these words, preceded by hymns of praise, to the god Agni.
O Agni, you who bring benefit to all the gods and are immutable in every way, enter [us] and protect us all; present us for the sake of Śaṅkara.
O best of gods, act in such a way that the divine Śaṅkara, having emerged,
may look upon us as we stand here bowed down and full of devotion.
Thus addressed by all the gods, the Consumer of Oblations replied:
"O gods, there is indeed nothing that ought not to be done by me on your behalf."
I do not have the power to behold Hara, the supreme Lord of the gods of gods, united with Pārvatī; and you all are greatly distressed.
"Your word is not to be transgressed, yet this hardship is exceedingly great for me. O gods, like a messenger, I shall enter [the fire] and perform a great act of daring.
Having spoken thus, he went quickly to that abode of the one with matted hair (Śiva).
There he saw Nandin, possessed of supreme vigor, standing at the gate;
blocking the entrance, he stood there wielding a blazing spear.
Having seen that and then looking all around, the Fire thought:
"There is no means here whatsoever, even for the smallest creature, to remain."
Thinking, "I shall enter," he went to him alone for refuge;
the god Agni, with palms joined in reverence, praised Nandin.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and homage to Caṇḍa, the wielder of the trident;
homage to the Lord of the armies, and always homage to the one whose self is Śarva.
Salutation indeed to Hālāhala Rudra, to Nīlarudra;
salutation to Iṭirudra and likewise to Ārdrapaṭa.
Salutations to you, the Rudra of dreams; salutations to you, the Rudra of ashes.
Salutations to the Rudra of the cremation ground; salutations to you, the ten-million-fold Rudra.
Homage to Piṅgalarudra, the lord of the Rudras;
homage to Pramatharudra, and homage to you, Bhūtarudra.
Salutations to you, Virūpākṣa, Rudra, Śvetarudra;
salutations to you always, O God; salutations to you always, O Śiva.
Salutations to you always, O gentle one; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees!
O God, [be gracious] to me, your devotee, who desires the welfare of the gods.
"Be a granter of boons, O Lord of Nandin; do not direct your wrath toward us, O Master.
Then Nandīśvara spoke to the Fire-god who stood there offering praise.
"O Vahni, O best of gods, I am pleased with this devotion of yours;
tell me, O god, O consumer of oblations, what pleasing thing may I do for you?"
Then the Fire-god spoke to Nandin, who stood there as the granter of boons:
"O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me," (72.77)
"O Lord of Gods, let me be granted entrance for the sake of the gods' business into the abode of the God of Gods; O All-pervading One, let this be my boon."
Nandī replied to him: "This boon must indeed be granted with difficulty;
you shall not be able to see that Lord of Gods when he has entered into yoga. (72.79)
"O Anala, although [I have already described] Maheśāna, the imperishable creator of the world, together with his Goddess,
nevertheless this very boon must indeed be granted by me to you."
Go, O Fire, becoming more subtle and difficult to perceive;
having entered, emerge quickly, your arrival and departure remaining unnoticed.
Permitted by Nandin, Jātavedas, filled with joy,
became subtler than light and merged with a ray of the sun.
Having entered the palace of Śambhu, he then approached a pillar made of jewels;
repeatedly illuminating that pillar situated amidst Vaidūrya gems, he stood there. (72.83)
There he beheld the Lord of Gods and the Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī;
then that bearer of oblations praised the two deities in his mind.
Thus being praised and showing his affection for the goddess,
Hara, perceiving her bashfulness, addressed these words to the goddess.
"O Goddess, O beloved, this jewel on the pillar, as if shining brightly, praises me along with you; I shall grant him an auspicious boon."
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, O Lord of the Gods, act thus for this devotee;
while he praises you together with me, grant him an excellent boon."
The God of gods said:
"I am pleased with your devotion and your humility, O you who dwell within the gem.
Speak whatever task you desire; all that shall be yours."
Agni said:
"O Lord of the World, the gods desire to see you from outside;
O Blessed One, act in such a way that they may all behold you. (72.89)
The God of Gods said: "So be it, O best of gods! Having emerged from the abode of the inhabitants of heaven, I shall grant you a vision, O Agni, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you."
Having been thus permitted, the Fire-god emerged from that place;
having informed the gods of his mission, he stood there, established in yogic concentration.
Then, having emerged, the Blessed One, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
went swiftly to the place where the gods were assembled.
Then, having beheld Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, all the deities bowed their heads in joy and, filled with delight, offered him praise.
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one and to the thousand-footed;
constant salutations to the Lord of the great, the Lord of the gods.
Salutations to the one who delights in the cremation ground, who is beautifully clothed in a tiger skin,
who severed the head of Brahmā, and who indeed granted boons to Viṣṇu.
Salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; salutations to you, O Tyambaka;
salutations to the lord of beings and to the churner of primordial matter.
Salutations ever to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand, the master of all yogas;
salutations indeed to the blue-crested one together with his consort.
Salutations to him who is unattached to desires, and salutations indeed to him who is attached to desires;
salutations to Śarva, the All-pervading, the wielder of the staff, and the one with matted hair;
salutations to him who has become the soul of all—grant us that which is in our hearts.
Thus being praised by all the best of the gods,
Mahādeva then replied to those deities who stood before him with bowed heads.
"I am well-pleased, O gods; tell me, what shall I give to you?
Having bowed down once more, those gods spoke these excellent words: || 72.100 ||
O Lord, O All-pervading One, that boon which was granted by you to us at our self-choice marriage—may we all together entreat you; it behoves you to grant it to us.
O Lord of the World, this yoga which you have practiced for many years for the sake of a son for the Goddess—withdraw it; salutations to you!
O God of great splendor, inauspicious omens are seen;
the earth is unstable, O Lord, and we are deeply distressed. (72.103)
Therefore, O Lord, you ought to act so that this [child] may not be born from the body of the queen as a son, but may instead be born [in another way]. (72.104)
Having heard those words of theirs, the God of gods spoke these words:
"This great boon has been requested by all you foremost of the gods."
Nevertheless, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you, I shall grant it;
however, for this long time, I have restrained my great splendor.
"For he beholds this supreme and unfailing station.
Then, O best of sages, having been addressed thus by the God, those gods—
The gods, led by Brahmā, remained together in silence;
then, from among them, Vahni spoke to the Lord of the World.
"O Lord, Protector of the Three Worlds, offer this supreme splendor into me.
Then Bhava offered that supreme splendor of his own into the fire. (72.109)
Having offered all of that into him, the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara was pleased; he said, "O Consumer of Oblations, choose a boon. || 72.110 ||
Then Vahni, having prostrated before the Lord, the omnipresent one, requested boons:
"I desire this son of yours to be celebrated by my name. (72.111)
"O Śaṅkara, may I be immune to the curse, may I behold you constantly, may I bear this with ease, and may I release it at will. (72.112)
"O wielder of the trident, may I be a consumer of all things yet remain untainted, and may no sin accrue to me;
may the gods and the sacrifices find their foundation in me. (72.113)
May I be Bhūteśvara and may I be Paśupati;
may I be your body, your very form, and your refuge.
"O Lord of Gods, I desire this boon to be granted by you.
"So be it," said the All-pervading Lord, and he bestowed all of that upon Vahni.
And having dismissed the gods from there, the bull-bannered God of gods entered his abode once more; and the Goddess addressed him.
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, where did you go to return here so swiftly? What was that most weighty task for which you departed? (72.117)
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke to Pārvatī, whose face was clouded with anger:
"O Goddess, O beloved, I have departed in haste at the request of the gods."
O lotus-petal-eyed one, [he was surrounded] by devoted and deeply distressed people standing outside;
then the Goddess spoke to the God, the Lord of the entire world. 72.119.
"How did you learn, O Lord, that the gods dwelling in the third heaven had arrived outside and were terrified? By whom was this told to you, O All-pervading One?"
The God of gods said:
"O Goddess, having entered and stationed himself by a jeweled pillar, the Fire-god announced to me all the gods standing outside while offering praise. (72.121)
"O Goddess, it was by your very permission that the boon was granted to him by me.
Thereupon, the blessed Pārvatī, filled with anger, spoke to Nandin.
"How did that fire enter you while you were standing at the door here, O evil-minded one?
Then she, becoming violently angry, [struck him] with a lotus placed against his ear.
Having seized that lotus, which was like a thunderbolt and blazed like twelve suns, he hurled it at Nandīśa.
Roaring as if bursting forth, he rushed toward Nandin for the purpose of slaying him;
then, crying out "Nandīśvara is slain!", Śaṅkara rose up.
Having said, "May it be well; take this lotus quickly," he took the lotus;
then the goddess Umā returned to her original form.
"Alas! What a great calamity has been committed by me under the sway of anger!
Somehow Nandin, the leader of the great hosts of attendants, has not been killed. (72.127)
Then the Goddess, taking that ear-lotus from the hand of the God, quickly cast it into the lake, saying, "May it be well with you."
Having spoken thus, the lotus from her ear was then cast by the goddess;
it shone upon the ridge of the Vindhya mountains as a lake filled with many lotuses and water-lilies.
Crowded with swans and cranes and adorned by ruddy geese,
it was known by the name Bhadrotpala, situated near Hemaśṛṅga.
Having bathed there, a person is quickly liberated from all sins;
there, gifts and the libations offered to the ancestors always become inexhaustible.
And a man who dies here goes to the same world as Nandīśvara.
Then the Goddess, the daughter of the Mountain, spoke these words again to the God.
"O God, what did the gods say to you, and what kind of boon did they request?
Then the Lord of Gods, whose banner is the bull, spoke to the Goddess.
"O Goddess, O fair-faced one, requested by the gods, I have emerged;
this yoga of yours, O Mistress of the World, was for the sake of a son for the Goddess. (72.134)
"Here, thousands of terrible and inauspicious omens are seen;
the entire earth is terrified, and we ourselves are deeply agitated. (72.135)
"Therefore, so that this son may not be born from the womb of the queen, let this boon be granted, by which he may become a praiseworthy offspring. (72.136)
Then, O Goddess, that splendor was offered into the fire by me for the sake of a son;
you shall have a glorious son with six heads and twelve eyes.
Having heard those words of his, he cursed the sons of the Mountain-dweller and the immortals:
"Since my son was not desired in their bodies by those evil-minded ones, therefore those gods shall not obtain a son from their own wives. (72.138)
And the Earth, too, her senses impaired by my curse, shall remain bewildered;
though she obtains many husbands, she shall never obtain a son. (72.139)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the goddess, having cursed the gods along with Indra, ceased;
she was known by the name Kaiṭabhā, auspicious and the bestower of many boons.
On a golden peak of the Vindhya mountains, there was the auspicious Girijā;
for that is indeed a holy sanctuary, as well as the stone known as Ramaṇā.
O Vyāsa, the man who goes there shall become a leader of the Gaṇas after death.
Then all the gods, together with Agni, the consumer of oblations, arrived there.
Pale, overcome with dejection, pregnant, and filled with shame—
Nandin announced those who had arrived as gatekeepers to Śaṅkara.
Having entered and been granted permission, the denizens of heaven said to the God:
"O Lord of the three worlds, we are unable to endure this splendor. (72.144)
"Save us, O Lord of the world of the gods, so that we may be free from our feverish distress!
The asura Andhaka is performing exceedingly difficult austerities;
therefore, O God, O All-pervading One, a very great fear of him is seen by us."
The God of gods said: "O gods, let there be no fear; I shall slay Andhaka, that excellent son of Hiraṇyākṣa who has exerted his prowess for your sake."
And you all go to the vast forest situated in the middle of Meru,
known by the name Śaravaṇa, which is twelve yojanas in extent and holy.
O preeminent deities, having split open your bellies there,
that supreme and radiant splendor of mine shall emerge.
"O best of gods, your wombs shall attain the state of gold.
Then, having heard those words, they bowed their heads to Bhava.
They went to the glorious and auspicious Mount Meru,
where, having then split open their bellies, he emerged from them.
Resembling the fire at the end of an eon and difficult for even the gods and asuras to behold,
Mount Meru quickly became glorious and exceedingly beautiful.
Everything was made of gold; the supreme splendor of Maheśvara shone forth, and a divine wind blew, carrying the fragrance of flowers from all seasons.
And as their bellies were split open, they attained a supreme golden state;
in heaven, divine drums resounded spontaneously, though not struck.
Showers of many fragrant flowers fell,
and there arose the sound of invisible beings offering salutations.
Seeing and hearing such things as these, O observer of noble vows, those best of gods went joyfully to the wielder of the Pināka bow; having reported everything,
they were sent back by Sthāṇu and returned to their own worlds with delighted faces.

Having heard these most excellent words spoken by the gods filled with joy, the goddess was delighted; having learned of the news of her son’s birth, she—the mother of Yoga, the bestower of boons upon the wise, and the Ordainer—remained there, her lotus-feet touched by the heads of the deities, and she attained great satisfaction in her heart.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of Skanda," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventy-third chapter.
Vyāsa said: Whose son was this Andhaka? What was his power, and what was his prowess?
And how was he slain in battle? Tell me all of this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence; I shall tell you everything, O twice-born one, exactly as it happened—this entire ancient account of Andhaka. 73.2.
The two sons of Kaśyapa by Diti were born as the two Daityas;
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother.
At that time, Hiraṇyakaśipu was the eldest king there;
when that hero had been slain by the wise Narasiṃha, [the kingdom passed to his younger brother].
Hiraṇyākṣa became king, honored by all the Daityas;
it is heard that, being childless, he performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son. (73.5)
Having reached Śaṅkukarṇa at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean,
the son of Diti performed austerities in order to see the god who wields the Pināka bow.
Vyāsa said: How did that divine, purifying, and world-renowned sacred field of Maheśa, known as Śaṅkukarṇa, which accomplishes all goals, come to be?
You ought to explain to me what that fruit and the perfection of merit are.
Sanatkumāra said: "In ancient times, indeed, the Lord God Kapardin Nīlalohita,
having come to the ocean of the Indus for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds..."
Then the Lord of the World began to perform an inconceivable penance, even for the gods and asuras,
for the sake of protecting [the world] in all ten directions.
He appointed thousands of troop-leaders, such as Nikumbha and others—
Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahādaṃṣṭra, Sthūlākṣa, and Sthūlanāsika.
It had short legs and a gaping, terrifying mouth;
it was covered with a tiger skin and had a leopard skin as its upper covering.
Having summoned the very powerful Gaṇeśa, who is known as Śaṅkukarṇa, to his side, the Blessed One spoke this to him.
"O child, protect this forest together with the lords of the Gaṇas, so that the gods may not enter it, for as long as this vow of mine lasts. (73.13)
Having thus performed that protection, Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull,
practiced there a great, formidable penance that is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, arrived there;
but being obstructed by Śaṅkukarṇa, they could not move even a step forward.
The gods said:
"O Gaṇeśas, we have arrived with a purpose to see the fierce god Śarva, who wears his hair in matted locks; O sinless ones, show him to us."
Agitated and unable to see him, we, the lords of the Pramathas, are perishing.
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"O gods, you are not able to see the Lord by any means.
Perform austerities—may it be well with you—and then you shall behold Śaṃkara. (73.17)
The gods said:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, O you of great splendor, let there not be the destruction of the worlds!
Therefore, grant us an entrance; show us favor, O Lord. (73.18)
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"Let the worlds perish, or you yourselves; entrance shall not be granted.
Even when they have perished, the Lord, the Sovereign of the World, will create them once again. (73.19)
He alone is the creator of all beings, and likewise their destroyer;
O gods, who else besides that omnipresent Lord is capable of destroying the worlds? (73.20)
"We shall not open the door; our command is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having been addressed thus, the gods reflected and went to the abode of Brahmā. (73.21)
Then those best of gods reported this to Brahmā;
thereupon Brahmā said to the gods: "O gods, [let us go] again with me. (73.22)
"Go to the leaders of the hosts until I bring you back to your original state.
Then those dwellers of heaven, together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [departed].
They returned once more to that very place where Śaṃkara was staying.
Then that lord of the Gaṇas besieged them once again.

Śaṅkukarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas, blazing as if with splendor, was then addressed by Brahmā with these conciliatory and meaningful words. 73.25. Śaṅkukarṇa,
O Lord of the Gaṇas, there is indeed no malice whatsoever among the gods;
by your grace, let the gods behold the bull-bannered God.
"The gods, led by Indra, bow their heads before you;
and I, together with Viṣṇu, entreat you, O Lord of the Gaṇas."
Having heard those words of Brahmā, that lord of the Gaṇas,
enraged, raised his sharp-edged spear and spoke these harsh words.
The gods are not more venerable to me than this salutation to you;
however, the command of Śambhu is weightier, for no one at all has permission to enter.
O Brahmin, how can we, though appointed for protection, transgress the command of our lord and grant entrance to those who are forbidden? (73.30)
Having heard those words of the high-souled Gaṇeśa,
Brahmā, filled with supreme shame, withdrew to a secluded place.
Then all the gods, seeing the Grandfather filled with shame,
spoke these words to the Lord of the Gaṇas, their bodies overcome with anger and wrath.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, you have no shame; how can you revile your guru?
For the Bull-bannered One will certainly not forgive you for speaking thus.
Furthermore, O Gaṇa, do not show us such contempt;
today, we shall exert ourselves to destroy your life.
Having heard those words of theirs, Śaṅkukarṇa, filled with rage,
looked askance at the denizens of heaven and spoke these words in great anger.
"O gurus, who are you to me, that I suspect you are the lords of the immortals?
Having propitiated Śaṅkara, you have attained this supreme divinity."
"You too, O best of immortals, have become attendants of the Lord of the Gods;
we too are masters of great yoga, the leaders of the hosts of that wielder of the trident."
"O dwellers of the third heaven, you are either equal to us or inferior to us,
since we behold and follow the Lord of the Gods."
"Therefore, we are always more worthy of worship than all the gods combined. Behold us fearlessly; enter, O immortals! (73.39)
Behold today the terrible power of the lords of the hosts—
whatever strength you possess, whatever yoga, whatever austerity, and whatever exertion you have.
"Show all of that to me, and then you shall behold my power.
Having heard those words of his, all the gods became exceedingly arrogant.
With weapons firmly grasped, they swiftly rushed toward Śaṅkukarṇa; O Vyāsa, as those gods who considered themselves heroes were charging forward, [Śaṅkukarṇa]—73.42.
The exceedingly powerful Śaṅkukarṇa seized their strength through yoga;
thus, all those foremost of gods had their power completely restrained.
They were unable to set foot forward and stood motionless like pillars;
when the gods had been thus restrained, Viṣṇu, the best among strikers, [acted].
He rushed with speed toward Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas;
then that powerful one paralyzed the body of Viṣṇu through his yogic power.
Resuming his yoga once more, Viṣṇu, endowed with sovereign power,
fought with Śaṅkukarṇa, and he in turn fought against him.
O best of sages, when those two lords of yoga were thus engaged, a truly great battle took place between them by means of their very yoga.
Having restrained Viṣṇu, that most wonderful Gaṇeśa, the beloved of Śarva, engaged my father in combat through his yogic power.
Having resorted to subtle yoga, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [remained there].
He beheld Śaṅkukarṇa standing right before him in various places;
then that lord, having cast off the gross elements, entered the subtle elements.
Then the Grandfather, whose soul was absorbed in yoga, established the senses, the principles, and the constituent states in their respective places, having resorted to the supreme yoga.
He beheld the mighty Sthūlaśiras, who had ears like spikes;
meanwhile, O Vyāsa, [the following occurred] regarding the trident-bearing God of gods.
For a thousand divine years, he performed the twelve-fold vow;
and thus, O Vyāsa, the observance of that high-souled one was completed.
