When that vow was completed, he, possessing a splendor like the fire at the end of a yuga,
gazed upon all the directions as if Śaṅkara were restoring life to them.
Seeing that all those inhabitants of heaven had been restrained,
the god then pacified Śaṅkukarṇa with gentle words alone.
"O child, O lord of the Gaṇas, you have carried out my command correctly;
release all these gods and do not disregard them, O lord of the Gaṇas. (73.56)
Thus addressed by the god, Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas,
dismissed all the deities and stood near the god.
Then all the Suras as well, filled with supreme shame,
bowed with the highest devotion to the Lord of the gods, the All-pervading One.
Then the God, who knows the self, smiling at them as they stood ashamed,
addressed Viṣṇu in a melodious voice while speaking together with Brahmā.

"O lords of the gods, this Lord of the Gaṇas is always devoted to my command. O best of deities, let whatever has been done by him pass over you. Tell me what must be done, for which purpose you have come here."
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, this illustrious Gaṇeśa Śaṅkukarṇa has indeed destroyed our strength through his yoga; let a boon be granted to him."
May you always grant us the vision of yourself from beyond.
The God of gods said:
"This very place shall become known by this name, 'Pavitra,' renowned throughout the world;
likewise, it shall be celebrated as Śaṅkukarṇa and the auspicious Sthūleśvara. (73.62)
Extending for a yojana in every direction and endowed with all sacred fords,
it is graced by the fruits of all sacrifices and possessed of the fruits of all acts of charity.
Whoever comes here, prepares an oblation, and honors me with diligence,
fasting for a day and night, shall go to my world.
Whoever, having undertaken some specific vow, should dwell here for a year,
shall attain supreme yoga and become equal to Śaṅkukarṇa.
And whoever, established in the observance, should here in this field give up their life-breaths, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become a great Gaṇapati.
"The śrāddha offered here shall become inexhaustible for the ancestors;
and you yourselves shall be endowed with sovereignty and possessed of the power of asceticism and yoga. (73.67)
"O gods, depart free from anxiety; you shall behold me eternally.
Then the Lord, the Sovereign, having granted this boon to the gods, [departed]. (73.68)
Having granted him a constant and full vision, he vanished right there;
when that Great God had departed, Brahmā was surrounded by the foremost of the gods.
Having installed a linga there, he established many sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the wheel:
the holy Daśāśvamedhika tīrtha and the Pañcāśvamedhika tīrtha.
Having established sacred fords for the gods, he departed for his own abode.
This, O Vyāsa, has been narrated to you regarding the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
But the supreme abode of the Blessed One is pure, world-renowned,
crowded with perfected beings and celestial musicians, and frequented by hosts of apsarases.
O Vyasa, having gone to that forest, which was endowed with many flowers and fruits and was always filled with the songs of birds, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa [remained].
For the sake of a son, he performed austerities while meditating upon the Three-eyed Lord.
Then the God, whose banner is the bull, arrived there accompanied by his retinue.
On the beautiful peak of the Snowy Mountain, renowned as Maināka,
the supreme lord of yogins remained absorbed in the eternal, supreme Brahman.
Then, having approached, she slowly stood behind the Goddess and,
with her two lotus-like hands, closed the eyes of Śambhu.
Thinking, "He does not know," the daughter of Himavat then played;
at that moment, O Vyāsa, the world became blind. (73.77)
For it was previously invisible, shrouded by darkness, just as it had been;
then the god, having seen that, opened his third, imperishable eye.
From his forehead, he created [the eye] situated above, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon;
by the splendor of that eye, the mountain was reduced to ashes.
Seeing her father thus consumed by the wielder of the Pināka bow, Pārvatī withdrew her hands and stood dejected at her husband’s side.
Then the god, seeing Umā with a dejected countenance,
looked once again at that mountain with a gentle eye.
As soon as he was seen in that state, he became his former self once again.
Seeing her father, the imperishable god, restored to his natural form, the daughter of the mountain king, her face beaming with joy, bowed down and spoke to her husband. (73.82)
"O Lord, for what purpose was this mountain reduced to ashes by you? And for what reason, O Master, has it been restored once more to its natural state? (73.83)
Having heard those words of hers, the Supreme Lord said:
"O Goddess, at the very moment your eyes were closed by you..."
Then all the worlds became blind, enveloped in darkness;
therefore, O Goddess, this eye was created by me for the sake of light. (73.85)
O auspicious one, it was by this very [fire] on his forehead that this best of mountains was scorched,
and it was because he perceived you to be distressed due to the slaughter of your father.
O lady of beautiful hips, for your sake I have been restored to my natural state, even though this world is swallowed on all sides by intense darkness. (73.87)
"O Goddess, in the same way, a blind son shall be born through my power;
I shall give that son to Hiraṇyākṣa when he is performing austerities. (73.88)
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One, surrounded by his hosts, took hold of Andhaka and,
having arrived at the ocean of the Indus, spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
"Behold me, O son of Diti! I grant you divine vision.
I am Śarva who has come here, O Daitya; choose a boon as you desire."
Rising up, Hiraṇyākṣa bowed his head to Bhava and quickly requested a boon from the god, saying, "Grant me a son. (73.91)
To him, who was bowing his head at his feet, the best of the gods said:
"O tiger among asuras, this son of yours is the eldest of a hundred sons."
O Lord of Asuras, do not treat him with contempt, thinking "he is blind," for he will become great, endowed with the power of asceticism, heroism, and strength.
"He shall not be subject to execution by anyone other than me.
Then that Blessed Lord, having granted him an auspicious son, [departed].
Taking Andha once again, that great asura Hiraṇyākṣa went back to the beautiful peak of Maināka.
Having gone to his own city of Aśmaka, he said to his high-minded wife:
"O Goddess, this son has been given to you by the Blessed One himself. (73.96)
"Nurture him through yoga; do not be negligent at any time.
Seeing him with affection, milk flowed from her two breasts. (73.97)
Being nourished over time, that Andhaka grew up;
and when he reached his youth, he reflected in this manner: || 73.98 ||
"Fie upon my life as a blind man! Death itself would be better for me, since I, being blind, do not behold my home, my possessions, and my kinsmen. (73.99)
Blessed are those men in the world who, having repeatedly gazed upon the faces of their kinsmen and addressed them as they pleased, depart themselves without distress. (73.100)
The task could have been accomplished with a clod of earth, or with grass, or even with a corpse;
it was not done by me who have received his grace. Fie on me, the doer of evil!
"Out of affection for his son, this Daitya father always protects me;
he does not kill one who ought to be killed, for he causes me to suffer the depletion of my treasury. (73.102)
Deluded by affection, he does not understand this agony of mine;
I alone shall perform that task which is to be done by the wisest of men.
"By performing great austerity, I shall indeed become possessed of sight.
Having thus reflected in many ways, the highly intelligent blind man [resolved]. (73.104)
Having taken leave of his mother and having bowed down to his father,
the wise one, having made his resolve and being firm in his determination, departed for the sake of asceticism.

In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the *Andhakopākhyāna*, [it is said]: "The blind one, his eyes overflowing with tears of grief, his soul exhausted by fatigue, was tormented by the sight of that intense sorrow and the pain of separation, and he sighed."
The seventy-third chapter, titled "The Departure for Asceticism."
The seventy-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O best of Brahmins, having gone there at that time, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa—
Gaṅgādvāra is a gateway to auspiciousness, an unsurpassed grove for ascetic practice.
There is a divine place named Kanakhala, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
there, all the trees of Kanakhala are indeed made of gold.
Where, in ancient times, Dakṣa performed a sacrifice together with the gods;
where, in the past, his sacrifice was destroyed by Mahādeva.
There, having bathed with a disciplined mind and worshipped the god, he paid homage to the deities and spoke these words: || 74.4 ||
Andhaka said:
"To all the gods and the various beings who dwell in this forest of asceticism, I go for refuge; may they grant me success in my penance. (74.5)
"From this day forward, I shall perform a severe penance, most difficult to practice, by which I may obtain my desired boons or meet death that destroys life. (74.6)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, O son of Parāśara, that one of great strength then subsisted on air for a year, free from fatigue.
Likewise, he bathed at the three daily junctures, offered oblations into the sacred fires,
was devoted to the worship of the gods, and remained intent upon silent recitation and burnt offerings.
At the completion of every year,
that great asura would extract a portion of flesh the size of a karṣa from his own body and offer it into the fire.
In this manner, O best of sages, a thousand celestial years passed for him as he offered his own flesh into the fire every single day.
That asura was as white as a conch shell, a pearl necklace, water, nectar, a kunda flower, or the moon.
He remained solely established in austerity, until nothing but his bones and veins remained.
Endowed with that ascetic power, he of immeasurable self then rendered the sun lusterless, as did the moon along with its planets and stars.
Just as that very sun illuminates with its brilliance,
so too did he dry up the ponds, the riverbanks, and the lakes.
Then that Andhaka, by means of his ascetic power, paralyzed the wind;
the Siddhas did not move through the sky, and their celestial chariots fell.
Having seen that form of his asceticism, Śakra suddenly created hundreds of obstacles; yet he did not waver.
Then Brahmā, approaching him, spoke to the Dānava Andhaka:
"O great Asura of mighty strength, you have performed terrible austerities;
I am pleased with you, O mighty-armed one of noble vows—become possessed of sight!"
"O Asura, let your body return to its natural state as it was before;
now speak another boon, whatever else resides in your mind. (74.17)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having then become possessed of sight and with his body uninjured,
he bowed down and spoke directly to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Andhaka said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, and if my ascetic penance has been successful,
O Grandfather, grant me invincibility against the gods in battle."
Great strength, as well as illusions and even immortality—
this I desire, O Lord of Gods, if you are a granter of boons to me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the all-pervading Lord laughed and spoke again these auspicious words to the son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
"O son of Diti, I do not grant immortality to the Daitya; however, there shall be a condition attached to it. You yourself state what that subsequent term shall be."
Andhaka said: "If there were a woman who is indeed the mother of the world and I did not bow down to her, then my death would come; otherwise, I am truly deathless. (74.23)
Brahmā said:
"Let it be exactly as you have spoken today;
you shall be known by the name Andhaka, and you will attain fame in the world. (74.24)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to Andhaka, that thorn in the side of the gods, the Blessed One departed for his own abode, and Andhaka ceased [his assault].
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and worshipped the god according to the prescribed rites,
and having offered oblations into the fire, the wise lord of the Daityas then took leave of the penance grove and went into the presence of his father along with his companions.
With a joyful heart, his great strength increased through asceticism, his desire fulfilled, and having gratified the enemies of the gods, he,
radiant and resembling a cloud driven by the wind, returned once more to the presence of his father.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Obtaining of Boons by Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventy-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone with those eight Dānavas to the vicinity of that city, he...
Having accomplished his purpose, Andhaka returned and announced himself to his father.
Then, O Vyāsa, Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the Asuras, gave many jewels as well as desired objects to the messenger of pleasant news.
Then the king himself, together with all his friends, his mounts,
and his women, went forth swiftly like the moon accompanied by the hosts of stars.
Having gone not very far into the forest, which was filled with *aśoka* and *campaka* trees,
that illustrious one encountered his son, who was like another glorious Soma meeting Budha.
Seeing his son’s purpose accomplished, the lord of the Dānavas was filled with joy;
out of affection, he embraced him and repeatedly smelled the crown of his head.
"How, by what means, at what time, and which boons were obtained by you?"—
being thus questioned, he related everything exactly as it had happened.
Having heard of that granting of the boon and likewise his majesty,
those tigers among the asuras roared like the oceans.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having placed his son Andhaka upon that chariot, Hiraṇyākṣa quickly entered his own city together with those friends.
Accompanied by his son, that Daitya shone with a fulfilled heart,
like the sun moving through the zodiac together with Saturn.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having entered, that lord of the Daityas spoke to his circle of friends,
just as an Adhvaryu priest addresses the other officiating priests standing by the Sānnāyya offering.
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"Listen now to that which has long resided in my heart as a task to be performed;
it must be carried out by all of you together, who possess terrible prowess. (75.11)
"Previously I desired that once my purpose was accomplished and I had returned here, I would indeed celebrate the Kaumudī festival in this city of Andhaka. || 75.12 ||
"I shall perform the 'Great Night of the Gods' (devarātri) for the god who destroys sacrifices; let all that be done without hesitation. (75.13)
"By my command, let it be proclaimed throughout this city— in its squares and assembly halls— that for fifteen days, beginning with the Kaumudī festival, [the streets shall be illuminated]."
And let there be for me three divine nights as those of Your Majesty,
as well as those of my friends— the lords of the Daityas and the Dānavas of great strength.
"May they also come here from all directions and take their delight;
and those auspicious brahmins on our side, beginning with Śukra,
as well as the nāgas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and likewise human beings."
May they all also come together and take delight with me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed by the wise Hiraṇyākṣa,
the lords of the Daityas then did everything exactly as they had been told by that enemy of the immortals.
O son of Śakti, he swiftly dispatched messengers to the Daityas together with the Dānavas, as well as to the other factions who were on his side. (75.19)
"The mighty King Hiraṇyākṣa invites you;
accompanied by your circle of friends, go there, desiring to see him. (75.20)
And Ghaṇṭika, wrapped in new garments and well-adorned, mounted a rutting elephant of snowy white and proclaimed aloud: || 75.21 ||
Victorious is King Hiraṇyākṣa, the powerful lord of the Daityas;
all those who hate the Daityas and the enemies of the Danavas have been slain. (75.22)
For the victory of the sons of Diti and for the fear of the Ādityas,
the king commands you all to observe the Kaumudī festival beginning from dawn.
And let the city be made ready with streets well-swept and strewn with offerings for the night of the god Rudra, the destroyer of the asuras.
"May all the city-dwellers be clothed in unwashed garments, wearing garlands, having bathed their heads, and having received and partaken of food in due order. (75.25)
Let the singers sing and let the actors and dancers dance;
let banners be raised in the houses, on the streets, and in the marketplaces.
And let the houses always be plastered,
adorned with heaps of flowers, and likewise with various kinds of incense.
Let all [the objects] be adorned with garlands and clusters of forest-wreaths;
let the Brahmins be fed, and let auspicious proclamations be made.
And everywhere there were the sounds of Vedic chanting and proclamations of auspicious days; and throughout the night, lamps were lit everywhere on the royal highways and within the houses.
"Let indeed uninterrupted wicks soaked in abundant oil be prepared;
let young men wander about on all sides together with women. (75.30)
Delighting, laughing, and singing, devoted to dance,
let the wives of the Daityas play musical instruments such as cymbals and perform dances.
And he performed the auspicious worship of Mahādeva with perfumes, flowers, and the like,
as well as various offerings and grand ceremonial ablutions.
There were abundant garlands, adorned with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten,
as well as lamps of diverse forms, drinks, and flavors.
"Offer various fruits, meat cooked in non-arid lands, and ornaments of gold and jewels to the Lord."
"Let animals be slaughtered here and let the best of the twice-born be fed.
If any inhabitant of the city should fail to do all this at any time, the highly illustrious king shall inflict corporal punishment upon him. (75.35)
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus made the proclamation, the bell-ringer mounted the back of an elephant and returned once more to his own home, while the Kaumudī festival drew near.
Then all those people in the city did exactly as they had been told;
and the king also, self-restrained, bathed, pure, and with a disciplined mind, [prepared himself]. (75.37)
Day after day, Vyāsa, exerting himself with diligence, bathed him with pure *pañcagavya* and fragrant oil. (75.38)
With milk, clarified butter, curd, and many auspicious juices;
with flowers, fruits, seeds, and gems, all accompanied by water.
With fragrant ashes and scented water,
the king himself [prepared] for each [of them] ten hundred jars.
Day after day, O Vyāsa, he should worship Tryambaka with perfumes, flowers, incense, recitations, and offerings. (75.41)
Having honored them, the king then fed other brahmins;
he did so with sacrificial animals, as well as with jewels and gems.
Praised with offerings of food, beds, seats, and other gifts, he went to his home;
likewise did the other lords of the Daityas, as well as the mighty Andhaka.
O best of sages, they all acted exactly as the king had commanded;
then the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa seized Andhaka.
Vyāsa said: "He caused him to fall with his feet; reciting this [hymn] to Rudra, he said:
'O son, may this gracious Lord always be well-disposed toward you. (75.45)
You should cultivate devotion toward this Supreme Lord;
he is to be saluted and worshipped, for there is no teacher higher than him.
You should always worship this Supreme Lord with devotion. (75.46)
Sanatkumāra said:

Having spoken thus and prostrated before Śaṅkara, that great Asura, the lord of the Asuras and Dānavas, the wise one, returned home filled with contentment, like the Lord of the Gods to his own abode. 75.47.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Kaumudīmahotsava," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventy-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, during that Kaumudī festival, the Daityas and Dānavas were together with their women.
The gods, their minds filled with passion, looked back like those who have gone to heaven.
There, a certain woman with beautiful outer corners of her eyes placed a divine lotus over her face,
as if out of fear of the moon, for the sake of protecting her lotus-like countenance.
Another, approaching with her foot,
struck her beloved as the moon strikes a full-blown autumn lotus with its ray.
Other noble women, unacquainted with royal highways, would take off their sandals upon seeing the ground paved with crystal. (76.4)
And others, O best of Brahmins, having lifted up their garments out of fear of water, walk along the royal roads upon seeing the ground strewn with jewels. (76.5)
A certain woman, abandoned by her lover and led away by another man who was enamored of her, emerged from her house; touched by the rays of the moon, she fell down, languid with passion.
Having fallen, that noble woman spoke thus to Soma:
"Once again you burn me with your sharp rays, as if you were a sun burning a lotus."
It is said that you revive medicinal herbs scorched by the sun;
why then do you not firmly revive me, who am utterly consumed by love?
Some beautiful women, swinging on swings,
appeared like the moon reflected in water, their forms flickering with the movement of the waves.
Some of the mighty Daityas sang together with women,
like Gandharvas in the Nandana grove accompanied by Apsarases.
In some places the royal highway shines, crowded with many women,
like that beautiful and divine celestial path in the sky.
In some places, the sound of anklets and girdles, as well as that of cuckoos,
shone forth, pleasing to the ear of the listener and subtly inflaming passion.
In some places, O Vyāsa, the sweet voices of women, impassioned by pleasure, are heard as they converse with their beloveds, causing agitation in their hearts. (76.13)
Thus, O Vyāsa, that most wonderful festival took place,
increasing the joy, happiness, and confidence of the Dānavas at that time.
When he had ceased,
O Vyāsa, the people returned once more to their former state, and those Dānavas assembled together.
Those who brought great joy to Bhīma entered the divine and enchanting assembly hall,
which had pillars made of gold and altars of diamond and lapis lazuli.
It was adorned with hanging strings of pearls and decorated with excellent garlands of flowers,
as well as diamonds, lapis lazuli, sapphires, great blue gems, and mango sprouts.
It was adorned with red gems, crystals, and emeralds as well,
encased in a divine lattice, and beautified by variegated tinkling bells.
It was endowed with trees that bore many flowers and fruits and granted all desires,
as well as with beautiful oblong ponds and numerous couches and seats.
Free from fatigue, with many outflows, devoid of all suffering,
fully endowed with all desired objects, and crowded with many women and men.
Enveloped in pride, the Daityas entered that divine assembly hall—Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Sini, and Vāṣkala as well. (76.21)
Virocana and Bali, as well as the renowned sons of Bali—
twelve thousand in number, of whom the exceedingly powerful one was the foremost.
There was a king named Bāṇa, a great master of illusion who possessed a thousand arms;
and Bāṇa had ten thousand other sons as well.
Mura, Dhamuṣumuṇḍa, and the Dānava Vipracitti; Kāla, Hayaśiras, Śambara, and Kālaśambara.
Viśruta, Indradamana, and the Dānava Kālanemi;
likewise Sundan and Nisundan, as well as Vipāka and Pāka.
Rāhu and Śataketu, Dhvaja, Tāra, and Satāraka; Mahiṣa and Dundubhi, as well as the exceedingly powerful Kālaka.
And Andhaka, as well as Ariṣṭa, Baka, and Śarabha;
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, Madhu, and Kaiṭabha.
Mahākāya, Śatānanda, and Śatadundubhi; Kārttasvana, Hastin, Bala, and Naraka.
Dhvāṅkṣa, Mūka, and Ivala, as well as Vātāpi with Asṛpuñjika, Kaṇḍala, Mīḍha, and the famous Durloma. || 76.29 ||
Dhundhu, Śatamāya, Śatāvarta, and Duḥsaha;
Candrasūrya, Nara, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka.
Brahmahā and Yajñahā, as well as Ilvala and Pilvaka;
and Maya, the best of the Dānavas, and the renowned sons of Maya. (76.31)
Of them, there were eight thousand, all of whom had made firm their resolve;
and Vṛtra, the best of the Dānavas, as well as Namuci and Bala.
Śatodara, Vyaṃsa, Tāthāya, Hradodara,
Keśin, as well as Pralamba, Kabandha, and Dhenuka.
Hāla, Gārgyaśiras, Kuśa, and likewise Śambhu;
as well as Gaganamūrdhan, Sāluka, and Śālva. (76.34)
And Meghanāda, as well as the famous Mahānāda;
then Khara, Khararoman, and the Dānava Sūcīroman.
Parigha and Aparigha, Daṇḍa and Kāśyapa,
the massive Dundubhi, and the group known as the Saiṃhikeyas.
Likewise, there were Hālāhala and Andhakāraka,
as well as the sixty thousand Paulomas and the renowned Kālakeyas;
and eight thousand Kālakañjas— these were the thorns in the side of the gods.
And there were three crores of the mighty Nivātakavacas;
all those enemies of the gods together are calculated to be sixty crores.
Excluding those humans, as well as the serpents,
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and even birds—
O Vyāsa, there were twenty crores of them at that time.
Having entered that assembly hall, all those enemies of the gods, out of pride,
shone like rain-clouds accompanied by lightning and meteors.
Resounding like clouds, like smoky mountains,
bellowing like buffaloes, those banners appeared as if they were approaching.
Like portents that have broken loose, like venomous serpents,
like elephants in rut, and like winds driven with speed.
Having filled that assembly hall, they stood there for the purpose of harassing the gods;
then the hall-keeper, having approached the king, spoke these words to him.
Then, O Vyāsa, the youth, having first bowed his head to him as he sat comfortably upon the throne, knelt upon the ground.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke with proper speech in smooth words and syllables:
"May the Lord, the bringer of victory to all the asuras, be victorious! (76.45)
"Prahlāda and all the others, led by Vipracitti, have arrived at the assembly;
let this be known. As for whatever else you ought to do," (76.46).
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard that all the enemies of the gods had arrived at the assembly hall,
the king suddenly rose up like the banner of Indra during a festival.
He wore a diadem, possessed great tusks, hair like muñja grass, and large jaws;
his mouth was gaped open as far as his ears, and his scalp was like a great umbrella.
With arms reaching to his knees, with rounded eyes and tawny eyes, and with hair standing erect;
possessing a body as firm as a diamond, he was a great yogi of immense strength.
He shone intensely with his crown, like the sun at its rising.
With his chest adorned by an excellent necklace, like a cloud accompanied by cranes,
Vyāsa set out with his son, appearing like the Himalaya mountain incarnate.
Then that best of the lords of the Dānavas, his earrings encircled by the rays of various jewels,
entered the assembly hall— which was crowded with the foremost of Asuras and Daityas— like the sky filled with risen planets.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Entrance of Hiraṇyākṣa into the Assembly Hall," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The seventy-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having gone to that assembly, he saw the Daityas and Dānavas.
Just as Indra [approaches] the intoxicated clouds that have appeared during the rainy season.
As he entered, all the enemies of the gods then rose up and cried "Victory!", just as the Vedas do for the Grandfather Brahmā.
"Arise! the lord of the Asuras said to them all, as a serpent possessing the fivefold illusion rises up like clouds sustained by the wind.
That great asura Hiraṇyākṣa shone before them like a rutting great elephant in the midst of a herd of young calves.
Then he sat upon an excellent seat made of divine Jāmbūnada gold.
Seated upon his lion-throne, that king of the enemies of the gods shone like a great cloud accompanied by lightning, having reached the peak of Mount Meru.
Then the Asuras sat down in silence,
desiring to create water like towering dark clouds at the proper season.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having perceived their gestures and knowing the time was ripe,
King Hiraṇyākṣa himself, the scorcher of the gods, spoke to those enemies of the deities regarding their intentions.
All of you, great māyās, listen with self-restraint and equanimity, like disciples to the words of a teacher—words that are timely and beneficial. (77.9)
My elder brother was indeed dear to me, as venerable as a father;
King Hiraṇyakaśipu was high-souled and true to his promise. || 77.10 ||
He was righteous, generous, a performer of sacrifices, a giver, endowed with asceticism,
a maintainer of the sacred fires, a knower of the four Vedas, and a bringer of happiness to all beings.
"He was slain for the sake of the kingdom by the gods, whose minds were perverted by deceit;
because of his suffering, O great Asuras, I am tormented and I wither away. (77.12)
Just as a blossoming lotus is drawn up from the water in the summer heat,
so am I able to inflict punishment upon those enemies of the Asuras.
I am indeed not exerting myself there for the sake of protecting you children;
rather, I, alone, shall personally inflict punishment upon the enemies of the gods.
I shall go, of this there is no doubt; let there be no fear in you, O Asuras.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, those Dānavas were filled with joy;
yet, overcome with great shame, they looked at one another.
Then his younger brother Vipracitti, who was possessed of great strength,
bowed down properly to that brother and spoke these meaningful and sweet words.
There is no doubt, O Great Being, that by you alone [the purpose] of the enemy of the Asuras [will be achieved].
If they do not stand firm in battle by resorting to some kind of illusion, they are weak, of this there is no doubt; but they are strong through deceit.
Having propitiated me with your head bowed, listen to what I say;
O Hiraṇyākṣa, this has been well-established by even children through sound reasoning.
"That is what is to be grasped," so it has been declared by those who know the scriptures.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu was our eldest and most excellent brother. (77.20)
Even he, though capable and thinking "I am able," was struck down by the gods acting as one;
and even the mighty Hari was forcibly slain by those who were powerless.
O King, O Lord of Asuras, we cry out in distress without you; therefore, I make this request to you: we are but children to you, but they are not.
"Endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga, and possessed of various illusions, we are capable in fair combat, yet we are unable to slay those defilers of their lineage. (77.23)
Remembering our enmity, we shall slay the gods,
just as you find no sleep because of the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Likewise, O Great King, do not act toward us as you would toward fools;
whether on even ground or uneven, O King, wherever you shall engage us in battle. (77.25)
We shall surely cross over that [host] like young fish crossing the ocean;
here is Prahlāda, together with his brother, his sons, and his circle of friends. (77.26)
Just as a single lion challenges all great elephants,
so too does this Bali, the lord of the Daityas, alone challenge all the gods, including Indra.
He is capable of oppressing all the gods, including Yama and the Lord of Wealth;
and this Bāṇa, his son, is a king who possesses a thousand arms.
These two brothers, Sundan and Nisundan, who are mighty of arm, are alone intent upon destroying all the gods. (77.29)
Both of them alone, intent on slaying the gods in battle—this valiant Maya, as well as Sāraka and Tāra. (77.30)
And there are other heroic Dānavas capable of harassing the gods;
they too are all exceedingly powerful, and we ourselves are always strong.
"We shall overwhelm all the gods like hunters in the forest with deer;
for this Andhaka is a glorious hero, having received a boon from Brahmā. (77.32)
He will surely force all of them in battle to the abode of Yama;
for it was by relying upon him that they were protected by him.
"We shall wage a great battle that will strike terror into the gods;
formerly we were all gods, and later they became the gods. (77.34)
"How indeed shall we fear them, like śarabhas before lions?
Having heard those words of his, Andhaka, the lord of the asuras, [spoke].
There he spoke these words, gladdening the lords of the Dānavas:
"O King, we are possessed of great strength, whereas those gods are devoid of power."
Behold all the gods, led by Yama, who have been slain;
today [I shall slay] that evil-souled wretch, the lowest of his lineage, the murderer of kings.
Today their mother Diti suffers this sorrow— [the rest of the verse follows].
"Stay, all you Dānavas! I am sufficient for these evil-minded ones who slay our kings; I have arrived as their death. (77.39)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, O Vyāsa, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa,
desiring victory over the enemies of the gods, spoke to the Dānavas.
Today the Puṣya constellation is present, which brings us strength;
this very day, let all the Dānavas, clad in armor, set out quickly.
Then those Dānavas, filled with joy, quickly equipped their mounts,
which were suitable for battle and capable of harassing the enemy.
"Make yourselves ready quickly; let us go toward the deities.
A most tumultuous sound arose from their mounts.
Like the sound of the Ocean of Milk stirred by a gentle breeze, he said:
"This lion is mine; this leader of the elephant herd is mine. (77.44)
"To whom does this chariot belong, so fully equipped with the implements of war?
Come, go forth with speed; wait but a moment! (77.45)
"Let all the lords of the Daityas depart; we shall follow behind them.
Ascend your own chariot, O hero; what need have I for a chariot today? On foot alone, I shall slay the enemies of the gods in battle."
Thus there arose from those enemies of the gods a sound most pleasing to the ear,
mingled with the resonance of flutes and lutes, like the cooing of women.
Then Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, a man of great asceticism, having arrived there,
spoke these words to Hiraṇyākṣa, gladdening the lord of the Dānavas.
"Peace has been established for you today by me, as well as protection against the Dānavas;
slay all the gods in battle, for there shall be no defeat for you."
I shall support you, along with your servants and kinsmen, as you fight, just as another sacrifice sustains the worlds through its own fervor.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having performed a circumambulation and bowing his head to Śukra,
he went out from the palace, placing the descendant of Bhṛgu before him.
Then there were kettledrums, conchs, *praṇavas*, *ānakas*, and *gomukhas*;
as well as *sāḍastamas*, *ḍiṇḍimas*, *bhāṇḍas*, and *paṭahas*.
Jharjharīs, darduras, sunavas, mardalas, kaṭaṃkaṭas, pepukas, and likewise ekapuṣkalas—[all these musical instruments were sounded]. || 77.53 ||
Pañcākṣas, saridhīkas, mukundas, and likewise murajas,
labhakas, and jalamattas were sounded by the thousands.
They were honored with auspicious rites by singers and bards who sang and offered praises,
and by divine women of noble lineage who had reached old age.
At the gate, Hara beheld a prepared chariot that was like a divine being—
divine, firm, made of Jāmbūnada gold, and marked with a measurement of a hundred nalvas.
With three thousand divine, unattached white steeds, swift as thought, moving at will like the immortals, and entirely free from the pain of fatigue; || 77.57 ||
O Vyāsa, the charioteer of that chariot was the famous son of Garuḍa named Makara, a beautiful bird capable of traveling at will.
Honored by that king with the title of "King" and with blessings,
he ascended the single-wheeled chariot like the sun.
Wearing armor, with his quiver fastened, armed with arrows, sword,
and bow, he had his finger-guards made of iguana skin bound on and likewise wore a neck-guard.
Adorned with a great banner and a parasol,
and with many victory-pennants, he was like a rain-cloud accompanied by cranes.
Then his parasol, resting upon his diadem,
shone like the moon on a full-moon night, manifesting the splendor of a cloud.
His skull-topped staff shone like a banner reaching toward the heavens,
appearing like a blazing comet risen for the destruction of the three worlds.
O Vyāsa, the chariot of the high-souled Andhaka was exactly like that of his son, possessing a sound like the roar of a great rain-cloud.
Then, addressed by him with the words "Now go," the charioteer urged on those three thousand excellent horses that were yoked to the chariot of the enemy of the gods.
Urged on, those seven swift horses, possessing the speed of the wind and capable of going wherever they desired, bore that great chariot like the steeds of the Sun.
Then, in front of him, Śukra appeared in a chariot rumbling like a cloud,
just as Budha appears before the rising sun in the sky.
And on his right side was the Dānava Andhaka,
like the sun reaching the southern solstice for the world.
Taking his stand on the second flank,
Vipracitti stood there like Himavat, the best of mountains, to the land of Bhārata.
Then other heroic Dānavas followed behind and ahead according to their pleasure, like the planets surrounding the moon.
O best of sages, that army as it marched shone like clouds at the end of the rainy season, accompanied by lightning and thunder.
He proceeded amidst the sound of neighing horses, the trumpeting of rutting elephants,
the leaping, the clapping of hands, the shouting, and the fierce lion-roars.

Indeed, that terrifying army of the Dānavas advanced, resounding with the noise of musical instruments and lion-like roars, the neighing of horses and the fierce trumpeting of elephants, and the sound of arms clashing together.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Departure of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 77.77 ||
The seventy-eighth chapter.
Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana said:
O Blessed One, when the sons of Diti had departed for Amarāvatī,
What did the immortals do? This I wish to know.
How did it vanish for them, what was the mantra, and what was their activity? And what answer did those gods receive through their diligent efforts? (78.2)
What did those deities do—those who were righteous, generous, learned, and whose doubts were severed, and who were beloved by the entire world? (78.3)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, how the gods obtained the upper hand and how the armored Asuras countered whatever was done against them. (78.4)
While the Daityas were thus exerting themselves, terrible portents indicative of fear for the gods arose intensely in Amarāvatī.
Flesh-eating birds wandered everywhere above there;
the garlands of the gods withered, and an inauspicious odor blew forth. (78.6)
The horses and other animals did not neigh, and the elephant became dejected;
even without clouds, blood fell in great quantities everywhere, portending fear.
O son of Śakti, weapons are blazing with smoke, headless trunks appear in the sun, and a battle is seen right here. (78.8)
O Vyāsa, the cries of "Alas! Alas! from these two men pervade everywhere, affecting both the displeasure of the gods and their very minds. (78.9)
The left eyes throb, yawning occurs, and birds shriek in other ways that portend fear;
moreover, the fire blazes there with a harsh and crackling sound. (78.10)
Having seen these and various other portents indicative of fear, Śakra spoke these words to his preceptor Bṛhaspati: || 78.11 ||
"O Blessed One, what is this terrible danger that has arisen for us, since these fierce and most dreadful portents are foretelling it? (78.12)
I do not believe these portents are without cause, for they are by no means insignificant to us;
indeed, these fierce omens are as terrible as the end of an eon.
Having heard those words of his, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods,
looked upon him, reflected with his intellect, and then spoke these words.
What you have said is true; it is not without cause. There will undoubtedly be a very great reason for this.
In ancient times, Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas, was the cause;
he was slain by the Man-Lion, and our kingdom has been regained.
Today, for twelve thousand years,
all the worlds have been enjoyed by you, the high-souled ones who are perfectly at peace.
The lords of the Daityas, together with the Dānavas, lie down devoid of energy;
and in Pātāla, the sons of Danu dwell, struck down by misery and grief. (78.18)
Hiraṇyākṣa, however, was the king of the Daityas and the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
he was surely seeking to avenge his slain brother. (78.19)
Surrounded by all the lords of the Daityas and the Dānavas,
the lord of the Daityas, possessed of great strength and prowess, approached together with his sons and grandsons.
And his son Andhaka was indeed made immortal by Brahmā;
that youth cannot be slain, and from this your fear has arisen.
Therefore, O beings of great courage, all of you, well-armored and clad for battle, wait until this portent has passed.
Having heard those words of his, Śakra then said to all the gods: "Prepare yourselves for battle, having made a firm resolve."
A great danger has arrived; do not remain inactive!
Lest the lords of the Daityas, having encountered us, slay us as the gods slay the intoxicated. (78.24)
Then Vāyu, having approached Śakra, the destroyer of all asuras,
spoke with palms joined in reverence in the very assembly of the gods.
This Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, surrounded by all the asuras,
approaches in order to slay the gods, remembering the slaughter of his brother.
Therefore, O Indra of the gods, being fully armored and endowed with great strength, arise together with us for victory and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed one, the high-souled Vyāsa, himself the king of the gods,
[gave him] an impenetrable, divine armor adorned with gold.
Having himself bound his soul in meditation, Śakra, whose voice resounded like clouds and drums, duly bestowed the mantra upon his son, the descendant of Aṅgiras, according to the prescribed rite.
Clad in that armor, the majestic Śakra shone like the immovable Mount Meru enveloped by clouds accompanied by lightning and meteors.
Then the divine Bṛhaspati himself bound upon him arm-guards of iguana-skin, finger-protectors, and radiant hand-shields with sacred mantras.
He also bound to him inexhaustible quivers and a sword born of nectar, which was indestructible by arrows and other weapons, using a mantra.
Then he properly gave him a most formidable bow, together with five arrows, consecrated by mantras and increasing victory.
The valiant one showed him auspicious objects:
a full jar, a weapon, and also the elephant Airāvata.
It was fashioned by many divine teachers dwelling in the Kalpa age;
it has been worshipped and incensed, and indeed incensed by those possessing the pride of wrath.
Then the god mounted that elephant,
which was endowed with the auspicious marks of a noble beast, possessed four tusks, and was exuding rut.
Mounted upon that elephant Airāvata,
the Lord then shone like the rising sun upon the crest of the Eastern Mountain.
O great sage, the king of the gods then shone with his white parasol, like the king of white mountains [the Himalayas] with the moon. 78.38.
Fanned by chowries, his exceedingly radiant face shone like a full-blown great lotus in autumn being fanned by swans.
Beside him was Śakra’s righteous son Jayanta,
who shone like Rudra’s beloved son Kārtikeya.
Then the mighty Yama, mounted upon his buffalo Puṇḍra and preceded by the Staff of Death (Kāladaṇḍa), arrived surrounded by ten crores [of followers].
And Kubera went forth, surrounded by many Rākṣasas,
as well as by Yakṣas, Puṇyajanas, and other deities.
Of them, there were twelve crores, twenty thousand,
eight hundred, and again eight more.
The god Varuṇa went forth with ten hundred sons;
they were all surrounded by aquatic creatures numbering twenty-one crores.
Then the god Anala, surrounded by ten crores [of followers],
went forth together with his son, along with his circle of friends and kinsmen.
Then Vāyu, of great splendor, all-pervading, and of great speed,
possessing immense strength, set forth with ten akṣauhiṇīs.
All the Ādityas went forth, surrounded by twelve akṣauhiṇīs;
and each one of them, O Vyāsa, was a warrior skilled in divine weapons.
Likewise, the Rudras, possessed of great power through their great māyā,
emerged one by one, each surrounded by sixteen akṣauhiṇīs.
The Vasus with ten [Akṣauhiṇīs], both Aśvins with eight,
and likewise all the divine Aṅgirasas, were surrounded by Akṣauhiṇīs.
The Yāmas, the Dāmas, the Sādhyas, and those Lekhas of great strength—
all of them also joined together with ten hundred crores.
There were twenty crores of high-souled Gandharvas,
sixty-four of Pannagas, and twenty of birds.
And fifty crores of Piśācas gathered there,
as did [crores] of high-souled kings.
All this divine force was assembled there;
having seen that vast and boundless, supreme army of the gods.
The king of the Jīvañjīvas, who was a supreme knower of dharma, said:
"O Blessed One, let an array be formed so that [we may overcome] those evil-minded ones."
Having heard those words of his— words concerning that which is unassailable, immeasurable, and which even Bhārgava does not know— the wise Bṛhaspati spoke.
In the presence of the gods, he said to Śakra, the lord of the deities:
"O great archer, there is nothing that the great Bhārgava does not possess within me. (78.56)
O Pākaśāsana, even he who does not know its divisions would not act [otherwise];
for Uśanas, the great yogin of great renown, knows it.
And I do not know that at all, for he is indeed superior to me;
yet, O Lord of Śacī, it was due to his sharpness and his pride.
He shows negligence toward them, and he is not found to be so everywhere;
yet I [behave] with a sense of discernment and with supreme gentleness.
Vigilant in all respects and protected by your troops,
O Lord of the Gods, I always surpass him in intelligence.
Therefore, I shall form for you an array of exceeding brilliance in the shape of a hawk,
by which you will defeat those Dānavas in battle for some time.
Then that Blessed One Jīva, the great yogin, assuming the form known as Śyena, created a brilliantly radiant array for the benefit of the gods.
Upon his neck, he placed the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), as well as Varuṇa,
Anala, Vāyu, and Jayanta, the son of Śakra.
Jīva made his head, Cūḍā, Yama, Mṛtyu, and both Kālas; Jīva made his mouth, and the Moon and Sun were his two eyes.
That twice-born one made all the Rudras his one wing,
the Ādityas his second wing, and Purandara his center.
The Vasus were his feet, and the Aśvins were his great soles;
the Gandharvas and Pannagas likewise took refuge in his nails.
The great beings among the birds and the mighty piśācas made his tail, while the serpents and other gods then formed his belly.
The kings stood at his feet and established upon the ground all the immensely powerful and highly energetic gods who were members of the assembly.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having formed that array of birds and having consecrated it with a mantra,
Bṛhaspati spoke these words to the king of the gods.
"This array was devised by me after creating the king of the Rākṣasas;
beyond this, no further action of the ritual remains for us. (78.70)
O Śakra, protected by the gods and by me with Atharvan mantras and the power of asceticism, conquer your enemies in battle.
Perform your duty according to your power, for you are indeed immortal, O King;
let even all the gods, the immortals, fight, O King of the gods.
O bull among gods, it is by our good fortune that victory has been won; it was not otherwise.
Slay the enemies, O mighty-armed one; let there be no fear for you in battle.
Then conchs and kettledrums, as well as paṭahas, ḍiṇḍimas, āḍambaras, nambhas, kṛkavākas, and cow-horns [were sounded]. (78.74)
The mṛdaṅga drums, the peṣukas, and various musical instruments resounded on all sides;
by that sound, a great joy for battle arose among the warriors. They let out lion-roars and performed the slapping of arms and the clashing of weapons. || 78.75 ||

Then the gods, led by Indra and other preeminent deities, went forth with conchs and drums, their hands radiant with all their infallible weapons; they were desirous of victory and longing for the destruction of the enemy.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Array of the Divine Forms," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 78.78 ||
The seventy-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, when the army of the gods had been arrayed and stood ready for battle, armored and prepared.
The terrible and fearsome strength of the Dānavas was clearly seen.
Seeing that strength of the Dānava, all the gods, together with Indra,
let out lion-like roars mingled with the sound of musical instruments.
That immense roar, O Vyāsa, like that of the ocean being churned,
filled the entire world with a sound like the thundering of clouds at the end of an eon.
Then all those tigers among the Dānavas, having seen the foremost of the gods,
drew up their army in formation and stood there, looking intently at one another.
Seeing those leaders of the Dānavas standing there gazing [at him],
O Vyāsa, Hiraṇyanayana himself spoke to Bhārgava.
Having formed this array, these gods stand here fearlessly;
they think, "In battle, we shall conquer the Dānavas in every way. (79.6)
Therefore, may you without delay create for us a counter-array of illusions that will break apart this very array of the gods. 79.7.
Sanatkumāra said: Having replied,
"So be it," he drew his crescent-shaped sword and strove to sever the head of that bird from its body.
Upon its peak, he placed Prahlāda, Andhaka, the Dānavas,
the Dhārās, the Nivātakavacas, the Paulomas, and the sons of Kālakā.
Virocana, Bali, and Vipracitti along with his younger brothers, as well as the brother of Prahlāda together with his circle of friends and kinsmen.
The great yogi made the back his seat and the king himself his middle;
then the descendant of Bhṛgu, the scorcher of enemies, spoke to him with confidence.
"O Hiraṇyākṣa, this [formation] is properly arranged, timely, and beneficial in every respect;
for this great array has been formed by you as a breaker of the enemy's divine formations."

"Act with diligence—may prosperity be yours! Protected by me, and guarding one another, all of you, skilled in various weapons and possessing great powers of illusion, must act so that none of the gods may overcome you. (79.13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and cow-horns, as well as āḍambaras, ḍiṇḍimas, and paṭahas with great sounds [resounded]. || 79.14 ||
And thousands of other various musical instruments were sounded,
which indeed bestow intoxication and strength upon both the gods and the dānavas.
Then, commanded by the lords of the Dānavas with the words "Crush them!", the Dānavas,
though struck on all sides, began to trample the army of the gods.
Those gods, moreover, being prepared and endowed with the power of austerity and yoga,
struck the Dānavas— who had committed offenses— with various weapons.
From the falling heads of elephants being struck down with swords,
there arose a most terrible sound, like that of splitting bamboo canes.
As the bows were drawn and the arrows were released,
there arose a great sound like that of mountains being split asunder.
With bhindipālas, śaktis, and tomara-javelins being hurled,
the entire sky became as if covered with fireflies.
With heads, feet, and arms cast down,
that battlefield in an instant became uneven.
With elephants resembling mountains, with excellent horses and the finest chariots,
and with headless trunks dancing about, the battlefield became difficult to behold.
With parasols and necklaces, with armor and also with hand-guards; with gold coins, threads, beautiful crowns, armlets, and earrings as well.
With various neck-protectors, fine silk garments, and jewels; with variegated saddle-cloths and even arms adorned with ornaments.
With pestles, trident-staffs, bells, and even goads,
the surface of the earth there shines like the sky covered with celestial lights.
Enraged, that great car-warrior, though himself deprived of his chariot, seized the charioteer by the hair and,
leaping onto the chariot, struck him down with force.
And there, another mighty-armed man, having swiftly struck the elephant,
hurled the chariot away like a handful of *kuśa* grass scattered at a sacrifice.
Having been thrown from the elephant, he leapt up— [the rest of the verse is missing].
With arrows resembling venomous serpents, he sent [them] to the abode of Yama.
Even though his horse was slain and he had fallen to the ground,
this self-possessed man attended to him from his feet, just as a disciple attends to a sleeping teacher.
When their driver and warrior were slain, these excellent horses bore the chariot like men who are intoxicated yet possessed of knowledge carry the sacred scriptures.
This other bull among the gods, though firmly bound by the Daitya,
encircled him with his two arms and proceeded toward the presence of the deities.
Behold, he severed the arm of the charging elephant.
He fell to the earth, slain by that very same elephant.
This one was joined with another; having come, he was slain by yet another;
and that one too was killed by another god, and he again by yet another.
These and many other foot-soldiers, having gathered together in great numbers, bewildered the chariot-warrior and struck him down fearlessly. (79.34)
Thus do the perfected ones who travel through the sky, as well as the ṛṣis and cāraṇas,
purify themselves, take delight, laugh, and recite prayers.
The Apsarases carry away the warriors slain there in battle;
even the Piśācas and the Nikumbhilās rejoice and dance.
That music of the Gandharvas, now shattered, broken, and torn asunder,
became the music of war, increasing the fear of cowards.
Then the gods and asuras, whose entire bodies were wounded by one another’s blows,
remembering their enmity and desiring victory for the sake of sovereignty, struck each other, having assumed forms resembling those of Rākṣasas.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle between the Gods and Asuras," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Eightieth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that great and terrifying battle was raging, [the following occurred].
Then the gods indeed surrounded the Dānavas on all sides.
Death, Time, Yama, Kṛtānta, as well as Strife, Deceit, Diseases, Enmity, and the powerful Wrath; 80.2.
All those hells, all the messengers of Yama,
the pretas, and the ancestors— these are the four classes.
And Vāmana, O gods, as well as the immensely powerful Kiṃkaras—
all these, having entered him, then struck down the Dānava army.
With their limbs torn apart by the messengers of Yama, their chests and bellies shattered,
the Daityas groan upon the earth like sinners in the hells.
Crushed by swords and shields, bound by the noose of Death,
and fallen under the power of the Ordainer (Kṛtānta), all the sons of Diti are being torn apart.
Being struck down by both Death and Yama, those lords of the Daityas, finding no protector anywhere, wandered here and there. || 80.7 ||
Thus, being tormented, they wandered here and there and struck one another;
then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within the army of the Dānavas.
"Excellent! Excellent!"—thus was there a cry from the gods as they honored Yama.
Then there was the son of Prahlāda, known by the name Virocana. (80.9)
Then, having approached on his elephant, he crushed the army of the gods;
that great illusionist rushed forward together with his elephant.
Having circumambulated Yama, like another Droṇamegha,
he [assailed him] with many sharp, iron arrows of unblunted points.
He rained down upon Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Vāyu as well;
having then shrouded the splendor of the sun with his sharp rays,
he overwhelmed the gods like the Saṃvartaka cloud.
With all their limbs pierced by those arrows and being struck again and again,
all the gods in an instant became deprived of their senses.
Whether he was going or coming, whether he had not yet reached his destination or had already arrived, and even when he was at a distance—
whenever and wherever the Daitya beheld him, he struck him from that very spot.
With his bow perpetually drawn, the Daitya became as difficult to look upon as the sun surrounded by a halo,
like the fire risen at the end of an eon.
Then, O Vyāsa, as he was shooting thus, the wise Varuṇa, threatening the lord of the Dānavas, cut down that very great bow.
Vāyu stripped away his armor on all sides with sharp arrows;
Dhaneśa destroyed his elephant with a thunderbolt strike.
Seeing him thus humiliated, both Bali and Bāṇa,
along with Prahlāda and his brothers, rushed toward the world-protectors.
As they were still attacking, the mighty world-protectors (lokapālas) crushed their wheel-protectors with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
As Bāṇa was drawing his bows with his arrows, Vyāsa, the wind suddenly severed those bows all at once; it was like a marvel.
His bow having been severed, he, filled with rage, then discharged javelins;
Vāyu hurled those back toward another direction with great force. (80.21)
Furthermore, with his straight-jointed arrows, he,
being exceedingly exerted, sent his horses along with their charioteers to the abode of Yama.
That mighty one, powerful as Balarāma, leaped down from his chariot in fury;
seizing his mace, he rushed impetuously toward Śvasana.
As he was thus rushing forward with his mace, the Wind-god swiftly cut that mace to pieces with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
And Bāṇa, the best among strikers, though his mace had been cut away,
seized another mace, hurled it, and laughed.
As Bāṇa’s mace, moving through the air, came rushing with speed,
Vāyu seized it and, like one undaunted, scattered it in another direction.
Then, O Vyāsa, seeing that his son was deprived of his chariot and severely afflicted by Vāyu, Bali quickly placed him upon his own chariot.
Those two lords of the Dānavas, joined together upon a single chariot,
shone like the sun and the moon when they have met on the full-moon day.
Then, at that time, a battle took place between them and those others—
[the gods and the asuras]—
having learned that they were being held back by the mighty world-protectors.
All the Nivātakavacas, the armored Kālakeyas, the Paulomas, the Saiṃhikeyas, Śambara, and Kālaśambara—[all these were slain]. (80.30)
And the great Daitya Andhaka, and the renowned Hiraṇyākṣa—all these Dānavas, eager for battle, did not abandon their formation. || 80.31 ||
Those of great speed exerted their force like mountains shrouded in clouds;
then the powerful Yama struck them with his staff as they were still rushing toward him.
They stood obstructed, fixed like figures on a variegated cloth;
seeing all those Daityas standing still out of fear of Yama, [he spoke].
Andhaka approached Yama and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Having arrived with his great chariot, he repeatedly twanged his bow.
The valiant one pierced Yama in the forehead with ten arrows,
Mahiṣa with five, and likewise Kāla in front of him with six.
Whirling his bow, which possessed a radiance equal to Indra’s rainbow, he [struck] Death with ten arrows and Kṛtānta with seven. (80.36)
Like a thundering cloud, Andhaka—the eldest son of Hiraṇyākṣa and possessed of great strength—pierced the god once more, saying, "I am he! (80.37).
"And a boon was granted to me by Brahmā," he proclaimed.
As he was speaking thus, the powerful son of the Sun quickly [arrived]. || 80.38 ||
Enraged, he shattered the chariot, striking it down with his staff;
for when that chariot along with its bow had been crushed there, Andhaka [acted]. (80.39)
Raising his mace with speed, he then rushed toward the Lord of the Dead;
but with a blow of his staff, the latter likewise crushed that mace to pieces.
Enraged once more, he struck him on the head with his staff.
Just as a sage who has conquered his senses remains unshaken even when touched by the objects of the senses, so too was the irresistible staff struck down by Andhaka. (80.42)
Seeing it repelled before them, the lords of the Dānavas laughed and let out lion-like roars accompanied by musical instruments and the resonant sounds of their arms.
They cried out, "Well done, Andhaka! and shouted thus again and again;
then Andhaka also approached, roaring like the ocean.
Striking with his palm, he cast Mahiṣa and the others down upon the ground;
then a cry of "Alas! arose from the gods, while the Dānavas cried out, "Seize him! Seize him! (80.45).
And the array of the gods was broken, O son of Śakti;
then those three—Death, Time, and Fate—[approached]. (80.46)
Overcome with rage, they bound Andhaka with many nooses;
but that exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas, having severed those very nooses,
the strong one bound Kṛtānta with the noose of his own arms.
Bound by the noose of his arms, Kṛtānta, frantic with rage,
lifted up Andhaka and, being powerful himself, carried him away by force.
Beholding his own son being led away, Hiraṇyākṣa struck Death most fiercely and firmly with sharp arrows.
That one of great strength pierced all his limbs and even his joints with sharpened arrows; yet, though transfixed, he stood firm.
Seeing that [opening] disclosed by the arrows, all the gods, including Indra, stood guard with their weapons raised in their terrible hands. (80.51)

Then, at that time, a most fierce sound of musical instruments arose from the armies of the Asuras and Suras, consisting of kīṭhara drums, mṛdaṅga drums, flutes, lutes, paṇava drums, sughoṣaka drums, and ḍiṇḍimānaka drums.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the Yuddha-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 80.80 ||
The eighty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Hiraṇyākṣa, seeing the Lord of the Gods approaching before him, [acted].
He said to the charioteer, "Take me to Indra. || 81.1 ||
Urged by him, and urging the horses in turn,
he then led them to that Indra of the gods, just as Agni carries the oblation offered to him.
Then, standing within the range of an arrow's flight, that bull among the asuras spoke to the thousand-eyed lord of the gods, who was mounted upon the shoulder of his elephant.
"O Śakra, whatever strength you possess, display it without delay;
for we are the former gods, and indeed the entire triple world belongs to us. (81.4)
O best of gods, having rightfully established [the kingdom] according to the order of seniority,
you have now abandoned that justice and killed my brother once again.
"Having become deceitful through misplaced trust, they later attained divinity;
we here are the ancient gods, and you are the new deities. (81.6)
I know the lives of all those who fight; having slain you here today along with your followers, I shall likewise make you an offering.

"I shall become free from debt to my brother who was slain by you through your magic power. Having spoken thus, the valiant one drew his powerful bow and pierced [Indra] on the forehead with five sharpened arrows, O Vyāsa. (81.8)
Pierced in the forehead by him with five arrows,
that king shone like Mount Meru enveloped by the rays of the sun.
Then, as he was walking about once more, Śakra took up his thunderbolt, severed his bow, and struck him again.
By that excellent stroke, he saw the quarters of the sky ablaze;
not seeing [the enemy], he took up another bow and drew it once again. || 81.11 ||
The king cut that down for him, as well as another and yet more;
then, seizing a spear, he angrily hurled it at him.
As that fierce weapon, with its blazing mouth like the very sister of Death, was falling upon him, the king cut it down with his thunderbolt; it was like a marvel.
Then, raising another splendid mace, the enraged Hiraṇyākṣa rushed forward with speed like a lion toward an elephant. 81.14.
As it was falling swiftly toward him, the king cut that gold-adorned mace into many pieces, just as an atheist destroys both dharma and artha.
Then Vipracitti, Śini, Vāṣkali, Maya, Śambara, and the Dānava Asiloma likewise [approached him]. || 81.16 ||
Tāra, Kāraka, as well as Indradamana,
Kālanemi, Ṣaṇḍa, Vipāka, and Pāka.
Ilvala, Namuci, Vātāpi, and Kālamuñjika—all these possessed of great māyā power—rushed against the Lord of the Gods. || 81.18 ||
Then, as they were still approaching, the furious Rudras and Ādityas hemmed them in,
just as powerful lions hold back elephants in a lonely place.
And between them there arose a most terrible battle, like that of rutting elephants colliding with one another in the forest. (81.20)
There, O Vyāsa, the Sun-god named Aṃśa, having drawn his bow, pursued the Dānavas with a chariot that roared like a cloud.
He struck Vipracitti with ten arrows, Śini with five,
Vāṣkali with three in that battle, and Maya with five as well.
And he slew Saṃvara with twenty arrows, as well as Asiloman,
Tāra, Tāraka, Ilvala, and likewise Namuci.
Vātāpi, Indradamana, Vipāka, and Pāka;
Kālanemi, Ṣaṇḍa, and likewise Āmī-sṛmuñjika.
He pierced all of them with ten arrows each;
and as they drew their bows in battle, that god, possessed of light-handedness like the sun,
simultaneously cut their bows asunder and let out a roar.
Then,
O best of Brahmins, as if laughing, he shattered their horses, charioteers, and divine, victory-bearing banners with his arrows in many ways.
Those great archers, their horses slain and their charioteers killed on all sides, all rushed with speed toward Aṃśa, sword in hand. || 81.27 ||
Then Āditya, remaining unperturbed, filled their knees as if they were the peaks of great mountains or like roaring clouds.
With their ankles and knees pierced by arrows,
those Dānavas then cast off their burden and fled swiftly in another direction.
Then the gods produced a great sound of musical instruments,
as well as vast lion-roars and abundant sounds of clapping arms.
Drawing even his own bow, which resembled Indra’s rainbow, the Blessed One wrought a great slaughter among the Dānavas and Daityas. (81.31)
The best of strikers, Aṃśa, struck down the heads of the lords of the Dānavas like ripe fruits falling from a tree. (81.32)
Some, rendered headless by arrows, run along on their limbs;
having fled from the battle with speed, they fall lifeless upon the earth. (81.33)
Others, possessed of great strength, with their arms and thighs severed,
fell down groaning fiercely like men situated in hell.
With all their limbs filled with arrows and bound by the fetters of shafts, they wander here and there like embodied beings in saṃsāra. (81.35)
There was no Daitya or Dānava of great strength there who did not have fierce arrows pierce him from the high-souled Aṃśa.
Just as a forest in full bloom appears like a grove of bandhujīva flowers,
or like that of aśoka and kiṃśuka trees, so did the army of the Daityas shine.
"This is a portion, this is a portion," "No, this is one, and that is another"—thus, O Daityas, afflicted by fear, they saw everything as consisting of portions. (81.38)
With his bow perpetually drawn like the sun encircled by a halo,
he pierced every Daitya wherever he beheld them with his feathered arrows.
At that time, neither taking up his portion nor even placing it there, nor drawing the bow, was he perceived by the Daityas and Dānavas. (81.40)
His great bow appeared drawn into a complete circle;
at that time in battle, he was seen like the sun at midday.
Possessing a divine bow, light-handed and powerful, with his bow always drawn into a great circle,
he consumed his enemies in battle like a fire fanned by the wind consumes a great heap of dry fuel.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the Yuddha [section] of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 81.81 ||
The eighty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those lords of the Daityas were thus being driven hither and thither by him through his partial incarnations (aṃśa).
Having seen him, Bala, the great illusionist, spoke this to his charioteer: || 82.1 ||
"Lead me where this evil-minded Aṃśa burns up our strength, so that with my sharp arrows I may send him to the abode of Yama. (82.2)
As he was thus rushing forward, that best of strikers then cut down his banner with one arrow and his horses one by one.
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he swiftly struck off the head from the body;
he also pierced him in the forehead with five arrows. 82.4.
Those five arrows shone upon the forehead of that Daitya like the rays of the sun emerging from the center of a cloud.
Then, O Vyāsa, the powerful Daitya, a bowman filled with rage, leaped into the sky and covered Aṃśa with many arrows.
Like a cloud after a good rain, like a thunderbolt [from the sky], as the sun [emits] its rays, and as the moon [emits] frost. (82.7)
Likewise, that Dānava, powerful and the best among strikers, out of pride,
showered Aṃśa with sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs.
And the lord of the Dānavas cut his banner into many pieces,
having rendered the horses speedless and deprived the charioteer of his chariot.
He shattered his bow with many arrows,
and he likewise struck down those fierce deities whom [the opponent] had stationed according to their respective positions.
The great illusionist rendered them motionless and let out a roar;
in one place resembling Bṛhaspati, in another resembling the sun.
In some places he was like the moon or fire; in some places he was equal to the stars and planets;
in some places he resembled a mountain; and in some places he assumed the form of a vulture.
In some places, entering the sky and becoming invisible, he discharged arrows;
his body, thus covered with arrows, was cut, pierced, and torn asunder.
Stunned as if mute, the entire host of gods appeared motionless;
the sound of musical instruments had vanished, and the neighing of horses was silenced. (82.14)
Resounding with the trumpeting of elephants and the fierce cries of exhausted warriors, that army stood motionless,
appearing as if it were depicted in a painting.
O Bala, whichever god there was who looked upward at him,
the exceedingly powerful Bala rendered his face invisible with his arrows.
And they remained devoid of all movement, as if established upon the path to liberation.
Seeing all of them thus despondent in that great ocean of an army,
Vāyu, Jayanta, Pūṣan, and Bhaga— those of immense strength— [approached].
Roaring, they warded off those arrows of his army,
just as Vāyu, O highly blessed one, disperses arrows shot from the clouds.
The mighty one seized those who were being released, those who were being liberated, and even those already freed;
Bhaga, as if laughing, cut asunder his divine bow.
Likewise, Dehatrāṇa and Pūṣan [were assigned] the two quivers, as was Jayanta.
The gods, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, tormented him with sharp arrows;
then that powerful bull among the Dānavas was thus afflicted by the gods.
O Vyāsa, he of terrible prowess fought with trees born in the forest;
those beautiful trees were then hurled by him in many ways with great force.
Then Kratu, with his arrows, struck the lord of the gods;
thereafter, he seized a great mountain peak, complete with its deer, wild beasts, and kinnaras.
Uttering an exceedingly terrible and great roar,
he fell with such force, like a powerful wind driven by its own strength.
He seized that very horn and struck it down upon the head of the Asura;
thus, he slew ten million powerful Dānavas in battle.
He struck down that mountain peak, which had been hurled by Bala and was making a great roar;
and the Dānavas, the sons of Diti, saw those [demons] slain by that peak.
Upon seeing those fierce gods, thousands [of beings] broke and fled—
charioteers with their chariots, cavalry with their horses, elephant-riders with their elephants, and likewise the foot soldiers.
Others, abandoning their mounts and seeking to save their lives,
fled by the thousands, letting out great cries of distress.
Then, as they were fleeing, that Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa,
the Danuja Vipracitti, and the mighty Prahlāda approached them.
Then Maya, the Daitya Andhaka, and Tāraka, the scorcher of Śakra,
spoke to all the Dānavas and Daityas who were overwhelmed with fear.
O tigers among the Dānavas, O Daityas, enemies of the gods!
Why do you stand here guarding? Do not be afraid, O Dānavas! || 82.32 ||
"Where have you Dānavas gone? Will you find happiness or not?
These gods were formerly possessed of great strength, yet they did not know your power. (82.33)
Even the foremost asuras do not crush those who dwell in the underworld;
yet these lowest of their kind will utterly destroy everyone, even in the underworld.
"Do not go; turn back and protect yourselves by all means! O Daityas, do not fear for your lives here; rather, [protect them] through fair combat. (82.35)
Where has your state of being Danujas gone? Where has your nature as Daityas gone? Where has your enmity with the gods gone, and where has the seizure of your kingdom gone? (82.36)
That fortitude which you possess, that pride of yours, your lineage and birth,
and that roar you previously uttered— the time for all of that has now arrived.
Then the Daityas spoke, saying, "We are not children;
moreover, each one of us individually is capable even of destroying the gods. (82.38)
This very time for him has now arrived here; why do you flee?
I shall know all of that boasting of yours today, and nothing beyond this.
"O Daityas, do not fall into vain fear here like autumn clouds;
turn back, O you who know not dharma, and fight with firm resolve! (82.40)
"Behold, O lowest of your clans, the great deed of me and my son!
O Dānavas, I am the illustrious Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Kaśyapa."
"And this son of mine, Andhaka, is as auspicious as the boon granted by Brahmā;
he possesses the prowess that belonged to Hiraṇyakaśipu, O best of Asuras. (82.42)
"I possess twice as much of that; behold it without hesitation!
And today, O Dānavas, witness all of them slain by me."
Even if all the gods were to stand before me in battle today, once the enemies of the asuras have been slain, the three worlds shall remain undisturbed.
"O best of asuras, freed from fever, you shall attain happiness through me, Indra;
let there be no fear for you here today, so that you may stand as virtuous men do, beholding me together with my son in battle. (82.45)
Sanatkumāra said: O best of brahmins, having been addressed thus, they all turned back, completely overcome with shame, like elephants tormented by the goad. (82.46)
With their lotus-faces covered by parasols, their countenances filled with shame and devoid of passion,
they did not stand before the face of that king, like distressed small fish in shallow water [avoiding] a whale.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Asuras' Outcry," in the Battle [section] of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 82.82 ||
The eighty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, those Dānavas retreated from the front of the battle.
Then they performed that difficult task with speed, like rivers rushing into the ocean.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Śini, Bāṣkala,
Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, and another Bala who was a thorn to the gods.
Vipracitti, Ṣaṇḍa, Hrada, Śatodara,
the Asura Yama, Vyaṃsa, Śatāvarta, and Hutodara.
Keśin and Namuci, as well as the asura Indradamana; Maya, Mura, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālin, and Prabhākara. || 83.4 ||
Tāra and Tāraka, the renowned Baka and Aṭi,
as well as Mūka and Kubha, both possessing the great roar of Kārtasvana.
Vātāpi and Celvala, as well as Ilvala and Kabalvala; Ketu and Śataketu, Rāhu and Svarbhānu.
Śambara, Namuci, and Kālaśambara,
as well as Dundubhi, Mahiṣa, and Śatadundubhi.
Kālanemi, Vipāka, Pāka, and likewise Duryodhana;
Hastin, Sunda and Nisunda, Śarabha, and Kāla as well. (83.8)
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatākranda, Śatāvarta, and then Dhenuka;
Pralamba and Vaka, as well as Gaja and Hālāhala.
The renowned Saiṃhikeyas, the Paulomas, the sons of Kālaka,
as well as the Nivātakavacas and the Bāleya hosts.
And all the sons of Bāṇa were renowned as the Kālakhañjas;
they were Vṛtra and Vṛtta along with their hosts, as well as others of great strength.
O best of Brahmins, as that army was roaring,
there then arose a great surge from the king of the Sindhus, like the mighty tide rushing toward the shore.
With abundant lion-roars mingled with the sounds of musical instruments, along with the rattling of chariot rims, the neighing of horses, and the trumpeting of elephants; (83.13)
That tumultuous sound, O Vyāsa, filled the three worlds;
even the gods stood there, fully prepared and exerting every effort.
With eyes long and copper-red with rage, they seized those Daityas.
With swords being hurled and with *śataghnī* weapons falling from all sides,
that sky then became as variegated as if filled with meteors.
O best of sages, heads pierced and cut by arrows indeed fall upon the earth like ripe fruits from palm trees.
With crowns, necklaces, armlets, and radiant waist-bands; with golden medallions, fine silken garments, bracelets, finger-rings, and earrings.
With elephant-ornaments, hair-combs, and ivory-handled fans; with fans made of young leaves, umbrellas, and even jewels.
With divine golden turbans and highly radiant armor, and with heads, feet, hands, and faces of great splendor; 83.20.
With goads, blankets, and yokes shining with gold,
that night of battle shone there like another sky filled with stars.
"Stay! Stay! Where are you going from me? There is truly no escape for you today! I am standing here; strike me! I have no fear; stay before me! || 83.22 ||
Why do you roar vainly in the sky like clouds in autumn?
Show your deed quickly; today your roaring shall be fruitless.
"Do not strike thus, O fool! Do not look [at me]; be firm!
Stay, stay! Where will you go after killing my beloved son? (83.24)
"Here I stand; today I shall lead you to the abode of Yama.
Today, O lowest of gods, I shall destroy all that unbearable arrogance of yours. (83.25)
"My arrows shall destroy you; stay, stay before me!
O lowest of Dānavas, I am a god; I am not afraid in battle."
Speaking thus, thousands of warriors there fought like intoxicated great elephants, intent upon slaying one another.
Having thus spoken to one another, all the Siddhas and Cāraṇas stationed in the sky dispatched them to the abode of Yama.
They achieve their goals, they rejoice, and they roar like clouds;
"This Dānava, my husband, has been slain by me in battle"—thus she was fashioned. (83.29)
"This god is your husband; do not set your heart on another.
Why are you thus possessed by greed, examining one best man after another? (83.30)
"There is no taking by force here; read the document, do not be in haste!
Why is your mind dissatisfied? Be content, O beautiful one. (83.31)
"This portion has been given to you by the gods; take it and go to your home.
Thus the Apsarases spoke here, and they laughed. (83.32)
When their warrior was slain in battle, they likewise raised a clamor;
the soft speech of those women was mingled with the sound of their girdles and bracelets.
Having heard [the challenge] again and again, those warriors fought on, free from fear;
with their leaps and the slapping of their arms, they made all the directions resound.

That battle shone forth, resounding with the trumpeting of elephants and the leaping of those agitated by it, echoing with the roars of lions, instilling fear in gods and dānavas, and bringing an end to life.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the section on the war.
The eighty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
At that time, that foremost sacrifice of war took place there for the sake of the kingdom.
