There, the powerful god himself, the thousand-eyed one, was a performer of sacrifices.
The lord of the gods, together with the deities, is considered to be his kusha grass;
and his various weapons are the sacrificial ladles (sruva) with which the oblation is offered.
The vital breaths are declared to be the oblation; Agni is Death of great splendor;
the mantras are the divine weapons, and the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) are the heads.
There, Soma was the victor; the Rudras were the Adhvaryus, the Ādityas were the Bahvṛcas, and the Vasus performed the office of the Hotṛ. || 84.4 ||
Brahmā himself was present there as the presiding deity, and Bṛhaspati and the two Aśvins performed the duties of the *śāmitra*; thus did the sacrifice proceed.
The Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, along with his followers, became the sacrificial animal there;
thus did that sacrifice of the Daityas shine forth, O Lord of Śiśira.
Hiraṇyākṣa became the sacrificer, the leader of the Daityas and Dānavas;
Vipracitti became the Hotṛ priest, and the Dānavas were the Prasthātṛs.
With Prahlāda as the Udgātṛ, Śukra as the Brahman,
and the thousand-eyed Indra as the sacrificial victim, that imperishable one thus performed the sacrifice.
While that great sacrifice was proceeding, amidst great terror,
Indra approached the exceedingly powerful Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa.
The mighty Vāyu quickly approached Vipracitti;
Aṃśa was held back by Saṃvara, as was Bhaga by Bala.
Virocana joined with Pūṣan and Mitra, while Bali was joined by Bāṇa; Varuṇa was with Sārdha, and Yama with Andhaka. (84.11)
Jayanta was with Nelvala, Candra with Maya,
Rāhu with Ahirbudhnya, and the Kāpālin with Śataketu.
Ajaikapād fought with Kālanemi, Jvara with Kārtasvana,
Aryaman with Prahlāda, and Dhara with Anuhlāda.
Dhruva was engaged with Hrāda, while other mighty warriors were likewise engaged with their respective opponents;
meanwhile, Hiraṇyākṣa firmly drew Indra’s bow.
The immensely powerful one pierced the elephant in the region of its frontal globes with a single arrow;
he struck the lord of the gods in the region of the collarbone with five arrows,
and again pierced the elephant on the forehead with six and then with seven more.
Pierced by those arrows, that elephant, with blood flowing from its wounds,
shone like the white king of mountains streaming with liquid red chalk.
Then Śakra, enraged, struck him on the temple with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt and let out a roar, O Vyāsa.
The powerful lord of the Daityas, disregarding that vajra-strike as if it were a mere blow against his own merit,
continued to afflict Śakra along with his elephant.
The elephant, pierced by him, appeared with blood flowing;
out of rage, it blazed like a fire fed with oblations, and it roared. (84.19)
Exerting great speed and urged on by the goad,
he swiftly seized Hiraṇyākṣa’s chariot by its pole.
Seizing him and lifting him up, that best of elephants hurled him away,
like the white-eared Meru mountain with its clouds being tossed aloft.
Having traveled for a moment with great speed, that excellent chariot shone like the sun,
together with its chariot, when it was formerly struck by Svarbhānu.
O best of sages, while that chariot of Hiraṇyākṣa was thus firmly established upon the ground, the elephant quickly approached, desiring to seize it.
With his trunk extended and his eyes, ears, and tail stiffened,
the elephant charged with speed like Garuḍa toward a serpent.
Beholding him rushing forward with such speed, that best of asuras then bore him in the sky like Garuḍa bearing a serpent.
The elephant likewise followed that revolving circle;
with his gaze, ears, and tail fixed, and his trunk extended, he moved about.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from both armies, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! likewise; yet once more, the hosts of gods and daityas became as if mute.
"Excellent, O Daitya! and "O Hiraṇyākṣa!"—thus did others cry out as that lord of the hosts of gods shone forth, whirling about while mounted upon the shoulder of his elephant.
Like a buffalo standing at the forefront upon Śailendra, the lord of mountains,
the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, the king of the Daityas, wheeled around three times.
Having warded off the elephant as if it were swift, the immensely powerful lord of the Daityas stood upon his chariot,
firmly drawing his bow while engaged in combat.
He surrounded the king of the gods on all sides with sharp arrows;
O Vyāsa, he was then struck by those arrows in his vital organs and joints.
With his vajra, he shattered his armor into a hundred pieces and cut through all the harnesses of the horses as well. (84.32)
The valiant Śakra, as if laughing, cut into many pieces the reins held in the charioteer's hand and the golden whip.
Then her horses, their traces severed, set out at will;
Hiraṇyākṣa also, having leaped down, struck them with his mace.
With his sword, that great asura struck both the elephant and the lord of the gods;
by that blow, the elephant abandoned that best of chariots.
O Vyāsa, discharging excrement and urine, the powerful one then fled,
trampling, roaring, and whirling about that best of gods.
Even when struck by the sword, the immensely powerful king of the gods felt no pain in the battle, nor did he suffer any distress.

Unable to endure being struck in battle by that lord of the Dānavas, a mighty elephant of great strength whose ichor flowed with a fragrant scent, he was driven away by Hiraṇyanetra as the latter crushed him.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Yuddha-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 84.84 ||
The eighty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Vipracitti, possessing great illusory power, [assailed] Vāyu with many swift arrows.
The son of Danu covered him, just as a rain-giver covers the earth with a downpour of water.
Then, O Vyāsa, with his bow drawn into a circle, he discharged sharp-pointed arrows like the ocean sending forth swarms of locusts. (85.2)
Just as rain showers come from clouds and the like, just as moonlight comes from the moon, just as rays come from the sun, and just as snow comes from the snowy mountain.
Thus, from his bow drawn into a circle, those multitudes of arrows shot forth from Vipracitti.
As those arrows were falling, covering the sun,
the powerful Lord Anila swiftly struck them down upon the asuras.
By those arrows, many of that Daitya's Dānavas were slain;
mangled and groaning, they lay upon the earth like men dwelling in hell.
Seeing them thus slain, the great asura Vipracitti leaped down from his chariot and fought Vāyu with his bare arms.
As he remained intent on battle, Vāyu’s strength increased;
and the gods thought that the son of Danu had been subdued. || 85.8 ||
Then, springing up with great speed,
the immensely powerful Hiraṇyākṣa struck Pavana firmly on the cheek with his mace.
By that excellent blow, he struck Hiraṇyākṣa; from that very moment, the Dānava was no longer at all [able to stand].
Having abandoned them, the mighty one quickly departed for another land;
and so too did Aṃśa and Saṃvara, O best of sages. (85.11)
A terrible battle ensued, increasing the joy of the spectators;
then the mighty Aṃśa swiftly rushed toward Saṃvara. || 85.12 ||
Display your skill! He properly severed the golden banner, split the bow into five pieces, and sent the horses to the abode of Yama.
Then he struck the head from the body of that charioteer and let it fall to the ground;
furthermore, he pierced him with sixty-four arrows.
That Dānava, having swiftly entered into a terrible and dark illusion (māyā),
[assailed him] with boulders, thunderbolts, maces, and even iron clubs.
O Vyāsa, on the field of battle, he struck down the god Aṃśa along with his chariot using spears, swords, slings, and iron clubs.
Beholding that great terror being unleashed on all sides,
the bewildered Aṃśa abandoned the battle and fled elsewhere out of fear.
Bhaga, having summoned his strength, spoke to that Daitya while standing in a chariot rumbling like a cloud, saying, "Stay! Stay! and pierced him with a feathered shaft.
Having seized the arrow, Bala, that great chariot-warrior among the Asuras,
swiftly struck Bhaga on the palm of his hand, pierced him through, and let out a roar.
Then, having approached him, as if laughing by means of his illusory power,
he struck him on the chest with his foot and returned once more to his own chariot.
Seeing his agility, heroism, lack of confusion, and prowess, all the gods and asuras honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent! (85.21).
Then Bhaga, overcome with shame, was struck by him with his foot;
likewise, he struck his horses, chariot, and charioteer with his mace.
Having then reduced them to nothing but their names, he roared like a cloud;
meanwhile, Bala abandoned his chariot, which had been shattered along with its horses.
Standing on the ground, the powerful one severed Bhaga’s divine bow and then struck him in the forehead with a sharp arrow.
Furthermore, O Vyāsa, he pierced his two hands with seven arrows;
and as he was grasping his bow, Bala cut it at the back.
Again and yet again, Bhaga then seized another mace,
that Kālamūla, which was destructive of all things and possessed the brilliance of fire.
Having said, "You are slain," he hurled that club which destroys strength.
As that mace came flying toward him, Bala, the preeminent among the Dānavas— || 85.27 ||
Nandin checked him with arrows, as one might ward off one's own death;
then, perceiving his club to have been repelled, that Asura once again—
With the tip of his bow, the powerful one struck him on the head;
then, seizing the chariot along with the charioteer, he held them fast to the pole.
Like Vāyu casting a mountain into the ocean, the god Pūṣan struck Virocana with many swift-flying arrows. (85.30)
Enraged in the battle, he pierced him,
and he in turn pierced him back with seven sharpened arrows, shafts capable of piercing the vital organs.
Then the powerful Pūṣan, having drawn his great bow, became enraged.
Aiming at his enemy, he released that terrible life-ending weapon, which possessed the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon, and said, "You are slain! (85.33)

And that great lord of the asuras, having leaped down and beheld him who shone like the sun,
considering him irresistible, abandoned his own chariot and, entering the sky, remained there.
Having reduced that chariot— drawn by horses, belonging to a great warrior, capable of going everywhere, and equipped with the finest weapons—
to ashes as if by fire, he quickly ascended to the divine sky, his form becoming invisible.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter in the Yuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 85.85 ||
The eighty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Dānava Virocana, whose chariot had been burnt, stood in the sky.
Quickly drawing his sword, he [discharged] sharpened arrows at Pūṣan.
The valiant one cut down all those [arrows] as they fell, and likewise struck him again on the head with his sword. (86.2)
By that excellent blow, his head streaming with blood, he quickly fell onto the seat of the chariot like a banner whose festival has ended. (86.3)
Having quickly seized him as he fell, that mighty lord of the Daityas roared like a cloud and hurled the king of the gods away.
Mitra pierced Bali in the region of the collarbone with three arrows;
Bali, with a single broad-headed shaft, severed his bow.
Then he struck him again in the heart with another [arrow];
stunned and nearly dead, he sank down upon the floor of the chariot.
O Vyāsa, the charioteer then drove away that dejected man who had approached him out of fear of death; thereupon, the Daityas raised a great cry.
Varuṇa pierced Bāṇa with a hundred arrows;
then the powerful Bāṇa [pierced him] with five hundred bows.
Drawing them back simultaneously, the enraged one discharged as many arrows;
then Varuṇa, being light-handed, [intercepted] those very arrows as they were falling upon him.
Having divided each [arrow] into five parts, he pierced Bāṇa with five;
then the powerful Varuṇa, laughing, [seized] all of his bows.
He cut [the bow] with sharp arrows, and that was like a marvel;
then the Daitya, his bow being severed, hurled a mace at him. 86.11.
Seeing that mace shattered, the powerful hero again created five more;
yet, being then intent upon one, he did not even notice those other maces.
And all those [arrows], without being wounded, fell upon him;
one, having crushed his crown, fell down upon the surface of the earth.
One cast her terrible bow from her hand,
while another hurled a firm, celestial standard onto the surface of the earth.
Then one [goddess], having struck the chariot, swallowed the dust;
others [struck] his chest, thighs, belly, and waist with those maces.
Falling with great ferocity and causing intense pain, they inspired great terror;
thus was he deprived of his chariot by that wise man with great difficulty. (86.16)
Varuṇa, having released him, went to another battlefield;
Yama, having encountered Andhaka, urged him on, saying, "Stay! Stay! (86.17).
Then he hurled a staff at his chariot from that position;
having shattered his chariot into hundreds of thousands of pieces, [it struck him]. || 86.18 ||
Having returned once more to the hand of Yama, he stood there just as before;
the mighty Andhaka also, abandoning his chariot, stood with mace in hand.
He rushed toward Yama, emitting fire as if out of rage;
as he was charging with such speed, Yama himself, the King of the Ancestors, [confronted him]. (86.20)
With his staff alone, he reduced the fierce mace to ashes;
then Yama, laughing, spoke forcefully to him.
That abode which once belonged to you has been destroyed by me;
now, this very day, I shall lead even you back to your own home.

"For I am the Lord, the cause of death for the entire world. Having encountered enmity with me, where will you find release for your life at the end? Today I shall slay you; let the world be made secure. (86.23)
"Or else, O Andhaka, having first gone to my city which is bound [in darkness],
you shall see all these enemies of the gods right there before you."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, as Yama was speaking thus in battle, the fearless Dānava Andhaka,
his eyes blazing with fire from rage, spoke to that enraged Yama.
"I am Andhaka, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of the gods;
endowed with the power of great yoga, I am no ordinary Dānava."
Having cut portions of flesh from his limbs and other parts, each weighing a karṣa,
he offered them as oblations into the fire for eight hundred and five years.
Brahmā, being pleased, granted him eternal and auspicious immortality;
I am that very one, known by the name Mahāsattva, the destroyer of death—of this there is no doubt. (86.28)
You have not brought about my death, like a hare for a lion in the forest;
rather, I shall be the cause of your death—of this there is no doubt. (86.29)
"Today, by slaying you, a wicked soul who strikes fear into all the worlds, I shall bring about the welfare of the three realms; such is my resolve. (86.30)
"You have always stood in enmity toward the gods and must be slain by them;
yet, once you are killed, you will become dear to them today. (86.31)
For never before have you taken the lives of any being, whether small or great; therefore, you are always free from fear.
Terrified by fear of you, the gods are incapable of slaying you;
therefore, they smear themselves with nectar and other substances and always worship you. (86.33)
If you, the cruel one, are slain today, they will undoubtedly find joy from the gods, free from all dualities; they will not experience such pleasure even if they were to obtain immortality.
Today, at the end of my life, I shall utterly destroy my pride, my arrogance, and even the greatness of my yoga, along with my very vital breaths.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus threatened by the lord of the Asuras, the son of the Sun struck that tiger among Asuras on the head with his staff.
And Kāla struck him in the heart with his very hand,
while Mṛtyu swiftly struck him on the head with a thunderbolt.
And Kṛtānta cast a terrible noose around his neck and struck him on the cheek with a club as if it were an iron bar. (86.38)
Struck by those unerring weapons and missiles, the Dānava Andhaka became as distressed as if he were being pelted by a shower of flowers.
Neither nooses, nor the staff, nor even the iron bar bind him;
furthermore, other intense sufferings do not lead to his distress.
Then a great shout was raised by all the Dānavas in every direction;
musical instruments were sounded, and Andhaka rejoiced exceedingly.
O Vyāsa, impelled by his own intoxication and prowess at their sound of satisfaction,
he roared like a cloud and rushed toward Yama himself.
Having gone there with great speed, although being struck by Yama’s servants,
he of mighty velocity struck Yama on the chest with his fist.
And again he struck the buffalo on its head with his foot;
both of them, being overwhelmed, wandered there for a short distance.
Then, O best of sages, having abandoned Andhaka, they both departed quickly;
Jayanta, reaching Celvala, pierced him with ten arrows.
Elvala quickly cut down his banner adorned with jewels,
as well as the harnesses of the horses and his golden whip.
Without their traces, his horses, becoming agitated, abandoned the chariot;
neighing loudly as they fled, he became carless.
Abandoning his chariot and standing upon the ground, the powerful son of Śakra struck down Ilvala’s horses, charioteer, and banner.
Then, both having been deprived of their chariots and each desiring victory over the other,
they pierced one another with sharp arrows from their bows.
Warding off each other's arrows and neutralizing weapon with weapon, the two roared like two oceans.
Then the glorious son of Śakra, having found an opening,
cut his bow with a broad-headed arrow and roared again and again.
That Daitya, his bow shattered, whirled a sword with the brilliance of blazing fire and hurled it; but he [Rāma] then cut that one down as well.
Having seized another's fallen mace, adorned with gold,
he whirled it and hurled it, then fled away with great speed.
Just as the son of Diti shattered that terrible mace with his straight-jointed arrows,
he likewise cut through his [the opponent's] bow.
Then, just as the son of Aditi seized his sword,
the Daitya struck him in the chest with his left foot.
The mighty Jayanta seized that very foot of his,
and whirling him around, he roared like a thundercloud.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of the asuras:
"Go! Save the lord of the Daityas, Ilvala, quickly! (86.57)
The gods uttered lion-roars and the sounds of conchs were abundant;
musical instruments were played, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! arose.
Then the powerful Jayanta, roaring like the clouds at the end of an eon, whirled the lord of the Daityas around as if he were a wheel.
Then Hiraṇyākṣa himself, as well as Andhaka, Bali,
Bāṇa, Vipracitti, Śambara, and Virocana— || 86.60 ||
And those Daityas— the Kālakeyas, the Paulomas, the sons of Siṃhikā,
and the Nivātakavacas— surrounded him on all sides.
He was struck violently by them with those arrows, maces, iron clubs, long spears,
and many other various weapons.
Being struck by him, that god Jayanta, the son of Śakra,
cast him onto the path of Hiraṇyākṣa and fled toward where the deities were.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the Battle [section] of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The eighty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Maya, overwhelmed by rage, assailed the divine Moon.
Roaring like one who is joyful, he [assailed him] with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
As he discharged arrows here and there, Candra, as if laughing,
split each one into seven pieces and pierced Maya with five [arrows].
Then he pierced him in the forehead with a spotted arrow;
and the god laughed again, putting shame upon him.
As he was laughing, that man, greatly distressed, quickly pierced him deeply in the forehead with a heron-feathered arrow,
just as an obstacle strikes one who is firm in his vows.
Then, making a great noise, the god cut down his banner for his sake and,
with swords, sent his wheel-protectors to the abode of Yama.
Seeing that restlessness of his, Maya, the best of the Dānavas,
then resorted to divine illusion and became Rāhu.
Having become Rāhu, that lord of the Daityas rushed toward the Lord of the Gods, who bears the mark of the hare,
just as Rāhu once did with his chariot that roared like a cloud.
Then the god, who is born of the nectar of immortality, having recognized that illusion,
pierced him— who stood in the sky as if at a non-junction— with three arrows.
That great asura Daitya, possessed of great illusion, warding off those arrows by means of his own magic power, rushed toward the cool-rayed moon.
Then the Daitya, seizing his divine chariot of great splendor, which was drawn by Nāgas,
struck it against the pole and let out a roar.
Having approached Rāhu, the eclipser of the moon,
Ahirbudhnya pierced him with five arrows and struck down his banner.
Leaping from his chariot,
the imperishable one struck him with a mace of terrifying form, completely crushing his bow, his standard, and his horses.
Greatly exerting himself, he seized the blazing thunderbolt with its hundred bells, like the daughter-in-law of Death, as Antaka seizes the noose of Death.
Whirling that fierce weapon, which resembled the staff of Yama,
he forcefully hurled it toward Rāhu, just as the king of clouds hurls lightning.
Blazing like a great meteor and as radiant as a thunderbolt from the clouds,
it fell upon Rāhu’s head like a thunderbolt upon a mountain peak.
Then, by that blow, he indeed felt no pain;
laughing heartily, the exceedingly powerful Rāhu exerted great speed.
Seeing him rushing toward Ahibudhnya like the king of birds against the enraged serpents, the Blessed One, the best of gods, [beheld him].
He went along his own path, leaving it like a serpent;
and the hero Śataketu followed him in a chariot that rumbled like a cloud.
Enraged, he rushed forward in battle and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
As he charged, the wearer of the skull-crown pierced his heart with heron-feathered arrows.
The thunderbolt hurled [at him] split him like a towering mountain peak;
with his heart thus pierced by that Rudra, the best of the grahas [fell]. (87.20)
Confused, he fell upon his own chariot like the lofty banner of Indra;
then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the Daityas, and they cried out, "Seize him! Seize him!"
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods cried out like thunderclouds;
then Andhaka, Hiraṇyākṣa, Vipracitti, and Virocana [spoke].
Śambara, Celvala, Bāṇa, and also Bali;
the Kālakeyas together with the Paulomas, and those who are the Nivātakavacas.
And many other Daityas surrounded that Rudra with arrows, maces, clubs, *prāśas*, and *tomaras*.
They obstructed that god, threatening him again and again. Being struck by those many [demons], O best of sages, that god departed with speed from the vicinity of the enemies of the gods. (87.25)
Ajaikapād challenged the lord of the Daityas, Kālanemi, who was armed with a mace and irresistible with his club,
just as Viṣṇu once challenged the powerful Madhu.
Those two of great strength, skilled in combat and with maces in hand, moved about like two planets intent on each other's conquest, tracing various circular maneuvers.
But Kālanemi, filled with rage, [hurled] a mace adorned with gold,
which had a hundred bells and a loud laugh-like sound, and was as wondrous as the tongue of Death.
Having whirled him around repeatedly like a bellowing bull,
the Daitya released [the mountain] toward Rudra, just as Skanda hurls his spear at a mountain.
Like a thunderbolt released by Śakra falling upon a mountain,
or like a mighty flash of lightning, that Rudra of terrible prowess [advanced].
Śveta, the best among strikers, swiftly deceived Rudra—the foremost of those who strike—as he cried out, "Stay! Stay!", as if he were Death itself approaching. (87.31)
Having whirled his terrible mace, he brought it down upon the Daitya;
by that blazing mace of fearsome form, the Daitya was struck.
Struck on the head, he saw all the directions as yellow;
then the Daitya, once again whirling his mace with skill, [struck him]. (87.33)
Having displayed various circular maneuvers, the one of great strength struck Ajaikapāda on the shoulder with his mace.
And he too, struck by him like a mountain by a thunderbolt, entered the earth, afflicted with grief; it was as if a marvel had occurred.
And rising up with speed, the mighty Rudra, filled with rage,
moved in a circular path, circling to the left of the Daitya while keeping him to his right.
Having whirled his mace once more, he brought it down upon the Daitya;
that mighty Daitya, having been struck by that blow, spun around three times.
Having steadied himself, he struck Rudra again in the belly with his mace;
impelled by that mace, he was like a tree shaken by the wind.
He fell to the ground with force, like the mountain Śataśṛṅga in ancient times;
then, approaching him as he lay fallen, [the king] took the one of noble vows by the foot.
Having whirled it around, he hurled it; yet that [demon], being subject to death, remained standing.
Rudra, the best among strikers, [then unleashed] the fierce fever of the golden sound.
He struck him simultaneously on both breasts with ten sharp, broad-headed arrows;
then, with a single shaft, he cut his radiant bow made of gold,
and pierced him again in many places with feathered arrows.
— Rudra, too, brandishing his staff which accomplishes all purposes, swiftly hurled it toward Kārtasvana’s chariot. (87.42)
Like a cloud striking a mountain with rain, he struck him— who resembled the fire at the end of an eon and possessed the brilliance of a hundred suns and fire— with a multitude of arrows.
Being struck by them, Daṇḍa blazed up even more intensely like a fire kindled by oblations,
and he rushed forward with great speed.
Knowing that his staff was irresistible, the powerful Kārtasvana abandoned his chariot and, with great speed, rose into the sky.
And the staff, having approached the chariot along with the horse, the driver, the banner, and the flag-staff, reduced them all to ashes and departed once more. (87.46)
As long as the punishment had not yet fallen upon him, the powerful Kārttikeya pursued Rudra in his chariot and assailed him with arrows.
Having cut down his banner and bow, as well as the harnesses of his horses,
he deprived Jvara of his chariot and struck him on the head with a sword.
His soul overwhelmed by the fear of the sword, that Rudra abandoned the assembly of his enemies and quickly fled elsewhere on foot, O best of sages. (87.49)
With his mind perverted by the blow of the sword, though he possessed the luster of red sandalwood unguent,
he abandoned that enemy of supreme prowess and fled hither and thither toward the divine army.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the Yuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The eighty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Aryaman [struck] Prahlāda, the bull among the Daityas, with many arrows.
He struck the terrible chariot and shattered its banner.
The heroic Prahlāda, too, having abandoned his excellent chariot, fled like Rāhu at the appointed time flees from the sun that dispels the darkness. 88.2.
And as his enemy rushed forward with speed, bewildered, Aryaman struck him with many arrows, just as a cloud strikes a mountain with rain.
Without even counting the arrows, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu rushed forward with speed,
impelled by anger, pride, and arrogance.
Seizing the pole of his gold-adorned chariot along with the charioteer,
he then struck it with his bow and roared out of joy.
Anuhrāda, having reached Dhara, was pierced by him in the middle of the chest;
drawing his sword with speed, he approached Dhara’s chariot. (88.6)
Having cut down his banner, his horses, his charioteer, and even his bow,
as well as the pole upon his shoulder, he returned once more to his own chariot.
By that deed, Dharā was severely afflicted by the Daitya;
and in this manner, other mighty gods were likewise [afflicted] by other lords of the Daityas.
Some were conquered, some were threatened, and others stood ready for battle once more;
then a tumultuous conflict broke out between the gods and the dānavas.
The battle between those desiring to conquer one another brought fear even to the timid;
then there arose kettledrums, conchs, and many large drums and cymbals.
O Vyāsa, thousands of jharjharyas, pepukas, ḍiḍṇimas, and goviṣāṇakas were sounded by both sides in the army.
Then [the river] flowed with currents of blood, with banners and flags for its trees,
abounding in elephants and horses for its crocodiles, and having excellent chariots for its turtles.
Abounding in hair-weeds, with bowstrings for its cords, with hissing weapons for its frogs, and foam-like silk garments and parasols; (88.13)
The excellent *uṣṇīṣa* was a swan, and the stones were her hands, feet, and head;
the necklaces and armlets were the sands, and the crown was a full-blown lotus. 88.14.
A terrible river, consisting of a mire of fat, blood, and phlegm, which destroys life and vitality, began to flow, carrying away elephants, horses, and chariots.
In that river, the Rākṣasas bathe, drink, and take their pleasure;
they also dance, inspiring fear in those who are not brave. (88.16)
Vultures, jackals, dogs, cats,
and crows took their delight, devouring eyes, hands, feet, and entrails.
"This is my elephant's foot; this is my bandage of fat;
this is my bright trunk; and this is my arm, which sheds blood. (88.18)
"This is mine, not yours; take it and look!"—thus did those cruel flesh-eaters engage in a quarrel there.
And other great chariot-warriors there, having abandoned their slain bodies,
departed for the assembly hall of Brahmā in celestial chariots crowded with women.
Others, performers of evil deeds, being struck by those blinded by wrath,
fall into a terrible hell, crying out again and again.
Some, uttering piteous cries—afflicted by arrows—men die in battle by the hundreds and even by the thousands. (88.22)
Some were chewing on grass, while others cried out, "O brother! O son! Wailing in terror, the people gave up their lives with great difficulty. (88.23)
Some great chariot-warriors among the gods and asuras, their lips bitten in rage,
fell upon the earth like trees, their vital organs pierced by arrows.
Inauspicious jackals howled, and the Rākṣasas let out loud bursts of laughter;
likewise, men, elephants, and horses uttered cries of distress.
There were lion-roars from the heroes, the loud sounds of arms being brandished,
the twanging of bowstrings being drawn, and likewise the sounds of musical instruments.
Then Indra, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Yama, the powerful Kāla,
Varuṇa, the Maruts, and all the Viśvedevas likewise [arrived].
Mitra, Jayanta, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Aryaman, as well as Rudra who bears the skull and the Vasus of great strength. || 88.28 ||
Nāsatya, Dasra, and the Pṛśnis—these and other preeminent gods among the deities, all possessed of mighty arms. (88.29)
The powerful ones displayed their force against the army of the Dānavas,
roaring like oceans or like fires at the end of an eon.
Like tempests out of season, like great mountains immovable,
like bulls bellowing, and like elephants trumpeting in rut.
Seizing like crocodiles and tearing like sea-monsters,
raining down like clouds and roaring like lions,
they all with sheer force checked the army of the Dānavas.
That army of the Danus and Dānavas, its momentum shattered by Devavega and though exerting itself with effort,
became supportless and utterly overwhelmed, like a blade of grass caught in the mouth of a fire.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Yuddha [section] of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 88.88 ||
The eighty-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Of those who were driven by that force, broken, and suffering once again—
For the sake of protection, Hiraṇyākṣa, his eyes blazing intensely, seized his foot.
And Andhaka, the great illusionist, and his brothers who were equal to him, [were there],
along with a hundred thousand chariots of all those who did not flee.
And Prahlāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, together with his brother;
and Vipracitti, together with his brother and those sons of Siṃhika.
Crying out, "Seize! Seize!", they then rushed against the gods;
a most terrible battle then ensued between them.
Like a thunderbolt against crocodiles, or like an elephant in the forest against other elephants,
Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Pūṣan held back Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having come together, they struck all their vital points with sharp arrows;
[they also struck] the variegated bows of those celestial beings as they discharged them.
The radiant lord of the Daityas, by the power of his illusion, paralyzed them;
they were then rendered motionless by the Daitya through his magic.
They did not bow as they had before, and for that reason they became agitated;
that Daitya of great illusion, too, having roared with a sound like a thundercloud, [continued].
He bound their limbs on all sides with the power of his illusory weapon;
and seeing those mighty ones thus bound and rendered incapable of action, [he spoke].
The charioteers quickly bore them away from the field of battle by means of their vehicles.
Then Kāla, Yama, Dhaneśa, and Mitra likewise [departed].
Varuṇa, all the Vasus, and the two mighty Aśvins, with weapons grasped and filled with rage, stood there crying out, "Stay! Stay! || 89.11 ||
They rushed with speed toward the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa;
as they were charging in battle, that Daitya was overcome with rage.
In the battle, he pierced the armor of all of them with his sharp arrows;
with their armor shattered, they all had faces blazing with rage.
Then they discharged their foremost weapons, which were indeed irresistible;
Yama hurled his staff at him, and likewise did Kāla.
Dhaneśa hurled his terrible thunderbolt, Varuṇa his noose,
Bhaga his fearsome mace, and the other gods likewise their various weapons.
That Daitya, undaunted in spirit, even as he laughed, checked them with arrows that pierce the vital organs,
just as Bhava [Śiva] checked the hand of Śakra.
Then, filled with joy, the great chariot-warriors of the Dānavas uttered cries of "Well done!
and, having honored the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, they celebrated him together.
Others said: "This is no marvel for the son of Diti in battle, who was begotten by Kaśyapa, nor for our lord, the king. (89.18)
Others, filled with joy, let out lion-like roars and loud shouts of "Bāhu," and likewise played all kinds of musical instruments.
Thus, in that great battle, many words of praise were heard from the Dānavas who were greatly rejoicing, O son of Parāśara.
Perceiving their great joy and that defeat of the gods at that time,
Vāyu, who moves through all living beings, rushed toward the asuras.
With that chariot, which was a thousand nalvas in measure,
adorned with banners on all sides and garlanded with hundreds of flags, he, the breaker of obstacles, [proceeded].
Restrained with effort by the charioteers despite its speed, it was suddenly seen filling all the quarters of space with a roar. (89.23)
Then that imperishable one, having struck the king of the Daityas with five sharp arrows,
quickly cast him away from that place for a distance of a yojana.
Then, having pierced Andhaka with sixty arrows, Vipracitti with seven,
and Maya with fifty, he struck each of them again with seven more.
At that very moment, he pierced all the Daityas and Dānavas,
as well as the sons of Puloman and the Nivātakavacas.
Pierced by him with many arrows, those foremost of asuras were scattered in all directions and remained at a distance of a yojana apart.
Whatever maces, clubs, and sharp-edged spears they discharged,
the blessed Vāyu caused them all to fall upon the Dānavas.
Struck and being struck severely by the weapons released by themselves,
they fled in every direction, uttering cries of distress.
That wind of great velocity also shattered the best of chariots,
and furthermore, it filled their eyes with a shower of dust.
Then, terrified by fear, they did not discharge their arrows;
likewise, they cast aside their other weapons and stood huddled together in a mass.
Having observed that deed of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa,
the son of Diti, spoke to all the Dānavas in reproach.
"Shame on all your strength, O Daityas! Shame on your pride! Shame on your prowess!
Abandoning the battle, go away unperturbed and attend to the duties of women! (89.33)
"You fools, who stood in the midst of battle while life still remained, have been shattered by a single gust of wind; fie upon that counsel you previously gave! (89.34)
Or rather, as for what I said—that you are children exhausted by pleasure—that is not so; there is no doubt that you have acted like children indeed. (89.35)
"All of you remain like children, guarding your own lives;
behold, I alone shall conquer this wind. (89.36)
Then that powerful and imperishable son of Diti, having become a mountain,
completely warded off that wind-force from all sides.
Having realized that Anila had been warded off by Parvata, Andhaka leaped forward and bound him with the noose of his arms. (89.38)
Then that powerful Vāyu, bound by the noose of his arms,
quickly seized Andhaka and leapt up into the sky.
As soon as he had risen up, seizing the Dānava Andhaka,
Rāhu swiftly brought down a most terrible mace upon his head;
and the mighty Vipracitti likewise rushed at him and seized him by the feet.
Like a great crocodile seizing fish in the vast ocean, he was seized; by that powerful blow, he became overwhelmed and fell within the range of living beings. (89.41)
With his hair clinging to his shoulder, he was whirled around by Vipracitti;
as he was being spun about, he appeared with his necklaces, garlands, and garments slipping off.
O best of sages, seeing it whirling like a blazing brand in the night, the gods together with Indra were once again struck with wonder. (89.43)
Those of great speed made a rush, crying out, "Seize him! Seize him!
But the Daitya Vipracitti [beheld] them, enraged and with weapons raised.
Beholding many [enemies] in the battle, the leader of the Dānava hosts roared like a cloud,
repeatedly emitting a terrifying sound like the wind.
He hurled his thunderbolt at Śakra as if toward a mountain;
and he too, having been struck by it, regained consciousness, O one of great strength.
Having manifested his power, he stood before the Lord of the Gods with palms joined in reverence;
then Vāyu and all the gods, together with their followers, did likewise.
Grasping their excellent weapons, they rushed against the lords of the Daityas;
a most terrible battle then ensued between them.
Like proud lions with śarabhas in a desolate place,
some there were struck down by a powerful blow and rendered unconscious.
Saying "Excellent! Excellent!", other mighty lords of the Danavas and Daityas, filled with joy, cast off their lives by stretching them upward. (89.50)
Protecting like a good son a hero struck down by an enemy, some of these noble sons of gods and dānavas, even after slaying very many [foes], [remained]. 89.51.
Some of the exceedingly powerful gods and daityas, though unscarred by sharp weapons, reproached themselves; others, having approached unarmed, [did the same]. (89.52)
Desiring a righteous battle,
many lords of the Daityas there, possessing terrible prowess, cast aside their weapons and fought without using them.
And those gods who are indeed not struck never strike [others] at any time; all the foot-soldiers there fight with foot-soldiers. (89.54)
The battle proceeded with horsemen against horsemen, chariot-warriors against chariot-warriors, and likewise elephant-riders against elephant-riders.
Thus, indeed, that battle between those gods and the Dānavas continued for eight hundred years, being most terrifying.
Then the Daitya Mahāmāya, mounted upon an elephant with the luster of a rain cloud,
bore a massive iron spear that possessed the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon.
Vidruta Virocana, who had the luster of a cuckoo, collyrium, or a cloud,
then rushed toward the gods as if they were rising up from their left side.
On an elephant with temporal secretions flowing, its face resounding with a majestic roar, he charged toward the Lord of the Gods and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (89.59).
Then, as he was still falling, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana (Indra) drove a terrible arrow into the region of his collarbone, and he cried out.
Having endured that blow, that Daitya of terrible prowess then pierced his [the opponent's] uplifted hand with a lance.
Then, from his hand pierced by the lance, that divine bow—adorned with gold and possessing a brilliance equal to a great thunderbolt—fell down. (89.62)
Then, while he was thus distracted, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas quickly pierced his elephant in the region of the frontal globes with a lance.
He was shattered by that Daitya in the forest like an elephant in rut without a goad,
for he could not restrain his own strength as it was unchecked.
Thus being struck by the Daityas and Dānavas, those Ādityas,
afflicted by fear, fled in all directions in every way. (89.65)
Then conchs and kettledrums, as well as various other musical instruments, were sounded;
and those esteemed by the Daityas and Dānavas let out lion-like roars.
That great army, protected by the gods, though its interior was cut, pierced, and torn apart by the elephant and further churned by the Daityas,
shone like the ocean lashed by Mount Mandara during its churning.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter in the Yuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 89.89 ||
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld that divine army [attacked] by the leaders of the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas...
O Vyāsa, he was being struck violently, like deer by hunters in the forest.
The enemy of darkness, possessed of great splendor, Soma, the best among strikers;
he of sharp form with most cooling rays, having the wind himself as his charioteer.
Both of them were properly clad in armor, both held their bows,
and both had their finger-guards made of iguana skin fastened on, as well as their quivers secured.
Equipped with swords and bells, and adorned with banners like two elephants,
both those heroes of great prowess stood ready to fight the Daityas.
Soma, however, pierced the heart of the Daitya, the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, with ten sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs.
With his heart pierced by Soma and violently shaken,
O Vyāsa, that Daitya fell into a state of delusion, like Mount Krauñca struck by a thunderbolt.
Having observed him thus, the charioteer drove away the chariot together with the Asura,
carrying off the master of great illusions like treasures being carried off from the Lord of Wealth.
Then there arose a cry of "Alas! from the Daityas, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! from the deities;
and cries of "Seize him! Seize him! from the Daityas, and "Do not seize him! from the deities.
Then kettledrums, conchs, cymbals, and cow-horns were sounded by the gods, indeed, to arouse joy and passion.
Then Andhaka, Tāra, Tāraka, Namuci, as well as Vipracitti, Śambara, and the Dānava Mahāmāya [all came forth]. (90.10)
Dhundhu, Kārtasvana, and the mighty Rāhu;
Śataketu, Śatāvarta, Puloman, and likewise Vilvaka. || 90.11 ||
Vātāpi, Kālanemi, Śatāvarta, Śatodara,
Mahāpārśva, Udara, Musuṇḍa, and Suṇḍa.
Durloma, Vakrabandha, Viroma, Rodha,
Mārīca, Subāhu, and Śvetakuṇḍali.
Vṛṣaparvan, Atikāya, Śarabha, and Siṃha,
as well as Narāntaka, Devahana, and he who is Yajñahana.
The two Daityas Sunda and Nisunda, as well as Śakratāpana,
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala.
Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, and the exceedingly powerful Vātāśva;
then Maya, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Prabhākara. || 90.16 ||
Dundubhi and Mahiṣa, Ariṣṭa and Riṣṭa, Keśin and Dhenuka, as well as Ajaka and Vyaṃsa. || 90.17 ||
Likewise, there were Gaganamūrdhan and the Dānava Asiloman;
also Sūcīloman, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, and Paratāpana.
Hastin, Duryodhana, Vipāka, Pāka, Bala, Mura, Naraka, as well as Mūka and Indradamana—these too [were slain]. (90.19)
Aśvagrīva, Śambara, and likewise another, Kālasaṃvara;
Śālva, Śatabhuja, Drumas, and the Dānava Vyāghra. || 90.20 ||
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, as well as Mahāsaṅgara,
the renowned Chāyāgraha, and the famous Saiṃhikeyas.
And all those famous sons of Bali, the Hālāhalas,
as well as all the sons of Maya and the Nivātakavacas.
The Paulomas, the Kālakeyas, and those who are the sons of Vipracitti—
these and many other Daityas and Dānavas highly esteemed [by their kind]— [90.23].
All of them launched their assault against the god who resembles the moon, like buffaloes attacking elephants or as lions do against a śarabha. || 90.24 ||

Just as obstacles [hinder] one who is striving, just as sensual desires [hinder] one intent on liberation, just as the objects of the senses [hinder] one engaged in yoga, and just as [worldly things] [hinder] one who is suffering; || 90.25 ||
Like serpents toward Garuḍa, or like bees toward a tree,
so did all those Dānavas, grasping their excellent weapons, [attack him].
They fled toward the cool god (the Moon), making sounds like great clouds;
as they were attacking, O Vyāsa, the enemy of darkness (the Sun) seemed to laugh.
He cut down all the uplifted weapons with his arrows in every way;
then that god, filled with wrath, [struck] them all once again.
And with sharp arrows he pierced their hearts and made them cry out;
likewise, the imperishable Lord of the Stars [shone] with cool frost.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he struck all the asuras;
pierced by his arrows and severely tormented by the cold, they were utterly overwhelmed.
The lords of the Daityas remained right there, as if fixed upon a painted canvas;
even the god Candra stood in the battle with his bow drawn into a circle.
Roaring like a cloud, he pierced all the lords of the Daityas—whosoever they might be, whether Dānava or Daitya, O best of sages. (90.32)
Then all those arrows remained fixed upon him;
for whenever the Daitya moved even a single limb, [the shafts would remain there]. (90.33)
With sharp arrows, the god pierced and roared at every Daitya warrior who spoke anything whatsoever in that battle.
Candramas also buried eight arrows in his mouth;
with all their limbs pierced by arrows, they appeared as if fixed upon a variegated cloth.
Just as that divine Lord Candra, the destroyer of the Dānavas,
so too did the blessed Vahni afflict the Dānavas in battle.
That formidable army, consisting of chariots, horses, elephants, and warriors, overwhelmed by falling drops of blood, was sinking like a herd of elephants stuck in the mud. (90.37)
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the section on the battle. || 90.90 ||
The Ninety-First Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
In that army, by means of that Soma of incomparable splendor, [the enemies were struck down].
While he was being struck, that great illusory Asura then regained his composure.
Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, filled with rage, spoke these words to the heroic son of Garuḍa, the charioteer in battle: || 91.2 ||
O Lord of Birds, you feel no shame here in this ocean of battle,
that you are now carrying me away from the fray by means of your chariot.
"What will all the asuras and the exceedingly powerful daityas say?
'Our king, the scorcher of his enemies, has been defeated by his foes in battle'? (91.4)
Seeking his own life, that evil-minded one has abandoned us, the foolish, and departed from the battle to some unknown place; shame on me, a doer of inauspicious deeds! (91.5)
Having become the son of Kaśyapa and the esteemed brother of the Daitya,
that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was endowed with the power of great yoga.
In the presence of all the Daityas and likewise the Dānavas, how was the king, the lord, and the hero conquered by his enemies? (91.7)
Or rather, you are indeed the son of Garuḍa, who belongs to the side of the gods;
you favor that very side and do not protect me. (91.8)
"O lowest of the bird-clans, I am not unable today to sever your head, adorned with its earring, from your body with this sharp sword."
"You were my friend in the past, and like a brother to me when I was a child;
therefore, having protected you, I release you—go, for you are free from fault. (91.10)
Having heard those words of his, the charioteer, the lord of birds,
spoke in gentle tones to the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa.
"Do not be angry, O best of Dānavas; O Daitya, I am not your enemy. I have been brought here quickly from the battlefield solely for the sake of protection. (91.12)
O Lord of the Dānavas, even the charioteers who are learned in the scriptures say that a husband and wife who are devoted to one another are like a chariot and its driver. (91.13)
Just as a charioteer must protect his beloved from the blows of weapons,
so too must he protect the chariot, for it is like a master who brings victory.
"Thinking that you, having been pierced and bound by the enemy in battle, would become incapable [of action], I quickly removed you for this very reason. (91.15)
Having regained your breath and summoned your strength, you shall again don your armor for battle and conquer your enemies in combat; it was only thus that you were carried away.
For those high-souled ones who retreat at the proper time and advance clad in armor at the proper time, victory in battle is not difficult for them to attain, O Daitya.
"And I am not your enemy; truly, I am always a doer of what is beneficial for you.
Do not harbor suspicion, O Lord of Daityas; I swear this by my entire truth. (91.18)
Nor is it unknown to you that an oath was made by me long ago:
"I shall die like a corpse; death does not exist for me. (91.19)
"I am the son of Garuḍa; having abandoned the gods, I have taken refuge with the Asuras out of affection for you alone, O Daitya. Do not harbor any suspicion toward me. (91.20)
This army has been hard-pressed by both the Moon and Fire;
protect us quickly, O mighty-armed one, for you ought not to succumb to grief. (91.21)
"O Great King, resorting either to illusion, or to your bow, or to your strength, slay the enemies; let not the sons of Diti become enraged."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that great asura, having embraced the king of birds,
rushed forward with speed in a chariot that thundered like a cloud.
Then, as he was still falling, both Sūrya and Candramas likewise severed his banner in battle with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, O Vyāsa, having pierced him in the forehead, those two gods, Śaśin and Pāvaka,
let out a loud roar like the clouds at the end of an eon.
Seeing that agility of theirs, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa destroyed that coolness with the foremost of weapons, the Āgneya.
Having burned him with a shower of snow, he then, having once more deluded him by means of his magic power,
quickly assumed the form of Rāhu and rushed at him.
Then, being seized by that Rāhu, the lord of birds abandoned the battle and fled elsewhere; thereupon the Daitya let out a roar.
For when that store of snow had vanished, all those Dānavas recovered their spirits and once again waged war against the hosts of gods;
they roared like clouds with thunderbolts, making the ocean resound.
The great chariot-warriors among the Daityas and Dānavas, those preeminent riders, were taking breath;
desiring battle once more, they were like great tusked elephants dwelling in the forest.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter in the Yuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 91.91 ||
The ninety-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen the Lord of the Constellations, the Blessed One, the Bearer of Oblations (Agni), [spoke].
Having fled out of fear of the Dānavas, he now stands on foot, prepared for battle.
With his arrows, he reduced the Dānava’s chariot—along with its driver, horses, banner, and pennants—to a state of union with ashes. (92.2)
Then, filled with rage, he rendered that divine bow stringless with a smooth-jointed arrow, and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (92.3)
Then Andhaka, Rāhu, Prahlāda, Maya, and other foremost Dānavas surrounded Kuśānu. (92.4)
Then, having leapt down, he burned their bows, chariots,
and variegated banners, and let out a roar.
Assuming a hideous form and making the quarters of the sky resound on all sides, that best of Vasus burned the various armor and heads.
O Vyāsa, as they were crying out "Alas! Alas! there the blessed bearer of oblations shone forth, burning with his tongue as he stood like a blazing fire within the cave.
Scorching those faces of certain Dānavas,
he of great luster was like the enemy of darkness (the sun) scorching full-blown lotuses.
But for some of the lordly elephants, the blessed fire— like a forest conflagration to serpents— consumed their trunks adorned with gold.
The blessed Fire consumed the arrows and the bows, as well as the sword-fittings; he likewise burnt the elephants and horses in their entirety.
Being struck down, those lords of the Daityas, deprived of their weapons and armor,
wandered here and there in great distress.
As those enemies of the gods were burning, set ablaze by fire,
Hiraṇyākṣa himself became King Parjanya.
Then that lord of the Daityas, having become like a cloud, violently extinguished that fire with showers of rain, like the Saṃvartaka cloud.
Beholding the fire-god thus pacified and distressed,
Vipracitti struck him on the forehead with sharp arrows.
Then, as he was crying out even more, Maya, the best of the Dānavas,
that great Asura, drove terrible arrows into his mouth.
O Vyāsa, as his mouth was thus split open, a terrible smoke, resembling collyrium, rose from his body like a gust of wind. (92.16)
By that smoke, O Vyāsa, the sky, the heavens, and the earth were entirely filled with that great mass, so that nothing could be discerned.
By that sound, by the calling out of names, by the proclamation of titles,
and even by the touch of hands, they then led one another to the abode of Yama.
Neither a god was recognized there, nor a Daitya, nor even a Dānava;
not knowing [the truth], they established such a state of affairs there. (92.19)
The Daityas there called the Āṭi bird "Vaka," while the deities called that Vaka "Āṭi"; at that time, I struck down those Daityas who were calling it "Vaka. (92.20)
And as he cried out "Sura!", that [conflict] turned back;
thus did the battle continue for a thousand years.
Indeed, there was great fear among the Daityas in the darkness along with the Suras.
In that darkness, there occurred a battle exceedingly terrifying and most cruel, causing the destruction of the world;
it was a torrential flow of blood from the gods and asuras who, though desiring the welfare of the world, were engaged in its ruin.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 92.92 ||
The Ninety-third Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at that time, that comet of fire arose.
And being struck by the wind, it indeed underwent intense dissolution.
Then the entire sky indeed became completely clear;
all the gods and the Daityas beheld one another.
Then conchs and kettledrums, as well as paṭahas, āḍambaras,
sughoṣakas, ḍiṇḍimas, and all kinds of broken drums [resounded] on every side.
Then, by the hundreds and thousands, they were slain in both armies;
then Śakra, the lord of the gods, Yama, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa— || 93.4 ||
Pūṣan and Bhaga—these two—and Aryaman and Mitra as well;
Jayanta and the Maruts, and all the Rudras and Ādityas. || 93.5 ||
With great speed, those of immense velocity crushed the Dānava army;
there, seizing a powerful bow that shone like gold, [he stood firm].
Yama brought the lords of the Daityas to the abode of Yama with his staff;
he, having pierced the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa with five arrows.
He laughed and roared at each and every one of the horses;
then all those best of Daityas and Dānavas became distressed.
He discharged arrows that resembled venomous serpents and were like misshapen prey;
he, being light-handed, cut each one of them into three pieces in that battle.
And again, as if laughing, he struck him with terrible arrows,
[piercing] Andhaka’s charioteer and his chariot along with the horses.
By the servant, the one of great heroism, Yama was led to his own city;
then Andhaka, mace in hand, roared like a cloud at the end of an eon.
He rushed swiftly toward Yama and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then the Lord of the Gods struck his gold-adorned mace with the thunderbolt.
O Vyāsa, those best of gods, having deprived him of his weapons and his armor, shattered him into a hundred pieces as he fell to the earth. 93.13.
In that battle, they struck him simultaneously with a rain of weapons;
Yama struck him on the head with his staff, and Śakra struck him with his thunderbolt.
Vitta gave him a thunderbolt, Varuṇa likewise a noose,
and other gods also [gave him] their own infallible and supreme weapons.
They rushed forward in great agitation, crying out, "You are slain!
yet at that moment, no pain whatsoever arose within that Daitya.
Then that Daitya, having leapt up and taken his stand behind Puṇḍra,
struck Yama with a blow of his fist and felled him from Puṇḍra onto the ground.
Likewise, seizing Indra’s elephant by the tail once more, the swift one whirled it around and hurled it far away, saying, "You are destroyed! || 93.18 ||
Then the Daitya, frantic with rage, seized the palanquin of Dhaneśa that moved at will and shattered it in many pieces.
Then, in that battle, elephants struck down elephants, foot-soldiers struck down foot-soldiers,
chariots [struck down] chariots, and horses [struck down] horse-riders.
Furthermore, even while being struck in the battle by Mahendra’s elephant,
he then leaped up and cast Śakra down from the elephant's shoulder.
Beholding that deed of the lord of the Dānavas in battle,
all the gods, seeking to save their lives, fled in every direction.
To the east was the Blessed Lord Indra, together with Āditya and the world-protectors;
likewise, to the south were the Rudras, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The Rakshasas and Pisachas fled toward the west along with the Pannagas,
while others likewise took to the north like deer.
When they were broken, the lords of the Daityas, with their weapons raised behind them,
rushed forward roaring and displayed terror to them.
Then, having gone for a moment, they were halted by Hiraṇyākṣa;
turning back, they all stood still, overcome by indignation.
Then Hiraṇyākṣa, skilled in speech, spoke these words as if laughing to those enraged lords of the Daityas and Dānavas.
O Daityas and Dānavas, what is the use today of these weaklings of yours—these wicked souls who are bound, imprisoned, and as good as dead? (93.28)
Those for whom this kingdom has been seized are already as good as dead; of this there is no doubt.
Their life does not exist today. Do not be so foolish and do not delay! (93.29)
Even those who are weak, though enraged and desiring life, [are spared] because they are invulnerable by force; thus they are indeed difficult to conquer, without a doubt.
"Regarding union and liberation, as well as their causes...
[so spoke Uśanas in the assembly]. 93.31.
"That which they call 'kingdom' is indeed the vital breaths of these great-souled ones;
he who would seize their kingdom seizes their very life-breaths. (93.32)
O lords of the Dānavas, today we shall fill the abodes of the gods with those deities who have been deprived of their positions by the darkness of those [enemies]. 93.33.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, those [demons], together with Hiraṇyākṣa, entered Amarāvatī;
they seized the jewels and proclaimed their victory.
There, those Asuras appointed guards for protection, and with their trusted agents,
they reassured both the citizens and the subjects.
With the word "O Master," and likewise with offerings,
excellent gifts, and blessings, they bowed down before Hiraṇyākṣa, the best of the asuras.
Having comforted them and seated himself upon the excellent throne, the lord of the Daityas performed the necessary duties for all and departed for the abode of Varuṇa.
With lion-roars, various musical instruments, leaping, slapping their arms, and shouting,
all those great asuras surrounded the lion among the Dānava kings from every side.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Journey to the Abode of Varuṇa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The ninety-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
[He beheld him] rushing forward with speed like Garuḍa in battle.
Having seen him, those sons of Varuṇa fled together with their father.
And all those Daityas, having reached that abode of Varuṇa,
stood with shoulders squared and directed their efforts toward that city.
The powerful messenger Vātāpin, sent by the king, went and entered that beautiful city, O great Asura. (94.3)
O Vyāsa, highly honored by the citizens, the king— the delighter of the Daityas and Dānavas and the sovereign of the entire world— spoke this to them with great pride.
The glorious and powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Kaśyapa,
having conquered all the gods in battle, constantly issues commands to you.
All of you, listen to my command and indeed carry it out:
bring forth the jewels and abandon the deities.
"Whoever belongs to the side of the gods who dwells here in this city, I grant him safety; let him go to the gods as if he were fearless."
O Vyāsa, Nārada and the other sages, having approached that Daitya, then spoke these words, full of conciliation, to that Asura.
A king is called a Bhoja, a Virāṭ, a Samrāṭ, a Bhūpati, a Kṣatriya, or a Nṛpa; what wise man would not honor him who is praised by these titles? (94.9)
Thus you are a king, a Bhoja, a Virāṭ, and likewise a Samrāṭ; you are a lord of the earth, a Kṣatriya, a Nṛpa, and a Sarvasaha.
The gods, including Indra, who possess great heroism, have been conquered by you.
Who in this world is equal to you, except for the one external Lord Rudra?
"You are the protector of all worlds, as well as their destroyer and creator;
O Great King, what evil-minded person could ever thwart your command?"
"O Lord of Daityas, O Dānava, we all desire a boon;
for you are the granter of boons to all beings, so become the granter of a boon to us. (94.13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, he said, "I am the giver of boons.
Then those who were skilled in speech spoke to the king of the Daityas. (94.14)
The sages said:
"O Daitya, that which has been spoken by you regarding hell, disease, and death—may it not be so; let this boon be granted to us. (94.15)
The Daitya said:
"O best of Brahmins, O you whose wealth is asceticism, my vow was made long ago:
'If I become the king of the world, I shall increase the happiness of the worlds. (94.16)
O best of sages, I shall not act in such a way that I would become one who has made a false promise,
untruthful, and evil-minded.
"Therefore, sirs, ask me for another boon that is very dear;
I shall do all of that accordingly, for I entreat you with my head bowed. (94.18)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having heard those words of his, all those sages once again spoke thus to the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa.
The sages said: "O bull among the Daityas, in ancient times all this was performed by Brahmā for the sake of setting the worldly order in motion, and dharma was likewise established. (94.20)
"Having considered this world, the Dharma has been set in motion;
let there not be that which was non-existent, O Daitya—be a granter of our boon."
That vow would prevail which results in the avoidance of suffering for the worlds;
and because of that, the imperishable work of Brahmā shall not perish.
"O Daitya, as long as you remain the king and the sovereign of the world, in this way you shall today fulfill your debt to Brahmā. (94.23)
Having heard their words and identified them as sages, the king of the Daityas said:
"Those who commit acts of hostility and those who break my commands are bound by the nooses of Śakra."
"For them alone shall there be death and torments in the hells.
Then the king said this, and they too spoke to the lord of men.
Having said to them, "So be it," he ordained their release from torment;
having liberated all those in hell, he entrusted them with the guarding of that place.
Then, O sinless one, having proclaimed his victory before the mighty Vipracitti, the king of the Pitṛs,
and having honored those twice-born brahmins,
the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa departed for the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Then those mighty Dānavas, protected by Andhaka, made that city of the Lord of Wealth resound;
surrounding Hiraṇyanetra, they then advanced like clouds toward a mountain.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Visit to the World of Yama," in the *Hiraṇyākṣa-digvijaya* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
The ninety-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus reached Laṅkā, the auspicious city of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera),...
Armed with armor and weapons, they stood nearby, brandishing their uplifted [weapons].
Seeing the Dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength, standing there, as well as all the inhabitants of Laṅkā and the guardians of the treasures, [they spoke]. (95.2)
The treasures, such as Śaṅkha and Padma, and the sages whose wealth is their asceticism,
having taken up the guest-offering and jewels, presented them to the Dānava.
And they said: "O Lord of Daityas, we are under your command, there is no doubt; O Lord of Dānavas, please instruct us as to what we should do. (95.4)
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"O Yakṣas, let there be no fear for you; you are mine, of this there is no doubt.
For this king is the best among you, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu. (95.5)
Prahlāda was the oppressor of all the hosts of gods;
therefore, having established that bull among the Daityas, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), there [in Alakā].
Having established the lords of the Dānavas in all their respective positions, he again filled the abodes of the other hosts of gods.
Andhaka consecrated him as Indra in Amarāvatī,
while the Daitya himself ruled over the entire Bhūrloka.
Furthermore, taking up his bow and arrow, which shone like the sun, the lord of the Daityas said to the Earth: "Reveal yourself to me. (95.9)
Terrified and trembling before that Daitya, she stood with palms joined in reverence,
saying "Victory!", like another Lakṣmī standing before Viṣṇu.
Like a tiger toward a doe, like the king of birds toward a female serpent, like a lion toward a tigress, and like the sovereign of the śarabhas toward a lioness— (95.11)
Like a mean crow seizing a female swan, or like a water-fowl seizing a peahen,
so did that son of Diti seize her with a face contorted by rage;
and, highly agitated, he spoke to the goddess who was overwhelmed with fear.
"O auspicious Earth, I have been appointed by Brahmā as your husband;
you should desire me as your venerable lord, for I shall indeed protect you. (95.13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having gone to Rasātala near his own city,
he bound her with serpent-nooses as if she were a wicked woman.
Then the very powerful and wicked Daitya lord Acala, with his conch, besieged Ārtā just as a valiant one might besiege a cave. || 95.15 ||
Then he appointed fourteen thousand Daitya lords named Kiṅkaras as guards, who were constantly engaged in her protection. || 95.16 ||
Having done exactly that, the lord of the Daityas shone with satisfaction, like a farmer who has beheld his field well-ripened. || 95.17 ||
"I have accomplished my purpose"—thus did that king form the thought, having united his eldest son with wives like a self-controlled and virtuous man. (95.18)
O observer of noble vows, no one else can gain access to him,
just as it is impossible for a Brahmin who lives with hypocrisy even while living with his own companions.
"O Dānavas, all of you, perform sacrifices and honor the Brahmins;
and bow down again and again to the trident-bearing God. (95.20)
Then he commanded: "Devote yourselves solely to the Dharma. Among them, there was not a single Daitya or even a Dānava who was unrighteous.
While he was ruling the kingdom, wicked conduct ceased to exist;
for he himself was indeed the wind, the moon, and the sun. (95.22)
Vyāsa became endowed with the power of asceticism throughout the worlds;
while that king was ruling, medicinal herbs sprang up spontaneously.
Without cultivation, they arise as the sustainers of the entire world;
yet that very king of the Daityas, having seized them, leads them to destruction.
He indeed crushed him and led him back to his home;
he alone became the wielder of the staff, for he was indeed the staff itself.
Through that very yoga, he protects everyone everywhere at all times;
no one among them falls ill, nor does anyone die. 95.26
Nor was there anyone ever addicted to another's wife, nor a slanderer; there were no violent people, nor were there any unrighteous ones anywhere. 95.27.
Ponds, lakes, rivers, and springs—even these exist everywhere and remain well-established even without rain. (95.28)
For him there are no rākṣasas, nor indeed any harmful piśācas;
for him there are no calamities, nor any dualities whatsoever. (95.29)
While that king reigned, the brahmins did not offer oblations into the fire, nor did they study or perform sacrifices; at that time, society became a single caste.
Those Bhrigus who were Brahmins, bringing joy to the Dānavas, study and perform sacrifices in this very manner in every respect, O Vyāsa. (95.31)
Everything became joyful and flourishing, free from the suffering of disease;
the world was equal for all people, transcending the distinctions of caste and stage of life.

While Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti and lord of the Daityas, was king, the world shone forth, ever engaged in the festivities of dance and song, sleeping in happiness, and devoted to the pleasures of love.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Reign of King Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 95 ||
The ninety-sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
While the auspicious Daityendra was thus the king and sovereign of the three worlds,
And when the earth itself was firmly established and all living beings were at ease.
"Deprived of their positions, those mighty gods were left without a foundation; afflicted by suffering, what did they do? Tell me all of this in detail. (96.2)
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Dharma, to the state that befell the gods, and what they all did there in due order when afflicted by suffering. 96.3.
Agni became the bearer of oblations for the gods, increasing their portions;
having cast him out, the Daitya then made another fire.
O best of Brahmins, in that ritual, there were mantras following it which,
when recited, brought about auspicious results for the portions belonging to the Daityas and Dānavas.
Then the Sacrifice itself approached the high-souled Daityas;
and when the Sacrifice had departed from the lord of the Daityas, all the gods were as if dead.
They lost their sense of direction, their vigor and prowess were diminished;
they were bereft of splendor, devoid of effort, without anyone to cry out to for help, and filled with anxiety.
Like serpents burnt by mantras, like mountains pulverized by the thunderbolt, or like venomous snakes whose poison has been neutralized when bitten by Garuḍa; || 96.8 ||
O Vyāsa, those gods, deprived of their kingdom and robbed of their splendor, were like trees stripped of water or women bereft of their kinsmen.
They brooded in their hearts, withered away, and lamented;
then the self-existent God, perceiving the gods to be in such a state, [acted].
From his celestial chariot, which was the color of the sun, the Grandfather spoke these words:
"O gods, you have lost your senses; why are you so deeply distressed?
O foremost of the immortals, I grant you today the power of asceticism and yoga."
"You are the creators and the destroyers of the world in every respect;
it is not fitting for you to stand here today like eunuchs."
"Abandoning both your own and my own yoga, O mighty ones, do not fall into sorrow; take it up yourselves, O gods! (96.13)
Just as darkness is not joined with the sun, nor heat with the moon;
just as frost does not belong to fire, nor nectar to a serpent. 96.14

There is no goodness in one who is not good, nor is there anything unseemly in one of noble birth; there is no unrighteousness for those bound by their vows, nor is there a lack of wisdom regarding the gods.
"O gods, it is not fitting for you, who are high-souled, that this should be so;
for those who abide in their own splendor do not despair even in times of calamity. || 96.16 ||
Having encountered this calamity, you ought not to grieve;
do not despair, for the kingdom shall be yours once again. (96.17)
"Endowed with the power of great yoga, Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, cannot today be slain by you with limited splendor. (96.18)
"O imperishable ones, you must await the exhaustion of this asceticism;
when his penance is spent, Viṣṇu will slay the lord of the Daityas in battle."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, those lords of the gods, having attained yoga, bowed down to the creator of all beings and spoke as follows. (96.20)
"Our great seats of yoga have been seized by the sons of Diti;
tell us, where shall we stay? Point out to us an imperishable place. (96.21)
Brahmā said:
"All your abodes have been taken away; this is known to me. Listen to where you must dwell by means of your yogic power (yogamāyā). (96.22)
"O most excellent ones, all of you enter into bodies through yoga;
O gods, from that you shall obtain sustenance from all quarters for the sake of living beings."
Through their various kinds of food and drink, as well as through their transformative activities,
the earth— though bound by the nagas— will nourish you all.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed by the God, all those gods, together with Vāsava,
acted exactly as Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, had spoken.
Remaining there, those best of gods continuously revolved,
abiding by the doctrine of the world-system as they observed the cycle of the four ages.
Then, through his yogic power, Hiraṇyākṣa, whose self was absorbed in yoga, beheld the gods established among the creatures; he became enraged toward them.
Whichever god he saw stationed there, that best of Dānavas would approach and slay him. (96.28)
I am constantly and ever-vigilant in protecting my subjects from fear;
yet those of wicked conduct increase my enmity as well. (96.29)
"Ungrateful, slayers of their masters, insatiable, and evil-minded—these wicked enemies of mine [should always be deprived] of food, drink, and other necessities. (96.30)
Those women of wicked conduct, who deserve my punishment, instead cause me to swell with strength; therefore, I shall deal with them.
Then, by means of his yoga, the Dānava dried up all the pools, lakes, rivers, and springs.
O you of excellent vows, those herbs that grew without being cultivated and which once existed there, he caused to perish;
he also crushed the trees and creepers.
With its trees, shrubs, creepers, and sprouts destroyed, its grasses, medicinal herbs, springs, and reservoirs of water vanished,
and with its rivers, ponds, wells, and leafy growths dried up, the world appeared like the back of a tortoise.
With the duties and restraints of the castes and stages of life lost, and with its cowherds, settlements, birds, and humans perished, [the world lay desolate].
Resounding with throngs of elephants, horses, infantry, and so forth, the world was like the fierce fire at the end of an eon.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Words of Brahmā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen the world in such a state, those gods were afflicted with grief.
Having reached the world of Vairāja, he beheld his grandfather once again.
Having all approached him and bowed down again and again,
they, being deeply distressed, told him the entire deed of the Daitya.
And having offered their salutations once more, they spoke again to the God, the cause of the world:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, we have been robbed of our kingdom and are likewise weak."
We are incapable of standing against that Daitya in combat;
nor do we see any place where we might remain there free from anxiety. (97.4)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the terrified inhabitants of heaven,
the blessed Brahmā spoke to all the gods.
The gods should not fear that great-souled yogin;
for that Daitya has already attained the entire fruit of his ascetic penance.
O gods, the time has arrived that brings an end to his life;
therefore, all of you go with me and entreat Viṣṇu.
"Sirs, you are indeed powerless today and incapable of resisting him; Viṣṇu alone is capable, and he shall deprive that Daitya of his life. (97.8)
For previously, when he was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"This one cannot be slain by a human nor by a god in any way whatsoever. (97.9)
Nor will this Great-Souled One be born among the animals, nor on earth, nor in fire; nor in space, nor even in the worlds. (97.10)
This very one, the lord of the Daityas, a high-souled and righteous deity, shall then be incapable of being slain by any living beings; he shall only be slain through sorrow.
Having assumed the form of a boar, it was neither divine nor human;
nor was it born among the animals, for it was indeed a man-boar (naravārāha). || 97.12 ||
Having entered even into the netherworld (pātāla), it is neither earth nor sky;
it is neither fire nor this world; it is entirely liberated from all things. 97.13.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they were all delighted, and having bowed down to the Grandfather, they said, "O Lord of Gods, let us go; for our time is passing away."
Then they all went to Śveta, the best of mountains,
to Viṣṇu— the patient, the victorious, the crusher of ten thousand Dānavas.
Having prostrated with great reverence, they praised him with desirable words:
"Salutations to the destroyer of all enemies and the end-maker of the Dānavas! (97.16)
Salutation to the unconquered god Vaikuṇṭha, the Great Soul;
salutation indeed to him who has shaken off all passion, and salutation to the Truth itself.
Salutation to the god Sādhya; salutation to the abode, the well-knowing one;
salutation to the god Yama and to Jaya—salutation, salutation!
Salutations to the son of Aditi, and to Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to Sumati, and let there also be salutations to Viṣṇu.
Salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana and to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
salutations to Rāma, to Rāma, and indeed to Atri’s son Datta.
Salutations to you, O Narasiṃha; salutations again and again to Dhātṛ.
Salutations to Sādhya, to the Veda, and indeed salutations again and again to the wielder of the discus.
Salutations to the slayer of Śakuni, and salutations to Dāmodara;
to him who performs austerities in the water, and to him who is fond of his bed upon the serpent.
Salutations to the Great Puruṣa who has the form of Kapila;
salutations to him who has the form of a cloud and is dear to Mahādeva.
Homage to the one whose form is half-Rudra and likewise to the one who has the form of Umā;
homage to the host of Maheśvara, who holds a discus and a mallet in his hands.
And let there always be salutation to Śipiviṣṭa, the bearer of the Śrīvatsa,
the heroic Dhundhumāra, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
To the four-armed Kṛṣṇa, who wears the jewel Kaustubha,
who stands in the sky as Trivikrama, and who is beautifully clothed in yellow garments.
Salutations to the slayer of Puruṣa, who wields the mace and the fierce sword;
to the yogin, the sacrificer, and the one who ravaged the wife of Bhṛgu.
To him who always has the form of a bull, the foremost of the Ādityas, the wise Cekitāna, the self-controlled Śauri, the kinsman of the Vṛṣṇis; || 97.28 ||
