Salutations to you for the destruction of Mura and Aśvagrīva, and likewise for the slaughter of the asuras; salutations to you who bear the Śārṅga bow and who brought about the ruin of Saubha and Śālva.
Salutations to you, O Padmanābha, who entered the body of Brahmā;
salutations to Jayā, to Śarva, and to him who was granted boons by Rudra.
Salutations to the Lord of all, who sets forth the lost dharma;
salutations to you, the most excellent Puruṣa, the one with a hundred arms.
"By your grace, O Puruṣottama, we shall indeed cross over this hardship.
We have all been robbed of our kingdom, yet you do not know it, O mighty-armed one!
O Vaikuṇṭha, destroy that Hiraṇyākṣa, O mighty-armed one! (97.32)
Sanatkumāra said: That mortal who, endowed with supreme devotion, constantly recites this Vaiṣṇava hymn, is liberated from all sins. (97.33)
And having died, he rejoices for fourteen million years in all the worlds, honored by all the gods; of this there is no doubt.
He who merely recites this for the sake of living beings is liberated;
without reaching the world of death, he wanders free from suffering.
Sanatkumāra said:—
[He] spoke this to the tigers among the gods, always honoring them. (97.36)
"From here that evil-minded Daitya, accompanied by his allies, hates the gods.
Assume for me the form of a boar in human guise; let me be sustained. (97.37)
That lord of the Daityas is indeed high-souled, powerful, and righteous;
he cannot be slain by me alone—I tell you this truly.
"Assuming that boar-form which consists of all the gods and increases my joy,
I shall slay that exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas."
In those forms, O best of gods, among all of us,
Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā, and Yama likewise became the Prasthātṛ.
There, O best of gods, Varuṇa was the Udgātṛ priest; from him came the sacrificial animal, Hiraṇyākṣa; and I, the mighty one, was the Śamitṛ priest for that sacrifice of his. (97.41)
Today let all beings behold both me and him alike.
Having heard those words and the roar of that great-souled one, [they were like] two rutting elephants dwelling in the forest for the sake of a mate. (97.43)
With eyes wide open in joy, they all gazed at one another and thought that the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas was indeed slain.
Their faces, with eyes like blossoming lotuses, shone with exquisite splendor;
that Daitya was slain by him in the form of Narasiṃha, just as his mighty preceptor had been slain in ancient times.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Means for the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Ninety-eighth Chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those tigers among the gods assumed his form.
The lords fashioned his body out of the seven worlds.
All his bones are mountains, and his channels are rivers;
his blood is the seven oceans, and phlegm, bile, and wind are his qualities.
His feces became the herbs, and his dharma was the semen;
his urine became the clouds, and the seven vital airs were the ones residing within his body.
The Sādhyas became his head, and Rudra occupied the crown;
Dharma was on his forehead, and the self-possessed Vāyu was his nose. 98.4.
The sun and moon became his eyes; the quarters of space became his ears;
his vital breaths became his eyebrows, and day and night became his eyelashes.
His mouth became the fire situated in the submarine mare’s mouth;
the intermediate space became his lips, and the serpents became his teeth.
Indeed, four great weapons and fangs were fashioned:
first the Pāśupata weapon, and second the discus. 98.7
The third was the Brahmadaṇḍa, and the fourth was the head of Brahmā;
Soma became his neck, and Rudra was situated upon his shoulder.
The two cheeks were likewise fashioned by the Ādityas, and his two hands by the Rudras;
his fingers were Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Siddhi as well.
— — — — and their movements, as well as their claws as weapons in every respect;
likewise, the staff of Yama, the staff of Time (Kāla), and the staff of Death (Mṛtyu).
Rudra and Daṇḍa were made the four arms and feet of the Lord;
the Sādhyas were his chest, and Soma was also his heart.
O best of sages, the great elements were his belly;
O best of Brahmins, Aditi, the mother, became his navel.
Prajāpati was his penis; Mitra was stationed in his anus;
the Vasus were on his sides, and Dharma was at his back. (98.13)
Death, Time, and Yama are situated on the soles of his feet;
the two Aśvins are his tail, and the ancestors reside in his joints.
Necessity, the noose of time, as well as Death and Strife, and whatever diseases there may be—all these have taken refuge in his glance. (98.15)
The Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, along with the Gandharvas and Pannagas,
all took refuge within his skin and stood there gathered together.
Likewise, all the meters, the Vedas, and the sacrificial offerings—all these remained individually within each of his pores. 98.17.
Gifts, religious observances, restraints, and all the Mothers;
the gods presiding over specific places, as well as beasts and birds.
All the hairs of that high-souled Boar became [the stars],
and the fingers of his two feet likewise became the Viśvedevas.
At that time, the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases became his gods;
all the sages were established within the pores of his skin and in all his limbs.
Thus, O Vyāsa, the Boar Nandivardhana came into being;
he shone in that form, touching both heaven and earth. (98.21)
In ancient times, when the blessed Svayambhū was about to lift up this earth,
the radiant Madhusūdana shone forth in that very form.
For at night he was brilliantly illuminated like the Himalaya mountain;
then all the sages, by means of their great ascetic power, [honored him] at that time.
Having each attained their own splendor, they further kindled his brilliance;
that Viṣṇu [was empowered] by the splendor of those ṛṣis of supreme energy.
At the end of time, he blazed forth like another fire at the end of an eon,
letting out a tremendous roar that shook the very earth.
He said to all those sages, "I shall slay the Daitya, the enemy of the gods;
having killed that king of the Daityas, I shall be like the lord of the śarabhas killing a lion. (98.26)
"Having entered the netherworld (rasātala) today, I shall liberate the distressed earth;
and having established her in her own place and restored the kingdom to the gods, you, O wealth-possessing ones,
should now recite prayers for victory and for our welfare."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said: "Exert your strength; this Daitya possesses exceedingly great power."
O Lord of the Gods, applying great effort and remaining vigilant, slay that king of the Daityas; this is my considered opinion regarding this difficult task.
In former times, there was no Daitya equal to him; this lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was possessed of great strength and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga.
Then, O Vyāsa, the blessed Lord whose banner bears the bull was there with the gods including Brahmā, and with the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
Having bowed to the Lord of Gods, he said: "O Lord, O Sovereign of All, please augment Viṣṇu with your own splendor so that he may slay the enemy of the gods. (98.32)
The Blessed One said:
"At that time, all the lords of the gods shall enter into Hari, who is composed of splendor;
thereafter, he will swiftly slay the Daitya."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Brahmā himself performed the protection of that high-souled one;
learn that duly from me today as I speak it, O you of pure vows. 98.34.
Brahmā said:
"O best of sages, may the Ordainer and the Creator protect you;
may Rudra and the Creator of all guard your deeds as you fight. (98.35)
May Kapālī, Tālaketu, Gandhādhipati, Rasādhipati, and Sūkṣmarūpa protect [you]. 98.36.
He who is the knower of touch, subtle, possessed of sound, and high-minded;
he who is the lord of the senses and indeed Nīlalohita.
May the Great Yogin protect you, as well as the Lord of the Seed, the Garland of the Empowerment of the Seed, and the Lord of Consciousness. (98.38)
He is the Lord who knows the time of both worldly engagement and liberation; He is the Lord who knows the course of dharma and adharma, and who bestows the fruits upon those who act.
He who provides the functioning of the qualities (guṇas), who is independent of actions, who is the ordainer of the rules, and who is the knower of all deeds; || 98.40 ||
And he who functions for the sake of instruments even without instruments;
he who is omniscient, omnipresent, and himself the presiding controller. (98.41)
There is nothing whatsoever that is not presided over by Him, nor does anything exist in any way [without Him].
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
He possesses ears everywhere, and His all-pervading movement is imperishable.
He whose sovereignty is inexhaustible and who possesses a thousand forms;
he who is the creator of all beings and of the principles (tattvas), and who is of great renown.
He who is the creator of this saṃsāra and likewise its bringer to an end—
he whom the followers of Sāṃkhya do not recognize, nor do the practitioners of Yoga who have mastered the scriptures.
The contentments and the cognitions constantly delude living beings with illusion;
yet within this Great Soul, all principles are woven like warp and woof.
He who pervades all things, beginning with the Puruṣa, yet is himself pervaded by nothing;
without knowing whom there is no liberation, and by whom this entire world is bound. (98.46)
By whom I was formerly made the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) of all the worlds;
by whom you, as well as Sacrifice (Yajña) and Viṣṇu, were created in the beginning, O Ancient One.
May that high-minded one bestow upon you great strength, vigor, and splendor,
as well as memory regarding weapons that is attained effortlessly in all circumstances.
And may the all-pervading Lord grant protection to you as you fight;
having been properly protected by me, go and destroy the Daitya.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O brahmins, the gods situated within the pores of his skin praised him with great reverence, using words of pleasing hymns. 98.50.
And all the various beings cried out, "Victory!
Then, auspicious celestial drums resounded in the sky without being struck.
There, where Varāha had become manifest, the divine beings cried out;
and showers of fragrant flowers fell everywhere upon Varāha, greatly increasing the joy of the gods. (98.52)
Then, saying "Success! and having offered salutations to Rudra, he went to the abode of Varuṇa while muttering the Rudra-mantra that brings victory.

Being attended by sages rich in asceticism, as well as by many victorious birds and numerous divine deer that moved clockwise for his success, the Lord proceeded toward the great ocean for victory. 98.54.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Journey of Varāha to the Abode of Varuṇa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The eighty-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
That righteous-souled one set forth, roaring like a thundercloud.
The Veda consisting of all the worlds, the Boar, the increaser of joy.
Then, having reached the ocean, that one of exceeding strength beheld it roaring like a cloud and submerging itself like a lion.
He moved like a dancing girl performing her dance, and like a warrior leaping about;
he traversed the earth with many varied and wonderful circular maneuvers.
Then Nandivardhana beheld that wonderful spectacle in its many forms— [the prince] skilled in wrestling and expert in mace-fighting.
He honored that Lord of Gods, the all-pervading one who embodies all the worlds,
with the arghya offering, as well as the gods and the sages who had assembled there.
Having taken him for victory and paid homage to the great ocean,
he turned back all living beings and entered the vast sea.
Plunging into the ocean with playful ease,
the Lord shone like a mighty elephant in rut having reached a vast lake.
Having entered very far within, he became invisible, like the sun with its full orb covered by a layer of clouds upon the earth. || 99.8 ||
Then, having entered the water and agitating the great ocean,
O Vyāsa, he appeared to the lords of the worlds like the moon reflected in the water.
He saw the *timi*, the *timiṅgila*, and even those that swallow the *timiṅgila*;
likewise others that swallow those, as well as donkeys and even elephants.
And likewise those resembling sea-monsters, conchs, and even horse-faced beings;
as well as others resembling birds, and yet other human-like forms.
And [they saw] enclosures in the shape of chariot wheels, as well as those with the faces of lions and tigers,
those with the mouths of śarabhas, bears, and cats, and likewise various kinds of fish.
Whirling them about, he of great splendor and immense strength proceeded;
some entered him out of curiosity, while others merely sniffed him.
Then fish with flaming mouths bite him by the hundreds and thousands;
yet he circumambulates the auspicious, divine Hayashiras from left to right.
In an instant, having passed through the midst of Maināka and also Bhogavatī,
he went to the city of Varuṇa, the wise lord of the waters.
Having reached the world-elephant Parjanya and performed a circumambulation,
they arrived at the city of Surabhi and beheld the cows of radiant luster.
O Vyāsa, that divine lake is the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīroda), where those twice-born ones who subsist on foam always flow with nectar and immortality.
Having drunk from that lake water which was as radiant as the nectar of glory,
and being duly honored by the foam-drinkers, he dwelt there for that night.
Having stayed there, he went to the imperishable city of Kaṅka;
and having reached the city of Vāsuki and that of the wise Takṣaka, || 99.19 ||
There, the Lord of the Gods granted Śeṣa immortality—immortality more delightful, charming, divine, and even superior to that of heaven. (99.20)
Having heard him, the king honored him with the guest-offering (argha);
bowing down out of great respect, the imperishable one invited him.
As he was thus worshipping him, the slayer of Madhu, filled with supreme affection, said:
"You ought not to cause an obstacle to the work of the world."
"O Lord, this great task must be performed for the inhabitants of the three heavens.
We shall do it again together with you, if you so desire;
let not this opportunity pass away for the sake of the Daitya."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having dismissed that serpent, he went to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
There dwelt a Daitya named Suprabha, the guardian of the ocean, who moved within the waters. (99.24)
He then beheld him approaching toward the city of Hiraṇyākṣa;
he also observed the subtle gods within the limbs of the boar.
And because of his form, that Asura did not approach him out of fear;
moreover, that evil-minded one was paralyzed by his splendor.
Indeed, wishing to inform Hiraṇyākṣa quickly,
he then exerted his speed toward the city ahead of the Boar.
Desiring to go to that king of the Daityas, the infinite and death-like one in the form of a boar,
he approached the Daitya— blazing with splendor and wearing garlands— just as the wind approaches the end of life.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Entry of Varāha into the Ocean," in the Skanda Purāṇa. 99.99.
Sanatkumāra said:
When that fear had arisen, which indicated the danger of destruction—
At that time, terrible portents occurred in the city of Hiraṇyākṣa.
The watchtowers crumbled and the deities seemed to cry out;
jackals howled within the houses and assembly halls of the Daityas.
Suddenly, there arose from the citizens a terrifying clamor;
trees fell to the ground uprooted even without wind;
the sun appeared like a headless trunk, and a battle was seen right there.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having observed these and other great omens at that time, the king spoke thus to the Asuras and Daityas.
O bulls among the asuras, great omens are being perceived;
these are certainly not without cause, for a great danger is seen.
"O lords of the gods, having been deprived of their kingdom, they will not remain inactive;
surely they are relying on something else as they prepare for battle."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best of the asuras, bowed properly to his father and spoke these words. (100.7)
Prahlāda said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, I am your son, and you are my father according to dharma.
O best of the Daityas, your intellect should not be influenced by those such as me."
Nevertheless, out of affection and desiring an imperishable kingdom, we spoke as children; you ought not to remember that.
"Last night in a dream, I saw that being in human form;
having assumed the form of a boar, he seized you. Act correctly so that this may not indeed come to pass. (100.10)
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "This is so; there is no doubt that you have seen it exactly as it is according to dharma at that time. This is indeed so; there is no uncertainty. (100.11)
Today I went in a dream to the abode of Tryambaka;
there the blessed Lord, whose banner bears the bull, spoke these words to me.
"O Daitya, this much alone shall be your kingdom and even the status of Indra itself: that you give this beloved daughter Suprabhā, along with the yakṣas, to my son. (100.13)
"Quickly bestow upon him today this crown and the necklace,
as well as the armlets, the bracelets, the sword, and the golden circlet."
Then, taking from me both the royal insignia and the fine linen upper garment against my will, he presented them to Śakra.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "O Daitya, you must always dwell near me from this morning onwards; what use have you for a kingdom?"
For that which has been seen by me here shall not prove false;
in every way, there is no possibility for the Daityas to exist here while I am present.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, all the Daityas then spoke:
"This is false; O King, these things occurring in dreams are proclaimed to be false. (100.18)
"Andhaka, who is invincible to all beings, powerful, and unconquered, shall fight with us together against the gods. (100.19)
Relying upon him, we shall all fight happily and free from anxiety. O crusher of the hosts of gods, do not you yourself fight against the deities.
All the vital breaths of the Daityas, together with the Dānavas, are established in you;
while you live, we live, but if you do not exist, how can we remain?
Abandoning the city this very day, let us all enter the great ocean.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa,
the best among speakers, laughed and spoke this to them properly.
He who is the creator of all beings, as well as their bestower and their destroyer—he who ordained what was done previously, who else could alter that again? (100.23)
"O Dānavas, if death has been ordained for me inevitably by him, then he will come and slay me while I am sitting here, not fighting. (100.24)
"Behold that place of mine, O all you best of asuras,
where death shall not come and lead me away while I am standing."
Or rather, O Dānavas, death has not been ordained for me by him in such a way that he will take me away while I am fighting as before.
How could one such as I perform this act, which is censured by the virtuous—having brought death upon a child and then casting my gaze upon another’s soul? (100.27)
O lords of the Dānavas, even one such as I, having alone repeatedly wrought the slaughter of enemies in battle, would turn my back upon them once again. (100.28)
Vipracitti said:
"All the gods have indeed been conquered by us many times and have perished in every way; yet they return once more. Therefore, we shall all strive so that this does not happen again."
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"Knowing ourselves to be immortal gods, and that our own selves are very difficult to attain, we shall regain them again even after living for a very long time. (100.30)
Understanding sovereignty in this way, they constantly flee from it;
but for us, O best of Asuras, there is no immortality at all.
Therefore, even for us who are ruined, there is no hope for life;
since that [hope] is absent, we see that whatever comes to pass is indeed better for us.
"Do not set your mind on destruction; my mind is fixed on battle.
Let our lives depart in fair combat in the fray, and not like cowards."
Sanatkumāra said:
While those enemies of the gods were thus speaking in the assembly, a Dānava appeared, agitated and panting with haste. 100.34.
He was thoroughly terrified, as if by a lion-king in the wilderness, like an elephant by the paw of a lion, or like a serpent by Garuḍa. || 100.35 ||
Then, with his fist clenched and looking toward all directions,
he went with speed and, sighing heavily, spoke to the gatekeeper at the door.
The Dānava said:
"O keeper of the assembly hall, announce to the king that Anala himself has arrived;
he is the protector of the ocean. He must be told to come quickly, for this is an untimely hour. (100.37)
Then, having laughed and addressed him, that gatekeeper, the warden of the assembly, said to him:
"Do not be afraid; O great asura, from what source could you have fear? (100.38)
"There is no lion here, nor a thief, nor any other beast of prey; there are no cattle, nor other animals. Cast away your fear and take heart. (100.39)
Thus addressed by him, that most excellent of Asuras remained unappeased;
filled with rage, he then let out a great roar, making the quarters of the sky resound.
Having approached King Vyasa, the lord of the Dānavas, they then said: "O Asura, tell us, what is it that you have seen today? (100.41)
O King, having properly consoled this Daitya, that highly illustrious one said:
"For the sake of the welfare of the Dānavas, ask him, O son of Diti. (100.42)
O best of Brahmins, O Vyāsa, having heard that Dānava, that king of the Dānavas, who possessed great strength, spoke these words to them.
"O Daitya, out of fear you are unable to come near me;
take heart and tell me everything exactly as it was seen, just as it is."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, that Dānava, his fever of anxiety gone, bowed down to the king with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words properly. (100.45)
May the king, who brings happiness to the Dānavas, be ever victorious for us!
May all our enemies, who bring us harm, perish! 100.46
"By your command, O Great King, I travel everywhere day after day, accompanied by men, as far as the edge of the ocean. (100.47)
"There today, O bull among the Daityas, I see that boar there,
resembling a peak of Mount Meru and blazing like a fire."
O great king, all the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity are seen stationed within its branches, assuming subtle forms. (100.49)
O Indra among kings, you are possessed of great strength and are always a source of fear to the gods;
yet Bhīma is even greater than you—indeed, no one such as he exists here on earth.
"O bull among the Daityas, neither seen nor even heard before in bodily form, I was struck by him with his gaze and fell violently to the ground. (100.51)
With their necklaces and garments slipping off, terrified as if struck by a thunderbolt—those Dānavas of fearsome prowess who were once my followers. (100.52)
They all fell down by his force, deprived of life;
O Indra among kings, he now approaches toward your very city.
Shaking the entire earth and agitating the oceans, O Lord of Daityas, he deprived the aquatic creatures of their lives. (100.54)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best of the asuras,
spoke these meaningful words to the king of the Daityas.
Prahlāda said:
O King, such as I have heard that form of the Boar to be, it consists of all the gods; the Boar is considered to be beyond the reach of nature (aprākṛta).
Therefore, you must act in such a way that he does not delude us. Having reached a firm decision, O Lord of Daityas, do this without delay. (100.57)
It is clearly manifested by Brahmā that this form of the Boar, which bears the discus and the plough,
is composed of all the gods.
"O Lord of the Dānavas, you are invincible to all the gods;
this illusion was indeed created by them because they were powerless, and not otherwise."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa spoke these meaningful words to the Daityas and Danujas. 100.60.
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"If this evil-minded slayer of my brother comes here, today at long last that desire in my heart will be fulfilled. (100.61)
Today, having repeatedly cut to pieces that evil-souled slayer of my brother in battle, I shall offer him as a propitious sacrifice to Paśupati.
Today, O Daityas, I shall cut off his head with its variegated eyes and earrings from his body and offer it to Rudra, the Supreme Soul.
That Keśava was not encountered by me previously in that battle;
today, having encountered him, I shall send him to the abode of Yama.
Now, once he is slain, all the gods will become hopeless and overwhelmed by fear; falling into a state of helplessness, they will surely fall into servitude.
Sanatkumāra said: Then he spoke to those heroic Dānavas and exceedingly powerful Daityas, the Dānavas known by the name Kiṅkaras.
"O you of great strength, go those ten thousand men and find out who this is; then I myself shall go. (100.67)
Thus addressed, all those great illusionists departed, joyful,
with their finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on and their feet armored as infantrymen.
Those sons of the Dānavas and Daityas, possessed of great strength, adorned with garments, necklaces, and strings of gold,
went forth like venomous serpents, uttering many cries in their extreme fury.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Command to the Kiṃkaras," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 100.100 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Those Daityas and Dānavas, having donned their armor, rushed forth with great speed.
They rushed toward the boar like distressed deer toward a lion. || 101.1 ||
O Vyāsa, those lords of the asuras, being led away by that boar-eyed one, appeared like consecrated sacrificial animals ready for slaughter. 101.2.
Having slain them and bound them with the noose of death by Kṛtānta, he then led those Daityas away like a man leading cattle. || 101.3 ||
Having traveled eight yojanas and emerged from the waters of the ocean, they all beheld a boar, like small deer seeing a lion. || 101.4 ||
Having gazed at him for a mere moment, those enraged Daityas and Dānavas rushed about on all sides, stretching their bows.
Then, beholding those Daityas approaching from all sides,
that most mighty lord of boars spoke these words to them.
Varāha said:
"O sons of Diti, why do you all attack me from every side? I have done nothing to offend you, nor am I your enemy. (101.7)
Then, as he was speaking thus, all those sons of Diti, the Daityas, filled with great wonder, surrounded that Boar and questioned him.
"Who are you, appearing here in the form of a boar, having crossed the surging ocean?
For what purpose have you come here, or where indeed are you to go? (101.9)
Having heard those words of theirs, that high-minded Varāha,
whose voice was like the rumbling of a cloud, then spoke to all the Dānavas.
"I am Varāha; behold my form, just as the Daityas do.
I have come to this place for the purpose of wandering about; of this there is no doubt. (101.11)
"O best of Daityas, my wife having been carried off by another, I am despondent;
as I wander about, I contemplate the household of that wicked man. (101.12)
The Dānavas said:
"This is not your way; this is the abode of the Daityas.
Disregarding the Daityas, how have you come to this place? (101.13)
"O lowest of the deer species, we shall all slay you today;
and having killed you, we shall carry you before the Lord of the Daityas. (101.14)
Then all those Dānavas struck him violently with their excellent weapons,
just as uplifted clouds strike a mountain with rain.
Even though he was being struck down by those Daityas, that powerful and most mighty divine-souled Boar spoke these words: || 101.16 ||
For I have committed not even the slightest offense against you here, O best of Asuras; I have not done so, I shall not do so, nor am I doing so now. (101.17)
"For what purpose do you all strike me with sharp weapons as if against an enemy? Indeed, there is no enmity here on your part toward me, nor is there any business for me with you. (101.18)
"If you have need of my flesh, O Dānavas, then slay me;
however, let not my life be taken by sharp weapons, lest I have cause for fear of you."
"O sons of Diti, I stand here with these two arms outstretched;
when you all come to a standstill, then I shall slay you all at once."
"Today, O Daityas, you shall know here the strength of deer; I shall destroy that pride of yours which has made you intoxicated after conquering the gods. (101.21)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the venerable Vyāsa stood with his arms outstretched like the banner of Indra, resembling the risen Lord Śaṅkara himself.
Having heard those words of his, those Dānavas, overwhelmed with rage and exerting themselves greatly,
struck him violently with various weapons and missiles in their hands.
As a great wind disperses the clouds, as Garuḍa the birds of prey, as a tiger the deer, and as a lion the hares. || 101.24 ||
Just as fire blazes when fed with oblations, or as an elephant [overpowers] jackals, so did that blessed Vyāsa, the boar who increases the joy [of his devotees]. || 101.25 ||
Being tormented by them, he stood firm like a mountain, counting [the blows];
when he was struck by those very arrows, as well as by maces, clubs, and spears— || 101.26 ||
Being struck by these and many other weapons— bhindipālas, bhuśuṇḍīs, swords, iron-tipped arrows, and others— the lord of beasts shone forth invisible; then they all rejoiced exceedingly.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, as they were roaring, the Boar Nandivardhana emerged from the heap of weapons and crushed their heads.
With his two hands, his two feet, and his fangs, he tore [his enemies] apart;
with the weapons released by them, he likewise cut down others and let out a roar.
All of them were likewise mangled by their claws and teeth as they were deprived of their weapons;
they were utterly exhausted, like vast hoards of wealth being constantly consumed by many.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Battle with the Kiṃkaras," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 101.101 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having beheld all of them slain by the Boar, he...
Having escaped with great difficulty from that hardship, he entered the city of Aśamaka.
Having gone there, with disheveled hair, covered in dust, and drenched in blood, he spoke these words at the door of that assembly hall.
"O Daityas, announce this to the wise lord of the Dānavas!
Thus urged, the gatekeeper, with his weapon raised, announced it to the king. (102.3)
Those best of asuras who had gone to see that king of beasts—
all those sons of Diti— were slain by him, having displayed his prowess.
"Do not fall into negligence, O Lord of Daityas; do not despise the king of beasts.
Do not wait for time, nor recognize him as a mere deer.
He is great; of this there is no doubt, and he cannot be conquered by the Dānavas. (102.5)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa,
becoming enraged himself, then sprang up from his seat.
He rose up like the banner of Indra, roaring like a rain-cloud;
with his face contorted by a frown, he blazed like a fire enveloped in smoke.
Then, as he rose up from there, the Daityas and the Dānava Vipracitti bowed and spoke these words to the Daitya in smooth syllables and phrases: || 102.8 ||
"You are the king of all the Daityas and the bringer of victory to all beings;
while we remain here, it does not behove you to go forth yourself."
"O Great King, having slain him along with the gods and those who are his protectors, we shall cut off his flesh and bring it here. (102.10)
Of the Ādityas, along with the Rudras, the Vasus, and the Aśvins;
together with the Pitṛs of the Bhṛgus, and likewise those of the Aṅgirases. (102.11)
And whatever Viśvedevas there may be, as well as the Sādhyas, along with the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and the Uragas; 102.12.
O Dānava, [this applies] to Gandharvas and birds,
as well as to humans who are prepared for death, together with the world-protectors.
The Daityas are capable of warding off [the gods] and even slaying the wicked-souled ones; they are also capable of restraining them at the proper time. Therefore, do not go from here yourself.
"Behold today, O son of Diti, how we, exerting ourselves, have slain him wherever our king, our master, and lord of subjects commands us. (102.15)
We shall all carry that out with our heads bowed, there is no doubt;
for even though we are all foremost among the Asuras, if we are unable to accomplish that task,
you yourself must be its doer— do not look upon us as if we were strangers.
For the sake of the deer, the immensely powerful king himself has gone out against the Danu-demons;
he is not among the Daityas, yet they shall speak of his strength.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king commanded all the Daityas,
just as Indra at the proper time commands the clouds that possess the luster of crushed collyrium.
Having received his command, those Daityas also, filled with joy,
equipped themselves for battle— those of massive bodies— and mounted their vehicles.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala;
Jambha, Kujambha, Vātāpi, Ilvala, and Virocana.
Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Śambhu, Kaśyapa, the great-bodied Śambara, and Kālaśambara; || 102.21 ||
The Dānavas Pradīpta, Asiloman, Śilīta,
Sarabha, Śalabha, Dhundhu, and the Dānava Mūka.
Śatodara was renowned, as was another named Hradodara; Tāra, Tāraka, Maya, and the famous Kāla were there as well.
Aja, Namuci, Vyaṃsa, Kārtasvana, Śubha,
Ilvaka, Bilvaka, Vipāka, and Pāka.
Hasta, Duryodhana, and the Dānava Vipracitti;
Hayagrīva, Mura, Naraka, and Kuṇḍa as well. || 102.25 ||
Śakuni, Vṛṣaparvan, Śataketu, Mahārava,
Maraka, Rāhu, Svarbhānu, and Kāla himself.
Virādha and Kabandha, Dundubhi and Śatadundubhi, Śālva and Druma—these two—and Mayūragrīva as well. (102.27)
Kālanemi, Meghanāda, and the highly powerful Andhaka; Mahiṣa, Ānanda, Śamaka, Vāṭi, and Baka as well.
Then those tigers among the Dānavas— possessors of great illusion and great strength,
all of them experts in every weapon and having attained their mark in combat— [prepared for battle].
O Vyāsa, others went on chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as on foot, like gods going against an asura to slay that boar. || 102.30 ||
And that powerful Lord Varāha, the increaser of joy, possessed of great splendor,
was likewise being praised by the sages who dwelt within himself.
Having slain all those servants, he arrived at the city of Aśmaka,
roaring like a cloud at the end of an eon that releases its rain.
Having gone there at that time, O Vyāsa, the Lord, who consists of the world,
circumambulated the city keeping it to his left and approached the southern gate.
There, by many Dānavas at the southern gate,
a tumultuous "halāhala" cry was raised, by which the city was provoked to anger.
For he, the imperishable one, having shattered the śataghnīs, the door-bolts, the mallets, and the spiked hammers, pulverized the wheels of time and the mechanical engines.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Dānavas, possessed by intense fury, arrived,
covering the lord of beasts with a fierce shower of weapons.
Then, struck by those lances, discuses, and slings,
he abandoned the gate, went forth, and took refuge on level ground.
O Vyāsa, perceiving that he too was broken, those Asuras then pursued him from behind, lacerating him with their excellent weapons.
While being struck by showers of arrows, javelins, great maces, clubs, and iron-tipped missiles,
he then emerged and fought against the sons of Diti, presided over by the hosts of gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Asuras," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 102.102 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, then those bulls among the Dānavas arrived at that level ground.
He spoke deeply to them all, like a lion to deer in a lonely place.
"O lords, all you Dānavas and Daityas of great strength,
fight once again most fiercely with me in battle, though I am but a deer."
O lords of the Dānavas, there is no shame in your approaching the battlefield;
yet either you possess no strength, or the gods were defeated by you only falsely.
"I am a powerful forest-dwelling deer, and I have many [followers].
O best of Dānavas, I do not believe that your minds are set upon a righteous battle."
"I possess no bow whatsoever, nor any weapon of that kind, with which I might fight against these many lords of the asuras who are equipped with weapons. (103.5)
If you all think thus, then lay down your weapons now;
standing firm in righteousness, fight me one by one.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, that Andhaka, lord of the Dānavas,
spoke to all the lords of the Daityas, roaring like a cloud at the end of an eon.
"It is even as this deer says, O great chariot-warriors of the Asuras:
'Let us all cast aside our weapons today, and let the warriors fight one by one.'"
Prahlāda said:
"O lords of the Daityas, this is a lack of wisdom, just as this lowest of deer [has spoken].
Among equals, it is praised for equals to engage in combat with one another. (103.9)
The deer possess neither weapons nor the strength of arms, yet they are constantly slain by weapons; this is considered the established law.
How can we, having abandoned our own duty as lords of the Dānavas, adopt the behavior of deer and fight like mere beasts? (103.11)
"This lowest of beasts is wicked; he is not to be slain by people such as us.
Let there be no consideration whatsoever regarding this deer on your part."
"Resorting to illusion, this certain evil-souled defiler of the gods, a Daitya of most wicked nature, desires to deceive us. (103.13)
O lords of the asuras, where have you heard or seen such hand-to-hand combat between deer and men in battle? (103.14)
This Viṣṇu is ill-behaved and evil-minded, a thorn to the Daityas;
being incapable by his own prowess, he remains here having resorted to illusion.
Sanatkumāra said: Thereupon, O Vyāsa, that powerful lord of the Asuras, filled with rage, overwhelmed him with many arrows from his bow and let out a great roar.
Andhaka and Vipracitti— all those Daityas and Dānavas—
showered him with sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Then the god, having been deeply pierced by those Dānavas who were violently enraged,
shone like the Himavat mountain when struck by the rays of the sun.
Having summoned a powerful impetus and shaking his sharp arrows,
the god proceeded with ease toward the Dānava Prahlāda.
Having gone there, he suddenly rendered both his charioteer and the chariot itself nothing more than a name,
using his tusks and his two hands.
Then, leaping down from his chariot even while being struck by the Dānavas,
the god struck that Daitya on the head with the chariot’s banner-staff.
Then Prahlāda also, springing up, struck the enraged [Hiraṇyakaśipu] on the chest with a mace of terrible form,
just as an obstacle strikes one established in righteousness.
Struck by him, the god then released his chariot and returned to that very place where he had previously been stationed.
Then Andhaka, Vipracitti, Śambara,
and Kālaśambara pierced Indravardhana with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
O Vyāsa, pierced then by those straight-knotted arrows and being split in many ways, he moved in circular maneuvers.
At times he leaps and roars like a lion,
and at times he casts himself upon the ground in battle like a tiger.
Having spread his bow, that hero of great prowess stood firm while enduring the arrows;
then, rising up on one foot, he shook them off like a bull.
Like a bird, that lord of beasts circled in the air in various patterns;
then the boar stood motionless, like a mountain.
Having thus traversed many kinds of paths, the one of great strength,
roaring aloud, seized both chariots with his two hands with sheer velocity.
The powerful Suprabha, having whirled both Vipracitti and Andhaka around for a moment along with their horses and chariots, [struck them].
Having lifted them up from the ground, he threw them down and again struck them with his foot;
and while they were standing upon their chariots, he struck them once more on the head.
Extremely enraged, those two raised their clubs and, rushing forward with speed,
struck Varāha on the head simultaneously and roared.
Powerful and enraged, with blood-red eyes, he seized those two maces with his hands by sheer force,
just as the lord of beasts seizes them.
Then Janārdana,
who was highly skilled with the mace, performed many various and wonderful circular maneuvers in perfect form.
The circle was drawn, then dispersed, and again not drawn;
it was raised up, then scattered, released, and likewise run.
The turned-back, the retreated, and also the half-moon; the fixed, the raised, and likewise the swan-whirled.
Skilled in the mace, having properly whirled it through various circular maneuvers,
he hurled the mace upward at Andhaka, making it resound.
And the powerful Nandivardhana [fought] against Aparā and Vipracitti;
those two Dānavas were exceedingly difficult to approach, wielding maces of great velocity.
Having deceived Varāha once more in battle, the two Dānavas rushed toward their destination like two winged creatures springing up with great speed.
As those two were still approaching, that mighty Varāha struck Andhaka with his fist and killed Vipracitti with his foot.
Andhaka and Vipracitti, both enraged, seized his fist and his foot respectively, crying out, "You are slain! (103.41).
Like two dark clouds thundering at the proper time,
those two then seized that high-souled one, the best of the gods.
Like Kāśyapa, the king of birds, he leapt into the sky with great speed;
standing in the air, that lord of beasts shone brightly as he bore the two Daityas aloft.
Like Garuḍa, the lord of birds, roaring in the sky and shaking his two wings, that powerful one [seized] the elephant and the tortoise for the sake of devouring them. (103.44)
And he hurled his foot at those two Daityas, who were like two serpents;
O Vyāsa, seeing those two Dānavas, intoxicated with the pride of battle, thus cast down, [he struck them].
The two of them rushed toward the earth like two terrible thunderbolts fallen from the sky;
and that powerful Lord of Gods, Varāha, the increaser of joy,
crushed the chariots of all the Daityas.
Seizing some by the forehead, he cast them into the great ocean;
striking others with his foot, he reduced them to union with the dust.
Having struck down a chariot with a chariot, a foot-soldier with a foot-soldier,
and an elephant with an elephant, he sent them to the abode of Yama.
Sanatkumāra said: All those tigers among the Daityas and Dānavas were likewise put to flight; overcome with the utmost shame, they retreated according to their strength.
Seeing one another’s faces, all those heroes, having been conquered by that single [boar], were filled with shame; they spoke again to the divine Varāha. || 103.50 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Battle with Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 103.103 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, those Dānavas, roaring fiercely, [pursued] that deer.
Then, filled with intense rage, they hacked at him violently with their weapons.
Like deer attacking a tiger or young elephants a lion,
those enraged Dānavas struck the Boar with showers of weapons.
And that tiger among deer, having sat down by the great ocean,
entered the waters and drank them in, like the submarine fire entering the mouth of the mare.
Then, opening his vast mouth wide, he swallowed the thousands of weapons hurled by those Daityas and let out a roar.
Having seized all those weapons,
that one of great strength rushed with speed toward the Dānavas like another ocean.
Just as a lion [overcomes] elephants, or the king of śarabhas [overcomes] lions, or as Garuḍa [overcomes] serpents, or as a tiger [overcomes] deer. || 104.6 ||
Just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds, or as the king of birds [Garuda] scatters pigeons,
so did that blessed Vyasa, the protector of the world, deal with the Dānavas.
He exerted such force that his mind was swiftly directed toward the senses;
and having reached those Daityas, he possessed a voice like the roar of a great cloud.
Like Rudra driving away herds of cattle, he put them all to flight;
being greatly enraged, he struck some with his feet and others with his hands.
There, with his fangs he sent others to the abode of Yama;
with his snout, he struck Śambara and Kālaśambara down to the earth.
He swiftly struck Naraka with a kick, Hayagrīva with his fist, Namuci with his chest, and Mahāmāya as well.
Striking them again and again, the enraged guardian of the gods felled them;
thus he drove them away while roaring like a lion.
Vipracitti struck that Varāha on the chest with his fist;
he, in turn, struck the fierce Vipracitti on the side of his body with his fist.
Struck by the boar, he, frantic with rage,
once again struck that boar in the chest with his sword, making it resound.
Unable to endure that blow,
the exceedingly powerful boar struck the Daitya on the head with his fist, which was like a thunderbolt.
Then, whirled like a wheel by that blow,
the Daitya fell violently upon the earth like a tree struck down by the wind.
Then, as Vipracitti,
the son of Diti, was fleeing, the Lord of Creatures, the God of gods, approached him as he fell and seized him by his two feet.
Then, having whirled him around and roared repeatedly, the powerful and great-souled Nandivardhana hurled him toward the city.
Hurled by him, that mighty lord of the Dānavas shone like a cloud severed by the lightning-flames of a thunderbolt.
With his pearl necklace and garments slipping off, and his garlands and ornaments falling away,
he fell with great force upon the palace of Hiraṇyākṣa.
O Vyāsa, that palace with its watchtowers, standing like a celestial chariot,
fell down being pulverized like a great mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, at that great sound, Hiraṇyākṣa himself,
the son of Diti and lord of the Dānavas, arrived with speed and beheld him.
That tiger among the Dānavas, being crushed by the boar,
became momentarily stunned by that very blow.
Then the king, the son of Diti, comforted him with cool water,
many palm-leaf fans, and jewels.
When the Daitya had recovered his breath, risen, and sat upon an excellent seat,
the king, overcome with great wonder, questioned him.
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "O Daitya, by whom today has the Himavat mountain, or the earth together with the oceans, been suddenly lifted up by one of great strength, as if by Viśvakarman? (104.26)
By whom has Mandara been cast down today? By whom has Death been defeated?
By whom have you, O Lord of the Dānavas, been hurled? Who is the powerful one on earth? || 104.27 ||
Just as the weighing of the earth, the shaking of Mount Mandara,
or the death of Death itself, so too is this great hurling of you.
Resembling Rudra, Indra, and Death, and terrifying to the world-protectors,
by whom have you been equaled in battle— like a strong man compared to one who is weak?
Whose is this inexhaustible power? By whom has such great strength been placed in his arms, renowned throughout the three worlds? O Lord of the Dānavas, let it be told.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, that exceedingly powerful Dānava sighed deeply and, looking at him again and again, spoke to him. (104.31)
Vipracitti said: "O King, O Lord of Daityas, this is superhuman, yet it surpasses even the gods and the Daityas; such a thing has never been seen or heard of anywhere."
"O King, such strength as that of Varāha is not found anywhere; indeed, I do not see anyone equal to that high-souled one. (104.33)
O Lord of Daityas, though being hacked by many missiles and weapons in battle, he felt neither pain nor suffering, nor did his consciousness fail him.
O King, for one who has been bitten even by a mosquito, there would be no relief;
yet for one who is slaying [the enemy], there is no fear from the Daityas or Dānavas.
Just as a lion [devours] small animals, or as a serpent [swallows] frogs,
so did he seize all those lords of the Daityas and Dānavas.
I do not consider that to be a deer, nor a god, nor even an asura;
it is surely some misfortune that has befallen the sons of Diti.
Struck on the head by that fist, I fell to the ground;
then, having been seized and suddenly lifted up, I landed upon your house.
"O Dānava, I do not know the whereabouts of the Dānavas, the Daityas, or the others; I believe they have all been slain."
"He is invincible, possessed of great splendor and strength, while we are weak.
Having heard this, do that which is for the benefit of the sons of Diti."
Upon her body all the sages are seen together with the gods;
it is my thought today that she has been created for your sake as a magical illusion (kṛtyā).
O Lord of Daityas, turn back your mind which is resolved upon battle,
and act for the benefit of the Daityas.
"He is powerful, while we Daityas are weak; he is immortal, whereas we are mortal.
He is unconquerable, yet the Daityas have been conquered [by him]. Do not involve us in battle."
"Having abandoned the city of Aśmaka, we have all taken refuge at Samudrastambha;
we remain here, O King—do not engage in battle with him again. (104.44)
"O Daitya, do not think in every way that this is merely a deer;
for even Narasiṃha was previously a deer, though he was empowered by him. (104.45)
"As long as you remain, O Daitya, bringing happiness to the Dānavas, so long shall all the Asuras continue to live; of this there is no doubt. (104.46)
"Let not the sons of Diti and the very foolish sons of Danu be provoked to anger;
O Lord of Asuras, let us depart from this city in every direction."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa spoke to the lord of the Dānavas, who was terrified of that great-souled one.
Without doubt, O best of Dānavas, that deer is a great-souled being by whom you, who are like Mount Mandara and possessed of immense strength, were weighed in the balance.
O bull among the asuras, four thousand very great divine years have passed while I have been enjoying sovereignty today.
When five times five [twenty-five] had arrived, even the gods were destroyed,
along with their hosts, as if they were powerless in many terrible battles.
Thus, though endowed with such power and having enjoyed a kingdom free from thorns,
how shall I remain like a serpent, having entered the water out of fear?
If that Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a deer, should take on the form of a boar, even so, O Lord of the Dānavas, let there be no fear; for that too shall be my task.
My strength, too, is inexhaustible, and for that reason I am powerful—
he who, out of fear of me, abandoned his own form and took on the state of a deer.
O Daitya of great strength, what need is there to speak of this mere deer, for he who could slay an elephant, a lion, or even a *śarabha* in battle—of him [this beast] would be no concern? 104.55.
Out of fear of me, that boar, presided over by all the gods, challenges me, O Lord of Daityas;
therefore, victory shall indeed be mine.
For you alone, O Daitya, are my messenger;
therefore, O bull among the Dānavas, go quickly to the world of mortals. (104.57)
"O Dānava, I swear by the truth that I shall not return without having slain him who killed my brother and who strikes terror into the Dānavas. (104.58)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having mounted the charioteer, he prepared the ready chariot;
to console his wives, he entered the house once more. (104.59)
Having had the auspicious rites performed for him there by those women, and having surveyed all those sons of Diti from every side,
the one of great strength took up everything that was radiant, fit for battle, and capable of warding off enemies.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Overthrowing of Vipracitti," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 104.104 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having equipped himself with a bow, armor, and bound on leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, he set forth.
With his quiver fastened to his back, carrying arrows and a sword, he was possessed of great strength.
With a tawny beard, four fangs, spike-like ears, and large jaws;
with arms reaching to his knees, long eyes, and a body as well-proportioned as a banyan tree. || 105.2 ||
He holds a lotus and a conch in his two hands, and a wheel and a fish in his two feet;
he has webbed hands, webbed feet, and small genitals.
With eyes resembling the rising sun and a complexion like a mountain of collyrium,
he then went forth, O Vyāsa, his face adorned with a frown.
And at the gate he saw the chariot prepared by the charioteer,
measuring a thousand nalvas in size and yoked with divine horses.
O Vyāsa, it was equipped with ten thousand [attendants], provided with all necessary implements,
furnished with a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and possessed a banner with the splendor of the sun.
Then, being addressed with cries of "Victory! by many Dānavas, he ascended like the divine Sun, the lord of splendors, ascending his chariot.
Mounted upon that chariot, the son of Diti then shone like a sapphire set within a golden vessel.
The crown upon his head shone with great brilliance,
like a forest fire situated on the peak of a mountain of collyrium.
And that Daitya urged his charioteer toward departure;
Vyāsa, Vipracitti was stationed at his side. (105.10)
Like a counter-image of a banner situated in the sky, [he was surrounded] by conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, tambourines, and flutes. || 105.11 ||
As musical instruments were being played, King Hiraṇyākṣa departed from the city of Aśmaka,
with [attendants] in front, behind, and on both sides.
All the asuras departed, O Vyāsa, like the planets before the sun;
and as they were leaving the city, birds appeared, foreboding fear.
Vyāsa saw that the lord of the Daityas did not take them to heart;
meanwhile, a serpent with a black body cut off his path. (105.14)
A vulture with a blood-red face perched upon the top of his banner;
and as his chariot moved along, the vulture wheeled in circles above it.
The great banner of the chariot, which possessed immense radiance, broke,
and the left side of his body throbbed again and again.
The horses did not neigh and the elephants lost their rut;
these and many other such things occurred, O best of sages, regarding the Daitya.
He repeatedly observed omens that portended danger for himself;
then, having gone out from the city not very far, he beheld the lord of beasts.
The Dānava beheld him fighting fearlessly in battle;
that illustrious chief of the Daityas, too, had his eyes bloodshot with rage.
Drawing his great bow, the mighty one rushed forward on his chariot;
the long-armed Varāha, having put the sons of Diti to flight,
charged with impetuous speed and fury toward Suvarṇākṣa.
As he was thus rushing forward, the exceedingly powerful Dānava swiftly loosed many sharp-pointed arrows into all his joints.
Pierced by those arrows in all his vital joints, O observer of noble vows, that lion did not waver; supported [by his own power], he stood firm. (105.22)
O Vyāsa, seeing that mighty one thus paralyzed,
the gods then rendered him free from the shafts by means of mantras that extract arrows.
Then, having been freed from the arrow by the gods, that great lord of beasts regained his speed and rushed once more toward the son of Diti.
Being struck by many arrows,
that great and imperishable lord of beasts approached the chariot of the lord of the Daityas and desired to seize it.
Making sounds as he seized it, O Vyāsa, he who assumes the universal form (Viśvarūpa) took up various positions;
and having formed a circle, the driver caused that chariot to whirl around.
The Daitya bound that exceedingly powerful deer with outstretched trunk using a serpent-weapon; thus bound, it fell to the ground.
And as he fell, the lord of the Daityas, their hands grasping various weapons,
exerting themselves intensely and overcome with manifold rage, struck him repeatedly.
Garuda swiftly liberated Nandivardhana from the lords of the serpents, even as he was bound, being struck, and fallen.
And having been released, that highly illustrious one then leapt up and, fleeing from the sons of Diti,
swiftly charged toward the chariot of Hiraṇyākṣa.
As he was running, O Vyāsa, the Daitya, roaring like a cloud, pierced him again in the heart with a straight-knotted arrow. (105.31)
And that lord of beasts, pierced in the heart, fell upon the ground, overcome by delusion, like the banner of Indra at the conclusion of a festival.
Then all the preeminent gods together cried out "Alas!
Alas!", while the sages offered hymns of praise; yet the Sun became devoid of luster.
Then, having been revived there by the sages who were most eminent in the knowledge of Brahman,
he regained consciousness and spoke these words.
"O gods, quicken me swiftly; I am utterly deluded.
This Daitya cannot be fought in battle by one of little prowess. (105.35)
Then all those deities and the sages whose wealth is asceticism completely gratified that god with their own austerity.
As he was being nourished by the sages and the deities,
his form shone with a splendor equal to the fire at the end of an eon or the god of death at the time of universal destruction.
Blazing with splendor, that great-souled one shone forth, praised by all the gods and the ṛṣis;
like seven suns, the god of gods then appeared radiant as if he were about to consume the worlds.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Nourishment of Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 105.105 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, although he was thus nourished, he became powerful and possessed the splendor of the sun.
Moving in circles, it was variegated, manifold, and swift.
Having performed leaps like a lion, he gazes repeatedly behind and before him; then again, he acts like an elephant.
Opening his mouth wide once more, he swallowed the weapons of his enemies;
then, with trees and rocks, he slaughtered the Dānavas.
Becoming a sky-traveler once more, he roamed about like the king of birds;
then, filled with rage, he laughed again, a sound resembling the crash of a thunderbolt.
And again, making himself subtle, he stood before him;
thus did the Dānava see him leaping and roaring.
With a face contorted by a frown, Hiraṇyākṣa spoke, making the air resound:
"O wretched beast, O evil-minded one, you shall not obtain liberation! (106.6)
"Having slain you by my own power, I shall offer you as a sacrifice to Rudra.
For by you, a wicked-souled man, my eldest brother was treacherously killed;
today you, that evil-minded one, have obtained the fruit of that deed."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of Hiraṇyākṣa in the encounter,
the Blessed Viṣṇu, proceeding with wrath, spoke to the son of Diti.
"That powerful Daitya was slain by me, that lion among men, after I displayed my prowess in battle; likewise, your own death is certain."
Even if you were to go to the sky, or to the netherworld, or beyond this, or even to a mountain or the ocean, you would still not be released.
"O Asura, whatever strength you possess, whatever ascetic power, and whatever magic you have—
that I shall today blow away from your body along with your life."
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"You were pinned by my arrow and released by the gods through their mantras;
and though you were again bound by a weapon, the king of birds liberated you. (106.12)
"O evil-minded one, you have died again and been restored to life by the gods;
yet I shall kill you once more, like a lion kills a deer in the wilderness. (106.13)
What power do you have here today, other than a boon from Maheśvara, even to touch me with your hand, like a man [attempting to touch] the sacrificial fire? || 106.14 ||
Having assumed this body composed of the elements and presided over by them all,
you have approached me in battle, having been fully nourished by them.
But I am endowed with my own ascetic power and strength;
nevertheless, you are not able to overcome me today, just as a deer cannot overcome a lion.
Whether to fight or even to advance together with the gods, that evil-minded one is no match for us; for this difference between the two of us is indeed very great.
He who is of noble birth or learned, and who stands firm on the path of the virtuous, should consider himself already victorious and thus abandon the battle. (106.18)
Who else but you could be so pitiless, shameless, a striker at vulnerable points, and possessed of such an evil soul? This does not belong to a mere beast, nor is it characteristic of a Daitya.
"You are not my death; rather, I am yours in this combat.
Let these thousands of Siddhas and Cāraṇas behold the difference between us as we fight in many ways in battle."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the enraged Hiraṇyākṣa struck the boar—who possessed the brilliance of a thunderbolt and lightning—with arrows resembling venomous serpents. (106.21)
Then, although being tormented by him, that exceedingly powerful boar,
filled with rage, rushed forward with speed, seized the chariot, and let out a roar.
Seizing him by the pole, the god dragged him along and tossed him up with great force; then, together with his horses and charioteer, he hurled him away and let out a roar.
But by his thrusts and side-blows, those horses had their traces severed;
they became wildly agitated, and the excellent chariot fell apart at its joints.
Then the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, abandoning his chariot and standing on foot with his bow,
struck the Lord of Beasts with a bewildering weapon.
Delusion entered that god Nandivardhana;
however, by the power of the mantras of the gods, his delusion was once again destroyed.
Indeed, this lord of the Daityas, filled with rage, struck him with various kinds of weapons;
yet he did not cause him any pain.
Then that immensely powerful boar, as if laughing,
uprooted a tree with speed and struck the Daitya on the head.
By that blow, as the Daitya was struck,
his bow fell away with force, along with his five-fingered hand-guard.
Then, crying out "Alas! Alas!", the deeply distressed Daityas and Dānavas, enraged, struck the Boar with many weapons. (106.30)
Being struck by those Daityas, that one of great strength opened his mouth wide;
he swallowed all their weapons and let out a roar.
Seeing him thus transformed, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa,
filled with rage, took up his trident while uttering a salutation to Rudra.
Then the enraged Daitya hurled a great trident of immense sound and exceeding brilliance, resembling the fire at the end of an eon, at the Boar.
Seeing him rushing forward, roaring in many ways, and vomiting forth flames and sparks, all the gods and hosts of Siddhas, their minds bewildered by fear, cried out, "Alas! Alas! (106.34).
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Hurling of the Trident," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 106.106 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
The deer did not see the spear as it was rushing toward him with great speed.
He was intent upon the alliance with the Daityas, which brought fear to all living beings.
Unobserved, O Vyāsa, that son of Indra was pierced in the heart by that spear and fell down, nearly dead.
Then, O best of sages, the invisible spirits cried out, "Alas!
Alas! The oceans overflowed their shores, and the sun became lusterless.
Meteors fell everywhere and the flowers of the gods withered;
there was a battle among the planets, and celestial chariots fell from the sky.
When Varāha had fallen, all the sages then cried out;
having paid homage to Mahādeva, Brahmā then called him to mind.
Then everything became free from darkness and beautiful as before;
having paid homage to Mahādeva, Varāha rose up.
The divine, Maheśvara-like splendor entered Madhusūdana;
his body invigorated by that, Mādhava drew forth his trident.
That mighty one suddenly became like fire;
then, with that very spear, the delighter of the gods [struck] that Daitya.
Enraged, he struck the Krauñca in the heart with a spear, just as Guha did;
that great asura, his heart pierced by that boar, [fell]. (107.9)
O Vyāsa, he did not suffer pain, remaining like a wise man in the midst of hardship;
having extracted that spear which was broken in the middle, he cast it away.
Drawing his sword with speed, he struck Varāha on the head;
by that powerful blow, Varāha Nandivardhana [fell]. || 107.11 ||
O Vyāsa, he did not suffer pain, nor was he drenched in blood;
rather, he became like the Himavat mountain, variegated with various minerals. || 107.12 ||
O observer of noble vows, the divine Varāha, the crusher of all asuras, shone forth as that Daitya desired to strike him once again.
With a blow of his open hand, he caused the sword to fall from [the other's] hand;
then both of them, skilled in wrestling, engaged in combat.
Like two elephants in a rage, like two buffaloes filled with pride,
like two lions roaring, and like two bulls in fury, those two were enraged.
Like two enraged śarabhas or like two pitiless tigers, they fought one another, each desiring victory over the other.
With goads, hand-ropes, lassos, and retreats;
and again with various maneuvers of drawing near, dragging, and pulling away.
With palms and fists, with arms and even feet, with nails and teeth, and likewise with other means, those two of great strength [struck one another]. (107.18)
Thus did the battle between those two, the gods and the Daityas,
continue for eighteen days and fourteen others as well.
There was another thousand of human years;
during that time, the Daitya became weakened. || 107.20 ||
Perceiving that powerful lord of the Daityas to be waning, a disembodied voice of exceedingly beautiful tone spoke these words in the sky: || 107.21 ||
Listen to this, O divine Boar, and having heard it, act accordingly;
for it is impossible for you to slay this exceedingly powerful Daitya in such a manner.
"Surely this cruel man has been rendered powerless by Maheśvara;
behold him indeed by his splendor, for his time has come."
"O Vaikuṇṭha, having released this king of the Daityas, slay him with the Cakra; then he shall meet his death by means of the Māheśvara weapon."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard him, the blessed Nandivardhana released the king of the Daityas, striking him on the chest with his foot.
Released by that god, that bull among the Daityas shone like the sun released from its eclipse by Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā.
The Blessed One, beholding that Daitya blazing with splendor,
then called to mind his discus, having paid homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then, O Vyāsa, all the directions appeared like fire-pits,
and there arose a tremendous sound resembling the clouds at the end of an eon.
The perfected ones (siddhas) fell to the earth and fear entered the gods;
then the sages cried out, "May it be well with all beings! (107.29).
The oceans dried up; the nāgas and birds perished;
and all the daityas and dānavas likewise entered their subterranean lairs.
Terrified by fear, living beings dropped torches from the sky as the brilliantly shining discus approached like the fire at the end of an eon.
That great wheel had edges like razors, it was the end-maker for aquatic creatures submerged within it;
it was difficult to behold, all-devouring, impenetrable, and obstructive.
Likewise, the divine, irresistible,
and deluding tusk of the Boar, which produced a sound like a hundred thunderbolts, came forth.
Beholding that most terrible [weapon] falling from every direction, all beings fell to the ground; they saw nothing at all.
Then that god, having assumed an immense and imperishable form that pervaded the three worlds, hurled it at the Dānava while making a roar.
Resembling the fire at the end of an eon, with edges as sharp as razors, it tore through the sky and swiftly pursued the Dānava, as if burning all the quarters of space.
Then that tiger among Dānavas, remaining unperturbed, struck the approaching Mahāraṇa with various kinds of missiles, O son of Śakti.
And that [weapon], O Vyāsa, reduced those great discuses and missiles, which resembled fire, to ashes; then it departed, making a great roar.
Then he created an illusion consisting of fire and earth,
as well as that of wind and water, and one of darkness whose essence was the senses.
In that very same way, he created illusions in the battle capable of causing flight, delusion, and paralysis, as well as those for turning back the enemy, crushing them, and others;
all of these were then destroyed by that wheel, which emitted a terrifying roar.
Having gone there, he tore his head from the body as if it were a mountain.
That immense head, with its foremost eye, resembling fire within a gaping mouth,
possessing fangs and emitting a most extraordinary and terrifying roar, was severed by him and fell like a lofty peak of Mount Meru.
His face, its form pressed by the rims of the chariot wheels, shone with no luster and appeared exceedingly dejected,
like the disc of the moon, devoid of rays, at the end of the night.
Biting his own row of teeth as if they were a mirror, and repeatedly gnashing his teeth,
the severed head of the Daitya fell like a massive peak from a mountain.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Skandapurāṇa 108.
Sanatkumāra said:
When that Daitya had been slain, all the gods offered their praises.
And sages endowed with ascetic power fell down, and showers of flowers descended.
Invisible celestial drums resounded with a great sound; there was peace for all beings, and the world shone in its natural state. 108.2.
Then the discus vanished from sight, and the gods, the sages, and all the worlds were restored to well-being; they beheld that Daitya slain.
All those Asuras also, having diligently closed the city gates on every side, stood ready for battle upon the ramparts.
Terrified, with disheveled hair, covered in dust, and afflicted by fear,
they stood upon the ramparts then, seeking to preserve their lives.
The Blessed One, like a fire kindled by oblations with blazing flames,
searched the earth while terrifying all the asuras.
Having searched everywhere outside and uprooted the trees,
he sought her on all sides like a cowherd searching for a lost cow.
Then, uprooting the mountains, he pulverized the gardens of the Daityas;
he destroyed the groves and the ponds, and let out a roar.
Then, having gone to the south for a moment, that best of gods reached Mount Śaṅkha and roared like a rain-cloud.
For even the Asuras, standing within the inner walls, watched in fear as that lord of beasts rushed toward them from every direction.
Then that god, having uprooted the excellent mountain Śaṅkha,
beheld the earth bound and guarded by the Dānavas.
Having cast that supreme mountain, Śaṅkha, into the waters of the ocean,
he slew all the Dānavas who were the protectors of the earth.
Then, having put the lords of the nāgas to flight and forcibly seized the earth,
he went forth, having delighted the Daityas and taken all kinds of jewels.
Carrying her, who was caught upon the tip of his fang,
that lord of beasts shone like a king of elephants carrying a hanging lotus stalk caught upon his tusk.
Carrying her through the midst of the ocean, he shone like the Lord of Beasts in the form of a boar,
as Brahmā once did with the earth at the end of the age.
Having crossed over the ocean, the Blessed One Nandivardhana established that earth once again in its own place.
Then that slayer of Madhu gave the three worlds to Śakra and said,
"O sinless one, you are our king today, and I am your friend."
Whatever other enemies there may be who become lords of the asuras, I shall undoubtedly carry out their terrible slaughter as well. (108.18)
Then all the sages and the deities, together with Indra, assuming their own forms, said to him: "Become as you were before."
Varāha said:
"O gods, this form was obtained by me, who possess supreme splendor;
yet no pleasure worthy of me has been found by me through it on this earth."
"Having spent some time here in happiness with this form, I shall become a god once again; I tell you this truly. (108.21)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, all the gods, together with Indra, circumambulated him and departed for their respective abodes in every direction. || 108.22 ||
When the hosts of gods had departed, the Blessed One Nandivardhana dwelt there in happiness, having slain that foremost of Dānavas.
There, thousands of radiant Vedic Apsarases appeared before him in the form of does; he took his pleasure together with them.
Wandering with them, that high-souled god Nandivardhana took his pleasure like a rutting great elephant with female elephants in the forest.
Like a lion with lionesses or a tiger roaring aloud,
he took his pleasure on the coastal marshlands like a second Airāvata elephant.
As he was sporting there, the Siddhas and the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
stationed in the sky, caused showers of beautiful flowers to fall.
Others constantly offered praise and circumambulated him; all the celestial drums resounded incessantly.
Then the Apsarases danced before this Boar,
while the Gandharvas played instruments and sang for the Great-Souled One.
The gods, led by Indra, as well as the Yakṣas who generate merit and those who are the folk of the gods, delighted that Boar.
Whatever Yātudhānas there may be, and all the Brahmadhānas, as well as humans, animals, and sages in their entirety— 108.31.
All the kṣatriyas, the rājanyas, and all the various guilds from every quarter came there, beholding the auspicious festival of the boar.
O Vyāsa, for that high-souled Varāha, there was always a great, divine festival filled with many wonders and many sights, which increased joy on every single day. (108.33)
Its lake was frequented by hosts of seers, and always resorted to by gods, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, rākṣasas, and vidyādharas together with the apsarases. (108.34)
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Festival of Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 108.108 ||
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Śakti, as he was sporting for a long time, Skandapurāṇa 109.1.
A son named Vṛka was born to his wife Citralekhā. || 109.1 ||
That powerful wolf, constantly roaming this earth, roared and slew hundreds of beings in the world as he grew great. || 109.2 ||
Then he reached the great mountain Himavat,
the lord of mountains, near Gaurīkūṭa, at the auspicious abode of Kārttikeya.
Not recognizing him, he then approached with force and insolence,
making the bright trees adorned with jewels and gold resound.
They yield flowers and fruits in all seasons and grant every desire;
they are white, made of stone and jewels, as well as of gold.
And other stones of green vitriol and red arsenic he likewise uprooted again and again with force and shattered, as if enraged.
Constantly roaring like another elephant in rut,
he shattered that beautiful forest belonging to the wise Kārttikeya.
At the sound of his roaring and the noise of the destruction of the forest,
the heroic leader of the Gaṇas emerged from Skanda’s abode.
Known as Kokavaktra, a firm favorite of Skanda,
that high-souled and powerful being went and gazed upon Vṛka.
Having seen him— of massive body, youthful, and pleasing to behold—
roaring like a cloud with his face slightly flushed with anger.
With a joyful heart, Kokavaktra spoke these words as if laughing:
"Whose son are you, a child who has arrived here at this auspicious temple of the gods? (109.11)
"Do you not know that this is the residence of the great-souled Skanda, frequented by the gods along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kiṃnaras? (109.12)
Having performed what was exceedingly dear and being highly honored by the Gaṇas as well,
Kumāra departed for Mandara together with all the lords of the Gaṇas.
"Having stationed me here for the sake of protection, I shall therefore ward off those [enemies] from you;
for I am pleased with your beauty, your strength, and likewise your form. (109.14)
"Rest, O you of great strength; for this reason I tell you:
I shall restore that which has been broken, exactly as it was before."
O Lord of Śūkara, for your sake I shall fully describe that god, so that he may not be angry with you and may grant you his grace. (109.16)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Vṛka, the lord of beasts, with eyes bloodshot with rage, then spoke these words to Kokavaktra. || 109.17 ||
I do not fear you, O prince, nor this evil-minded one;
for this prince, together with his hosts and lords, is not my equal in strength. || 109.18 ||
Whatever strength and pride you possess, display it without hesitation;
I shall leave you with nothing but your names at the end of this forest.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having uprooted a golden tree with leaves of lapis lazuli,
he hurled it at Kokavaktra and bellowed like a bull.
Then, laughing, Kokāsya seized that very tree and,
filled with rage, struck Vṛka on the head with it.
Having whirled in a circle due to that powerful blow,
the deer fell senseless upon the ground like the great banner of Śakra.
Then, seeing him fallen, Kokāsya laughed and bound him with many nooses, leading him into his house.
Seeing him bound and fallen, all those deer who were his companions fled suddenly, afflicted by fear and desiring to save their lives.
Then, at that time, Kārttikeya arrived, surrounded by many leaders of his hosts, accompanied by his followers and his warbling peacock.
Kokavaktra, the lord of the Gaṇas, related that to him and showed him the mighty Vṛka bound with nooses.
Kokavaktra said:
"O Blessed One, the illustrious Vṛka was indeed the son of the one who assumed the form of a boar;
he was the one by whom the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa, the thorn of the gods, was slain. (109.27)
"This evil-minded one, together with his companions, has destroyed your grove;
therefore, he has been bound by me with snares—now do what must be done next."
Skanda said:
"I cannot release this lowest of the deer-kind here today;
if I were to release him, I would incur reproach in the world, of this there is no doubt."
"The god will surely speak to me; it is Skanda, undoubtedly afraid, he who released his son, the boar, though he had committed an offense. (109.30)
"I have been told by Sthāṇu, the Supreme Self, that I have gone today;
do not show him mercy, for he might call you to take on the form of a boar. (109.31)
And this exceedingly radiant power was bestowed upon me by him today;
it is renowned as Saṃvartikā, the destroyer of the strength of all weapons.
"Therefore, let this evil-souled one of wicked conduct, who oppresses the whole world,
be seized and swiftly executed by force once he has been exposed."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all the leaders of Skanda’s hosts bound him outside with various kinds of nooses and tormented him by the thousands.
Being dragged along, afflicted by suffering, he lamented like a man of evil conduct dwelling in hell, tightly bound by his own deeds. (109.35)
Seeing him being pursued, Nārada, of great ascetic merit,
went and informed that Varāha of immeasurable soul.
"This son of yours, Vṛka, bound by numerous nooses, is being led away like a wicked man by the servants of Kārttikeya. (109.37)
"Indeed, Skanda does not show deference to you, O Lord, who are striving for the sake of the world, because of his childish nature and his anger. (109.38)
Or rather, Skanda considered himself stronger than you;
therefore, he bound his own son with your nooses. (109.39)
