Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, before he has caused his death, you must go and set him free without delay. (109.40)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, Varāha, the increaser of joy, with his face flushed with rage, roared like a cloud at the end of time. || 109.41 ||
Then, from his anger, an exceedingly brilliant fire issued forth from both his eyes,
as if destroying the entire world with its splendor.
Rising suddenly from his seat and casting a piercing gaze upward, the Lord himself, like a lord of beasts, set out for the divine peak of Gaurī.
Making the entire earth tremble while being praised by great beings,
and beholding the portents that had arisen, he proceeded unimpeded.
As that god was going along, a serpent cut his path;
and a fang, having struck a tree, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Blood flowed from his mouth and his heart trembled;
fear arose within him as he was struck by that forceful impact.
The winds blew contrary to him as he fell to the earth upon his chest;
and as he remembered his beloved, an intense longing arose within him.
Disregarding these and many other such portents indicative of danger, that mighty lion among men proceeded on his way. (109.48)
Seeing him set forth, O observer of noble vows, and observing the auspicious omens,
the gods of the celestial realm prepared their offerings.
Followed by hosts of Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and great serpents,
as well as by throngs of Rākṣasas, Cāraṇas, and Kiṃnaras, that high-souled one went to the peak of Gaurī.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Binding of Vṛka," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 109.109 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Kumāra, having emerged from his own delightful abode, also departed.
He took delight together with the lords of his hosts through many auspicious games.
The Lord brought that son of Varāha as well;
releasing Vṛka from his bonds, the omnipresent one let him go while smiling.
He seized again with great speed the boar as it was released and running away;
letting him go once more, he caught him again and again.
Thus he sported with him, and the boar approached him.
Seizing a massive rock, he, enraged like the God of Death,
hurled it at Kārttikeya, making a sound like a thundercloud.
As she came rushing through the air, roaring in many ways, her form resembling Death itself and possessing extreme velocity like a blazing meteor, Kokāmukha seized her with great speed. || 110.5 ||
Then the Lord hurled a thousand-spoked wheel, radiant as the fire at the end of an eon,
at the undistracted host of Vināyaka.
Then that discus, resembling the end of time and the slayer of all enemies of the gods, quickly entered along with its attendants; thereafter, it turned back.
Then Viṣṇu did not seize that wheel which had turned back, nor did he make a brilliant effort; rather, he disregarded it at that time. (110.8)
Then that discus, unworshipped by Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Dānavas, quickly departed toward its own abode. || 110.9 ||
When that wheel had thus passed away, the Lord Nandivardhana,
having uprooted a tree with great force, struck the prince.
Disregarding that blow, the Blessed One, the son of Agni,
in a fit of rage hurled the Saṃvartikā spear and let out a roar.
Scorching as it were all splendors and roaring in many ways at that time,
the spear sped forth like a divine arrow to slay the boar.
The Blessed One Nandivardhana, roaring like a king of lions, swiftly struck that Āpamantī with many kinds of missiles.
Having reduced them to ashes, that auspicious Saṃvartikā spear entered his heart like a firm and beloved mistress.
With his heart pierced by her through that supreme yoga, he, like a yogin, abandoned that body and remained with another body. (110.15)
Having assumed another body, that best of gods,
surrounded by all the deities, went to the abode of Bhava.
There he beheld Mahādeva, wearing a crown of matted locks,
who dispelled the mass of darkness with the flood of rays from the crescent moon.
Seated upon a noble golden throne adorned with jewels,
he was shining exceedingly with splendor, with Pārvatī stationed at his side.
He was constantly surrounded on all sides by many hosts of diverse forms who could assume any shape at will and were ever fond of dance and song.
Having beheld Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, with a serene inner soul,
praised him with various hymns and spoke these words in a melodious voice.
O Blessed One, having assumed the form of a boar and exerting my prowess in battle through the strength augmented by your splendor, Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by me.
O Lord, you are the eternal cause of both creation and dissolution;
by you, whose form is unmanifest, this entire world is pervaded.
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace, Brahmā, I myself, and Śakra, as well as the other inhabitants of heaven, are constantly honored in the world. (110.23)
O Mahādeva, O Lord, when you are pleased, we all are pleased;
if you are angry, our destruction will surely follow—of this there is no doubt. (110.24)
To Viṣṇu, who was thus praising him, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara— the moon-crested one possessing the splendor of a thousand suns— spoke with delight.
"I am pleased with your devotion, O Viṣṇu, and with your exertion for the sake of the gods' purpose.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever resides in your heart. (110.26)
Viṣṇu said: "O God, if you are pleased with us, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then you ought to prescribe that divine vow which removes all sin. (110.27)
Relying upon whom we all, together with Śakra, shall be freed from suffering and grief and conquer the Daityas in battle, achieving every desire.
The God of gods said:
"Behold, I shall declare to you this eternal secret, the divine Pāśupata vow, by which you shall attain all your desires. (110.29)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods, desiring the welfare of the deities,
took his leave of the goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, and departed for heaven.
Then the Lord Śarva, whose beautiful form is like the snowy mountain, mounted his excellent bull; accompanied by the hosts of gods, the Master set out for Sumeru, intent on imparting the vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Departure of the God of Gods to the World of the Devas upon the Withdrawal of the Boar Form during the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Skanda Purāṇa 111.
Vyāsa said:
When Mahādeva had gone to heaven to prescribe the supreme vow,
What did the Great Queen do next when she was all alone? || 111.1 ||
Sanatkumāra said: When Mahādeva had gone to heaven, the illustrious goddesses, the mothers of the world, approached the Goddess, the daughter of the best of mountains. || 111.2 ||
The daughter of Agni, Bharata, is renowned as Mālinī;
and Śucāvatī is the imperishable daughter of the god Parjanya.
Sāvitrī, Devamātā, Gāyatrī along with Durgā, as well as Śrī, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, and likewise Prajñā. || 111.4 ||
Khyāti, Diti, Danu, Aditi, Siṃhikā, Khaśā, Rākā, Kuhū, Sinīvālī, and likewise the auspicious Anumati. || 111.5 ||
The Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī, as well as other auspicious rivers;
the wives of the ṛṣis, and those of the gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
and likewise those of the uragas, birds, and gandharvas. || 111.6 ||
Having approached and paid homage to Pārvatī, all these women, who were knowers of all dharma and devoted to the purpose of dharma, questioned her regarding dharma. || 111.7 ||
"By what dharma or by what austerity, O Lord of Gods, O lady of auspicious countenance, is very great merit obtained? And what is proclaimed to be inexhaustible? (111.8)
The Goddess said:
"O you of excellent vows, for the sake of your own welfare and that of the worlds, I shall explain the Dharma exactly as it is, in due order. (111.9)
Indeed, there is no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of food;
for all beings arise from food, and therefore it is remembered as the most excellent. 111.10.
He who, having prepared food with great care, bestows it upon a twice-born man,
obtains all his desires and is honored in heaven.
The giver of food indeed goes to heaven in a celestial chariot that is yoked with peacocks and swans, which fulfills all desires and possesses the brilliance of the sun.
If that best of men should ever return to the human state,
he will be of noble birth, handsome, and possessed of abundant wealth and grain.
But that man who gives according to his ability day after day,
by that deed he attains the same world as Prajāpati.
Even if one should give food that has been consecrated with mantras only once,
for him that merit shall be a hundredfold and even a thousandfold.
He attends upon [beings] in the worlds, and even here he shall be happy, though he be disregarded, despised, or even treated with disrespect. (111.16)
O auspicious goddesses, whatever kind of food one gives, even if it be of such a nature,
he goes to a terrible hell while being driven by rākṣasas.
If that man should ever return to the human state again, he would attain manifold satisfaction through whatever [merit] has been produced for him. || 111.18 ||
Among the Mlecchas he becomes an enjoyer and delights like an immortal; for food is indeed distinguished in this way, and there is nothing superior to it on earth. 111.19
Food is declared to be Prajāpati, and he is considered to be the year;
the year is the sacrifice, and in that sacrifice everything is established.
From that arise all beings, both stationary and moving;
therefore, food is indeed superior to all things—such is the sacred revelation (Śruti). 111.21.
Indeed, there is no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of food;
for all beings arise from food, and therefore that gift is highly praised.
Listen to the fruit of the gift of one who bestows upon brahmins water that is fragrant, cool, and endowed with divine flavors. (111.23)
Having ascended a celestial chariot resembling the sun and resounding with the voices of throngs of Apsarases,
he goes to heaven, to dwell in the same world as Varuṇa.
Having dwelt there for eighty thousand years, happy like a god,
he is born into a great, unadulterated family, possessed of wealth and grain.
He who gives a vessel full of water to a Brāhmaṇa finds that essences attend him, and having gone to heaven, he is honored there.
And he who gives vessels that are well-filled, O fair-faced ones,
shall become a vessel of enjoyments and shall deliver his ancestors from fear.
He who constructs a prosperous reservoir of water,
wherein all living beings indeed drink the waters, O goddesses of the waters— (111.28)
And having delivered his fathers,
as well as his grandfathers and great-grandfathers, that bird [resided] among the worlds of the Kāmikas.
For six hundred thousand years he lived like a god among goddesses;
and again, in the world of men, he was entirely free from all diseases.
He becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and is born as a king;
he is a donor, a performer of sacrifices, powerful, radiant, and pleasant to behold. (111.31)
O women of pure smiles, that man who should dig a pit and fill it with water, and then feed the Brahmins there according to the prescribed rules, [attains great merit]. || 111.32 ||
It was adorned with eight variegated banners,
and further embellished with a victory-standard and flowers.
Having delivered his ancestors, that best of men travels in a celestial chariot to the world of Varuṇa, while being sung to by Apsarases.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who would give gold, or wealth, or land, or sesame seeds, or even jewels, to all living beings. || 111.35 ||
Accompanied by his entire retinue, he reaches the world of Indra in a great celestial chariot and rejoices like a god.
And having fallen from there, that righteous-souled one, possessing the fulfillment of all desires,
is born into a great family in this world and becomes truly fortunate.
But that man, O gentle lady, who plants a tree on a path that provides shade, flowers, and fruit, truly delivers his ancestors from the world of Yama. (111.38)
In the same way, having given [the land] to the Brahmins and having redeemed it again, listen, O you of great splendor, to the fruit that man obtains. (111.39)
As long as embodied beings make use of the tree's flowers,
and once it has borne fruit, its fruits are eaten by living creatures.
Having delivered even his ancestors for as many thousands of years as there are syllables,
he reaches the world of Soma and shall obtain the fruit of immortality.
He who, with a concentrated mind, should offer fruits to Brahmins,
shall indeed partake in many fruits and become fortunate.
O Goddesses, that best of men who provides firewood to Brahmins during the winter season attains the world of Agni.
He who offers a vessel made of gold and adorned with jewels rejoices in heaven upon a celestial chariot crowded with hundreds of apsarases.
He who bestows auspicious silver vessels upon the Brahmins,
having attained the realm of the Gandharvas, rejoices together with Urvaśī.
He who gives a copper vessel, especially to Brāhmaṇas,
shall become a Yakṣa endowed with strength under the king of the Yakṣas.
He who bestows a house endowed with the fulfillment of all desires,
having reached the world of Brahmā, is served by all objects of desire.
Having dwelt there for four entire kalpas by virtue of that deed,
he is born as a householder who is both a donor and possessed of enjoyments.
He who bestows medicinal herbs and various kinds of grain attains the world of Soma, which is purified by the fulfillment of all desires.
Having remained there for seven thousand years,
that man is then born again here, endowed with all wealth and possessed of enjoyments.
But he who bestows a field that is already productive and bears fruit,
having become a lord of fields, attains the realm of Prajāpati.
But he who bestows land upon a high-souled Brahmin shall be happy in all the worlds, traveling in a resplendent celestial chariot.
For many thousands of years he wanders, able to assume any form at will;
yet, through the turning of time, that man eventually returns to human birth.
In that regard, for him who, being of great renown, bestows a garment upon a brahmin, the earth becomes a cow of plenty for him in every respect. (111.54)
Having attained the world of Virāj, he shall dwell in happiness for ten million years,
he who indeed offers a covered seat to a Brāhmaṇa.
That best of men who provides a well-spread bed attains a position of sovereignty and reaches heaven, free from all distress.
He enjoys many beloved wives who are goddesses and devoted to him;
and he who bestows a well-adorned maiden upon a Brāhmaṇa— (111.57)
Having gone to the world of the ancestors, he shall indeed dwell there for a hundred thousand years;
and being born again here, he will be endowed with all his desires fulfilled.
He obtains wives and devoted followers, and he is born with many offspring—this is the result for one who bestows a horse that is adorned with gold and possesses auspicious marks. (111.59)
By that deed, he enjoys the world of the Gandharvas among the goddesses;
[he obtains] a chariot, a horse, an elephant, a female slave, a maiden, and even a house.
And he who bestows land is born as a king upon the earth.
Through the ritual accompanied by mantras, his reward of merit is great;
that [earth] stands before him as a cow that milks all desires.
And he who gives a water-cow obtains the great fruit of that gift by providing auspicious drinking water,
or a pond, or even a well that is very abundant.
Having filled the jars to the brim and adorned them with perfumes and garlands,
and having honored the best of the twice-born with various kinds of flowers.
When they have been well-satiated with various kinds of food and drink, one should cause them to be given vessels of sesame seeds;
one should give them abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and then cause them to touch those [vessels].
May the auspicious and gentle waters satisfy my ancestors;
may the ancestors always be granters of desires and move according to my will.
Having thus given that cow, and having then purchased it back,
one should cause that water-shed to be used, O goddesses, which bestows the world of Brahmā.
And having given sesame vessels, as well as a pair of new garments, the presence of gold, and various kinds of fruits; || 111.68 ||
Then, having bathed and become pure, one should give to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
Cows produce ghee; ghee is established upon the earth.
Ghee is Agni and the gods; let ghee be bestowed upon me.
Having given in this manner according to the prescribed rule, a man who bestows a cow together with her calf and a bronze milking vessel shall attain the world of Brahmā.
With golden horns and silver hooves, draped in fine linen and silk,
provided with excellent bedding and coverlets, and endowed with many flowers and fruits.
After the Brahmins had been gratified, at the time of her being given away, she was adorned with perfumes and garlands; then the gods took refuge within her limbs.
Brahmā stands upon her head; Śakra is situated in her anus;
the moon and sun reside in her eyes; and Vāyu is established in her nose.
Fire took refuge in her mouth, and the Lord Soma himself in her tongue;
all the quarters of space resided in her ears, and the Rudras took shelter in her veins.
All the world-protectors are in his two feet, and the mountains are his bones;
the seven oceans are in his belly, and the suns are situated in his neck.
The Ganges, the best of rivers, is her dewlap; the auspicious Vasus dwell on her two flanks;
Prajāpati is her udder, and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) are her urine. (111.77)
Her feces became Śrī, and from her, the Nāgas and all weapons emerged in every way; the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the worlds remained situated, taking refuge in her tail.
The mantras, sacrifices, gifts, and restraints, together with the sages; the lunar mansions, the planets, and all those things that exist in the form of stars—[all these were created by him].
The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Paṅkti;
likewise the Anuṣṭubh, the Ṛg, the Yajus, the Sāmans, and the Atharvaṇa.
The mothers of the world, the clouds, and the rain; Dharma, Tārāyaṇa, all living beings, and likewise the rivers. || 111.81 ||
Resorting to her pores, the gods are stationed there,
as are the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and the piśācas, together with the birds.
Sacrifices and sacrificial fees, as well as beautiful Apsarases, high-souled Gandharvas, and others of this kind. || 111.83 ||
O Vyāsa, all the fruits of sacrifices and gifts, as well as the various types of destinies, are entirely supported by the two horns of that [cow]. (111.84)
All [the sages] took refuge in Vatsa, who was entirely composed of the auspiciousness of the gods;
he was presided over by the deities and honored by all the worlds.
With a well-composed mind, he should place into the hands of the Brahmins, accompanied by the sacred mantras,
kusha grass, gold, seeds, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds.
Then, O observer of noble vows, one should give a cow along with water while reciting this mantra—a cow who embodies all the gods and likewise embodies all the worlds. (111.87)
"For the sake of all the world as its sign, and for the welfare of all the world, I bestow this auspicious [gift] upon the Great Beings for the sake of the inexhaustible. || 111.88 ||
Having thus given that cow, wherever he is born,
there she goes and delivers that person from fear.
It is indeed the cow that milks all desires, likewise the bestower of all worlds;
it is the giver of all knowledge, and likewise the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having gone to all the worlds by means of her, he rejoices like an immortal; and being born here, he likewise attains that very same woman who moves at will.
Born from her, he becomes a human being endowed with a thousand cows, possessed of great strength, handsome, wealthy, and having many sons.
He who gives a cow that is in the process of giving birth, with both mouths [the mother and the calf],
according to the prescribed injunctions, shall obtain the memory of his past lives.
But he who bestows a cow upon Brahmins according to the prescribed rule—
he too that Lord protects from fear and even from hell.
He who gives a black antelope skin to a vow-observing celibate student obtains the fruit of the earth, and yoga proceeds for him.
He who, self-restrained, bestows a dwelling upon yogis, celibate students, and Brahmins,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
O you of excellent vows, having attained supreme memory, he obtains the Āptoryāma sacrifice, the Pauṇḍarīka, and a thousand cows, and he attains yoga.
O goddesses, that best of men who gives a water-pot to a brāhmaṇa attains eternal righteousness through that deed.
O brahmin-sage, he who rescues to the best of his ability one who is diseased, miserable, deluded, and senseless, shall be liberated from the sin of killing a brahmin.
O deities, he who bestows gold upon a poor twice-born man obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
O Goddesses, he who gives all these gifts that have been described in their entirety simultaneously shall become the sole sovereign on earth.
O highly fortunate ones, whoever should constantly hear this, give it according to their ability,
and recite it, shall also go to the third heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 111.111 ||
In this very way, through fasting, dharma is attained. || 112.1 ||
O Goddess, he who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa eating but a single meal a day shall,
by that deed, O Goddess, always become possessed of cattle.
By performing [the rite] in the month of Pauṣa, one obtains many righteous sons;
and by doing so in the month of Māgha, one further attains beloved ones.
One who constantly observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Phālguna attains good fortune among women, and women become most dear to him.
That best of men who passes the month of Caitra eating but one meal a day shall be born handsome and into a family abundant in wealth and grain.
The man who passes the month of Vaiśākha eating but a single meal per day goes to the world of the most excellent beings, honored and possessed of wealth.
He who observes the practice of eating only one meal a day for the month of Jyeṣṭha-mūla becomes the eldest among his brothers and attains abundant enjoyment.
He who observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Āṣāḍha shall attain honor from kings and obtain abundant desires.
And that man who likewise observes this vow during the month of Śrāvaṇa,
having attained the position of a general, is born powerful.
O Goddesses, he who observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Bhādrapada is born wealthy as a result of that deed.
Furthermore, for one who subsists on a single meal during the month of Āśvayuja,
his trade bears fruit, as do his agriculture and his herds of cattle.
He who passes even the month of Kārttika eating but one meal a day attains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Agni.
That best of men who passes his entire life subsisting on a single meal per day goes to the world of Śakra in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun. 13.
He who subsists on a single meal for a full year becomes equal to a king and protects the earth like the great Indra.
If a supreme man observes a fast for one day and night,
he obtains the auspicious fruit of ten pieces of gold.
That best of men who observes a fast for one day and night every month becomes pure through that deed; he becomes wise and righteous.
He who passes a full year without exception, fasting for a day and night on both the fourteenth and the eighth days of each fortnight; || 112.17 ||
Endowed with that karma and freed from all evil,
O goddesses, he does not go to hell, nor does he behold Yama.
The wise man who performs a three-night fast every month,
having reached the realm of Kubera, shall find supreme happiness.
The man who, being self-restrained and pure, eats on the fourth day,
attains the station of the Gandharvas and rejoices in heaven like Śakra.
He who eats on the fifth day of every month without weariness,
having reached the world of Vāyu, goes to the heavenly world.
He who, established in his vow, always eats on the sixth day,
having reached the world of Varuṇa, shall also find the great state.
He who eats on the seventh day, having conquered the pairs of opposites and being firm in his vow,
reaches the world of the Sun and shall find the great state.
And the man who, being pure, eats on the eighth day itself,
having reached the world of Viṣṇu, shall become possessed of supreme luster.
The man who, established in his observance, eats on the ninth day,
becomes dear to the Vasus and wanders together with the Vasus.
Having eaten on the tenth day, one obtains the fruit of ten days;
becoming equal to the two Aśvins, one always blazes like the sun.
Furthermore, having attained human birth again, he obtains ten wives;
he possesses inexhaustible gold and does not die an untimely death.
But the pure man who eats on the eleventh day,
having obtained the fruit of Ekādaśī, shall attain the status of being a member of Rudra’s retinue.
Having remained there for eight hundred years, endowed with supreme happiness,
he attains the status of a Brahmin and is born here as a performer of sacrifices.
That man who always eats on the twelfth day,
having reached the world of Śakra for twelve days, shall attain it.
Having dwelt there in happiness, that best of men is born again here as either a king,
a royal official, or a very great archer.
But the man who always eats on the thirteenth day shall dwell in the abode of Bhārgava, endowed with divine happiness.
If that person is born again as a human being,
he is born auspiciously into a noble family, well-supplied with wealth and grain.
But the man who constantly spends fourteen days [in this manner],
having reached the world of Tushita, shall become an excellent lord of the hosts (Gaṇapati).
He who passes half a month always thus, without weariness,
becomes equal to the king of the gods and dwells in heaven.
In this world, a king is born again and again as a great sovereign on earth—
he who, being wise, has spent a month with anger conquered and the senses subdued.
Surrounded by celestial nymphs in a divine chariot,
he was honored like a god and praised from every side.
Blazing like the sun, he enjoys eternal happiness and dwells in all the worlds for many tens of thousands of years.
Then, having reached the assembly of Brahmā and being highly honored by Brahmā himself,
that best of men dwelt in the world of Brahmā just like Brahmā.
But if he returns again, he becomes a lordly Brahmin;
he attains yoga therein and enjoys the sovereignty of yoga.
Then, having become a lord of yogis, he shall become a leader of Śambhu’s attendants;
[he shall also know] the procedure for all fasts, which bestows supreme merit.
"O goddesses, listen from me to another [account] in due order and according to the truth:
having bathed, being pure, having sipped water, having offered oblations into the fire, and being well-composed. (112.42)
Having thus consecrated himself, the wise man should observe a fast;
he should bathe at the three periods of the day and likewise offer oblations into the fire.
Restrained in speech, free from anger, self-controlled, righteous, truthful in word, and compassionate,
he should constantly recite the Gāyatrī and the purificatory hymns at all times.

Then, at night, lying upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having spread out kuśa grass according to the rules, he should worship the Rudras or the Gaṇas, remaining strictly secluded from women and Śūdras.
Then, free from sorrow and devoid of envy, one should eat along with the goddesses;
for as many days as one remains there, for that long one should feed the Brahmins.
Then, when the time has indeed come, having honored a hundred or even a thousand excellent Brahmins according to one's ability in every way, || 112.47 ||
Having given sacrificial food, cows, and garments in sequence,
one should cause gold and a vessel of sesame seeds to be given to each individual;
thereby, one obtains that fruit which is difficult to attain through other vows.
O highly fortunate ones, that best of men who would release a bull with a dark-blue body, or even another [animal], shall deliver his ancestors from suffering. (112.49)
As many hairs as there are on that great-souled bull,
for so many thousands of years does he rejoice in heaven.
He who, with a pure mind and well-composed, having reached the new moon day of the dark fortnight, should give sesame vessels to Brahmins; || 112.51 ||
Having gratified the ancestors, that bull among men attains the world of the ancestors and enjoys happiness for a long time in an inexhaustible manner.
O fair-faced ones, this rule for the fast has been told by me;
now listen once more with full concentration to the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance as prescribed, with a well-concentrated mind,
shall reach the world of Soma and attain equality with Soma.
Whoever performs the Prājāpatya penance, whether once or many times,
having become equal to Prajāpati, is glorified in his world.
But that best of men who performs the Sāntapana penance delivers himself from distress and goes to the world of Agni.
And he who, with a very great mind, performs the Mahāsāntapana penance,
attains omniscience and finds the world of Brahmā.
And that best of the twice-born who performs the tulāpuruṣa rite,
being liberated from all sins, shall go to heaven with great splendor.
With great difficulty indeed a man may go to the abode of Śarva;
likewise, through the kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance, he may attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
But that best of men who performs all the *kṛcchra* penances attains whatever desire he may pray for.
Whoever among these may be the performer, being well-composed,
he becomes purified by that act and even attains divinity.
If a man should dwell for a full year constantly subsisting on milk, or consuming barley-gruel prepared with cow urine; || 112.62 ||
Whether subsisting on oil-cake and fruit, or even eating food free from pungent and salty flavors,
he attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice and enjoys the world of Brahmā.
Completely liberated from all evil and freed from all bonds,
he moves about like Brahmā in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
But that best of men, a high-souled one whose sins have been destroyed, who practices all these very [observances] individually, remains [in this state] as long as he breathes. || 112.65 ||
That Great Being, having attained either the worlds according to his desire, or even liberation,
or great sovereignty, remains resplendent.
And all these very same gifts and austerities are always available in every respect even for Śūdras, provided they are performed without mantras.
It is ordained, without doubt; thus spoke Prajāpati:
"All those Śūdras who are free from blemish are remembered as being without mantras. (112.68)
For women, the husband is the deity; nothing else is ordained besides him. He is their goal, his house is their supreme abode, and he is remembered as their highest dharma. 112.69.
Therefore, she who is authorized by him to practice this Dharma shall,
being well-composed, obtain the fruit of that Dharma.
But she who, without being authorized by him, performs any religious duty, does not obtain the fruit thereof; however, being virtuous, she does obtain the fruit.
But that woman who, permitted by her husband, having performed the dharma most excellently,
gives [the merit] to her husband, for her the fruit shall be infinite.
Whatever one desires, whether in this world or in the next, all that one obtains, O goddesses; moreover, one becomes fortunate.
Her husband shall be under her control, and she will then be dear to him;
she shall have sons and progeny, and she does not experience suffering.
"This dharma has been declared by me to you, O mothers of the world. Beyond this, what else do you wish to hear, O beautiful ones? (112.75)
For this Dharma, O noble ones, is exceedingly great and most radiant, yet it is extremely difficult for those of unrefined self to practice;
therefore, one who knows the Dharma should not speak of it to anyone else who is deceitful or unrighteous.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those goddesses, the mothers of the world, having together honored Mahādevī, spoke with joyful hearts. || 112.77 ||
"O you who are honored by all the immortals, oh, the Dharma has been proclaimed by you!
By practicing it, one swiftly attains a most great fruit. (112.78)
"O Queen, let us look from here at this auspicious forest of the mountain,
filled with various species of flowers and teeming with flocks of many birds."
Then, having risen together with the divine mothers, that goddess went to see that supreme, celestial forest on Mount Mandara.
The great yoginī wandered about, bestowing the eye that removes suffering,
as she gazed upon the peaks of realgar and those made of gold.
The Daughter of the Mountain was delighted upon seeing the lovely mountain cascades with their white waters,
the lakes filled with lotuses, the most enchanting ponds,
and Nandin standing by her side.
Then the daughter of Meru, named Śubhāvatī, who possessed a slender waist, spoke to the daughter of Himavat while pointing out the auspicious forest. (112.83)
"O Daughter of the Mountain, behold this forest, auspicious with its playful arts and endowed with all seasons, just as you have well-spoken of it."
This great work brings forth [wisdom], and it shines with its chapters; for the wise, well-spoken words are as appropriate in times of distress as they are in prosperity. (112.85)
Thus the excellent mountain peak shines with its golden stone,
like a learned man possessed of auspicious marks who has just chanted the Sāman hymns.
And this mountain peak, possessing jewels and ever radiant,
shines like the rising sun at both ends of the great age.
This peak of lapis lazuli, with its surface of sapphire stones,
shines as it bears the image of Śarva upon the Lord of the Earth, Hara.
"This elephant is intoxicated by me, as if surrounded by rutting female elephants;
having performed anointment with your lovely-browed limbs, O fair-hipped one, you now bow your head with its sprouts. (112.89)
"Oh, look at this beautiful form, endowed with a row of forest trees, O auspicious lady!
He truly appears like Jayanta consecrated in the office of crown prince by means of chowries."
And behold this tree, O Śarvāṇī, with its sprout-like branches,
as it dances near its mother like a beloved son born of her own body.
I believe this is the beloved dwelling of the deity of the forest;
its splendor appears exceedingly beautiful, the like of which I have never seen before.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of Śubhāvatī, the imperishable daughter of the mountain, the daughter of Himavat, gazed upon the young tree. (112.93)
Thus that goddess of gods, wandering upon the great mountain,
beheld a young Aśoka tree in full bloom, radiant as the rising sun.
Seeing him standing there with his hands joined in reverence like hundreds of copper-colored young shoots, O Sage, the goddess Girijā attained supreme delight.
And he thought in his mind: "This tree is my son;
this son of mine shall be praiseworthy and a bringer of joy. (112.96)
"When the Blessed One has arrived, having been authorized by the Self-Existent One, I shall take this beloved son of mine, who is like a young *aśoka* tree. (112.97)
And for me, who am childless, this best of trees shall become a son—the foremost among those with sons, and the destroyer of the grief for a child. (112.98)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus resolved, the beautiful Umā then moved away from that tree toward another region and beheld it there.
Then, in the meantime, terrifying portents occurred there;
there was a great force of wind that felled mountains and trees. (112.100)
The peak of the lord of mountains fell without any calamity, and trees were uprooted even without the wind. (112.101)
Meteors fell from the sky and an inauspicious wind blew;
moreover, O son of Kālī, the left eye of the goddess throbbed. || 112.102 ||
Seeing them, the goddess was struck with wonder and spoke thus to Śailādi, to her companions, and to all the Kāleyas who were skilled in speech: || 112.103 ||
The goddess said:
"This mountain appears intoxicated, covered on all sides by those trees;
I consider this a great danger, for it is not thought to be accidental."
Nor do these ill-omened portents arise without cause;
therefore, act in such a way that these inauspicious signs do not bring fear upon me.
Then Nandin, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, said to the Goddess of gods:
"O Bhavānī, from what source could there be fear for you, who are the mother of the dwellers of heaven? (112.106)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, while she was speaking thus to the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe,
the Daitya Andhaka then departed from Pātāla for Mount Mandara.
Surrounded by thousands of Daityas and Dānavas headed by Prahlāda,
the illustrious great Daitya appeared like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of gods.
By the counsel of the most eminent Daityas, that great Asura came to Mount Mandara to see it, just as Indra goes to the Nandana grove.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Śini, and Bāṣkali;
Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Vātāpi, Bali, Bāṇa, and Virocana.
Ilvala, Namuci, Vyaṃsa, the great asura Vipracitti,
Sunda, Nisunda, Naraka, Dhenuka, and Ariṣṭa as well.
Mura, Kārtasvana, Hastin, Duryodhana,
Maya, Tāraka, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Prabhākara.
Hālāhala, Kumbha, Saṃvara, Kālasaṃvara, Dhundhu, Indradamana, Hayagrīva, and Śatodara. (112.113)
Meghanāda, Siṃhanāda, Dundubhi, Śatadundubhi,
Kālanemi, Baka, Daṇḍa, Vipāka, and Pāka.
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatāvarta, Puloman, and likewise Śarabha; Bala, Gaganamūrdhan, and the highly illustrious Sūcīroman.
Asiloman, Pralamba, Śambhu, Devāntaka,
Mahiṣa, Bhīmasena, Vāyu, and Vāditra—
these followers of Andhaka also arrived at Mount Mandara.

Armed with weapons, having conquered the hosts of gods, possessed of great majesty, yet fallen from the path of dharma—all of them were indeed heroes who never retreated; together with Andhaka, they went to Mount Mandara.
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Kālī, that host was like a herd of rutting elephants, like raining clouds, and like well-horned serpents. || 112.118 ||
Like a fierce and great herd of arrogant boars,
that host of Dānavas likewise moved about upon Mount Mandara.
Wandering there in his blindness, he then beheld the goddess of the gods together with her companions,
like a wolf seeing a lioness.
O Vyāsa, having seen the Blessed Goddess, that Daitya, his mind deluded, did not offer salutation; he merely stared at her.

Seeing that Daitya gazing at the daughter of the Mountain with unblinking eyes, the highly intelligent Prahlāda spoke these meaningful words: 112.122. Having seen that Daitya gazing at the daughter of the Mountain with unblinking eyes, the highly intelligent Prahlāda spoke these meaningful words.
This imperishable daughter of Himavat is the mother of the world;
she is renowned in the universe as Umā, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga.
He whose son was Brahmā, who bestowed the office of Prajāpati, and who,
by virtue of his son's boon, attained the status of Brahmā among those who possess sons.
He who grants auspicious boons to us and to the gods—he of great renown is to be propitiated by all the worlds and by the gods alike. (112.125)
He who, having entered the entire multitude of beings without exception, abides within them;
by whose self this imperishable world is sustained.
She who, by her own will, could contract all this universe in half a moment—she is the wife of that wise Supreme Lord;
for she is capable, O Lord of the Daityas, of destroying the entire world in an instant. (112.127)
Whether to burn her, or to seize her, or to cast her into hell—
how is it that you, O Daitya, deluded by passion, did not offer her obeisance?
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, while the enemy of the gods was thus speaking words endowed with righteousness, the Goddess, together with her divine consorts, vanished in an instant.
— those women, the mothers of the world, became invisible. || 112.130 ||
Then, when those [creatures] had perished, they reached the auspicious forest of Mount Mandara on foot,
which was filled with many sights to behold.
With *balā* trees, groves of *kalanī*, *sāti*, *muktā*, and *priyaṅgu*; with *campaka*, *bakula*, *lodhra*, *aśoka*, and those called *nāga*.
It was adorned with *puṃnāga* trees, *tilaka* trees, forests of *devadāru*, *sarala* trees, coconut palms, and clusters of lotuses.
Neither by its deep ravines, nor its ridges, nor its caves, nor even its waterfalls, is there anything on earth found anywhere more delightful than that.
Then all those lords of the Daityas roamed about on the great mountain,
which was filled with many waterfalls and crowded with various trees.
While wandering there, they beheld the seven great sages, the Siddhas, established at a certain waterfall, absorbed in yoga.
Seated upon a stone slab, they were conversing with one another about stories that were consistent with the Dharma, varied in their meaning, profound in their essence, and bringing great joy.
Seeing them, that Andhaka asked Prahlāda, the best of the Asuras:
"Who are these sages here, and for what purpose have they gathered in this place? (112.138)
Then the wise Asura,
the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, having perceived that the thorn in Devaka’s side had reached his own center, spoke to him.
Prahlāda said:
"O Andhaka, these seven high-souled sages have assembled here:
Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras. (112.140)
Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha, those great-souled ones perfected in yoga and rich in asceticism, have come here, their sins consumed by austerity.
"O Lord, I do not believe this arrival of Mandara is without cause.
Remaining here in this secluded spot, all of us lords of the asuras shall find out what these practitioners are doing here. (112.142)
"O lords of the Daityas, these beings are indeed silent; having become quiet according to their strength, let us all adopt the opinion of those who remain silent."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those foremost of Asuras, having made an agreement, remained there,
saying, "Whoever among us should say anything [to the enemy], he shall be put to death by us."
While those evil-minded Asuras were thus situated there, those sages devoted to austerity spoke these words to one another: || 112.145 ||
"O twice-born ones, this region of the mountain is not pure today; let us go elsewhere, for the arrival of the most wicked Daityas is seen here. || 112.146 ||
Bhavānī too has gone elsewhere, tormented by fear of the asuras—
those evil-minded asuras for whom this destruction is certain.
All those who destroyed the Dharma have gone to their destruction;
had this cruel act not been committed by them for the sake of the kingdom, the Dharma would not have perished.
If they had remained content with their own kingdom, none of those enemies of the gods would have met such destruction;
they too would have been honored in all the worlds like the gods.
Sanatkumāra said: Aṅgiras spoke this to them: "For those among them who are lustful and engaged here for the sake of sovereignty, unrighteousness has arrived. (112.150)
Indeed, for one who desires [the kingdom], it is dharma alone that secures the kingdom;
therefore, he should never practice unrighteousness, for there is no stability whatsoever in a kingdom [attained through such means].
Atri said:
Those who desire sovereignty through unrighteousness always conquer in battle;
they become dear to the world and live for the welfare of others. || 112.152 ||
Having slain their enemies without hesitation, those who act in accordance with dharma are soon firmly established in their kingdoms; therefore, one should take refuge in dharma.
But those who, abandoning righteousness, take sovereignty by force alone and delight in what is evil—
even though they desire it— never attain that kingdom at any time.
Furthermore, whatever kingdom is obtained by them through cruel deeds shall not endure for long; moreover, they become objects of hatred.
Bhṛgu said:
"This dharma, which brings fear to the Asuras, was established of old by Brahmā, desiring to create; yet they do not practice it. || 112.156 ||
And by their very nature, they are all indeed cruel by birth;
because of their cruel approach, they have resorted to that [cruel] deed.
Sanatkumāra said:
While they were thus speaking to the Asuras,
those three— Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Kṛtānta— then arrived.
Having honored one another according to the prescribed rites,
those three sages sat down upon the very rocks, remaining devoted to each other.
When they were seated, the ṛṣis saluted them with great respect and said,
"O sustainers of the world, where have you set out for today?"
Dhātṛ said:
"O twice-born ones, having returned from the world of Brahmā, we have today come here;
we were commanded by Brahmā to go to the presence of Kaśyapa. (112.161)
Once again the sages spoke: "The twice-born Kaśyapa has been liberated.
Then Dhātṛ told the sages what Kaśyapa had said.
"O Brahmin, since you have informed me that Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, has said:
'The Asuras are my sons, and the Devas are also dear to me, O Lord. (112.163)
O Creator of the World, O Best of Gods, may I attain peace by acting in such a way that there shall be no mutual enmity among them.
In this regard, O great sage, commanded by Brahmā,
I shall tell you how the war between the gods and the asuras occurred, as well as their mutual friendship.

O most excellent of sages, you have related everything— the production of the nectar of immortality, the kingdom, and its entire establishment— as well as all that is destined to happen in the future, O Blessed One.
Lokeśa related the deeds of the gods and asuras; having reported all of that to him, he said, "We have been sent by Brahmā and have come here to see the Blessed One, the daughter of Himagiri."
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, when they had spoken thus, all those sages, whose wealth was their austerity and who were self-restrained, questioned them once more at that time.
O auspicious ones, we wish to hear that account of the past and future events of the gods and asuras, if your minds are inclined toward showing us favor.
Furthermore, O best of gods, what has been requested by you?
Tell us all of that, if indeed we are worthy of your favor. (112.170)
Having heard those words of theirs, those three most excellent gods of great power spoke these words: "You, Kṛtānta, must explain [this]."
Then he related to them the future in its many wonderful details,
exactly as it had been ordained of old by the Creator, including the true cause of the world, the gods, and the asuras.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Ascent of Mandara," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
That which was told to them by that high-souled Kṛtānta—
Tell me all that which was previously told to the sages on Mount Mandara.
Sanatkumāra said:
There shall be among the Asuras a son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
the mighty and wise Indra Prahlāda, the bull among the Asuras.
Having secured the nectar together with the gods, that lord of the hosts of deities,
the preeminent Daitya, having conquered the gods in battle, carried the nectar away.
He will be defeated in battle by Viṣṇu and will consecrate his son upon the throne.
Vyāsa said: "O son of Brahmā, how was that nectar churned by the gods and the mighty asuras? This I wish to know. (113.4)
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, having approached Brahmā, Prahlāda, the bull among the Asuras, was then consecrated in the sovereignty of Śakra and protected the Asuras.
Then a battle between the gods and the asuras took place;
and the gods took counsel together with the blessed Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, the gods are being slain by the asuras in battle like mortals.
O you of noble vows, command us so that the gods may not die."
Thus addressed, Brahmā said to those gods, including Indra:
"Go quickly and produce the nectar from the Ocean of Milk!"
In all the Manvantaras, whichever gods there may be,
they all produce the nectar from the Ocean of Milk together with the Asuras.
Then the lords of the gods eat, and by that they attain satisfaction;
they rise up even from death, and having drunk it, they do not die.
The gods said:
"O gods, how do you, the lords of the manvantaras on earth, produce that nectar? Tell us all the means for that. (113.11)
Brahmā said: In the city of Soma, belonging to Varuṇa, lies that auspicious lake Kṣīroda,
where those seven auspicious oceans are always present.
Irā, Mālā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, Irāvatī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Surabhī, and Kadrū. (113.13)
There were Aditi and Diti, as well as Devikā, the source of the universe;
there were cows, all-enduring and auspicious, who yielded every desire.
There, the affectionate cows yield milk of six flavors that is like nectar;
there dwell the foam-drinking sages, whose nature is defined by austerity, self-restraint, and tranquility.
O best of gods, whatever herbs there are in this world—
those of the village, the forest, the celestial, and the human— they exist there by the thousands.
Having cast in trees, creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, and other such things, as well as medicinal herbs and King Soma himself.
Prosperity, fortune, as well as renown, fame, contentment, and likewise glory, faith, retention, as well as reasoning and reflection; || 113.18 ||
Strength, righteousness, and vigor; the goddess Tṛpti and Sarasvatī;
all sacred fords (tīrthas) and various kinds of gifts—[all these he beheld].
They invoked the bull, the chariot, the banner, as well as the elephant and the horse;
they invoked the eight auspicious symbols there, as well as the Vedic meters.
The Vedas and whatever sciences there may be, as well as these mothers of the world;
the mantras, the sacrifices, gold, and the implements for the mantras—[all these he gave].
Having cast into it whatever was beautiful, satisfying, and flavorful, he then began to churn it with the churning-stick.
[They placed] Mandara, the best of mountains, and the tortoise Akūpāra;
and upon his back, they set Mandara, the lord of mountains, as the churning-stick.
Having made Vāsuki, who was seized by Viṣṇu, their rope,
the Daityas were on the side where his mouth was, and the gods were on the side where his tail was.
Pulling that churning-stick, they shall churn for many years;
then, after a thousand years, the horse will emerge from it.
The cows along with their calves, the auspicious intoxicated elephant, the bull with its terrifying roar, and the maidens who were like flutes of kīcaka reeds. || 113.26 ||
The eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalaka), as well as the physician Dhanvantari, Śrī, Lakṣmī, and others such as Vāruṇī, who is intoxicated with wine; 113.27.
Likewise, the divine herbs— both those of the village and the forest, as well as those belonging to humans—
and all those beginning with trees, as well as King Soma himself, [were produced] from that.
Having gathered that nectar and that unassailable poison,
as well as all those [offerings] beginning with the sacrifice, and whatever else was collected there— ‖ 113.29 ‖
In this manner, during the various Manvantaras, the gods, along with the asuras and humans, churn you for the sake of nectar; and thus, O gods, that nectar is produced.
Therefore, O gods, having gone from here together with the Dānavas, churn the nectar quickly; from that you shall obtain your welfare.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Brahmā, the creator of the world, those lords of the gods returned to this world and acted accordingly in every respect.
While that [ocean] was being churned, poison indeed arose first;
it caused terror to both gods and asuras, and Śaṅkara then drank it.
Then, from that ocean, once again various wonderful jewels emerged, and the deities took them up.
The Asuras seized these [auspicious objects] and then cursed those Asuras;
because they disregarded auspicious things, they met their destruction. || 113.35 ||
The jewels said:
"Since you wicked and cruel ones do not rejoice in us, therefore that which you desire shall not come to pass. (113.36)
The Asuras did not even take the Vāruṇī wine, which brings on the intoxication of pride;
because of that, those Asuras were indeed wicked-souled in every respect.
Then there was the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, most magnificent;
and a four-tusked elephant, and the highly renowned physician.
Ghṛtācī, Pūrvacitti, the goddess Rambhā, and Manoramā were there;
then Soma took the nectar and rose up, O gods. || 113.39 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having cast aside those jewels, the Asuras, exceedingly arrogant, seized the nectar by force from the hand of Soma. 113.40.
The gods, having approached them together while they were deluded, spoke to them with conciliatory words:
"It is not right for you to act thus; we shall all enjoy [this] together. (113.41)
"Let there indeed be a very firm friendship between us; O lords of the Dānavas, do not, out of pride in your strength, undergo this suffering here in vain."
To all of them who were speaking thus, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas and a master of great illusion, spoke these words, having cast virtue behind his back.
Prahlāda said:
"O lords of the gods, when you indeed took the jewels that had emerged from the ocean, you were not addressed by us in any way at all."
"O deities, we shall all take this very jewel;
for indeed, we will not give it up today without a fight. (113.45)
"O gods, this nectar of ours is the source of all auspiciousness;
if you have need of it through battle, take it if you are able."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by those cruel ones, the gods became as if terrified;
with pale faces and dejected, they did not say anything to them at that time. || 113.47 ||
Ashamed, those great beings, the lords of the gods, turned back;
indeed, they became devoid of energy, thinking, "We have been defeated."
While they were thus reflecting, the thousand-eyed Purandara said to them: "What is the use of despondency? Let us slay them in battle."
Viṣṇu said:
"O lords of the gods, this lack of foresight regarding war belongs to Śakra;
for it is not possible to slay all the Asuras in battle, as they possess great strength. (113.50)
"Therefore, while they have not yet drunk that auspicious nectar, I shall seize it by employing an artifice through deception. (113.51)
"Arm yourselves, all you gods; having formed a battle array, take your stand.
O dwellers of heaven, remain here until I have secured the nectar."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, assuming the deluding illusion (māyā), O lords of the gods, I,
as the glory of the sacrifice (yajñaśrī), approached the Dānavas who were arrogant in their strength.
May all you dānavas, enemies of the gods, accept me;
for those gods have met their destruction, while you are the gods—of this there is no doubt.
Then the Asuras rose up, and Prahlāda the Dānava likewise;
having circumambulated him, they placed the water-pot into his hand.
The god spoke to the Dānavas, whose minds were captivated by her female form:
"O sirs, you ought not to hurl this [weapon] at me today in any way whatsoever. (113.58)
O wise ones, you never employed illusion against him;
for they were all of wicked conduct and relied upon deceitful magic.
Prahlāda said:
"I know that they are indeed masters of illusion and powerful through deceit;
yet, well-prepared ourselves, we shall slay them by means of illusion alone. (113.60)
"Those of evil intent who know deceit must be slain with deceit;
and those skilled in illusion must be met with illusions—thus has the Dharma been proclaimed. (113.61)
But you alone are our refuge here today, and likewise our ultimate resort;
we shall subsist upon everything given by you, O beautiful one.
If you do not grant this to us, it will indeed be for your own supreme benefit;
and likewise, we shall all never again hold you in contempt.
Then that wise one of auspicious appearance, smiling, said to him:
"I shall do for you that which you have spoken; it is the truth."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, while they were looking on, the omnipresent Viṣṇu, assuming his own form and taking up the nectar, flew up and gave it to the gods. (113.65)
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Nectar," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 113.113 ||
Skanda Purāṇa 114.
Vyāsa said:
How did that terrible poison arise, possessing the brilliance of ten thousand suns?
How was it drunk by the Blessed One Śaṅkara of immeasurable splendor?
And how did the blue color arise upon the neck of the God of gods, which possesses the luster of the kunda flower and the moon? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
"In what highly meritorious region did this supreme narrative take place,
O one of great splendor, and at what time was it told to the one preceded by Brahmā?"
O ascetic, tell us this correctly and exactly as it happened:
how did the blue-throated god Śarva, the lord of the three worlds, [become so]? (114.4)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this was heard by me previously as it was being narrated by Vāyu, the life-breath of the universe, during a thousand-year sacrificial session.
"By what cause is the throat of the trident-bearing God of gods blue?
I shall proclaim that; listen, you who are devoted to your vows. (114.6)
To the north of the king of mountains are lakes, rivers, and pools—[in] regions strewn with [these] and upon the mountains. (114.7)
On lofty mountain peaks and in forest glades within the caves,
there dwell high-souled sages of celebrated vows who subsist on roots.
There they worship and praise Mahādeva according to the prescribed rites, with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with dance, song, worship, and other such offerings. || 114.9 ||
When the wheel of the luminaries had set in motion and the sun had reached the meridian.
At that time, when the gods have completed their observances, all those deities of self-restrained souls remain for that portion [of the day]. || 114.11 ||
Having entered among them, the Wind, the source of life for all living beings, said to Sadāgati: "Salutations to you, O Blue-throated One! (114.12)
Having heard that, the sages of purified souls and firm vows,
known as the Bālakhilyas, who travel in the company of the sun, [spoke].
Eighty-eight thousand sages,
whose vital energy was drawn upward and who subsisted on air, leaves, and water, questioned Vāyu.
The Bālakhilyas said:
"O best of winds, O Prabhajana, we wish to hear by your grace that which was spoken by you regarding 'Nīlakaṇṭha'. (114.15)
"By what means did the throat of the Lord of Ambikā become blue?
We wish to hear this correctly from your mouth, especially. (114.16)
That which we have asked is indeed for our supreme benefit;
for all the words that proceed forth are uttered by you alone.
When the wind has reached the locations of the phonemes, the process of speech proceeds;
O Wind, from you proceed knowledge, discernment, and energy.
By means of yoga, all the castes have been set in motion;
from which words turn back, and which are difficult to attain even for those bound to a body. (114.19)
Even there, O Wind, you exist as a real presence, omnipresent at all times;
O Samīraṇa, there is no other omnipresent deity besides you.
And this very world of living beings is supported by you, O Wind;
for this world of life is visibly present before you as the source of its own existence.
"Do you know the Lord, the Master of Speech, the Guide of the Mind?
Tell me, by whom and in what place was this transformation of his form brought about? || 114.22 ||
Having heard those words of the sages whose minds were purified by meditation,
the highly effulgent Vāyu, who is saluted by the worlds, replied.
Vāyu said: O Brahmins, in former times, during the Kṛta age, there was a righteous-souled mind-born progenitor named Vasiṣṭha, who was devoted to the determination of the Vedas. || 114.24 ||
He questioned Kārttikeya, who indeed has the excellent peacock as his vehicle,
who brought about the end of Krauñca’s body, and who is the delighter of the Goddess’s heart.
To Mahāsena, the high-souled child appearing in disguise, who steals the collyrium from the eyes of the wives of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
At that time, the great ascetic Vasiṣṭha requested a discourse endowed with many auspicious qualities that destroys all evil.
Vasiṣṭha said:
I take refuge in the pure one, the giver of boons, the protector of Brahman, possessed of immeasurable splendor;
who is ever compassionate toward his devotees, omniscient, and of pleasing aspect. (114.28)
Salutations to you, who were born in the reeds; salutations to you, the son of the Kṛttikās.
Salutations to the twelve-eyed one; let there be salutations to you, the six-faced one.
Salutations to you, who hold a spear in your hand, whose divine arrows— [text fragmentary] —[text fragmentary].
Homage to Hiraṇyaretas; homage to you, the source of all beings! Homage to him who holds a cock in his hand, and likewise to the one who is fond of goats.
Salutations to you who are clothed in red; salutations to the one with the blue crest;
salutations to the eternally youthful one, worshipped by all the deities.
Salutations to the destroyer of Krauñca, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
salutations to you, whose form is the ocean... || 114.34 ||
Salutations to you who have the form of a child and who are playful in your madness;
this auspicious [form] of Śiva which is seen here resembles bright collyrium.
For what purpose has that arisen in your throat, which resembles a kunda flower or the moon?
This I ask you, who are trustworthy, self-controlled, and devoted, as I inquire of you.
"Speak a discourse endowed with auspiciousness and resting upon merit.
Thus was he praised by the sage Vasiṣṭha, whose soul was purified.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the immensely radiant enemy of the Daityas, who was born from the fire, replied.
O twice-born one, as for the question which you have asked me, listen, O best of speakers, to this being told by me. (114.39)
Just as it was heard by me previously, when I was seated upon his lap:
the conversation between Pārvatī and the high-souled Śaṃkara.
I shall relate that to you exactly as it is, O Great Sage,
on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals.
Resembling the rising sun and like molten gold,
it possessed stairs of diamond and crystal and floors of variegated silk-like stone.
In that divine place made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with various jewels,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and abounding in various flowers, fruits, and waters.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by ruddy geese, its lotuses resonating with the songs of bees and echoing with the sound of falling rain.
Its caves resounded with the cries of intoxicated cranes and peacocks;
it was crowded with throngs of Apsarases and graced by Kinnaras.
It resounded with the cries of pheasants and gallinules,
was sweet with the songs of cuckoos, and was frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
In that place rich with the lowing of bulls and resonant with the thundering of clouds,
the mountain caves were abandoned by elephants agitated by fear of the Vināyakas.
Amidst the resonant sound of bamboo flutes that captivated the faculty of hearing,
and amidst the graceful swaying of swings attended by women and perfected beings (siddhas), [he wandered].
It was filled with the clamor of bells hanging from banners on swaying swings,
abounding in the sound of lutes, and crowded with the activity of dancing.
With mouths [emitting] sounds from drums and cymbals, and likewise with leaping and the slapping of arms,
the mountain caves resounded with the cries of playful movements and diversions.
The Lord of the Gaṇas was sporting with faces that were terrifying and distorted, causing great alarm by their laughter, and with various forms of bodily postures.
With faces like those of tigers and lions, and even with mouths like snakes and rats;
with other faces like those of deer and sheep, and likewise with faces like elephants and horses.
With fierce faces like those of cats and forms resembling jackals—
some short, some tall, some emaciated, some stout, with protruding bellies and massive paunches.
With short shanks, with protruding lips, and others with shanks like palm trees;
with ears like those of cows, with a single ear, with large ears, and with no ears at all.
With one foot, with great feet, with many feet, or without feet;
with a single head, most fierce, or with many heads, formidable.
And with the leaders of the hosts who were headless, as well as those with massive heads;
with those having a single eye, great eyes, and many eyes in every respect.
And with other leaders of the hosts who had the forms of headless trunks, who were eyeless, who had a single nose, large noses, many noses, or no noses at all; (114.57)
With single mouths, great mouths, many mouths, and mouthless faces;
with single tusks, great tusks, many tusks, and tuskless faces.

Surrounded by such beings of great yoga— some with one hand, some with large hands, some with many hands, and some handless; some of universal form, some deformed, some beautiful, and some devoid of form— the Lord of Beings was thus encompassed.
Seated comfortably upon a delightful golden stone slab, her limbs adorned with ornaments of pure jewels,
the daughter of the Mountain King addressed these words to the destroyer of the body of Madana.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, whose banner is marked by a bull!
O Mahādeva, that which resembles a dark cloud shines upon your neck."

"O Lord, destroyer of the bodies of Kama, what is this auspicious, bright, and not overly intense [light] resembling a mass of black collyrium that shines upon your neck? O Ishvara, what is the cause or what is the reason by which this has become blue?"
I wish to hear all this in its true essence, according to the proper method.
Then, having heard the words of the goddess Pārvatī, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī, related a narrative filled with auspiciousness.
Maheśvara said: Formerly, while the nectar was being churned in the Ocean of Milk by the gods and the Dānavas,
a terrible poison arose first, possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction.
It appeared like Death itself at the end of time, possessing the splendor of the sun at the dissolution of the eon;
resembling the sun that destroys the three worlds, it blazed forth on all sides.
Having seen him, O lady of excellent countenance, all the hosts of gods and the Daityas,
with dejected faces, went into the presence of Brahmā.
Seeing the hosts of gods terrified, the immensely radiant Brahmā said:
"The eightfold sovereignty has been bestowed upon you by me."
"You are all lords of the three worlds and free from all affliction;
you all travel in celestial chariots, and you all move according to your own will."
Honored by the subjects and always highly esteemed by me, for what reason are these women of great wisdom so deeply distressed in heart? (114.69)
"By whom has my sovereignty been revoked, that they have come before me?
There is no one here who can turn me back from the creation of beings, for I am ignorant of nothing. (114.70)
You are always capable of acting with regard to the internal, the elemental, and the celestial, as well as concerning the ripening of the karma of living beings.
"What is the task? What is the cause? Or from where has fear come, by which you are so agitated like deer tormented by a lion? (114.72)
"You ought to relate all this quickly and according to the proper method.
Then, having heard those words of that great-souled Brahmā, [the gods spoke].
Then the lords of the gods, daityas, and dānavas, together with the ṛṣis, spoke,
O Brahmin, while the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras.
The terrible poison appeared, resembling a serpent or a bee, like a dark blue cloud, with a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
It had arisen like the death-bringing Time, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon;
it shone forth on all sides with the brilliance of the sun that destroys the three worlds.
Seeing that immense mass, like a confluence of splendors,
suddenly arisen before them, they all became dejected of countenance, beholding the great poison that had emerged.
By that poison rising up, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
Janārdana— whose body was once fair with a reddish hue— was scorched and turned black.
O Brahman, having seen Janārdana— whose limbs were once reddish-fair but now made black—
we are all terrified and have come to you alone for refuge.
Having heard the terrifying words of both the gods and the asuras,
the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, replied.
"Let all the deities and the sages whose wealth is asceticism listen:
that which arose at the beginning when the great ocean was being churned."
The poison known as Kālakūṭa, resembling the fire of universal destruction, was produced;
at its mere emergence, the gods could no longer shine.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor I, nor all the foremost of the gods are able to withstand his impetus, except for Śaṅkara.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā— the one born from the lotus, possessing the luster of its interior, not born from a womb, and the best among those who know the Vedas— began to praise me in this manner.
Brahmā said:

Salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa; salutations to you, the one with many eyes. Salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand; indeed, salutations to the one who holds the thunderbolt in his hand.
Salutations to the one who holds a trident in his hand, whose hands bear a staff, a noose, and a sword;
salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, salutations to the Master of all beings.
Salutations to the slayer of the enemies of the gods, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire;
salutations to you who are indeed Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. 114.87
Salutations indeed to Sāṃkhya and to Yoga, and to the multitude of living beings;
salutations indeed to the destroyer of the body of Manmatha, and to the Death of Death.
To Rudra, whose seed is wealth, the god of gods,
the impetuous one, the turbaned one with the beautiful face, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful giver.
To Kapardin, to Karāla, to Śaṅkara, and to Hara;
to Virūpa, to Surūpa, to Śiva, and to the Giver of Boons.
Salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, the slayer of Makha, and the lord of the Mātṛs; salutations to the Awakened One, the Pure One, the Liberated One, and the Absolute One.
To the creator of the three worlds, to Śakra, the giver of boons,
to the fierce one, and likewise to the most terrible one, to the brahmin of infinite vision.
Salutations indeed to Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas; to that whose source is the Unmanifest; to the eternal, to the non-eternal, and to that which is both eternal and non-eternal.
Salutations indeed to the manifest and to the unmanifest, and to that which is both manifest and unmanifest;
salutations indeed to the conceivable and to the inconceivable, and to that which is both conceivable and inconceivable.
Salutations indeed to the subtle, to the non-subtle, and to the one who is both subtle and non-subtle; salutations to the destroyer of the afflictions of devotees and to the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
To Śarva, the beloved of Umā, whose lap is marked by the face of Nandin;
to the half-month, the month, the fortnight, the season, and the year.
Salutations to the one of many forms, to the shaven-headed, to the bearer of the staff, and to the protector;
to the rider of the chariot, to the wielder of the bow, to the one with matted hair, and to the perpetual celibate student.
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the three-eyed Lord; salutations to you, O Blessed One, Śiva, who is the Supreme Person and the Lord in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. 114.98
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Creator of all beings!"—to you, who are thus praised with such deeds and worthy of praise, let there be homage.
Bowing with my head, I am prostrate before Rudra, the teacher of the world, the best of gods, the three-eyed one;
O storehouse of splendor, you who are subtle and attainable through the excellence of yoga, you approach the manifest Rudra.
O God of gods, having recognized my devotion, be gracious, O you whose hair is drenched in the waters of the Gaṅgā!
I have come with effort to seek refuge in you, the auspicious one, whose vehicle is adorned with the bull Saurabheya and clouds. || 114.101 ||
Thus, at that time, I was praised by that Brahmā, the creator of the world, with various hymns originating from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Then, being pleased with that high-souled Brahmā,
I addressed the Grandfather with the foremost of salutations.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Sovereign of beings, O Great Ascetic!
What task for you must I perform, O Brahman? Tell me, O observer of noble vows.
Having heard these words, O lotus-eyed one, Brahmā then replied:
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of the past, future, and present, O Sovereign of Causes, listen,
O God, while the great ocean is being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras."
The terrible poison appeared, resembling a peacock or a bumblebee, like a dark blue cloud, and possessing a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
It appeared like Death itself at the end of time, possessing the splendor of the sun at the dissolution of the age;
it shone forth on all sides, resembling the sun that destroys the three worlds.
By that poison rising up, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
Janārdana— whose limbs were once red and fair— was scorched and turned black.
Seeing Janārdana, whose limbs were once reddish-fair, now made black,
we were all struck with fear and have come to you alone for refuge.
Drink that, O Mahādeva, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
for you are indeed the first consumer, you are the best of gods and the Lord.
You alone are capable of restraining his great impetuosity;
no other man in this world of mobile and immobile beings is able to do so.
O Mahādeva of great splendor, you alone are capable of drinking [it] from that very one who possesses fierce power and a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
"O Mahādeva, there is no one else capable of withstanding his force.
While the supreme Brahmā was speaking thus, O Goddess— || 114.113 ||
"Very well," O fair-faced one, having accepted those words, I began to drink that poison which was like the God of Death himself. || 114.114 ||

For the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, while I was drinking the most terrible poison in the presence of the lords of the gods and the Daityas, O you who are honored by the gods and Gandharvas,
it quickly became black in my throat at that very moment, O lotus-eyed one.
Seeing that great poison, which resembled the petals of a blue lotus, clinging to his neck like the serpent Takṣaka, the king of snakes, licking its fangs like a serpent; 114.116.
Then the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"O Mahādeva of noble vows, you shine with this throat."
Having heard these words of his, O daughter of the mountain king, O lady of beautiful countenance, while the hosts of gods and the Daityas looked on, I [acted].
Because the terrible poison was worn upon the neck by the yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, piśācas, uragas, and rakṣasas, I am therefore Śrīkaṇṭha.
O daughter of the mountain king, seeing that Kālakūṭa poison of fierce splendor held in his throat, the entire assembly of gods and demons was delighted and attained the highest wonder. (114.120)
Then all the hosts of gods, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas, spoke with palms joined in reverence, O Goddess who moves like a rutting elephant: 114.121.
Oh, what strength, vigor, and prowess you possess! Oh, what a body and power of yoga this is of yours!
Oh, what majesty you have, O God of gods, whose moon-crested head is bathed by the waters of the Gaṅgā!
You alone are Viṣṇu and you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are the sun and you are the moon;
you alone are Time and you are Destiny; you alone are Death and you alone are the Giver of Wealth.
You alone are the subtle, imperishable Puruṣa; you alone are subtler than the subtle.
You alone are the manifest, you alone are primordial nature (prakṛti), and you alone are both existence and its source.
You alone are the earth, you alone are the water; you alone are the fire, you alone are the wind;
you alone are space, the past, the future, and the present; you alone are the being joined with existence and non-existence.
You alone are the sacrifice, you alone are the discipline; you alone bring about every dharma.
You alone are the distinct distributor of all that is moving and unmoving, and the protector at the time of dissolution.

Having spoken these words, the lords of the gods and the hosts of Siddhas, joyful and free from grief, bowed to me; with the Soma duly distributed, they departed in their celestial chariots, swift as the wind.
This supreme secret, greater than the meritorious and exceedingly great, is a hymn that destroys all sins, spoken by Svayambhū himself. (114.128)
But he who, devoted to Me and established in self-restraint, constantly retains this auspicious hymn sung by Brahmā, which destroys all diseases— 114.129.
I shall declare the destiny of that embodied being both here and in the next world;
for him, O lady of excellent hips, poison—whether stationary or mobile—is likewise [ineffective]. (114.130)
O lady of beautiful hips, having reached his body, he is quickly struck down;
having attained peace, he removes the terrible and inauspicious evil dream.
He becomes beloved among women and in the assembly of the king;
he attains victory in debate and in battle—of this there is no doubt. (114.132)
As he travels on his way, safety and strength arise within him;
O fair-faced one, I shall describe his destination after the dissolution of the body.
With a tawny beard, a blue throat, and hair marked by the crescent moon,
he is three-eyed, invincible, wielder of the trident, whose banner bears the bull, and possessed of great strength.
Possessing a body equal to Nandin and prowess equal to Nandin,
that perfected one (siddha) wanders through the entire sevenfold world by my command.
His course cannot be obstructed, like that of the wind in the sky;
having become my attendant, he shall remain so until the dissolution of all beings.
Moreover, O lady of excellent hips, I shall declare the fruit for those men who always listen to this, O you who possess a thousandfold fruit.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya gains the earth;
a Vaiśya obtains profit; and a Śūdra attains a good rebirth. 114.138.
The diseased is freed from illness, and the bound is released from bondage;
the pregnant woman gives birth to a son, and the maiden finds a virtuous husband.
One recovers lost wealth both in this world and in the next;
it is the fruit of a hundred thousand cows properly given as a gift.
A mortal who hears this narrative obtains that same fruit,
even if it be but a single syllable, a quarter-verse, a stanza, or even half a stanza.
Alternatively, that man who daily recites this entire chapter in an assembly of gods and brahmins, with his inner self absorbed in me—
