One who is faithful and ever-exerting is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Recite this, O Goddess—may it be well with you—and teach it to your kinsmen.
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a hymn superior to this;
neither yakṣas, nor piśācas, nor bhūtas, nor vināyakas [have composed one]. (114.144)
They shall create obstacles in that house where this hymn remains;
just as among fields, a field is designated as the most excellent when it is liberated [from weeds]. || 114.145 ||
Likewise, this hymn, composed by Brahmā, is the most excellent among hymns;
whoever should cause even a single foot of it to be heard by Brāhmaṇas at a śrāddha ceremony, [attains great merit].
Indeed, inexhaustible food and drink attend upon his ancestors—
whatever has been mentally conceived and whatever has been uttered by speech.
Everything is accomplished for one by the recitation of this hymn;
even those who are of sinful birth, upon hearing this supreme secret. (114.148)
Even women and Śūdras here go to the world of Rudra;
when, after the lapse of time, they occasionally attain the state of humanity once more.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences is born into a pure family;
he becomes a devotee of the gods and then practices righteousness.
This meritorious history, which destroys all sins,
has been told by me here out of my own satisfaction, O lotus-eyed one.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Mahādeva Composed by Brahmā," in the section on the Churning for Nectar within the Amṛtamathana of the Skanda Purāṇa, concerning the narrative of Nīlakaṇṭha.
Skanda Purāṇa 115.
Vyāsa said:
When that nectar had been stolen by Viṣṇu in a disguised form, [the gods were distressed].
And what did the Daityas and the Dānavas do immediately after that?
Sanatkumāra said: Deprived by Viṣṇu through his anger, all those lords of the Dānavas then girded themselves for battle and, censuring Viṣṇu, spoke as follows. (115.2)
"Fie on your strength! Fie on your heroism! Fie on your prowess, O wicked one!
You are a constant betrayer of trust, a man of base deeds and evil soul. (115.3)
In the past, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by you through deceit, as was Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the Daityas; and this nectar has been carried away by you.
"You possess no strength in battle, for you are strong only through deceit. Stand firm in combat; you shall not escape us. || 115.5 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king of the Daityas, enraged and vomiting flames of fire,
rushed toward Viṣṇu on a chariot that roared like a cloud.
Then Vipraciti, the lord of the Daityas, challenged the thousand-eyed Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who was mounted upon his elephant, with his own elephant. (115.7)
But Virocana, filled with rage, charged on his elephant toward the Lord of Wealth, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas,
just as a rain-cloud rushes toward the sun.
Bali, the son of Virocana, likewise rushed toward Yama, the lord of the host of ancestors,
with his chariot, like one obstacle rushing against another obstacle.
And Anuhrāda, the lord of the Daityas and son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
rushed toward Varuṇa like the current of a river toward the ocean.
But Maya, the best of the Dānavas, as well as Tāra and Tāraka,
were engaged with the Ādityas like elephants with great elephants.
Śarabha, Śataketu, Bala, and the Dānava Mūka rushed toward the Rudras like lions attacking lions in the forest.
Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Mahāmāya,
and Śambara were engaged with the Vasus, just as calamities are joined with the virtuous.
Then Naraka, Hayagrīva, and the asura Indradamana were closely joined by the two Aśvins, like stars accompanied by two planets.
And other Dānavas of great illusion and great strength, together with various other gods, fought one another, calling out to one another in fury. || 115.15 ||
Vipracitti, possessed of great illusion, afflicted the thousand-eyed Indra with three arrows,
making the ten directions resound with his roar.
As he was shooting, the powerful Indra, possessing a light hand,
shattered that variegated bow into a hundred pieces with his hundred-edged thunderbolt.
Then, as he was taking up another bow while mounted on his elephant, [the opponent] crushed him with the elephant;
he fell down like a mountain.
As that Dānava leaped down from the elephant, the powerful king of the gods struck him with his thunderbolt, just as Guha struck Krauñca with his spear in battle.
By that blow of the thunderbolt, the Dānava, his consciousness bewildered, fell swiftly to the earth like a tree shattered by the wind. || 115.20 ||
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of the Dānavas, while the gods let out great lion-like roars, crying, "Excellent! Excellent! (115.21).
Then, having regained consciousness, he used his terrifying power to send that intoxicated elephant to the abode of Yama.
Then that foremost of gods shattered his rear guards and his brilliantly shining armor; having abandoned the battle, he departed.
Bali, Yama, Puṇḍra, Kṛtānta, Kalaha, as well as Kāla, Niyati, the Kiṅkaras, and Pāśa.
As he looked at each one, he pierced them with five sharp arrows each,
and he struck Yama himself in the heart with sixty-four.
As he was crying out, Yama, becoming enraged, then laughed and,
striking his chariot with his staff, reduced it to ashes.
Seeing the chariot with its driver, horses, and footmen destroyed, Bali, crying out "Stay!
Stay!", rushed toward Yama with a roar.
As he was falling, Yama swiftly hurled his staff at him;
by that blow upon his head, he then fell to the surface of the earth.
Then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of Dānavas;
some cried out, "Seize him! Seize him!", while others exclaimed, "Woe! Woe! (115.29).
But the mighty Anuhrāda, filled with rage, struck Varuṇa in the heart with an iron shaft and felled him onto the seat of his chariot.
Rising in an instant, that powerful god drew his mighty bow,
fixed arrows upon it, and severed his [the opponent's] bow.
He struck the horses and caused the charioteer’s head to fall from his body;
as he was leaping down from that excellent chariot whose horses had been slain, [he struck him].
He quickly pierced his heart, and he fell down like one dead;
Tāraka and Tārakākṣa severely struck the Ādityas.
They, too— Śarabha, Śataketu, Bala, and the Dānava Mūka— deprived all of them of their chariots with three hundred arrows each.
Making the earth resound with various kinds of Rudra-weapons, they afflicted [the enemy] in battle;
but those of great strength, having warded off those weapons of theirs, [remained firm]. (115.35)
Like locusts, they destroyed the fields in an instant;
being driven away by those many Rudras, they were then deprived of their chariots.
Abandoning the battle, Mahāmāya, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, and the great illusionist Śambara fled in every direction. (115.37)
In the battle, they rushed at the Vasus like elephants charging against elephants;
then all the Vasus discharged the sleep-inducing weapon (*svāpana-astra*) upon them. || 115.38 ||
Stationed upon their chariots, they appeared like sleeping deer;
the charioteers then bore those who were asleep away from that battlefield.
And as they were carrying them away, they struck off the heads of the sons;
then, when the charioteers had been slain, the horses bolted in confusion.
While still asleep in the battle, all the sons of Diti were wandering about—
Naraka, Hayagrīva, and Indradamana as well.
The two Aśvins were well-prepared for battle, as were those lords of the Asuras;
then, as they were charging forward, those two gods, the best among physicians, [confronted them].
With their staff-like weapons, they rendered them all chariotless;
then [the others], maddened with rage, rushed forward again, all armed with maces.
In that battle, they suddenly struck them down with the Vāyavya weapon;
and other gods likewise then crushed the sons of Diti.
Just as herds of deer gathered together in the forest are torn apart by lions, so too was Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, overcome when he encountered Viṣṇu. || 115.45 ||
Having then fought a great battle, he became deprived of his chariot;
his horses were slain by the discus, and his charioteer and followers were killed.
Seizing his mace and leaping forward, he rushed at Janārdana; as he was thus rushing with his mace raised, O great sage— (115.47)
Janārdana swiftly cut that mace with his very discus;
then those Dānavas had their prowess shattered by those heroic gods.
They broke apart out of fear, like herds of deer in the forest before lions;
seeing them broken and being broken, [the others] abandoned the battle and fled. 115.49.
Prahlāda also, abandoning the battle, followed after them alone.
When they had been broken, there arose for Indra a highly honored cry of victory.
Then the gods, together with Nārāyaṇa and the world-protectors, made everything equal;
they uttered various lion-roars and sounded musical instruments.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Battle in the Churning for the Nectar," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, did that churning of the nectar take place.
And there was indeed a most terrible battle with Prahlāda as well.
After a long time, having indeed fought hundreds of battles,
that lord of the asuras bestowed the kingdom upon his son, Virocana.
Furthermore, O Vyāsa, the exceedingly powerful Virocana was slain in battle by the highly energetic Indra, the lord of the gods, for the sake of the kingdom.
Vyāsa said:
"How did that battle between the Āṭi and the Baka occur, so full of great terror?
O Blessed One, I wish to hear it, for my curiosity is indeed great. (116.4)
Sanatkumāra said: Again, in this world, there arose friendship between the gods and the asuras; and they, with faces filled with wonder, beheld it from afar.
In that region of Ilāvṛta, there was a terrible,
fierce Atharvanic sorcery (kṛtyā) of deformed appearance, which caused terror among the Asuras.
Seeing her, those deities said, "Who is this Āṭi? while the Asuras said, "It is Baka. Thus a dispute arose between them. (116.7)
Then that terrible *kṛtyā* revealed herself to the gods;
she became a crane (*baka*) for those Asuras, known as Āṭi.
O great sage, they made a wager there concerning the kingdom:
"Whichever of us is defeated shall become the slave of the other; the victor shall be the master. (116.9)
Then she, in the form of Āṭi, showed herself to them all.
Thereupon, those defeated [Asuras] said to the gods, "We have not been conquered. (116.10)
"This is clearly a crane; you have been defeated, there is no doubt.
This is not a crane that is a crow, nor indeed is this a crow that is a crane. (116.11)
Thus, as they disputed for the sake of the kingdom, a terrifying battle broke out between those chief Dānavas and the gods. (116.12)
Indeed, after Virocana had been slain for a thousand years,
and once Virocana was killed, Brahmā [conferred sovereignty] upon Bali, the great Asura, among them.
He consecrated him in the sovereignty of Indra, and he indeed became the king;
thereafter, O Vyāsa, that imperishable one overran the three worlds by his power.
He was born as the lord of the three worlds and indeed the sovereign of the Asuras;
having conquered the Lord of the Gods in battle, that powerful one displaced him from his station.
The one of great strength also assumed the state of Indra and the state of Yama;
he himself became Varuṇa, as well as the Lord of Wealth and likewise Agni.
The Sun and the Moon, and Parjanya who releases the rain—
he alone always performs everything that is to be done in the world.
While he thus ruled the kingdom, there was then no happiness for the gods;
deprived of their sovereignty, those great-souled ones wandered about like birds.
O Vyāsa, having consoled those great-souled ones who were suffering in many ways, Brahmā, the best of gods, out of compassion bestowed his wisdom upon them.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, this Bali cannot be harmed by you;
he is high-souled and righteous, and he is immortal—of this there is no doubt."
"He is devoted to Brahman, powerful, and has likewise obtained boons;
let this Viṣṇu go to him in the form of a Brahmin and entreat him. || 116.21 ||
Assuming the form of a dwarf, he will take three strides of the earth;
having seized it, let him stride over it in every direction.
He will undoubtedly make the entire earth level with his stride;
then Dhātṛ himself will place his second stride in the intermediate space.
"And I myself shall bestow the third step as well;
thus, O gods, this recovery of your kingdom is seen to be possible, and not otherwise."
At the time when this Viṣṇu sets out for heaven,
at that very time, you must guard the Dānavas with every effort.

Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, those lords of the gods, being of great courage, deliberated in many ways on what was auspicious and said to Viṣṇu: "Let the word of Brahmā be carried out. (116.26)
"O Lord, that best of Asuras has indeed been initiated today for a horse sacrifice; go to his final purificatory bath tomorrow morning and beg him [for the horse]. || 116.27 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been told by him, "So be it," the gods, clad in armor for battle, then all took their positions with Śakra at their head. || 116.28 ||
Then Nārada, having gone there and being honored by him with devotion,
sat down comfortably and spoke these words, he who is the best among those who speak.
"I am pleased with you because of your righteousness, as are the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
O best of Dānavas, this conduct of yours is free from any demonic influence."
For all the Dānavas are cruel, slayers of Brahmins, and thorns to the worlds;
you, however, are devoted to Brahmins and likewise a benefactor to the worlds.
Therefore, O bull among the asuras, you must always contemplate what is auspicious for yourself,
so that, O King, whatever may be auspicious for you shall indeed be ever-present.
This Viṣṇu, dispatched by the gods, has assumed the form of a Brahmin;
intent on the kingdom, he will demand three strides from you.
Therefore, you must not grant him that kingdom, lest it be lost to you later.
Beyond this, O King, Lord of Asuras, you are the authority.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, O Vyāsa, Bali, the son of Virocana and lord of the Dānavas, then spoke to Nārada while bowing down. (116.35)
"O Great Sage, they are my firm enemies and I am theirs;
if they should beg from me, then indeed I would have achieved my purpose. (116.36)
If Madhusūdana, having completely abandoned his own duty,
should entreat me with a distressed soul, my life will have been fruitful.
And this is my vow, O Brahmin, O great sage:
when entreated, I shall never say, "I will not give," O Lord. (116.38)
O best of brahmins, the vital breaths of one who asks "give" depart upwards;
however, for one who says "I will not give," they depart toward hell.
"Give me! is the name of weeping; "I have nothing" is the response to that weeping. O Nārada, may other people not see me while I am weeping. (116.40)
O Great Sage, this is the way for every man:
that he who gives to me as I beg shall obtain that fruit which is imperishable. (116.41)
Therefore, if I do not give this great thing requested by my enemies,
I shall undoubtedly fall into the hell named Raurava.
For that lowest of men who does not give to one who begs destroys the beggar by cutting off his hope; of this there is no doubt. (116.43)
"You are clearly my father, and I am your son, bound by affection;
O best of Brahmins, I shall not refuse you—may this bring you peace."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having taken leave of him and being duly honored by him,
he ascended to heaven unperturbed, reflecting upon how [the goal] might be achieved.
Then, on that very day at nightfall, that highly illustrious one,
having become a brahmin in the form of Vāmana, approached Viṣṇu and made his request.
And that king, O best of Brahmins, [gave] jewels and riches,
villages, female slaves, queens, cattle, horses, chariots, and elephants.
And various vehicles, gold, couches,
beds, coverlets, garments, ornaments, and houses.
Whatever object the brahmin requested, however much, and in whatever manner, that lord of the Daityas granted it without hesitation.
To him who was thus behaving, the highly illustrious Vāmana said:
"Give to me that which I shall tell you."
Having honored him with the water for the feet, the water for the guest-offering, a seat, and other such rites, he said: "O best of the twice-born, tell me what you desire."
Vāmana said:
"O King, if you grant [this] to me who asks out of my desire, then I shall speak; otherwise, O Lord of Asuras, I will not speak. (116.52)
Bali said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, having understood the matter, I would promise it if it were something that ought to be given;
and if it were possible for me to give it, then I would venture to give it."
Vāmana said: "O best of Asuras, this has always been your vow:
'Whatever a Brahmin requests, I shall give that to him. (116.54)
O lord of the asuras, having been initiated for the horse sacrifice, you give whatever a brahmin asks for;
of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed, that king, skilled in speech, reflected and then spoke once more to him of great prowess, smiling as he did so. (116.56)
Bali said: "You are Viṣṇu in the form of a brahmin, yet you beg of me through a disguise;
having abandoned the duty of a kṣatriya, you speak with such wretchedness. (116.57)
"Even to all who are destitute, I shall give when asked;
for with the exception of the kingdom, O God, I will grant you whatever you desire. (116.58)
Vāmana said:
"This is true; I am Viṣṇu, and our kingdom has been taken away by you.
We have no desire for the kingdom today, for we are indeed free from longing."
We entreat you for a dwelling where I may live in peace.
Bali said:
"O Lord of the Gods, what is the measure of that house for which you beg?
Of what kind is it, and where shall I give it? Tell me everything, O Vāmana. (116.60)
Vāmana said:
"O King, grant me, who am seeking a dwelling, a large house endowed with the qualities of all lands, measured by my three strides."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, Śukra of great asceticism spoke to Bali:
"O great king, this one of great power is Viṣṇu; he must not be given [the earth]. (116.62)
"This is that invincible slayer of all the Dānavas;
Viṣṇu has come here in this manner through a disguise—release him! 116.63.
Disregarding his words, the son of Diti said:
"O Viṣṇu, I shall give you a house such as you request."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Madhusūdana spoke to the sinless King Bali in the presence of everyone.
Vāmana said:
"O sinless one, I am the god Sādhya, the son of Dharma and a grandson of Diti;
therefore, O mighty one, there is no fault in my accepting this gift."
"O King, Lord of Asuras, if you have no regret later regarding this middle house that is to be given, then pour water into my hand. (116.67)
Sanatkumāra said: Then,
saying "So be it," that mighty one began to offer a great house to Vāmana with a golden pitcher.
Then those cruel Dānavas, eager to oppose him and intensely intent upon Bali, arrived there, O great sage.
Prahlāda along with his brothers, Maya, Jambha, Ardhalocana,
the valiant Vipracitti, and others of great strength.
Having gone there and placed Prahlāda at their head,
O Vyāsa, they spoke to Bali, the son of Virocana, while reflecting upon his impending defeat.
Prahlāda said:
"What is this great resolve you have formed, O evil-minded son?
This destruction of the sons of Diti is not a deed that should be done, O one of great strength. (116.72)
"This Viṣṇu is a great deceiver, an evil-souled slayer of Daityas;
he will surely traverse even the three worlds, there is no doubt. (116.73)
"You are our refuge, O son; you are our strength, you are our prowess.
Our very life depends upon you; do not destroy us so quickly."
O son, King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa do not equal even a sixteenth part of you, the king.
"O mighty one, give this house to that wise man; I tell you this, for it is for the welfare of all and for you as well."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the high-souled Prahlāda,
the righteous and highly illustrious Bali bowed down and spoke this.
Bali said:
"I know indeed that this god is Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all asuras;
yet this is my very vow: whatever is asked of me must be given by me."
"I am renowned as a lord of generosity, famous throughout the three worlds;
O givers of gifts, while I still live, how could I act otherwise? (116.79)
"It is unrighteous, laborious, not leading to heaven, and brings great fear;
how indeed could I commit a falsehood? Such is the vow I have undertaken. Having given my word, how could I again act otherwise for the sake of dharma, O Asuras? (116.80)
Prahlāda said:
O son, among the Dānavas and Daityas, dharma was established by themselves; yet the sons of Diti and the Dānavas always prosper through unrighteousness. (116.81)
Deceit, falsehood, hypocrisy, the slaughter of all beings,
and the plundering of sacrifices— this indeed is our auspicious dharma.
Therefore, O Lord, do not grant [the boon] to that evil-minded one after having promised it;
for in that way our prosperity would be secured, whereas otherwise there would be great danger here.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the wise Bali, that tiger among asuras and skilled in speech, reflected and spoke these words. || 116.84 ||
Bali said:
"O best of asuras, this dharma which has been urged upon you by means of unrighteousness— surely its fruit for such a cruel act cannot be eternal."
King Hiraṇyakaśipu did not attain ultimate happiness, nor did Hiraṇyākṣa, nor his son Andhaka. (116.86)
"You are our grandfather; yet, because of such a cruel deed, no learned people whatsoever praise this. || 116.87 ||
"Behold, O sages, how by truth and righteousness the gods are established in heaven; they conquer exceedingly, and the planets indeed shine."
No one at all is seen in the sky; thus, by my cruel deed, I seek to propitiate you and ask for your forgiveness. O Lord of the Daityas, I speak to you.
Prahlāda said:
O Dānava, whether it be wicked or cruel, or even auspicious, one’s own great ancestral duty must not be abandoned. (116.90)
"O son, O great sage, this has been practiced by your fathers and likewise by your grandfathers; it must not be abandoned by you."
Bali said:
"O Grandfather, listen to me regarding that which was performed by my ancestors without hesitation, as well as that which is censured by the virtuous. (116.92)
There was a sage of undepressed soul known as Vāmadeva;
upon seeing Urvaśī, his seed fell from him out of infatuation. (116.93)
It is said that a mare swallowed that [semen] while it was still in the ground;
she immediately conceived a fetus, and he became a mule.
Out of affection for his son, that sage nurtured her for many years;
then there arrived at that place a powerful royal sage named Aṣṭaka.
O Indra among kings, he saw her in the midst of the sage’s hermitage;
and filled with supreme joy, he thought this in his heart.
"This woman is equal to my wife in her perfection of auspicious marks;
if the brahmin gives her away, it would be most excellent for me. (116.97)
"And this brahmin will not give her to me, for she is very difficult to obtain;
yet I shall employ a stratagem by which he will give me that radiant woman."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king, having approached Vāmadeva, spoke to him with great reverence after bowing down, O son of Śakti, free from all deceit. (116.99)
The king said:
"O great sage, I have a certain need for this she-mule;
being thus entreated, grant it to me for a full year. (116.100)
"Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, when the task has been fully accomplished, I shall give it back to you, O chief of brahmins;
if it is to be given, let it be given."
Then that tiger among sages gave her, the blameless one, to him;
having received her, the king departed, delighted at the thought, "I have obtained her."
Then, when a full year had passed, that best of sages spoke to him;
the brahmin then said to him, "Give me the auspicious she-mule."
For that evil-minded ṛṣi did not give it; instead, he struck him out of anger.
Thereupon, his son became the king, a bull among men.
Then the brahmin said to him, "He did not give her back then," and consequently that evil-minded man died from the anger of the brahmin.
He had a son who became a king, the best of the Daityas;
then the brahmin said to him, "Give me the female mule. (116.106)
Then, having been entreated in that manner, even he, being of very wicked soul, said:
"I will not give [it] to that evil-souled murderer of my father. (116.107)
Then that brahmin, filled with rage, deprived him also of his life;
thereafter, the king's young son became a monarch of exceeding splendor.
Enraged by anger, that brahmin spoke to him as well:
"I shall destroy the lineage of that evil-minded Aṣṭaka."
Having heard those words of his and having honored that brahmin, the boy looked at his ministers and said, "I shall give the daughter of the Vāḍava later."
Then the lord of the Dānavas, having summoned his ministers, asked:
"Tell me, should this auspicious female mule be given away or not? (116.111)
The ministers said:
"O lord of men, this female mule was formerly requested by your father from his grandfather for one year and brought here. (116.112)
When a full year had passed, O great sage, although the brahmin continued to beg, the gift was not given; and out of anger, that brahmin died.
Then your grandfather became king, O lord of subjects;
likewise, he too died from the wrath of a brahmin after failing to give her away.
But if you follow the conduct of your ancestors, then this evil-minded Death, appearing in the form of a Brahmin, must not be given [the gift]. (116.115)
Having heard those words of his ministers, the one of great asceticism, filled with indignation, rebuked those ignorant of dharma and said this: || 116.116 ||
In the past, having resorted to folly, you committed an act that was exceedingly cruel,
unrighteous, disgraceful, and censured by the virtuous.
I shall by no means follow their path—
those ancestors and grandfathers of today who were devoid of wisdom.
"I shall deliver those situated in the pit, as well as my very great lineage. Having spoken thus at their passing away, a highly intelligent son was born.
The king formed a firm resolve to give a mule to the brahmin;
then, having honored that ṛṣi with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, O King. || 116.120 ||
That lord of men gave him his own she-mule,
and having indeed given him wealth as well, he propitiated that seer.
Then that tiger among sages, the powerful one, with a joyful inner soul,
raised up that tiger among kings and spoke these words.
O mighty-armed one, by you, a virtuous son, your fathers and grandfathers dwelling in hell have been rescued and enveloped in the merit of the Brāhmaṇa-sacrifice.
"I have no need for the jewels, nor for the mares, O lord of men;
being satisfied with you, I bestow all of this upon you, O ruler of men."
O mighty-armed one, if that evil-minded Aṣṭaka had indeed acted thus toward me,
or his son, or even your father, O you of wicked intent.
They would not have met with destruction, and I too would have been satisfied in every way. Therefore, I take my leave and shall depart; this wealth of yours remains as it is.
Then that tiger among sages departed for the forest itself;
and the king, having obtained the female mule, enjoyed himself with her as he pleased.
"For thus do all the twice-born, O King, and others who speak of dharma, condemn an action that is devoid of righteousness, even if it honors one's ancestors. Therefore,
I shall give the kingdom to the high-souled Vāmana."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among asuras duly poured the highly honored water into the hand of Vāmana. (116.129)
As soon as that [discus] of the high-souled Viṣṇu was cast into the water,
a shower of flowers then fell upon the lord of the Daityas.
"Excellent! Excellent! was the sound of invisible beings, and the celestial drums themselves resounded there without being struck.
And the auspicious Maruts blew forth, carrying pleasant fragrances;
and there arose a sound saying, "All you Dānavas are slain! (116.132)

Then, having observed that deed which was so exceedingly difficult for him to perform, all the sages whose wealth is asceticism praised the Lord of the sons of Diti and bowed from afar to Madhusūdana.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter in the Vāmana section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 116.116 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke to that bull among the Asuras.
I stride with my heroic steps; behold me, O lord of the Dānavas, O you of radiant splendor!
"O Dānava, if what has been given is not sufficient, then another portion of land must be given by you; be true to your word. (117.2)
Bali said:
"Stride out, O best of Vāmanas, with three strides today in every direction;
if they are not filled, I shall be the giver—I tell you this truly. (117.3)
Sanatkumāra said: Then the imperishable Viṣṇu, intending to take his stride, bowed with supreme devotion to Mahādeva, the Lord of the gods and the husband of Umā.
Then the gods, well-prepared, armored, and eager for battle,
those beings of great power and great strength, arrived there through the sky.
Then, having assumed a form of supreme radiance on Puṣkaradvīpa, that Viṣṇu strode across both the earth and the sky.
Placing one foot on the mountain Udaya and the second on the lord of rivers, he went from there to this world via Puṣkara. || 117.7 ||
Then, as he was taking his stride and lifting one foot,
the lord of the Daityas named Ajaka seized that foot.
Lifting him up along with the Asura, Madhusūdana cast him away;
O Vyāsa, that Asura has not returned even to this day.
Then, having resorted to Rudra’s second supreme yoga,
he became a single stride alone in the intermediate space, the Bhuvarloka.
Then, O Vyāsa, having again established himself in yoga, Brahmā traversed the entire heavenly world in a single step from the intermediate space.
Having reached that world which had emerged, the best of gods reached Janaloka,
and there it came to an end.
And as he was departing from there, the Daityas, with weapons and missiles in their hands, rushed forward with speed; the gods repelled them.
At that time, ten thousand sons of Bala, his offspring,
were slain while fighting with various weapons in their hands.
"Bāṇa and Vāta—these two sons of Bali were possessed of great strength;
therefore, O Sage Vyāsa, they both fled from that battle. (117.15)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, having approached the Lord of Gods and released him from his bonds, established an agreement with him.
O Bala, you have handed over the entire kingdom of the gods to them;
remaining firm in truth and your promise, do not desire the kingdom again.
For as long as this Manvantara lasts, this auspicious agreement of yours must always be observed, my child; now go as you please.
You will undoubtedly obtain the full fruit of this sacrifice,
and by my grace, you shall indeed attain yoga once again.
Having been thus released, she took leave of him and entered Pātāla;
the gods, too, having regained their own kingdom, rejoiced greatly.
Vyāsa said:
Of what nature was that Blessed One Viṣṇu, who, having abandoned his own exalted dharma, recovered the three worlds, yet no misconduct whatsoever occurred on his part? (117.21)
Sanatkumāra said: As that god Viṣṇu proceeded, his form shone with the brilliance of a blazing fire; it was exceedingly fierce and difficult to behold even for the gods.
Then the gods, together with Indra, having accomplished their purpose, praised and extolled Viṣṇu, the supreme deity of great power.
Endowed with supreme joy and all bearing celestial weapons,
[they stood by] us as we were being tormented by the Dānavas, O Lord of the Gods.
O best of gods, you have indeed been our protector and the bestower of sovereignty;
through you, we all are made happy, just as those who perform meritorious deeds are by their own good works.
"O Lord, by your power we shall enjoy the kingdom free from anxiety, just as the sons of the gods did in former times through the power of the Sun. (117.26)
For you indeed are our supreme abode and likewise our ultimate goal;
you alone are the highest purifier, except for the god who is the lord of Umā.
Sanatkumāra said:
As the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was thus being praised by the gods,
he then experienced extreme satisfaction as well as great self-regard.
Then, O Sage, through his arrogance, that supreme yoga of his fell away,
just as fire is extinguished when sprinkled with water.
Then, O sage, having found that opportunity, that sinful and demonic woman,
being greatly delighted, entered into Janārdana with great joy.
O Vyāsa, that imperishable Viṣṇu, possessed by that evil,
did not shine there despite his brilliance, like a virtuous man who has encountered a cruel person.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Traversing of the Three Worlds," in the Vāmana section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, at that time he was thus joined with that sinful, demonic nature.
The best of gods assumed that very form of a dwarf.
But as he was acting in that manner, all the gods, including Indra, said to him: "O Lord, what is this strange transformation of yours? || 118.2 ||
Having heard those words of theirs, the sages of celebrated vows—
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Aṅgiras, and Kratu— [spoke].
Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Ruci;
Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, and likewise Auśija. || 118.4 ||
Gautama and Śaradvat, Kaśyapa and Uddala, Vatsāra, Naidhruva, and the self-possessed Cyavana. || 118.5 ||
Dadhīca, Ṛcīka, and the renowned Jamadagni;
likewise Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, and Agastya of great asceticism.
Bṛhaspati, Śuka, Śakti along with Parāśara, Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, and he who was Sārasvata; || 118.7 ||
These and other sages, O Vyāsa—Nārada along with Parvata—then spoke to the gods, having been urged by Brahmā. (118.8)
The sages said: "O lords of the gods, we have arrived here today from the world of Brahmā, having been swiftly commanded by Brahmā for the sake of this deity. (118.9)
That this high-souled Vaikuṇṭha, a kinsman of the gods, having abandoned his own duty, accepted the kingdom as a gift. (118.10)
Then that [form] of the Asuras which was terrifying to all living beings completely abandoned the Asuras and entered into Keśava.
Overwhelmed by her, this god is incapable of resisting his enemy;
indeed, behold that his splendor is no longer as auspicious as it was before.
If you consider him to be well-composed at sacred fords,
let him bathe there and then perform the horse sacrifice again together with the gods.
Then, having seen the wielder of the Pināka bow and being purified by him in every respect, the Grandfather spoke thus: "You shall become liberated from all evil."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those gods, together with the hosts of sages,
undertook a pilgrimage, taking that imperishable Viṣṇu with them.
They [saw] that beautiful lotus pond, renowned as Suṣumṇā,
covered with groves of lotuses and resounded by the joyful cries of birds.
It was endowed with many trees and groves, beautified by blooming lotuses,
rich in numerous orchards and trees, and possessed sands of fine gold.
Marked with blue diamonds and lapis lazuli, with its banks of sapphire and emerald,
it was rich with the cries of various birds and frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*.
Sweet with the songs sung by kinnaras and frequented by apsarases,
rich with the songs of intoxicated bees, it was the very abode of the residence of Śrī.
O observer of noble vows, having bathed in which, mortal men go to the abode of the immortals in their own bodies by means of a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun.
Having reached that Suṣumnā river then, the gods, together with the sages,
gathered lotuses, stalks, and fibers.
Then, having uprooted and taken from there a magnificent great lotus, full-blown and most enchanting, covered with a thousand petals, Agastya— || 118.22 ||
Then he cast it upon her bank and bathed at his pleasure;
and the omnipresent Lord Indra, unseen by anyone, seized it.
Then Agastya, having emerged, did not see that lotus;
and having addressed them all, the high-minded one said this: || 118.24 ||
Agastya said:
"O gods, by whom has my great, well-blossomed lotus been taken?
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those sages and the gods,
O sage of noble vows, each one individually exerted various efforts at that time.
Indra said:
"He who steals your lotus shall dwell eternally in heaven, performing many sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees. (118.26)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they all thought, O Vyāsa, that the lotus had been seized by the high-souled Lord of the Gods; and Indra spoke to him. 118.27.
Indra said:
"How may we hear the principles of dharma from the sages?
Therefore, this means has been devised; accept this water-born [lotus]. (118.28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having worshipped there the fires, the gods, and the ancestors, and having gratified the Brahmins, they likewise offered prayers for Viṣṇu. (118.29)
O Vyāsa, many sages and gods, being well-composed, went to other very meritorious and auspicious sacred fords. || 118.30 ||
Then they saw a single tree, a great withered trunk; and in its hollow they saw a parrot, wasting away, his senses agitated. (118.31)
Having seen him, those illustrious inhabitants of heaven, having perceived Śuka with their divine vision and being gratified, questioned him regarding Mahendra.
Indra said: "O Lord of Birds, why do you remain upon this tree now that it is dead—devoid of flowers, fruits, and leaves, withered and no longer a source of sustenance? (118.33)
Śuka said:
"In former times, this tree was indeed very great, like the Kalpa-tree;
it was long lived upon by those who subsisted on its fruits, which were like nectar."
When even a lord of the forest returns to this state through the power of time, how could a wise and grateful person like me ever abandon him? (118.35)
O Lord, I would be ungrateful were I to abandon this one who is as good as dead;
O Lord of Śacī, may those worlds that belong to this tree be mine.
Indra said: "O king of birds, you are wise, intelligent, high-souled, and a knower of the principles of policy; why do you make yourself appear as if you were a fool? (118.37)
"O virtuous one, this tree is his constant duty;
O lord of birds, it was performed by him out of its own nature, not through prior deliberation. (118.38)
This thought occurred to him: "Let the birds dwell with me constantly; let them eat fruits as they please. (118.39)
For just as fire, water, and wind are in reality insentient, they nevertheless act for the benefit of living beings by their very nature and not otherwise. (118.40)
In the same way, O bird, having understood that the action of this tree is born of its own nature,
abandon it and go elsewhere, where there may be happiness.
Śuka said:
"I am not deluded, O Lord of the Gods; do not disregard my words.
Listen, O Lord of the Devas, O Master, to what I say according to my own understanding. (118.42)
For just as fire, water, and wind are indeed insentient in their true nature,
O tiger among gods, so too are trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like.
For this cycle of existence has been ordained for all who perform actions;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods, there is no lack of consciousness in the trees.
And just as is the disposition of trees, so how may we act in every way for the benefit of living beings? Listen to that from me. (118.45)
Having created these primary beings, the highly illustrious Svayambhū spoke to them:
"Act in every way for the benefit of all creatures."
Therefore, O Lord of the World, they exist for the benefit of all beings, even down to their fruits, flowers, bark, and sprouts.
O Lord, what is unknown to you—that the wind, fire, and water, as well as the auspicious mountains, all proceed according to their nature through the power of intelligence? (118.48)
Indra said: "How did you obtain this knowledge? What is your duty, and what is your toil?
We wish to know this; tell us, O Lord of Birds. (118.49)
Śuka said: O Lord of Gods, from birth until now, my mind has never been inclined toward betraying a friend, even when death itself had arrived. (118.50)
I am devoted to my parents and likewise intent upon my own wife; I do not hold living beings in contempt, and I approach my wife only during her season. (118.51)
"I do not eat the grain of others, O Lord of the Devas;
therefore, O best of gods, my stainless knowledge has arisen. (118.52)
Indra said: "I am pleased with this virtuous intellect of yours, O best of birds. Choose a boon; I shall grant whatever you deem auspicious. (118.53)
Śuka said:
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace let this lord of the forest live;
therefore, O God, I would choose no other supreme boon. (118.54)
Indra said:
"The destinies of living beings are proclaimed to be determined by their own actions; one falls by one's own action alone. O intelligent one, what use have you for this [other]? (118.55)
"Having ascended this celestial chariot given by me, O best of birds, go quickly to my world while being praised, as a man [is honored]. || 118.56 ||
Śuka said:
"I do not desire worlds, nor celestial chariots, nor even happiness. Grant me that which has been requested; this tree indeed belongs to those who live. (118.57)
Sanatkumāra said: Having understood his true nature and everything about him, that best of gods restored the tree, endowed with all its qualities, just as it was before.
And Śuka, by virtue of that deed, as well as through his firm devotion and his assistance to the distressed, went indeed to the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter in the Vāmana-tīrtha-yātrā of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 118.118 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those deities [went] to the city named Kṛmilā.
For they, having approached, beheld this there, O great sage. || 119.1 ||
The Brāhmaṇī named Gautamī was like another Rudrāṇī;
she was righteous, generous, and had burnt away her sins through asceticism.
While she was devoted to her ascetic penance and her husband had gone to the world of Brahmā,
her son was bitten by a great black serpent and died.
He arrived at that place, where a hunter named Arjunaka was also present;
having arrived there, he then saw him overwhelmed by poison.
Having gone there, he said to Gautamī: "O lady rich in asceticism, this son of yours has been bitten by a snake and has quickly perished; why do you not perceive him? (119.5)
Thus addressed, she approached and, seeing her son whose life had departed,
that woman of great vows wept profusely, O Vyāsa, like one whose child has died.
While she was thus lamenting, that hunter Arjunaka then dug up the hole, drew out the serpent, and bound it securely.
Bound by him, that wicked-souled black cobra, being extremely distressed,
then spoke to that hunter who was known as Arjunaka.
"What is the use of my being bound by you? Do you not perceive this as unrighteousness?
We are not even fit to be eaten by mortals; why do you not release me? (119.9)
Arjuna said:
"Having cut you into pieces, I shall give you as food to the peacock, since this son of a seer was devoured by you and has indeed died. (119.10)
The serpent said:
"Impelled by Time, I bit that son of the ṛṣi.
O Arjunaka, you ought not to reproach me for this fault in accordance with the truth. (119.11)
Arjuna said:
"O serpent, if you have been impelled by Time and have bitten me, you are indeed merely the instrument of my death; therefore, I shall strike you severely. (119.12)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, that Gautamī, afflicted by supreme sorrow, brought about her own death; Kāla, fearing her, then approached her.
Kāla said:
"I am indeed the Time of all living beings; there is no doubt about this.
Urged by Death itself, I have slain the son of the ṛṣi."
Arjuna said:
"Whether instigated by you or by Death himself, he bit me;
since he is the cause for my killing him, therefore I shall slay him. (119.15)
Sanatkumāra said: Then Death, of great mind, having approached that place out of fear of Gautamī’s asceticism, spoke these words in a melodious voice. || 119.16 ||
"I too, being well-composed and bound by destiny, am killing him; you ought not to find fault with me, O lady of excellent vows."
Arjuna said:
Whether it be destiny, death, or even time that is the cause, the black serpent is nevertheless the instrumental agent; therefore, he must be slain without a doubt. || 119.18 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Niyati arrived there, O Vyāsa, and being afraid, she spoke these words at that time to the sorrowful Gautamī. (119.19)
"O virtuous one, O lady of excellent complexion, ever unwearied, I bind living beings with my snares under the power of Kṛtānta and bring them under the control of Death. (119.20)
Kṛtānta said:
"O virtuous lady, I am indeed the servant of the great-souled Yama;
impelled by him, I lead living beings to the abode of Yama. (119.21)
Arjuna said:
"Whether it be Yama, or Kṛtānta, or even these [deities] who are the cause of this, such a man of evil conduct shall never be released in this manner. (119.22)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, the high-minded Yama himself came there and spoke thus to that Gautamī.
Neither I nor these great beings are the cause of your son's death;
look into the matter of his passing and listen also to my words.
O auspicious lady, the union of living beings with a body is caused by merit and demerit;
likewise, their separation from the body occurs again through the exhaustion of those very two.
For embodied beings, dharma alone is said to be the sole cause of life;
when that is exhausted, death is declared, and that is remembered as both time and death.
In the Kṛta age, the time-period is said to consist of four thousand years;
in the Tretā, it is three thousand, and in the Dvāpara, two thousand.
In the Kali age, O observer of the great vow, they say the lifespan of a living being is indeed a hundred years;
at any other time than that, it is declared to be otherwise—listen now to that death as well.
Those gods who dwell within his senses, O best of bipeds,
all those most excellent deities take away one portion for themselves.
For one who sees with the eye what is wicked, and likewise speaks of what is wicked, as well as for one who hears it, reflects upon it, understands it, and even perceives it; ||| 119.30 ||
Likewise, for one who touches, smells, or even eats, as well as from grasping, moving about, and the discharge of pleasure; || 119.31 ||
Furthermore, living beings indeed carry off another portion, and diseases likewise carry off yet another portion that is most wicked among them. (119.32)
Furthermore, the ancestors have one portion, and the gods another;
likewise, the seers, the sacrificial fire, the moon, the sun, and the planets have yet another.
O virtuous lady, as long as food has been brought for that embodied being, so long shall he live; and that is what is called untimely death.
And how a living being dies at an untimely hour when asceticism has been intensified—listen now to me as I speak of this here, O lady of excellent complexion. (119.35)
As long as the lifespan of that being is not exhausted in the Great Vow, so long does he obtain life; at its conclusion, he dies once again.
Whatever offense it was for which the gods took away his life,
by that a great unrighteousness (adharma) arose within him, bringing an end to his existence.
Then, O virtuous lady, a disease manifested that cut through his vital organs;
with his vitals thus severed, he was rendered helpless and cast off his body, O observer of great vows.
Having attained another body, he proceeds to another state;
that which does not inflict disease upon him through its favor is indeed unrighteousness.
Even that [karmic residue] of the gods dwelling in bodies is indeed destroyed by another means—
through poisons, the falling of weapons, various kinds of creatures,
and many other terrible things; for one who perceives this, there is no fault.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having perceived him through her ascetic power, Gautamī, who was firm in her great vows and freed from sorrow, spoke these words to that Arjuna: || 119.41 ||
Gautami said: "Release him, Arjunaka; this serpent does not deserve death from me.
He was possessed by unrighteousness and by the gods that he bit my son. (119.42)
Those great-souled lords, having entered both sentient and insentient beings, employ them all here according to their respective natures.
"He has died according to his own dharma; there is no fault on the part of the ascetics. Go, all you deities, to your own homes; why remain here? || 119.44 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, all those goddesses, having been sent by the wife of Brahmā, spoke these words together to that Gautamī: || 119.45 ||
The gods said:
"We are pleased with you, O knower of dharma, whose sins have been burnt away by asceticism.
Let this son of yours live, and may he remain steadfast in his own duty."
"O virtuous lady, this serpent is Adharma himself standing here in embodied form; and this one, in the shape of a lizard, is Dharma. Behold these two, O lady of great vows! (119.47)
O you of great vows, this examination has indeed been performed for you by these gods;
all the worlds shall be imperishable for you, without a doubt.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those gods, led by Indra, suddenly beheld everything there exactly as it had occurred, and I reported all of that to them.
Having bathed, all those highly fortunate ones, with concentrated minds, went again to another sacred ford, and likewise to others, repeatedly.
Proceeding in due order, they arrived once again at the place where the Kṛtyā had previously been slain by the highly powerful Indra, the lord of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
By whom was that Kṛtyā produced, for what purpose, and for whom, O Lord? And how was she slain again? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a king of great power known as Tṛṇabindu;
skilled in speech, he spoke these words to the seven sages. (119.53)
"O Brahmins, perform the sacrifice for me; indeed, I shall give you much wealth.
They replied, "O virtuous lord of men, we will not perform the sacrifice for you. (119.54)
When he had been initiated for the sacrifice, a great drought occurred;
then those [sages], overcome by hunger, arrived at the sacrificial ground by chance. || 119.55 ||
Then the king said to them, "Tell me, what shall I give to you?
They replied with angry words, "O King, give us our son! (119.56)
Having paid them due honor, that king, bowing with great respect, bestowed upon them his son and his wealth, O descendant of Parāśara.
Likewise, O ascetics rich in austerity, having abandoned the substance of that very Anata, they come taking his son with them because of the child's extreme delicacy. (119.58)
Afflicted there by hunger and thirst, and further exhausted by the journey, he died.
Having placed him in a forest fire, they stood watching.
While they were looking on there, O lord of men, Vyāsa arrived;
wearing divine earrings, he spoke thus to those sages with a smile.
Tṛṇabindu said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, you did not accept gifts from me;
nor, O sages strengthened by penance, did you officiate as priests for us. (119.61)
"O twice-born ones, you see no fault here in the death of this child; yet it is unrighteous and disgraceful! Alas, your minds are indeed set upon unrighteousness! (119.62)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, disregarding him and without saying anything at all, they departed for another direction in the forest, tormented by hunger. (119.63)
And at that time, O Vyāsa, Tṛṇabindu, desiring their comfort and welfare, created many trees there in an instant through his ascetic power.
And having reached that forest, O Vyāsa, they beheld many trees laden with fruit; at that time, they attained supreme satisfaction.
Having taken them, they broke them open and beheld therein gold, food, delicacies, and likewise silver of great luster.
Those sages, endowed with ascetic power, considered that [destruction] to have been wrought by Tṛṇabindu.
Thereupon, those seven ṛṣis of firm vows abandoned that forest and departed for another direction; and Tṛṇabindu became enraged.
Then that lord of men, his soul overwhelmed with grief and deeply agitated, approached those sages and spoke to them, bowing down with palms joined in reverence.
Tṛṇabindu said: "O Brahmins, I have not fallen from my status, nor am I a doer of evil deeds; I have not been shunned by the Brahmins, nor am I a non-sacrificer, nor a committer of sin. (119.69)
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I am born into the pure lineage of lords of men;
I protect my subjects properly—why do you not hold me in high esteem? (119.70)
Having heard those words of his, those sages of great vows said: "O King, we will by no means accept them. (119.71)
"You are excellent, endowed with virtues, a protector of subjects and a lord of creatures.
We are well-pleased; we do not accept wealth from you, O King. (119.72)
Sanatkumāra said:
O sage, having spoken thus to the king, they all departed;
and that king, filled with great wrath, [then entered] the blazing fire.
He invoked a magical spell (kṛtyā) from that [fire] and created one of immense power;
known as Yātudhānī, he then spoke these words to her.
"O mighty one, go and devour the seven sages in this task;
for you must recognize by their names those ascetics, Vasiṣṭha and the others."
Having gone to the auspicious and divine lotus pond named Śubhā,
she reached its bank and stood there waiting for them.
Those sages, too, being deeply distressed and their senses agitated by hunger and thirst,
searched for other regions and then came upon that auspicious pond.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having seen the fault in their departure, Purandara approached them in the guise of a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), accompanied by a dog. || 119.78 ||
Seeing him laughing, his arms outstretched and his hand occupied with a triple staff, they all spoke to one another in a gentle manner. (119.79)
The sages said: "Surely, because he has been eating here day and night, always without weariness,
from whichever direction he came, it was from that very place that he became fat."
Or perhaps this man, with hands ever outstretched, is a constant beggar;
he has become fat by selling his asceticism and his Vedic study.
Having thus imagined him in many ways, those sages whose wealth was their asceticism asked that one of immeasurable soul, saying, "Who are you? (119.82)
Indra said:
"O best of Brahmins, I am a wandering mendicant coming from Daśeraka;
I shall go to the auspicious pool, for my name is Śunaḥsakha. (119.83)
"Dogs have always been dear to me, and I have always been dear to dogs;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, I am known by the name Śunasakha (Friend of Dogs). || 119.84 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they went together with him to that auspicious lotus-pool;
they beheld the Kṛtyā there and were repelled by her. (119.85)
Or if it pleases you, O wise ones, to plunge into this river,
then tell me your names here and wander at ease, O imperishable ones.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they said to that maiden, "So be it.
And then, O subduer of enemies, her brother spoke thus to all those sages.
"O Brahmins, this is a sorceress; she is not an ordinary human being.
For there must be some purpose behind her speaking to you in this manner."
If you consider this to be the highest good and most beneficial, then speak out your names in such a way that she does not recognize them. || 119.89 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," O Vyāsa, those auspicious sages,
having caused her names to be heard, entered into their respective abodes as they desired.
They spoke of their own names, which were difficult to understand and etymologically obscure; she did not comprehend them, and so they entered the water. (119.91)
Sanatkumāra said: Without having ascertained their names, that Śikhodbhavā spoke to Śvasana: "Tell me [their names], and then you may go or not. (119.92)
Śvasakha said:
"I am a friend of dogs, and I am associated with cruel dogs;
therefore, O night-roaming Yātudhānī, know me as Śvasakha. (119.93)
The Yātudhānī said:
"O lowest of men, speak your name only once more;
then you shall go into the presence of the Brahmins, known by me. (119.94)
The Dog-Friend said:
"I am a friend of dogs, O goddess; my friendship with dogs is unfailing. As a friend of dogs, I shall therefore slay you, O sorceress; listen! (119.95)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to that cruel woman, the Lord of the Gods struck her on the head with his triple staff; by that blow, she was instantly reduced to ashes.
And that son of Tṛṇabindu, having been killed by a mere magical rite, was quickly restored to life by Śakra and approached his father. (119.97)
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Śakti, having thus slain her, Indra, the friend of the serpent, once again seized the lotus stalks, roots, and lotuses belonging to the sages. (119.98)
Then, having safely crossed over but not seeing him, those brahmins, filled with rage and bound by their mutual vows, pronounced curses upon one another.
Then all those best of sages, having approached Śvasakha, said:
"We have doubts regarding you; tell us how you may be liberated from them. (119.100)
Śvasākha said:
"He who plucks your roots, flowers, and fruits—may he eat sweets with happiness, together with his friends and his family. (119.101)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those sages, O Vyāsa, spoke to Purandara:
"The substance that was taken by you from us—give that back to us again. (119.102)

O Vyāsa, the Blessed One, being pleased, took all their roots and fruits and spoke these words to those sages: 119.103. "O Vyāsa, the Blessed One, being pleased, took all their roots and fruits and spoke these words to those sages."
Indra said:
"O Brahmins, this *kṛtyā* (magical spell) created of old for your sake has been destroyed by me with my triple staff for your benefit, O you whose wealth is asceticism."
"This was done to you by King Tṛṇabindu when he was enraged."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having approached him, the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity bathed that Viṣṇu in the sacred ford honored by hosts of seers.
Then, having arrived at the Himavat mountain, those men of firm vows, filled with joy, caused Viṣṇu to be worshipped with an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
While he was sacrificing, Tryambaka, the Lord of Gods and Master of the Ganas,
filled with joy toward the sacrifice, arrived through the sky.
Vyāsa said:
"O son of Brahmā, alas! You have related to me this account of the Yātudhānī, which is supremely secret and very difficult to understand. (119.108)
For this is a supreme secret, full of great significance, ever glorious and most purifying;
it has been correctly proclaimed by you, O Great Yogi, like the nectar of immortality possessing the luster of the full moon.
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter in the Vāmana-tīrtha-yātrā, within the Yātudhānī-upākhyāna, of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 119 || 119 ||
Vyāsa said:
Hereafter, I shall relate how that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Controller, departed.
Having observed him performing the sacrifice with the ritual, tell us [the truth].
Sanatkumāra said:
That divine Lord, the wielder of the trident whose banner bears the bull,
spoke these words on the eighth day of the dark fortnight to the Goddess, the daughter of Himavat.
"O auspicious goddess, today in this world is the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight;
tonight we shall go to behold the cremation grounds."
The Goddess said:
"O God, O Protector of the World, let it be as it pleases you; whatever is desired by you, O Mahādeva, that shall indeed be twice as much for me. (120.4)
Then, O great sage, on that day in Ujjayinī,
the young son of a brahmin— pure and learned— passed away.
Having prepared him for you and adorned him according to the prescribed rites,
they led him to the cremation ground, wailing and weeping.
Having then led that young Raktapādaka to the cremation ground, they,
overwhelmed by grief, wept piteously and profusely out of affection.
Then, seeing them weeping, the vulture, filled with hunger and provoked to anger,
spoke to those twice-born ones as if he were wise, having first given them instructions.
"O brahmins, listen to my words, which I speak to you as humans;
you are clearly devoid of wisdom, so attend to my speech throughout this night. (120.9)
This man has indeed died by the power of time; why do you grieve like the ignorant?
He will not come back to life through weeping; perform your own duties, free from feverish distress.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, they then departed, leaving their son behind while looking back at him again and again; then the jackal spoke to them.
"Alas! Shame on all you humans! Behold, how devoid of intelligence, lacking affection, and ungrateful you are, that you depart indeed, having abandoned him. (120.12)
A son is obtained with difficulty and is likewise born with difficulty;
moreover, he grows up cruelly, afflicted by disease.
"Indeed, he has forgotten many endearing things you did;
this boy has done these other things—oh, what a lack of affection on your part! (120.14)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, having heard the words of the jackal, they gathered together and stood weeping, surrounding him in that cemetery.
Then at night the Lord of Gods, the one with matted hair, arrived together with his beloved,
surrounded by all his attendants and accompanied by Nandīśvara.
Approaching them, that Lord, who brings happiness to all beings,
replied to those who were weeping there, saying, "I am here as the giver of boons."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, with voices full of sorrow and eyes clouded with tears, they said:
"O Lord, by your command, this son shall not be Jīva. (120.18)
Having restored their young son to life there,
the Blessed One granted him the status of Gaṇeśa and an eternal, imperishable residence in that very place.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus spent that night, he went according to the prescribed rite to the cremation grounds and proceeded to the auspicious Vaidūrya peak of the Himavat.

He of blazing splendor, the omnipresent and imperishable soul, the wielder of the Pināka bow who dwells upon mountain peaks, spoke to those consecrated for the supreme sacrifice: "Choose a boon, you who have taken refuge solely in the triple heaven."
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 120.120 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having beheld Mahādeva, the sole kinsman of the seven worlds, they...
With palms joined in reverence, they all spoke, bowing their heads down upon their knees.
O Blessed One, O best of gods, Hari, desiring the welfare of the world, formerly accepted a gift from him; therefore, let sin pursue him.
Therefore, O Lord of this world, O Lord of the gods, being entreated by us, perform what is for the welfare of this devotee who bows before you.
"Let this sacrifice be completed; let Hari be released from evil;
and let all the gods, together with Indra, regain their own vital energy."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the Blessed One, with a joyful countenance,
completed the sacrifice and split that mountain with his trident.
From that [lotus], because of its division, waters as white as nectar, conch shells, and the moon issued forth;
there, they then bathed Viṣṇu.
Then, as soon as he had bathed, there emerged from his body a most terrible, deformed demoness of evil, with a distorted face.
"Though they have rushed against the gods to slay them and were restrained by the kinsman of the gods—[he] said to her:
'None of the gods, including Indra himself, should be killed. (121.8)
And right here shall be your highly honored abode,
more meritorious than all other sacred fords and the destroyer of all sins.
"You shall constantly deliver seven ancestors and seven descendants;
you shall be renowned in the world as 'Sandhyā,' the auspicious and most excellent of all sacred fords."
This auspicious and divine stream of water bestows the fruit of all sacrifices;
by worshipping you, men shall cause seven generations of their lineages to cross over [to liberation].
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those deities, having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, according to the prescribed rule, at the word of Rudra, [departed].
Having constructed a temple for the god, they departed for the third heaven.
When the hosts of gods had gone, Hari then [remained] on Śivakūṭa.

Having then performed the horse sacrifice, he remained there worshipping the God. After six thousand years and six months of that [sacrifice] had been spent, the Lord of Gods, whose banner is the bull, was gratified.
Soma, joyful and accompanied by his retinue, spoke this again to him:
"Rejoicing and with a most satisfied soul, tell me, what shall I give to you? (121.15)
Viṣṇu said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, O Dispeller of Time, tell me how I may avoid the destruction of my worlds, whether it be through sin or even through ascetic penance."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, laughing, the Lord of Gods, the Prajāpati, being well-pleased, addressed Viṣṇu and said, "Perform this secret and great vow. (121.17)
Then, having performed the protective rites, he [taught him] that auspicious yoga, the yantra, and the vow which bring about all dharmas and accomplish supreme sovereignty.
Having performed that divine Pāśupata rite which fulfills all desires for twelve years, he attained supreme sovereignty.
The trident-bearing god himself, being pleased upon seeing him in such a state, gave him half of his own body; thus it became Viṣṇu-Śaṅkara.
That mortal who should always hear this on every sacred festival day (parvan),
and worship Śiva and Viṣṇu, shall go to the supreme goal.
Thus, having conquered, that Viṣṇu Vāmana, possessed of great strength,
restored the three worlds entirely to all the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O bull among sages, when the three worlds had been overrun by the gods,
those asuras who remained after the slaughter took refuge with the two Dānavas.
Tāraka and Maya waged war against the gods;
both Maya and Tāraka were surrounded by their sons and grandsons.
Vipracitti, the son of Danu, and those who are known as his sons—
the Nivātakavacas, all the Paulomas, the sons of Kālakā,
the valiant Saiṃhikeyas, and likewise the host of Bāleyas. || 121.25 ||
These and many other dānavas, arrogant in their strength,
equipped for battle and filled with rage, then challenged the gods.
Seeing them calling out, even the gods, well-prepared for battle, approached them and, desiring combat, then engaged in a struggle with them.
Between them there occurred that tumultuous battle, hair-raising,
for eight hundred and sixteen thousand years.
Despite their divine weapons, victory did not fall to either side in the battle;
then, in that conflict, the gods were confronted by the sons of Siṃhika, who were difficult to overcome.
The great beings were defeated like herds of animals by lions;
having observed their strength, the thousand-eyed Purandara [acted].
He went for refuge to Rudra, the imperishable Lord of the gods;
having gone there, he reached the peak of the mountain Suvarṇacūḍa, where the deity had made his abode.
He beheld Mahādeva together with the Goddess, surrounded by his attendants,
blazing like fire, difficult to be seen by those who have not disciplined their souls.
Having been previously described by Nandin, that best of gods,
upon seeing him, bowed his head in salutation and spoke these words.
O Lord, sixteen thousand and eight hundred divine years have passed since that battle of the gods.
Tāraka and Maya, those two Dānavas intoxicated by war,
relying upon them, all the Asuras slaughter the gods as if they were mere cattle.
O best of gods, grant life to those gods who are being slain, or do whatever is appropriate, O Lord.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull reflected upon them and then, O Rāma, spoke the name "Rāma. (121.37)
The Blessed One said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! You have performed very great ascetic penance.
Go and, through fair combat, make all the gods free from their feverish anxiety."
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, the powerful Rāma, son of Jamadagni, bowed down with great reverence and spoke in a piteous voice. (121.39)
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, I am of little prowess and am greatly emaciated by asceticism;
moreover, O Lord of Gods, I am unskilled in weapons and shall not be able to withstand battle, O All-pervading One. (121.40)
Devāvaha said:
"Go, O Brahmin; you shall be able to fight today, so do not grieve.
I will empower you; do not be distressed, O Bhārgava. (121.41)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lord Hara spoke to Indra, the lord of the gods:
"He shall slay your enemies; give him a chariot. (121.42)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Śakra, having bowed down and taken Rāma with him,
went to that very region where the battle had occurred.
Then Śakra, Purandara himself, having equipped him with that preeminent chariot, said to Rāma: "Summon the sons of Siṃhikā."
With that preeminent chariot, Rāma— the best among strikers—
was equipped with armor, fastened his quiver, and took up his arrows, sword, and bow.
Wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, and bearing raised banners and flags,
he rushed with speed toward the unassailable sons of Siṃhikā.
A most terrible and fearsome battle took place between them and him, like that of tigers in the forest against a lion. || 121.47 ||
There, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas beheld a marvel:
that even he who was but one was seen on the stage as possessing many forms.
At that time, the descendant of Bhṛgu was not seen taking up his variegated arrows, nor likewise in the act of fixing them, nor while drawing back his bow.
At that time, his great bow was seen by his enemies as being drawn into a complete circle, and he himself became difficult to behold.
Turning back, O Vyāsa, that mighty descendant of Bhṛgu, filled with rage,
discharged ten sharp arrows at each of them, one by one, into their mouths.
There they beheld the marvelous lightness of that wise one; a great sound of "Excellent! Excellent! arose there from all living beings.
Sanatkumāra said:
With their faces pierced by those arrows, the mighty sons of Siṃhika fell to the earth along with their elephants, like palm trees struck down by the wind. || 121.53 ||
Then that host of ten thousand enemies of the gods was consumed by the descendant of Bhṛgu, just as the world is consumed by Time.
Then the gods, along with the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and cāraṇas, having exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! to him, praised him with joyful countenances.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having observed that deed of his, the Lord Pākaśāsana,
together with the deities, honored Bhārgava with great respect.
The one of great splendor, having embraced him again and again, said this:
"This deed belongs to you; its like is not found among others even in heaven. (121.57)
If those sons of Siṃhikā were slain by you so suddenly,
this great feat of yours is equal to that of the Three-Eyed Lord (Śiva) at Tripura;
there is no one equal to you in the world— this I tell you as the truth.
These were not equal to you, O King; they were not equal to any human being.
Invulnerable to all living creatures, they have been slain by you alone.
Therefore, being pleased with you, we grant you invincibility,
as well as inexhaustible strength in battle and supreme fame upon the earth.
And Tryambaka, being pleased by your divine and desired boons, will grant them to you;
and in battles, you shall conquer the assembled host according to your wish.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having been addressed thus by those gratified gods, that ascetic of great austerity went to the god Tryambaka with a joyful and contented mind. (121.62)
Then even the gods, well-prepared for battle, swiftly assailed Tāraka, who was intoxicated with war, together with Maya.
Their own momentum checked by the force of the Daityas, those mighty warriors, possessing a speed like that of the ocean,
fell upon the hosts of Daityas and struck them violently, just as forest-dwelling lions pounce upon elephants.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon the Son of Jamadagni," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having witnessed the slaughter of Saiṃhikeya as well as the victory of the gods, the Skandapurāṇa 122 [continues].
Suddenly, the Daitya armies were shattered on all sides.
Vipracitti, Ṣaṇḍa, and the great asura Prahlāda,
followed by Kālanemi, then became enraged against Keśava in the encounter.
Mounting his great chariot, which was equipped with a hundred shafts and bore a lofty banner,
the Dānava rushed with speed toward Keśava.
Then, O Vyāsa, as he was rushing forward, Keśava discharged a great, irresistible discus; at that moment, he [the demon] brought it to a standstill.
Seeing him thus standing firm, all the gods, filled with fury,
were indeed defeated by Kālanemi, who was now without weapons.
Having put them to flight, that lord of the Daityas turned them back;
having accomplished this, the imperishable one then assumed the office of the world-protector.
Then, pervading both the earth and the sky, that one of great strength moved through the three worlds by means of his supernatural power, like the Self-born Creator himself.
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing that Daitya situated in such a state, the gods, together with Indra,
terrified by fear, then went for refuge to the imperishable Hari.
And that Lord of Gods, Hari, the refuge and kinsman of the three worlds,
granted them protection from fear with the desire to slay the Dānava.
Then, having pervaded both heaven and earth in every way with his form,
he called to mind that lotus-wheel which had been fashioned by Rudra.
Then, O Vyāsa, he [Indra] struck off the great head of the Dānava,
just as a violent wind sweeps away a ripe fruit from the top of a palmyra tree.
When that Daitya had been slain,
the great warriors Tāraka and Maya retreated with great speed toward Pātāla.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, O Vyāsa, did that fierce battle take place on account of Tāraka,
wherein Kālanemi was slain and Virocana became renowned.
And the valiant Saiṃhikeyas, the great asura Tuhuṇḍa,
Surocana, Satāvarta, Hāla, and likewise Gārgyaśiras.
Vipāka, Saha, Pāka, Caṇḍa, Kārtasvana, and Kubha—
these and other lords of the Daityas were slain during the Tārakāmaya war; furthermore,
the cruel Vipracitti was killed along with his younger brother upon the banner.
Vyāsa said:
How did that battle between the gods and the asuras come to pass?
And how did his name indeed become "Dhvaja"? (122.17)
And having performed that deed so difficult for all beings to accomplish, Jāmadagnya, the upholder of the Bhṛgu lineage, came into the presence of Tryambaka.
I wish to know this: what was said to him by the God of gods? 122.18.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the son of Jamadagni, sent by the immortals themselves,
went to the secret city of the god, the abode of Candra.
Vyāsa said:
O you of firm vows, tell me how that divine city of Purīcandra came to be—that secret abode of Maheśa. 122.20.
Sanatkumāra said:
O high-minded one, I shall now relate to you that which is difficult to attain, hearing which even a doer of evil deeds may go to the supreme goal. (122.21)
In former times, there were two high-souled sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
it is said that for the sake of the gods' mission, they committed the killing of a Brahmin.
Overpowered by that evil, those two gods, though once exceedingly powerful, became utterly devoid of consciousness; they fell completely into the state of animal births.
Then, when a divine year had passed, the immeasurable-souled Brahmā himself came there along with the deities and the ṛṣis.
Then he attempted to awaken that god and his attendant;
yet even so, they did not perceive him, being completely shrouded by their own karma.
Then Brahmā spoke to all those dwellers of heaven:
"For the sake of Nārāyaṇa, you must practice the highest dharma."
"Then the god, together with men, shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
To him who spoke thus, all the gods, bowing their heads in reverence, then said with palms joined in salutation: "Instruct us as to what penance and ritual act we must perform."
Brahmā said:
"All of you, being self-restrained, subsisting on air alone, and having conquered your senses, recite the *Hṛdaya* of the Rudras correctly; then you shall attain yoga. (122.28)
Sanatkumāra said: Having replied, "So be it," those lords of the gods, dwelling in the waters, performed silent recitations together with the sages for six hundred thousand years.
Then, after a long time, for those of disciplined soul,
a subtle yoga manifested, from which auspicious fire arose.
By that fire, the sin of killing a Brahmin was then consumed;
having abandoned it, she entered the water.
The waters, though pervaded by the *nāstya* [demon], did not become flavorful;
they were indeed odorless, colorless, and lacked luster. The earth became deficient in vitality, and its fiery energy ceased to be sharp. || 122.32 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having seen him in that manner, they joined [in yoga] once more;
with their minds concentrated, they meditated upon the heart-mantra of the Rudras.
Then the blessed Lord Śūlapāṇi, whose banner bears the bull, arrived;
being pleased, he said to the gods, "I am gratified; tell me what you desire."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those deities, having beheld Rudra perfectly, took their delight;
bowing down, they praised him whose vehicle is the sacrificial cloud.

The gods said: "Salutations to the supreme deity, whose splendor is like the fire at the end of an eon; salutations to him who is performing penance within the waters, and to the heart of the Rudras. (122.36)
Salutation to the one who holds the great axe in his hand, to the golden-bodied one,
to the lord of the Vasus, and to the lord of the gods.
To the pure one, to the one who repeatedly licks [the oblation], to the wrath that has just been born,
to the lord of the planets (grahas), and to the heart of the planets.
Homage indeed to the King of Planets, who is followed by the great planets; homage to him who is fierce in self-restraint and tranquility, and who wields a formidable staff.
Salutations to Yama, the Lord of Restraint, and the bearer of the staff of Yama;
salutations to the supreme deity, the highest of all things.
Salutations to the Lord of the great ones, to the bearer of the water-pot, to Vāmadeva, to the Eldest, and to the Lord of creatures. 122.41.
Salutation to the Lord of Pradhāna, to the one who sets Pradhāna in motion;
salutation to the thousand-faced one, to the wielder of the mace, salutation to the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to the creator who is the form of the wind and possesses many forms;
salutations to the destroyer of ritual sacrifices and the extinguisher of the fire of desire.
Salutations to him whose form is the limbs of the Vedic meters, and to the one with deformed eyes;
salutations to the destroyer of the collection of the senses, and to him who has reached the end of the Vedas.
Homage be to the destroyer of the thunderbolt, and to him who is beyond the mind;
homage to you, who wear a garland of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and who are adorned with a lotus garland.
