Salutations to the one who burns the mountains, to the one born from that which is born of the mountains;
to the great one of universal form, and to him who is honored by the great.
To the one with a hundred thousand eyes, to the one with an eye on his forehead,
to the leader of great yoga, and likewise to Tatpuruṣa.
Homage to the secret of the Vedas, who is praised by the gods and the Vedas;
to the yogi who is meditated upon, who laughs with the falling thunderbolt.
Homage be to you who dwell in the heart; homage to you who are omnipresent;
to the lord of the best of youths, and to the progenitor of the youth.
To him who wanders with staff in hand, the Ender, the Unconquered;
to the Auspicious One, of auspicious form, who sets forth all that is auspicious.
To Śiva, who possesses an auspicious form, who is eternally the pervader of all,
who is the secret of the science of archery, and the originator of the science of archery.
O Lord of Gods, who destroys all sins and dispels all evils, you who are auspicious and gentle, grant us that which is in our hearts.
O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, whatever we have spoken improperly, you ought to forgive all of that out of your affection for your devotees.
O Lord, this kinsman of the gods, whose soul was once overwhelmed by sin,
shall become as pure as the moon when he is with Nara, O Lord of Gods.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, that man who, being devoted and self-restrained, constantly recites this hymn to Tryambaka, is liberated from sin.
One shall be liberated from all sins and recover what was lost;
and one does not fall into an evil rebirth, even if one has indeed committed great wickedness.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by the gods, that blessed Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the gods, was pleased and spoke to all the deities, O son of Satyavatī. (122.57)
The God of Gods said:
"O gods, I am thoroughly pleased; choose the boon you desire.
I shall grant it, O ones of great wisdom; do not remain silent, but speak everything."
The gods said:
"O Mahādeva, this Hari has his mind overcome by sin;
quickly dispel that [sin] from him, as the sun dispels the mist. (122.59)
O Lord of Gods, this one of great power performs his work for the benefit of the world and the gods; indeed, destroy his evil.
And may we, standing in the midst of the assembly, obtain equality with you and membership in your host,
O Lord of all gods, if you so deem it fit, O All-pervading One.
Sanatkumāra said: While the gods were speaking thus, O best of sages,
the blessed Lord Śarva, with a joyful mind, spoke laughingly.
"O gods, this Viṣṇu shall be instantly liberated from this sin;
and this highly fortunate woman, the personification of sin, shall be born upon barren soil. || 122.63 ||
The resin of trees, the foam of the waters,
the scent of great serpents, and likewise the censure of women.
The mention of the impurity of a consecrated Brahmin, the reviling of Brahmins, and the disparagement of cows; 122.65.
The kindling of fire and the damming of rivers—
if a man, possessed by passion and delusion, should perform these acts,
he would incur this [sin] in this world, even if he were the Self-born Lord himself, the protector of the worlds.
But when Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva,
then this man, Nara, shall enjoy her in embodied form.
Having enjoyed there the boon granted by Hari, he shall then be born as his own sister;
being further liberated from sin, he will wander through this world.
However, so that even this sister of his shall not cause him any hindrance,
let him practice this formidable asceticism, which is exceedingly difficult to perform.
"And you, together with the sages, remain right here, well-composed and undistracted; perform the preparatory rites at my command."
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the Lord, all those gods then spoke to Hari: "Perform severe austerity; from that you shall indeed attain the highest good."
Then, having ascended Candra, the king of mountains, he practiced very great austerity with a well-concentrated mind, which scorched the collection of his senses.
The high-souled gods, together with the sages of firm vows,
performed austerities with concentrated minds on Hiraṇyavarṇa, the king of mountains.
Then, when their vow was completed, the wielder of the Pināka bow instructed them in that great and radiant Pāśupata vow.
With a satisfied soul, he addressed the foremost of the gods,
speaking in a voice as deep and grave as the resonance of clouds and kettledrums.
The God of gods said:
"O guardians of the worlds, this very *puraścaraṇa* has been well-performed by you yourselves.
Having practiced this *Pāśupata* rite, you have become free from suffering and devoid of fear. (122.76)
This is the supreme and most purifying vow, superior even to Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
there exists nothing higher than this, nor anything subtler anywhere.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, naked, and truly pure,
by bringing stability to the body, he worships Rudra and is liberated from all sins.
After bathing while wet, the application of ash is improper; for while wet, the killing of living beings is certain.
One should know that the "wet" is the primary nature (prakṛti), and that this primary nature is indeed bondage.
For the sake of abandoning the primordial nature (prakṛti), bathing with ashes is prescribed;
for by means of this, neither nakedness nor impurity shall ever arise again.
There is no other supreme machine among machines than this, which possesses six limbs, fulfills all desires, and is honored by all the worlds. (122.81)

Pure, the most purifying, auspicious, and the destroyer of all sins, may they practice this with concentrated minds; it increases ascetic merit, and that machine is to be known as sinless and is remembered as primordial nature (prakṛti). 122.82.
Bondage is said to be threefold, as is the fruit of renunciation;
therefore, for the sake of abandoning everything, one should practice this discipline.
He who never decays in this world is always honored;
having attained the supreme yoga, which is the greatest among all yogas.
Because there is nothing higher than this six-limbed [yoga] which fulfills all desires,
by means of which the yogi, once liberated, does not fall again into death and the like.
Having fully attained that yoga, perfected through divine action,
the great yogi is not smeared by actions done or left undone.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus commanded by the God of gods,
those inhabitants of heaven completed that formidable vow and became the attendants of Śaṅkara.
Having attained the status of attendants to that trident-bearing god, they,
intensely purified by their asceticism, took possession of that region.
The gods said:
"Because our preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa) were well-performed here even to the very end, therefore this is remembered as the secret abode of Maheśa. (122.89)
The city known as Puṣkarāvatī was radiant throughout the three worlds;
it was five yojanas in width and of the same extent in length, and was beautiful.
Crowded with perfected beings and celestial musicians (cāraṇas), resounded by throngs of apsaras, filled with the cries of many birds, and abounding in rivers and waterfalls,
this grove of ascetics, whose wealth is penance, shall become a place of great merit.
Whoever comes here, prepares the sacrificial porridge (caru), feeds a Brahmin,
and worships the Lord of the Gods, shall rejoice in the world of Rudra.
And whoever, having made a vow here, remains for even a moment as one who bathes in ashes and is firm in his observances, shall attain the state of being among the Gaṇas.
Inexhaustible and immortal, free from old age and disease,
he shall become a leader of Rudra’s hosts and attain the sovereign power of yoga.
Even one of very evil nature who acts according to his own will, if he should dwell here for a single day,
attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice and is liberated from all sins.
Even one of evil conduct who, possessed of desire, should here give up his life—
he too, having reached the assembly of the gods, shall move about together with the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those deities, having attained that supreme austerity,
performed sacrifices and ritual ablutions for the Lord, the Supreme Self.
Then all those inhabitants of heaven, having accomplished their purpose and endowed with the power of great yoga, set their minds upon going toward Hari.
Approaching him who was like the blazing sun, O Vyāsa, those of great strength beheld the imperishable Hari on Mount Hariścandra.
After a long time, that one of great asceticism, having shaken off all evil,
attained equality with the gods at that very moment, his soul filled with joy.
Then, O best of sages, rising up with speed, he descended quickly from the peak and stood in their midst. (122.101)
Then, filled with joy and having properly united with Hari,
they crowned that peak of the mountain with its fruit.
Because this Hari shone here as stainless as the moon through his great ascetic penance, he is therefore known as Acaleśvara.
"He shall become known as Hariścandra, of this there is no doubt;
because he has again made a descent here by means of that which was not his natural state, therefore let this Bhṛgu be meritorious in every way throughout the world. (122.104)
O Lord of Gods, whatever man comes here and accomplishes his purpose by leaping from the Bhṛgu cliff, he shall go to the exceedingly radiant world of Hari.
Even one who is joined with great sins and afflicted by disease,
if he gives up his life here, shall be liberated from that great fear.
Or whatever else a man constantly desires here at this precipice, he shall obtain all that before long; so indeed it is remembered.
Sanatkumāra said: "The knower of dharma who recites or even hears this story of Hariścandra, who was formerly Purūravas, destroys his own sin. (122.108)
But that man who, pure and free from malice, always recites this in an assembly of the twice-born and the gods,
he dwells in heaven like a choice immortal, stainless and blazing with splendor like the sun.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Mount Hariścandra," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O son of Śakti, having reached that city of Purīcandra, that Rāma—
With his mind afflicted by the asuras, he beheld the Supreme Lord.
Having seen Mahādeva together with Ambā and his attendants, the imperishable one,
he stood before him, bowing down with palms joined in reverence and deeply humbled.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that high-minded god, the source of all speech, being pleased, spoke these words of profound resonance to the son of Jamadagni.
Covered as if with *kiṃśuka* flowers and as if sprinkled with sandalwood paste,
he was likewise drenched on all sides with blood,
like another great mountain from which red mineral ore was flowing.
The God of gods said: "O son of Jamadagni, a great deed has been performed by you today in battle out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, as you have slain the sons of Siṃhikā."
"O mighty-armed one, I am well-pleased with this deed of yours;
I shall grant you seven boons—name them as you wish."
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, O Lord, grant me yourself the origin of all knowledge as set forth in all the Vedas. (123.7)
"May I be invincible in battle; grant me the science of archery (dhanurveda), as well as an axe that destroys all things and an unimpeded chariot. (123.8)
"And grant me this vast collection of weapons, as well as imperishable immortality—bestow these boons upon me, O God; salutations to you."
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, as he was speaking thus, the Lord Hara laughed and said,
"All this shall come to pass for you by my command."
"You shall observe the vow of the science of archery for one year;
therefore, O scion of Bhrigu's lineage, you must remain right here."
Then the Blessed Three-eyed One himself commanded him a formidable vow, and he, being self-restrained, performed it.
When the vow was completed, the god himself, the destroyer of sacrifices,
came in person and bestowed upon him the science of archery, together with its mantras and its complete collection.

He [received] the vast collection of weapons, together with their cords, their protective coverings, their mechanisms for discharge, and their methods of withdrawal, as well as the corresponding counter-weapons.
Ishana bestowed that upon him and spoke these words in a melodious voice:
"This exceedingly powerful science of archery, along with its weapons, has been given to you."

"Remember my command that [this] must not be given to the Kṣatriyas. If, however, you should ever give it to the Kṣatriyas out of delusion, you will suffer humiliation at their hands, and you shall have no victory in battle. (123.16)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having given him the axe and the chariot that moves at will, which was inexhaustible and appeared before him as soon as it was thought of by the mind, [he departed].
Borne by the charioteer Yakṣarāja Amara,
the wielder of the Pināka bow suddenly vanished from his sight.
Having received those boons, O Vyāsa, he went to the presence of his father;
however, he did not see him there, for he had been slain by the sons of Kārtavīrya.
Even that powerful Rāma, having failed to perform his duty toward him,
cleared the earth of the kṣatriyas seven times and thrice over.
With that blood, O Vyāsa, he created seven lakes and there,
at Samantapañcaka, he gratified the ancestors.
Then, having rid the earth of the kṣatriyas, that best of the Bhṛgus shone as the lord of the three worlds through the grace of Mahādeva.
To him [came] prosperity, contentment, and fortitude, as well as accomplishment, renown, and fame;
likewise faith, intelligence, forbearance, freedom from envy, and self-restraint.
For Reasoning (Ūhā), Refutation (Apohā), Logic (Tarka), Self-restraint (Dama), and Tranquility (Śama)—all these personified mothers approached Bhārgava. || 123.24 ||
Then he said to them all: "Enter me without hesitation;
let this ill-behaved Śrī remain far away. (123.25)
Sanatkumāra said:
To him who spoke thus, the virtuous Śrī said to Mahābala:
"O mighty-armed one, why do you not welcome me, who am so difficult to obtain? (123.26)
Rāma said:
"O beautiful one, you are fickle, alluring, and unstable;
therefore, I do not welcome you. Stay far away from me! (123.27)
If every man possessed by you were himself a lord, he would, deluded by the intoxication of power, engage only in improper acts. (123.28)
Sanatkumāra said:
That illustrious and high-minded king of the Bhṛgu lineage performed sacrifices;
and in former times, O twice-born one, the earth sank down during his sacrifice. (123.29)
Vyāsa said:
For what reason did the Earth enter Pātāla during his sacrifice? What do you consider to be the cause in that matter? I wish to know this. 123.30.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone to Kaśyapa, the best of sages, that protector of the earth said,
"O best among the virtuous, become my officiating priest."
O Vyāsa, while he was speaking thus,
Kaśyapa, being enraged, spoke there to the lord of men, censuring the best of the Bhṛgus.
"You are fallen, of evil conduct, broken in character, and a doer of great wickedness;
how indeed shall I perform a sacrifice for one who has committed the murder of a learned Brahmin?"
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, by those words, he spoke to that best of sages:
"O best of munis, do not remain within my domain today."
"O Brahmin, I am the master of the world; go elsewhere where I am not.
Thereupon, he abandoned that place and departed.
And he did not reach that place where the Lord was not present;
failing to find him, he then took refuge in the forest and,
having become invisible, wandered there for many years.
Then he saw a pigeon perched upon a tree, sitting there,
overcome by passion and rendered helpless by his union with a female pigeon.
The pigeon said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, from the moment I first beheld you, O lovely one, I have been withering away; I find no pleasure, O beautiful one. (123.38)
The female dove said:
"Do not speak thus, O man of evil conduct; for it is never right to act unrighteously.
The male dove said:
"If you will not give yourself to me here, O slender-waisted one, I shall take you by force; therefore, yield to me, for I bow at your feet."
The female dove said:
"O cruel one, why do you have no fear of the mighty son of Jamadagni, that you now rejoice here over me, a devoted wife deprived of her husband? (123.40)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by her, O son of Śakti, that pigeon spoke: "O Rāma, who indeed is this person who is equal to me? There is no one like me. (123.41)
While he was speaking thus, an arrow marked with the name of Rāma swiftly struck off his head; Kaśyapa witnessed that.
Seeing him behaving in such a manner, that high-minded one became afraid of that mighty man and caused the king to perform a sacrifice for Jamadagni’s son.
Kaśyapa said: "O King, O best of the Bhṛgus, I shall perform the sacrifice this very day,
provided that you grant me the desired sacrificial fee."
Rāma said:
"There is no doubt regarding what you say; O one of great asceticism, I shall grant it.
Perform the sacrifice for me according to the rule; today I stand under your authority. (123.45)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, there took place for him that very great horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) with abundant sacrificial fees, in which the gods attained satisfaction. 123.46.
Then, at the time for the sacrificial fee, the powerful son of Jamadagni said to Kaśyapa: "Tell me, what sacrificial fee shall I give to you?"
He said: "Give me the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, as well as whatever wealth you possess in your house."
Having done that for him in such a manner with a pure inner soul, he took up his bark garments and said to Kaśyapa, "What shall I do? (123.49)
Kaśyapa said: "O descendant of Bhṛgu, abandon this region and go to another land; you must not dwell in my country today."
Sanatkumāra said: Having replied, "So be it," and having performed a circumambulation, he went to the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa and the source of all rivers. || 123.51 ||
Having gone to that fearsome ocean, the descendant of Bhṛgu said:
"O great ocean, grant me a place for my residence."
The Ocean said:
"Since you are now under my control, employ me according to what is right;
standing near the shore, draw your powerful bow."
O Rāma, release your arrow, desiring to reach that supreme region.
"As soon as that arrow, impelled by your breath, has been discharged,
at that very moment I shall grant you a dwelling."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among the Bhṛgus, having shown respect and remaining unwearied, drew his powerful bow and fixed an arrow upon it, O Vyāsa. (123.55)
Having then formed the resolution in his mind, "He shall indeed go a hundred yojanas," he consecrated him with mantras.
Then Sāgara praised Śambhu for the sake of pacifying him,
desiring the welfare of the gods and for the purpose of drying up the ocean.
That incomparable arrow, discharged by the son of Jamadagni, was intercepted;
having traveled twelve yojanas, it fell down like Rudra himself.
And at that moment, the ocean withdrew its waters as if laughing;
likewise, the son of Jamadagni, endowed with great splendor, dwelt there.
The son of Bhṛgu, resembling the lord of the gods, with a joyful heart, made that region— which was frequented by herds of deer and flocks of birds,
and resounded with the terrible cries of lions, lordly elephants, śarabhas, and bears— like a glorious city of the deities.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter in the Rāmamāhātmya of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In that manner, that earth was given by the son of Jamadagni to the high-souled one.
Then she descended like a mountain peak falling from above.
The sage, filled with anger, said to her: "Stay, stay, O Vasundharā!
For what reason, O auspicious one, do you abandon me and go beneath? (124.2)
The Earth said:
"O sage, with my heart captivated by his virtues, I am unable to remain without my beloved husband Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who possesses exceeding splendor. (124.3)
If you do not grant me to Rāma today, O bull among sages, I shall go down [to the underworld], O Lord; I will not remain otherwise than this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of hers, Kaśyapa, the best of ascetics, spoke to the Earth, as if burning her with his splendor in his anger. || 124.5 ||
Kaśyapa said:
"Go, O woman of wicked conduct, down again to the lower state!
I shall become the earth; behold the power of my asceticism! (124.6)
Then that Blessed One Vyāsa, having resorted to supreme yoga,
attained the state of the earth and sustained human beings.
When this earth had shone for many thousands of years,
the Earth, being despondent, then propitiated Kaśyapa.
The Earth said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, by virtue of your asceticism, your yoga, and your power, there is no one at all equal to you, whether in heaven or on earth. (124.9)
I propitiate you with my head bowed; your supreme power has been witnessed by me.
Whatever wrong I have done, O great sage, please forgive that.
"By your command, O best of brahmins, I myself would indeed become the earth among the worlds; you ought to show favor to me, who am distressed. (124.11)
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing her thus standing before him, the Blessed One, the best of sages, then spoke with a smile to the goddess Earth who was bowed down in prostration. 124.12.
Indeed, it was solely through your own transgression that I have done this to you;
now, enjoy the sovereignty of the earth granted by me.
"O Vasundharā, having become my daughter and being born in the lineage of Kaśyapa,
you shall become known in the world as Kāśyapī."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, that earth, having gone downwards, was established once more;
having regained its nature as earth, it became free from distress.
This state of the earth belonging to the great sage Kaśyapa,
as well as the arrival of the earth and its subsequent transformation— [all this has been told].
Indeed, whoever, having become pure, should always listen to or recite this,
shall obtain imperishable worlds as well as the fruit of the earth.

O Sage, that best of men who, having repeatedly bowed here to her who is the source of all worlds, shall always recite this [account], attains the imperishable world of the Rishi, as well as the earth that bestows wealth. || 124.18 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Becoming Earth of Kaśyapa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the powerful battle of the banners.
It is the ancient destroyer of the yoga of both the gods and the asuras.
There was a glorious and mighty son of Danu named Vipracitti; it is heard that, with a disciplined mind, he performed austerities at Bhastrāpada. (125.2)
Having propitiated the three-eyed Lord there, the divine master of the gods,
he chose the boon of immortality, and that lord of the gods granted it to him.
The divine, all-pervading, auspicious golden banner, composed of illusion,
spoke to that lord of the Dānavas with a gratified soul.
"O son of Danu, this Viśvarūpa here is your supreme banner;
by relying upon him in battles, you shall become invincible."
And if you, O mighty-armed Amara, do not make a sound, then by your good fortune, victory in battle shall be yours; otherwise, it will be otherwise for you.
Thus addressed by the god Dhvaja in that great battle,
O best of Brahmins, he challenged all the gods along with the Danujas.
That battle became terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising;
it was exceedingly fierce for eighteen hundred years.
There they beheld a marvel performed by the wise son of Danu:
that with his banner of universal form, he alone slew many.
And as he fought in battle, relying upon his standard through his illusory power (māyā),
the gods did not strike him, for though they beheld him, they were bewildered.
They did not see the sons of Danu nor the Daityas in the battle;
all those bewildered dwellers of heaven saw only the banner.
The unfailing weapons which the denizens of heaven discharged were indeed rendered invisible by the dense mass of shadows from the banners.
In front, behind, on both sides, and even above, they saw only the banner; they saw neither the Daityas nor the Dānavas.
There, O Vyāsa, those sharp arrows, blazing like the flames of fire,
issued forth from his banner and tore asunder the foremost of the gods.
Maces, iron clubs, slings with missiles, and javelins,
as well as other weapons, were seen issuing forth from the banner.
Taking refuge at that banner, those gods were completely broken by that Daitya in battle; deprived of their senses, they were rendered devoid of prowess.
Seeing all those best of gods broken and being broken,
the Dānava roared like a rain-cloud while leaning upon his banner.
Perceiving that opening and observing his banner, the Lord Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
being filled with supreme wrath, hurled his thunderbolt.
Resembling the blazing sun and emitting a terrifying sound, that thunderbolt brought the lord of the Dānavas, along with his banner, within its range of action.
Having fixed his aim upon the banner, the high-souled Lord of the Gods slew all fourteen thousand of those Dānavas.
Perceiving those beings of great majesty, who were like the lords of the gods, to have been slain by that sound,
all those who bore signs equal to Indra’s placed them upon their banners and, with the power of the lord of the gods, struck them with thunderbolts.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the Battle of the Banners.
Vyāsa said:
O imperishable son of Brahmā, you have spoken of that which is called Bhastrāpada.
How did that situation come to pass? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
A lord of subjects named Bāhu, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku,
had his entire kingdom seized by the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas.
O best of Brahmins, having been robbed by force, he went to the forest together with his wife.
Having gone to the hermitage of Ṛcīka and being hospitably received by him,
he dwelt in the middle of the forest together with his pregnant wife.
But at the time of her delivery, O son of Śakti,
her co-wife, out of passion and delusion, administered poison to her.
Having experienced that sensation, she, tormented and filled with pain, cried out, "Cool water! and fell to the ground in a swoon.
Seeing her fallen in that manner, the king, consumed by grief, took his water-pot and went to the river for water, even though he was old. || 126.6 ||
Having filled that jar and taken it upon his shoulder,
he fell down and died from the exhaustion caused by old age and toil.
When the sages had thus proclaimed, "He is dead,
he is dead," that goddess, struck by grief for her husband, rose up from her swoon.
Stricken then by the heat of the poison and by the death of her husband,
O Vyāsa, she wailed aloud like a female osprey.
All the sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, having assembled, performed the piling of the altar correctly and consecrated it with the purificatory rites. || 126.10 ||
As she was entering that fire, Śaivyā was defiled by her pregnancy;
she was forbidden by the sages, O Vyāsa, and by the high-souled Aurva.
On that day, O Vyāsa, in the evening, that embryo, which was like fire in its brilliance and was the destroyer of wrath, emerged from her along with the poison.
Then the sage gave him the name Sagara and,
filled with compassion, performed for him every consecratory rite.

He bestowed upon him the science of archery (dhanurveda) as well as the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga), a vast collection of celestial weapons, and an unimpeded, inexhaustible chariot.
With that preeminent chariot, he indeed struck down his enemies in battle;
and by aiming the Aurva weapon, he destroyed their dharma.
Having slain them in that manner, O Vyāsa, he then obtained the kingdom,
as well as Śaivyā, the slender-waisted sister of Vainateya.
Childless, the mighty-armed lord of men, possessed of great splendor, propitiated Tryambaka, the best of gods, for the sake of obtaining a son.
To him, the Lord, the powerful master, granted sixty thousand sons of great soul who would perpetuate his lineage.
Sanatkumāra said: Having obtained that boon, the high-minded king spoke to his two wives— the sister of Vainateya and Śaivyā.
Sagara said:
"The Lord has granted me a single auspicious son to continue my lineage, as well as sixty thousand sons of great soul. (126.20)
"In this matter, which of you two goddesses chooses the boon that is auspicious and beneficial?
Speak; I shall not make a division among you who have realized the Self. (126.21)
Vainateyasvasā said:
"O lord of men, let me have sixty thousand sons.
Śaivyā said: "Let there be but one son for me who shall perpetuate my lineage. (126.22)
Sanatkumāra said: Then Śaivyā gave birth to the son of Asamañja; she gave birth to a great egg, the sister of Vainateya.
From that vessel,
O Vyāsa, those ten thousand [beings] were multiplied by six, and thus they came into being as beings of great strength.
Then Sagara abandoned his son Asamañja, knowing him to be unrighteous and established in improper conduct. (126.25)
His son was Aṃśumat, who was exceedingly virtuous even as a child;
Sagara, the best of kings, then took great delight in him.
Having renounced Asamañja, he was consecrated for the horse sacrifice;
he appointed sixty thousand [men] for the protection of the horse.
While those high-souled ones were thus exerting themselves to tend the horse,
Śakra, having become invisible, carried off that excellent steed.
Having gone everywhere throughout the worlds and not seeing that best of horses,
they approached their father who was consecrated for sacrifice and reported the matter concerning the horse.
Then that king, enraged and as if burning his sons, spoke with eyes copper-red from anger: "Perish this very day, quickly! (126.30)
"O cruel ones, do not come here today without the horse; search for it elsewhere! What use have I for you, my sons? All of you go to the abode of Yama! || 126.31 ||
Sanatkumāra said: O best of Brahmins, having been addressed thus, they then searched the entire three worlds and dug up this whole earth.
Then, having seen those world-elephants and the sages of firm vows supporting the entire earth,
and having seen them, he bowed down to them.
They beheld the sage Kapila sleeping in the pool of water;
not far from him, they then saw the horse and became enraged.
Impelled by the destined purpose and ripe for death at that time,
they spoke to Kapila, the best of sages, because of their father’s curse.
"This wicked-minded one has stolen our excellent horse while we were asleep;
today we shall all lead him before our father. (126.36)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those mighty ones, bound by the noose of Time and subject to the power of destiny, struck him with their feet.
Oppressed by them, he became enraged; then, like a king of serpents suddenly releasing its breath, he emitted ten thousand years' worth of arrows.
Issuing forth from his mouth, that wind, consisting of fire,
burned all the oceans that were excluded from justice and righteousness.
When all of them had been consumed by fire, the sages, Nārada and the others, related to Sagara exactly what had occurred— that most difficult of events.
Then that high-minded king, afflicted with grief, steadying himself by his own effort, commanded his beloved grandson Aṃśumat.
Sagara said:
"Mount this chariot and go to that excellent horse;
bring it back here, O mighty-armed one, so that our time does not pass us by. (126.42)
You should act according to those words so that this best of sages does not direct his anger toward us; then our lineage will certainly endure through you.
Sanatkumāra said:

Thus addressed, that high-souled king, honored by gods and siddhas and possessing the prowess of the lord of the gods, mounted his chariot and proceeded with speed to where the yogin, like the Destroyer himself, was manifest. 126.44.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Sagara," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone to that region frequented by great elephants, he then [proceeded].
He saw them turned to ashes and the sage, radiant as fire.
Then, having bowed down in his presence with words joined in praise, he asked for forgiveness for all the evil deeds previously committed.
Kapila said:
"O King, here in this secluded place I was standing absorbed in yoga, free from all distress.
Being suddenly assailed by them, I released wind from my mouth. (127.3)
That wind, which had been restrained by me for ten hundred years,
was suddenly released and consumed all those ancestors of yours.
"O King, they were not burned by me intentionally, nor even out of anger;
they were slain because their time had ripened, just like birds struck down by the fruit [of their own karma]."
"This horse standing by my side has been taken away by someone who knows his own self for the destruction of those [enemies]; do not be angry, let the horse be led back. (127.6)
Sanatkumāra said: With his permission, O Vyāsa, that high-minded lord of men, Aṃśumān, proceeded to fetch water for them to drink. (127.7)
Vainateya said to him: "O mighty-armed one, this water of mine must not be given to my sisters' sons; it shall not go to them. (127.8)
Aṃśumān said:
"O son of Kaśyapa, how may my ancestors indeed attain those divine worlds? I desire this to be told by you. (127.9)
Vainateya said:
"In the world of the gods there is a holy river named Gaṅgā, which removes all impurities.
With its waters, let your bones be reunited here with your kinsmen in every way."
When these are touched, O King, then they shall attain liberation from evil, O tiger among kings; otherwise, what use have you for water? (127.11)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, having taken back the horse, that virtuous king returned and presented the horse to his grandfather. 127.12.
Then that high-minded king, having performed the horse sacrifice,
being tormented by the slaughter of his sons, set his mind upon the destruction of the ocean.
Then the lord of rivers, having bowed to him and propitiated him,
attained the state of being his son and spoke these words to him at that time.
"O King, O illustrious one, I must indeed be filled to the brim with the water of the Gaṅgā by someone born of your lineage, O mighty-armed monarch. (127.15)
"Do not be angry; I am your son, the bringer of glory and of immeasurable luster.
I shall give you jewels; come to peace with me, O Lord. (127.16)
Then the anger of that king toward the ocean was pacified;
and Viṣṇu, being pleased with him at that time, granted him his desired boons.
He shall obtain more than a hundred horse-sacrifices, an imperishable residence in heaven,
an eternal and undecaying lineage, and likewise preeminent and inexhaustible fame.
Likewise, he obtained friendship and remained firmly established in the ancient dharma;
having received these boons, he enjoyed his kingdom free from all thorns.
Then he went to the forest, and having performed austerities there, he ascended to heaven;
thereafter, King Aṃśumān shone forth, righteous and true to his promise.
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom with the intention of descending to the Gaṅgā,
he of great strength and prowess ascended to heaven after performing austerities.
Then his son Dilīpa, a high-souled and mighty king like the lord of the gods,
having ruled the kingdom, went to the forest, O Vyāsa.
There, having exerted himself for the sake of the Gaṅgā and performed austerities, he went to heaven;
yet, without having attained that desire, he was born again as his son.
There was a virtuous king named Bhagīratha, the auspicious lord of Jambūdvīpa; he was righteous, truthful in speech, and heroic, like Dharma incarnate.
O best of sages, O Lord, from the very moment of his birth, there has remained in his heart the thought:
"How might I bring down the Gaṅgā? || 127.25 ||
Then, after a long time, having performed all his duties,
the king practiced very great austerity by which the Lord of the World was gratified.
Then Brahmā himself, having approached that one of firm vows, said to him:
"Speak, O lord of men; what shall I grant you? Choose your boons."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king, having seen him and bowing down with a joyful countenance,
spoke concerning the inexhaustible dharma as well as the imperishable residence in heaven.
Make the lineage truly imperishable, and grant me a hundred excellent sons—
heroes who are righteous and never retreat in battles.
And constant victory in battle, as well as imperishable fame in the world,
and also the unsurpassed descent of the river Gaṅgā.
"And how she may become most renowned in the world as Bhāgīrathī—this I desire, O Lord of Gods, if you so deem it right, O All-pervading One. (127.31)
Sanatkumāra said:
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One, the Creator himself, bestowed all this upon him in its entirety and spoke these words to that king.
"O tiger among kings, you shall lead the Gaṅgā from heaven to the earth;
for indeed, no one is capable of supporting her as she falls from the sky,
except for the God who is the teacher of the worlds, the three-eyed wielder of the trident."
Therefore, with your vows restrained, propitiate the Lord of the gods;
that omnipresent one will clearly sustain you by means of a boon.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, that lord of kings, subsisting on air and with unblinking eyes,
remained there on the auspicious peak of the Himavat without drawing breath.
The Lord, the god Kapardin Nīlalohita, was pleased with him who, devoted to that [practice] for a thousand years, had sought his blessing.
Having said, "I am the giver of boons," the Lord spoke again:
"O best of kings, I grant you divine vision; behold me!"
Having seen that great archer, the three-eyed lord of the gods, he said to the river-goddess, "O goddess, hold back [the flood]; I choose a boon."
"O Imperishable One, if you are pleased with me, let the divine Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, [descend];
O Mahādeva, this is my desire: that my deceased ancestors and grandfathers [be purified]."
"Having rescued them from hell, I shall lead those virtuous ones to heaven.
O Mahādeva, this effort has been undertaken by me for their sake;
through your grace, they shall go to heaven after being bathed in the Gaṅgā."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull spoke to that tiger among kings with a deeply satisfied inner soul. 127.41.
The God of gods said:
"O Bhagīratha, it shall be exactly so for you; of this there is no doubt.
And by my grace, that Gaṅgā shall become your daughter."
"And for your sake, O best of kings, I shall sustain that [earth] as it falls from heaven,
for the purpose of astonishing the worlds and for the welfare of all."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, said: "O best of gods, which one shall sustain my force? || 127.44 ||
Today, having seized him suddenly and with great force,
I shall go without a doubt to the most difficult-to-reach netherworld (pātāla), which is exceedingly hard to endure.
Whether he be that self-existent Brahmā, or Śakra the lord of the gods, or even Viṣṇu the son of Aditi—I shall surely lead him away; of this there is no doubt.
"Today let the worlds behold my great and unassailable momentum as I fall upon the earth; thus did that river speak. (127.47)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of hers, which were full of arrogance, Śaṅkara formed the resolve to subdue that best of rivers. 127.48.
By his mere resolve, a fever indeed entered the gods;
the garlands of them all withered, and portents arose.
The world was overturned and the celestial palaces trembled;
the Asuras, intoxicated by their own power and appearing possessed of immense strength, were seen challenging the sons of Diti, who blazed with the splendor of fire and the sun.
Sanatkumāra said: Having observed that transformation, the gods spoke to Śatakratu: "O Lord, this reversal could not have occurred without cause; let it be investigated quickly. (127.51)
And at that time, confusion arose for that god along with the sages;
Brahmā, having approached them, enlightened them.
Brahmā said:
"O all you dwellers of heaven, do not remain despondent.
Listen to what I say; let not this time pass you by."
This god, the great archer with matted hair who rides upon the clouds,
possessed of terrible prowess, set his mind upon destroying the Gaṅgā.
"Therefore, since the destruction of the world has been thus conceived by the mind of the gods,
act without delay so that this reversal may not come to pass."
"Go from here with me and, having met with the sages, seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, out of a state of distress. (127.56)
Sanatkumāra said: Then those gods, together with Brahmā, the lotus-born,
went to the peak of the Himalayas, which was adorned with all kinds of jewels.
By name it was called Hiraṇmaya, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
and there the gods beheld that Lord of the Gods through their austerity and devotion.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, beholding him as if enraged, possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon,
and difficult to look upon, they then sought refuge with the Goddess.
The gods said:
"O radiant one, you are the mother of the worlds together with the gods;
therefore, O Rudrāṇī, you are our bellows. Grant us the state that bestows fearlessness. (127.60)
"We have come to you for refuge, O Mother; we are your sons, O auspicious one.
Protect us, O Goddess of the gods; this is what we desire."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of the gods who were terrified and seeking refuge, the Goddess granted them an unsurpassed boon that bestows fearlessness.
Then, having bowed her head to the Blessed One, the wielder of the Pināka bow and Lord of the gods of gods, the daughter of the Mountain spoke like one who was terrified.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord raised up that frightened woman, who was prostrate with her head fallen at his feet,
using his hand which possessed the luster of a lotus petal.
And then he said to the virtuous lady, "O daughter of Himavat, you are afraid; for what reason? And what is your fear, O fair-browed one? Tell me, O lady of beautiful countenance. (127.65)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, the daughter of Himavat then spoke to him like one terrified:
"O God, I am greatly afraid upon seeing your exceedingly radiant form. (127.66)
Resembling the fire of universal destruction and difficult even for the gods to behold,
O Lord of Gods, the worlds, along with the deities and the sages, were despondent.
All these lords of the gods wait upon you, trembling with fear;
O Mahādeva, I am afraid of you, yet these gods are even more afraid than I.
They have come to me for refuge; grant them freedom from fear.
You are the creator of all the worlds, together with the gods and the seers.
Do not destroy them; having done so, I entreat you with my head bowed low.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of hers and having seen the gods, the destroyer of the sacrifice said, "O best of the thirty deities, you have no fear from me."
But this river, by her very nature as a woman, O daughter of the Himalayas, having set a wicked mind upon me, will fall upon me. (127.71)
I shall arrest that river as it falls from heaven;
you too, O sinless ones, may go to your respective abodes with confidence.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard those words, the foremost of the gods bowed down and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke with voices full of shame: 127.73.
The gods said:
"This best of rivers was created by you for the sake of the welfare of the world;
yet rivers are fickle, and such is the very nature of women. (127.74)
By virtue of that very nature of hers, and because she has taken refuge with us,
she has assumed great pride and boasts, being entirely fearless.
"O Lord of Gods, O you of terrible prowess, hear from us why this river possesses such pride that she boasts in this manner; do not be angry. (127.76)
"For everyone becomes arrogant when requested for the sake of some task;
O Lord, this is so even in the world regarding one as small as this, how much more so for this best of rivers? (127.77)
O Mahādeva, this very river, which you desired for your support, now boasts because she has been favored by the most excellent of gods. || 127.78 ||
Supported by you, the lord of the gods, this best of rivers shall become sacred in this world,
destroying all sins.
O Lord of the Gods, whatever deity might be capable of holding back this river as it flows downward, no greater benefit would come from that.
Therefore, O best of gods, being entreated by the deities and by this king Kāla, become auspicious and sustain this river. (127.81)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus was that Blessed Lord addressed by the gods, together with Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and the lords of the worlds— with words that were truthful and entirely free from contradiction.
Having repeatedly considered that granting of the boon to the king, the Lord of Gods spoke these words in a deep voice: 127.83.
"O best of gods, it is for the sake of this king, whose senses are overwhelmed by hunger, and at the request of you who are worthy of honor. (127.84)
"O sinless ones, listen to what I say regarding the destruction of this pride; I shall not destroy this river, O great beings. (127.85)
There shall be a great destruction of this pride by the lord of mountains;
furthermore, the righteous-souled Anujahnu shall destroy his pride once again.
And this great river, corrupted by fish and of wicked conduct, having encountered a human husband, destroys his seven sons. (127.87)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, Śarva, the best of deities, then said:
"Tell me what else you desire; I shall grant it to you as you wish."
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, we desire a place for the god of great supernatural power—
a sacred field (kṣetra) called Samantapañcaka that shall never be bereft of you."
Because we addressed the imperishable daughter of the Himalayas as "Bhastre," and because they desire a state of fearlessness, it is therefore remembered as Bhastrapada.
Whoever should come here, observant of the rules, and worship the one whose banner is the bull,
shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice and attain the world of Rudra.
O best of gods, he who offers a sacrificial oblation (caru) after fasting for a day and night shall become equal to Nandīśvara.
O Lord of Gods, whatever man here should give up his life while observing the rules of restraint, or even without restraint, O God, by means of death occurring by chance; ||| 127.93 ||
Having thus become equal to the Gaṇas, he shall remain until the dissolution of all beings,
endowed with a divine body and having entered into the service of following you.
"Salutation to Bhastreśvara"— he who, having performed this, remains ever pure,
whether rising or sleeping, rejoices in the world of Śakra.

Whoever should constantly recite this great, divine [hymn] of infinite benefit in the assembly of the twice-born and the gods, shall become a high-souled leader of the Gaṇas and possess great speed; O God, he becomes divine through taking refuge in Your praise.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter in the Gaṅgāvatāra section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 127.127 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
In that delightful abode of Sthāṇu, the gods, together with Brahmā, [resided].
Having installed the *liṅga*, all the holy sites (*tīrthas*) performed their respective rites individually.
Rudratīrtha, Sthāṇutīrtha, and the Tīrtha of Brahmā;
Indratīrtha and that of the Vasus, and another known as that of the Aśvins. || 128.3 ||
There is another sacred ford of Yama, and then another sacred ford of Vāyu;
there is also another sacred ford of Viṣṇu, renowned and worshipped by the gods.
O brahmin-sage, having bathed in these, prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru), and offered it,
one indeed wanders through these divine places free from fear from any quarter.
Even today, O Brahman-sage, that sweet sound is heard there,
mingled with the jingling of girdles and bracelets, and intensified by the resonance of flutes and lutes.
O Vyāsa, there were beautiful apsarases who were constantly singing, dancing, and likewise praising the Three-eyed Lord.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those gods, together with Brahmā, spoke to the best of deities: "O Blessed One, may we behold this supreme dhāraṇā."
The God of gods said:
"O lords of the wise, you shall see me tomorrow at dawn as you desire,
holding the river that flows through the three paths, which is proud of its own virtues."
Having been addressed thus, they bowed to the Lord and then went to the vicinity of the Gaṅgā;
thereupon Brahmā spoke to that goddess who brings happiness to the world.
"Do not be proud, O Gaṅgā; do not meet with destruction.
Abiding in rectitude, you shall fall, O best of rivers."
Praising Tryambaka, Soma, endowed with supreme devotion, said:
"Having understood your intention, that Lord is prepared for my destruction. (128.12)
Śambhu was propitiated with great difficulty out of a desire for your very welfare;
do not commit an offense again, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
"O best of rivers, from your destruction, the certain ruin of the worlds would follow.
Having thus consoled her, the gods, together with Brahmā, then [departed].
On the second day, the lords of the world arrived, desiring to see the great and divine peak of the Himalayas known by the name Vajropala.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Ananta, as well as men and sages;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts.
The Sādhyas, the gods, along with the Pitṛs, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
as well as the Piśācas, the Asuras, the horned creatures, and the Pṛśnis. || 128.18 ||
The sages Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Marīci, Pulaha,
as well as Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, and Kaśyapa.
Auśija and Vāmadeva, Gautama of great asceticism, Cyavana, Bharadvāja, and Indrapramati as well. || 128.20 ||
Raibhya, Jamadagni, the powerful Kuṇibāhu,
Atharvan, Śvetaketu, and the renowned Dattātreya.
Ruci, Dharma, Dakṣa, and those who are the Sāvarṇi sages;
Agni, Vedabāhu, and he who is named Śaṅkhapād.
Ambarīṣa is renowned, and Ketumān is another;
these and many other sages as well as deities [were there].
And all the celestial chariots, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
the Jambhakas, the Seasons, and all the various classes [of beings] from every side.
Then all those gods of supreme splendor, filled with joy, arrived there while they were stationed in the sky and beholding [the scene].
On that most excellent peak, which resembled Mount Meru and Mount Mandara,
the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Umā, suddenly became visible.
Shining with a mass of matted hair, tawny like a flash of lightning,
he stood tall and addressed Bhagīratha.
The God of gods said:
"O Bhagīratha, where is that Gaṅgā who delivers your ancestors? Summon her, O mighty-armed one; I shall sustain her, of this there is no doubt. (128.28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among kings, O Vyāsa, having remembered those words of Brahmā, bowed his head with joined palms and called to mind the river. (128.29)
Summoned by that mind, the goddess, the river whose abode is the heavenly world,
arrived in an instant at the earthly realm (bhuvarloka), bringing auspiciousness.
Having reached that world, that river, swift as the wind of the mind,
possessed of great velocity, and the source of hundreds of auspicious things, adorned it all.
Then, having come obliquely from the sky,
that great river became known as the Ākāśagaṅgā, indeed by the name Oghavatī.
That great river, the Ākāśagaṅgā, possessing great velocity, [flowed] further;
because she said, "May there be auspiciousness for me," from that half-path of sin,
she was then called by the name Śivagaṅgā, for she is indeed most auspicious.
Making a vast sound like the roar of a thunderbolt, the river was seen by the gods;
therefore, it is known as Devagaṅgā.
Seeing her, all the sages and all the inhabitants of the world of the gods suddenly recited prayers for peace, their hair standing on end with joy.
O Vyāsa, as they were chanting those [mantras], that river which brings happiness to the world,
as if praising them and terrified, split into three parts and fell to the earth.
As she was falling with great speed, Mahādeva caught her with his mass of matted hair in three swift movements, even in the very presence of the gods.
Having reached that mass of matted hair, the triple-streamed river became gentle;
yet, obstructed by his power of yoga-illusion, she could not find its end.
Because she then fell down, trembling with fear while offering praise,
she is therefore called Bhītagaṅgā and Stotragaṅgā.
Because that most excellent river fell with three currents,
she is therefore called Trisrotas by those who discourse on Brahman.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having fallen there, she was sustained by the god through his power of illusion;
searching for the opening in his matted locks, she dwelt there for many years.
When a full thousand years had passed while she remained in her hut of matted locks,
all the gods beheld her as if she were situated within the hollow of a tree.
Then those gods, O Vyāsa, suddenly prostrating themselves before the bull-bannered Lord, spoke with despondent minds: "Do not destroy the river. (128.43)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs and having seen the king himself,
the God of gods, who is full of compassion, shook out his mass of matted hair.
As he shook his mass of matted hair, drops indeed fell there;
they resembled pearls and were as pure as the rays of the full moon.
They made Bindusaras divine, possessing a splendor like that of the ocean;
from it, seven great streams issued forth.
The Nalinī, the Hrādinī, and the Plāvanī flow toward the east;
the Sītā, the Cakṣus, and the Sindhu—these three indeed flow toward the west.
The middle stream followed the path by which King Bhagīratha had gone;
therefore, that Gaṅgā is called "Bhāgīrathī" by those who discourse on Brahman.
Then, tearing her way through, that best of rivers went toward the Himalayas;
she was obstructed at the foot of the Himalayas by a mountain peak of jewels.
Then, O Vyāsa, seeing her thus obstructed, King Bhagīratha, with a dejected countenance, remembered Brahmā in his mind.
Then the blessed Brahmā said to the great elephant Supratīka: "Tear apart this mountain with your tusk-like thunderbolts."
Where that king of mountains was pierced by the elephant Supratīka,
that place is called Gaṅgādvāra, and it is remembered as being exceedingly meritorious.
As long as the highly illustrious elephant did not stand facing him,
he was carried by the current for a distance of twelve yojanas.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Vyāsa, this most meritorious descent of the Gaṅgā which I have described is the sacred place known by the name Bhastrāpada. (128.54)
That mortal who shall always hear this on every sacred festival day (parvan),
having attained the world of the gods, shall wander together with the deities.

He who, with an undaunted mind, constantly hears this auspicious liberation from great evil—which is the enticement of the celestial nymphs of the divine chariots—goes to the worlds known to the dwellers of heaven. (128.56)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter in the Gaṅgāvataraṇa section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the Hālāhala [poison] in its entirety.
The battle between the sons of Diti and the gods, which brought terror to all.
O Vyāsa, the host known as Hālāhala, possessing formidable prowess, appeared among the Asuras—terrible and a thorn to the Brahmins. 129.2.
When the sons of Danu had departed, that host, frantic with rage,
mustered its strength and challenged all the gods to battle.
Between them and those others, a most terrible battle took place;
and victory always accrued to the Asuras.
Then all those gods, their pride shattered and their prowess destroyed,
having been deprived of their kingdom, approached Brahmā, the cause of the world.
Gathering together, they said to him: "O Lord, we have now been deprived of our kingdom;
by what means may we regain our kingdom through your splendor? (129.6)
Having heard those words of theirs, the god born from the waters said to the gods, "Propitiate the Lord of Gods without delay."
That three-eyed god, possessed of great heroism, shall be your giver of strength,
by which you will conquer all those enemies in battle through your prowess.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods and propitiated Śaṅkara through austerity, the gods spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O Slayer of the Sacrifice, grant us strength. (129.9)
While they were thus engaged in silent recitation, Hara, gratified by their austerity,
bestowed upon them an invincible mantra, the most excellent of all mantras.
Having obtained that [knowledge], O brahmin-sage, the gods, having performed their protection,
all acted among the Asuras like those who were deluded, though they were themselves undeluded.
Then the Asuras, seeing all the inhabitants of heaven thus bewildered,
thought, according to the facts, that those of evil conduct were indeed fools.
"Deprived of their sovereignty by these gods with their deluded minds, they wander about like madmen; behold them, O you who are not gods! (129.13)
Others, reviling them, struck them cruelly; some bound them at will, while others released them.
Thus, O Vyāsa, as those of auspicious deeds were conducting themselves at that time,
a very great dharma arose which destroyed the Asuras.
Due to that misconduct of those evil-minded Asuras,
the hosts of deities perceived that their strength had waned because of the destruction of dharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those wielders of divine weapons, having been addressed by Brahmā,
challenged the tigers among the Asuras and slaughtered them all in battle.
Where Bala was slain in battle by Devendra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt after the latter had displayed his prowess, he is therefore known as Balahā (the slayer of Bala).
Sanatkumāra said: There was another most terrifying battle known as Andhakāraka, which lasted for ten thousand years and ten hundred more. 129.19
There was once a glorious son of Danu known as Devatāntaka;
desiring to master the power of illusion (māyā), he propitiated Rudra in ancient times.
When a thousand years had passed and the time for the boon had arrived,
O Vyāsa, Brahmā granted a boon to that wise son of Danu.
He chose that tamasic illusion which afflicts all beings— an illusion that is impenetrable, irresistible, and which no one knows.
He gave that illusion to him and then spoke these words to him:
"O mighty one, this illusion shall indeed be as described to you;
provided, O son of Danu, that you do not make a sound according to your will."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, that Asura, having obtained the boon and being concealed by his illusory power (māyā), oppressed all the worlds together with many Dānavas. 129.24.
Even the gods did not remain before him out of fear; all the gods, agitated by terror, did not stand at all in his presence. Abandoning their stations, they took refuge here and there. (129.25)
Though summoned by the harsh cries of the Dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength,
the dwellers of heaven nevertheless did not stand before them.
Having reached them, all those sages, filled with indignation, said:
"Protect the worlds; do not remain hidden! (129.27)
"And we, O gods, shall sustain [the world] through austerity while remaining self-restrained.
Let there be no fear for you; fight and make the world free from fever."
Thus addressed by those sages, O Vyāsa, for the sake of the welfare of the world,
they did not remain at all before that robber out of fear.
When they did not remain [in their places] even though thus addressed, those best of sages then spoke of another means to the dwellers of heaven.
"O best of gods, summon all the apsarases and dispatch them to the presence of the asuras, whose minds are possessed by lust."
"O gods, having shown your prowess in battle, you shall by force slay those who are attached in heart to those women, who are intoxicated by drinking maireya wine, and who are stronger than you."
Then those women, sent by the gods for the purpose of deceiving the enemies of the deities,
were accompanied by cranes whose ears were pricked by the resonant sound of their tinkling anklets.
With their long necklaces cast across the expanse of their full and high breasts,
they possessed long eyes resembling those of startled young does.
Others had pale cheeks rubbed by swinging earrings and wore smooth garments with the luster of a peacock's neck.
With rows of lower lips as red as freshly cut coral,
their sprout-like hands were clinging to the ends of their garments and to flower-crests.
Their arms were adorned with armlets set with various gems radiating light,
and their beautiful, curly hair resembled the plumage of peacocks.
Adorned with garlands of flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling trees,
their breasts were set off by bodices as green as the body of a parrot.
They possessed the playful, graceful, and swaying gait of rutting elephants,
and their speech was as melodious as the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos and water-hens.
The causes of destruction for his enemies revealed themselves as obstacles even to the great austerities he had undertaken. 129.40.
Then, upon seeing those apsarases, the sons of Diti were deluded by desire;
for the sake of those beautiful-limbed women, they struck one another.
With maces, iron clubs, discs, swords, spears, and hammers;
with bows, thunderbolts, sharp-pointed javelins, slings, and axes.
"She belongs to me, with her lovely limbs and slender waist; she does not belong to you.
Or rather, let battle be the bride-price; release her and strike at me!"
Having spoken these various words, the Daityas, impelled by Time,
encountered one another's slaughter and went to the abode of Yama.
But those Dānavas who remained there, their prowess extinguished,
were all likewise slain in battle by the gods of fierce splendor.

The man of pure intellect who recites this account of the destruction of the lords of the Dānavas in an assembly shall obtain in this very world young women whose beauty is equal to that of the Apsarases. (129.46)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the section on the Battle with Andhaka.
Vyāsa said:
How was that Daitya Andhaka struck down by Hara?
Under whose power the entire three worlds stand in subjection out of fear.
Sanatkumāra said:
In the beginning, there was a lord of the Daityas named Andhaka, a thorn to the three worlds;
having obtained boons from Brahmā, he was incapable of being slain by gods or men.
When he is enraged in battle, neither Viṣṇu, nor Śakra, nor Yama is able to stand before him; how much less so the other inhabitants of heaven?
Once, while wandering this earth, arrogant in his strength,
he beheld on a ridge of Mount Mandara the goddess who was the daughter of Himavat.
Beholding her, that lord of the Daityas, his mind struck by passion, thought wickedly toward the goddess: "I alone am the master. (130.5)
Having reflected upon this, he spoke to his Dānava followers:
"Bring this daughter of the mountain quickly into my presence."
Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best among speakers, whose mind was possessed by the god of love, spoke these words.
O Lord of the Dānavas, since that speech which is beneficial and pure for the future must certainly be spoken by me, especially out of affection for my kinsman. (130.8)
This is the daughter of Himavat and the wife of the wise Śarva;
you must not entertain ill-will toward her, lest she consume us with her splendor.
O tiger among the Dānavas, you ought not to revile Umā here—the goddess who is the mother of the world, worthy of worship, and possessed of a brilliance difficult to behold. || 130.10 ||
Why, with a foolish mind, do you wish to cross the deep-swirling, terrifying river by binding a great stone around your neck? (130.11)
O Lord of the Dānavas, having become a moth through delusion, why do you wish to touch the blazing crest of the fire for your own destruction? 130.12.
O Lord of the Dānavas, do not bring us all to destruction along with our very roots;
let your mind be turned away from the Goddess, for this is not fitting for the wise.
You are wise, of noble birth, and born into the lineage of the noble;
you are a performer of sacrifices and ever-devoted to dharma—this [act] is not fitting for you, O Lord.
You have many wives, all of whom possess perpetual youth;
they are naturally endowed with beautiful limbs—let the Queen’s heart be turned away from this.
"He who, pleased by our asceticism, grants the boons we desire—
to that God of gods, you, O Goddess, wish to do evil."
You wish to take away the half of the body of that God of gods, by whom Dakṣa, Kratu, Kāla, and Kāma were brought to destruction.
How can you disregard the Goddess, the sustainer of the world, who is worshipped in the Liṅga by gods, asuras, and great serpents? 130.18
And you must not conceive of that god, the wielder of the Pināka bow, as being one alone;
for if he so desired, he could create hundreds and thousands of forms.
Thousands of Pramathas, yogis of fearsome deeds,
march before him just as your Dānavas do for you.
He who would take away the radiance from the sun, the luster from the moon, the forbearance from the earth,
or the fangs from Vāsuki— he might as well carry off Pārvatī.
The entire head of that fool who would insult that noble lady, the wife of Śarva, shall shatter into a hundred pieces.
You ought to remember those words spoken to you by your grandfather, the lotus-born one, at the conclusion of the granting of the boon.
"O son of Diti, this prosperity which has been granted to you by me is very difficult to attain;
through your own misconduct, O Danu, it shall go elsewhere. (130.24)
Those men who, possessed by misconduct, do not listen even to the bitter but wholesome words of their kinsmen, go to their destruction.
"O Lord, for the sake of your welfare, we shall seek out Śaṅkara;
having met him, we shall all follow you to the abode of Vaivasvata."
Thus addressed by that kinsman with these auspicious words, he,
impelled by Time, laughed and said, "It is not so."
In that which is unavoidable, both what must be done and what must not be done are dear to me;
if there should be destruction for me in battle, even that destruction would be victory.
For it is Time alone that ordains the auspicious and the inauspicious for all beings by means of the mind; whether in this way or otherwise, it will bring it about.
Then, having rejected Prahlāda out of passion, the lord of the Dānavas set his mind upon touching the goddess, like a moth toward a flame of fire.
Then the Blessed Lady, having perceived the wicked intent of the evil-minded one,
commanded her hosts of great strength to go to battle.
Then, informed by the goddess, they, with various weapons in hand and led by Somanandin, set out facing the Dānavas.
Having waged a truly great battle with the followers of the Dānavas,
they were scattered by the Lord of the Dānavas like clouds driven by the wind.
In the meantime, seeing that Andhaka had risen up, the Goddess herself,
taking up her bow with an arrow, rushed toward him.
She struck Andhaka between the breasts with twenty-five sharp-pointed arrows; he fainted and fell. (130.35)
Then, regaining consciousness after a moment, that proud Dānava quickly rose up with great speed, his formidable bow raised.
Then, rising up once more toward the goddess, that great asura released showers of arrows like a rain-cloud pouring down its waters.
Then, as the goddess raised her trident— blazing with the splendor of fire—
and began to slay Andhaka, the Lord gently restrained her.
"This lord of the Dānavas is to be disciplined by me alone; do not trouble yourself.
I myself shall pierce his heart with my trident in battle."
Thus addressed by the God of gods, the goddess Pārvatī then desisted from the battle and became invisible.
Then the God himself spoke to Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas:
"Summon all the Gaṇas from every side and fight together with the Dānavas. (130.41)
Then, having summoned all those hosts by the command of Śarva, Nandin spoke again to the Lord of Gods: "Listen to these hosts who have arrived. (130.42)

These eternal beings were created by you yourself in the act of creation as distinguished and beloved ones; their true nature, which manifests as diversity through the state of progeny, is very difficult to describe.
These Rudras, who have the bull as their emblem, the bull as their vehicle, and are adorned with portions of the moon—
these dear ones of yours, O Rudra, have arrived.
O Lord, there are one hundred times ten million times ten million of these great-souled ones,
as well as as many thousands and hundreds.
And there were sixty thousand of those blue-throated deities, great-souled Nīlakaṇṭhas, for whom no equal is found.
These heroes, fierce in their forces, possessing formidable and intense prowess,
will gladden your heart as they fight.
Corresponding in power to these very Rudras,
the gatekeepers were indeed composed of the subtle elements (tanmātras), being valiant and possessed of fierce wrath.
Thus these lions among monkeys, possessing the strength of lions,
will fight with the Dānavas in battle like elephants against elephants.
The Rudras, the sons of Rudra, and those who are the attendants of the Rudras—O Lord of the Rudras, there is indeed nothing that cannot be accomplished by them. (130.50)
O best among those who have sons, each one of these Rudras has five sons of great prowess, and they all wear the side-locks of hair like crows.
Those who arose suddenly from you while you were eating, born of your wrath—
these very ones have arrived here, placing Vīrabhadra at their head.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, sixty crores and sixteen thousand of these leaders of the Gaṇas, who are dear to you, have arrived here.
"Thus, O Lord, for the sake of pleasing you, the prosperous sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed by them;
O slayer of cities, behold them now as they have returned."
O sinless one, those who were proclaimed by you as having fallen into calamity—
those known as the hundreds of thousands of millions (koṭīśatasahasra)— they too have now arrived.
Just as great fires, together with the wind, consume trees that are already ablaze,
so shall these [beings] utterly incinerate the Dānavas who are intent on your destruction.
Even while Guha was sporting with the gods in his mountain dwelling,
hundreds of leaders of various beasts with diverse faces were given to him as attendants for the sake of his pleasure.
O Maheśvara, thirty koṭis of those leaders of the Gaṇas, like blazing mountains, have arrived, O sinless one, to do what is pleasing to you.
These lords of the hosts, wearing red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents,
born from the blood of Oṣṭhaja, are named the Raktas.
These sixty thousand crores of Aṅgāraka’s followers, possessed of great strength and prowess, have now presented themselves here.
O sinless one, you should not consider even this much as your own power;
for these eightfold sovereign powers, O Lord, are born from your grace.
O Great Lord, these beings, being fully prepared, will bring forth many worlds,
including gods, asuras, and humans.
In battle, these arrows— resembling kunda flowers and adorned with golden lotuses— would consume the gods and dānavas until the end of the yuga.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, all these heroes are armored and eager for battle; they are devoted to Brahman and adorned with crescents of the moon.
"O Lord of Rudras, behold these Rudras who have arrived, eager for battle;
they possess the luster of the rising sun, are equipped with weapons, and have four arms. (130.66)
For these gatekeepers, O Lord, have faces like those of the lords of monkeys;
they wear red garments, red garlands, and are anointed with red sandalwood paste.
Devoted to Brahman, bestowers of boons, heroic, and lifelong celibates from their youth,
they were all mounted upon intoxicated peacocks, each holding a spear in hand.
These heroic youths named Skandas,
who wear golden garlands and possess horses equal to Uccaiḥśravas, have displayed their prowess.
O God, they shone as they stood there, dressed in yellow silk garments,
possessing a luster like that of the rising sun, with eyes like the petals of young blue lotuses.
O God, those whom you behold here, clad in white garments and with white faces, are your sons named Viśākhas, the Rudras who hold spears in their hands.
Many who were radiant with their physical forms like risen moons,
wearing side-locks of hair, shaven-headed, and adorned with red crests upon their heads.
These boys of renowned prowess,
who stand here among the goats and sheep with the luster of *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* flowers, are the ones known as the Śākhās.
Brave, magnanimous, and with faces like the gods in their childhood,
they possess retinues equal to those of your son Naigameṣa.
These divine youths, who resemble dark clouds and possess voices like those of dark clouds, are indeed known as the Naigameṣas.
"O God, these Pramathas born from your hair have presented themselves before you;
and here are these many red-hued hosts who crush the forces of the enemy. (130.76)
They were all shield-bearers, armored warriors, chariot-fighters, and versatile combatants;
they all carried various weapons and were all experts in warfare.

All were skilled in action, fierce in battle, and fully armored; they possessed the splendor of white and black clouds or of mountains, and like surging oceans filled with crocodiles, fish, and sea-monsters, they were formidable.
With faces like lions, tigers, and boars, and with iron clubs and thunderbolts in their hands—
these Pramathas have arrived before you solely through your grace.
These indeed are the heroic attendants of Skanda, the Supreme Self;
given by the gods for his play, they have all presented themselves before you.
O Lord, it is my conviction that this vast army of Pramathas, arrogant and exultant, is capable of breaking the host of the Dānavas.
Setting aside all other tasks and maintaining the highest reverence,
he immediately began to destroy [the enemy], for the sake of the ruin of the gods' foes.
O Lord, these leaders of the hosts of Gaṇas, possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun and a radiance like the gateways of Mount Kailāsa, are indeed prepared to conquer the army of your enemies.
O Lord of the Moving and the Immovable, then Andhaka, standing in the fray, attains equality with you;
O All-pervading One, surrounded by hundreds of hosts of Gaṇas, release the prostrate lords of the Gaṇas.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa, at the commencement of the battle with Andhaka. || 130.130 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed One beheld the leaders of the Gaṇas who had arrived.
With their own numerous divisions, they were fully armored and eager for battle.
And Diṇḍi, and Bhārabhūti, and Somaśarman, and Karika, and Meghanāda, and Udaremaṇi. || 131.2 ||
Āsatti, Dhūtapāpa, and Candramauli; Ādityamāla, Vikrānta, and the mighty Sukeśa.
Tālaketu, Jvara, and the powerful Daṇḍapāṇi—
these and other renowned leaders of the Gaṇas, both secret and manifest.
Having worshipped Mahāgaṇapati as well as Khoṭhāmudgara, the Blessed One propitiated them all again and again.
He, whose roar was like a thundercloud and whose voice resounded like a hundred drums, said:
"O best of beings, you together with the Dānavas ought to fight for me."
"You yourselves, O leaders of the hosts, are sufficient to harass them;
therefore, O beings of great power, go forth with your hosts and followers for their total destruction, for I have been honored by you, O mighty ones. (131.7)
Thus addressed by the god, those high-souled ones bowed their heads to Hara and departed; the god, too, then established himself [in his abode].
Then there arose a sound like that of the ocean being split asunder,
from the army of the Asura Andhaka as it approached Mount Mandara.
Hearing the roar of the Dānavas, which caused extreme distress to the ears,
the Pramathas roared fiercely like clouds at the end of an eon.
Those two oceans of armies, tossed by each other's force,
became like two great seas being churned at the end of a cosmic dissolution.
The God of gods said:
"O Brahman, offer oblations for the destruction of our enemies and for our victory;
and you too, Nandin, protect [them], surrounded by all these hosts."
"May these enemies, who roar like clouds pouring rain while stationed in the sky,
afflict those Dānavas who likewise move through the sky."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, the two began to carry out the word of the Blessed One;
Bṛhaspati offered oblations into the fire, and Nandin protected him.
As the great beings exerted themselves, Mount Mandara, the crusher of all,
appeared as if it were about to collapse, with its elephants and lions falling away.
Then, like a lion’s strength against the pride of Andhaka’s host,
he quickly shook that mountain-like [host] as it was surging forward.
Then a tumultuous roar arose from the Pramathas:
"Let the Daityas be warded off in battle with trees, stones, and arrows! (131.17)
But the Dānavas, though being held back by the Pramathas who appeared victorious, then quickly tore through the army of the Pramathas and ascended [the mountain]. || 131.18 ||
For even the Pramathas, resolved that they must fight without attachment,
cut down, pierced, and struck the enemies of the gods.
"Seize him! Release him! Stay where you are!"—such were the words that arose from both the hosts of the Pramathas and the Asuras as they stood ready for battle.
The pitiless Pramatha demons crushed one another with excellent trees from root to tip, as well as with mountains covered in vegetation.
Then, by the sons of Dākṣāyaṇī, those destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice were unable to be turned away, for they were not averse to devotion.
Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving that the enemies had been defeated and were unable to ascend the mountain peak,
the gods restrained the Pramathas from all sides.
The God of gods said: "O leaders of the hosts, let the sons of Danu ascend Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves; for the sake of my sport, do you fight with them."

Then they beheld a region filled with flowers from trees broken by the onset of herds of elephants spreading out, and where the terrifying roars released by lions dwelling in many beautiful groves resounded.
The darkness within its beautiful stone chambers was dispelled by the lamps that were the crest-jewels of the lords of serpents;
and the openings therein were revealed through the masses of great rocks shattered by the force of the cool, pure waters of the mountain torrents.
In some places, the mass of rays from the young sun was obstructed by the tips of fresh copper-colored sprouts;
in other places, there were clearly fashioned beautiful patterns of leaf-designs upon the moon-like faces of celestial nymphs.
In one place, he beheld a region of the forest variegated by clusters of lovely blossoms shaken by the wind,
where his own body was being gazed upon by a troop of monkeys seated upon slabs of crystal gemstone.
