It was delightful with the soft warbling of kalahamsas resting in water fragrant with the pollen of lotus petals, while throngs of siddhas were awakened by the pleasure of hearing the cries of the peacocks in the dwellings of the wine-servant maidens.
In some places, the gold ore was melted by fire trickling from sun-stones heated by the rays of the sun;
in other places, the waters were scattered by mountain rivers flowing from moon-stones through which the fallen rays had entered.

In some places, its broad banks were adorned with heaps of pearls burst forth from the frontal globes of great elephants when struck by the thunderbolt-like tusks of boars, appearing like scattered clusters of white flowers.
The intermediate space was filled with the great roar of the loud, joyful laughter of the hosts of Bhairavas;
it was delightful with the dancing of joyful siddha-wives hidden within the bowers of trees and thickets of creepers.
It was a place where intoxicated elephants roamed through many encampments, where the waters of mountain torrents were drunk by many young deer,
where there were many rugged slopes, precipices, and groves, and which was filled with various shrubs, climbing vines, and spreading trees.
The tops of its trees were variegated by the radiance of emeralds, rubies, and peaks;
its beautiful forest interiors resounded with the abundant, sweet warbling of swarms of bees and the cries of cuckoos.

In that place, the Siddhas—conquerors of death and grief, perfected through the use of yellow pigment, collyrium, and mineral ores, and masters of hidden treasures—dwell forever joyful, accompanied by their consorts, wearing beautiful necklaces as radiant as moonbeams. (131.35)

There, the Vidyādharas, their passion bound to their beloveds, paint various flower-ornaments upon the full, high-sloped breasts [of their consorts] with streaks of mineral pigments in green, red, and ochre hues. (131.36)
In which [place], the Apsarases— whose slender bodies were always exhausted by amorous dalliance, and whose lotus-like hands were placed in the grasping hands of their beloveds—
most joyfully enjoy the breeze that has arrived, exceedingly cooled by its intimacy with the waters of the mountain torrents.
The swans were awakened by the tinkling of anklets; the lotuses were brushed by the downy feathers of those swans;
the pure water was reddened by the pollen of the lotuses; and the golden peaks were adorned by the waters. || 131.38 ||
There were sandalwood trees rising from the mountain peaks, with flocks of cuckoos perched upon the branches;
there was the trumpeting of lordly elephants released by the herds, and bears and hyenas agitated by fear of that roar.
Its groves were inhabited by bears and hyenas; from the mouths of its bower-caves issued forth lions;
many frontal globes of elephants had been torn open by lions; and pearls and gems had fallen out from those frontal globes. (131.40)
Its surface was illuminated by the rays of jewels, with the foot of Śaṅkara resting upon that surface;
there were groves of trees rising from its base, and paths strewn with heaps of flowers from the creepers of the thickets. || 131.41 ||
The road was variegated with jeweled archways, and the jeweled archways were adorned with colorful cloths;
upon those cloths flowers were placed, and bees were kissing those flowers.
Its slopes were variegated with various minerals, delightful with bowers of diverse flowering creepers,
resounded by the cries of various intoxicated birds, and inhabited by siddhas perched upon its many peaks.

Then all those Daityas, desiring victory for themselves and permitted by the Blessed One to enter, ascended that delightful Mandara mountain, which was inhabited by various throngs of Cāraṇas and Siddhas and had been personally chosen as his dwelling-place by the Three-eyed Lord.
Then, released by the Pramathas, the sons of Diti climbed [the mountain],
thinking quickly that the Pramathas, being terrified, had turned back.
Then, on the back of Mount Mandara, which was crowded with various kinds of trees,
the Daityas stood with their shoulders hunched, possessing a radiance like that of the sun.
That Mount Mandara, with its formidable rocks, stones, and trees, and its many tigers, hyenas, and elephants,
was violently scattered by the great asuras with their proud horses and elephants, like a cloud dispersed by the winds.
In some places, those resembling white clouds hurl boulders and, uprooting trees, roar like thunderclouds;
though being warded off, they crush the Pramathas as lions in the forests crush the leaders of deer herds.
Then, surrounded by those elephants, chariots, horses, and Dānavas, that place, possessing the splendor of the agitated great ocean,
shone like a forest protected by the arms of the sons of Diti, as if guarded by the arms of the Lord of Beasts.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Mandara," at the commencement of the Battle with Andhaka, in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 131.131 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Having reached the peak of Mount Mandara, that Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, [proceeded].
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke this to Śakra, whose splendor was like that of Indra and the sun.
Andhaka said:
"O Blessed One, we have reached Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, where the surface of the rocks is crowded by the Pramathas of terrifying appearance. (132.2)
The leaders of the Gaṇas—those who move through the air, those possessed of illusory powers, and the yogins of great strength—cannot be forcibly conquered by the Dānavas. || 132.3 ||
For generally, even those who are powerful act with skillful means at the outset in their undertakings; it is only later that they act otherwise.
"Adopting that means, being especially composed,
let us utterly crush the Pramathas, or do as it pleases you."
Therefore, O Lord, desiring our victory and for the sake of conquering the Dānavas,
form the mountain-array that shatters the enemy's formations.
And those here who possess bodies with the splendor and color of ten million suns,
standing in the midst of the hosts of Pramathas, behold me repeatedly.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard the words of Andhaka, the preceptor of the Daityas became enraged and spoke to the lord of the Daityas, as if pointing out Gopati. (132.8)
Śukra said:
"This one with honey-colored, tawny eyes, the three-eyed one adorned with the moon,
wearing a tiger-skin garment— this is the god who wields the Pināka bow."
But he who has the face of a lion among monkeys, wears blue garments, and possesses four arms—
he who shines like the rising sun— is this Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas.
Slender and tall, resembling fire, he who blazes like this very fire is Bṛhaspati, the lord of Brahmins, possessed of vast intelligence. || 132.11 ||
This one standing not far away, who bears a trident and has a bull as his emblem—
this is the great-bodied Andhaka, the excellent Mahāgaṇapati.

He who, possessing great strength and holding a spear in his hand, shines while mounted upon a peacock that calls out—a peacock with variegated plumage resembling the light of the rising sun—[is this one]. (132.13)
Devoted to Brahman, delighting in Brahman, a celibate student of restrained vows—
this Skanda is indeed the leader of the gods against the Dānavas in battle.
He who stands upon the copper-crested [mountain], possessing the luster of a copper-crested stone,
shines while brandishing his spear like a cloud flashing with lightning.
For he, who bears the side-locks of youth, whose face resembles the full moon, is named Viśākha;
though a youth, he is devoted to lifelong celibacy.
Young and possessed of youthful wisdom, like a tree endowed with branches,
this son of Svāhā is indeed named Śākha, of great splendor.
For he who stands there, having turned toward his left side, repeatedly points with his forefinger both at me and at you. (132.18)
Mounted upon a ram, this powerful youth stands ready;
known as Naigameṣa, he is the son of Andhaka and Hara.
Surrounded by these four sons,
this slayer of asuras appears just like the Grandfather (Brahmā) when he is joined by the four gods.
O best of Asuras, protected by my mantra, you shall fight against the god Īśa, the great archer who is preceded by the son of Nandin.
"I shall raise up the Daityas slain by the Pramathas by the hundreds and thousands,
just as a rain-cloud raises up crops."
Sanatkumāra said: Having addressed that lord of the Dānavas as "O Bhārgava," he then proceeded to array that army in a mountain formation against the Dānavas.
Having made the base blind with darkness, along with the horses and the charioteer,
he indeed rendered its feet [immobile] by means of many thousands of foot-soldiers.
Upon those thousands of feet of the mountain array,
Bhārgava caused the Dānavas to construct masses of trees, crags, and rocks.
With ten crores of those high-souled Dānavas,
the Lord of Planets (Rāhu) struck the hips of those copper-eyed beings.
On the slopes variegated by the outflow of minerals,
the descendant of Bhṛgu also stationed the Dānavas like blades of grass and like shrubs.
With another thirty crores, he who possessed a splendor equal to the sun fashioned the peaks of the mountain-array for the enemies of the lord of the thirty gods.
Then, upon those lofty peaks, the descendant of Bhṛgu pointed out the armed Dānavas, saying, "These are the precipices. (132.29)
Standing on the precipice, those Daityas, possessing the luster of dark rain clouds,
remained there as if joyfully discharging showers of weapons like water.
Those Daityas who are strong, endowed with speed, and thorns to the gods,
having whirled about like hawks, shall then lie hidden within the mountain range.
The divine descendant of Bhṛgu rendered all the Nivātakavacas, who bore various weapons, like the peaks of a mountain formation.
Then [he slew] Prahlāda, Saṃhrāda, Anuhrāda, as well as Śini,
Jambha, Kujambha, Tāra, Maya, and Namuci.
He likewise meditated upon Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Kārtasvana, Kuśa, Śambhu, Aṅga, Ilvaka, and Bilvaka.
Vita, Vṛtta, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Daṇḍa the Dānava, Añjana, Ruṣaṇa, Rāhu, Svarbhānu, Ajaka, and Gaja. || 132.35 ||
Hastin and Duryodhana, as well as the Dānava Dhundhu—these and other powerful Daityas who were thorns in the side of the gods. || 132.36 ||
"Guard the array! Fight! thus spoke the lord of the asuras, who was like Himavat, the king of mountains, or the Vindhya with its wondrous caves.
That mountain array, with its trees bristling with weapons, shone like a massed darkness or a gathering of clouds. || 132.38 ||
Beholding the mountain-array again and again, the Pramathas were filled with wonder;
likewise, those stationed within the mountain-array gazed upon that mountain-formation.
Those tigers among asuras roared like clouds at the end of an eon, and they said:
"Indeed, this cannot be broken even by the gods together with Indra."
"What can the Pramathas do, they who possess so little strength and prowess?
Śukra will bring us back to life even if we are dead; of this there is no doubt.
Fight, O best of Dānavas, with fearless hearts! (132.41)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen the mountain-array constructed by the best of the Bhṛgus, the god Kapardin spoke thus to Bṛhaspati of vast intellect: 132.42.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen the mountain-array constructed by the best of the Bhṛgus, the god Kapardin spoke thus to Bṛhaspati of vast intellect.
O Lord of Speech, behold this mountain-array constructed by Śukra,
which, with its peaks and caves, resembles the Himavat mountain.
If this mountain-array is neglected, it will swallow the worlds, along with the netherworlds, Viṣṇu, and the Grandfather (Brahmā).

Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the nāgas, nor likewise the mountains, would be able to shatter this [fortress], even if they were prepared for the task, were it not for these leaders of the hosts.
"O best of Brahmins, O wise one, I see no other means of breaking the mountain-array than the great Vajra-array, which is capable of piercing all arrays."
Therefore, O best among the knowers of Brahman, form today the Vajra array, which shatters even mountain ranges and is surrounded by ten thousand Pramathas.
Thus addressed by Śambhu, Bṛhaspati, the lord of brahmins,
then arrayed his forces against that array with the Vajra formation.
The wise one stationed many thousands of mighty-armed devotees and leaders of the hosts in the midst of the diamond-array (vajravyūha).
By the heroic attendants of Skanda, who were slayers of gods and asuras,
a thousand sections were composed for that Vajravyūha.
That twice-born one established ten million of the Pramatha strikers— heroes among heroes— at all the points where the vajra-shards fell.
The divine Aṅgiras made Kumāra, Viśākha, Śākha, and likewise Chāgamukha the buds of the Vajravyūha formation.
At the tip of the bud stood Nandin, four-armed, with the face of the lord of monkeys, the destroyer of enemies; he held a raised thunderbolt in his hand and possessed the radiance of the sun.
He placed Kuṇḍodara, Nandiṣeṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa,
and Mahodara at the rear portion of that thunderbolt, where it was like a flower bud.
But before him stood the lord of the Gaṇas, Somanandin, who has the face of a tiger;
he resembles ten thousand suns and moons and stands holding a paṭṭiśa weapon.
The gatekeepers of the Rudras, as well as the Rudras themselves and those who are the sons of Rudra,
have been stationed here and there as protectors of the adamantine array.
Established upon an excellent chariot in the midst of the Vajravyūha array stood the Lord Bhava, Śarva, Kapardin, the blue-and-red one.
His great banner, white and radiant, shone like Indra’s standard;
it was like Mount Mandara, its peak graced by the orb of the moon.
With its hundred streams and many joints, adorned with beautiful buds,
the array of thunderbolts became like one desiring to shatter the mountain formation.
Seeing that manifested array, the gods, gandharvas, and guhyakas, their eyes wide with wonder, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (132.60).
Then, amidst the hosts of the Gaṇas, lion-roars arose, mingled with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs;
they struck terror into the sons of Diti and resembled the roar of the agitated waters of the ocean.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Formation of the Array," in the *Andhakamathana* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen those two arrays formed by the Pramathas and the Asuras, the gods—
With ten million celestial chariots, they quickly obstructed the sky on all sides.
The entire expanse of the sky shone, filled with splendors,
like the beautiful forest on the peak of Mount Meru being consumed by fire.
Rich with the sound of celestial drums and crowded with hundreds of divine women,
that divine assembly shone like the orb of the sun.
Strewn with celestial flowers, perfumed with divine fragrances,
and filled with hundreds of spectators, the surface of the sky shone like a divine arena.
Musical instruments were struck, and the celestial singers sang;
Rambhā and other divine women with beautiful side-glances also danced.
Then the two arrays of diamond-mountains, each desiring victory over the other,
clashed together with great roars like two oceans tossed by the wind.
Though addressed by the high-souled Śukra with the words "Do not hasten," and though being restrained,
the warriors engaged in unrestrained combat.
Then conchs and kettledrums, cymbals and cow-horns,
āḍambaras, ḍiṇḍimas, maṇḍūkas, and even small drums were sounded.
Kettledrums, war-drums, clay drums, and kīṃkharas and ānakas were sounded vigorously by the thousands on both sides of the army.
Then, upon hearing the sound of musical instruments from the two armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras, the hosts of gods, along with the Gandharvas and Cāraṇas, raised shouts of acclaim.
At the sound of Bala’s musical instruments and the lion-like roar of the gods,
lions, tigers, and elephants roared fiercely on Mount Mandara.
To the sound of that resonance of musical instruments, those Pramatha asuras, possessing immeasurable prowess, fought while breaking through their own battle array.
But at their first encounter in battle,
those who were disciplined in combat let out a terrible roar, like the trumpeting of elephants.
The gods and asuras, desiring to slay one another in battle, distinguished themselves by the thousands with weapons held in their hands.
Due to the extreme joy caused by the severe blows of spears, thunderbolts, stones, trees, and arrows,
the battle of the Asura attendants increased in ferocity, like the transition from the Yuga to the Tiṣya age.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: While the tumultuous conflict between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras was raging, the Skanda Purāṇa 134 states:
The sounds of bowstrings and terrible lion-roars are being heard.
With their fingers interlaced, the gods, cāraṇas, uragas,
and guhyakas raised the hems of their garments and cried out, making sounds born of the excitement of battle.
Stirred to valor by that sound of the heroes' roars,
the proud Pramatha demons performed deeds that were unbearable.
Severed by long swords, their chests split open by spears,
and their vital organs mangled by arrows, the Pramatha demons fall.
In that battle between the Pramathas and the Asuras, heaps of falling heads were seen there, along with arms together with thighs.
With their wheels shattered, their banners torn, their fenders destroyed, and their poles broken—
seen by the hundreds, they were without horses, their charioteers slain, and rendered chariotless.
Adorned with banners, armlets, armor, weapons, and standards,
the preeminent elephants fall with their tusks and trunks protruding.
With their limbs mangled by the strike of arrows,
horses resembling the steeds of the sun— resplendent with their crests of yak-tail plumes— are brought down along with their riders.
With its terrified horses bolted and its dānavas fleeing along with their chariots,
that army appeared like a frenzied ocean with its crocodiles wandering in confusion.
With garments, parasols, crowns, jeweled earrings, necklaces, half-necklaces, armlets, finger-rings, and the finest garlands; 134.10.
Covered with severed hands and fallen feet,
the battlefield shines like the sky filled with risen stars.
Clad in garments dripping with blood and adorned with various ornaments,
the earth, with its limbs covered in red cloth, shone like Death itself.
Then a terrible river began to flow, carrying the blood of the multitudes of horses and elephants as its water, leading toward the abode of Yama.
It was teeming with deer, elephants, donkeys, horses, camels, and great sea-monsters;
it had flesh, fat, and liver for its mud, and hundreds of bows and banners for its trees.
With hundreds of stones for its severed heads, five-headed serpents for its hands, moss for its matted hair, and the strings of hundreds of bows for its fibers; (134.15)
Indeed, it was filled with the joy of white-robed women, crowded with crowns and turbans,
brimming with drums and lutes, and resounding with the croaking of excellent ornaments.
It was teeming with arrows and fish, difficult to approach due to swords as its crocodiles,
with great chariot-wheels as its large crocodiles, and churned by maces as its aquatic monsters.
With its sand scattered by broken necklaces and its foam produced by phlegm,
it was like a garland of red lotuses or like a discarded wreath of saffron.
Like the tongue of the king of serpents, like the wondrous command of Yama,
that river— terrifying to the timid warriors and increasing the joy of the heroes—
flowed forth with waters of blood, carrying them toward the heavenly realm.
With smoke increased by the enraged lords of the Daityas and its interior ablaze with the fire of Nandīśvara,
that army shone with a roar like the ocean, like the world at the time of universal destruction.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter in the Gaṇayuddha of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: As that battle between the attendants and the asuras was increasing in intensity, the Skanda Purāṇa [continues].
Standing upon mountain ranges and precipices, those best of Dānavas were filled with rage.
In their wrath, those tireless ones rained down a shower of spears, javelins, darts,
and maces upon the army of the Pramathas, like clouds pouring forth rain.
Though struck many times by the falling rain of weapons,
they disregarded it all and set their minds solely upon battle.
For just as clouds [destroy] crops, as elephants [crush] trees, as tigers [slay] spotted deer, and as śarabhas [overpower] elephants; || 135.4 ||
Like thunderbolts [shatter] mountains, like messengers of Death [seize] men, like obstacles [impede] those seeking peace, and like lack of discipline [corrupts] statesmanship; || 135.5 ||
Just as beings are like beings, and faults are likewise like faults,
so too did the heroic Pramathas strike down the Nivātakavacas by the hundreds and thousands with showers of spears, javelins, and arrows.
With chests torn open by spears, heads split by clubs,
and limbs withered by the blows of thunderbolts, the Dānavas fell upon the earth.
The exceedingly terrible roars of those crying out were heard on all sides,
like the thundering of the clouds of universal destruction.
Pierced in many places by arrows,
with their hips and spines broken, the asuras writhed upon the ground like serpents with shattered backs.
Then, beholding that excessive slaughter, hundreds of great asuras there, their eyes bloodshot with rage, turned back. || 135.10 ||
O Vyāsa, those Pramathas, being violently pierced by them,
were filled with shame and closed their eyes, like bulls under a falling rain.
The Pramathas endured that rain sent forth by the Dānavas;
and they too, having waged a tumultuous battle, were then afflicted at its conclusion.
Broken, turned away in flight, with their limbs and joints shattered and mangled—
when that army had been routed, the foremost of the Pramathas then [attacked] Prāmatha.
Ten [monkeys], equal to a hundred great elephants, created a mighty force;
there was the powerful Śaṅkukarṇa and the heroic Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
Mahākāla, who is dark-hued, and the renowned Nandiṣeṇa; Piṅgala, Lohitākṣa, and the heroic Somanandī.
Vināyaka and Nandin, Chāga and Kuṇḍodara, and Skanda seated upon his excellent peacock. || 135.16 ||
Together they emerged like water-bearing clouds, and they entered the army of the asuras like makaras entering the ocean. || 135.17 ||
The Daityas were slain by Śaṅkukarṇa, torn asunder by Ghaṇṭākarṇa,
struck by the arrows of Nandiṣeṇa, and driven away by Mahākāla.
With their weapons and ornaments pulverized by the force of Kuṇḍodara’s mace,
and agitated by Piṅgala, they perished, torn asunder by the spear of Skanda.
With their faces split by blows from fists, their heads struck by palms, and being cast hither and thither by blows from open hands, [they lay there]. (135.20)
With their weapons, garments, and armor fallen away, and the bindings of their hair loosened, the Dānavas were utterly shattered; thus, the breach of the formation occurred swiftly.
Being split apart, the mountain array appeared terrible to behold,
like the great Vindhya mountain struck of old by Indra’s thunderbolt.
Then the Pramathas, appearing victorious, rushed by the hundreds toward the Daityas whose battle arrays were broken, like birds toward ripe trees.
Then once again there occurred a battle,
tumultuous and fierce, between the heroic Pramathas and the Asuras.
Furthermore, when those [armies] met in that terrible encounter like a clash of elephants,
the gods, along with the gandharvas and siddhas, rejoiced and shouted in heaven.
Then, various kinds of tumultuous sounds produced by the retinues of the Dānavas were heard,
as terrible as the roaring of thunderclouds.
On elephants resembling the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), on chariots equal to the celestial palaces of the Gandharvas,
and on horses with speeds like the wind, the Daityas indeed move fearlessly in battle.

The lords of the Gaṇas and the foremost of the Dānavas set about destroying one another with spears, javelins, lances, *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons, and arrows, as well as with mountain boulders, discuses, tridents, and thunderbolts.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter in the Gaṇayuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, Virocana, the lord of the Daityas, who was as radiant as the sun, [spoke].
He entered the host of the Pramathas, as the sun enters a mass of clouds.
Mounted upon an elephant adorned with tusks, which resembled the peak of Mount Mandara, possessed trunk-tusks, was dripping with rut, and had four tusks; || 136.2 ||
There, that bull among asuras shone upon the ridge of the Naga mountain,
like the thousand-rayed sun blazing while stationed at the peak of its rising.
With his maces and arrows, which possessed the radiance of the sun’s rays,
he struck down the Pramathas by the hundreds and thousands.
Just as Vainateya [Vishnu] puts the serpents to flight, or as a lion puts the bulls to flight,
so did the heroic Virocana put the Pramathas to flight.
Whether moving away or coming toward him, whether not yet reached or already reached, and even when standing at a distance—
whichever Pramatha the Asura beholds, he rends him asunder.
Just as deer upon seeing a lion, or serpents upon seeing Garuḍa,
so did the Pramathas flee in fear upon seeing Virocana.
Seeing the strength of Gaṇeśvara, Vināyaka, the excellent lord of the Gaṇas and leader of the Pramatha host, quickly turned back.
Stretching out his terrible trunk like Airāvata in former times,
he rushed toward Virocana as a tiger springs at a deer.
Beholding that sharp-toothed elephant-faced one rushing toward him,
the Dānava pierced him between the temples with a lance.
Drawing that javelin from the tip of his trunk,
Vināyaka tore Virocana apart with that very weapon hurled by his hand.
Pierced by that lance and distressed by the blow of the hand,
Virocana trembled, overwhelmed, and bled profusely.
Then, observing the lord of the Dānavas, Virocana, reeling,
Vināyaka pierced him with his two teeth, which were as white as the moon.
Beholding that deed of Vaināyaka, the gods, together with Śakra, let out loud cries of acclaim;
a garland of flowers fell upon his head, just as the triple-pathed river [Ganges] falls upon the Lord.
Adorned with that garland of various flowers, the god then shone resplendent in battle,
possessing a beauty as charming as a row of star-clusters, standing like another lofty Mount Meru.

Seeing Vināyaka with his mouth agape, his blood flowing, and his face wide open as he tore [the foe] apart, Jambha—who resembled a dark cloud—cried out in distress and fled, saying, "Do not fear! (136.16).
As Jambha approached, roaring in many ways like an immeasurable cloud in the sky,
Nandin checked him and struck him with his mace, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt, when enraged, strikes a mountain with his vajra.

From that blow of the thunderbolt, he became slack in his actions like the son of a Dānava fallen from heaven; he fell to the ground and rose again repeatedly, like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter in an assembly hall.

When Jambha had been struck down and the enemy force was subdued, the six Dānavas, with faces like those of enraged Mlecchas, hacked at that elder brother of the Six-faced One with axes, spears, swords, and battle-axes.
Vināyaka, having been struck by them, tore out two tusks from his own body and released him,
who was drenched in blood, just as Rāhu releases the sun after half-eating it.
Released by him, Virocana— his splendor shrouded by excessive pain— did not shine with his usual charm,
like the full-orbed moon in the sky during the season of new clouds when it is obstructed by rain-clouds.
That Vināyaka, resembling a six-faced deity, drove away those six Dānavas who were themselves like Vināyakas,
with blows from his broad teeth that were like thunderbolts, just as a lion scatters lordly elephants.
With an elephant’s face, raising his trunk like an elephant of the gods filled with pride,
he drove away those foremost of Dānavas, just as a proud lion cub drives away elephants.
Like bulls watched by a lion, like men watched at the hour of fate,
or like those whose end has been signaled by a leader, terror then seized the watching armies.
Whichever way that god looked, raising his own hand like an elephant,
in that very direction the army of the Daityas was shattered, like a flowering forest by a fierce wind.
Seeing that army overwhelmed by the powerful one, this son of Bali, the best among the strong,
set out with the intent to slay Vināyaka, like a rutting lord of elephants against another intoxicated elephant in battle.
As he rushed forward like the enraged Lord of the Scorching Rays (the Sun) or like Time (Kāla) himself with bow in hand at the battle,
Kuṇḍodara advanced to block him and to fight in the fray, like one lion against another lion.
Like two lion cubs filled with pride, or like two young elephants with their trunks extended,
Kuṇḍodara and the son of Bala met together, intoxicated by the passion for battle.
Drawing five hundred bows that resounded like thunderbolts,
he discharged excellent arrows at Kuṇḍodara, roaring like a rain-cloud.
Then Kuṇḍodara struck all those sharp-pointed arrows of Bāṇa, which were like enraged serpents,
with a mountain-peak, just as an obstacle thwarts one's desires.

Seeing those arrows, which were struck down by the enemy of the gods and lay fruitlessly upon the ground, that foe of the enemies of the gods (Kumbhakarṇa) struck Kuṇḍodara with a spear, just as Guha struck the Krauñca mountain, the king of mountains, with his spear.
From the chest of Gaṇeśvara, that spear drank the blood of Bāṇa, just as the wife of the wielder of the thunderbolt drinks the beautiful, fragrant nectar brought by Śakra. || 136.32 ||
Struck by the blow of the spear, the yakṣa Kuṇḍodara, who resembled Mount Dardara or Mandara,
fell down, losing his great consciousness like a tall tree consumed by a forest fire.
Seeing Kuṇḍodara slain, Vināyaka— his lotus garland fallen away—
rushed toward Bāṇa, desiring to kill him, like an elephant with its trunk raised high as if holding a golden water-pot.
With arrows resembling thunderbolts, Bāṇa struck that leader who was already stretched out;
having pierced him through the face, he then roared like a cloud in the sky at the end of summer.

Disregarding the falling arrows as if they were the dropping of blades of grass, he whose face was like that of a lordly elephant shattered Bāṇa’s chariot— along with its fender, wheels, and charioteer— with a single arrow.
As that Vināyaka was tearing apart Bāṇa’s horses and had fallen to the ground like an elephant,
Rāhu, the son of Siṃhī, pounced upon him like a lion and bound him with his noose-like arms.
Bound by Rāhu around his pair of arms, the Leader, wearing a garland of a thousand serpents,
quivered like an elephant crossing the celestial river with its trunk-tip whirling.
Seeing Vināyaka, whose movements were then restrained by Rāhu’s arms, the gods dwelling in heaven—including Śakra, along with the Yakṣas and Siddhas—cried out "Alas! Alas! again and again. (136.39)
Then Kuṇḍodara, that best of Yakṣas, having recovered his breath like a crop drenched with water,
took up an axe and struck Rāhu between the collarbones with a clenched fist.
Struck by the blow of an axe and firmly beaten with fists by that preeminent Yakṣa, Rāhu,
though possessed of terrible strength, released Vināyaka just as a man of noble birth abandons an evil deed.
Turning toward him like a rutting elephant dwelling in a forest thicket, Gajānana,
whose trunk was formidable, struck Rāhu with his feet, his tusks, and his outstretched trunk.
Struck by Vināyaka, Rāhu—the enemy of the immortals—abandoned his pride, arrogance, and strength; like a cloud devoid of water, he stood like a lordly elephant struck down by a lion.
While Rāhu was being tormented by Kuṇḍodara with blows from his fists and Vināyaka himself,
Kujambha, Saṃhrāda, Maya, along with Tāraka, Huṇḍa, and Tuhuṇḍa, then approached him.
Māya struck Kuṇḍodara with a trident in the belly, as Tāraka did with a spear;
but Bala struck him, who resembled a hanging cloud, with a fist like a thunderbolt.
And the son of Hiraṇyanetra’s younger brother struck Vināyaka of terrible strength with his palm;
and his son also, the powerful Tuhuṇḍa, having gone there in a rage, likewise struck him. (136.46)
Then Vināyaka, moving with terrible speed, seized Tuhuṇḍa in battle with his trunk,
and having hurled him down and tossed him up, he cast him far away like a messenger of Yama.
Having struck Prahlāda and then Maya, that god, whose chest was like intoxicated collyrium,
uprooted him and roared with a terrible sound, like a cloud filled with white water in the sky.

And Kuṇḍodara, that best of Yakṣas, having struck Bala along with Satāra and Kujambha—those two leaders of elephant herds standing on the battlefield, their garlands shaken off and their wrath greatly aroused—[fought]. (136.49)
The two of them discharged a fierce shower of arrows, like two ancient clouds releasing a torrent of rain.
Then again, they unleashed weapons that produced sounds like the crashing and thundering of clouds;
those hosts of the Asura’s attendants had reached a state of supreme intensity in their engagement.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then there occurred once again a conflict between the armies of the attendants and the asuras.
It arose like the wondrous [roar] of sea-monsters from the agitation of the ocean.
Armed with spears, swords, and bows, the Dānavas and the Pramathas shone there like clouds charged with lightning, eager for battle.
"Endure! Strike! "Perish! You are already destroyed!"—such were the words repeatedly heard from those very people as they spoke. (137.3)
With spears, tridents, and discuses; with *huṇḍa* weapons, whirling clubs, *bhindipālas*, hand-held missiles, and even scattered arrows.
With ṭaṅkas, kaṭaṅkas, spears, nooses, axes, and sharp-edged spears; with blows from trees, stones, and rocks, and even with the peaks of mountains.
With these weapons, they indeed slaughter one another:
"I am Ghaṇṭākarṇa, O Asura! I am Jambha, the lord of the Pramathas! (137.6)
"I am Somanandi, O enemy of Indra; I am Kujambha, O lord of the Gaṇas;
I am Bilvaka, and I am the Yakṣa, the Dānava named Piṅgala. (137.7)
"I am Prahlāda, I am Nandin, I am Śaṅkukarṇa, and indeed I am Bala.
Who are you? I am Kuṇḍodara; I am Vṛtra, O Kuṇḍakodara! (137.8)
"I am Nandīṣeṇa, I am Śambhu, and I am indeed Mahākāla; I am Viśākha, I am Bali, I am Bāṇa, and I am Guha. (137.9)
"I am Prahlāda, I am Śākha, I am Naigameṣa, I am Andhaka"—
thus spoke the terrifying ones among the Dānavas and the Pramathas.
Due to the excess of their pride, insults are heard from those fighting in battle,
like the trumpeting of rutting elephants or the rumbling of clouds at the onset of the rainy season.
It was as if mountains were being split apart, like oceans at the time of their destruction,
or like the great winds rushing with speed at the end of the dissolution of the world.
As they struck one another, there arose a great clamor;
with weapons resembling the staff of Brahmā and even like the staff of Yama,
they slaughtered each other, being intensely provoked by mutual rage.
Then, as the weapons were being hurled, there arose a crackling sound like that of thunderbolts striking mountains or of bamboos burning.
Struck with great force by the Śaktis discharged by Gaṇeśvara,
they fell down screaming like clouds accompanied by meteors.
With their limbs shattered by blows from trees and their joints pulverized by maces,
the Dānavas fall upon the earth like horses deprived of life.
With their banners and flags severed, and their axles, yokes, and poles broken,
chariots resembling celestial palaces were seen there in ruins.
With elephants, horses, and shattered chariots,
that ground became impassable, as if the Vindhya mountains had descended upon it.
There, the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and kiṃnaras,
filled the sky many times over with the rich sound of their loud acclamations.
A rain of divine flowers, most variegated and fragrant like nectar, fell where they were fighting in battle.

Thus, those sons of Diti and the arrogant hosts of Pramathas, roaring with sounds like the thundering of clouds and discharging arrows, swords, spears, double-edged blades, and maces, fought one another with great intensity as they closed in upon each other.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: While the Daityas were thus suffering, the leaders of the hosts of Daitya commanders—
Those of great speed exerted their force, like the oceans at the ends of the eons.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala;
and those four sons of Prahlāda who were of terrible prowess.
Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Kubha, Karabha, Namuci, Tāra, Tāraka, and Indratāpana. || 138.3 ||
Añjana, Rūṣaṇa, Vyaṃsa, Gaviṣṭha, Pṛthivījaya, Ilvaka, Pilvaka, and the Dānava Dhundhu and Mūka. || 138.4 ||
Kharas, Muru, as well as Naraka, Keśin, and Dhenuka; Lamba, Pralamba, Ajara, Bhāvaya, Vyoma, and Mārdava—[all these were slain]. (138.5)
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatāvarta, Gavākṣa, Gomukha, as well as Saram,
Nisunda, and Sunda— all of whom possessed great strength and prowess.
Pāka, Vipāka, Santāpa, Hastin, Duryodhana, Mohana, Mathana, Sacakra, and Cakra. (138.7)
Kālakāvadana, Kāla, Kālanemi, Kalidruma, Hayaśīrṣa, Indraśiras, Triśiras, and Śaṅku as well. (138.8)
Likewise Gaganamūrdhan, Aviroma, Mahāmanas,
Asiloman, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, and the Dānava Vṛtra.
Daśagrīva, Bāli, Meghanīla, Prabhākara,
and he who, arrogant in his strength, seized the wheel from the chariot of the Sun.
That Vipracitti, together with his army, clad in armor and abiding in truth,
along with these and other sons of Diti, was like elephants in their fury.
They made an effort to advance, having crushed the Pramathas in battle,
like lions for the sake of prey or like elephants for the sake of a female.
In the same way, the Dānavas entered, desiring to slay the Pramathas.
As those enemies of the gods rushed forward, their onset was terrible,
like the fearsome current of the lord of rivers filled with crocodiles and sharks.
With weapons, stones, rocks, trees, and thunderbolts in their hands,
they were indeed obstructed by the exultant Pramathas, like the currents of rivers by the oceans.
Nandin, the lord of the hosts of Gaṇas; Mahākāya, who is full of vigor;
Ghaṇṭākarṇa; Śaṅkukarṇa; Kuṇḍodara; and Mahodara. || 138.15 ||
Nandiṣeṇa, Somanandin, Karika the lord of the Gaṇas,
Vighna, Vināyaka, and he who is the Sarvavināyaka.
Piṅgala, Lohita, Mayūra, and Kukkuṭa as well;
Pañcākṣa, Vīrabhadra, Viṭpati, and Pāvakārdana. || 138.17 ||
The nourishment of the Ādityas, the nourishment of Soma, another which is the nourishment of the ocean, and likewise the nourishment of the purifier (fire). || 138.18 ||
Varabarhidhvaja, Viśākha, Śākha,
and the powerful Naigameṣa— all possessed of the vigor and prowess of Rudra.
And those Pramathas of terrifying form, born of Bāhuleya,
rushed at the Dānavas in battle like bulls against bulls.
And between them there arose a tumultuous battle,
as fierce as that of scent-elephants against śarabhas in a place devoid of people.
Like elephants with great elephants, like mountains with mountains,
like oceans with oceans, and like fires with fires.
Likewise, the gods, their pride aroused and enveloped by the fire of wrath,
were restrained by heroic attendants, just as obstacles are held back by those devoted to dharma.
Mountain peaks, torn apart on all sides by pickaxes,
fall by the thousands upon the earth, resembling circles of vultures.
Discuses were shattered by discuses, spears were split asunder by spears;
arrows, pierced by arrows, fell like serpents.
With faces resembling the moon and lotus, and with arms like iron clubs,
the earth shines as if covered with garments of tiger skins.
The terrible battlefield became like a forest of cremation grounds, marked by the mud of fat, marrow, and bones, and strewn with the filth of hair.
Horses, elephants, and even chariots were seen crushed here and there upon the surface of the earth by the lords of the Dānava hosts.
"O enemy of the king of the gods, you must now be examined in the assembly of the non-gods."
Then, as Nandin was speaking thus, Kujambha— whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra, Indra, and Vāyu, and who resembled Indra himself—
knitted his brows into a three-fold frown upon his forehead and spoke to Nandin.
"O monkey-faced one, do you wish to frighten me with your words?
I am the grandson of Hiraṇyakaśipu; I am no ordinary demon. (138.31)

Standing on the battlefield, I feel no fear from Varuṇa who wields the noose and inflicts punishment upon himself, nor from Indra with his thunderbolt, nor from the Lord of Wealth with his mace; I have no fear of the Daityas, nor do I flee from them.
Today here, let this unworthy face of yours— with its tawny, rolling eyes—
fall to the earth, mangled and hideous by my arrows, like a fully ripened palm fruit falling from a palm tree.
Having spoken thus, the cloud that was the king of the Dānavas covered Nandīśvara with a rain of a multitude of arrows,
just as a lion, letting out a great roar, covers a lordly mountain with a cloud.
Just as birds enter a tree laden with ripe fruit, or fierce serpents a high anthill,
so did the arrows released by the king of the Dānavas— with their blazing tips— enter Nandīśvara.
But the wielder of the thunderbolt, having warded off those floods of arrows with his own thunderbolt— just as a mountain resists torrents of rain—
hurled his vajra at Kujambha and roared loudly like a cloud in the sky.
With a terrifying form arising from its sparks, emitting a roar as it struck and released a cry,
the thunderbolt rushed toward the asura to slay him, just as the thunderbolt of the king of the gods [Indra] strikes a mountain.

In that same way, Kujambha struck Vajra with many sharp teeth, well-sharpened, positioned nearby, and smeared with poison; he shattered him into a hundred pieces, just as a cloud at the proper time extinguishes the fire of universal destruction.
Struck by the force of his arrow, that thunderbolt— released with extreme velocity from Śailādi, possessing unfailing speed,
and once hurled back after being struck by Kujambha— was given as if in a state of deranged frenzy.
Beholding the excellent thunderbolt held fast and hearing the roar released by Kujambha,
Nandi, filled with rage, rushed toward that enemy like Rahu toward Tamon-dhra in the sky.

Seizing the chariot by force with his hand at the tip of the pole, that protector of the Pramathas dragged it back and hurled it along with its driver and horses; having thrown it, he roared again most terribly.
With its wheels bewildered, its horses unharnessed, its charioteer, sword, head, and rim fallen away,
Kujambha’s vehicle tumbled from the sky like a mountain whose wings have been severed by the thunderbolt.

Therefore, having descended from the chariot driven by the elephant Nandi, Prahrādi, whose spirit was undaunted, took up a spear; with his courage unyielding, he stood firm like a rain-cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder.

Jambha released that crest toward Nandin—a crest flickering like the tongue of a serpent, eager to devour like a death-goddess afflicted by hunger, and blazing like the flame of a great fire. (138.44)
That spear, released from the arm of Indra’s enemy, fierce and blazing like a Kṛtyā of Aṅgiras,
was struck down and consumed by the fire from Nandin’s mouth, just as a female moth is consumed by a flame.
Having burnt that spear with the fire of his mouth, the lord of monkeys, who possessed the splendor of the sun,
swiftly struck him with his own thunderbolt, just as the blessed Lord Indra struck Mount Meru with his thunderbolt.
With his bones crushed by the blow of the thunderbolt, his teeth shattered, his eyes destroyed, and his knees broken,
Kujambha fell to the ground hunched over, like a mountain struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt.
When he was slain, all the hosts of gods and the Daityas, who were the enemies of the gods, raised a great cry;
and the Lord of Beings honored the god who is the Lord of Creatures and bears the mark of the moon.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Jambha in the Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Having seen Kujambha slain by Nandin, the delighter of the gods, [the demon]...
The gods, the cāraṇas, and the great serpents raised a roar.
At that sound of the gods and at the destruction of Kujambha,
Jambha, that tiger among the Dānavas, summoned a great rage.
From the limbs of him who was enraged, sparks of fire flew forth on all sides,
like those from Mount Meru when struck by the thunderbolt.
Jambha, who resembled a cloud flashing with lightning and was overwhelmed by rage,
rushed toward Nandin to kill him, like a lion-king attacking an elephant.
Carrying a massive, terrible iron club weighing five hundred bhāras,
that Daitya rushed toward Nandin.
"Stay now, you of evil conduct! Having been seen by me, where will you go?
This iron club, resembling a thunderbolt, shall crush you to pieces. (139.6)
Having spoken thus with a terrible voice in the presence of Nandin,
Jambha hurled his iron club at him like a second Yama.
Released from his hand, that iron club— resembling a serpent freed from its slough and like the fire of cosmic destruction— advanced to slay Nandin.
Nandin struck that great [mace], which resembled the serpent Vāsuki and was like the staff of Brahmā,
with his thunderbolt as if it were the strength of the king of the gods.
Regarding the blow of the thunderbolt as if it were a blade of grass, he seized his iron club;
rushing toward Nandin, he was as difficult to behold as Indra or Agni.
A great roar was raised by the Pramathas by the thousands;
hearing the roar of the gods and seeing the iron club approaching, [they were struck with fear].
Śaṅkukarṇa, impelled by speed, rushed toward the iron club;
it was as formidable as Karkoṭaka and difficult to ward off, like a great weapon.
Seeing that Śaṅkukarṇa had seized an iron club by force, [he struck him]. || 139.13 ||
The gods rejoiced and shouted, and they praised Śaṅkukarṇa;
the powerful Śaṅkukarṇa, for his part, again seized an iron club.
He roared, aiming at Jambha, and that lover of battle rushed forward;
then that tiger among Dānavas, eager for combat, charged after him.
Then, from the army of Gaṇeśvara as well as from the army of the Dānavas,
there arose the sound of musical instruments mingled with lion-like roars.
Then, in the vault of the sky, there arose a sound resembling the roar of the agitated waters of the ocean,
as the denizens of heaven heard that battle between the lord of the hosts of Danu’s sons and Isha.

The foremost hosts of Pramathas, along with the Nāgas and Rudras, and the best of the Asuras together with Andhaka, having ceased their strife, then stood watching the battle between the Lord of the Gaṇas and the Dānava. || 139.18 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 139.139 ||
The one hundred and fortieth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
The exceedingly powerful [hero] rushed toward Jambha, who was running with his ears pricked like spikes.
Vṛtra rushed toward him to slay him, like a lion toward an elephant. || 140.1 ||
Having abandoned Jambha, Śaṅkukarṇa, the preeminent leader of the Gaṇas,
rushed toward Vṛtra himself, just as a destroyer pursues one who has committed an offense.
Then Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, struck him with an iron club,
just as Śakra strikes a great mountain with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Then Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas,
being struck excessively with an iron club, reeled about like a tree shaken by the wind.
Streaked with streams of blood from that well-dealt blow,
he shone like the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala) disgorging molten gold ore.
While Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas, reeled after being struck violently by the iron club,
the gods and Gandharvas shouted in joy, honoring the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Then, having recovered after a long time, Vṛtra, the bull among the Dānavas,
uprooted a mountain peak and rushed toward Śaṅkukarṇa.
He hurled that mountain peak, along with its trees and bears, its minerals, stones, and serpents, at Gaṇeśvara; and it both crashed down and roared.
Nandi shattered that great mountain peak, which had been released by Vṛtrabhuja,
with his thunderbolt, as a lion strikes down a mighty elephant.
Then those two leaders of the Gaṇas and Daityas, both skilled in hand-to-hand combat, joined together with arms like enraged serpents, making a terrible sound.
They were like two suns roaring, like two blazing fires,
like two thundering clouds, and like two elephants trumpeting.
Like two intoxicated tigers, like two hissing serpents,
like two roaring lions, and like two leaping bulls.
Like two great mountains in motion, like two oceans surging, like two clouds filling the sky, and like two rivaling sea-monsters; 140.13.
Thus Śaṅkukarṇa and Vṛtra, the bull among asuras,
both skilled in combat, engaged in battle with a mutual desire to slay one another.
With fists like thunderbolts, with palms resembling lightning, with terrible kicks of the feet, and likewise by tossing [them] upward; || 140.15 ||
By means of reproaches, as well as distractions, draggings, and thrustings away;
by fierce demonstrations of prowess, and even by the hearing of his names.
By goring with the tips of their claws, by seizing the throats and restraining them,
with lion-roars accompanied by musical instruments, and with trees, mountains, rocks, and stones— || 140.17 ||
Śaṅkukarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas, and Vṛtra, the son of Danu,
then struck each other, each seeking the other's weak point.
But Vṛtra, like a tree with deep roots, was suddenly uprooted by Śaṅkukarṇa,
who seized him by the hands and cast him down upon the earth.
Then, when Vṛtra had been struck down, a loud cry of "Excellent! arose from the army of Gaṇeśvara as well as from the host of Dānavas.
Then, having struck Vṛtra with his fist and cast him down upon the earth,
Śaṅkukarṇa departed swiftly like a bird fleeing for its life.
But Vṛtra, though possessed of great heroism, became overwhelmed by the blow of the fist;
he rose up like the banner of Indra and fled from the Lord of the Gaṇas.
As he was charging, Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, struck him with a śāla tree and cried out, "Come here! || 140.23 ||
Vṛtra, having been struck by Śaṅkukarṇa in his anger with a śāla tree,
approached and forcibly seized Śaṅkukarṇa by the foot with his strength.
Seizing Śaṅkukarṇa like a serpent seizing a bird, Vṛtra whirled him around helplessly, as delusion assails the world when it has arisen.
As Śaṅkukarṇa was being whirled about in every direction by Vṛtra,
his ornaments fell away from his body by the thousands.
Seeing him being thus tormented by Vṛtra, all the gods and Gaṇeśa then cried out "Alas!
Alas! and, grasping their weapons and arrows, they fled for the sake of his liberation.
Beholding all those lords of the hosts approaching with sharp weapons in their hands, Vṛtra released Śaṅkukarṇa in that assembly, just as Garuḍa, the king of birds, releases a serpent.
But the mighty leader of the hosts, Śaṅkukarṇa, having been released from Vṛtra,
turned back toward Vṛtra again, desiring to fight like a lordly elephant.
Then again, from all sides in that army, there arose the roars of lions and the sounds of kettledrums; and a heart-stealing cry of "Bravo, Śaṅkukarṇa! broke out in the battle for him.
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having whirled Śaṅkukarṇa around and having cast Vṛtra down upon the surface of the earth, [he...]
He crushed the army of the Pramathas, just as an elephant in rut crushes a forest.
Having struck Nandin, Nandiṣeṇa, and Somanandin,
and having put them to flight, he roared like a rain-cloud.
Then, as he was roaring, Rudra, the best of the Viṭpatis,
released an arrow that was like the fire of the thunderbolt and brought about the destruction of his enemies.
Released from Viṣṇu’s hand, that arrow, radiant as the rays of the sun,
pierced Vṛtra and entered him like a perfected being entering the sky.
Then, raising his hand like an elephant with its trunk, that Dānava rushed at the Lord of the Gods in battle,
as the wind charges toward a cloud.
The large-bodied Nandin struck that Dānava with a trident,
Somanandin with a thunderbolt, and Nandiṣeṇa with an axe and a palm-strike.
And in the battle, the Lord of the Viśvedevas, being exceedingly enraged, pierced Vṛtra with a thousand arrows,
and again with another twenty-one.
Afflicted by the leaders of the herds, that Dānava, who resembled a mountain,
cried out loudly as he was being cast down, like a tree inhabited by deities.
Then Māyābala, Mūkatāra, Jambha, Namuci, Gaṇa, Elvala, Bāṇa,
and Bāṇaputra stood with various excellent arrows and weapons, seeking to ward off the most heroic of the hosts' leaders.

Adorned with beautiful golden necklaces of radiant luster and shimmering waist-bands, resembling the great Indra himself, these sons of Diti, possessing forms of extreme joy yet appearing as Death itself, roam among the hosts of the Pramathas. (141.10)
Their mouths were torn open by clubs, halas, and arrows; their limbs were crushed like mountain peaks by thunderbolts and vajras.
Sprinkled by the drops and droplets from their wounds, with their white necklaces, ornaments, and garlands fallen away,
those hosts of Pramathas, their faces trembling with fear and severely tormented by their enemies, fled in all directions.
Like white, stainless clouds raised high in the sky,
the sons of Diti released a shower of arrows— terrible in their great velocity and capable of causing affliction— just as fresh clouds pour down rains of new water.

Then the chief Daityas, resembling clouds over Mount Kailāsa and possessing splendor equal to the blazing sun, struck the hosts of Pramathas with nets of stainless, sharp arrows they had discharged. 141.14.

Then, having entered the battle, the hosts of the enemies of the gods, striking fear into their foes, advanced and spread across the field with iron clubs, arrows, swords, and spears discharged from hundreds of mechanical engines held in their hands.
Excellent elephants resembling mountain peaks and many preeminent horses with swift gaits,
as well as formidable chariots like the abodes of the gods, fall at the front of the battle, broken and burnt.
Hewn down firmly by arrows as if by axes, their wounds smeared with fine ointments,
and their eyes, courage, and lives having departed, hundreds of the sons of Danu were struck down.
With the fallen white boar-bristle necklaces, earrings, crowns, diadems, gems, garlands, and garments,
the earth at the front of the battle shines like Urvaśī adorned with exquisite and beautiful ornaments.
Like the great ocean agitated at the time of the deluge, or like the vast sky [filled with clouds],
so did the host of the Asura army become, with its swift elephants, horses, and Dānavas.

Yama, Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth, and Vāsava; Bhaga, Vasu, Sūrya, Śaśāṅka, and Māruta—all these, their lotus-like eyes and faces blooming with joy, stood guard over him who was exalted as the crusher of the hosts of his enemies.
With the lordly elephants acting as clouds and the galloping horses as the blowing winds,
the storm at the edge of the battlefield— turbulent with hundreds of thunderbolts, arrows, and lightning flashes— did not cease.
With the faces of the excellent sons of Danu, whose eyes resembled lotus petals and who were like the sun and moon to the day-lotus,
the earth shone as if covered with lotuses.

The battle was exceedingly fierce and terrible, where the lords of the hosts of Dānavas were crushed; it was stained by the sprinkling of blood and fat, and watched over by the forces of Garuḍa and the Piśācas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 141.141 ||
The one hundred and forty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that battle between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras was proceeding,
The sound of bows is heard, resembling the roar of clouds in the rainy season.
There were the roars of trumpeting lordly elephants and the neighing of horses,
as well as the cries of the immortals and the Rākṣasas, who were devoted to the music of battle.
Terrible sounds, causing distress to the ears like the roar of thunderbolts, are indeed heard; for the interests of those who act unrighteously truly increase.
Then the Dānava named Kārtasvana, whose voice was like the roar of a cloud, struck down the Pramathas in battle, like Time itself arrived to slay mortals.
Equipped with a chariot, a bow, arrows, armor, and earrings,
he consumed the army of the Pramathas like fire consumes dry grass.
Great arrows released from golden bows,
having pierced the *pramatha* demons, tore through the battlefield without obstruction.
Like locusts [devouring] fields, like rivers [overwhelming] men, like birds [flying through] trees, or like Garuḍa [seizing] ripe serpents—so did he [treat them]. || 142.7 ||
Thus those broad arrows, released from his golden bow,
threw the Pramathas into utter confusion, just as birds agitate the trees of Indra.
Multitudes of arrow-showers fall upon the ranks of the army like [torrents] upon a mountain.
With the sound of musical instruments silenced and greatly agitated by the blows of arrows,
the army of the lords of the hosts appeared like a forest of bandhujīva flowers.
Just as the wind disperses thick clouds, as Vainateya [Garuda] devours serpents, as a tiger destroys spotted deer, and as the sun destroys masses of darkness. || 142.11 ||
Likewise, the enraged Kārtasvana, with his most terrible thunderbolt-like arrows,
scorched the leaders of the hosts like the world-destroying fire at the end of an aeon.

Seeing the army of the lord of the Gaṇas burnt, devoured, and afflicted by disease, the divine Lord of the Earth, filled with wrath, then spoke to Kārtasvana: 142.13. Seeing the army of the lord of the Gaṇas burnt, devoured, and afflicted by disease, the divine Lord of the Earth, filled with wrath, then spoke to Kārtasvana.
Then, as the arrow reached its mark, Rudra, whose prowess is fierce,
being provoked to anger, drew an arrow from his quiver and aimed it at the lord of the Dānavas.
Your strength, heroism, and majesty are supreme, O son of Kārta-vīrya;
why then do you slay these weak ones, the lords of the hosts of Dānavas, O lord of the Dānavas?
"Come, if you have the power or if you possess strength, engage in combat with me! Do not merely roar; behold my might! (142.16)
"O Daitya, today I shall strike down your head— adorned with earrings and embellished by the sprouts of your fangs— just as the wind blows a fruit from a palmyra tree."
"Even though the Dānavas protect you in this pitch-dark battle today,
nevertheless, O disgrace of the Asuras, I shall take away your life."
While the lord of the Viṭpas was thus roaring,
the shouting Dānava discharged an arrow and, having released it, roared like a rain-cloud.
Blazing like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter, that arrow,
radiant as the sun at the height of summer, sped toward the Lord of the Rakshasas.
There the sun became lusterless before the radiance of that bird;
by the sound of its golden wings, the birds fell to the earth.
That Bāṇa, though endowed with splendor like the fire of universal destruction,
was submerged in the king's bracelet like a wicked man in hell.
Then, having extracted that very arrow sent by the Dānava,
the Lord of the Viśvedevas hurled it at Kārtasvana and let out a roar.
Released from Viṣṇu’s hand, that arrow which destroys the Dānavas took the head of the Dānava charioteer along ten paths through the air.
As he drove, his horses— fickle and dappled— became bewildered in battle and,
seizing the chariot, bolted away like hawks toward a piece of meat.
"Go toward the chariot adorned with gold! Why do you sit idle?
Seize them!"—such was the great roar that arose from the lords of the Dānavas.
Wandering upon the vast plateau of Mandara,
that best of chariots shines like the excellent chariot of the seven-horsed Sun as it circles Mount Meru.
Then, leaping down from that excellent chariot drawn by swift horses,
Kārtasvana, bow in hand, rushed toward the lord of the Viśas.
Then, as he was eager to fight again with the Lord of the Demons on his golden chariot, a roar of "Excellent! Fight! arose from the two armies.
That Dānava covered the lord of the Viṭpas with many sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts,
just as a cloud covers a mountain with torrents of rain.
Though being filled by the floods of gold-tufted arrows like the ocean by masses of clouds,
that lord of the people did not experience any distress at all.
Then, drawing his bow with force as far as his ear,
that powerful one cut each of the Daitya lord’s arrows into two or even three pieces.
Having struck down those arrows with feathered shafts that consume the life-force of his foe,
he pierced Kārtavīrya’s golden armor with a thousand more and let out a roar.
With those arrows whose points were visible from behind,
the Dānava shone like a mountain with excellent serpents half-emerged from its crevices.
Then the powerful and enraged Rudra cut asunder his bow, sword, and quiver— five in all— and he struck him down.

Then the Lord of the Viśvedevas, possessed of noble strength, released the arrow— which was like Indra’s thunderbolt, enraged and hissing like the lord of serpents— straight-flying and destined to afflict the son of Diti.
That king of arrows, dispatched by the boon of Rudra, spreading a cloud of smoke upon the field of battle,
forcibly struck off the head of the Asura in combat, just as a sage of noble intellect plucks a lotus.

Then, as he was gazing upon that enemy's face which had been struck down in battle by the subduer of the submarine fire, a roar was raised by the gods, the best of sages, and the Pramathas with terrifying sounds.

But that lord of the *viṭ* (the Gaṇas), the commander of the Pramatha army— skilled in the arts of war, the subduer of the lions that are the enemies of the gods, and himself a subduer— having been approached and honored for a long time by the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*), [remained there]. Thus ends the section on the battle of the Gaṇas in the *Skandapurāṇa*.
The one hundred and forty-second chapter. || 142.141 ||
The one hundred and forty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Having slain the enemy Kārtasvana with a golden arrow, [he...]
The Lord of the People consumed the Daityas like fire consumes moths.
That god, with his bow drawn taut and wearing beautiful golden earrings,
roared while discharging arrows at the Dānavas, like the sun emitting its rays.
Those arrows, with shafts made of gold and feathers from the wings of Garuḍa,
fell upon the Dānavas like calamities sent by the gods.
With their faces severed, their hands severed, and their feet, bellies, and thighs mangled,
hundreds of Dānavas fell upon the earth like mountains.
Some were struck on their backs, some were torn on their sides;
others were pierced in their eyes, while still others wandered about like the blind.
As a tiger [devours] deer, as Garuḍa [devours] serpents, as an ungrateful person [destroys] good deeds, and as the sun [dispels] the darkness; || 143.6 ||
Then the god Viṭpati, the consumer of oblations, destroyed those asuras with sharp-pointed arrows that had the faces of fire and thunderbolts.
Deprived of their chariots, with their elephants struck down, and their horses distressed by arrows,
the Dānavas fled in terror, driven by the shafts of the Lord of the Viṭpas.
Then, having seen the army of the asuras— with their weapons cast aside and their splendor vanished—
broken in battle by the Lord of the People like a forest by an elephant.
Whosoever among the sons of the gods were there of exceeding strength and renowned,
they were pursued by the Lord of Wealth like other beasts by a lion.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini,
Bāṣkala, Jambha, Virocana, Bāṇa, and that Dānava Bali.
Ajaka, Namuci, Vyansa, Ilvaka, Vilvaka, Vipracitti, Tuhunda, Hunda, and the Danava Vakra; || 143.12 ||
Maya, Tāra, Tārākṣa, Vidyunmālī, Prabhañjana, Ariṣṭa, Riṣṭa, Añjana, Ruśabha, and Kubha. (143.13)
Kāla, Kālanemi, and likewise Kālākavada; Sampāti, Ilvala, Bala, and Naraka as well.
The sons of Madhu and Kaiṭabha were the Dānavas Dhundhu and Mūka, as well as Hasti, Vipāka, Pāka, Vikarṇa, and Śambhu.
With many uplifted weapons, radiant like falling meteors,
they rushed at the lord of the clan, roaring in their fury like lions.
With spears, stones, and mallets, and with arrows sounding like thunderbolts,
they struck him with terrible roars, like clouds striking a mountain.
Just as clouds driven by fire release a rain of water,
even so did those Dānavas discharge a shower of arrows upon the god.
The Lord of the Foes, the crusher of the hosts of enemies, swiftly cut down that shower of weapons from the foe, just as a quarrel is brought to an end by mutual affection.
Then those sons of Danu and Daityas, stationed in the sky toward the Lord of the Viśvedevas,
let forth a rain of mountains like roaring clouds.
And others, standing upon the peaks of Mount Mandara like garlands of Mandāra flowers,
released Sāla, Sarala, and Devadāru trees toward the Lord of the People.
He, the lord of the people, being severely afflicted by the Dānavas stationed both in the sky and on the earth,
turned away from them like a fire drenched with water.
Seeing their lord turned away and covered by the Dānavas with mountains,
those renowned lords of the Gaṇas, possessed of terrible strength, could not endure it.
Somanandin, Nandin, and Nandiṣeṇa were his attendants,
as were Prabhāmaya, Vīrabhadra, and Sūryāpyāyana.
Pañcākṣa, Kopapāla, Trinetra, Piṅgalekṣaṇa, Rākṣasa, Piṅgala, Śmaśānanilaya, and Annada. (143.25)
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, and the powerful Kuṇḍodara; Airāvatamukha, Annapāla, and Kapāladhṛk.
These and other leaders of the hosts, hundreds in number as proclaimed by the Gaṇas, entered to consume the Dānavas, like fires entering dry trees. || 143.27 ||
Surrounding Viṭpati on all sides, like young elephant-lords trumpeting,
those lords of the Gaṇas, with tridents, discuses, arrows, and *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons in their hands, advanced with intent for battle.
Then, between those various warriors who were exultant in battle, there ensued a close-quarters combat,
like that of great elephants intoxicated with rut and accustomed to living together in the forests.
Beholding that great battle between the Dānavas and the lords of their hosts,
those inhabitants of heaven moved through the sky in divine celestial chariots, shouting cries of "hiṃsana" and delivering blows with their swords.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter in the Gaṇayuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those Pramatha-asuras were filled with excessive fury and were arrogant.
Having committed offenses against one another, they fought in a closely joined battle.
Kālanemi, who was like Death itself, fought Viśākha with his hand brandished by Śakti, as Kumāra conquered the earth.
And he who, arrogant in his strength, had seized the wheel from the chariot of the Sun—that Vipracitti, eager for battle, became entangled with Śākha. || 144.3 ||
Naigameṣa, the son of Agni, caused Hayagrīva, Sugrīva, and the lord of the Dānavas to fight,
just as Madhunihā fought Madhu.
Jambha fought with Nandin, and Tuhuṇḍa with Somanandin;
Huṇḍa, the burner of the world, waged war against the heroic Vināyaka.
Mahākāya, along with Kāla and Ghananāmuci, as well as Piṅgala and the two Gaṇeśas, Ilvaka and Pilvaka— these were there.
Hrāda was encountered by Śaṅkukarṇa, Viṭpati by Anuhrāda, and Rudra Ādityāpyāyana by Saṃhrāda.
And Kuṇḍodara, the lord of the Yakṣas, and his attendant Ghaṇṭākarṇa,
were engaged with Balei and Ulūka, like two elephants contending with two lions.
The Dānava who was the progenitor of Bali was joined by Pañcākṣa along with Rudra, who possesses the splendor of the sun,
and by Vīrabhadra.
Sumukha rushed against Tāra along with Maya, while Mayūra attacked Vajraroman, and Kukkuṭa went against Mura. (144.10)
For the remaining leaders of the hosts, having come together with the remaining Daityas,
were locked in combat with one another like elephants against lions in battle.
Like bamboos being consumed by fire in a deserted place,
there arose a "taṭataṭa" sound from weapons being struck down.
"Run not! Stay! "Look! Look!"—shouting thus, the hosts of Dānavas, locked in combat with one another, struck each other down.
With their limbs smeared with fat and marrow, their faces, hands, and thighs severed,
the Dānavas and Pramathas fled, mangled by weapons.
With faces, thighs, and feet; with hands, teeth, and eyes;
and with scattered necklaces, armlets, garlands, garments, and ornaments—144.15.
With the elephant-kings' blankets, rugs, and weapons,
that battlefield shone like the sky with stars and planets.
With the variegated drops of blood produced by the tips of nails and teeth,
the ground, its limbs smeared with red sandalwood, shone like a woman.
Having discharged that arrow of solar brilliance at Vināyaka, Tuhuṇḍu laughed aloud,
further increasing his wrath.
As he was laughing, that Vināyaka severed his face, adorned with large earrings, with a sharp-edged sword.
Seeing Tuhuṇḍa slain, Huṇḍa, tormented by the slaughter of his brother,
hurled a spear at the mouth of the Nāga, just as Śakra hurls the thunderbolt at a mountain.
That power of Vināyaka, concentrated in the jewel, fell upon Maṇi and,
resembling a blazing crest of fire, drank his blood out of wrath.
That spear, having struck Vināyaka’s chest,
shone forth like a streak of gold upon a sapphire gem.
Drawing forth the Huṇḍa-weapon from his lotus-like hand— a weapon resembling a ray of the sun—
the Lord suddenly struck Huṇḍa with it, just as the younger brother [of Indra] struck Mount Krauñca.
Seeing that Tuhuṇḍa and Huṇḍa had been caused to be slain by Vināyaka,
the subduer of enemies, the entire army of the leaders of the Gaṇas became like the overflowing Gaṅgā.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Huṇḍa and Tuhuṇḍa had been slain by Vināyaka,
That battle between the lords of the Gaṇas and the Asuras appeared tumultuous.
Roaring like clouds swollen with water at the onset of the rainy season,
they rushed forward with great speed, fighting one another in combat.
With their limbs smeared with streams of blood and their lips bitten,
they struck one another with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and battle-axes.
Of spears being hurled, of swords being brought down,
of names being proclaimed, and even of bows twanging.
Having heard sounds that caused distress to his ears, Jambha, the best among the strong and indignant at the slaughter of his brother, entered the army of Prāmatha.
Having pierced the lord of the Gaṇas, Vyāghrapūrva, with his trident,
Jambha roared like a forest-dwelling lion after slaying a buffalo in the woods.
Then, as he was roaring, Maga, the foremost of them,
struck his head with a spear and fled from the remaining Daityas.
Then those renowned leaders of the hosts, famous for their prowess, glory, and learning,
advanced against the asuras in battle like śarabhas against elephants.
Then there occurred a great assembly of the lords of the asura hosts,
like a clashing of thunderbolts together with mountains of gold.
Virocana and Andhaka, both indignant and highly enraged,
rained down showers of arrows like two clouds pouring forth torrents of water.
By Svayamprabha, those two Daityas, who were discharging showers of arrows,
were afflicted by excellent shafts and turned away from the front of the battle.
Svayamprabha, with numerous arrows discharged from his bow-mechanism, dried up the ocean-like army of the Dānavas,
just as the sun with its blazing orb dries up the ocean at the end of the world.
Then Andhaka, the charioteer of the world of the Dānavas, with eyes rolling in anger, said to his own charioteer:
"O charioteer, drive toward Śukra; he is our preceptor who always removes our suffering. (145.13)

Saying "So be it," he brought that chariot, which was yoked with excellent horses and resounded like a cloud, to where Śukra, the best of planets and a twice-born one, stood amidst the hosts of Dānavas. || 145.14 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 145.141 ||
The one hundred and forty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Andhaka, the best of the Asuras, having withdrawn from that battle, [departed].
Approaching Śukra, he spoke these words with his face bowed low. || 146.1 ||
"O Blessed One, relying upon you, we always consider even the gods along with their followers to be equal to blades of grass; I speak this as the truth."
Like elephants before lions or serpents before Garuḍas, the gods are always afraid of us through your grace. (146.3)
Protected by you, the Daityas fearlessly entered that impenetrable array of the hosts of gods, like those tormented by heat entering a lake.
Having taken refuge in you, we shall stand as motionless as stones and slay the Indra among the best of Brahmins in battle without hesitation.
And because of our state of misfortune, we— along with our wives and sons— serve your feet, which grant us happiness, day and night.
Constantly protect us who have come to you for refuge, just as Nārāyaṇa protects the gods in times of fear. 146.7
Behold Huṇḍa and Tuhuṇḍa, Kujambha and Jambha,
as well as Pāka, Kārtasvana, and the great Asura Vipāka.
And that hero Indradamana, who strikes down even the heroic gods,
was assailed by the Pramathas of terrifying prowess, who had overcome the pain of death and other such afflictions.
These fallen ones have been slaughtered like sandalwood trees by lions;
for her who, having formerly inhaled the smoke of grain-chaff for a thousand autumns,
obtained from Hara the boon of knowledge— the time for that has now arrived.
Now let all the Pramathas and all the worlds behold with wide-open eyes that fruit of your knowledge as you bring those Dānavas back to life.
Seeing the Dānavas restored to life by you in battle,
all the Dānavas, casting aside the fear of death, will fight with the Pramathas.
—Indeed, that knowledge was [obtained] by you, who were seeking the welfare of the Dānavas. (146.13)
"Having propitiated the God, she has attained this; show her to me, salutations to you!
Having heard these words of Andhaka, the sage Bhārgava, firm in his resolve, [replied].
Then, with a slight smile, he said to the lord of the Dānavas:
"O lord of the Dānavas, that which was spoken by you is indeed true."
"Indeed, this acquisition of knowledge for the Dānavas was accomplished by me after drinking for a thousand years the most unbearable smoke of grain-husks."
This lore, which brings happiness to my kinsmen, has been obtained by me;
by means of this lore, I shall [revive] these Daityas who have been slain by their enemies.
I shall raise up the crops that have withered, like a cloud;
I shall restore them to be free from wounds, free from disease, and healthy, as if they had risen again after sleeping.
In this very moment, O Lord of Dānavas, you shall behold the Dānavas;
having seen the Dānavas risen up, you shall see them slain in battle by the lords of the Gaṇas.
And out of both wonder and fear, the lords of the Gaṇas will flee.
Having spoken thus to the lord of the Dānavas at that time, that descendant of Bhṛgu—
Addressing each Daitya individually, the wise Brahmin recited the Vidyā; indeed, by means of that Vidyā being thus repeated there by the Brāhmaṇa, [the Daityas were overcome].
The Dānavas, who had been asleep, rose up like those awakened from sleep upon their beds;
they arose like the meanings of the Vedas when practiced, or like clouds at the appointed time.
Just as comets meet their destruction at the appointed time,
so were those Daityas utterly destroyed by Śukra along with the Pramathas.
When they were raised up, those lords of the Gaṇas shone like ancient beings restored to health,
seeing those Dānavas brought back to life by Śukra.
"This is a marvel, O lords of gods! they said to one another.
Seeing those great asuras, Tuhuṇḍa and the others, restored to life, those ancient gods roared like clouds filled with water.
Seeing those thousands who had risen up, others with axes, thunderbolts, lightning, and spears in their hands rushed toward the army of Śaṅkara’s servants, which resembled a surging great ocean.
Once again, a gathering of the hosts of gods and asuras took place there with a most terrifying roar,
like the surging of oceans driven by the winds at the end of a Yuga.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Revival of the Daityas in the Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Daityas had been raised up by Bhārgava of fierce deeds, [the battle resumed].
The gods, along with the gandharvas and the dānavas together with Andhaka, raised a clamor.
Then there arose the sounds of mṛdaṅgas and kettledrums mingled with the blast of conchs, along with lion-roars together with the clamor of chariots and elephants.
Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Jambha, Kujambha, and the great asura fought against the enemies of the gods with mountain peaks, spears, and blows from rocks.
Pāka, Indradamana, and that Bali, son of Kārtasvana,
crushed the army of the Pramathas, desiring to take revenge for their enmity.
Having checked their momentum, even the proud Pramathas,
all bearing rocks and trees in their hands, rushed toward the Dānavas.
In that most terrifying battle, the lords of the hosts of gods were heard making the sounds of their bows and the fearsome clatter of their chariots.
Others, intent on conquering the Pramathas as well as the Dānavas,
raised a terrible clamor and shouted partisan cries in the sky.
A roar arose from the troops as they shouted and ran,
like the sound of oceans surging at the end of an eon.
And the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, intoxicated by the excellence of the battle,
cried out and scattered heaps of various flowers.
Various kinds of flowers falling down shone like the stars released by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas at the end of the night.
The musical instruments of the gods and gandharvas resounded many times;
for those whose minds were intent on battle, they ceased again and again.
But Jambha, remembering his defeat in battle by Vināyaka,
rushed furiously toward him like one elephant charging another.
Seeing the Dānava Jambha charging at him in battle,
Vināyaka, enraged like a lion against an elephant, blocked his path.
