Raising his trunk, which resembled the trunk of Airāvata, that Vināyaka, whose face was like that of an elephant, struck the Dānava in battle.
But Jambha, that elephant among the Dānavas, pierced him between the two temples with a preeminent arrow,
just as a perfected one pierces the orb of the sun.
That arrow indeed sank between the two frontal globes of that elephant,
like a lightning-charged cloud between the two peaks of the lord of mountains.
His mind incensed by that arrow, he shook his head and hand together; then, bending down the great Daitya with the tip of his hand and striking him, he roared aloud.
But Jambha, quivering as he was, being struck by Vināyaka’s hand,
became enraged and assailed Vināyaka with fierce arrows.
Like locusts entering a field or bees entering a tree,
those arrows of Jambha then entered the god Vināyaka.
With their faces torn by triple-barbed arrows and dripping with blood,
those shafts shone upon the leader like serpents taking refuge on Mount Meru.
With his limbs deeply pierced by Jambha’s arrows, his eyes drenched in blood flowing from his temples,
and shaking both his hand and his head, the god rushed toward Jambha like one parched with thirst for water.
Having struck him repeatedly with his firm hand, and having roared again and again,
that powerful one seized the chariot in battle and hurled it away along with its horses, standard, weapons, and wheels.
With its flags and banners shaken down and broken, and with thousands of swords, spears, double-edged blades, and arrows fallen away,
the chariot of the Asura’s delight fell like the intense desire of a man destitute of wealth.
But Prahrādi, possessing the splendor of Indra’s rain-cloud, having abandoned the chariot that was about to fall, stood in the sky wielding his spear;
he shone like one who stands in the sky wielding a spear.
The son of the asura king Vināyaka, his power fully aroused, hurled at him that spear, which was adorned with a bell, bright as gold, and blazing like a streak of fire.
Falling from the sky like a female serpent with a blazing face, that weapon-woman,
struck by the arrow of her husband, fell like a supreme spear dropped upon a man whose life-force has been destroyed.
While that sacrifice of battle, which was a source of wonder to the Pramathas and the Asuras, was thus proceeding,
the son of Śilāda, provoked to anger upon witnessing the deeds of Bhārgava, approached Maheśa.
Having said "Victory!", Nandin spoke to the fierce Jayayoni, who was as bright as gold:
"O Lord, that feat of battle performed by the lords of the Gaṇas is difficult even for the gods led by Indra to achieve."
"Today Bhārgava has rendered our efforts fruitless, for by him these lords of the Dānavas have been restored to life.
Indeed, here are those leaders of the Dānava hosts who have returned today from the abode of Yama."
Scattering the Pramathas, they roam like proud sharabhas among elephants in battle;
for if he so desires, he can always revive even those foremost Daityas who have been cast down.
"O Maheśa, how indeed can there be victory, and how can there be peace for the lords of the Gaṇas?
For this Śukra stands positioned on the side of the enemy; moreover, O bull-vehicled one, he is not to be slain as he is not fighting. (147.31)
There is no destruction at all through your grace, and you grant that very grace;
O Lord, let it be as you intend—that he be slain so that your victory may be constant in battle.
Act accordingly, O Buddha of supreme intellect, for there is none equal to you, O Great Lord, in wisdom. (147.32)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Nandīśvara, the lord of the Pramathas, the God of gods, the Lord,
then spoke with a smile to Nandin, the leader of all the hosts of attendants.

"Nandin, go with extreme haste; having torn him from the midst of the sons of Diti, that best of the twice-born, bring him here, just as a wealthy man who has been robbed brings back his sacrificial offering."
Thus addressed by the bull-bannered god, he whose banner is the bull and who utters the roar of the bull-lion,
quickly entered the army and proceeded to where the lamp of the Bhārgava lineage was located.
While he was being guarded by those sons of Diti, who held nooses, swords, trees, stones, and spears in their hands,
Nandin— like a sharabha seizing an elephant— agitated the Daityas and carried off Śukra.
Seeing him with his garments fallen, his ornaments cast off, and his hair disheveled as he was seized by the enemy,
the enemies of the gods rushed forward, uttering lion-like roars as if to set him free.
Like fierce clouds raining down, those lords of the Dānavas rained a shower of thunderbolt-spears, arrows, and axes, along with discuses, staffs, stones, and tremors, upon Nandīśvara. (147.38)

Having reached Bhārgava, Nandīśvara—the foremost of the hosts of Gaṇas—burned his hundreds of weapons with the fire from his mouth; then, seizing Śukra by the hand, he approached the leader of the Dānava hosts.
Then, from them all, there arose the most terrifying descent of released weapons and missiles;
a great battle of those crying out "Kill! and "Seize!", which brought delight to the minds of the gods.
In that interval, Nandīśvara, his eyes discolored with rage, approached Bhava and quickly reported to the Lord: "O Blessed One, here is that Śukra! || 147.41 ||
And that God of gods took up the semen, like an offering presented by one who is pure;
the protector of beings swallowed the semen situated in his mouth without saying anything at all. (147.42)
Then, once again, the lords of the Gaṇas struck down that army of Dānavas and Daityas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Seizure of Bhārgava," in the "Battle of the Gaṇas" section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, when Śukra had been swallowed by the Lord of Śukra, like food by a serpent—
All the Dānavas became like impoverished men, devoid of activity.
They were like bodiless living beings, like Garuḍas without their wings, like elephants with their trunks severed, and like bull-elephants without their tusks. || 148.2 ||
Like lordly serpents freed from poison, like twice-born brahmins devoid of ignorance,
like oceans drained of water, and like winds that have lost their force.
Like clouds that are silent, like fireless streets,
like days from which all joy has departed, and like trees stripped of their flowers.
Like deer terrified by a lion, like wingless birds, like planets whose luster has faded, or like crocodiles dragged from the water; || 148.5 ||
When Śukra had been carried off by Nandin and even swallowed by Kapardin,
the Dānavas were born as heroes whose pride and prowess were dejected.
Having reached a state of supreme despondency in the battle against the Dānavas, that Dānava Andhaka, standing in the fray with a voice like the roar of clouds, spoke.
"By Nandin, the best among those who know the right course, having displayed his prowess while leading Śukra away, the lives of all of us have today been taken; of this there is no doubt. (148.8)
Who else, other than Śukra Bhārgava, will restore to life the Daityas slain by the Pramathas? Who else will sustain us? (148.9)
Fortitude, valor, splendor, courage, heroism, strength, and steadfastness—
all these have been taken from us by our enemies now that the divine Śukra has been carried away.
"When the descendant of Bhṛgu has been carried away, my mind too is distressed;
yet, even if assailed by the Pramathas, I shall not abandon the battle."
"Steady yourselves! Do not fear; fight with the enemies!
I shall slay all the Pramathas along with Nandin."
Today, having rendered these gods helpless and having slain them as well,
I shall liberate the descendant of Bhṛgu, just as one releases Hari from his cage.
And even if that yogin, by means of yoga, were himself a master capable of emerging from his body, he would still be one who protects what remains for us. (148.14)
Having heard these words of Andhaka, the Dānavas, roaring like clouds and having resolved upon death, began to torment the Pramathas.
There, with showers of sharp vajras and jagged stone fragments,
they hacked at one another and wrought a great slaughter.
A most dreadful sound arose from the drawing of bows, the discharge of feathered arrows, and the falling of swords.
Their banners and flags were broken, their weapons exhausted;
they were variegated with streams of blood and blossomed with the flowers of wounds.
Thirsty, exhausted, and with their horses and elephants slain,
the armies on all sides became like the ocean-girt earth.
Then again, by that lordly elephant, who roared, possessed four tusks, resembled a mountain of collyrium, and had the luster of a black elephant; 148.20.
Equipped with a quiver and a banner, and goaded by his hook,
Jambha, that tiger among the Dānavas, rushed toward Nandin.
Mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant, the Daitya Jambha, bearing his spear,
shone like a cloud with a flight of cranes resting upon the peak of a black mountain.
With his tail, eyes, and ears motionless, and his great trunk extended,
the mighty elephant rushed forward when urged by the lord of the Dānavas.
Just as the speed of the ocean wind at the end of an eon is incomparable,
so too was the speed of that elephant as it ran incomparable.
The horses, the elephants, and the Pramatha demons fled from his path, just as men flee from death.
That powerful leader, exerting his prowess, restrained that intoxicated elephant as it rushed forward like a thundering cloud.
That best of gods, Dantī, struck that elephant, which resembled a mountain,
in the face with the tip of his extended trunk.
Struck by Vināyaka, that leader of all elephants was driven by a terrible pain and became senseless for a moment.
Then, having rested his horse and gathered himself, the elephant,
trumpeting loudly, struck Vināyaka on the region of his chest with his trunk.
Struck by that elephant, who was like the peak of the Vindhya mountains,
the Great Being, the Leader, did not move even a single step.
Seizing that elephant of the Dānavas by the trunk with his own trunk,
Vināyaka, who possessed the stature of a great mountain, hurled it down and cast it to the ground.
Like a lion struck down by another lion in the midst of the forest, he,
quivering like a serpent or a cloud driven by the wind, let out a roar.
As that elephant was falling, vomiting blood from its mouth,
he swiftly pierced it with a lance, just as the sun with its rays pierces a cloud.
Then Vināyaka struck that best of Dānavas, who was releasing his feet from his neck,
with that very same lance.
Struck by that excellent blow from Gajavaktra, the Dānava Jambha bled profusely,
like a mountain discharging waterfalls.
Furthermore, desiring to slay him, the valiant one seized his sword; as he raised the blade, roaring and seeking to cut off Jambha’s neck—
Kuñjambha cut that sword as Garuḍa cuts a serpent;
and then he [the demon] likewise [cut it] with a well-drawn arrow that drank blood.
For Kujambha struck him on the arm with his thunderbolt, as Indra strikes a mountain;
struck firmly by him, he reeled like a *sāla* tree.
The god, with his trunk raised high, rushed toward that Dānava as a lion rushes toward an elephant, and he charged at Kujambha like a lion toward an elephant.
Vināyaka, like Airāvata, appeared as one exultant in his strength;
he ran toward Vyaṃsa, desiring to slay Kujambha. (148.40)
Having gone there, he seized him with his shoulder and cast him down upon the earth;
having struck the shoulderless one with his own shoulder, the mighty Nāgavaktra [overcame him]. (148.41)
He reached the presence of Kujambha like a śarabha reaching a lion;
then Kujambha, having pierced his upraised arm with an arrow, [struck him]. (148.42)
He struck him on the head with a mace and on the chest with a club;
smeared with blood from those three blows, Vināyaka shone resplendent.
Then Vināyaka, possessed of great heroism, seized Kujambha from the earth and hurled him away, just as a man might cast down an offering for the spirits.
When Kujambha, who resembled Mount Mandara, was hurled by the arms of Vināyaka,
all the Dānavas became enraged and began to afflict Vināyaka.
Though afflicted by hundreds of Dānavas and mangled by various weapons,
the god moved among the Daityas like a lion among deer.
Enraged, he crushed the Dānavas with his tusks, his feet, and his extended trunk, just as an elephant crushes reeds.
Then the Gaṇeśas, seeing Vināyaka pierced by hundreds of weapons by the Dānavas,
seized their own weapons and, possessing the prowess of elephants and lions, let out a roar and charged forward by the hundreds.

Then once more there occurred a great battle between the hosts of Ganas and the Asuras, which was pierced by thousands of weapons, unbearable due to the falling of arrows, swords, spears, and double-edged blades,
destructive of life, and wherein horses and elephants were slain.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and forty-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Brāhmaṇa was swallowed by the one who bears a portion of the moon.
What did Bhārgava do while staying within the belly of that God of gods?
And how was that twice-born one, the best of ascetics and a yogi, not released from the body of the god by the power of yoga, despite his great austerity? (149.2)
And how did Andhaka, the best of the Asuras, when deprived of Bhārgava and pursued by the lords of the Gaṇas, manage to maintain his hold at that time? (149.3)
O best among those who know the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, tell me all of this in its entirety; for I am not satiated as I listen to the deeds of the Lord.
Sūta said: Then, as Vyāsa was thus questioning him, Sanatkumāra, the best of sages, related the deeds of Śukra.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Bhārgava had been swallowed by that Bhūtamātṛ, the kinsman of the gods,
Andhaka became lusterless, like the sun obscured by a cloud.
Seeing his own army being repeatedly crushed by the Pramathas,
Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed toward the Gaṇas.
By those blows of arrows like vajras and by those strikes of thunderbolts,
the Pramathas fell upon the forest like waterless clouds falling to the earth.
Pierced by arrows in their chests, thighs, cheeks, backs, arms,
and bellies, the Pramathas shrieked like elephants.
Whomever he saw— whether going or coming, not yet reached or already reached, or even standing at a distance—
he pierced that very person violently with arrows.
He pierced one with a hundred, and again a hundred with a hundred;
a thousand with a thousand, and likewise ten million with ten million.
Banners, flags, variegated Vaijayantī streamers, goads,
elephant blankets, chowries, diadems, earrings, and garments.
Whatever among the forces of the Pramathas trembled or even fled,
the Dānava Andhaka swiftly cut all of that to pieces with his arrows.
Just as fire emits sparks, as a cloud pours down torrents of rain, as the king of rivers produces waves, and as the sun sends forth its rays; 149.14.
Like lions in the forest letting out roars, or like elephants spraying their spray,
he discharged sharp-pointed arrows capable of crushing the enemy host.
While Andhaka, the best of heroes, was fighting with resolve,
the Asuras also fought with resolve following after Andhaka.
Those Nivātakavacas, who were all exceedingly similar to one another,
fought a battle with many of the Rudras.
The sixty thousand Kāleyas, great Asuras who were like Death itself,
fought with sixty thousand Pramathas born from his arms.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini,
Bāṣkala, Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, Kujambha, and then Avaniñjaya.
Añjaka, Kālanemi, Namuci, and Vyaṃsa—
these eleven are renowned, possessing the splendor of eleven suns.
Eleven Pramathas, seeking a quarrel,
tormented Vīrabhadra, who was composed of light, as well as Viṭpati and Piṅgala.
Vegapaṃ and Pavanāda, as well as Somārkāpyāyana;
Saṃvarttakānala and Pāvakāpyāyana.
The Yakṣa Annada, the powerful Rākṣasa Vidyunmālin,
and these Dānavas headed by Prahrāda— [these were the enemies] of the foremost of the gods.
The gatekeepers of the Rudras, as well as the sons of the Rudras, were deprived of their hands, weapons, and armor; they were covered by hundreds of weapons. || 149.24 ||
Those who were the attendants of Skanda and those who were the lords of the hosts of Śaktis—
those fond of strife, resembling the God of Death himself— engaged in combat together with the sons of Danu and those belonging to the lineage of Danu’s offspring.
While that battle was thus proceeding, with necklaces, ornaments, garlands, and weapons shattered,
and garments disarrayed, the gods and hosts of Siddhas stationed in the sky cried out in joy, their beautiful eyes wide with wonder.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 149.149 ||
The one hundred and fiftieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
[I shall describe] the illusory power and the heroic might of Andhaka, the enemy of the gods.
It was perfectly created by the Blessed One, arising from the signs of the form of a deity.
Since the sage Bhārgava was swallowed by the God into his body,
what did he do while remaining within the body of the God of gods?
And how did that twice-born descendant of Bhṛgu emerge from his asceticism and the power of yoga, like the moon emerging from white clouds? || 150.3 ||
O best of sages, this curiosity has arisen in me today;
please tell me the life-story of the wise Bhārgava Īśāna.
Sūta said: Thus addressed by Vyāsa, the lord Sanatkumāra, the son of Padmagarbha, related the emergence of Śukra from Śiva.
Then, within the body of that Śambhu, his semen, its luster destroyed,
wandered about seeking an exit, like the wind which has no fixed abode.
He beheld worlds with the radiance of fire, surrounded by hundreds of millions of Rudras,
traversed by Rudra-maidens, within the body of Rudra.
Of those with the color of jasmine, the moon, or a conch shell; of those possessing fangs and claws;
of those endowed with long tails; of those full of pride yet possessed of great patience.
They had hair with the radiance of blazing fire, bore the *nandyāvarta* mark,
possessed tongues with the luster of *kiṃśuka* flowers, and had bodies as massive as Mount Kailāsa.
The descendant of Bhṛgu beheld upon the body of the God of gods a thousand lions of terrifying form, bound by the fetters of fire.
Remaining within his body as a mountain, he beheld the gods together with Indra, the Ādityas, the hosts of Apsarases, and humans, as well as the battle between Gaṇeśa and the Asuras.
Wandering for a hundred years in the armpit of Bhava,
he did not perceive any flaw in him, just as Kali finds no opening in a man of pure conduct.
Mahādeva also stripped away his yoga and his sovereignty endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā*, even though his mind was restrained by speech.
Then a great clamor arose between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras;
hearing that sound, Bhārgava was awakened and became alarmed.
Having entered within the presence of the Lord of Umā, that Brāhmaṇa, strengthened by his ascetic penance,
praised the god Soma, who is adorned with the moon, with beloved hymns of praise.
To him who had fallen into a state of calamity, the trident-bearing God granted the favor of his arising [from it] by means of a command: "Depart through the linga. || 150.16 ||
Then, having become subtle in form, that Śukra, the best of sages,
emerged like semen from the linga of the wise God of gods.
Since the delighter of Bhṛgu’s lineage issued forth from his penis like Śakra,
that best among those who possess movement attained the renown of "Śukra."
And as he was paying homage, he was addressed by that one whose banner bears the lord of the clouds:
"O descendant of Bhrigu, since you have emerged from me today like Śukra..."
"By that very deed you are Śukra, and you are my son; you may go.
Thus addressed by the god, Śukra, whose splendor was like that of the sun, [departed].
He entered the army of the Dānavas like the moon entering a mass of clouds;
seeing him, who resembled the moon and whose appearance was like the rising of the moon, [the demons were struck with wonder].

Just as there was joy among men at the rising of the moon, so too did those enemies of the gods, the sons of Danu and Daityas, feel upon seeing Śukra, who possessed a radiance equal to the moon. 150.22
All those who had been slain by the Pramathas, who appeared victorious and eager for battle, let out lion-like roars in great joy.

Upon the arrival of those [demons], the great asuras considered themselves as having come from the very jaws of death because of Bhārgava’s approach; they paid him homage, rejoiced, and were filled with joy. (150.24)
That great ocean of Dānavas attained the joy of Śukra’s rising,
just as the ocean, joined by the Rākṣasas, always does at the rising of the moon.
Then Śākha and Viśākha, Chāgavaktra and Caturmukha, Nandin and Somanandin, and the heroic Nandiṣeṇa;
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kuṇḍodara, and Mahodara.
And Viṣpati, Vīrabhadra, and that god who consists of light.
Saṃvartaka, Anala, Urva, Yaśodīpta, Vibhākara, Vegavan, Śikhaṇḍin, Tāmracūḍa, and Kukkuṭa.
The Yakṣa Piṅgala, the food-giver; Piṅgala the clever boy;
Vidyutkeśa and Sukeśa, the two invincible Rākṣasas.
These and other leaders of the hosts, possessing splendor equal to that of the world-protectors,
entered the army of the Dānavas, which was emboldened by the rising of Śukra.
Then the sounds of musical instruments, together with the roars of lions,
became fierce in both armies, causing all living beings to tremble.
Then, having encountered one another, they struck each other down with terrible weapons and with palms that had been cooled by their beaks.
Placing Nandīśvara and the six-faced Kārttikeya at their head,
the Pramathas crush the Daityas in battle, just as Tārkṣya crushes serpents.
With their heads severed by falling swords and their skulls crushed by clubs,
the Dānavas lie upon the ground like mountains split apart by thunderbolts.
Pierced and shattered by arrows, their thighs and arms broken,
the Daityas fled in battle like serpents tormented by Garuḍa.
With their thighs and hips shattered and crushed by thick arrows,
the Daityas, afflicted with pain, shrieked like clouds filled with thunder.
During that exceedingly fierce crushing of the Gaṇas and the Daityas,
the earth became filled with Daityas, just as the sky is filled with clouds.
With crowns, diadems, necklaces, bracelets, ornaments, and armlets; with bangles, bracelets, waist-bands, and earrings.
With brilliant jeweled head-ornaments,
radiant necklaces, garlands of beautiful flowers, and eyes [set with gems], they possessed arms whose foreparts were adorned with jewels.
With missiles, weapons, garments, and umbrellas possessing a luster like that of the moon,
her limbs were variegated with red saffron and she was adorned with various ornaments.
The battlefield shone here and there like women adorned with abundant wealth,
resembling either proud lions or mighty elephants.
The Gaṇeśvaras, as they were crushing the Dānavas, became filled with zeal.
Being struck down, defenseless, and afflicted by fear, they sought refuge. || 150.42 ||
Pursued by the Pramathas, the Dānavas took refuge in the ocean;
they saw that army abandoned by the Dānavas who were tormented by the Pramathas.
And when the Daityas had entered the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
the descendant of Bhṛgu, possessed of great splendor, blazed like a fire that has reached its full intensity.
Enraged, he severely cursed the Daityas who dwell in the ocean:
"Since you have abandoned me—who am as beneficial as a father—along with your allies," (150.45)
"O weak ones, you have entered the ocean for the sake of saving your lives;
therefore, remain right there, shameless as you are, struck by my curse. (150.46)
Having entered the state of fish, you shall be born again and again as long as the worlds exist, along with the mountains and the oceans. (150.47)
"For that long you shall be fish in the water, creatures that move within the water;
sinful eaters of human flesh, you shall become devourers of men. (150.48)
"You shall exhaust my curse for hundreds of millions of years.
Having thus rendered the remaining ocean-dwellers victims of his curse,
the immensely radiant Śukra, whose splendor was like that of the moon, became silent.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those Asuras, struck by the preceptor’s curse, were seen in the waters of the ocean, still equipped with weapons, wearing armor, and clad in mail.
Then Śukra, touching Andhaka—who was overwhelmed by the fear of his enemy—with his hand, spoke to him as if restoring him to life with these words: ||| 150.51 ||
"Do not fear, O best of Dānavas; fight against your enemies!
I shall sustain you as food sustains life. (150.52)
Thus addressed by Śukra, that lord of the Dānavas, Andhaka,
saying "So be it," besieged the Pramathas in battle.
Then, when the asuras had entered the ocean and were being struck down by the followers of Śaṅkara,
Andhaka held back all the Pramathas, just as the ocean with its vast waters holds back rivers and streams.
Then that Dānava Andhaka pierced Nandin with twelve arrows and the son of Agni with five;
he struck Viśākha and Śākha with ten each, and the Naigameṣa with a hundred.
He pierced Vīrabhadra, as well as Viṭpati, the radiant Piṅgala, and the excellent Yakṣa,
with arrows adorned with gold, just as an elephant-driver strikes an elephant with the tips of his goads.

There was no horse, nor elephant, nor man, nor any other creature, before him or behind him, who could withstand the arrows discharged by Andhaka—arrows resembling the blazing fire of time and the sun. (150.57)
Torn apart like sandalwood by the lords of the hosts, they stood repeatedly with their arms, bellies, chests, and heads mangled;
deprived of all effort, those who delighted their enemies remained like elephants confined within the bondage of a cage.
Then the asuras let out lion-like roars, intensified by hundreds of conchs, kettledrums, and drums;
once more, a terrifying battle broke out between the lords of the hosts and the lords of the dānavas.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Curse of the Asuras," in the Gaṇa-yuddha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the battle with Andhaka was proceeding and the Gaṇas were fleeing, [the following occurred].
The Grandfather spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Behold them, may you be blessed, O Lord of the Immortals, turning their backs as they are being crushed in battle by the terrible Dānavas and by Andhaka. 151.2.
As Śukra remains reviving the Dānavas slain again and again by the Pramathas in battle,
he is like a rain-cloud bringing crops back to life.
With his bow drawn, resembling a cloud accompanied by Indra’s bow,
Andhaka discharged a rain of arrows, destroying his enemies.
For this oppression of the Pramathas is indeed harmful and brings dishonor;
why did you remain patient during this defeat? || 151.5 ||
For once this Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, has conquered all the hosts,
he will utterly uproot even our very foundations.
Therefore, before he can bring our Pramathas to destruction with his arrows,
we shall seize the flanks of the one clad in animal skins.
"In this way, O Lord of the Devas, your purpose will be accomplished, and a great favor will indeed be done for Rudra as well. (151.8)
Having heard the words of Svayambhū, the Lord of the Gods, the destroyer of Bala and Vṛtra,
said to the gods, "This is fitting," and then spoke.
"Having taken up our armor, weapons, and missiles, we of swift prowess shall quickly provide assistance today to the hosts fighting in battle."
Then Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, the two lords of men, and Candra;
Svayambhū, Anala, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Dharmada. || 151.11 ||
Pūṣan, Aryaman, Bhaga, Mitra, and Yama, the son of the Sun;
Aṃśa, Tvaṣṭṛ, Jaya, and Jayanta, the son of Śakra. || 151.12 ||
The Maruts, Vasus, Sādhyas, as well as the Aśvins, Garuḍas, and Uragas;
the Tuṣitas, Lekhas, Viśvedevas, and Guhyakas. || 151.13 ||
The Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, and those others who belong to the side of the gods— all of them rushed into the battle, desiring to slay Andhaka.
Then, the sounds of kettledrums and terrifying lion-roars arose among the divine armies, bringing joy to the Pramathas.
That army of the Dānavas was churned by the descending gods,
like a lake with abundant fish and dwindling water being stirred by royal swans.
Then, amidst the army of the Dānavas, which was crowded together and inhabited by deities, there arose an exceedingly terrifying tumultuous roar.
As the ocean is by dense waves, as the sky is by clouds, as the body is by phlegm and bile, and as serpents are by Garuḍas; || 151.18 ||
In that same way, by the power of the inhabitants of the triple heaven, that entire army of the Andhakas was,
in a mere moment, rendered helpless, its armor and banners cast down.
On one side were the gods led by Indra, and on the other were the lords of the Gaṇas;
the army of the Dānavas was being driven away like a flock of goats by hundreds of wolves.
The god who holds a raised vajra in his hand, the bull among gods,
was their leader, like the syllable *oṃ* is for the Vedas.
With the fire of his vajra-weapon, Indra consumed his enemies in battle,
just as the fire of expiation burns away all misdeeds.
While the army was being struck down by both the gods and the Pramathas, Andhaka,
the lord of the Dānavas, blinded by rage and passion, spoke to the Dānavas.
"Having provoked enmity with Rudra for the sake of protecting all the worlds,
it is not possible for you, even with the gods, to defeat the Pramathas without becoming despondent."
"You must not fear death; fight, O Daityas and Dānavas!
For here stands Bhārgava, who will restore us to life."
Therefore, O lords of the hosts of gods, do not spare your lives;
resist them fearlessly according to your strength and according to your zeal. 151.26.
"By means of many secret and hidden illusions, restrain in battle all these assembled gods who have assumed concealed forms."
Thus addressed, they performed terrible deeds like clouds at the end of an eon. || 151.28 ||
Making sounds with their bows and likewise uttering lion-like roars,
the Dānavas, urged on by Andhaka, rushed toward the gods.
Having drawn his great bow, the Dānava Andhaka, who roared like the ocean and the clouds,
rushed with speed toward Rudra.
As that lord of the Dānavas, difficult to restrain, was charging forward,
Śailādri warded him off, just as one whose mind is fixed on righteousness wards off evil.
Andhaka, pressing his arms together in rage, pierced Nandin in the middle of the chest with three arrows that resembled blazing suns.
Severely mangled by that Dānava, Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas,
then reeled like a tree shaken by the wind.
Reeling, Nandin shone with his polished earrings as ornaments,
like an aśoka tree rich with swaying sprouts and flowers.
Then, having recovered after a long time, Suyaśas, the lord of Suyaśas,
raised his powerful thunderbolt and hurled it at Andhaka.
Andhaka checked that powerful thunderbolt, which had arrived resembling the radiance of fire,
with floods of arrows, and he laughed aloud.
As he laughed, drops of tears flowed from his eyes and beautiful eyebrows,
like rays from the blazing orb of the sun.
Then the King of the Bhūtas, having uprooted that tree with its agitated foliage and crying out,
"O Andhaka, you are slain!", hurled it and roared.
As he runs through the sky, bees fanned by the wind from the trees follow him, just as friends follow one who has fallen into misfortune. || 151.39 ||
And Andhaka cut that [bow] of his as well with arrows adorned with beautiful gold,
just as the slayer of serpents [Viṣṇu] cut the embryo of Diti, the supporter of the worlds.
When the tree had been cut down, Nandin then uprooted the peak of Mount Mandara, which was filled with wild animals, beasts of prey, and serpents, and rushed toward Andhaka in the battle.
But Nandin, whose abode is the forest of Mount Girikūṭa,
hurled that mountain peak at his chariot, just as the slayer of serpents hurls a thunderbolt at the Vindhya mountain.
Struck violently by that bull Nandin with his horn, the chariot—along with its wheels, pole, and horses—was reduced to a state of union with the dust. (151.43)
Then, seeing Andhakāratha’s chariot shattered along with its wheels and axle,
the gods, together with the gandharvas, the pramathas, and the guhyakas, raised a great cry.
Then Andhaka, having roared like a dark cloud,
struck Nandin with his trident, as a lordly elephant strikes down a tree.
Beloved of the trident and struck by that very trident,
Nandin, with all his limbs overwhelmed, trembled like the moon beneath the waters.
As Nandīśvara reeled, severely afflicted by the blow,
a roar like that of lions repeatedly arose from the army of the asuras.
By that lion’s roar, Nandin was awakened from his enemies;
then the kinsman of beings struck Andhaka with a battle-axe.
Struck by the battle-axe, the Dānava Andhaka bled profusely,
like sandalwood exuding its own resin when struck by an elephant’s tusk.
Seeing Andhaka deprived of his chariot, the enemies of the gods protected him;
just as the gods remained stationed in their respective quarters, so did they protect this world.
Then Bāṇa, the son of Bali, the Dānava who possessed a splendor like that of the Bāṇa flower,
placed Andhaka upon his chariot.
Then Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, ascended that chariot,
just as the blessed Sun-god rises with his full orb.
Then again, the gods and dānavas prepared themselves, desiring to wage a most terrible conflict;
in that battle, the fire, incensed by tridents, thunderbolts, lightning, and arrows, blazed forth with even greater intensity.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Battle between Andhaka and Nandin," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
[He saw] Viṣṇu, the destroyer of Dānavas, tormenting the Dānavas.
The Dānava Jambha, letting out a roar like a rain-cloud, rushed forward.
But seeing Jambha approaching with a roar like that of a cloud,
the god was not at all alarmed, just as a lion is not when it sees an elephant.
Kujambha and Jambha, the younger Dānava mountain,
obstructed the infinite end of his enemies and roared aloud.
Vṛtra, resembling Mount Añjana and appearing like the fire of universal destruction,
approached Indra roaring like a cloud, desiring to seize him.
As that Dānava, who resembled a mountain, was running and roaring, Purandara, the hundred-eyed one, struck him in a mountain cave.
Meditating upon Vāyu, the wielder of the mace who grants a hundred-year lifespan in battle, the warrior,
desiring to fight, quickly advanced, roared, and laughed.
The two great asuras Tuṇḍa and Huṇḍa fought with the Aśvins; Bhaga fought with Prahlāda, and Virocana with Aṃśa.
Aryamā and Yama fought against Bilva and Kelvala,
as did those great asuras led by Vipracitti who were foremost among the powerful.
Those lords of the Gaṇas and the gods fought by the thousands;
meanwhile, Andhaka, the bull among Dānavas, approached Nandin.
He was struck deeply by Andhaka with arrows released from his bow that pierce the vital organs;
he was mangled by those shafts for many years.
Nandin became enraged and, filled with fury, rushed toward Andhaka in the battle,
raising his hand which held a thunderbolt as radiant as the rays of the sun.
Enraged like a rain-cloud at the time of universal dissolution, Nandin,
that lord of the Gaṇas, struck Andhaka with his hundred-edged thunderbolt.
He pulverized the horses, the charioteer, and likewise the chariot;
then [he struck] Andhaka on the root of the ear, which was adorned with earrings and curls.
He who grants boons, possessing beautiful earrings and a voice deep as a thundercloud, struck him;
then, with his hand resembling an elephant's trunk, he too drew back [his weapon].
Struck by that Dānava with a backhanded blow, the Lord of the Gaṇas was cast down onto the chest of Nandin, as if by an elephant in battle.
He retreated eight steps, which he then fell back upon;
"Excellent! Excellent! the Daityas then cried out to Andhaka.
Enraged by that excellent blow directed at the Dānava, he summoned a fierce wrath and indeed rushed toward him. || 152.17 ||
Having gone there, he shattered his wonderful bow and his armor of great luster into pieces with the hundred-edged thunderbolt.
Having bound him with the noose of his arms, the Lord of Beings himself desired to crush him upon the ground, but Andhaka released him.
Having liberated himself and resorted to a deluding illusion, he rushed toward Śailādi, crying out, "Stay! Stay! (152.20).
As he was rushing forward with speed, all the great lords of the Gaṇas, their minds filled with rage and various weapons in hand, [advanced against him]. || 152.21 ||
Nandiṣeṇa, Somanandin, Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahodara,
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Vīrabhadra, and that god Prabhāmaya.
Protecting their master, those foremost of his attendants fought Andhaka, like lions attacking the elephant of Śakra.
Nandisena struck him with a spear, Somanandin with a fist,
Virabhadra with an arrow, and Ghantakarna also with a sword.
With their tree-like arms, whose tips were trembling,
those radiant gods severed Andhaka, just as the Draviḍas cut sandalwood.
But Nandīśvara, the leader of the Gaṇas, struck Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, on the head, even though he had been turned away by the other Gaṇas.
Seeing the lord of the Asuras pursued by the gods and the leaders of the Gaṇas, a cry arose within the army of the Asuras: "Run! Seize him! || 152.27 ||
Then the Asuras, led by Prahlāda, quickly assembled;
Viṣṇu alone held them all back as they came for battle.
Seeing him thus displaying his prowess at the forefront of the battle with the discus in hand,
Andhaka, overwhelmed by rage, launched a truly great assault.
Whether he was striving, motionless, charging forward, or roaring,
wherever the king beheld him, he pierced him with arrows.
Broad, yellow, and sharpened arrows, bearing the marks of Garuḍa’s body,
terrible and inexhaustible, fell from Andhaka’s bow.
Pierced by Andhaka in their mouths, gums, bellies, and trunks,
the elephants, though exceedingly intoxicated, shed their rut.
Some take refuge in the Lord of Gods, others in Indra, the sovereign of the gods;
some in the god Nārāyaṇa, and other hosts in Nandin.
Other gods stood taking refuge in Śākha and Viśākha, and others in Kumāra as well, like birds perched upon trees.
Just as mortals [fear] from the dread of the thunderbolt, as deer [fear] from the dread of the lion, and as serpents who devour serpents always [fear] from Garuḍa; || 152.35 ||
Likewise, the gods who were enemies of the deities, standing in battle against Andhaka, were terrified by the host of the Suras and wandered about like those who are bewildered. || 152.36 ||
Just as a forest of bandhujīva trees shines when bent down with blossoms,
so did that host of attendants appear, their limbs drenched with blood from their wounds.
Just as trees in the forests tremble when stirred by the wind,
so too did the gods, terrified by the fear of Andhaka, shake at the front of the battle.
Then Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, and the powerful Śakra, as well as the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the twelve Ādityas [appeared]. (152.39)
Nandī, Viśākha, Śākha, Vīrabhadra, Prabhāmaya, Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandī, and Vināyaka. || 152.40 ||
While their forces were being struck down by Andhaka with his surging armies,
the gods fled, still clutching their weapons, from that lord of the hosts of Dānavas.
Surrounding that best of chariots, which had the appearance of a Gandharva’s palace,
they shattered it and roared like clouds.
The great chariot of Andhaka was shattered by the gods,
just as a desire set upon unrighteousness is thwarted by obstacles.
That Dānava struck Śakra with his discus,
Ananta with a single arrow, and Vināyaka with a trident.
With his fist he struck Nandin, with his sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa) the radiant Prabhāmaya,
with a crescent-headed arrow (bhalla) Pūṣan, and with his mace Yama.
Having swiftly struck down all his enemies in battle,
Andhaka leapt up and roared in the sky like a cloud intoxicated with water.
That deceitful warrior, resembling a mountain himself,
hurled mountain peaks along with trees, shrubs, and serpents, and let out a roar.
That terrible rain from the mountain peak, along with trees, bears, and great serpents,
fell upon the divine armies like cool water upon lotuses.
Without ceasing, without resting, breathless and agitated by fear—
With their noses, eyes, teeth, and lips severed, and their feet, hips, and hands broken,
the Pramatha demons were seen terrified, bewildered, and trembling with fear.
Showering stones from the peaks of his palaces like weapons, the asura shines as he repeatedly hurls them while stationed in the sky; [may he protect] me...
Having intensified the roar of the surging ocean, that enemy of the hosts of gods, stationed in the sky,
repeatedly pours down a great rain of water, just as the cloud at the time of universal destruction pours down fierce torrents.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Battle with Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Andhaka, resembling a mass of great clouds, stood in the sky.
Just as a cloud releases its rain of hailstones. || 153.1 ||
Again, seizing his bow which resembled the rainbow of great Indra,
he released a downpour of arrows, and it became an exceedingly dark storm.
Then [there were arrows] with feathers like those of the Suparṇa bird,
with plumes made of Suparṇa feathers, flying like the Suparṇa bird, and possessing beaks as high as the Suparṇa bird.
The lord of the Dānavas unleashed a hundred [missiles] that pierce the body and consume the very essence of the body; then, filled with pride, he roared aloud.
Drawn and discharged from the fully drawn bow, they were surrounded by those moving through the field of battle;
acting as guides for their own paths of flight, they were equal to thought and wind in speed.
Those great arrows of Andhaka fall upon the gods like the rays impelled by the sun falling upon mighty mountains.
Elephants struck by arrows, horses struck by arrows,
and the lords of the hosts of deities were struck by arrows on every side.
With their entrails and blood protruding, their necklaces and ornaments scattered,
and the binding of their hair loosened, they fall down in intense agony.
Whether standing, moving, rising, running, or leaping,
he perceives the horse, the elephant, or the deity exactly as they are, from whatever direction they may come.
Then Andhaka, having forcibly struck down that enemy with arrows whose forms were like darkness,
roared like a cloud at the onset of the rainy season.
With the cries of those afflicted by wounds having ceased and the horses wandering aimlessly,
the army shone like a river whose roar has been stilled.
It was torn asunder, cut, split, scorched, devoured, and shaken down,
like a forest whose trees have been destroyed by elephants blinded by rut.
Some were struck on their faces, others in their eyes; others were struck on their chests and bellies, and likewise some were struck from behind.
Just as the *śataghnīs* were covered with arrows,
so too the hosts of Maruts and the groups of terrible prowess, being struck down, did not reach the ground.
Then a river carrying the water of wounds was set in motion by the gods and asuras;
it was teeming with great elephants as its crocodiles and had beautiful chariot wheels for its tortoises.
With the severed hands of serpents for its [cut] branches, with bows and excellent banners for its trees,
with the crests of crowns for its frogs, and with bowstrings for its binding cords— (153.16)
With its scattered pearl necklaces for pebbles, its white garments for foam,
and its waters most destructive to gods and asuras, this river was set in motion by the gods and asuras.
Then the Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, whose splendor surpassed that of collyrium and who laughed with the brilliance of lightning flashes, were exceedingly emaciated by thirst.
Just as they had drunk the excellent nectar of wine, so too did they drink blood;
then once more, a tumultuous and wonderful battle ensued.
At that time, Andhaka was struck by the great arrow of Nandin.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Battlefield," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that army was being struck down by the gods together with the lords of the Pramathas, [the following occurred].
The twenty-four fierce Dānavas, filled with pride, became enraged.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Saṃhlāda, Śitibāhu and Āṣkulī,
Jambha, Virocana, Vṛtra, Bali, Bāṇa, and Avaniñjaya.
Likewise, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Kubha, Śambara, Vipracitti, Ilvaka, and Pilvaka; || 154.3 ||
Maya, Tāra, Tāraka-akṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Pramohana—
these twenty-four Dānavas were overcome by the power of indignation.
They rushed toward the god Nandin, who stood there armed,
he who resembled a mountain of collyrium approaching the golden mountain.
They struck Nandin with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and battle-axes;
thus was he indeed beaten and obstructed by those enemies with their weapons.
Then Nandi was neither agitated nor did he fall into distress or pain;
thereafter, the Blessed One drew back his great, fully drawn bow.
With three arrows at a time, he swiftly pierced all those foremost of Dānavas;
with the streams flowing from the paths of his arrows, those Dānavas began to bleed profusely.
The lords of mountains appeared as if they were exuding liquid gold;
then Nandin, uplifted with joy, was restored to life once more by Śukra.
With terrible arrows, he sent Kārttavīrya to the abode of Yama;
having encountered that which destroys life, that great mountain-like Dānava fell.
With its stones shattered, it fell instantly like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
as it was falling to the earth, Nandin was slain, struck by Bāṇa.
Having uprooted a mountain peak, he hurled it toward Nandin;
that mountain slope, along with its minerals, wild beasts, predators, bears, and trees, [was cast down].
The serpents and other creatures rushed with speed toward Gaṇeśvara, who was like a tree shaken by a gust of wind, as Bāli had been released from Śṛṅga.
Like kinsmen abandoning a man who has fallen into distress,
Nandin, endowed with great prowess, pierced that mountain peak as it was falling with his arrow;
he shattered it like a great wind dispersing the clouds, and let out a roar.
Having split that mountain peak, the one whose abode is on a mountain peak pierced Bali with an arrow, as if Bali were a risen obstacle.
Struck by Gaṇeśa and brought under his control, the son of Prahlāda suddenly fell to the ground like a tree felled by the wind.
Then, when Bala had fallen and Nandīśvara had struck the drum,
the Dānavas, afflicted by arrows, fled from the battle.
Then Andhaka, whose form resembled a cloud, having reached the earth from the sky, spoke these words to the Dānavas who were like spreading clouds: || 154.18 ||
"O sons of the daughter of Dakṣa, listen today to my words;
if you have any regard for me, do what I have spoken as it is for your own welfare. (154.19)
Born in noble families, heroes who have mastered all weapons—why do you flee, driven by sharp iron arrows? 154.20.
Where are those conversations held in the assembly, and where now is that great enmity with the gods? (154.21)
"Defeated by a single Nandin by the hundreds and thousands, how indeed do you feel no shame while prattling thus in the courtyard of our home? (154.22)
"Turn back, O you who are ignorant of dharma! Fight! What is the use of fleeing?
There is no place to be found where death does not exist for us. (154.23)
"Standing to one side, free from enmity and devoid of envy,
you judges, behold now this single combat between him and Nandin."
Having heard these words of Andhaka, all those Dānavas in the battle turned back once more for combat, seizing their excellent weapons.
Then, mounting another chariot adorned with banners and measuring a *nalva* in size,
that Andhaka advanced toward Nandin together with the foremost of the Dānavas.
Sharp-pointed, fashioned of gold, broad, and beautiful to behold,
great arrows discharged from Andhaka’s bow fly forth.
Like fields by locusts, like trees by bees,
like lordly elephants by clouds, and like oceans by sea-monsters.
By Andhaka, with great arrows released that possessed a radiance equal to serpents and suns,
the gods were made like the finest *śataghnī* weapons.
Just as the winds are unimpeded, as is death, as is old age, and as are well-spoken blessings from Brahmins, so too are they invariably unimpeded. || 154.30 ||
Thus, those sharp and fierce great arrows of Andhaka were like raised staffs of Brahma; for they were irresistible and unfailing.
Wheresoever all the Asuras and that enemy Andhaka were in battle,
from there the Pramathas, together with the gods, were shattered.
With his bow perpetually drawn, he too released volleys of arrows like the sun radiating its beams, appearing like the sun encircled by a halo.
Encountering the pain of his arrows, all the leaders of the Gaṇas and the gods together with Vāsava falter like trees on a riverbank. || 154.34 ||
Having pierced Viṣṇu with one arrow, Ananta with two, and Śakra with three,
and having torn through Yama, Soma, the Lord of Waters, and the Vasus, he let out a terrible roar.
Having pierced the two Aśvins with two arrows, as well as Bhaga, Aryaman, Candra,
and Pūṣan, the one of fierce deeds then mangled Nandīśvara and the lords of the Gaṇas with his shafts.
Thus did the assailant Andhaka consume them, just as the Lord Fire consumes moths;
those chief warriors of the immortals were then warded off and torn apart by arrows by Andhaka.
In that battle, they were unable to stir or even to look at Andhaka, just as men on earth cannot gaze upon the sun in the sky.
Then, abandoning their blazing glories, the gods— including Nārāyaṇa and Devapāla—
fled, tormented by the arrows of the Dānava Andhaka and exhausted by the slaughter of the Dānavas.
Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, Ananta,
and Śatakratu were all broken in battle by Andhaka with arrows resembling flames of fire.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the two Aśvins, the best of gods,
were shattered in battle by Andhaka with blows from his thunderbolt, like birds struck down.
The Tuṣitas, the Viśvedevas, and the gods who consume the svadhā offerings were shattered by Andhaka with his arrows, like trees by the wind.
The blessed Moon, Vahni, and the Rākṣasa Vittapāla were broken in battle by Andhaka with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, serpents, Garuḍas,
and Mahoragas were broken in battle by Andhaka, pierced by arrows resembling fire.
Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandī, Prabhāmaya, Piṅgala, Nandiṣeṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Mahodara. || 154.44 ||
Vidyutkeśa and Sukeśa, and that god Vināyaka, as well as other heroic Pramathas led by Vīrabhadra. || 154.45 ||
Broken by Andhaka in battle by the hundreds and thousands,
the entire triple world, including all mobile and immobile beings, was forcibly overcome.
Having been broken by Andhaka in battle, that divine host— including Nārāyaṇa and the gods—
released the one Lord of the Gaṇas from within it.

No one at all remained standing before him who wore a crown of great jewels. Then, within the host of the asuras, there arose a terrible, great lion’s roar produced by all the living beings, along with a wondrous sound of musical instruments.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Victory over Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
In the meantime, all the gods, led by Śakra, [arrived].
Accompanied by Brahmā, they went to the wielder of the trident, the one worthy of seeking refuge.
Having bowed down to Mahādeva, they, afflicted by fear, said this: "We have all been utterly defeated; why do you overlook Andhaka? (155.2)
Then the God of gods spoke to the gods, headed by Brahmā:
"Because I have granted him a boon, you have been utterly defeated."
"He was disregarded by me in battle merely for the sake of sport;
now, for your sake, I shall subdue Andhaka."
Then the god, having smiled, looked at the trident standing at his side;
the trident, knowing the true intent of the god, blazed up at that very moment.
Having rushed swiftly toward Andhaka, who appeared victorious,
he suddenly displayed his prowess in battle and pierced him between the breasts.
Then, having pierced that blind one of great strength,
the spear brought that lord of the Dānavas, who possessed a massive body, into the presence of Śaṅkara.
From those drops of blood that flowed from him as he was pierced by the spear, men arose upon falling to the ground; and they too fought on, difficult to withstand.
Equal in form to him and equal in prowess,
they too, wielding various weapons and missiles, fought against the lords of the hosts.
With their hands raised high, some of those exceedingly powerful ones struck even the fleeing hosts. 155.10
Among those fighting, not a single lord of the hosts remained;
out of fear of the lords of the Dānavas, they all fled from the battle.
Seeing all those hosts together with the lords of the gods thus fleeing, Mahādeva unleashed— [the weapon]. || 155.12 ||
"—or else, having been informed [of our situation], you ought to grant us your command. (155.13)
Then the God of gods said to all those who were ready with their weapons:
"Devour these great asuras born from drops of blood."
Thus addressed, all those powerful mistresses of yoga,
having slain the asuras again and again in battle, devoured them.
The god who brought about the end of Andhaka also spoke to the flaming trident:
"Cook Andhaka in the fire of the sun for a hundred thousand autumns!"
For even Andhaka, while being cooked on the tip of a trident by the heat of the sun for a full thousand years, attained a state of sattva.
Having attained a state of pure goodness (sattva) and shaken off passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas),
he recognized the bull-bannered God as the cause of the worlds.
Having realized this, he then, with devotion and a stainless inner self,
though remaining with nothing but sinews and bones, praised the God who bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Andhaka said:

"I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who is the creator of this entire world with its moving and unmoving beings, as well as the author of what has been created; who likewise bestows pleasure and pain, and who is also the cause of dissolution at the time of the end. (155.20)

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, whose divine nature is immeasurable, whom yogis—whose delusion, darkness, and passion have departed, whose minds are one-pointed through devotion, and whose desires have ceased—meditate upon with resolute intellect. 155.21.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who out of love bears upon his head the stainless crescent moon with its expanding rays, and who gave half of his own body to the daughter of the King of Mountains. 155.22

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who bore upon his head the Gaṅgā—whose beautiful waters are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and which falls from the sky with the force of great waves—as if she were a garland of unfading flowers. 155.23.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who, by the pressing of his lotus feet, held fast the peak of Mount Kailāsa even as it was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who himself resembled a peak of Kailāsa.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, by whom the sons of Diti and the sons of Danu, as well as the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas, have been repeatedly endowed with all boons; and by whom the best of sages, subsisting on fruits and roots, were likewise joined [in their goals]. 155.25.
He destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the eyes of Bhaga, and likewise the row of teeth of Pūṣan;
he paralyzed the arm of great Indra, which was equipped with the thunderbolt—to that Śaṃkara, the giver of refuge, I go for protection. 155.26.

Those who have attained liberation from the threefold bondage, yet are not even endowed with the qualities of knowledge, spiritual lineage, or sacred learning—those persons who take refuge in Him and enjoy happiness; to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, I go for shelter. 155.27

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who at the outset of the nectar possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns, who terrified the foremost of the gods and the Dānavas, and who drank the violently surging Kālakūṭa poison. 155.28.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, the blessed Maheśa who granted many boons to Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and Ṣaṇmukha, and who, as the Lord, rescued Nandin from the jaws of death. 155.29.
And Kāma, the wielder of the bow with five arrows on earth, was rendered bodiless at that time by the Blessed One out of derision;
yet in ancient times, he destroyed Tripura with but a single arrow—to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, I go for shelter. 155.30.

Salutations ever to Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, who is attainable through the supreme reality; he who was propitiated with intense austerity in a Himalayan bower by means of the smoke-vow (dhūmavrata) in a mind inaccessible even to others, and who bestowed the Saṃjīvanī [herb]. || 155.31 ||

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who is worshipped by the hosts of immortals together with the world-protectors, and by the powerful lords of the Gaṇas—who have faces resembling various kinds of elephants and cats, and who are the destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 155.32 ||

For the sake of sport alone, the Blessed One created the seven worlds—adorned with various rivers, birds, and trees, together with Brahmā and beneficial to those of virtuous deeds; I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge. 155.33.

I go for refuge to that Śaṃkara, the giver of shelter, to whom this entire world is eternally subject, who enjoys the worlds through his eight very bodies, and who is the cause even of the greatest causes. 155.34.
Having bound [it], I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge. 155.36
Regarding the faults of sovereign power—those who are bound by them experience the departure [of that power] just as I have. 155.39.
Indeed,
through his grace,
you, performing auspicious deeds, have then fashioned the world of Śiva. || 155.40 ||
Sanatkumāra said: While he was thus offering praise, the god Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident whose banner bears the bull, being pleased at the completion of a full thousand years, spoke.
"O son, I am pleased; may it be well with you. You have now become stainless.
I grant you divine vision; behold me, O lord of the Dānavas! || 155.42 ||
"Whatever supreme fruit you desire, I shall grant it all to you; speak, O best of Dānavas! (155.43)
"Attain the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Indra, which is difficult even for the gods to reach;
or else, become the king of all the worlds as you were before."
Andhaka said:
"The state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, characterized by return [to rebirth]—all that is known to me even by the mind. (155.45)
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, grant me the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (gāṇapatya),
which is unsurpassed, pure, and forever imperishable."
The God of gods spoke— [he who is] honored by all the worlds. 155.47.
The great yogin, the great being of great power, capable of assuming any form at will, endowed with the qualities beginning with *aṇiman*, is the beloved, most excellent of persons.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having granted that most difficult-to-attain boon, Mahādeva, having become [invisible], vanished right there. 155.49
Having approached the adorable god, the giver of boons, who is devoted to sacred knowledge and possesses immeasurable splendor— [he spoke]. 155.51
— with speech and mind. || 155.55 ||

O Lord, those others whose bodies are submerged in the mire of the filth of false treatises, even though they seek liberation, they nevertheless praise Your feet; yet they are as deluded as deer in the forest who pursue mirages. (155.56)
On the bank of the Śaṅkita river, the sun, by his movement, makes the water clear with the masses of his stainless rays. || 155.57 ||
On one side, he performs penance by which even the moon, reduced to a mere crescent, steals away the splendor at the soles of your feet;
yet at night, with its laughter of rays, it whitens the faces of the quarters of the sky with its full-orbed body.

—O Lord, the Vasus, the Maruts, and the Aśvins, as well as the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, have attained perfection and reached their goals through the grace of the boon-bestowing lotus-feet of you, the Siddha. (155.60)
To the god who dwells on Kailāsa, whose anklets are marked by the sound of tinkling bells,
the lord of yoga with a supreme and elevated beautiful form, may he be bound in posture for the prosperity of the great world.
— — — — — you were never seen before; such a person inspires great longing in the people.
Therefore, O Lord, through the union of half your body with her, as with the moon and the matted locks [of Śiva], you honor her as something unprecedented, even as you do the Gaṅgā. 155.62.
On Kailāsa, Meru, Malaya, Udara, and Mandara, you are worshipped by Vidyādharas, sages, great serpents,
and Kiṃnaras with sweet words, O descendant of Kuṭāyana.
With devotion, those who are steadfast behold your essence—the undecaying, which is to be known by the self—through the vision of yoga; O Śiva, they enter into you alone, never to return. 155.65.
Having come together with him who possesses learning and age, those capable ones, emitting splendor, were sent swiftly—
[the rest of the verse follows].
The sacrifice of Dakṣa, for which all protections had been arranged by the best of gods and whose Vedic hymns were sung by the eminent sages such as Bhṛgu and others—
O Lord, that was effortlessly destroyed by you with a single wrath-born attendant who bore the excellent trident and discus.

Hara is that which takes away the *liṅga*, and Hari is that which places it below; as for me, I declare it to be above—among those speaking thus, who else here, being of small intellect, could speak so skillfully in the midst of these learned disputants? (155.70)
You are Śarva; you are all-pervading and the bestower of all fruits. You are Yoga, the bearer of Yoga, and the foremost among those who know Yoga.
You are the mother and the father of the world, the imperishable Lord. You are the peaceful, you are the auspicious, you are the supreme, and you bring about auspiciousness.

Whoever, having risen at dawn, constantly recites this foremost hymn of pure meaning sung by Brahmā in the assembly of the twice-born, shall experience happiness here in this world and, after death, shall be born into a lineage prosperous with wealth and gold. 155.72
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 155.155 ||
The one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus praised by Brahmā, the Lord with the odd number of eyes (the three-eyed Śiva) [responded].
Then he spoke to all those gods, together with Brahmā.
"I am pleased, O gods; depart! The thorn of the gods has been destroyed. What other dear service may I perform for you today, O sinless ones who have granted me this boon?"
Thus addressed by the God of gods, all the deities spoke,
praising the Lord of gods with bowed heads and joyful minds.
O God, you alone are the supreme refuge for all of us;
you are the father of all the worlds, and by you this Andhaka has been destroyed.
Having spoken thus and prostrated before Śaṅkara, all the gods,
together with Brahmā, departed for their respective abodes filled with joy.
Then the high-minded Lord of the Gaṇas, having duly honored the hosts who had exerted themselves in battle, dismissed them.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus conquered Andhaka and made him the leader of his attendants,
the God, the destroyer of the afflictions of the gods, dismissed the deities and sported.
Indeed, the brahmin who recites this "Slaying of Andhaka" in an assembly of twice-born men obtains protection; of this there is no doubt. (156.8)
One attains a body, yoga, form, and dharma;
having heard this, one is joined with the state of a leader of the Gaṇas upon the transition of the body. (156.9)
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 156.156 ||
The one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having shown favor to Andhaka and having dismissed the gods along with their hosts, the Lord—
Tell me truly what the Lord of the moving and the unmoving did.
Sanatkumāra said: When the gods had gone to heaven and Andhaka had been made a leader of the Gaṇas, the Lord of the Gods, together with the Goddess, [dwelt] with Andhaka and Nandin... || 157.2 ||
After a long time, the moon-crested Lord of the Pramathas entered his home and brought delight to it, as if he had entered the palaces of Mount Meru.
Hara, who has the crescent moon as his tilaka mark, is seen in the midst of his companions— Soma and those speaking of Soma— just as Rohiṇī is seen among the stars. 157.4.
Seeing the Lord of Gods, the bull-bannered one, approaching, the Goddess also rose quickly from her seat at that time, together with her female companions. || 157.5 ||
Placing his joined palms upon his head like a lotus bud,
he paid homage at the sage’s feet with a heart full of joy.
The lordly god, having raised her up, sat down upon the throne, which was suffused with the rays of jewels, accompanied by her alone.
And Śaṅkara recounted how Andhaka had been conquered in battle by the Goddess out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her, and how he had subsequently been made preeminent.
"This Andhaka, your son, was born from my very eyes;
having been made to abandon his demonic nature, he indeed has shown contempt for you and us. (157.9)
When Śaṅkara, the lord of gods, had spoken thus, the Dānava Andhaka,
bowing down with palms joined in reverence, made a request to Pārvatī.
"O auspicious goddess, I am Andhaka, upon whom the King has bestowed his favor;
I have come to serve you, so look upon me with a gentle eye. (157.11)
"O Mother, that which was done by me against you, born of my nature as a Dānava, has passed.
I have been favored by the Lord, and your laughter is my servant. (157.12)
"O Mother, know me to be one who is patient, self-controlled, and devoted, having you as my sole refuge; I stand here established in a state of pure being. (157.13)
Having spoken thus to Girijā, Andhaka, who resembled a mountain peak,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and praised her with words worthy of an oblation.
Vibhāvarī, Vāricarī, Śarvarī, Śarvavallabhā, Dhṛti, Mati, Kīrti, Dīpti, Prāpti, and Pramohinī. || 157.15 ||
Medhā, Sudhā, the virtuous Sādhvī, Svadhā, Svāhā of great splendor, Puṣṭi, Iṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Gṛṣṭi, Dṛṣṭi, Truṭi, and Taḍit. || 157.16 ||
Memory, joy, longing, loss, speech, languor, compassion, action, fortune, splendor, humility, faith, illusion, and she who is worshipped by the upholders of illusion. 157.17.
Aditi, Diti, Kadrū, Siṃhikā, Surasā, Danu, Rākā, Kuhū, Sinīvālī, Carṣaṇī, and Sukhadāyinī. || 157.18 ||
She is initiation, the most excellent skill, protection, and instruction; she whose abode is the armpit;
she who is fragrant, fortunate, and auspicious; she who brings about the past, the future, and the present.
Dharaṇī, Dhāraṇī, Dhanyā, Vīraṇī, and indeed Guhāraṇī; likewise Lā, Golā, and Maṅgalāvidhā. || 157.20 ||
— being established in the *ro-vṛt* state — and — — she who delights in the *kṣatra*.
The sky is variegated with stars; the earth is action; mindfulness is free from greed. 157.21.
She is purity, purification, the wise one, fame, the wearer of the hide, and she who is fond of the lower lip;
she is the bowstring, the victorious one, the worshipful, the sacrificial offering, the path, and the bestower of victory. 157.22.

She is the excellent one, the most worthy of choice, the bestower of boons, the noble woman, the purifier of speech; she is prosperity, the mother of all beings, the performer of good deeds, the well-disposed, and delight.
Bhāratī, Bhāsā, Āyuktā, Yuktaraktavacodharī,
Ājñā, Prajñā, Saṃjñā, Ulkā, Nāsāsamudbhavā,
Vedamātā, Gāyatrī, Durgā, and Sāvitrī as well. (157.24)
She is the possessor of attributes, the mother of all qualities, the sharpening flame, the most excellent among splendors;
she is the night, the delighter, the steadfast one, the source, and the forest-eyed goddess.
Seeking wealth, she was a river of gifts; she possessed the meaning of sacred learning and was more learned than the most learned.
She wore bracelets like firebrands and bore a girdle, being herself the wearer of a girdle.
"May Umā, the sustainer of the world, dark-complexioned and clad in dark garments, be pleased with me"—
thus was the Lord praised by Andhaka, who had already been extolled with hundreds of hymns.
Andhaka was greatly pleased, and being well-pleased, she said this to him:
"I am delighted, my son, that you have obtained this auspicious status as a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya). Now, O best of the excellent, choose quickly a boon that is dear to you. (157.28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld Bhavānī, the bestower of boons, that Andhaka, the foremost of the Gaṇas, bowed down with palms joined in reverence and spoke to Umā, the daughter of Himavat. (157.29)
And whatever boon you grant me, O Goddess, beloved of Ishana,
by means of that entire [boon], may my devotion toward you remain steadfast.
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed Aparājitā then approached Andhaka and, being well-pleased, spoke to him once more.
"I am indeed pleased, my son, by this auspicious knowledge of yours;
for you have today requested from me devotion to the Supreme Lord."
O sinless one, this leadership of the Gaṇas was granted to you by the God of gods himself solely because of your own desire; and for that reason, I have been well-pleased with you.
And because of that cooking of the sun, O dear son, and because of your excellent combat, there was a great expenditure of your sin; by that, you have been rendered preeminent.
Immortal, abandoned by old age, powerful even among the powerful, an ascetic, inexhaustible, and a conqueror—you shall become like Nanda. (157.35)
"You shall be beloved by my god and likewise by me;
become, O sinless one, a glorious servant, the lord of the lords of the Gaṇas. || 157.36 ||
And those who shall glorify you by day or even by night—
for them there shall be renown, fame, heaven, and indeed righteousness.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, Andhaka— honored and esteemed—
was granted leave by Pārvatī and rejoiced as he went to the side of Hara.
Thus, having bestowed his grace upon Andhaka, the god who removes the affliction of darkness sported on that mountain as he pleased.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having made Andhaka a leader of the Gaṇas, Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, [departed].
What did he do after that? Speak further and dispel my curiosity.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having then conquered Andhaka and made him the leader of his hosts,
the destroyer of the afflictions of the gods sported together with the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Then the Mother of the Lord of Beings, who had manifested as the six-faced one,
the best among those skilled in questioning, asked a question concerning her son.
For what purpose, O Lord, is this supreme verse sung by the virtuous:
"Five trees are better than ten storehouses"? (158.4)
A son is born after breaking through the sixteen limbs of the embryo;
how then can a son born from the womb be superior to that son born from the chest? || 158.5 ||
To Umā, who was peerless and who thus asked about inquiry, training, fault, action, and thought, the God spoke these words: || 158.6 ||
"O girl with thighs like plantain stalks, O beautiful-faced one, this matter you ask about is subtle;
I shall explain it to you, O imperishable daughter of the lord of mountains. (158.7)
Since a son born from the womb is superior to one born from the soil,
[the latter] dwells in the Śālmalī, the Vaitaraṇī, and the forests of sword-leaves.
In Kumbhīpāka, Raurava, and Mahāraurava,
as well as in other such hells,
they were surrounded by their own evil deeds and punished at the command of Death by Rākṣasas of cruel actions.
O Goddess, a virtuous son thus protects his ancestors when they are surrounded by terrible misfortunes and afflicted by Rākṣasas; no one else who is resolved upon evil can do so.
Not all men, moreover, possess virtuous sons;
indeed, he alone among them is truly such who delivers his ancestors from fear.
Among them, those of wicked conduct did not attain the status of sons, just as a rogue bull or a eunuch does not, O lord of men. (158.12)
In this regard it is further questioned: "The wise know that suffering is hell;
because he protects his ancestors from that, he is therefore remembered as a 'putra' (son). || 158.13 ||
O Goddess, there is no other connector between father and son;
therefore, the father protects the son, and the son likewise protects him from fear.
But due to the power of the senses, O Pārvatī, they commit even sinful acts toward their own sons; thus they become "unworthy sons" (asat-putra).
"O Goddess, for these trees have had their senses destroyed by Dakṣa’s curse;
they do not commit evil deeds, as their faculties are restrained."
For this reason, O Queen, even from among a hundred sons born of the womb, a single son born of the earth is praised, but not one born of the womb. (158.17)
"O sons, the night-stalkers are causing felling, splitting, terror, and rending of the trees, as if they were the ancestors themselves."
Umā said:
"How do the trees ward off the cutting, the splitting, and the terrifying [torments] by the hell-bound Rākṣasas for the ancestors in the abode of Yama? (158.19)
The God of gods said:
"Listen, O daughter of the Naga, to the division and the separation of the ancestors in the abode of Yama,
and how indeed these trees enable them to cross over."
O Goddess, these trees are devoid of effort and indeed destitute of sense organs;
they are sought after by the gods in sacrifice—[they are the trees]. 158.21.
"O Blessed One, by the curse of Dakṣa, our senses have indeed been impaired. (158.22)
Having reached a state of great abundance of darkness, they are inactive and unable to move;
they are miserable, devoid of sense organs, and enveloped by a vast gloom.
"Bring us, who are devoted to dharma, to this same state.
Having heard these words of theirs, the god born from the waters [spoke].
For the sake of the sacrificial tree, the Lord of Trees spoke these words:
"O stationary beings, welcome to you! I am pleased with those who seek refuge.
My child, I shall destroy this darkness brought about by Dakṣa’s curse. (158.25)
Śāla trees, bilvas, palāśas, varuṇas, and likewise kiṃśukas, as well as rohītakas and whatever other trees originate from the components of sacrifice. || 158.26 ||
Having been well-employed in sacrifices as bark, leaves, fruits, and branches,
you shall attain radiant forms and dwell in my world.
"O you who are followers of these sacrificial trees, go forth as materials for sacrifice; may you attain the same world as they. (158.28)
And by worshipping the Sthāṇu-liṅga with devotion,
you shall purify your bodies through dharma and attain your desired goal.
And as you proceed to the sites of the sacrificial ground,
freed from the darkness of Dakṣa’s curse, you shall move about in my world.
And that man who is childless, he shall have sons through you;
protect him from fear as well, for your dharma shall be great. || 158.31 ||
The trees said:
"How can we [save] those fathers of ours, who have sons, yet are destined for hell?"

Those who sell Soma, those who betray the trusting, those who are intent on the slaughter of living beings, and those who eat the flesh from the back [of an animal while it is still alive]. || 158.33 ||
Those who reviled kings and those who stole their alms-food are enveloped by these terrible, hair-raising consequences of their own deeds.
They are cooked in the terrible hell, crying out with horrific shrieks:
"Alas! We are violently assailed by inauspicious torments! (158.35)
"They will be threatened with death by Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess;
how shall we rescue our ancestors who are being thus tormented and beaten by the Rākṣasas, and who are submerged in hell? (158.36)
Brahmā said:
"You shall uplift those ancestors who are thus being tormented and crushed by the Rākṣasas, and who are submerged in hell. (158.37)
O trees, with attentive minds, listen to me as to how you shall deliver these ancestors who reside in hell. 158.38.
"O sinless ones, you who are devoted to your sons, wherever you may be destined to go, you shall quickly reach that place as soon as you are remembered. (158.39)
"O you who are stationary, listen to this so that you may provide happiness for our ancestors who have fallen into hell and are tormented by sufferings. (158.40)

Furthermore, that man who, according to the rules and with the recitation of mantras, performs for you the purificatory rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) and so forth, may designate you as his sons. || 158.41 ||
And those who have been born before you, whom you shall make free from possessions according to the prescribed rule and establish in the status of sons— you shall deliver them as well.
"And you shall grant all desires as well as supreme happiness;
you shall bring about the exhaustion of the karma of all beings, and likewise the imperishable worlds. (158.43)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the daughter of the mountain asked once more about that supreme procedure;
to her as she was questioning him, Mahādeva spoke these words.
O Goddess, whose thighs are like the trunk of the king of elephants, who moves with the gait of the king of elephants,
listen to the procedure by which a son born of the earth is obtained.
"O Pārvatī, on the following day, thinking 'I shall take hold of the Bhūviruha,' a woman should remain fasting, pure in conduct, and firm in her vows. (158.46)
Then, when the sun, whose rays are like a hundred thousand lotuses, had set behind the western peak,
and the stainless moon had risen, O lady with a face like the moon—
O fortunate one, O supreme mistress, when in a state of calamity, you should invite at night Brahmins who are purifiers and exponents of the Vedas. (158.48)
O lady who is the foremost among the leaders of the wise, these brahmins are indeed mines of the Vedas, like oceans are of jewels; they are to be honored by the thousands.
Where learned Brahmins who know the mantras do not consume the supreme oblation,
there the gods, O Lord of Gods, never partake of the offering at any time.
It does not overflow, it does not cause distress, and darkness does not overcome it;
this is the most excellent of all gifts—that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa. 158.51.
In the state of being a Brahman, O Great Being, the element of space (ākāśadhātu) is for consumption;
