because he consumes the Brahman, he is therefore remembered as a Brāhmaṇa. || 158.52 ||
But those who are born again and initiated by great-souled men—therefore, O Goddess, the name "twice-born" (dvija) should always be applied to them. 158.53.
"Vyoman" is said to mean the sky; the verbal root "vi" is traditionally understood in the sense of reaching.
O Goddess, because these brahmins cause one to reach heaven (divam), they are therefore known as "vipras. (158.54)
For these brahmins were created by the Self-existent One as being composed of the essence of truth;
success cannot be attained through them when they are displeased, even by the gods themselves.
"I am Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Brahmā, Śakra, Anila, and Śikhin;
we do not rejoice in that gift, O Brahmins, in which we are not honored. (158.56)
A wise person should honor those Brahmins by whose grace long life, dharma, strength, happiness, prosperity, fame, and residence in heaven are easily obtained.
Then, having invited the Brahmins, she— clad in pure garments and possessing a radiant smile—
should lie down upon the ground strewn with darbha grass, offering her salutations.
Having passed that night, when the sun has risen, he should take food to be chewed and food to be eaten and go to where there may be a tree. (158.59)
Then, having placed that tree— complete with its banners, its parasol, and its ornaments—
a woman followed the shade of the tree.
Having fed the best of the twice-born with whatever food was available,
he should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) performed by the officiating priests or by himself.
And when the Brahmins were satisfied, he revealed his own inner intention in accordance with the truth, directed toward the Supreme, with the highest sincerity.
"O Blessed Ones, I am childless; I wish to take a tree that has the nature of a son. O sinless ones, you ought indeed to grant me permission to do so."
Then, O beloved, having been authorized by them, one should take that young tree as a son in the presence of the gods of the earth (the Brahmins), O dear one. 158.64.
By this rite, O Goddess, the tree-son [Madhu] was taken;
he released the honey and rained it down for the ancestors dwelling in hell.
O fair-browed one, this son of the tree has been taken according to this rite;
when performed auspiciously, it leads to happiness, but if done otherwise, it brings suffering.
O Goddess with a face like the moon, even from among a hundred virtuous sons,
a single tree planted as a son is considered superior in the status of a son.
Thus has this been taught to you by me, O you whose path of speech is most refined:
that a son born from the womb (kṣetraja) is superior to a son born of the field (koṣṭhaja), just as a tree growing on the ground is superior to one produced from a seed-vessel.
Then, having again prostrated before Maheśvara, the goddess of gods, out of affection and curiosity, spoke these words: || 158.69 ||
"O Lord of Gods, while I was wandering on Mount Mandara during your absence, I beheld an Ashoka tree, tender and most beautiful. (158.70)
And then this thought occurred to me: "This young tree will become my son when I have returned safely from Rudra, free from all obstacles. (158.71)
And from these two breasts of mine, O Mahādeva, purifier of the twice-born, milk issued forth—a stream of nectar, bestowing happiness out of affection for my son. (158.72)
"O Lord, I would take that tree which has my son as its very nature, if you grant me your permission;
for I am subject to your will. (158.73)
"O sinless one, when the gods cast me as the fruit of a son, that young tree was indeed intended to grant satisfaction to me, who am childless; it shall become my son."
To Bhavānī, who was speaking thus, the blessed Lord Bhava,
the scorcher of enemies, spoke these words that issued from his very being.
O Goddess with eyes like full-blown lotuses, how indeed could your son not become one who possesses supreme sovereignty through my ascetic power? 158.76
"O blameless one, you are capable of giving birth to sons through your ascetic power;
and I, too, shall grant you most excellent sons. (158.77)
Or rather, O beloved, this Ashoka tree is to be favored by you;
permitted by me, O Queen, make the Ashoka tree your son.
Knowing her husband to be favorable, that lotus-eyed woman, satisfied and bowing down, spoke thus to the imperishable Maheśvara: || 158.79 ||
"O King, I know the dharma as it truly is: that for women there exists no deity other than their husband, who is indeed the one to be worshipped. (158.80)
"For whatever a woman gives or worships without first addressing her husband, she does not obtain the fruit thereof; such is what we have heard. (158.81)
But that woman who, having consulted with her husband, practices dharma—for her the gods are pleased and her merit is very great, O Lord. (158.82)
But that woman who, disregarding her husband—the deity and the guru—performs meritorious acts according to her own will, she falls into hell. (158.83)
Even in the past, that beautiful woman who, having duly obtained her husband's permission, would inquire after him as if he were still living— 158.84.
For she, O Lord of Gods, having been authorized by him with a joyful heart, obtains abundant fruit in her religious duties. (158.85)
Austerity, fasting, charity, straightforwardness, and truthfulness—even these together are not worth a sixteenth part of service to one's husband. (158.86)
For even she who is fickle in one respect is truly regarded as virtuous if, out of sincerity, she performs service for her husband while on his bed or seat. || 158.87 ||
Having thus spoken to the Lord of the Mountains on the mountain peak, which was variegated with heaps of flowers from the mountain trees,
the beautiful Bhavānī, the foremost of women, wandered there together with him, like the radiance of the sun accompanied by the sun itself.
Thus those two, honored by the gods and honoring one another,
wandered together, revered by the foremost of lords.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sons of Bhūmija," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lord Tryambaka, having understood the resolve of Pārvatī, [acted accordingly].
The best among those skilled in speech addressed the yakṣa Piṅgala Sumāli.
There, the Lord Śaṅkara himself [beheld] Nandin, who was standing by his side— a devotee, a great yogi, and a Gaṇa who had previously received boons.
She will take as her son the tree, the Aśoka, which is the offspring of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains;
all of that depends upon you, therefore act according to my command.
"O hero, Lord of the Gaṇas, act in such a way that wherever the Aśoka tree is found, there food may be seen in great abundance."
O Lord of Yakṣas, arrange it so that this region of the mountain, where the Aśoka tree stands, shall become as delightful as possible.
Thus addressed by the Supreme Lord, Piṅgala, whose eyes were tawny,
spoke together with Somā to the Lord of the thirty gods.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, O Destroyer of Sacrifices, I shall do exactly as you have commanded,
so that both Soma and Nandin will be well-disposed toward me."
Having spoken thus and being granted permission, that Yakṣa, the giver of food to the world,
then prepared an excellent meal beside that Aśoka tree.
When Sumāla had departed, the three-eyed Siṃhakrodha,
a mass of splendor, spoke to Nandin and Diṇḍicaṇḍeśvara.

"O highly intelligent one, tomorrow at dawn, Queen Nandin will worship the Brahmins, who are devoted to Brahman, with a sacrifice; for that purpose, there is need for the Brahmins to be present there. (159.10)
Therefore, O Lord, sent by me, go wherever I tell you and there,
at each step, invite the brahmins.
O Virūpākṣa, those Brāhmaṇas born of Brahmā who dwell in the depths of Pātāla worship Varuṇa in Audakī. || 159.12 ||
Invite without delay those known as the Phenapas, who drink the supreme essence of the juice of the gods, Asuras, and others.
O Lord of Beings, invite those Brāhmaṇas who dwell in Saṃyamanī and wait upon Yama, for they are equal to Brahmā himself.
Likewise, on the peak of Mount Udaya, there is a great lake named Satya,
frequented by royal swans and covered with lovely lotuses.
There dwell those truthful ones, whose wealth is austerity and who are known as the Truthful; it is by their truth that the sun perpetually carries out its daily course.
Having bathed in that lake, the stainless Lord Divākara,
the performer of auspicious deeds, makes his daily departure from it.
Having bowed your head to them and offered yourself,
O Nandīśvara, invite them while manifesting your true devotion before them.
And those Atharvāṅgirasa sages who constantly travel surrounding the chariot of the Sun— invite that host of twice-born ones as well.
And those perfected ones who wander with wheels, those who subsist by gleaning like pigeons,
and those who wait upon Śakra— invite all those twice-born ones as well.
Then, having gone to the assembly hall of Brahmā, he invited those devoted to Brahman and dear to Brahmā,
as well as Brahmā himself together with his wife and the Brāhmaṇas.
"Invite the Bālakhilyas, who dwell in the forest of asceticism and reside on the shores of the Ocean of Milk, having come from the abode of Brahmā."
Those who, together with their wives, their sons, and their sacrificial fires and implements, are my devotees—
to them I am ever well-disposed in my favor, being their leader.
O Lord of Speech, O husband of Suyaśā, having become well-renowned yourself, address those Bālakhilyas who are as difficult to approach as venomous serpents.
Moving through the three worlds like the unimpeded wind,
invite all those brahmins whom you see wherever they may be.
And whatever Pramathas are within your range, O slayers of the enemies of the gods,
may they all come here as servers of food for the brahmins.
Thus addressed by Kapardin, Nandin, who possessed a splendor equal to the sun,
raised his flaming trident and set out for the abode of Varuṇa.
Clad in bark, he whose range was the forest reached the ocean, which appeared like the sky and was surging like an elephant in an arena.
That leader of the Pramathas entered that ocean filled with whales like the blazing sun entering a mass of clouds.
On the surface of the earth and in the netherworld, he of the prowess of the lord of elephant-kings beheld the cow Gā, who was flowing with divine milk, that very source of the nectar of immortality.
Having saluted Surabhi, Nandin, the follower of Śaṅkara and subduer of enemies, entered where Varuṇa sat with his retinue, duly honored.
He beheld the protector of the waters, adorned with divine garments and ornaments, accompanied by hosts of sons and grandsons, and resembling ten thousand suns.
Having been announced beforehand by the gatekeeper,
Nandin then entered the residence of Varuṇa.
And that king, seeing Nandin from afar, was filled with joy;
rising up as he beheld him, he honored the destroyer of Manmatha.
Having personally offered him the guest-offering, a cow, and water for his feet, Varuṇa himself,
the guardian of the waters and the best among speakers, questioned him as he sat there.
"O Blessed One, why have you waited so long today before looking upon us?
We consider the sight of you to be equivalent to the sight of the God of Gods."
"O sinless one, your face appears like that of a thirsty man; it is protected by indragopa insects.
Speak all your intentions; I shall fulfill them for you, there is no doubt. (159.37)
Thus addressed by Varuṇa, who was intent upon that task, the son of Śilāda then spoke to Varuṇa,
who had been undefeated by the Dānavas.
Hara invites you to take his son Aśokataruka, for he is being invited by Umā to sport together with her. (159.39)
Therefore, O son of a god, surrounded by your wives and accompanied by the foam-drinkers,
go tomorrow to Mount Mandara and increase the joy of the Wielder of the Trident.
Having spoken thus and being granted permission by Varuṇa,
that lord of the Gaṇas emerged from Varuṇa’s abode like the sun from a white cloud.
Being honored by the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and even the gods,
Nandin reached Mount Udaya like the arrow of Śiva reaching Tripura.
Then, on the peak of that mountain, which was reddened by the scorching rays [of the sun],
the bird Garuḍa alighted, as if upon the path of the wind.
There he beheld a lake resembling the ocean, adorned with golden lotuses, rich with waves of withered blue lilies, and surrounded by celestial nymphs.
On the shores of that lake, among thousands of *aśoka* trees,
he beheld true sages who resembled ten thousand suns.
Seeing those ascetics, who were as radiant as the sun,
Nandin approached them with his hands joined in reverence and paid homage to the twice-born ones.
Having abandoned all their observances, those ascetics, though established in their vows, attached themselves to Nandin like birds to a tree that provides shelter. || 159.47 ||
Enveloped by them— who had drunk the rays of the sun and wore yellow garments— he, Nandin, shone like Jambudvīpa surrounded by mountains.
Being thus honored by truthful ascetics whose wealth is their austerity, that truthful leader of the hosts shone exceedingly, O Vyāsa, like Maheśvara among sacred fords.
Those ascetics, whose wealth was their austerity, their faces and eyes wide with wonder, spoke with words agitated by joy to Nandin as he sat at ease, saying: "O Truth, you are Truth! (159.50)
O Nandīśvara, after a long time, today indeed there is a rising, a rising radiance;
for by you, O dear one, it has been overtaken as if hell were overcome by Dharma.
"O sinless one, has the Lord of Gods, the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura, come here to sport? It was after seeing that god that you were seen by us. (159.52)
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, we shall behold Śaṅkara here through truth, pure conduct, and pure austerity, together with the sacrifice performed along with you. || 159.53 ||
Thus the son of Śilādā, whose face was like that of the lord of monkeys and who was truthful in speech, spoke these words to the ascetics who were paying him homage: || 159.54 ||
"The Unborn One would never abandon Mount Mandara under any circumstances;
however, I have come to this hermitage of yours on account of a specific task."
The daughter of the mountain will take the Aśoka tree as her son;
there Śarva invites all of you, O best of the twice-born. (159.56)
"Honoring Lord Ambāpati along with Ambā, all of you, who are constant in austerity, go quickly tomorrow to Mount Mandara, the upholder of the earth. (159.57)

There you shall behold Śiva, the Lord who is the sovereign of all, the master of the immortals, adorned by the lord of the stars (the moon), the subduer of the Asuras, the remover of the affliction of the gods, and the destroyer of Hara.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Invitation of the Brāhmaṇas for the Seizing of the Tree-Son," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixtieth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having addressed all those sages who were possessed of truth, heroism, fame, and sacred learning, [he spoke].
Dismissed by them, Nandī went toward Sūryaratha.
At the command of Hara, that lord of beings approached the divine Sun with those seven excellent horses and the best of birds as his charioteer.
He saw those ascetics, who subsisted on rays of light, seated comfortably amidst the thousand sunbeams like birds in the shade.
Then he quickly approached the chariot of the Sun, with Aruṇa as its charioteer,
as well as Aṃśumālin, Atri, and also Atharvan and Aṅgiras.
Then the auspicious Nandin addressed the gods, the ṛṣis, the serpents, and the horses,
desiring to please Rudra with the Ādityas, Aśvas, and others.
Having said "So be it," the Lord of Beings then quickly departed from Sūryavāha,
after taking leave of the gods, the ṛṣis, and the serpents.
Swift as the wind or like Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā,
Nandin reached Kailāsa, the abode of the Lord of Wealth.
Beholding that mountain, the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), which resembled a white cloud and possessed the luster of kunda flowers, the moon, and silver, he rejoiced.
That Lord of Beings, who carries out the word of the Lord of Mountains, reached the auspicious golden palace on the summit of the mountain belonging to the Lord of Wealth.
Situated on the peak of Kailāsa, possessing a splendor equal to the peak of Kailāsa itself,
it was endowed with mansions and palaces, appearing as if it were the very embodiment of prosperity.
It resounded day and night with banners and flags adorned with rows of tinkling bells, and with the laughter and clamor of the city dwellers.
Amidst the sounding of hundreds of musical instruments, including the most terrible drums,
the members of the assembly— accomplished in sacrifice and Vedic study— take their seats there.
Then, he reached that assembly hall of Rudra, graced with splendors,
where the son of the sage Viśravas was seated.
Nandin beheld the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), endowed with supreme supernatural power and likewise attended by splendor, served by a host of celestial women.
Śuktikarṇa was surrounded by yakṣa lords named Śuktikarṇas;
he, whose eyes were long and tawny like those of a monkey, was being praised with songs by the gandharvas.
Intoxicated by his friendship with Maheśvara and by the pride of granting boons, he was adorned with a pure and shimmering necklace of gold.
And Dhanada, seeing that excellent follower of Śaṅkara,
quickly rose from his seat while paying homage to Śaṅkara and Soma.
Rising from his golden seat,
the giver of wealth shone like the sun rising from a lofty mountain peak abounding in blossoming *aśoka* trees.
As he sprang up swiftly toward the lord of the yakṣas, the yakṣas leapt up after him,
like blazing planets following the lord of the planets at the waning of the day.
Then that giver of wealth, having offered the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya) to Nandin,
bowed mentally to Hara along with his sons, wife, and ministers.
Then, after engaging in various kinds of conversation concerning Maheśvara,
Dhanada asked Nandin why it was that he had come after such a long time.
Nandin said:
"The daughter of the mountain will take her son, the Ashoka tree;
there Maheśvara, the Lord of Wealth, invites you. (160.22)
"Tomorrow, O Lord of Wealth, go to Mandara together with your sons, your wife, your followers, and the hosts of Apsarases; the Lord of Gods is pleased with you."
Having thus addressed the Giver of Wealth, Nandin, who resembled Yama himself, was dismissed by the Giver of Wealth and departed for Saṃyamanī, the city of Yama.
That leader of the hosts saw Yama, the proclaimer of dharma, the lord who takes away living beings,
together with Agni, Dharma, and Vyādhi.
Seeing Nandin approaching, Yama, surrounded by hundreds of spirits,
then fell at Nandin’s feet with both his feet and was filled with joy.
Having performed an unsurpassed worship of him as if he were Rudra himself,
Yama earnestly asked Nandin about the reason for his long absence.
Nandi said:
"The Daughter of the Mountain will take you, her son, to the Ashoka tree;
there the god Śaṅkara invites you along with your followers."
And those twice-born ones who dwell within this realm—
the god addresses them, honoring them with great respect.
"Since the Blessed One has risen at dawn, and it is the auspicious hour, you ought to go to Mount Mandara, honoring the Lord Īśāna who is fond of the proper time."
Having been told "So be it" by Yama and by those twice-born ones who were like fire,
Nandin then departed from the abode of the Son of the Sun and went to the world of Śakra.
Nandi quickly entered that wondrous world of Indra, the abode of the virtuous, just as the slayer of serpents [Garuḍa] enters the womb of a serpent.
Nandin beheld Śakra in the Sudharmā hall, surrounded by the immortals in the Sudharmā assembly, listening to celestial music.
And Śakra, having placed the god Nandin— the servant of the God of gods—
before his thousand eyes out of joy, gazed at him intently.
Having received worship equal to that of Rudra, he of immeasurable soul sat upon an excellent seat near Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods.
Sitting near him as he sat, Śatakratu, the subduer of enemies, did not reach satiety even while drinking him in with his thousand eyes. (160.36)
Then Vṛtrabalāri, with joy, questioned Nandin, who was as radiant as the sun: "Why have you returned after such a long time?"
Thus addressed by the god who dwells in heaven, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the divine one,
scented with mandāra flowers, replied composedly.
The daughter of the mountain will take Aśokataruka as her son;
there the Lord, the protector of beings, invites you along with the gods.
Śaṅkara also invites those twice-born ones who were previously there, as well as those who now dwell in your abode, together with their sons and wives.
Tomorrow, O Lord of Gods, by the command of the God of Gods, you shall go to Mandara with your wife and sons; go and pay homage to the Lord of Mountains.
O best of gods, when you have gone to the festival of the Aśoka tree, the Lord of Gods, the remover of the suffering of gods and men, will attain supreme joy. (160.42)
Having prostrated before the Lord Maheśa— the wielder of the crescent moon and the trident, the bearer of the Pināka bow, the husband of the daughter of the king of mountains,
and the majestic one— you shall once again go to the assembly of the celestial realm.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Summoning of the Brahmins," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been granted permission by Śakra, Nandin, the leader of the Pramathas, [proceeded].
The one of great splendor resolved to go to the abode of Brahmā.
In a moment, that attendant of the Four-faced One, possessing great speed like the wind of great velocity, reached the Vairāja abode.
The radiant Nandin entered that assembly hall, which was free from fatigue like Mount Meru, just as a ray of the sun enters it.
Like a story full of wonderful meanings, endowed with many diverse themes,
Nandin beheld that assembly hall, which was filled with many marvels.
In that assembly hall,
Nandin beheld the wondrous lotus-born Brahmā seated together with ascetics, surrounded by the five classes of gods.
As he was expounding the meaning of the Vedas to those ascetics who were questioning him, and as he heard all those masters of the commentaries saying "Excellent! to him, || 161.6 ||
Nandin quickly and duly worshipped the Grandfather;
thereupon, the Grandfather spoke to Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas.
"Why have you returned so late? he asked, and he replied to him:
"The daughter of the mountain will take the Aśoka tree as her son. (161.8)
"O Blessed One, there the god Śaṅkara invites you, as well as these [sages] who shine like fire through their asceticism, who possess the Vedas, and who proclaim the Vedic teachings. (161.9)
The Lord of the Gods, having invited ten million sacrifices, invites you,
along with all the ascetics, to Mandara, which possesses wonderful caves.
"Go, O giver of honor to the gods; the Unborn One issues this command.
Having heard these words of Nandin, he who is the fulfiller of such speech [replied].
The Grandfather, appearing joyful in form, spoke thus to him who was fond of recitation:
"O Nandīśvara, go forth with success and auspiciously."
I too shall come to Śiva’s presence along with these;
and this Aśoka shall be released from the darkness caused by Dakṣa’s curse.
"The goddess, the daughter of Himavat, shall take this boy as her son.
Having been addressed thus, the beloved and foremost follower of the Lord paid his respects to the Lord.
Departing quickly from the abode of Brahmā, he went to the Ocean of Milk,
which was like a garland for the sea, though its shore was not adorned with garlands.
The chief of the assembly of Gaṇeśvaras approached those Brahmins, the Bālakhilyas, whose wealth was their asceticism, who were as difficult to withstand as the winds that blow at the shore.
The Lord of the Gaṇas beheld them joined by various observances;
and seeing Gaṇeśa, the husband of Suyaśā, bowing before him, [he spoke].
Those whose wealth was asceticism rejoiced with favorable benedictions;
standing in their midst, Nandi shone amidst the joyful ascetics.
Just as the moon, situated in the midst of the planets of gentle form, [shines],
so too [does he shine] through the offering of water for the feet, the arghya-offering, and indeed by the granting of fruits.
Having worshipped the god Nandin, the Bālakhilyas said to him:
"O Lord of the Pramathas, why have you come here after such a long time?
Shall we behold the Lord of Gods, Bhava, the husband of Ambā, together with Ambā?"
Then Nandin, the most excellent lord of the Pramathas, addressed these words to the best of the twice-born, who were adorned with ornaments, in that assembly of brahmins: || 161.21 ||
"O ascetics rich in austerity, Lord Śaṅkara, accompanied by Ambikā, does not come here to Mandara; hear from me now why he has come here."
The Mountain’s Daughter shall take Aśokataruka as her son;
there the divine Lord Śaṅkara invites you.
"Tomorrow, O foremost of brahmins, all of you, together with your wives, disciples, sons, and sacred fires, go to Mount Mandara; show favor to me and my mother."
Thus addressed by Nandin, the great sages, the Bālakhilyas,
spoke these words to Gaṇeśa out of their intense devotion to the Lord.
"O Nandin, O Lord, we shall come tomorrow at dawn;
go without hindrance to Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves."
Bowed down by the Bālakhilyas and honored by them, he invited all those best of the twice-born to three steps;
then, having returned, he went to Mount Mandara where he remained together with the Goddess.

Then the Lord of the Gaṇas, having approached the Lord of Beings, the Master of the Gods, the bestower of boons upon Kubera, who was like a bee at the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, addressed him thus:

161.28. Then the Lord of the Gaṇas, having approached the Lord of Beings, the Master of the Gods, the bestower of boons upon Kubera, who was like a bee at the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, addressed him thus:

O Destroyer of Tripura, O Destroyer of Time! All those brahmins who roam in heaven and on earth, endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, discipline, purity, and goodness—they have all been invited by me at your command.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Invitation of the Brahmins for the Seizing of Taruputra," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: When the Brahmins had been invited to the three steps of Nārāyaṇa...
Then, when Nandin, the leader of the hosts of the Gaṇas, had returned, || 162.1 ||
The Blessed One, the destroyer of those who desire sacrifice, the shatterer of Pūṣan’s teeth, wearing a garland and a crown, powerful and like Time itself, spoke these words at the proper time.
O Ambikā, all Brāhmaṇas in the world are equal to a Brāhmaṇa;
being invited, O lady of beautiful hips, do that which is in your mind.
"Where that *aśoka* tree stands, my dear son, there Piṅgala, the giver of food, prepares a meal for you, my beloved. (162.4)
"O Goddess, Daughter of the Mountain King, act in such a way that tomorrow at dawn we may go with Nandin to the side of the Aśoka tree, O Joyful One."

O Mother of the World, O Daughter of the Mountain, for the sake of your welfare, the entire universe— including the sky, the network of stars, and the netherworld— will indeed be gathered together there.
And by this Nandin, as he was addressing the best of the twice-born,
were traversed the three steps of Nārāyaṇa that had been stepped over by Trivikrama.
Therefore, O lady of excellent hips, O most noble one, O giver of boons,
O bestower of boons, I shall grant you a boon, O beloved, if it is pleasing to you.
Then the Goddess spoke to her beloved Hara, the Lord of Heaven, the master of Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa,
the bestower of boons, who is adorned with the crescent moon.
"This god Nandīśvara is our supreme benefactor;
he deserves thousands of millions of boons from you, without a doubt. (162.10)
For you are the granter of boons to the worlds and the lord even of the worlds;
if you are pleased, O Lord of the Mountain, grant a most excellent boon.
Then the god Kṛttivāsas, having smelled the head of Nandin, said to the lord of the Pramathas: "Let a desired boon be chosen."
Then Nandin, the beloved of Śaṅkara, who had the face of the lord of monkeys and a splendor like that of the lord of the gods, bowed his head and spoke.
"By your power, O Lord of Gods, I am a granter of boons, free from old age and death;
I am possessed of enjoyments and honored by gods, dānavas, and kinnaras who are themselves worthy of worship. (162.14)
"What need have I for a boon, O Śarva, since I behold your two feet, worshipped by millions of boons and honored by the Pramathas, together with Ambā? (162.15)
O Lord of Cows, if you are pleased with this boon of mine,
O Maheśvara, let my devotion toward you and Sāmba be eternal.
O best of gods, you have been made the lord of the hosts by me for the sake of the remaining groups who are superior to me; what else will you do beyond this?
Thus, as Nandin was speaking with humility,
the three-eyed god, who has the moon as his crest-ornament, looked upon him with affection.
Then, having wiped [his face] with a hand as blue as a lotus, the Blessed Lord Hara spoke with joy, greatly gladdening Nandin.
"Nandī, you possess devotion toward me, along with your wife and your retinue;
and honoring that devotion, I have placed you by my side."
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, compared to truth, dharma, austerity, charity, cows, and the Vedas— compared to all these, you are dearer to me."
O Lord of the World, whoever shall proclaim your name at dawn will obtain the full fruit of a properly performed horse sacrifice.
Whoever hates you is hateful to me, even if he is devoted to dharma;
whoever is dear to you shall always be dear to me.
The man who, having uttered "Salutation to Nandīśvara," goes to sleep,
shall indeed have no fear from the kings of the Kuṣmāṇḍas.
While Brahmā was thus speaking this hymn of praise for the qualities of Nandīśvara, the exceedingly fierce twilight approached his body.
The Lord, who knows the proper time and who is Hara, the destroyer of Time itself,
perceiving that the hour for his dance had arrived, considered it to be the right moment.
Then, having touched water with his hands, the Lord, the creator of the waters and protector of the three worlds,
sat for the twilight prayers, guarding the established order of the world.
With his hands outstretched and his knees placed in the lotus posture,
the god appeared like the sun in the sky with its rays extended.
Having recited that supreme mantra, which is born from the essence of the three Vedas,
Bhava, the four-faced one, danced skillfully and with agility.
Seeing her husband dancing with his sprout-like hands entwined,
the queen, his partner in dharma, danced along with him, consoling her husband.
Seeing the couple dancing, Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas,
began to dance with loud laughter, bringing joy to the two deities.
Beholding the god, Ambā, and Nandin dancing,
the Pramathas, resembling dark clouds, began to dance to the sound of musical instruments.
Then the kettledrums, the jharjharas, the kikhis, the ānakas,
the maṇḍukas, the āḍambaras, the ḍiṇḍimas, and the conch shells all resounded together.
Ambikā performed a graceful dance again and again;
Nandin let out a laugh, and the fierce Pramathas roared aloud.
Rich with the sounds of excellent musical instruments, the fierce twilight shone like a thunderbolt from Śiva, resembling the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha). || 162.35 ||
Some danced and laughed, while others muttered prayers;
still others sang most sweetly, like Gandharvas, being the Lord's attendants.
Then, when the full-orbed moon, exceedingly pure, had risen and pressed against the surface of the sky,
the one adorned by the moon as his ornament [appeared].
Having completed the observance, the Lord, accompanied by Ambā and the attendants of Nandīśa, ceased from that festival and spoke thus to Pārvatī: || 162.38 ||
O you of immeasurable prowess, having stayed this night,
tomorrow you shall take the son of the Ashoka tree.
Holding the darbha grass, she who bore the dhāraṇīs lay down upon that blade of grass;
at the word of the gods, she of firm vows slept for a single night.
Then, when the sun, the thousand-rayed one, had risen,
the Sun-born said to Umā, "Let us go where your son Aśoka is."
Then the Blessed Lady Dhanyā, the giver of wealth, who is honored by the Giver of Wealth, spoke to Bhava, her ornaments jingling: "Let us depart. (162.42)
Traveling on foot, the Blessed One Hara— the protector of trees—
accompanied by Nandin and Ambikā, reached that Aśoka tree.
There he saw the yakṣa Piṅgala, resembling a blazing fire, together with the Pramathas, preparing food for the giver of food.
Then, the lord of all that is to be chewed, eaten, sucked, and licked— the best among those who know how to heap things together— beheld there mounds resembling mountains.
Then, seeing the food prepared by the yakṣa, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
together with Ambikā and Nandin, experienced incomparable joy.
Then the divine Grandfather, together with the gods, apsarases, and serpents,
went there filled with joy to where Samba, the lord of Ambika, was.
Having bowed down to Mahādeva and being honored by him in return, those gods then surrounded that Aśoka tree and spoke these words in the presence of Hara: || 162.48 ||
"O dwellers of heaven, from this day forward, this tree shall be endowed with happiness on all sides, liberated from the darkness of Dakṣa’s curse."
Immortal, abandoned by old age, and freed from all suffering;
richly adorned with all ornaments and flowers, and endowed with every fragrance and flavor.
"He shall indeed be the granter of all desires, possessing flowers and fruits according to one's wish; of this there is no doubt, and he will be very dearly beloved by the Goddess."

Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord of the Mountains, the dispeller of the distress of those who bow before him and the granter of desires, spoke to the daughter of the Mountain King, saying, "Behold these mountains of food."
Beholding those towering heaps of food and drink that resembled mountains,
Piṅgala’s mother, the mistress of the gods, was deeply gratified.
The daughter of the mountain joined the excellent Yakṣa Piṅgala, who was possessed by Sumālī, with a boon; and Maheśvara spoke to her.
"O Queen, all this excellent food, both solid and soft, is ready for you;
do whatever you desire to do—why do you remain seated? (162.55)
Then she, exceedingly delighted and dwelling in celestial raiment,
took leave of Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, who possesses the speed of thought.
The goddess Vibhāvarī, who bestows sorrow upon the Daityas,
affectionately adorned that Aśoka tree with various kinds of ornaments.
And before him, the Daughter of the Mountain held aloft a parasol, illuminated by strings of pearls and adorned with peacock feathers.
And with fragrant sandalwood of various colors, the queen marked her body from head to foot with excellent streaks of paste. (162.59)
And with bands made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with jewels,
he decorated his beloved Aśoka tree on all sides.
Pārvatī fastened strings of pearls upon its branches and twigs;
with them, it shone like the moon among the stars.
Then Guhāraṇi, the mother of the worlds, longing for her son, clothed that Aśoka tree in pairs of white garments.
Then the bestower of boons to the gods offered an incense composed of a mixture of śrīveṣṭaka, nameru, guggulu, and clarified butter.
Then, with the sounding of conchs and the noise of divine trumpets,
Bali’s wife caused him to break his fast as he was performing austerities.
As she was thus worshipping that tree, which possessed the luster of nectar and was adorned with a necklace of moonstones,
milk flowed from her breasts due to the intense surge of maternal affection for her son.
Honored by Umā, that Aśoka tree, the illuminator of the forest,
shone exceedingly there like the beautiful Spring personified.
Having given to those Brahmins, who were equal to Brahmā himself, whatever they desired, Nandinātha caused them to recite the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Then, at the conclusion of the proclamation of the auspicious day and the pronouncement of blessings for both,
the queen, having obtained her husband’s permission, spoke to those sages.
"O Blessed Ones, I am childless; today I shall take this Aśoka tree as my son. You should deign to grant me your permission. (162.69)
To the goddess Pārvatī, who was speaking thus and longing for a son, all the twice-born spoke in unison: "Take whichever you desire. (162.70)
Then a divine sound from the conch shell, accompanied by the sounds of all musical instruments, resounded,
filling the entire threefold domain of Nārāyaṇa.
The Brahmins recited the Vedas, the throngs of Apsarases danced,
and all the Pramathas, along with the Gandharvas and great serpents, raised a shout of joy.
And the six seasons, exultant with their respective collections of flowers,
adorned both the Aśoka tree and that circle of deities.
The gods, filled with joy, beheld that festival at the Aśoka tree, where celestial music was played and throngs of Apsarases danced.
Playing his kacchapī lute, Nārada, the best among lute-players, danced with joy like a fire fanned by the wind. || 162.75 ||
Rich in the wealth of asceticism and honored by the gods as the giver of riches,
she shone there while being worshipped, like the radiance of the sun.
Having completed her vow and taken the aśoka sapling,
the daughter of the mountain king shone like the earth sprinkled with water.
Then, commanded by Nandīśvara, those thousands of Pramathas,
who were devoted to the brahmins, quickly offered their own seats to the brahmins.
There arose the sound of seats made of gold, silver, and radiant crystal, being strewn about by the Pramathas.
The roar of the Pramathas, as they carried their seats like great rain-showers upon the peaks of Mount Meru with blades of kusha grass, resounded loudly.

Like roaring clouds at the end of the rainy season, [they were like] those desiring the choice food of the year, with [weapons] resting on their shoulders, in their hands, and even upon their heads. 162.81.
Seated upon their thrones, the Pramathas shone like mountains with the sun and fire;
some brought things quickly, while others held them steady.
Those Pramathas, joyful in appearance and possessing great seats,
were seated upon thrones each a hundred yojanas in width and separated by intervals of a yojana.
A row of seats, unattached and fashioned by Viśvakarman, was created on the auspicious slope of Mount Mandara; from these rows of seats, the brahmins emerged.
From all the heat-radiating [rays] that have emerged, there is an equal lack of moisture from the clouds.
Having seen them like two bathed paths, their seats and ornaments trembled;
those thousand rows were spread out upon the vast Mount Mandara.
Having summoned the twice-born, who were anointed with yakṣa-unguents mixed with mud, wearing crests and garlands of flowers, and standing ready with uplifted [offerings].
With *mandāra* trees and their clusters of blossoms, as well as with *pāribhadra* trees,
the twice-born ones shone like gods accompanied by the songs of their consorts amidst the breezes.
Then the gods scattered very fine, fragrant, and golden-hued scented powders all around those gods of the earth.
Marked with the paste of divine sandalwood and sprinkled with divine powders,
the brahmins shone as they stood together in one place, like so many sacrificial fires gathered in a single spot.
Having caused divine incense to be wafted everywhere,
he then [beheld] one resembling crystal, as if gathered from the pollen of lotuses.
After the attendants of Śaṅkara had provided them with water for washing their hands in a moment,
those heroes, girding their loins like elephants with tightened girths,
began to surround the bulls among Brahmins. (162.92)
Then, in a mere moment, the gods humbly presented the twice-born with vessels made of gold, silver, and crystal. (162.93)
Having repeatedly cleared the path with their staffs, they created a circle of water;
then they properly provided food, edibles, meals, and drinks on all sides.
He who possesses the meaning—whether it be the cities of Hari, Puru, Asura, or Rāṭ;
whether situated in the eye, in the heart, in the mouth, or indicated by the hand. (162.95)
The lords of the Pramathas gave to the Brahmins and the learned;
some offered water that increases virtue from golden jars.
Some move about proclaiming, "Water!
while others [attend him] with fragrant chowries that possess the luster of moonbeams.
The delighted Pramathas, who are the very essence of ascetic power, greeted the Brahmins;
as did the celestial women dwelling in the three worlds. 98.
There, each of the brahmins was served like Vāsava by throngs of Apsarases adorned with every ornament.
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, Tumburu, and Parvata likewise danced, stealing the minds of the gods in every direction.
Kustumburu, Śāliśiras, Parjanya, Gaṇḍamaṇḍaka,
Citrāṅgada, Citrasena, Citra, and Citraratha.
These divine Gandharvas, fond of musical instruments and beloved by Hara,
sing songs that kindle passion amidst celestial melodies.
There, an excellent incense made from *nameru* and *guggulu*, mixed and sprinkled with streams of clarified butter, was being wafted about by female door-keepers.
For whose sake this verse, marked with three incense marks, wanders through the three worlds of Nārāyaṇa while being honored by the gods, including Indra. (162.104)
The gods attain satisfaction from guggulu, nameru, and the smoke of clarified butter, just as they do at the sight of beloved ones. || 162.105 ||
The winds could not obstruct the course of these three types of incense:
that of guggulu, that of nameru, and indeed that of the clarified butter incense.
Seeing that festival of the trees, the Lord Śiva,
who bears the moon upon his crest and bestows joy upon Pārvatī, repeatedly experienced unsurpassed delight.
While Paśupati, the lord of vows, was repeatedly rejoicing, O Hari,
the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, were filled with joy at the sight of Paśupati.
With Apsarases dancing in turn, perfumed with divine incense,
and strewn with seasonal flowers, that assembly hall appeared like the sky.
Then, with that rice cooked in milk,
which was like nectar, all those best of the twice-born,
honored by the world, were satiated with various kinds of food, edibles, and drinks.
Then there arose the auspicious sound of "Puṇyāha! uttered by the Brahmins, filling the three worlds—a sacred sound that delights the ears and strikes terror into the Rākṣasas and Asuras.
Then, having greeted Sāmba, Aśoka, Sahara, and Nandin with blessings accompanied by flowers and unbroken grains,
all those great ones— possessing beautiful voices and wearing sacred threads and matted locks— [spoke].
Having paid homage to Virūpākṣa, the brahmins departed as they had come.
And the gods, having been honored by the wielder of the trident with gifts and words of praise,
all departed as they had come, surrounding Śatakratu.
And all the hosts, together with their leaders, honored by Gaṇapāla,
went each to his own dwelling, their garments fluttering with joy.
"Oh, what great good fortune for the Goddess! Oh, how dear Hara is to her!
Oh, we have indeed observed such agitation on the part of the God for the sake of the Goddess!"
How can she who is not so beloved by her husband as the Daughter of the Mountain is by the Lord be called fortunate? And why does she even bear the nature of womanhood? || 162.117 ||
I consider the asceticism performed by the Daughter of the Mountain to be supremely radiant,
for by that asceticism the bull-bannered Lord, the bestower of boons, was won over.
Oh, how subtle is the power of women, which is exceedingly difficult even for the gods to overcome;
by it, lords equal to Rudra have come under the sway of women.
There, other high-souled lords of the Gaṇas said to them:
"This is surely a god who remains here in the form of a wife. || 162.120 ||
"Do not despise that goddess; why do you two not perceive her through yoga?
Speaking thus to one another, those best of the Gaṇas departed for their own abodes, shining like fires.
The god, together with Nandin and his beautiful consort Ambā,
sat beneath an ashoka tree, honored by Ambikā.
Then, having bowed to the boon-granting Lord who is adorned by Soma,
the source of all speech addressed her husband, the lord of the hosts of beings.
I have become completely fulfilled, O destroyer of Tripura and Andhaka,
since I have made the Ashoka tree my natural-born son.
O Creator of the World, by your power, the entire three worlds, both collectively and individually, have assembled here for the festival of my son’s tree.
Surely, O God, my well-performed austerity has become supremely radiant, since you, the Lord and Master of all beings, have been found by me, O God. || 162.126 ||
And that fruit of a beloved son which was formerly stolen from me by the gods— all of that has been restored to me upon obtaining my son, the Ashoka tree.
"O Lord, there is no other woman in the three worlds more fortunate than I, O Hero, since you, the Great Lord, are my husband and the master of my conduct. (162.128)
Having spoken thus out of affection, Bhavānī, wearing a string of pearls,
fell at the feet of the God, her eyes filled with tears.
Having raised her up and embraced her as she lay distressed, Giriśa placed his own thigh against her thighs and spoke these words with affection.
O beloved, you are my goddess, virtuous, chaste, and my partner in dharma;
you are devoted to Brahman, a source of refuge, and always dear to me.
"Therefore, O Goddess, even that which is not to be done has been done by me for your sake;
how much more so this act, which is mingled with glory and endowed with righteousness?"
"O Goddess, the Brahmins and the gods along with their hosts have been gratified by you;
and this dear little son, O beloved, has been taken up by you from the Ashoka tree. (162.133)
"Come, O Queen, let us go home; your heart's desire is fulfilled.
We shall see that son of yours once more, adorned with clusters of blossoms. (162.134)
Thus addressed by her husband, that virtuous woman, her face and eyes filled with joy,
spoke these words there to the green horse, she who had eyes like a deer’s.
"O deer-eyed Hari, protect this son of mine, this excellent son, who stands here; guard him with effort from lions, elephants, horses, and even from the fall of an egg-born bird."
Or even if this little Aśoka tree of mine should be adorned with clusters of blossoms, then you ought to come and see me. || 162.137 ||
Having thus instructed Harita, the goddess Umā, whose eyes were like those of a startled doe,
cast a sidelong glance with her eye and entered her abode together with her husband, like the splendor entering the orb of the sun.
Thus, together with Paśupati, the Goddess, having taken her son— the young Aśoka tree— into her arms,
entered her own abode with a joyful heart, standing in the midst of her delighted attendants.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Seizing of the Son by the Aśoka Tree," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-third chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having taken up the splendor of Śarva, what did Vahni do then?
How was Skanda born, and in what place did he of great splendor arise?
How was he consecrated as commander-in-chief by the best of the gods?
For what purpose was he consecrated, and in which region, O Lord? (163.2)
"And how was Tāraka slain by him at the forefront of the battle?
O great sage, I desire to know this through your grace. (163.3)
Thus addressed by Vyāsa, whose actions are untainted,
the wise son of the Grandfather, the best among speakers, then spoke.
Sanatkumāra said: "Even the radiant Pāvaka was not able to sustain that three-eyed splendor, which had arisen from the resolve of his son."
Although he was burning with that brilliance and causing pain to all living beings,
he entreated Gaṅgā to bear his fiery energy.
Requested by him, that goddess who dwells in the three worlds, Agni, spoke with a sweet voice and a sense of apprehension: "So be it. (163.7)
Then the radiant bearer of oblations, himself full of splendor, transferred that energy of the God of gods into the Gaṅgā by means of his yogic power.
Although she knew it was difficult to fulfill, that fair-faced one consented,
for the best of rivers fears the fault of failing those who come to her with requests.
Then, by the power of his splendor, she quickly became slow-moving and languid,
with her face and breasts turning dark.
With her slender line of body hair, which had the luster of crushed collyrium,
she shone like a streak of the moon at the end of the rainy season across a dark mass of clouds.
Then the queen, her eyes somewhat clouded, fell into a state of languor; she found no pleasure at all in her couches or seats.
Although touched by the cool, nectar-dripping rays of the moon,
that sinless woman withered away, being consumed by his splendor at that time.
On that auspicious day, in a place resplendent with clusters of reeds, he then discharged that fierce energy of Hara.
From the midst of the arrow, there emerged a boy of youthful prowess,
with six faces and twelve arms, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Having kindled the fire there according to the prescribed rites, Viśvāmitra, whose splendor was like that of fire, then performed the birth-rites for the noble-born child.
Then the Kṛttikās, seeing him, their breasts overflowing with milk,
approached his side.
The Vedas, along with the Upavedas and the Saṃgrahas,
all the arts and sciences, Lakṣmī, Medhā, and Sarasvatī, waited upon him.
Beauty, virtue, compassion, forbearance, fortitude, courage, valor,
yoga, splendor, strength, wisdom, steadfastness, profundity, and noble conduct.
Then, having taken up a divine bow, he of wondrous prowess effortlessly fixed an arrow and released it at the mountain.
Suddenly split by him, that excellent peak of the mountain fell down instantly,
while the birds, terrified and panicked with fear, flew about in confusion.
Seeing that great marvel, wonder and fear arose simultaneously among the beings dwelling there. (163.22)
Then, perceiving that danger from him,
the destroyer of Bala dispatched the Mothers for the destruction of the one of immeasurable luster.
Having arrived there and seen that treasury of splendors, the mothers,
their minds captivated by his brilliance, sought refuge in him alone.
Then the subduer of Pāka, enraged, arrived together with the hosts of the gods,
mounted upon the back of the elephant Airāvata.
Seeing the gods approaching, the one of great splendor roared loudly and,
filled with rage, rushed toward them like a lion toward elephants in rut.
By that roar, the inhabitants of heaven were repeatedly stupefied;
even the flow of rut from the temples of Airāvaṇa was brought to a halt.
And the three-eyed son of those gods, the destroyer of the pride of the gods, discharged thousands of blazing rays.
The faces of the enemies of the asuras, their luster destroyed by the flames,
became like lotuses in the lakes scorched by frost.
Then, taking up his thunderbolt, which blazed with the brilliance of fire,
Śatakratu, the corners of his eyes copper-red with rage, hurled it forth.
By that vajra-strike, he then became two-bodied;
and with both bodies, he rushed toward Purandara.
Then, quickly casting aside his pride, the subduer of Pāka bowed down to that treasury of splendor and, being utterly defeated, spoke thus: (163.32)
"Accept even this kingdom, which is desired by the wise;
you alone, O son of Agni, are fit for the protection of the worlds."
Even though there are other luminaries capable of dispelling darkness, it is into fire alone that the meritorious oblation is offered. || 163.34 ||
—the best among the powerful, having smiled, spoke to the lord of the gods: || 163.35 ||
"O Śakra, you yourself rule this kingdom which you have long desired!
O Purandara, I have no need for it because of its many faults. || 163.36 ||
Having heard those words of Skanda, whose mind was untiring,
the glorious Lord of Śacī spoke again in speech that was meaningful and gentle.
Show us the various kinds of manifold effects—those that are united and those that are divided. || 163.39 ||
When he had spoken thus, the one possessing the brilliance of fire replied with these words,
preceded by a smile, in a voice that was both affectionate and deep.
O Śakra, my mind cannot be forcibly shaken;
nor is water heated by the flames of the lord of rivers. (163.41)
O lotus-eyed one, O subduer of Pāka, I do not desire sovereignty— even in my mind— as it is the eternal abode of faults.
Having heard those words of his, he desired to speak again,
as if bathing Skanda with eyes that were dripping with nectar.
O Lord, this is not surprising in you, who are a praiseworthy mine of splendors;
for those who possess such power do not become attached even to very great enjoyments.
"Be consecrated to the generalship of the gods for the accomplishment of their purpose;
I shall honor your form here, O Lord, but I do not issue this command. (163.45)
Then, having heard those words, the twelve-eyed one of great arms and immense prowess spoke thus to the thousand-eyed Puruhūta:
The glorious, imperishable Lord of the worlds, who is without another, the immeasurable Self, whose banner bears the bull— Purandara— is my sovereign.
"O Śatakratu, having propitiated that Lord with devotion, receive his command;
I shall carry out whatever that Lord shall give me. (163.48)
Having understood his intention, the God of gods, whose banner bears the bull,
arrived together with his wife, desiring then to see his son.
Vahni accompanied by Svāhā, Gaṅgā the best of rivers,
and the Kṛttikās, all greatly rejoiced at Śveta, the foremost of mountains.
Then, arriving there simultaneously upon that most excellent peak of Śveta,
they wondered, "To whom indeed will Skanda now advance?"
Then, having understood their intention, Skanda, the lord of yogins and the best among the wise, became sixfold with great power.
Skanda went to Mahādeva; Viśākha went to the daughter of Himavat;
Naigameṣa went to Gaṅgā; and the highly effulgent Śākha went to Agni.
Filled with joy, Guha, wearing side-locks of hair like a crow's wing, went to Svāhā;
and the glorious six-faced one rushed toward the Kṛttikās with speed.
The Lord, the son of the God of gods, the master of yogins, simultaneously fulfilled the desires of them all with his various forms.
Then Śambhu gave him the fourfold collection of weapons,
and Pārvatī gave him the crest-jewel that dripped with drops of nectar.
With her eyes wide open in wonder, Guhā gave him a single-strand necklace that was as pure as the Gaṅgā, originating from nectar and purified by her own mind.
The Fire-god gave to his capable son a heavy, radiant, and unfailing spear that takes the lives of enemies.
Svāhā gave to the high-souled one a great, divine, red banner, radiant as a blazing fire and resounding with the tinkling of small bells.
And the Kṛttikās gave him a garland of excellent fragrance, in full bloom, tinged with its own pollen, and with curved filaments.
Then all the gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
arrived at the beautiful peak of Mount Śveta, desiring to behold the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva).
Then Mahādeva honored all those celestial beings who had arrived there together with a gracious look.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the gods of gods and received his permission, the inhabitants of heaven,
possessed of immeasurable splendor, sat down upon rocks as white as the moon.
The mountain, though already lofty-peaked, white, and radiant,
became even more resplendent by the convergence of those splendors.
Then, urged by all the gods, the lord of the gods,
the best among speakers, bowed to Mahādeva and made this request.
O Lord, our prosperity was forcibly seized by the one named Tāraka;
his thunderbolt met with bluntness against his hard chest.
The thousand-spoked discus of Hari, blazing with the blazing power of that foe of the gods,
reached his throat and became as soft as wool.
Even the staff of Vaivasvata, blazing with the brilliance of kindled fire,
was extinguished like a firebrand in a torrent of water upon the chest of Dānava.
In battle, the great noose of Varuṇa, the lord of the waters,
fell upon his neck as if brought under control by a mantra.
Having forcibly uprooted the wish-fulfilling trees in the Nandana grove,
he planted them according to his desire in the garden grounds of his own home.
In his presence, the wind acts as a palm-leaf fan out of apprehension;
the seasons, fearing him, wait upon him with their own clusters of flowers.
That son of Diti, the god of gods, forcibly seizes the oblation offered into the fire while all the deities look on. (163.72)
"O Śaṅkara, having consecrated the immensely radiant Skanda as the commander-in-chief, the gods desire to conquer the lord of the Daityas through your grace. (163.73)
Thus addressed by the wielder of the thunderbolt,
the bull-bannered god granted his permission for Skanda’s consecration as commander-in-chief.
Then he, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, worthy of adoration, the destroyer of Madana’s body, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament—
beholding his son, his eyes blossoming with affection— quickly vanished within the mountain white as the rays of the moon.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Authorization for the Consecration of Skanda," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the gods, led by Brahmā, took Skanda with them.
Those of immeasurable splendor arrived at the meritorious Samantapañcaka.
On that bank of the Sarasvatī, which was level, sloping toward the northeast, extensive, and free from pits, stones, thorns, and saline soil; (164.2)
Then all those foremost of gods, their minds filled with joy and possessing the splendor of blazing fire, sat down on every side around Skanda.
That merit, joined with that of the immortals, became an even more meritorious place,
like the waters of the Yamunā united with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then,
when the consecration of Skanda had taken place, the Earth herself, her eyes blossoming with joy, arrived at that place in embodied form.
Then that region quickly became one of golden sands,
variegated on all sides with diverse, shimmering rays from radiant jewels.
Whatever region those great-souled ones, free from envy, inhabited, that place became rid of evil through their majestic powers.
Then Himālaya, together with the mountains, arrived bringing a divine, well-fashioned golden throne.
Taking golden jars filled with jewels, medicinal herbs, perfumes, and meritorious waters, and adorned with garlands of blooming lotuses.
Greatly agitated, with their jeweled earrings swaying and their chests radiant with necklaces, they arrived there in great haste.
The Gaṅgā [bore] beautiful jars made of jewels, flashing with brilliance,
their necks adorned with golden lotuses, and filled with the most excellent water.
Taking them all with her, that best of rivers then came forth in joy, stumbling even on level ground.
Having caused well-prepared consecration jars to be brought forth,
which were reddened by the radiance of various jewels and thus rivaled the rays of the sun, [he performed the rite].
Accompanied by many goddesses of the celestial dwellers,
Pārvatī arrived, as if overwhelming all splendors with her own radiance.
Having caused them to take well-prepared, bright crystal jars, filled with supremely holy water and radiant with the luster of jewels.
And he wore a great, praiseworthy crown, radiant and beautiful in form,
its interior shimmering with the mass of rays from various jewels.
And a necklace, stainless and pure, with the brilliance of moonbeams—
lovely, a canopy of pearls, enchanting, and perfectly clean.
Then the lord of aquatic creatures arrived there, greatly delighted,
his armlets scarred by the tusks of the elephants belonging to the lords of the Dānavas.
The Lord of Wealth, taking beautiful and radiant jeweled armlets— the very essence, as it were, of all riches— approached.
Taking up fly-whisks with jeweled handles— long, radiant, and as white as the rays of the moon— the one of great splendor [proceeded].
Vaivasvata also arrived in his presence, wearing upon his chest a necklace as pure as the rays of the full autumn moon.
Under the pretext of a royal parasol, he bestowed upon that great-souled one the entirety of the fruit of sovereignty over the gods, just as Vāsava himself might.
Then the seasons, with joyful hearts, arrived at that place, adorning the trees there with the appearance of clusters of sky-flowers.
Arundhatī, Śacī, Svāhā, Sinīvālī, Girīndrajā, Aditi the mother of the gods, Niśā, Sānumati, and Kuhū. || 164.24 ||
Hrī, Śrī, Puṣṭi, the Quarters, and Dyau were all daughters of Prajāpati;
as were Rākā, Dhiṣaṇā, and Surabhi, who are the wives of the gods.
The personified medicinal herbs, the goddess of the forest Kauśikī,
the days, the kāṣṭhās, the muhūrtas, the months, the years, and the kalās.
Airāvaṇa, Supratīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Mahāpadma, and Sārvabhauma— the elephants of the quarters—
brought all the requisites for the consecration of the high-souled one.

Having bound up their matted locks, which possessed a radiance equal to blazing fire, those excellent sages dwelling on the Himalayas— rejoicing and empowered by the strength of their intense austerities— approached the son of Fire.
Delighting in the abode of the gods, blazing with splendor, their lotus-feet worshipped by the thrice-ten,
the hosts of sages— whose vigorous and constant rites of austerity were restrained [by his presence]— hurriedly approached Guha.
Assembled together with minds eager with joy, the sons of the Lotus-born Brahmā,
possessed of great majesty and bearing lofty renown, approached that son of the Three-eyed One, the source of preeminent power.
The lords of serpents, spreading canopies of light from the jewels upon their own hoods,
though bearing poison, assumed exceedingly gentle forms and hastened toward the son of Fire, whose prowess was insurmountable.
And the Garuḍas, free from envy, arrived with great speed, their power increased by being mounted upon the king of serpents;
they possessed a luster like that of the rising sun and caused trees to tremble with the force of the wind.

The Apsarases, endowed with long, tremulous eyes and possessed of the essence of various emotional graces and the qualities of supreme youth and beauty, danced all around, joyful and languid with delight.
Then the winds blew, their forms reddened by the pollen of various flowers, carrying fragrant scents;
they were entirely free from dust, moved with extreme gentleness, and brought delight to the hearts of the gods.
Having performed the ritual for his consecration, Bṛhaspati properly kindled the fire and carried out the rites for the one born in the reed-thicket.
Then the sages, having embraced the son of Śiva— the abode of blessings— with their own blessings, praised him who is worthy of praise with the most excellent hymns.
The Gandharvas and Nārada sang auspicious songs for him,
having then tuned their lutes to a high, resonant, and steady pitch.
Then, having taken him by the right hand while the auspicious rites were performed,
the preceptor seated him upon that lion-throne, facing the east.
Then, in the sky, the unstruck drums of the denizens of heaven resounded loudly;
likewise, various wonderful kettledrums, captivating the mind, were struck with great force.
Showers of flowers fell—variegated, fragrant with holy scents, possessing the reddish luster of their own filaments, and accompanied by the songs of intoxicated bees. (164.40)
Praising Skanda with words from his four mouths, Prajāpati took up the first jar, which was filled with meritorious water.
Then Viṣṇu, having put on his yellow garment,
took up the pitcher of the Kaustubha gem, which was touched by its own rays.
Then Indra, the subduer of Pāka, quickly adjusted his upper garment, which was inlaid with the luster of jewels from his armlets, and took up the water-jar.
Having bound their matted locks, which were marked by the crescent moon and tawny with fire,
the Rudras— adorned with bracelets made of serpents— took up their water-pots.
Though possessing supreme brilliance, the Ādityas, whose forms were pleasant to the touch,
received full jars filled with holy waters.
The Vasus also, whose chests were wounded by the tusks of the elephant of the enemy of the lord of the gods,
took jars there filled with meritorious water.
Then the Aśvins as well, perfectly refined by meritorious deeds and filled with water,
took up two golden jars that were garlanded with the rays of jewels.
There, the blazing ones, radiant with light, took up jars that were covered with golden lotuses and variegated by the rays of jewels.
The kings of the Nāgas and Gandharvas, the world-protectors, the hosts of Maruts,
the Bālakhilya sages, the ancestors, and the lords of birds— || 164.49 ||
He is Dharma, the Sustainer, the Ordainer, Time, Death, and the Earth;
he is Twilight, Splendor, Fortitude, Intelligence, Fame, Prosperity, and Sarasvatī.
The oceans, rivers, Vedas, sacred fords, mountains,
and planets brought jars there filled with the most excellent water.
Then, with joyful minds, they all consecrated the highly energetic son of Pāvaka as their generalissimo.
Then all the inhabitants of heaven and the assembled sages raised a shout of "Victory! for the victorious son of Śarva.
Maghavat took his white sunshade,
which was like a halo encircling a canopy formed by the mass of radiance from all its jewels.
And the world-protectors fanned the one of great splendor on all sides with long yak-tail whisks, pure as the rays of the autumn moon and possessed of jeweled handles.
The daughter of Himavat placed upon her son’s head a divine crown that had arisen from the nectar of immortality and was brought by Pracetas.
The best of rivers fastened a necklace upon his broad chest, which was as white as gold and possessed the luster of the moon's rays.
"Is it the chest that is adorned by the necklace, or is it the necklace that is held upon the broad chest?"—
such was the deliberation that arose then in that assembly of the gods.
Arundhatī fastened well-ornamented armlets upon the arms of the mighty-armed one, which were as thick as the pillars used for tying elephants.
Then the son of Pāvaka became even more radiant;
like a fire kindled at a sacrifice by the offering of clarified butter, he blazed forth with great splendor.
The four-faced Lord, being pleased, gave to that high-souled one great attendants who were heroic, powerful, and able to assume any form at will.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa with blood-red eyes, the invincible Nandiṣeṇa,
and the fourth, the renowned Kumudamālin, the best among the strong.
Sthāṇu gave the highly powerful great attendant Kratu when that terrible Tārakāmaya battle had commenced.
Enraged, he slew fourteen million Daityas;
and the gods gave him an army teeming with Nairṛtas.
Vaivasvata gave him both of his great attendants, who were invincible, possessed of universal forms, and the destroyers of Daityas and Yakṣas.
The Sun gave him two followers, Unmātha and Pramātha, who possessed great heroism and prowess, as well as Subhrāja and Bhāsvara.
Greatly delighted, he [gave] to Kārttikeya those two who were exceedingly invincible in battle,
who resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, and who were adorned with white garlands and unguents.
The Moon also gave him the Maṇi and the Sumaṇi; likewise, Vibhāvasu gave Jvālājihva and Jyotis to his son.
Being supremely delighted, he gave them two weapons for the destruction of the enemy host:
the Parigha and the formidable Paṭaha, as well as the Dahati and Atidahana.
Aṃśa also gave five attendants to the wise Skanda:
Utkrośa, Satvara, and both Vajra and Daṇḍadhara.
Being pleased, Śatakratu gave to the son of the God of gods the discus Vikramaka, as well as Saṃkrama, which is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
The highly illustrious Viṣṇu, being pleased, gave to the son of Agni both Vardhana and Nandana, who were masters of all branches of knowledge.
And the two mighty Aśvins, being pleased, gave to Skanda the fierce Kundura,
Kumuda, and the very powerful Kumuda.
The Creator gave both Ḍambara and Aḍambara to the son of Agni,
as well as the powerful Vakrānuvakra, who had the faces of rams and were invincible in battle.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave two great masters of illusion to Skanda as his attendants;
and Mitra gave Suvrata and Satyasandha to the high-souled one.
The Creator gave to Skanda Suprabha, Mahāmāya, and Śubhakarmā— those two who are destroyers of the enemy host.
Pūṣan gave two attendants to Skanda of immeasurable splendor: Pālin, who possesses great heroism, and Kālaka, who possesses great strength.
And Vāyu, being pleased, bestowed upon the high-souled Kārttikeya two beings of immense bodies and great strength, namely Bala and Atibala.
Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose, gave to the son of Agni two sons, Ghasa and Praghasa, who had mouths like whales and enormous bellies.
Himavat gave to Skanda both Suvarcas and Ativarcas, who were of great heroism and exceeding splendor, and possessed of immense strength.
And Meru gave two attendants, Kāñcana and Mahāmāya, as well as Jīmūtamālin, both to the son of Agni.
Furthermore, Mahāmeru gave to Skanda of immeasurable splendor both Sthira and Atisthira as his two attendants.
Vindhya gave to Skanda, who possesses blazing splendor, two beings of great strength, Ucchṛṅga and Viśṛṅga, who fight with rocks and stones.
Then he bestowed upon Kārttikeya two great attendants, Saṃgraha and Vigraha, as well as Samudra and Gadādhara.
Pārvatī gave to her son Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, and the invincible Śaṅkukarṇa—all of great heroism and great being. (164.85)
The Nāgas granted victory and great victory to the Great-Souled One;
and the Bull-vehicled Lord, being exceedingly pleased, bestowed these upon Skanda.
Many heroic attendants, invincible by enemies in battle—
Gajakarṇa, Nikumbha, Padma, and Kumuda as well.
[He saw] Sananda, the twelve-armed one, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Upakṛṣṇa,
Kṛtagrīva, Kapiskandha, Kāñcanākṣa, and Jalandhama.
With eyes that seemed to swallow him whole, he was dull-witted, with a neck curved to his side and a massive belly;
he had but one eye, twelve arms, a single foot, and great matted locks.
He had a thousand arms, disheveled hair, and the face of a tiger; he made the earth tremble.
He had a face on his back, a beautiful nose, and large faces on his sides.
[He saw] Parisruta, Kokanada, Priyamālyānulepana, Ajodara, Gajaskandha, Skandhākṣa, and Śatalocana. || 164.91 ||
With a tongue of flame, formidable, with white hair and a protruding belly,
possessing eight tongues and four fangs, he roared like a cloud and had a vast abdomen.
Vidyudakṣa, Dhanurvaktra, Jaraṭha, Mārutāśana,
Udarākṣa, Jhaṣākṣa, Vajranābha, and Suprabha.
Samudravega, Gokarṇa, Śailakampana,
Patrameṣa, Prabāhu, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka.
Dhūmra, Śveta, Kaliṅga, Siddhārtha, Varada, Priyaka, Gardabhāsya, Gonarda, and Bhūtatāpana. || 164.95 ||
Ānanda, Pramoda, Svastika, Dhruvaka, as well as Kṣepavāha, Sujāta, Siddhayātra, and Mahāvara.
Govraja, Kanakāpīḍa, Mahāpārśva, Mahodara,
Gāyana, Hasana, and the lord Bāṇakhaḍgadhara.
The Vaitāli, the Atitāli, as well as the Śaṭhika and Vātika,
the Māṃsaja, the Paṅkadigdha, and the imperishable Samudronmātha.
Raṇotkaṭa, Prabhāsa, Śvetamūrdhan, Acyuta, Kālakaṇṭhaśarīra, Kuṣmāṇḍa, and Śatrutāpana. || 164.99 ||
Gomāyuvaktra, Śyenāsya, Bhūtalonmāthana,
as well as Yajñavāha, Pravāha, Kākāsya, and Kākalocana.
Mañjula, Vakranāsa, Mahānāsa, Gajodara,
Tuhana, Tuhāna, Citradeva, Aja, and Khara.
A sweet and very gracious crown, preeminent with its diadem;
a garment honey-colored, and a jar with a pot-like belly.
Revanta, Manmathakara, Sūcīvaktra, Gajānana,
Śvetavaktra, Suvaktra, Cāruvaktra, and Pāṇḍara.
Kaṇṭhabāhu, Subāhu, Baka, Kokilaka,
as well as Acala and Kanakākṣa, the foremost leader of the forces.
And Saṃcāra, Kokamukha, Gṛdhrāsya, Jambuka, as well as Lomaśa, Jarāsya, Uṣṭragrīva, and Kamaṇḍalu. || 164.105 ||
Daṇḍaka, Dīrghavaktra, the mighty Haṃsavaktra, Tuṇḍuka, Śatapāda, Śatākṣa, and Cāpapṛṣṭhaka. || 164.106 ||
Śikṣaka, Āpavaktra, Śākhavaktra, and Kuṇḍaka—
these great yogins and great beings were constant practitioners of celibacy.
Invincible, of great heroism, slayers of enemies in battle,
wielding various weapons and missiles, diverse in form, and possessed of great splendor.
The leaders of the Gaṇas were surrounded by hosts with various faces;
they were clothed in the skins of lordly elephants, or wore garments of tiger-skins and black antelope hides.
Others had red hair and tawny beards, some were shaven-headed and naked, while others wore matted locks, had tawny eyes, and girdled themselves with snakes. || 164.110 ||
Brave warriors who wore serpents as armlets and had lordly snakes for their earrings,
their limbs were smeared with purifying ashes white as the moon.
[He saw] the leaders of the hosts, surrounded by many other hosts, dancing and leaping with eyes wide open in laughter. 164.112.
With faces like those of tortoises and cocks, with faces like hares, iguanas, and wolves, with terrifying faces like those of donkeys, camels, and horses, and with faces like boars and buffaloes.
With human genitals and faces, with the faces of dogs, jackals, and wild beasts,
with terrifying crocodile faces, and with the faces of porpoises and fish;
with the faces of cats and wolves, with long faces, and with faceless ones.
With faces resembling those of mongooses, owls, hawks, and lotuses,
and with mouths like those of mice, tawny rats, and cats— [they were] difficult for enemies to conquer.
Others had faces like those of goats and sheep, or mouths like parrots and ducks; some had the countenances of bears and tigers, and others likewise had the faces of elephants and lions.
With terrifying elephant faces and likewise the faces of hyenas,
with the faces of Garuḍas and jackals, and with the faces of crows and cuckoos.
With others having the faces of cows and monkeys, as well as the faces of hawks and vultures;
with great bellies, feet, and limbs, and with eyes like stars, they were possessed of great strength.
Others had faces like pigeons, as well as faces like cocks;
some had faces like quails and partridges, and others even faces like chameleons.
Some wore garments of yellow silk, while others were clad in rags and bark;
some had their bodies entwined by lordly serpents, and others wore bracelets of variegated snakes.
With large bellies and thin limbs, with thick limbs and thin bellies,
with short necks and large ears, they were adorned with various kinds of serpents.
[The army was] with heroes clad in the skins of lordly elephants, invincible in battle,
possessing faces on their shoulders, faces on their chests, faces on their backs, and faces on all sides.
By heroes of various forms, terrifying with various serpents, possessing various guises, great yogins dwelling in various places; || 164.123 ||
Others wore various garments, others various garlands and unguents;
others wore various skins as clothing, and others wore various ornaments.
They were adorned with ushnisha-crowns and tiaras, possessed necks like conch-shells and well-proportioned statures;
some wore diadems, some had five topknots, and others bore matted locks and crowns.
Some had three tufts of hair, others two, and likewise some had seven;
some wore crests, others had long matted locks, some were shaven-headed, and others had tawny hair.
With variegated eyes, variegated faces, and adorned with colorful garlands and unguents,
those heroes wore variegated garments and were constantly fond of combat.
With faces black and fleshless, long backs, and thin bellies;
with thick backs, large necks, pendulous bellies, and massive stomachs.
With great arms, great mouths, short necks, and thin faces;
with hunchbacks, long shanks, and ears and necks like those of elephants.
With long lips, long tongues, long eyes, and long noses;
with great tusks, excellent tusks, and variegated tusks—[they were] possessed of great strength.
With well-proportioned bodies, radiant and well-adorned,
they had tawny eyes, large ears, spike-like ears, or were entirely without ears.
With long fangs, broad chests, thick lips, and tawny hair;
with various feet, lips, and fangs, and with various hands and necks.
Covered with various skins and draped in diverse garments,
they were joyful, leaping about, and dancing with loud cries.
Some had long ears, broad chests, blue throats, and three eyes;
some resembled the belly of a parrot, while others were like collyrium in hue.
With white bodies, red necks, and tawny eyes, they were fearsome to behold;
their hands and feet were speckled, and they possessed the luster of jasmine and vermilion.
With [gems] resembling golden crests, white with red streaks,
those with the color of lapis lazuli, and those with a luster like a peacock's plumage.
Some had their hands raised with nooses, with gaping mouths and loud roars;
they were tawny-eyed, blue-throated, and possessed arms like great iron clubs.
With *śataghnīs* and *śaktis* in their hands, with maces and clubs in their grasp,
and with spears and swords in the hands of some, they were of massive body and great strength.
With heroes holding *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons and spears in their hands, with axes in their grasp, with nooses and mallets in their hands, and with discuses and javelins in their hands; 164.139.
Surrounded by heroes bearing variegated weapons who covered every direction,
their limbs were bound with networks of bells and they wore clusters of tiny tinkling bells.
Surrounded by hosts, the leaders of the hosts— beings of great essence and great strength—
waited upon the high-souled and illustrious Kārttikeya.
And he gave him mothers born from the body of Kauśikī—
women of great strength and great courage, unconquered in battles.
Prabhāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Palitā, Vṛṣanāsikā,
Śrīmatī, Bahulā, Siṃhī, Vijayā, and Bahuputrikā.
Gopālī, Suprabhā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Bṛhadambālikā, Kṛśā, Jayāvatī, Mālatikā, Dhruvaratnā, and Prabhākarī. || 164.144 ||
Suprabhā, Vasudā, Viśokā, and likewise Nandinī;
Vajracūḍā, Mahācūḍā, Vajranemi, and Mahāprabhā.
[Aja begot] Añjanī, Bharatsenā, Kamalākṣī, Śaśiprabhā, Śatruñjayā, Mahānāsā, Krodhanā, Śalabhī, and Khaṣī. || 164.146 ||
Mādhavī, Śukavaktrā, Kīrtinemi, Aninditā,
Gītapriyā, Mahāmāyā, Vāyasī, Amṛtā, and Satī.
Sarasvatī, Bhogavatī, Subhrū, and Kanakāvatī; Lakṣmī, Vīryavatī, and the mighty Vidyujjihvā. || 164.148 ||
Padmāvatī, Sunakṣatrā, Kandarā, Bahuyojanā,
Santānikā, Śivā, Kamalā, and also Maladā.
[Sudāmā], Bahudāmā, and the illustrious Suprabhā;
[and] Nṛttapriyā, who has beautiful hips and a white mortar for a girdle.
Śataghaṇṭā, Śatānandā, Śatanetrā, Yaśasvinī, Vapuṣmatī, Śīlā, Bhadrakālī, and Bhairavā. || 164.151 ||
To Saṃhārikā, Niṣkuṭikā, Bhūtā, Catvaravāsinī, Sumaṅgalā, Svastimatī, Vṛddhikāmā, and Janapriyā. || 164.152 ||
Dhanadā, Aṃsupradā, Bhavadā, Sukhadā, as well as Ailī, Bhelī, Samelī, Vetālī, Jananī, and Niśā. || 164.153 ||
