Kaṇḍū, Piṅgalikā, the illustrious Devamitrā, Lambuṣī, Sanakā, Citrasenā, and Acalā. || 164.154 ||
Kukūnikā, Śaṅkhinikā, as well as Jharjharikā, Kuṇḍālikā, Lokavilā, Kaṇḍarā, and Śatodarī. || 164.155 ||
[He gave] Utkvāthinī, Jurelā, Mahāvelā, Kaṅkaṇā, Manojavā, Kaṇṭakinī, Vighasā, and likewise Pūtanā. || 164.156 ||
Vaiśayā, Carcikā, Vāmā, Krodhanā, Mukhamaṇḍikā, Maṇḍodarī, Tuṇḍā, Koṭarā, and Meghavāsinī. || 164.157 ||
Subhagā, Lambinī, Lambā, Vāmadhūlī, Vikatthanā, as well as Ūrdhvaveṇīdharā and Lalāṭanayanā. (164.158)
Pṛthubarhā, Mahākāyā, Madhukumbhā, Taḍitprabhā,
Manthānikā, Unmanikā, Jarāyu, and Jarjarānanā.
Khyātā, Dahadahā, and likewise Dhamadhamā;
Khaṭaṅkhaṭā of great prowess, Vṛṣaṇā, and Maṇituṇḍikā.
Baddhaveṇī, Dharādhārā, Piṅgākṣī, Lambakarṇikā, Āmodā, Pramodā, and likewise Lambapayodharā—[these were the daughters]. || 164.161 ||
One with the face of a hare and an owl, dark-complexioned, with legs like those of a donkey and a great roar;
another with the face of a porpoise, white, with blood-red eyes, and terrifying to behold.
Jaṭālikā, Kāmacarī, Dīrghajihvā, and the greedy Lolupā; Kanelikā, Vāsanikā, and the very powerful Mukuṭā. || 164.163 ||
Lohitākṣī, Mahākāyā, Haripiṇḍī who is difficult to conquer, Paśudā, Vittadā, Vīrā, and the mighty Aṅgadā. || 164.164 ||
Payodā, Gopradā, Śaṅkhā, Suniṣaṇṇā, Tarasvinī, Pratiṣṭhā, Supratiṣṭhā, Rocamānā, and Surocanā. || 164.165 ||
Gokarṇī, Aśvakarṇī, Aśirā, Kharikā, as well as Kacakracā, Megharavā, Meghamālā, and Virocanā. || 164.166 ||
These and many other mothers were the givers of the Maruts:
Ekākṣarā, Sugandhā, Kṛṣṇakarṇī, and Dāruṇā.
Kṣurakarṇī, Catuṣkarṇī, Karṇaprāvaraṇā, as well as Catuṣpathaniketā, Gokarṇī, and Mahiṣānanā. || 164.168 ||
Kharakarṇī, Mahākarṇī, Bherīsvanā, Mahāsvanā, Śaṅkhakumbhaśravā, and Aparājitā in battles; || 164.169 ||
Gaṇā, Sugaṇā, and likewise Vātī who goes at will;
Catuṣpatharavā, Bhūtinī, and Vanyagocarā. || 164.170 ||
Following Kārttikeya were thousands of followers of various forms—
those with long teeth and excessively long nails, and those with long faces and terrifying countenances.
They were clever and sweet-spoken, in the prime of youth, and well-adorned;
endowed with majesty, they could assume any form at will and possessed great strength.
Some had fleshless limbs and were white, while others possessed a radiance equal to that of Jāmbūnada gold;
some were black with the hue of clouds, and others had smoke-colored hair and were most terrifying.
The Asuras had large fangs and long fangs, wore white garments,
had upright ears, tawny eyes, and long girdles.
They had pendulous bellies, protruding lips, and long ears, breasts, and eyes;
they had copper-colored eyes and copper-colored faces, with tawny eyes and golden hair.
Dwelling in trees and at crossroads, making their homes at the junctions of four paths,
they reside in caves and cremation grounds, and have their abodes in mountains and waterfalls.
Wearing various ornaments, adorned with diverse garlands and unguents,
they were dressed in various garments and likewise bore various weapons.
Delighted, Kauśikī gave these and other [attendants] to Skanda;
she also gave him the Vaijayantī garland with its beautiful filaments.
Viṣṇu [beheld her] rich with various ornaments, radiant and beautiful to behold,
wearing two stainless garments with the splendor of the rising sun.
Being well-pleased, Pārvatī gave to Skanda, whose mind was joyful,
a water-pot filled with the nectar-like water produced from the Amṛta.
Ganga, being pleased, gave to the prince of profound intellect her beloved son, the peacock Śikhaṇḍin with variegated plumage; and Garuḍa gave his own dear son.
Being well-pleased, Aruṇa gave to Skanda a powerful bird capable of assuming any form at will;
he gave the heroic Tāmracūḍa, who has feet for weapons.

Varuṇa gave to Skanda a most powerful goat, endowed with the speed of the vigor of existence, pleasing to behold for Skanda, capable of bearing a great burden, able to go anywhere at will, and able to assume any form at will. 164.183.
Brahmā gave to the one devoted to Brahman a pure black antelope skin for a garment,
which was as dark as the depths of the eyes of a woman agitated by amorous play.
Greatly delighted, Bṛhaspati gave that treasury of splendors, Skanda, a staff and a beautiful garland of gold.
Having duly consecrated that son of Agni as their commander-in-chief, the assembled gods, with hearts full of joy and possessing great power,
set out on an expedition together with Jayantī, the daughter of the enemy of the gods, for the sake of slaying the lord of the Daityas.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Consecration of the General," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Placing Skanda at their head, all the gods quickly prepared their army for battle.
Having struck hundreds of kettledrums with large, firm mallets variegated with gold and jewels.
The leaders of the army, having brought elephants from the quarters that resembled the peaks of mountains and whose bodies were drenched with the waters of the Mandākinī,
honored them with various perfumes and garlands.
Then they fastened variegated armor upon their flanks with the greatest effort;
through their diligent exertion, golden trappings were likewise applied to the foremost elephants and horses, as well as to their weapons.
Variegated banners and standards with beautiful golden poles were raised up;
they fastened various garlands of razor-edged arrows to the sides and hung bells upon them. (165.4)
And they yoked the chariot— whose wheels were beautiful with gold and which was variegated with the rays of its jewels— with celestial horses of noble appearance and joyful hearts.
Śakra fastened upon his chest a precious armor, bright as the interior of a lotus,
smeared with yellow sandalwood, and radiant with a brilliance flashing like a thunderbolt.

Restraining their tawny matted locks with hissing serpents, the delighted Rudras bound them high upon their chests— those large locks which were variegated by the wounds inflicted by the tusks of the Daitya-elephant.
Wearing his variegated armor, the one of great luster— equipped with a girded sword and finger-guards,
and bearing a ready bow— though possessed of blazing prowess, did not abandon his innate gentleness, just as the moon does not lose its natural coolness.
Then the Sūryas, with their own radiance slightly glowing, carefully fastened their armor—
made of impenetrable iron, beautiful, adorned with gold, and indestructible by arrows.
With his radiant armor fastened, his excellent bow ready, and a broad sword girt at his side;
holding his staff and with his crown secured, even Yama himself became exceedingly terrifying.
Enveloped in an exceedingly great radiance, his forebody repeatedly quivering and held high,
the noose seems to proclaim the defeat of the enemies in the assembly of Varuṇa.
Even the Lord of Wealth, wielding a mace and possessing arms as thick as iron bars, with eyes tawny like fire,
knows through his own mastery over the Lord that destruction awaits the enemies of the gods at the blow of that mace.
Then, in the army of the enemies of the gods, great meteors with flickering sparks of fire fell;
the sky resounded dreadfully even without clouds, and the earth, along with its trees and mountains, trembled.
Dust, grey as the back of a donkey and driven by the wind, fell everywhere from the sky;
banners with sturdy golden staffs fell down, and the clouds released a rain of blood-red water. (165.14)
Again and again, the waves released lukewarm tears, their hearts overwhelmed by dejection;
and the ichor of the elephants, dark as the throat of a pigeon, ceased from the surfaces of their temples.
In their radiant dwellings, flocks of birds, wild beasts, and horses shrieked loudly with piercing cries;
the garlands of flowers all around began to wither, and a harsh wind blew with increased force.
The great and joyful army of the gods advanced, rejoicing, toward the lord of the Daityas;
and the Daitya, having learned of the arrival of the gods, then caused his own army to arm itself.
Those armies of the gods and the asuras, with weapons raised, encountered one another;
they were exceedingly agitated like the waters of the great ocean at the time of universal dissolution, when the eastern and western waters meet.

Hearing the sound of the battle trumpets, the Daityas—powerful, filled with burgeoning pride, and eager for victory—set out for the fray with their weapons grasped, their auspicious rites left unfinished due to excessive joy. 165.19.
The dust raised by the chariots, horses, and infantry on the field of battle, greyed by the throats of monkeys,
and their exceedingly terrible and great roar then pervaded the sky and all the directions.
With the raised weapons of the Dānavas and gods, as well as with banners, flags, and sunshades,
the sky then shone like the vault of heaven containing lightning, the moon, the bow of Indra, and rows of swans.
As weapons were hurled at one another by the Daityas and the gods upon their scarred limbs, which were as if covered with fine threads, they produced a sound mingled with the sparks of flashing fire.
Seeing the asuras endowed with the strength of beings, some of the gods, disregarding their companions,
retreated like elephants in rut whose temples are darkened by the flow of ichor.
Having rushed forward with great speed from afar, the vanguard of the gods and asuras,
displaying their prowess, abandoned all hope for their own lives and struck one another down.
Then, among those whose minds were intent on excessive enmity and who sought to slay one another there,
that tumultuous clash of gods and asuras became like that of the Anavas in a great battle.
Horses pierced by iron clubs and spears fell down, struck by arrows;
and warriors, vomiting blood from their mouths with foam due to the forceful blows, fainted from the heavy strikes.
In that great battle, the lotus-faces of the Dānavas and the gods, adorned with earrings, fell severed by sharp razor-headed arrows as they displayed their mutual pride and wrath toward one another.
Then those Mothers and their hosts roamed about in battle,
crushing the multitudes of enemies with blows of the fist, strikes of the palm and the heel, and by dragging, twisting, and squeezing.
In the battle against the Dānavas, the leaders of the Mātaṅgas struck down the elephants with rutting tuskers, the best horses with steeds,
the chariots with chariots, and the throngs of infantry with foot soldiers.
Leaping up with speed, the leaders of the Gaṇas struck the warriors of the lord of the Daityas— who were mounted upon elephants—
with sharp arrows, fist-blows, and the fierce falls of thunderbolts, so that their brains were shattered and their eyes protruded.
Filled with intense rage, they lopped off [the enemies] with battle-axes, hacked them with swords, and pierced them with spears;
moreover, they crushed their foes with their arms, which were as exceedingly thick as the trunks of great elephants.
The goddesses also struck those hosts of Daityas who had taken up their weapons in the great assembly—
those mounted upon excellent horses, those stationed in chariots, and those standing on the necks of elephants— by leaping up against them.
Then that demonic army, its foremost leaders crushed by the lord of the hosts,
was violently agitated like the unfathomable great lake of the ocean when struck by the wind from Garuḍa’s wings.
Then, beholding his forces being violently slaughtered by the leaders of the hosts, Tāraka—
his long eyes turning copper-red with rage— advanced, protected by his crown and his army.
Having drawn his bow, which resounded like Śakra’s thunderbolt and blazed with the luster of jewels,
he covered the expanse of the sky with a shower of arrows— feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks— that pierced the vital organs.
Having learned of the arrival of that lord of the Daityas, the son of Anala then roared loudly,
beholding the spear held in his own hand, which was adorned with beautiful bells of variegated gold.
Then that roar of Kārttikeya, having pervaded the sky, the intermediate quarters, and the cardinal directions,
forcibly bewildered the minds of the enemies of the gods in that great assembly.
Then, beholding Tāraka approaching in that great battle, protected by a vast force,
Guha released a spear blazing with the brilliance of fire for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Released by that son of Fire, it enveloped the sky and the quarters with its flames;
becoming manifold in the firmament, it was most terrible, like an illusion bewildering the Daityas.
With irresistible speed, she fell simultaneously upon the chests of the assembled enemies of the gods, who wore variegated armor; having rent their breasts, she swiftly entered them all at once.
All those enemies of the gods were struck down; with their wide, red eyes rolling and their tongues and lips bitten, their limbs failing them, they gave up their lives while vomiting blood.
Just as the sun pierces through the darkness with its rays without obstruction,
so did the son of Agni shatter the forces of his enemies on the field of battle with his spears.
Having slain all the enemies of the gods on the field of battle— those possessed of towering pride and valor— the spear,
like the radiance of the sun after scorching the worlds, then returned to Skanda.
Having slain Tāraka, the king of the Daityas, at the forefront of battle together with the hosts of the sons of Diti who were free from distress,
he was praised by the joyful leaders of the assembly of the gods.
Possessing immeasurable splendor, he returned to the presence of the trident-bearer.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter in the Tārakavadha section of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 165.164 ||
The one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, endowed with the power of great yoga!
I have heard this entire great life-story of Skanda in its entirety.
O supreme lord of yoga, from you [I have heard] the supreme secret of the Blessed One;
thereafter, that lord of gods, the enemy of Tripura, whose banner is the bull— || 166.2 ||
Having dispatched Guha as the great commander-in-chief together with the gods, and having entrusted the deities to Skanda, what else did the Lord do? (166.3)
Where did the Lord of Gods go, and what did the Daughter of the Mountain say?
What did Umā say to him? Tell this to me as I ask. (166.4)
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā, who possessed great ascetic power and knew the supreme meaning of all the scriptures, began to relate [the account]. (166.5)
Sanatkumāra said: Having entrusted the gods to the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), Bhava, the god of gods,
then departed for Mount Mandara, which has golden caves, accompanied by the Goddess.
He stood there upon that great, radiant golden throne,
strewn with various jewels, as lofty as a golden peak.
Standing by his side, the goddess, daughter of Himavat, shone like Rohiṇī beside the full moon in a cloudless sky. || 166.8 ||
Then Girijā, having bowed to the Supreme Lord, spoke:
"Since I am your partner in dharma and exceedingly dear to you... (166.9)
And because I have obtained this through former affection, I ask you without hesitation about your purifying and holy names, O granter of desires.
"O Lord, I wish to hear these meaningful accounts as they are told by you. Thus questioned then by Gaurī, the lord of the gods spoke everything.
O Goddess, the awakening to the meaning of my names is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices;
it is my supreme secret, which even Brahmā and the other gods know.
I shall declare that to you, O Goddess, by which divinity is attained; for because I cause all diseases to flee from the world, I am called Rujādrava. (166.13)
"O beloved, because I destroy weeping (rudana), I am Rudra;
for at the time of the end, I indeed withdraw the entire universe."
Because he removes death, he is celebrated as Hara;
and "pura" is declared here to be the body of all living beings.
Since that city, which is my bed, is present within all living beings,
therefore my name is "Puruṣa," the one of great supernatural power.
Never indeed was I born, nor does my birth exist anywhere;
therefore, O Goddess, I am proclaimed as the unborn at all times.
Having gone to non-existence within me, the world of the moving and the unmoving comes into being again from me; therefore, existence is defined by that.
Since I alone am greater even than the great gods,
and there is no other greater than me, I am therefore Mahādeva.
Because I protect the animals and create them according to my will,
and because I am their lord, I am therefore known as Paśupati.
I am indeed the Lord of others, yet others do not rule over me;
I lead my devotees to lordship, and for that reason I am celebrated as the Lord (Īśa).
For the directions are my garments; I dwell in all directions.
Since I am the garment of the directions, I am therefore remembered as Digvāsas (the one clothed in the directions).
Because I am the bringer of welfare to all beings, I am remembered as Śaṅkara;
because I perform what is auspicious for the worlds, I am therefore remembered as Śiva.
Because that which was blue became thoroughly reddened upon my body with a crimson luster,
I am therefore celebrated as Mīnalohita.
When "Śūlin" is uttered with "Śūla," and "Lākulin" with "Lakula," O Goddess, when "Rudra" is thus proclaimed, it is remembered that the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is obtained. (166.25)
If "Hare" is uttered, one obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice;
if "Bhava" is proclaimed, one is immediately liberated from all sins.

By saying "Puruṣa," one attains supreme happiness; by saying "Aja," one attains the same world [as the deity]; by saying "Īśāna," one attains great sovereignty; and by saying "Mahādeva," one attains the imperishable.
By "Digvāsas" (the sky-clad) one attains supreme liberation; by "Śaṅkara" (the benefactor), great happiness;
by "Śiva," extreme auspiciousness; and by "Śūlī" (the trident-bearer), supreme strength. || 166.28 ||
By praising Lākulī, the supreme one, a man obtains fame throughout the worlds;
by praising Nīlalohita here, he obtains the fruits of all sacrifices.
O Goddess, my devotee obtains an imperishable dwelling within me.
Thus, O Vyāsa, has been told the explanation of the meaning of the names. 166.30.
By the wielder of the trident, the god of gods, out of a desire for the pleasure and welfare of the Goddess—what else do you ask, O Brahmin? Speak, and I shall tell it to you.
Vyāsa said:
O sage, O knower of the supreme dharma, you previously stated that Rudra is the bestower of white life; tell me that in brief. (166.32)
O Lord, how did Īśāna give that life back to the sage?
For what purpose and where, O Master of Yoga? And who is this one called Śveta? (166.33)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, my child, to how a second birth was granted by the wielder of the Pināka bow to Śveta, whose life had expired and who was being carried away by Yama.
There was a sage named Darbhadhvaja, equal to Bṛhaspati,
whose self was disciplined by all branches of knowledge, and whose son was Kuśadhvaja.
He became possessed of great splendor, like another Viśvāmitra;
he had a beloved son named Śveta, who was of great luster.
From the very moment of his birth, devotion to the bull-bannered god Śiva was ever-present in that son of Kuśadhvaja, like a shadow that never departs.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, or performing austerities,
the great sage remained meditating on the Lord of Gods with his whole being.
Then, O best of Brahmins, in due course, the powerful Dānava named Vipṛthu went to Śveta’s father and chose his daughter.
He did not give his daughter to that enemy of the gods;
moreover, Darbhadhvaja was slain by him at night through sheer force.
And he desired as his son-in-law Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus and mace,
the supreme soul of righteousness, O you of excellent vows, through his daughter.
Having learned that her father had been killed by him,
that virtuous woman of great vows went into exile for the sake of penance for the benefit of another.
Śveta, having understood that from him, established himself in supreme detachment;
reaching the bank of the Narmadā, he became single-minded and conquered his senses.
With his state entrusted to Rudra alone, devoted to him and having him as his supreme goal,
that ascetic rich in penance remained engaged in yoga, performing severe austerities.
Then a very long time passed while that wise man was performing austerities;
the lifespan ordained for him by the Creator reached its end.
Then, perceiving that Śveta’s lifespan was exhausted and that he was subject to the movements of death,
the son of Vivasvat joyfully [beheld] Kāla, Mṛtyu, and their attendants.
He dispatched his servants to bring that best of the twice-born;
then those messengers, having approached him, stood there with the intent to seize Śveta.
Seeing those messengers of Yama standing there, Śveta, terrified of death and overwhelmed by the pain of fear, cried out, "Alas! Alas! (166.48).
He reflected with an undistracted mind upon Śaṅkara for his protection;
then, as soon as he had been thought of, [Śiva], stationed on the peak of the lord of mountains, appeared.
The God who bestows grace upon his devotees perceived Śveta, who was afflicted; knowing him thus to be distressed, a devotee who had fallen under the power of death. || 166.50 ||
Laughing, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods, said this to the Goddess:
"O Goddess, there is a sage named Śveta who is devoted to me and has grown great through his ascetic penance. (166.51)
His life was exhausted; he became deluded, bewildered by the noose of death.
This established order was created of old by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
O Daughter of the Mountain, even Brahmā becomes deluded when the lifespan of living beings declines and the duration of the world-age comes to an end, even as he creates the worlds.
Since even he, being deluded, creates worlds beset by death and suffering,
that Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is nonetheless exceedingly devoted to me.
And because of her special devotion and reverence toward the daughter of the Mountain King,
this creation, accompanied by the seasons, was authorized by me as well.
"O Goddess Pārvatī, because that sage has dedicated all his actions to me and possesses such singular devotion, I am deeply pleased with him."
"I shall be his protector; I will restore that sage to life.
Then, having heard her husband's words, the Daughter of the Mountain spoke these words: || 166.57 ||
"O Great God, act thus to grant the desired favor to your devotee;
for what other refuge could there be for that devoted sage? (166.58)
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the god of gods, whose banner is the bull,
the lord of the Gaṇas, spoke to those leaders of the Gaṇas headed by Nandīśvara.
The wielder of the trident dispatched Śaṅkukarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas, as well as thousands of others,
for the protection of the sage Śveta.

Having received the command from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, those lords of the Gaṇas, possessed of great power, went swiftly to the presence of the white sage, like the messengers of Death desiring to consume [their enemies]. 166.61.
Having gone there, they beheld Śveta being tormented by the messengers of Yama,
like a single deer in the forest surrounded by many hunters.
Bound at the neck by the noose of Time and restrained at the hands and feet,
he was dragged away by Death himself, whose eyes were streaming with blood.

He was being hurled from all sides by the most terrible messengers of Yama, who had deformed faces and great fangs, whose beards and hair were blood-red, whose eyes resembled lightning, and who held fierce iron clubs in their hands.
Seeing the sage thus distressed and crying out repeatedly, "O Lord!", the lord of the Gaṇas quickly released the sage from those bonds, just as the Lord releases the fetters of bound souls (paśus).
"Go away, servants of Yama! Leave this sage here with his firm bodies; for he is devoted to Śambhu—the unborn Lord of gods and asuras, the cause of the world.

He who is the creator of wind, fire, Indra, and the Maruts, who is worshipped by Brahmā and others, and who is the protector—he is the unconquered one whose banner bears the bull-king; Yama shall not behold him."
Seeing those leaders of the hosts, the messengers, preceded by Kāla and Mṛtyu,
stood at a distance and, releasing the sage Śveta out of fear, spoke to him.
"The time for this sage is complete; his lifespan is exhausted, O lords of the Gaṇas!
What is the use of him? Release him; let us lead him into the presence of Yama. || 166.68 ||
Then Nandīśvara, as if burning them with his wrath, said:
"Go quickly, unhurt! You wretched servants of Yama!"
As long as these extremely wrathful lords of the Pramathas do not become enraged,
let them not strike you all at once— like lions in the forest attacking elephants maddened by rut— and thus deprive you of your lives. (166.70)

Then, having been addressed thus by Nandīśvara, the leader of the hosts and possessor of immeasurable prowess, those messengers of the King of the Ancestors fled in fear; and having gone, they reported the matter to Yama.
Having then heard those harsh words spoken by Nandīśvara,
the son of the Sun (Sugrīva) was provoked to anger and, out of delusion, resolved to go there himself.
Then he advanced, his eyes reddened with rage, surrounded by all those [demons] led by Death;
sighing like a fierce serpent, as if alone he desired to incinerate the entire world.
Seeing the white sage, free from delusion and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas whose forms resembled Śiva’s,
the son of the king of the planets said to Nandīśvara and the others, "Release him with speed!"

"Who are you, O Yama, that seeks to lead away the white sage Śveta, who is blessed by Bhava and devoted to the Lord of the Pramathas? Go away, O fool of unrefined soul, for he is being protected by the Lord himself! so said Nandin. (166.75)
Then, having heard those harsh and great words of Nandin,
Yama, filled with rage, spoke thus to the lord of all the gaṇas.
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, this Brahmin's life has departed; he remains here like one who is deluded.
Release him; do not undergo vain exhaustion. (166.77)
For even if he is protected for a long time, he will surely come back to me;
when his time is fulfilled, someone here has their lifespan exhausted.
Even a learned man, though endowed with austerity and righteousness, does not live [long] if the action he has performed is either unrighteous or censurable. (166.79)
"Having cast off this body, let him attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas;
for the examination of this entire multitude of beings is under my control. || 166.80 ||
"There is a constant discernment between meritorious and sinful actions;
therefore, quickly deliver this white horse to me, whose life has come to an end."
Or else, let all of us, the lords of the hosts, take him here and go into the presence of the wielder of the trident; he will certainly release him.
Having heard the words of the King of the Ancestors, those led by Nandīśvara said to Yama,
who was overcome by anger, "So be it."
Then all of them together, including Śveta, that best of sages,
went to the Vindhya mountain to behold Hara, the Lord of the World.
Nandī, the leader of all the hosts, having bowed with supreme devotion to Bhava of immeasurable splendor, reported everything exactly as it had occurred.
Having heard the words spoken by Nandin,
the Blessed One spoke directly to Vaivasvata with a voice that was both affectionate and deep.
O Lord of the hosts of the departed, Śveta possesses supreme devotion toward me;
therefore, even though his lifespan is exhausted, death shall have no power over him.
O scorcher of foes, because his mind was purified by great austerity and devotion toward me, Śveta has conquered death through my grace.
"By my command, you must not cause his defeat either.
Do you not know, O son of the Sun, that these foremost of men are my devotees? (166.89)
Even when the dissolution of the body has arrived, they do not see your abode;
for you have been thoroughly gratified by his extraordinary and supreme devotion.
"I shall grant you immortality with this very body. Thinking thus, free from doubt, go quickly to your own abode.
Having heard these words of the god and having bowed down, the son of the Sun, not yet understanding the ultimate truth, spoke thus to the wielder of the Pināka bow: || 166.92 ||
"O Blessed One, this ancient order was created by you alone;
I am appointed to this task of investigating birth and death. (166.93)
For when his term of office has ended, O bull-bannered Lord of the Gods, even Śakra was created by you alone, as were both Pavana and I, O Lord of the Suras.
O Mahādeva, this path, which consists of the destruction of time and death, has never been transgressed by anyone, because it maintains the suspension of time.
O Lord of the Gods, having thus reflected upon this supreme creation,
you ought to release the foremost of brahmins when his time is full and his life has reached its end.
Thus my status shall remain undiminished, and I shall not be disgraced;
moreover, Death, who dwells within the body, shall attain that white [state] as his end.
Having heard these words spoken by the King of the Pretas,
he whose banner is the bull was like a glowing ember or like the fire of universal destruction.
Then, as if the very world were suddenly being shaken,
the wielder of the Pināka bow took his stand upon the shoulder of Nandīśa.
Seeing Yama standing there, Vyāsa spoke these words:
"Aha! What deceitful speech this son of the Sun-maker has uttered! (166.100)
Behold the harshness of my words as they were uttered in reply:
"Śveta has been saved by me; go to Yama! (166.101)
"Release Śveta," he said to me, his mind already gone;
is he perhaps truly a fool, or is he merely arrogant in his own prowess? (166.102)
"Go!"—when I commanded this, who was able to remain there?
Standing before me, he gave me this reply once more: || 166.103 ||
Having thus spoken of the cause of the world's origin,
the Blessed One cast a sidelong glance and looked at Yama with wrath.
Burned by that eye,
he fell to the surface of the earth like a great tree in the forest felled by a mighty wind;
he was quickly reduced to ashes, and then Bhava laughed aloud.
Then the enemy of the Tripura Asuras touched the white sage as he bowed down, dejected by the fear of death, speaking with a faltering voice: "Do not be afraid. (166.106)
The wielder of the trident granted him a boon, saying, "O Brahmin, death shall not be yours.
And the Lord, being well-pleased, bestowed upon him the status of a permanent attendant and spoke thus to him. (166.107)
"Since I became angry at the son of the Sun on this most holy mountain, therefore I shall dwell here upon the summit of the king of mountains;
thus, I shall become known here as Krodheśvara."
In the region of Vindhya, frequented by immortals and Siddhas, at the holy mountain Krodheśvara,
those men who cast off their bodies free from delusion— my teaching holds that their destination is equal to that of Śveta.
And those who behold Śveteśvara here shall also become my own divine Gaṇapas.
Moreover, this most meritorious river shall be known by your very name as the Śvetagaṅgā.

"As soon as the Lord of the Universe had spoken these words— 'In this [city] there is an exceedingly vast place for the ancestors that grants the heavenly realm, where various kinds of abundant offerings are made'— the sage Śveta assumed a divine body."
Possessing qualities equal to those of Nandīśa and Caṇḍeśa, he bowed to the god and stood before him;
then, seeing his son lifeless, the Sun, tormented by grief, quickly rushed forward with speed. (166.112)
Together with Brahmā and the others, headed by Śakra, they came to the Cause of the World;
then those immortals made their request for the sake of restoring the life of the son of Āditya.
Since this fool has gone from that hardship to this intense suffering by the Lord of the World, be gracious, O Lord of Gods; show favor so that this King of the Host of Pretas may live.
"O Lord of gods and asuras, let him now be as he was before; indeed, cut away our suffering! Such is the petition of the inhabitants of the three heavens, headed by Brahmā, Śakra, and Arka. (166.115)
Hearing that Yama, the Lord, feeling compassion, spoke, saying, "Arise, my son!
Then the son of the King of Planets assumed a divine body, resembling a mountain as before.
Rising up quickly, he immediately bowed to the Blessed One, suddenly grasping him by the feet.
Then Brahmā and the hosts of the lords of the gods, seeing them prostrate, spoke to them.
The Lord of Brahmā, the Sun, Viṣṇu, and Agni; the sole creator of the gods and the sovereign of the gods;
the Lord of the Suras, whose crown is half-adorned with the matted locks of the Moon—O gods, depart for your own abodes! (166.118)
"This communication has been made by you with its fruit; do not, however, fall again into self-delusion.
Having spoken these words to the Lord of the Dead, the hosts of gods then departed after bowing down.
Having quickly seized Sauri, the King of the Ancestors, Śveta also stood there, freed from death;
just as Nandin was free from the state of suffering, so too was the brahmin devoted to the Supreme Lord.
Thus has this been told to you, which destroys the white death (the untimely death) of Śambhu, the Lord Īśa, the husband of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain;
it is the fruit of unerring devotion, a particular excellence of the attainment of prosperity—the one refuge in the world, whom I honor as the worthy protector. 166.121.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Granting of the White Boon," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
This supreme and secret majesty which has been proclaimed by you—
This could not belong to anyone else except for Hara, the remover of the world's suffering.
O great sage, these are the holy shrines here belonging to the trident-bearing God of gods, by beholding which people no longer grieve over birth and death.
Tell those to me, O knower of dharma, if I am worthy of your favor;
thus, O best of sages, having accomplished my purpose, I shall be liberated.
Having heard the words of Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā spoke this: "Excellent, O Vyāsa of great intellect! You are devoted to Śaṅkara. (167.4)
O you who possess great yoga, you who desire to hear of the meritorious places of Śūlin— you have achieved your purpose and are liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Listen, my child, I shall tell you this supreme secret of mine:
a description of the abodes of Śambhu, which removes the fear of birth and death. (167.6)
On the auspicious peak of Mount Vindhya named Ādityabandhana,
a highly resplendent liṅga was installed there by the Sun-god.
Having seen that auspicious peak of the Himavat mountain named Hemasomodbhava, O Vyāsa, a person does not grieve over birth. (167.8)
That holy place was manifested there by Cyavana;
those men who approach that abode of Śambhu [attain merit]. (167.9)
They do not fall back from heaven even when the dissolution of the world has arrived;
rather, they dwell on the sacred mountain at its rising, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas).
There is a meritorious lake named Satya, covered with golden lotuses,
where those sages known as the Satyas dwell, possessing the splendor of fire and the sun.
The high-souled ones sustain the chariot of the Sun with their blessings;
there, they established a holy shrine of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
O Vyāsa, that abode, worshipped by the immortals and surrounded by Siddhas and Vidyādharas,
was seen by those devotees of Bhava who travel through the sky.
Having become beloved of Bhava, they become lords of the Pramathas;
there, on Mount Uśīrabīja, the king of mountains, is a great hermitage.
O Vyāsa, there is a very lofty linga made of sapphire, worshipped by gods and dānavas, belonging to Āgastya Tṛṇāṅga; it is located in that place.
In that abode, the great seer Tṛṇāṅga,
assuming the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, constantly praises the matted-haired Rudra;
by worshipping him, the inhabitants of heaven become lords of the Gaṇas.
To the north, on the lofty summit of Mount Meru, which is devoid of light and bereft of sun and moon, a great golden [palace] was established.
O Vyāsa, there stands the linga of the Blessed One where the Wielder of the Trident himself resides,
[worshipped] by the son of Uttānapāda, whose soul was devoted to Bhava.
O great sage, that Liṅga, which is constantly worshipped by Dhruva, remains there;
it is inaccessible even to the gods, except for Dhruva, who is the supreme boon.
On the king of mountains, by the sage Jaigīṣavya,
a very great liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods was established.
Having seen that, O Vyāsa, a person shall attain the world of Rudra;
they become masters of the knowledge of liberation and experts in Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Having seen that most wonderful liṅga, men become [filled with joy], for it is the supreme liṅga established by the king of the gods in the Nandana grove. || 167.22 ||
Having seen that brilliant linga made of refined gold which the deities worship, those deities attain the supreme state. || 167.23 ||
In the ocean of milk, there is a divine, great, and holy sanctuary created by the Bālakhilyas themselves,
frequented by Siddhas and Kinnaras.
In that place was the crystal Liṅga named Candraprabha, adorned with jewels;
having worshipped it, the Bālakhilyas attained the same world as Īśa.
On Mount Gandhamādana, the Yakṣa king established a divine golden linga of the Blessed One known by the name Kubereśa.
Having worshipped that Great Lord with devotion using divine mandāra flowers and golden lotuses, Kubera became filled with joy.
To those gods and asuras by whom that abode of Kubera was seen,
the bull-bannered god bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
O one of great intelligence, hear now of those most meritorious places belonging to the moon-crested Lord, which are accessible here to human beings. (167.29)
On the auspicious peak of Himavat, the king of all mountains,
is the primordial abode of the Self-Existent One, renowned as Mahālaya.
There, O Vyāsa, are all the immortals led by the four-faced Brahmā,
as well as the perfected sages and those who are masters of yoga on earth.
Having worshipped Hara with devotion,
they attained that supreme state where Mahādeva himself has set his own foot.
Having approached that Lord who dwells in Mahālaya, all men who bow down to him are liberated from all sins. (167.33)
Having attained the dissolution of the body— wherever and in whatever manner—
that mortal who has reached the unsurpassed perfection is not born again.
Even those men who are doers of evil and ignorant of dharma do not see him;
there stands the mighty Mahāgaṇapati, stationed at the gate.
He obstructs the path of those men who are evildoers,
as well as of the yogins, ascetics, gods, perfected beings (siddhas), and supreme seers.
Having bowed to him, they attained perfection and went to the holy abode of Paśupati;
by his mere resolve, [they thought], "I shall see the Mahālaya."
A living being is liberated from those karmas designated as "great sins" by [visiting] Mahālaya,
the great and auspicious field that bestows the attainment of liberation.
A man who visits seven generations on both sides of his family is saved;
beyond that, O Vyāsa, is the most meritorious place known by the name Kedāra.
To the north of that very mountain is the auspicious supreme abode of the bull-bannered Lord;
indeed, it is there on that best of mountains that the god Hara himself resides.
From the mass of his matted locks, he released holy water;
that which issued from the crest of Hara’s head became [a stream] there. || 167.41 ||
O Vyāsa, those men who drink that auspicious water, which resembles nectar, become the Kuṣmāṇḍa hosts, beloved of Rudra.
Possessing great forms and great souls, even more joyful and beloved,
they beheld the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, dwelling at Kedāra.
Brahmā, Śakra, as well as Viṣṇu, Soma, and the lord of the hosts of Yakṣas.
Those high-souled men who have drunk the water of Kedāra worship the Supreme Lord stationed there with devotion. (167.45)
How is it that they grieve, O Vyāsa; what happiness indeed have they not attained?
For from their heads flowed the penance performed upon the field at the peak of the Himavat mountain for Soma, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and the all-pervading Creator, the wielder of the trident.
May those who delight in unrighteousness, who do not obtain it to drink without the grace of Śiva,
become liberated from the terrors of the bonds of worldly existence by drinking that [grace].
Madhyameśvara is the very first station of Umāpati;
having gone there to that lord of gods as well, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati. || 167.47 ||
There too, O sage, the Lord himself is eternally present;
by approaching that Īśāna, one shall not grieve regarding death.
O Vyāsa, in this region of the Himavat mountain, which belongs to all three worlds, this place is the most excellent, auspicious, and bestower of all perfections.
Merely by approaching him, the fruit of all sacrifices is said to be attained;
even for one who has failed due to negligence, the superior goal is the state of being a follower of Gaṇapati.
"There is nothing more meritorious than this to be found in all the worlds:
either universal sovereignty over the three realms, or death upon this mountain."
Therefore, death here is superior to the status of a universal monarch;
endowed with supreme sovereignty, one attains union with Śambhu.
"Is this creature dead here? What higher state than that could there be? Or is this another great peak of the Himalayas, frequented by the Siddhas? (167.53)
Where the Goddess performed austerities with the desire to obtain a fair complexion,
that place became renowned throughout the three worlds as Gaurīśikhara.
Those men who go to that holy Gaurīśikhara, at the sacred ford known as Kucakuṇḍa which was created by Umā— || 167.55 ||
Having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, they go to the supreme goal.
[They see] another horn of Rishabha, resembling a diamond or crystal.
There, at that peak of Ṛṣabha—a holy place of the Lord of Umā—Nandin performed austerities and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara. (167.57)
Having seen it, one is liberated from sin and attains the world of Rudra.
Another peak of Himavat is there, possessing a splendor equal to Hemakūṭa. || 167.58 ||
There is a beautiful sanctuary of Rudra named Bhastrēśvara;
on that mountain, the god Rudra is known as Bhastrēśvara. (167.59)
To that Mahādeva, the Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas paid homage—
those men who were terrified of death and likewise afflicted by the sufferings of birth.
Having reached that sacred site and taken as many steps as one desires,
O Vyāsa, a person who beholds it shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
At Gaṅgādvāra, the auspicious gateway, a highly meritorious place established by the high-souled Dakṣa for the sake of devotion to the matted-haired Lord (Kapardin), there stands a liṅga.
There were trees named Kanakhala, which were composed of gold; yet because of the lack of virtue among men, they appeared as mere wooden logs that had been cut down.
There dwells Śambhu, the soul of the universe and lord of all, together with Ambikā;
he is known by the name Bahurūpeśvara and bestows many boons upon living beings.
Those men seeking liberation who do not behold this birth [of the Buddha] obtain the merit of ten horse-sacrifices (vājimedha) by merely seeing it. || 167.65 ||

Seeing the Lord, who resembles a mass of dark blue clouds, the hosts of gods, vidyādharas, and siddhas, as well as the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and dānavas, do not fall again into the mire of saṃsāra.
There is another shrine of the Lord known as Japyeśvara,
where in former times a twice-born man, having performed his silent recitation (japa), established a linga.
Those men who, having reached that Lord Japyeśvara, shall give up their lives,
will be liberated from birth and death and shall dwell in the abode of Śiva.
O Sage Vyāsa, there is another abode of the one who wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, which is renowned in the world as Mahābhairava. 167.69.
There, the god who bears the trident, the bull-bannered one himself,
assumed a terrifying form, formidable with his hosts of Nandī and Umā.
Seeing which, the daughter of Himavat became overwhelmed with fear—
that place where Bhava, for the sake of sport, terrified the daughter of the Mountain King.
He became once more of gentle form and consoled the daughter of the mountain;
thus that sanctuary is called Mahābhairava.
O Vyāsa, he who, having approached Bhairaveśvara, beholds the wielder of the Pināka bow,
shall not undergo birth and death again.
Whatever merit belongs to those in the stages of life (āśramas) and likewise to those who observe the vows of the Lord, that fruit a preeminent man obtains simply by beholding Bhairava. (167.74)
And likewise Kumbhakāreśvara, as well as Utkaṭukeśvara,
Chagalaṇḍeśvara, and the site born of Mahābhairava.
By beholding these three places, one becomes the lord of the three worlds;
furthermore, another abode of Śiva called Rudrakoṭi is also mentioned.
O Vyāsa, by reciting [the mantra] three hundred million times there, Nandin attained from Śaṅkara the status of an excellent Gaṇeśa.
Those by whom that sacred abode was seen attain the supreme goal;
and in the Devadāru forest, there is also the excellent abode of Bhava.
It was covered with forests of devadāru trees and fragrant sarala trees,
and was constantly frequented by gandharvas, uragas, and kinnaras.
There dwell the Vaikhānasa brahmins, devoted to the worship of Śiva,
rich in asceticism, and resplendent like the sun or fire.
It is said that the wielder of the trident entered that forest for the sake of alms;
there, the Lord of the Gods was seen by the sages with his organ erect.
Out of envy, O Vyāsa, that great liṅga of the god was cast down by deluded sages in the hermitage of the Devadāru forest.
When that linga had fallen, the world became devoid of lingas;
both the stationary and the moving worlds shone forth entirely as neuter.
Then the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Siddhas seeking liberation,
realized that everything was born of Śaṅkara and that its destruction would be most terrible.
Having praised Śaṃkara with various hymns and fully gratified him,
that liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow then became as it was before.
And from that moment, the world attained masculinity;
there, a liṅga of the Supreme Lord was installed by them with devotion. (167.86)
Having seen that, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Thus, O great sage, does the holy Dāruvana forest belong to Īśa.
Having approached it, men are quickly liberated from all sins;
for by Dadhīca, this great, divine, and meritorious sanctuary was established. (167.88)
Renowned as Sthāneśvara, it is famous throughout the three worlds;
having reached Sthāneśvara, the man who casts off his own body [attains liberation]. (167.89)
Having attained mastery through yoga, he rejoices in the heavenly world by means of the serpent Takṣaka, who was firmly devoted to Śaṃkara.
Thus, Takṣakeśvara was established on the bank of the Jāhnavī,
where the supreme presence of Rudra, the God of gods, resides.
Having seen that god, a person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
There is also another great and meritorious sanctuary established by Agastya.
O observer of noble vows, having beheld with supreme devotion that deity renowned in the world as Āmrāteśvara, a man of pure conduct [attains his goal]. (167.93)
Having attained the dissolution of the body after seeing the Linga of the Lord of Umā on Mount Kālañjara, one shall reach the world of Śarva.
Having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, one shall attain the world of Rudra;
[there is a place] known as Puṣpabhadraka, situated on a plateau of the Vindhya mountains and covered with trees.
There is the meritorious abode of Bhava, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
which was established by the rākṣasa Meghanāda, the son of Rāvaṇa,
to gratify Bhava, the lord of all beings.
There, Mandodarī’s son had his desire fulfilled by Śiva, the moon-crested one, through the gift of a chariot of illusion.
Having seen that, having gone there, and having bowed to the Lord of the World,
men go to heaven, endowed with divine yoga.
And in the Andhra country, there is another shrine of Śarva, the Supreme Self,
named Citraratha, which bestows the boons of yogic perfection.
O Vyāsa, there [is described] the chariot of the wise god during the destruction of Tripura,
which was adorned by the immortals, including Soma, Āditya, Yama, and others.
Whatever fruit has been declared by the wise for a correctly performed horse sacrifice,
a human being attains that very fruit upon reaching Citraratha.
There is another auspicious abode of existence called Anyaduktaratha,
which is beautiful and always frequented by gods, kinnaras, and gandharvas.
There is a mountain named Śrīparvata, the abode of Śrī;
it is filled with hundreds of Siddhas and gods, that most excellent field of spiritual accomplishment.
There, O Vyāsa, a thousand meritorious lingas of Śūlin that grant boons were installed by the high-souled Śilāda.
Those men who behold that Lord dwelling on Śrīparvata shall never again experience the fear of birth and death.
In that very field consisting of worldly existence, brahmins devoted to the practice of yoga attain their desired perfection with this very body.
O Sage, those men who even mentally visit Śrīgirī do not go to the abode of Yama, even when death has arrived.
Then [he went] to Uttaragokarṇa, the hermitage marked by the liṅgas of Hara,
where fierce austerities were performed by flesh-eating rākṣasas.
In ancient times, after performing austerities there and propitiating the wielder of the Pināka bow, the illustrious Rāvaṇa and others obtained their desired boons.
Having beheld that, a man obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices, as Rāvaṇa attained the status of a universal monarch over the three worlds. || 167.110 ||
And one who dies there attains union with Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Beyond that is the holy site of Gokarṇa in the south, belonging to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Where, on the peaks of the Malaya mountains in Laṅkā,
the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of all the foremost immortals, is worshipped with *spṛkkā* flowers that grow there.
There, a single tiger among Rākṣasas, Vibhīṣaṇa, even today enjoys his kingdom without fear, having duly worshipped the Lord of the Immortals.
Those men who go to the hermitage of the Gokarṇa shrine obtain the auspicious fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
The mountain known as Hariścandra, which possesses many waterfalls,
is there that the hermitage was established by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Where the gods, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Kinnaras, as well as those observing vows and practitioners of yoga, all bow down to the Bull-bannered Lord.
O Sage, those by whom the peak, the summit of Mount Hariścandra, has been beheld, do not dwell among mortals; having become gods, they do not return again.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, at a distance of one yojana along the path,
is the great sacred site of Kārohaṇa, the abode of the Three-eyed Lord.
There, where the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) ascended the female crow as she was performing austerities—in that very place where he ascended the crow—[he remained]. 167.119.
Therefore, that region is celebrated by the name Kārohaṇa;
and in that very place, the Blessed Lord whose banner is the bull descended.
Understand from me that this land is more meritorious than all other lands;
O Vyāsa, when the Kṛta Yuga had waned and at the dawning of the Tretā Yuga—
In that [Kṛta age], Dharma, oppressed by Adharma, released one foot;
when the Dvāpara age arrived, he released a second, and in the Kali age, a third.
And because the Blessed Lord Rabhu established himself there for the fourth time,
that region is thus remembered as most meritorious due to its association with Dharma.
Having become Bhārabhūti in that region,
the wielder of the Pināka bow bound the burdens of the twice-born and cast them into the Narmadā.
Out of compassion and with the desire to liberate mortals from birth, Mahādeva,
in the Tretā age, cut off the heads of Diṇḍi and Muṇḍa.
And in the Dvāpara age, having become a blue jay, Śiva himself favored him with a dance;
thus, O Vyāsa, in that region, Śiva himself [manifests] in every age.
Having descended and favored those Brahmins of pure mind,
O observer of noble vows, he established shrines for all of them.
By whom these have been seen, he shall attain the world of the Lord Īśāna;
for even in the present Kali age, having recognized that the world is afflicted by suffering. || 167.128 ||
Having created four persons from his own four faces,
the Supreme Lord spoke out of a desire to show favor to the worlds.
"All of you go to the earth and become ascetic brahmins;
O lords of yoga, having led these brahmins to the supreme state, you shall come back to me. (167.130)
Having spoken thus, O Vyāsa, they then became separate individuals among men,
those brahmins devoted to the dharma of liberation.
In Ujjayinī was the eldest elder, known by the name Kauśika;
the second was Gārgya, who dwelt at Jambūmārga;
and the third was the high-minded Mitra, who was in Mathurā. (167.132)
The fourth, however, was a celibate student (brahmacārī) born of a noble lineage, O descendant of Kuru.
The Blessed One, the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Amareśvara,
[bestowed this upon] Somaśarman, who was born of the lineage of Atri.
Having assumed a white-bodied form, he went to the auspicious home of Atri;
there the Lord [approached] that knower of Brahman, the sage Ātreya, together with his family.
Śaṅkara favored him by bestowing the perfection of yoga;
having thus favored that best of the twice-born along with his family, O Vyāsa. (167.136)
The god went to Ujjayinī and entered the cremation ground;
there, he whose banner is the bull covered himself with ashes.
Taking a firebrand in his left hand, the Lord sat down there;
first, he took the disciple Kauśika.
The Lord of the World, having bestowed grace upon Jambūmārga as the second, then another at Mathurā, and then yet another at Kānyakubja; 167.139.
The Lākulī gave his own established doctrine and spoke this yoga;
for this is indeed the supreme secret known as the Pañcārtha.
"You have been granted this [power] by me to liberate the brahmins from mortal bondage;
through this initiation, lead the brahmins to the supreme state. (167.141)
Your dwelling, free from attachment, shall be on the pure and holy banks of rivers, in sacred shrines, in empty houses, or in the forests.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, all those disciples of Paśupati, who were themselves possessed of the splendor of Bhava, performed exactly as they had been commanded.
Since Bhava descended upon that land marked by the footprints of Dharma,
that region is therefore considered the supreme and most meritorious of all places.
There is the hermitage of the yogins where the destroyer of sins has appeared;
this place of the Great-souled One is known as Aṣṭāyatana.
O Vyāsa, those men who behold it and those humans who go to Kārohaṇa, the abode of Śiva, attain the supreme state.
O best of sages, for those [who dwell] between the Mahī and Narmadā rivers and within the region of the Sahya mountains, there shall be no fear of the womb-bed.
This is the ancient field of Paśupati, praised by the seers.
O Vyāsa, having come here, even if a man has been a perpetrator of great evil,
he shall be liberated from all sins and attain his desired goal.
The place Kārohaṇa is exceedingly meritorious, O wise one, where there are shrines of Śiva;
having gone to those places of great fruit, men do not enter the house of saṃsāra again.
And there is another meritorious sanctuary, O best of sages, adored by the seven worlds, located in Vārāṇasī where Hara is ever present. (167.150)
There, the holy Bhāgīrathī flows toward the northern direction;
it is a field of perfection, a vast field, renowned throughout the three worlds. || 167.151 ||
It is known by the name Avimukta because it was not released by Hara;
for there, one beholds the Lord Avimukteśvara, the consort of Umā.
O great sage, the destination of those devoted to Gaṇapati is said to be reached at the time of death,
where the mighty Gaṇapa Vidyutkeśa stands at the gateway.
By the command of the Self-Existent One, the wielder of the staff, possessed of great splendor, does not see Hara, the Lord of the gods, as long as he himself has not seen him. 167.154.
Even for great-souled yogis, a sight of him is meritorious;
having seen the pure Gaṇa Daṇḍapāṇi, who has received a boon from Hara.
Having attained happiness in this world, they go to his same world,
where the great-souled Siddhas dwell, endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty.
Having circumambulated him, they bowed down to the Self-Existent One:
Śakra, Pitāmaha, Viṣṇu, Dhaneśa, Varuṇa, and Yama. || 167.157 ||
The consumer of oblations (Agni), the wind, the moon, and the sun himself, as well as the seven seers, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, and the Pannagas. || 167.158 ||
Those of firm vows worship the god Avimukteśvara;
therefore, according to sacred tradition, there is no field of spiritual attainment more meritorious than this.
Wherever a living being who has met with calamity attains liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra through the grace of Śambhu—this is remembered as the supreme secret. (167.160)
The Gaṅgā is to the south of it, and Varāṇasī is to the north;
that field between those two is the Avimukta of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Whatever fruit is obtained from a Linga of Śambhu installed elsewhere,
that is said to be multiplied a thousandfold when it is established in Avimukta.
Whether a woman or a man, whoever installs [the Liṅga] according to the prescribed rule, by him a thousand Liṅgas of the Lord have been installed. (167.163)
Having become a three-eyed leader of the Gaṇas, he shall attain union with Rudra.
Therefore, O best of sages, after this, Liṅgas were installed there by all the supreme gods, headed by Brahmā and Āditya.
In that field of the Blessed One, in the city of Kāśī, many liṅgas established by high-souled beings are seen even today. (167.165)
Even if one who has not attained liberation through remembrance remains at the very edge of the earth,
that living being is freed from impurities and, upon death, attains happiness.
The Brahmins who know the true meaning of the Vedas, as well as the Siddhas and the Pāśupatas who desire liberation from the bondage of worldly existence, do not abandon that [dharma]. || 167.167 ||
Having reached the holy Vārāṇasī, that unsurpassed field of spiritual accomplishment, what living being would have the mind to depart elsewhere again? (167.168)
O Vyāsa, that sacred field of the moon-crested Lord is sung of in the Vedas;
it bestows liberation, perfection, and the supreme goal upon embodied beings who cast off their vital breaths there.
O Vyāsa, those men who dwell in Avimukta, being devoted to Rudra, dwell in the abode of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, eating, performing action, or even laughing, for that embodied being who remembers Avimukta, whence can there be fear of birth? 167.171.
There is no field superior to Avimukta; there is no state superior to Avimukta; there is no merit superior to Avimukta; there is no goal superior to Avimukta. (167.172)
Whatever destination belongs to one who meditates constantly and merges into the supreme Brahman,
that same destination is ordained for one who gives up their life-breaths at Avimukta.
This is the sacred field of Umāpati, always frequented by the best of gods for the sake of spiritual perfection;
it is Avimukta, which Brahmā and others have cultivated for the sake of peace.
Those mortals who, devoted supremely to the Lord, serve this place for the attainment of tranquility—[they shall find their goal].
Freed from the fear arising from cyclic existence, they go to supreme liberation.
And at Prayāga, the field of asceticism, there is a great sanctuary of the God;
having seen it, a person shall properly attain the desired goal.
Having seen the great abode of Rudra, the God of gods, at Naimiṣa, one is liberated from sin and attains the heavenly world.
In the field of Dharma, at Kurukṣetra, there is a great place belonging to the Lord of Yoga;
by seeing it, O best of Brahmins, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati.
Upon death, he shall attain the world of Rudra, which fulfills all desires;
in this verse lies another auspicious station of the Lord, the Master.
Known by the name Gṛdhrakūṭeśvara, it liberates one from all sins;
having seen it, the best of men are not deluded at the time of death.
There, by applying sacred ash, one is liberated from all sins;
even a twice-born man who has observed the twelve-year vow shall obtain that fruit.
This is the meritorious āyatanam of Pinākin in Magadha;
in the city of Pāṭaliputra, it is known by the name Prahasiteśvara. (167.181)
By approaching that Lord, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
It is recorded that there are eight sites of the Moon-crested God (Śaśimaulin) in Magadha.
Those places where Nakulīśvara wandered, surrounded by his disciples—having seen which, a man would immediately become free from sin. || 167.183 ||
Among the Yavanas, there is remembered another holy place of the Lord of Umā;
by beholding that Lord, a human being attains Tripiṣṭapa. (167.184)
In the land of Aṅga, there is said to be a supremely meritorious place belonging to the wielder of the Pināka bow;
by seeing that shrine named Hemacūḍeśvara, one is no longer deluded.
There, O Vyāsa, at the confluence of the Bhāgīrathī and the ocean,
there is the meritorious liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) established by Brahmā.
By merely approaching it, one is liberated from all sins;
by beholding it, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having seen the wielder of the trident at Prabhāsa, one becomes a Gaṇa upon the dissolution of the body;
having seen Śaṅkara at Puṣkara, one shall not grieve over birth and death.
And having approached the auspicious abode of Rudra at Mahendra, the best of mountains,
a wise man shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Having approached the god Mahākāleśvara in Ujjayinī, the wise man who observes the great vow shall attain the status of an attendant of the enemy of Tripura.
Having beheld the god Drimacaṇḍeśvara, a man is saved;
he rescues seven generations of his lineage on both sides and attains the fruits of all sacrifices.
Having beheld Śaṅkukarṇeśvara on the peak of the Himavat mountain, which is frequented by Siddhas and Kinnaras, a man shall no longer grieve over death.
Having approached and beheld that great abode of Rudra known as Ḍiṅgeśvara, and having seen that god, the lord of the world, [one attains merit]. 167.193.
O Vyāsa, one who is devoted to Śiva shall attain all desires;
and for such a high-souled person who has died, the destination is declared to be the state of being a Gaṇapati.
The supreme station of the God of gods is remembered as Suvarṇākṣa;
having seen that, O Vyāsa, a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (167.195)
Having beheld the holy site of Kapardin at Saptagodāvara,
a man, having obtained the fruit of a horse-sacrifice, shall dwell in the heavenly world.
There is another most meritorious place, celebrated as the best in the world,
known by the name Bhadreśvara, frequented by gods and gandharvas.
O Vyāsa, by beholding him, a human being obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
whatever great inauspicious karma has been committed since birth [is destroyed]. (167.198)
Upon seeing Hara Bhadreśvara, everything perishes at that very moment;
even if a man dies anywhere else, he shall obtain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Blessed are those men, O Vyāsa, who possess great luster and are devotees of Rudra,
who behold Bhadreśa, the remover of the fear of birth and death.
Having seen the abode of the Lord at Ekāmra, one shall attain heaven;
having seen Hara at Virajā, one shall obtain the merit of a horse sacrifice.
And in Nepal, having beheld the Lord Paśupati, the ruler of gods, one obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and goes to the world of Rudra. || 167.202 ||
And upon the dissolution of the body, one is liberated from the state of a bound soul (paśu). There is another place on the Himagiri mountain, presided over by Naikatuṅga Īśvara. || 167.203 ||
Having seen that, O best of sages, a mortal is not born again;
it is remembered as the granter of all desires to those who are devoted and prostrate before it. || 167.204 ||
Thus, O Vyāsa, these meritorious abodes of Rudra have been described by me, by which an auspicious destination is attained.
The bull-bannered God bestows upon that Brahmin who recites these daily with a disciplined mind the state of union (sāyujyatā).
A pure man should constantly recite the names of Śambhu’s abodes, for it is supremely auspicious, meritorious, purifying, and the remover of all fears. (167.207)
Thus, this dwelling in the world of Viṣṇu— the bearer of the Gaṅgā and son of the king of mountains— is the granter of all desires for you;
it is refined by the sons and disciples of the best of sages and is the purifier of all sins.
Speak, O Vyāsa; what else may I say to you? 167.208
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Abodes of Śiva," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard the narrative concerning the sacred abodes of the Lord whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon’s orb, [the sages asked:]
The sage Vyāsa spoke these words to that lord of sages, the son of Brahmā, who was a knower of Brahman.

O Blessed One, this secret discourse, righteous and highly meritorious, has been duly imparted to me by you. What other sage would be capable of fully knowing these beloved abodes of Śambhu? || 168.2 ||
"I desire to know how Tripura was consumed by a single arrow from the wielder of the divine Pināka, who formerly granted boons to his devotees; O Sage, tell me that as it actually occurred."
Thus questioned by the sage, the lord of sages explained the matter exactly as it was, saying these words:
"O son, listen to how that Tripura was burnt. (168.4)
When that lion among the bulls of the Daityas, the heroic son of Hiraṇyākṣa,
had been slain and the Dānavas had been broken, Maya became consumed by the sorrow of his lack of resolve.
Deprived of the royal splendor of the foremost of the Dānavas, that creator of all was like the fish-bannered god of love separated from Rati;
for he had taken with him the Daityas Tārakākṣa and Vidyutprabha, who possessed power equal to that of Indra.
Ahinakarma performed severe austerities, as did those two Daityas who were equal in prowess to Andhaka;
they stood upon snowy mountains during the cold season and were scorched by five fires during the summer.
In the rainy season, they practiced their austerities with diligence on ground-sites drenched by rain even under a cloudless sky;
thus, a thousand divine years passed for them as they remained steadfast in such intensely severe penance.

With only skin and bone remaining, yet possessing the brilliance of fire through the power of their extraordinary austerities, those lions among the sons of Diti became heroes equal in splendor to the sun and shone with the very form of the sun.
The Grandfather, having approached them all and spoken many kind words, addressed them: "Your asceticism has been performed and your delusion has vanished; now, being joyful, choose a boon. (168.10)
With palms joined in reverence, his knees resting upon the ground, Maya bowed to the Lord of the Gods and addressed him:
"Grant me invincibility, incomparable strength, divine knowledge, and supreme bliss. (168.11)
"O God, grant us this desired boon so that death may not come to us;
and I shall construct a fortress, O Lord of the Gods, consisting of three cities resembling divine celestial chariots."
"May that [city] be inaccessible to all the gods, with its own independent arrangement, movement, and activity.
When he had spoken thus, Brahmā addressed these words to Maya, the lord of the Danujas.
"This boon cannot be granted to you; therefore, choose another that is superior or different.
O son, ask for that, and I shall grant it; let there be no further anxiety on your account regarding the sons of Danu."
Then Maya, being utterly bewildered, spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Gods, let that boon be granted to us exactly as it was requested; and whatever else I say, you ought to grant that to me. (168.15)
When a full thousand years have passed, O hero among the gods, the three cities shall come together for but half a moment; at that instant, when those three divine cities have converged— 168.16.
O hero among the gods, when a full thousand years have passed, the three cities shall come together for but half a moment; at that instant, when those three divine cities have converged—

"May he burn those three cities with a single arrow; may he be the destroyer of Tripura. Having heard those words of Maya, Brahmā, his inner soul thrilled with joy, granted that desired boon to the lord of the Danujas, and having given it, he quickly departed for his own city. (168.17)
Then Maya constructed that triple city, just as the Creator fashioned the primordial cities at the beginning of the kalpa;
he first made one of iron, and thereafter another of silver, resembling a mountain.
Then he quickly created another third city, golden and as lofty as a peak of Mount Meru;
once created by Maya, that triple-city stole away the divine splendor of heaven.
It was well-furnished with charming doors, balconies, and windows, and with courtyards and squares made of gold;
it possessed palatial towers whose floors were touched by the rays of the moon and which were pleasant to enter due to the refreshing cool breezes.
It shone exceedingly with various banners— adorned with pearls, corals, and fragments of gems, resembling the brilliance of variegated lightning—
which were suspended and shaken by the wind, their streamers fluttering to and fro.
Adorned with fragments of jewels set in rows of palaces, which resembled the luster of great moon-like gems,
and featuring lofty gateways and the tops of mansions, that triple city shone resplendently.
It was surrounded on all sides by very tall trees laden with blossoms and fruit of every season that were pleasing to the mind,
and it was endowed with hundreds of delightful gardens where bees, peacocks, and swans wandered about.
That abode of the Daityas shone likewise with ponds crowded with birds and covered with blooming blue lotuses, as well as with lakes where cranes were dancing.
Likewise, it shone exceedingly, crowded with women whose breasts were pressed by their nails, whose eyes had reddened corners, and who gazed with slightly tremulous looks and modesty. 168.25.
Having constructed that iron city, Maya gave it to Tārakākṣa;
and he gave a second city, made of silver, to Vidyutprabha, the lord of the Asura kings.
The third [city], made of gold, was divine; King Maya himself took it for his own sake.
Then that triple city became presided over by those three lions among the Danava kings.
Having conquered all their own powers from every side, accompanied by their beloveds, friends, and servants,
they enjoyed various pleasures there, unconcerned with the cares of the three worlds.
Bound by pride and delusion, their passion was such that they considered the gods inferior in strength;
and having resolved this, they fell upon them violently and inflicted all manner of extreme torments.
Led by Vaibhrāja, they stripped the groves of their creepers and flowers;
led by Rambhā and others, they drained the ponds and stripped them of their lotuses. (168.30)
The celestial women, their limbs trembling with fear, caused great agony to others by those [demons];
and thus, a very long time passed while they were performing these acts of destruction against the gods.
Then, having become enraged, all the lords of the denizens of heaven assembled together and quickly reported everything exactly as it had occurred, without omission, to the Grandfather.
The god seated upon the lotus throne spoke to them all, consoling the lords of the gods:
"Those immensely powerful lords of the Tripura asuras cannot indeed be slain by you through force."
Therefore, Viṣṇu, I, and you, having taken hold of one another, shall go for refuge to Śambhu.
O lords of the gods, the wielder of the trident, the moon-bearer, is our eternal resort; he will slay them by force.

"So be it," they replied; and those gods—Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Anila, Pāvaka, and the others—having prostrated themselves, went to Kailāsa and, having beheld Hara, the Lord of the lords of the gods, praised him with their purposes fulfilled.
Homage to him who is worshipped by the Lord of the Three Worlds, whose lips are beloved, and whose prowess is immeasurable;
homage be to him whose crest is illuminated by the radiance of the mass of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon.

Homage be ever to the god of the three worlds; likewise, homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow. Homage be to him who bears the blazing sword and battle-axe; homage be ever to the one with the trident in his hand.
Homage, homage to the bestower of boons upon Nandin, the refuge of the world, the lord of the gods;
homage always to the bestower of boons upon his devotees, and homage be to the bestower of boons upon the lord of the yakṣas.
Salutations always to you who eternally abide on Himavat, the king of mountains, and dwell upon Kailāsa;
salutations to you whose abode is Vimukteśa, and salutations be to you who are present everywhere. 168.39.

Homage be ever to him whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who wears matted hair, who is seated upon a bull, who is clothed in the directions, who grants the supreme white boon, who is endowed with all prosperity, and who is the creator of the world. 168.40
Salutations to the Creator of Hari, Arka, Śakra, Agni, and Pitāmaha; salutations to the God who is the source of all;
eternal salutations to the subtle, eternal Supreme Lord, the omnipresent Sustainer. 168.41.
Homage to the Supreme, who is beyond the supreme, the Primordial Person known as the Twenty-sixth;
let there be constant homage to Śarva, the wielder of the bow, to Sarva, the source of all.
Homage be to the creator of the body and other elements consisting of moon, wind, sun, fire, water, earth, and space;
homage always be to Pūṣan for the destruction of teeth, and homage be to him for the destruction of the bodies of women. 168.43.
Homage to the Primal One, to the Supreme Person who is attained through yoga; let there always be homage to him.
Homage, repeated homage, to the one who possesses both fierce and gentle forms, and to the creator of the entire world.
Homage be to the creator of knowledge, homage to the creator of dharma; homage to the creator of sacrifice, gods, and asuras;
homage to the bearer of the third eye, and homage, homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin! 168.45
Let there be constant homage to the Supreme Person; let there always be homage to him who dwells in the cremation ground.
Let there be homage to the destroyer of the Daityas and Andhakas; let there always be homage to the destroyer of delusion.

Salutations ever be to the destroyer of darkness; salutations ever be to the destroyer of ignorance. Salutations always to the bestower of the boon of liberation; salutations always to him who abides in the immortal.
Homage to the husband of the daughter of the mountain-king; may there always be homage to the father of Kumāra.
Homage be to the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Wealth; homage always to the bestower of boons upon Śukra.
Salutations be to the one who is Brahman itself, the creator of Brahman; salutations, salutations to the creator of the gods, the Ordainer.
Salutations be to the slayer of Dakṣa, Amara, and the sacrifice; salutations be to the bestower of boons upon Caṇḍeśa.
Salutations be to Rudra, the supreme abode, the Lord of Yoga praised by the immortals;
salutations be to Hara, Śarva, Śiva, the Protector, to Bhīma and to Śambhu.

Salutations ever be to the Puruṣa who is devoid of qualities, yet exalted by qualities, who transcends qualities while abiding in qualities; who is sung of in the Sāṃkhya, and who is established in the Upaniṣads of Yoga.
Salutations ever to the Great Puruṣa, who is higher than the highest, who is both gross and subtle.
Being propitiated, O Supreme Lord, show us favor; being pleased, grant us a boon.
Thus did Śambhu [speak] to the gods, led by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Sun, as they offered praise.
Pleased by her exceptional devotion in this hymn of praise, he spoke these words of most wonderful meaning:
"I am satisfied, O gods; choose quickly today whatever you desire, if there is anything at all.
I shall grant it all to you today without exception; there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given to you. (168.53)
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon the Deities," at the commencement of the Destruction of Tripura, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter.
The gods said:
"O Lord, by the three Dānavas—Maya and the others—who have been granted boons by Brahmā..."
Having made that Tripura an impregnable fortress, he was being harassed by those who were arrogant in their strength.
"All the Apsarases have been carried off and the forests have been destroyed;
we shall slay every single god today, or tomorrow," they said. (169.2)
"Even Brahmā, the Grandfather, or Viṣṇu, or even Mahādeva, is not capable of subduing them; therefore, we have a very great fear."
Just as Tripura might be destroyed and they might be slain, so act, O best of gods; let this boon be granted to us.
Thus addressed by all those foremost of gods, Śambhu,
possessed of great splendor, spoke these words as if to reassure the deities.
"O lords of the gods, having each taken a hundredth part of my splendor and becoming composed of Rudra's energy, you shall slay the Dānavas. || 169.6 ||
Then those gods spoke these words again to the Lord:
"We are not capable of bearing even a thousandth part of you."
O Lord of the Gods, what power do we have to behold or even to sustain your supreme, great Maheśvara splendor? O Lord, show us favor.
"We are by no means able to slay those Dānavas by force.
O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, you yourself must destroy Tripura. (169.9)
It is said that a boon was granted to them by Brahmā:
"After a thousand divine years have passed, the wielder of the trident shall come to the three cities."
In that very instant, within half a blink of an eye, the powerful one will discharge this single arrow once and utterly consume these three cities and the Dānavas.
"That shall be your death; for there is no other way for you to die. We are not able to do otherwise, so grant us your favor. (169.12)
Then that Blessed Lord, whose banner bears the bull, spoke again to the anxious dwellers of heaven, consoling them as they bowed before him.
