"If it be so, O tigers among the gods, I shall, by discharging a single arrow once, consume this great and inaccessible Tripura in the twinkling of an eye."
"For the sake of pleasing Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and for the benefit of Śakra,
I myself shall mount the chariot Tripura and destroy it."
"Let that chariot be made ready, mounting which I, O dwellers of heaven,
shall consume the three fortresses of Tripura, which have been overrun by the three Dānavas."
O foremost of gods, the chariot must be made such that it is as strong as the Himalayas and capable of carrying me.
Then the gods, bowing to the Lord, became joyful in mind;
and all together they fashioned an excellent chariot.
Then the blessed Brahmā, as well as Viṣṇu and Hutāśana,
fashioned that supreme, divine chariot composed of all the gods.
Dhātṛ, Bhāskara, Śakra, Pavana, Dhanada, and Yama;
the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Gandharvas, and the two Aśvins.
The Garuḍas, mountains, Nāgas, Guhyakas, along with the great oceans,
the Ṛṣis, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and likewise the Grahas— [all these he beheld].
— as well as the bright and dark fortnights, the lords of the forest (trees), the days, the muhūrtas, the kṣaṇas, and likewise the kāṣṭhās and lavas. || 169.22 ||
He [knows] the solstices, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and likewise the years;
as well as whatever is stationary and whatever is moving, and the lunar mansions as well. (169.23)
They arrayed those eight classes of gods upon that chariot;
some they placed upon the two wheels, [others] upon the pole.
The preeminent gods yoked other chariots;
having made four gods into horses, they harnessed them to that chariot.
They made the year into a wheel, the mountain into a bow,
and they made the Goddess of the World, the sustainer of the universe, the bowstring for that bow.
The gods fashioned for him such a supreme chariot,
making that best of vehicles consist of all the gods and resembling a mountain.
Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, and Agni, having bowed down to the Supreme Lord, said, "The chariot is ready for the destruction of the enemies of the gods. || 169.28 ||
Then the Blessed Śambhu, being praised by the three classes of gods,
gazed upon the divine chariot fashioned from all the deities.
Saying, "Well done! Excellent!", he took up that great bow;
having grasped that supreme, blazing bow which was composed of all splendor.
Having gazed both downward and upward, the Lord of the World was gratified;
then, looking toward the Grandfather, the Lord of Speech spoke.
"O Brahmin, this chariot and this bow have been well-prepared by you;
now quickly bring that arrow with which Tripura is to be consumed. (169.32)
Then Brahmā, having bowed to the bull-bannered god, said to him:
"O Lord, this chariot has been fashioned by me for you, as well as this bow."
"The Blessed One himself ought to make that arrow suitable for its purpose.
Then, seeing Viṣṇu and Hutāśana standing by his side, Śambhu—
With a mere glance, that subduer of enemies summoned those two gods;
they both joined their palms in reverence and stood before the Lord of the Gods.
Then Śambhu himself fashioned Viṣṇu into the most excellent arrow;
he fixed Soma, the lord of herbs, upon its shaft.
He then made Śalya his charioteer and addressed Brahmā:
"O Brahman, who has been appointed by you here as the charioteer for this chariot?"
Then Brahmā, approaching his lord with palms joined in reverence, said to him:
"If you grant me the command, I myself shall indeed be the charioteer."
"O God, what else shall I obtain from you that is superior to being your charioteer?
Having said, "Everything shall be auspicious," the god who wields the Pināka bow then [departed].
Taking the Lord of Gods by the hand, he ascended the excellent chariot;
and those attendants of Rudra, headed by Nandīśvara, [did likewise].
And those led by Śaṅkukarṇa, as well as Caṇḍeśvara and the others—
the lords of the Gaṇas, great yogins, three-eyed, with battle-axes in their hands— (169.41).
They were skilled in various weapons and missiles, experts in diverse modes of combat, adorned with various ornaments and garments, and proficient in many branches of knowledge.
Sounding together many musical instruments, including the sounds of kettledrums and conchs,
those fourteen thousand leaders of the hosts arrived.
Thousands of showers of various kinds of flowers fell upon the head of the wielder of the Pināka bow as he stood upon his chariot.
And all those who were yoked to the chariot of the trident-bearing God of gods themselves sounded musical instruments in every direction.
Unable to bear the burden, the gods were utterly bewildered;
then the Lord of the gods, perceiving those denizens of heaven to be confused, [acted].
The gods made their bodies capable of enduring [the heat], and consequently they were bewildered;
then, O Vyāsa, in that interval, the venerable sage Nārada appeared.
He went quickly to Tripura with the desire to see Viśvakarman. Then, seeing that the Ṛṣi had arrived, Viśvakarman Maya [welcomed him]. 169.48.
Having worshipped him with supreme devotion, he bowed to that best of sages; the sage, having bestowed blessings upon him, sat down upon a cane seat.
Having sat upon that seat, the great sage said to Maya:
"This bull-bannered god has been propitiated by all the deities. (169.50)
The Lord of the World has arrived here to destroy Tripura; having mounted his divine, god-fashioned chariot, do what is right in this matter.
Having made Brahmā his charioteer, Śaṅkara himself came forth;
having heard the words of Nārada, that lord of the Dānavas then [prepared].
Having summoned Tārakākṣa and Vidyunmālin,
as well as his other asura brothers led by Bāṇa and Nemi.
Then he caused everything that had been told by Nārada to be heard;
having heard that, Tārakākṣa, the king of the Daityas, spoke as follows.
"There is no one equal to you in the three worlds, O preeminent among the asuras; whoever would fight you would do so without fear, so do not harbor such anxiety."
"What is there to deliberate upon here, O King, since we are all invulnerable? Which Dānava possesses the power to destroy that Tripura? (169.56)
O Lord of the Daityas, if all the gods have assembled here to fight, behold them today as they are being slain by me alone. (169.57)
A weak man employs sowing dissension, bribery, conciliation, or even prostration before a superior enemy; but we are always strong.
"The weak enemy must be subdued by force through valor by one who is strong and desires victory," so said the preceptor Śukra at that time. (169.59)
Therefore, we Daityas are powerful while the dwellers of heaven are weak;
having slain them all with our staff, we shall remain at ease in happiness.
Having heard the words of Tārākṣa, Vidyunmālī spoke these words:
"This auspicious speech of the king is also exceedingly pleasing to me. (169.61)
Deprived of their strength, those deities will not be able to fight with us;
if they do fight, being utterly deluded, they will then go to their destruction.
"However, we shall employ a stratagem against them instead of fighting one another;
for by means of battle alone, the Daityas always achieve supreme victory."
"Having slain all the gods today, rule the kingdom in Triviṣṭapa;
enjoy the three worlds in peace and become Indra, the creator of all. (169.64)
O Lord of the Daityas, having called to mind Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, we behold you today as Purandara, the Lord of the seven worlds.
"O King, you shall enjoy the sovereignty of the world; go to the destination of those two.
Having heard what Vidyunmālin had spoken, O Vyāsa, Maya [replied]. || 169.66 ||
"O foremost of Daityas, this is not so," he said, shaking his head repeatedly, "for a foe who is equal or inferior in strength to oneself [is not to be treated thus]. (169.67)
Even if one should be a child, provided he is the eldest and possesses the physical form of a single caste,
the wise apply those four means toward him.
"O foremost of Asuras, the inhabitants of heaven are equal to us in strength;
it is fitting for us to employ conciliation and other such means toward those gods."
This Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, the Lord of the lords of all beings, is our creator and destroyer; he is the Master of both us and the gods.
He comes himself to slay; what is his means?
Prostration and seeking refuge—these are the two qualities that serve as the means for Kapardin.
It is my opinion that these two means should be employed against him:
if we fight the wielder of the Pināka bow by resorting to violence. (169.72)
By his mere sidelong glance, the asuras were then struck down;
thereafter, Brahmā and the other gods, being tormented, went to Śambhu for refuge in order to find peace.
O Daityas, for him who is himself engaged in this [struggle], who could be his refuge—he by whom this entire world, from Brahmā onwards, is pervaded? (169.74)
Through meditation alone, even that which is the cause of liberation and the cause of the world would perish in an instant. (169.75)
"What kind of battle did we have with that Śambhu, the God of gods? Do you not know the difference between the intelligence of a child and that of a mountain of clay? (169.76)
O sirs, having become like mere clods of earth, you seek to challenge Umāpati, who is like a mountain,
deluded as you are and bound by the noose of Time.
"I am a devotee of Mahādeva; I know his inner power.
I shall attend upon him with prostration, but I will not fight with Śambhu."
If you too are wise and wish to heed my words, do not engage in battle with Śambhu; go instead for refuge to Śiva.

Having heard those words spoken by the powerful Viśvakarman, the blessed Nārada addressed these words to the destroyer of the Dānavas: The blessed Nārada spoke these words to the destroyer of the Dānavas, after hearing that which was thus spoken by the powerful Viśvakarman.
"O Viśvakarman, all that has been spoken by you in detail and with meaning is entirely logical; however, this is not the time for it. (169.81)
"O Dānavas, that ascetic power of yours has been exhausted and your sovereignty has indeed been enjoyed;
even as you act with cowardice, you shall perish."
Śambhu, surrounded here by all the immortals for the purpose of slaying you,
will kill even you who are prostrate before him for the sake of his own favor.
How is it that you kings, though born as sons of Danu and arrogant in your strength, are afraid and seek to conquer death like wretched Dānavas? || 169.84 ||
If you were to abandon your lives in battle, you would attain even greater sovereignty;
however, if you perish without fighting, your destiny will be inauspicious.
Moreover, O lords of the Pramathas, if you are slain by the trident-bearing God of gods, then you will undoubtedly become [his attendants]. || 169.86 ||
There is no merit for you in remaining in a state of conflict with the gods;
your inclination toward war is improper, and that [intention] is now manifest, as are we.
O Daityas, the bull-bannered Lord may one day be pleased by your valor and grant you boons; through him, your prowess shall become even more excellent.
"And I shall provide you protection that wards off the blows of weapons;
arise, O sons of Danu, with the desire to fight for victory! (169.89)
Having heard the words of Nārada, the exceedingly powerful Tārakākṣa,
the lord of Daityas Vidyunmālī, Bāṇa, and the other great Asuras [prepared for battle].
"Afflicted by the noose of Time, deluded, their merit exhausted and their lives departed, they said, 'This which has been spoken by Nārada is excellent; it is beautiful. (169.91)
Having understood those words of mine and realizing that destruction was at hand, he spoke these words:
"What Nārada has said is excellent. (169.92)
Nārada also, being delighted, performed a protection-rite through his illusory power (māyā) and,
having rendered the Asuras eager for battle, proceeded toward the chariot of Śarva.
Then all those Dānavas, having resolved upon battle and equipped with various weapons, became eager for combat.
Tārakākṣa, Bala, Bāṇa, and the Dānava Vidyunmālī—
all having equipped themselves, stood together at the front as kings.
Then, thousands of conchs and trumpets were sounded amidst the terrible army of the Dānavas, which struck fear into the hearts of the timid.
"This charioteer is coming here; that other one is seen there.
"How was he struck?"—thus they spoke words to one another. (169.97)
Free from fear and despondency, the hosts of Daityas from Tripura approached the fire from his mouth like sacrificial animals.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Asuras," in the Tripuravadha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventieth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that chariot arrived at the summit of the western ocean, where that Tripura was situated.
With his head resplendent and variegated with various banners, he was like Meru, the king of mountains, composed of golden stones.
Beholding the impregnable Tripura, the leaders of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandīśa and Caṇḍīśa,
being well-prepared and desiring to fight with the lions among the kings of the Dānavas, those great heroes together raised a roar.
And Caṇḍeśvara, the high-souled hero among the lords of the Pramathas, possessing a fierce body and holding a blazing, flaming, and terrible axe in his hand,
stood before the god Śambhu with his mouth wide open.
Grasping a blazing trident, the three-eyed Nandin, whose stature was equal to that of Hara, set forth;
and Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, stood at his side, wielding a flaming mace.
Bhṛṅgin, whose soul is Hara, as well as Vīrabhadra and hundreds of heroic lords of the Gaṇas,
stood there filled with joy, eager for battle, with thunderbolts, tridents, swords, and bhuśuṇḍi weapons in their hands.
Beholding that chariot arrived, the Daityas, overcome by delusion, rushed forth for battle;
those great heroes, headed by Tārakākṣa, equipped themselves and stood with various weapons blazing in their hands.
Overcome by anger, the sons of Danu waged war together with the lords of the hosts;
yet even the God, whose crest is the abode of the half-moon, did not discharge his arrow to consume the city.
He remained there just as before, repeatedly observing that battle between himself and the hosts of Daityas;
then Nandin engaged in combat with the foremost heroes of the Gaṇas, who were undaunted in spirit.
Vidyutprabha, his eyes clouded with rage, pierced Bhṛṅgin with ten arrows;
yet, having struck Bhṛṅgin, those shafts were unable to cause him any pain.
Then Bhṛṅgiriṭi struck Vidyutprabha on the back with his blazing trident;
struck by that trident, he reeled and, abandoning Bhṛṅgin, fled, overcome by fear.
Thus shattered, that lord of the sons of Diti abandoned Bhṛṅgin, the chief of the Gaṇas,
and pierced Vināyaka in the region of the shoulder with seven sharp, whetted arrows.
Furthermore, having once more struck that elephant-faced one in his vital organs with sixty-three and ten arrows, Vidyunmālin— having achieved his mark— provoked the wrath of this lord of Vināyakas.
Then that lion among lordly elephants, having encircled the neck of the lord of the Daityas with the tip of his trunk,
tore the head from the body, just as a wild elephant plucks a lotus from a lake.
The severed head of the Daitya shone forth from his body, which resembled the lord of the Vindhya mountains,
like a lotus quickly uprooted from a lake that resounds with the songs of swans and ruddy geese.
Then two other lords of the Daityas, Suyatta and Nemi, who were nearly equal to Andhaka and were well-prepared for battle,
approached Śaṅkukarṇa in a rage and pierced that lord of the Gaṇas with stone-tipped arrows.
Śaṅkukarṇa, attacking them with force, deprived them of their chariots by severing their standards and horses;
mounting two other chariots, the two of them once again encountered that leader of the Gaṇas.

Then the enraged Lord of the Gaṇas, having gazed intently for a long time at those two kings of the Daityas, struck them violently with many kinds of exceedingly sharp arrows that resembled the impact of a thunderbolt.
Having struck those two heroes with his blazing mace, he dispatched them to the city of Yama;
and other Daityas dwelling in Tripura, emerging in anger, were likewise overcome by the lions among the leaders of the Gaṇas.

With iron arrows, discuses, swords, and axes in their hands, those lords of the Daityas waged a most terrible and great battle against the lords of the Gaṇas, who were equal to Hari and had obtained the grace of Śiva.
They were indeed slain and deprived of life, like deer at the edge of the forest by lions;
their various weapons, garments, and necklaces fallen away, they carried blood with their severed arms.
Struck by the vajra, those who were like mountain peaks fell into the ocean;
then, having heard that the two Daityas named Bala and Nemi had been forcibly slain by Śaṅkukarṇa.
Having emerged from the city, that Tārakākṣa, filled with rage, personally rushed toward the lord of the Gaṇas;
Śaṅkukarṇa swiftly [assailed] that sovereign of the sons of Diti as he was discharging a fierce shower of arrows.
With a broad-headed arrow, Gaṇeśa violently struck the Daitya, who resembled a mountain, on the head;
falling down slightly, that lord of the Daityas, struck by that arrow, fell into a swoon.
Rising up quickly, Tārakākṣa indeed hurled a discus at that leader of the Gaṇas;
thereupon, Saṅkukarṇa became enraged and [attacked] that Tārakākṣa. || 170.24 ||
Having struck him down, he beat him on the head with his fist; thus struck, he too fell into distress. He reeled, wandered, fainted, stood still, fell down, and cast away his excellent weapon.
He released his rage, cried out intensely, and afterwards died, having cast off his life-breaths;
seeing the lord of the Daityas fallen, the demons seized him and went to the abode of Maya.
Having gone and informed their lord, the king of the asuras, they raised a clamor with various lamentations;
then Maya, the lord of the asuras, spoke these words, consoling those weeping lords of the gods.

"O Daityas, this nectar of immortality created by me remains here; with it, quickly restore him to life! Then, taking that supreme nectar, the joyful leaders of the Daityas restored Maya to life just as before, and they bowed their heads to him again and again.
Then that Tārākṣa, desiring once more to fight, quickly went forth onto the path of battle.
Perceiving that he who had previously died was now swiftly restored to life,
the Grandfather spoke these words to the lord of gods and asuras, making known the Daitya through his left-hand manifestation.
"O Śaṅkara, although this Tārakākṣa was slain by Maya, he was quickly restored to life;
for that lord of the asuras possesses the supreme nectar of the gods, with which he brings the asuras back to life. (170.31)
"This is a great fault, O Lord of the Gods, that he revives those who have repeatedly died in battle;
therefore, Śambhu quickly seized that nectar which was contained within him by mere meditation. (170.32)
The Grandfather, being once again delighted, bowed to the wielder of the Pināka bow and spoke these words to him:
"I have witnessed this battle of the Gaṇas with the lords of the Daityas, who possess undiminished strength. (170.33)
A thousand divine years have passed, yet this Tripura has not gone to its destruction.
O Lord of the Gods, hurl that flaming arrow; let those enemies of the gods meet their end.
O Lord of the Gods, when the thousand [years] were complete, Tripura came together again and became disordered;
the arrow was discharged by you, O God of gods, but it did not strike—was this by some yoga, O Lord of the Gods? (170.35)
"O Lord, this Tripura, the abode of the Daityas, meets its destruction through mere thought;
if I am to be honored by you, O Lord, then quickly release that arrow at Tripura. (170.36)
Thus addressed by the four-faced one, the slayer of Ananga turned back;
having drawn his bow with great force, he fixed that blazing arrow upon the Pināka.
Then, by mere volition, that God, the creator and destroyer of the world, fashioned those three cities together; and immediately, the entire world became motionless.

The god discharged that fierce arrow, which was of the nature of Viṣṇu, with fire and the moon as its feathers, blazing like the destruction of the three worlds; and having shot it, he cried out, "Alas! Shame! (170.39).
Then Nandin, having approached Maheśa and bowed down, spoke these words: "What is it?
The Blessed One said to that Nandīśvara, desiring to perform a favor for his devotee Maya.
"O Nandīśa, Viśvakarmā is devoted to me; just as fire does not burn his city, so you must go and, by my command, restrain the god Agni and the two gods Soma and Hari."
Then Nandi, having received the command of the Lord of the Gods, went quickly to that city of the Creator;
possessing a speed equal to his own, he arrived even before Jyotiṣmat.
Seeing there that lord of the Dānavas, his body bowed with his head to the one whose banner is the bull,
afflicted by the fear of death and seeking refuge, Nandin comforted him as he was devoted to the Lord.
Having seen Nandīśvara and heard those dear words, "Do not fear; you are protected by me; you shall become a Bhava," that king of the Dānavas spoke thus in response to Śiva’s gracious favor. (170.44)
Just as he had bowed his head to Rudra, he likewise offered salutation to him;
then Agni arrived, desiring to consume Tripura, having set it ablaze on all sides.

Resembling the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon, blazing as if to consume the world, that Nandin addressed the Fire-god—who had arrived there, the abode of Viṣṇu, the Creator of the Universe, and joined with the Moon—as he was burning, saying by the command of the Lord: "This is not to be consumed by you, O Consumer of Oblations. (170.46)
Then that Fire said to the god, "Why should this not be burned by me? Nandin then replied to Hutāśa, "Maya dwells here; he is a devotee of the Lord of the Immortals."
Then Vahni quickly spoke these words to the asura king Maya: "Depart from here immediately!
Taking the golden liṅga of Maheśa, Maya, the lord of the asuras, departed from the city.
Joyfully offering salutations to the beloved of Umā, Nandīśvara quickly entered Pātāla;
having approached the presence of the Lord of the Gods and reported [the matter], he then stood there waiting.

Then Tripura became ablaze; its machines and bolts were shattered, its houses destroyed, the fierce roars of many asuras were released, and it was filled with the terrified wives of the lordly Daityas.

On the balconies of their palatial mansions, women with moon-like faces and full breasts lay sleeping on couches, their eyes clouded with intoxication; they repeatedly sought the path of their beloveds.
With eyes reddened by the glow of their bodies, with dark yet radiant complexions and broad hips,
the wives of the Daityas saw themselves ablaze as they were embraced by the fire of the arrows.
Residing in the palaces, they set out, afflicted by fear like kinnarīs on a mountain trembling with terror;
then, beholding their beloveds returned, they embraced them closely and fell into a deep swoon.
Then those sons of Diti, having seized their beloved ones, fled swiftly with their desires frustrated;
as soon as they emerged, bewildered by the power of Śiva and deprived of their strength, they fell into the ocean.
Then, as those Daityas fell into the ocean, great fish resembling mountains,
along with fierce crocodiles and terrible makaras, devoured them while they were deprived of strength and bewildered.
Other great sea-monsters, with their necklaces shattered, fell upon those women;
deprived of their beloveds, they began to devour them, possessing formidable tusks and gaping maws. (170.56)
Being devoured, those young women fell down; having glared many times in anger at their beloveds, those maidens, tormented by great agony, wailed most piteously. || 170.57 ||
Then, that furious gaze of those Daitya women shone intensely,
like that of women exhausted at the end of dalliance who, desiring to approach other lovers, look upon their own husbands with anger.

Then all those bull-like Daityas, together with their wives, being scorched by the fire of Tripura, sank into the ocean; there they were torn apart by sea-monsters and, their lives departed, fell under the power of death.
And that arrow, whose essence was Agni, Indra, and Janārdana, having consumed that entire city of Tripura and been cast into the ocean,
attained tranquility and returned to the hand of Śambhu.
When those Daityas had been slain and the three cities burnt, the God, who is the cause of creation, dissolution, and so forth, once again made the gods seated upon their chariots,
endowing them with divine bodies just as they were before.
Brahmā and the other lords of the inhabitants of the triple heaven bowed down and spoke these words to the Lord:
"O Blessed One, this deed you have performed is impossible; it is a great and auspicious act, yet one even more terrible than Raudra."
The Daityas have been slain, Tripura has been consumed by fire, and peace has been established for us, O Lord of gods and asuras!
Homage be to you, the creator of the gods, who is ever-present everywhere, O Supreme Lord;
homage, repeated homage, to you who are eternal, whose movement is unknowable, and who are omnipresent. (170.63)
Then the Lord Brahmā spoke to those lords of the gods—Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Indra, Dhaneśvara, and the others:
"O gods, you must always provide for them and protect them, just as I would my own sons. (170.64)
With their desires fulfilled and their enemies destroyed, they departed joyfully for their own abodes;
then the gods, having bowed to the best of gods, went to their respective dwellings. 170.65.
The three-eyed creator of the world, accompanied by the lords of his hosts— Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśvara, and Vīrabhadra— also went to the peak of Kailāsa while being saluted by the Siddhas.
Thus, O Vyāsa, this unbearable deed of the God of gods, known as the burning of Tripura, has been narrated by me to you.
That pure man who studies this, being a devotee of Śarva, becomes freed from sin, attains heaven, and is born among the gods. (170.67)
Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter in the Tripuravadha section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventy-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, I have heard this account of the burning of Tripura."
Who indeed will relate this account of such diverse events exactly as they occurred?
Why did Guha, in his anger, rend that Krauñca, the lord of mountains? And why did Vāsava sever the wings of all the lords of mountains? (171.2)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, to that which you ask me concerning how the Krauñca mountain, the son of Maināka, was split by Kumāra. 171.3.
Then, having approached Meru, the king of mountains and the abode of all the gods,
Vāsava beheld Skanda like a mass of splendors.
Having seen the youth, who possessed the brilliance of fire, in a grove of reeds,
Śakra— intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty over the gods— questioned the six-faced one.
"Who are you, O youth of divine form, who have taken refuge on Mount Meru?
Having seen me, the king of the gods, arrived here, why do you not honor me? (171.6)
To Śakra, who was speaking thus, the son of the Trident-bearer replied:
"Brahmā and the others, as well as the Siddhas and those who know the Vedas, recognize me."
O Śakra, what purpose was served by you knowing that his kingdom, obtained through asceticism, would soon go to ruin; or what was gained by honoring him? (171.8)
Then Śakra spoke again to that son of Anala: "There is none superior to me, except for Śarva and the Grandfather."
"How is it that you spoke thus to the lord of the gods when he had arrived, O sinless one, if in your mind you consider yourself greater than me? (171.10)
For this is the son of Maināka, the Krauñca mountain, frequented by the Siddhas;
it is a vast and great mountain with many flowing waterfalls.
"Come, come with me; quickly perform the circumambulation.
Whichever of us two first completes this shall [win] it. (171.12)
"By his power and by his splendor, he shall indeed become our great protector.
Having said, "So be it," the six-faced Kumāra then [departed].
Having met with Śakra and mounted his excellent peacock,
he proceeded before Mahendra and circumambulated Mount Krauñca.
Then Mahendra, realizing that he was inferior to Anala,
mentally performed a circumambulation, desiring to win back the youth.
Having done this, he remained seated upon the stone surface, deeply satisfied; then the prince, having swiftly performed a circumambulation of that Krauñca mountain, [proceeded].
Seeing him, he quickly declared to Indra, "I shall be the victor.
Śakra said to Guha, "I alone am the victor. (171.17)
While those two sons of Śakra were speaking thus repeatedly, the land-dwelling Krauñca bird approached and spoke these words: "What is this? (171.18)
Then Śakra spoke these words to the prince:
"This very crane, possessed of great strength, is the witness to our victory."
"For this excellent grandson of the Himālaya will not speak a falsehood;
let Śakra be questioned—what harm is there? so said the son of Agni.
He spoke respectfully to Śakra: "Tell me, why have you performed a circumambulation from the summit of the mountain? For you are indeed the authority for both of us. (171.21)
Then the mountain Krauñca, his mind bewildered, reflected for a very long time:
"This lord of Śacī has performed a circumambulation of me here first."
Laughing at the gods, the Lord of Mountains spoke thus;
even as he was speaking these words devoid of truth, the mountain [trembled]. 171.23.
The peak fell swiftly, as if struck by a thunderbolt.
Whatever beings were there upon that lord of mountains, beginning with the gods,
they quickly abandoned it and fled in every direction.
Vāsava also rejoiced in his mind, honoring the mountain;
then the six-faced son of Rudra became enraged at Mount Krauñca.
Then Vāsava, enraged, went to see Guha;
their splendors were then united like those of fire and the sun combined.
Then, raising a spear that possessed a radiance equal to the fire of Yama,
the Lord Skanda, filled with wrath, hurled it with the intent to slay Krauñca.
That spear fell swiftly upon the summit of Mount Krauñca,
like the noose of Death upon a man whose life has come to an end.
But that best of mountains, Krauñca, his vital organs pierced by that spear and all his limbs severed on every side, began to flow with torrents of blood.
Deprived of consciousness and life-breath, he fell to the ground in embodied form; seeing their husband slain, his wives were deeply distressed. (171.30)
Lamenting piteously, they then fell upon Mount Krauñca;
[as did] Meru, Himācala, Vindhya, Kailāsa, and Gandhamādana.
Pāriyātra, Sahya, Niṣadha, Udaya, Vāmana, and Maināka, the best of mountains and the progenitor of Krauñca; || 171.32 ||
All the kings of mountains, afflicted by grief, arrived;
surrounding Mount Krauñca, they wept, being deeply distressed.
Having learned that her brother’s son had been slain, the goddess of the gods, daughter of the mountain king,
who observes great vows, came to Mount Krauñca accompanied by Śarva.
Seeing her own kinsman, the Krauñca bird, slain by the prince,
the queen was then overcome with pain upon seeing her father tormented.
Seeing the great mountain Himavat distressed by the death of his grandson,
Girijā grieved, looking again and again at the Lord of the Gods.
Then those of great strength, though deeply tormented by grief, paid homage to the Lord Pinākin as he arrived together with the Goddess. || 171.37 ||
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, Himavat, the best of mountains, with a dejected soul and overwhelmed by pain and grief, made this request: || 171.38 ||
"O Blessed One, by this Śakra, who holds himself in high esteem, my grandson Krauñca-parvata has been brought to his destruction. (171.39)
O King, what rivalry can there be for him with your son, the prince, since out of pride he perceives no difference between himself and the prince? (171.40)
"Now that my grandson has been slain by the prince after a contest,
let this Vāsava remain at ease, his pride extinguished and his heart at peace."
O Mahādeva, now that my grandson is slain, I am submerged in an ocean of grief;
I am unable to live and shall follow the path of my grandson.
As he was thus lamenting, his kinsmen, led by Meru and Vindhya, cried out, tormented by grief and pained by the loss of their kinsman.
Seeing her father in distress, as well as her other kinsmen and the mountains,
Girijā, the sustainer of the world, was also consumed by grief.
Then, seeing them all afflicted with grief, he whose vehicle is the bull said,
"Do not grieve," and spoke to his six-faced son.
"O son, great men such as you do not commit an evil act even against a kinsman who has committed an offense; why then have you slain the Krauñca? (171.46)
"O Six-faced One, this great mountain Krauñca is the son of your mother's brother; how is it that you have slain this, your own brother? (171.47)
"This action is not worthy of you, my son who is made of me.
Speak now; what do you consider to be the proper course of action here?"
To his father, the god who was speaking thus, the six-faced one then spoke these words, which were both modest and most wonderful: ||| 171.49 ||
"O Lord, because he disregarded Śakra’s command, this Krauñca has been slain by me;
since he did not heed my counsel, hear now another request. (171.50)
"By your grace, O God, I shall restore Krauñca, the best of mountains, to life;
for nothing is difficult for me, as I am indeed your son. (171.51)
Then the six-faced one said to his brother Krauñca, "Arise!
Thereupon, the lord of mountains, Krauñca, assumed his former body in an instant.
Vyāsa rose up free from disease; that was a marvel at that time.
Thus, with his life restored and remaining unshakable, Ṣaṇmukha shone with the brilliance of fire.
Remembering the insult from Rudra, his eyes bloodshot with anger,
the mighty one [stood] in the presence of all the gods and of Śakra.
Having prostrated before the God of gods, the Lord, the father together with Umā, as well as Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Yama, and the high-souled Brahmā; 171.55.
The God, assuming the excellent form of a youth, spoke these words:
"O Lord of Gods, this has been spoken by Śakra here in my very presence. (171.56)
"Great as you are, I am even greater"—it was this thought that filled me with wrath.
Out of that [wrath], this great spear was buried in the surface of the earth. (171.57)
"Except for the god who wields the Pināka bow, what immortal is capable of lifting it?
Let him therefore uproot this great [bow] from me, for he alone is able to do so. (171.58)
Having spoken thus, the god, whose radiance was like that of the rising sun,
became silent with a joyful heart and stood by his father's side.
Then Indra, filled with the pride of sovereignty in the midst of the gods, strove to uproot that spear which had entered the earth. || 171.60 ||
And even with great effort, the lord of the gods was unable to move him;
then, filled with extreme shame, he departed from that place.
Then other supreme deities, led by Yama and Anila, resolved to rescue him; girded with effort, they exerted themselves according to their power.
And the best of the immortals were unable to move that power;
then Viṣṇu, of immeasurable soul, beheld the gods whose vigor was destroyed.
I strove to lift up the spear in the presence of the inhabitants of the triple heaven;
yet, because that spear, though being moved by me, remained fixed upon the surface of the earth. (171.64)
Endowed with great heroism and possessed of the splendor and strength of Skanda, she did not waver;
then Viṣṇu, whose self is immeasurable, knowing the true state of affairs, became intent upon her.
Worshipping the Kumāra with devotion, he desisted from raising his spear;
then all the immortals, O Vyāsa, as well as Viṣṇu, the best of gods, [did likewise].
Having praised the six-faced god, those of great majesty said this:
"The Lord, the son of Mahādeva, is the master of the gods."
He is the Lord, the protector, the creator, the destroyer of affliction, the most excellent and the great one.
O Lord of Gods, with you as our protector, we are all perfectly at ease.
"We all stand here together; protect us from every side against this transgression toward Śakra, committed out of folly and delusion."
"Out of affection, you ought always to forgive what we have requested.
Thus was the Blessed One, the Youthful One, praised by all the immortals.
He abandoned his anger toward Śakra and was gratified with the inhabitants of heaven;
then all those mountains and the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, [were likewise pleased].
Then Śakra, the king of the gods, joyfully honored Guha;
and the Blessed One, being well-pleased, granted boons to his son.
And the leader of the hosts of Mothers went together with Guha and the Goddess to the divine and auspicious peak of the Himalaya mountain.
The mountains Meru, Vindhya, and others, together with Krauñca,
as well as Śakra, the king of the gods, each returned to their own abodes.
It is even so, just as the Krauñca mountain, inhabited by cranes and saras birds, was split by Guha with his spear and subsequently made immortal. || 171.75 ||
Moreover, that wound caused by the spear on Krauñca, the best of mountains—which was vast and great, and where many deities dwell—is still visible. (171.76)
All this has been told to you, the wondrous rending of Krauñca;
that mortal who hears this is liberated from all sins.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, how is the Supreme Lord the leader of the Mothers? Who indeed are these Mothers? Please explain this to me as I ask. (171.78)
How were the groups of Mothers born, and for what reason? O Lord, what is their vigor and what is their power, by which those hosts came into being?
And what is their support by which these auspicious groups function? By whom were they created, or are they self-existent? This I wish to know. (171.80)
Sanatkumāra said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you the auspicious origin of the Mothers.
For in ancient times, the Lord Brahmā, having created these various progenies, [proceeded further]. || 171.81 ||
Looking about, O descendant of Kali, the lord of the gods wandered;
once, when the time of twilight had arrived, that presider over creatures [proceeded].
Having reached a beautiful region on the shore of the great eastern ocean,
he performed his twilight devotions there for ten million years without weariness.
Then the god, having performed his twilight rites and seated upon his lotus throne, reflected: "This region is delightful and enchanting to the sight. (171.84)
"I shall create here a beautiful city, endowed with all objects of desire.
Having thus reflected, O Vyāsa, that blessed Lord, the creator of all, [proceeded].
In that delightful region, he built a supreme city of immeasurable splendor,
with foundations of red, black, and golden stone.
It was filled with loud, boisterous laughter and cries of "khātaka," and it stood like a four-legged creature with its crossroads and squares.
In the center was the Mandākinī, a divine and enchanting river with a large pond, surrounded by opulent houses featuring moats and excavated ditches.
Covered with groves of lotuses and resounding with the songs of joyful birds,
Brahmā, having created that city, adorned it with gold and jewels.
Vyāsa spoke these most wonderful and meaningful words:
"Those who, eating the fruits of their good deeds, shall dwell in this delightful and excellent city—" || 171.90 ||
Free from old age and endowed with splendor and strength, these highly fortunate ones shall become invulnerable through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Then that Blessed Lord, the best of the gods, spoke once again: "In this place, O best of the gods, there shall always be all desired objects."
"The god indeed rains down ten million [coins], and by that the people here are happy.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
went to his own divine assembly hall, which is frequented by many perfected beings (siddhas).
When he had departed from there, O Vyāsa, that city was indeed occupied by all the Asuras who spoke with the speech of Daityas, [and] by those who were thorns to the Brahmins.
O Brahmin, their husband was free from ill-will and anger, the best among all wielders of weapons;
yet he was a slayer of Brahmins, a destroyer of sacrifices, and the annihilator of gods and demons.
Siṃhanāda, Bhīmanāda, Mada, and others—
then the Daityas, led by Haimakuṇḍa, having assembled and stationed themselves in that excellent city, inflicted manifold afflictions.
For those haters of the world have slain thousands of Brahmins;
by those lowest of Asuras, the sacrificial rites such as the *homa* and others have been cut off.
Having learned that they had acted in this manner, all the inhabitants of heaven approached the world of Brahmā and reported everything to the Lord.
Having heard the words of the celestial dwellers and having understood the Daityas' machinations,
Brahmā said, "This cannot be accomplished by me," and departed together with the foremost of the gods.
He came to behold the delightful forest of the snowy mountain,
where Gaurī performed austerities while bearing half of her husband’s body.
All those gods, beginning with Brahmā, who entered there,
instantly became women by the power of Pārvatī’s ascetic penance.
Then the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the trident, questioned those foremost of deities who had become women: "For what purpose have you come? (171.102)
Then they all together first informed Śambhu of the crushing of the Daityas, and afterwards of their own miserable state as women.
When those men said, "May we become as we were before," the Lord of the Gods then spoke to the deities who had assumed the form of women.
"Go, all you gods, having become women, to the presence of the Asuras;
for those Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, are to be slain by women alone. || 171.105 ||
Having assumed embodied forms, O auspicious Mothers,
you shall thereafter become exactly as you were before, O best of gods.
Then, bowing again to the Lord, the deities spoke these words:
"O God, manifest for yourself also a female form in bodily shape."
"O Supreme Lord, with whom shall we together slay the Daityas by force?
Thereupon the God created the goddess Rudrāṇī, the auspicious Mother.
Assuming a deformed form, he [approached] his second mother,
Bahumāṃsā by name, who embodies the destruction of the world.
Then, by the command of the God of gods, the Lord Viṣṇu also brought forth two mothers: Vārāhī, who belongs to Viṣṇu,
and Brāhmī from Pitāmaha (Brahmā), as well as Śarvāṇī from Śaṅkara.
Kaumārī [arose] from the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), and Vaiṣṇavī from Viṣṇu;
the goddess Vārāhī from Mādhava, and Māhendrī from Purandara.
The auspicious goddess Sarvatejomayī, the most excellent among the Mothers,
possessing abundant flesh and great knowledge, was born from the one whose banner is the bull.
And from the bodies of all the goddesses, auspicious Mothers,
who destroy the Daityas and possess their own forms and powers, emerged.
The mighty goddesses of the northwest, the west, the south, and the north;
likewise Mahākālī, the goddess of the southeast, and thousands of others.
Having gone to that beautiful city, the goddesses slew the Daityas of terrible prowess in various ways with their fearsome and horrific roars.
They made that foremost city, adorned with gold, free of Daityas;
then, all the Daityas having been slain, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, [rejoiced].
He arrived at that region with the desire to grant a boon to the Mothers;
he saw all those Daityas, the enemies of the immortals, already slain. || 171.117 ||
Then, being well-pleased, the bull-bannered god granted them boons:
"You shall become mothers of the world, acting as motherly beings. (171.118)
Those who shall be your devotees, whether they be bulls among men or highly fortunate women— indeed, no violent beings shall harm them.
Even my deceased attendants shall become free from old age and death;
this place of yours is known as Koṭīvarṣa.
It shall become renowned throughout the world as the liberator from all sins;
for I am indeed the cause of you, since you were created by me alone.
"I shall remain here under the name Hetukeśvara as the bestower of boons;
established in the role of leader, I shall dwell together with you. (171.122)
But he who shall worship you along with me according to the prescribed rite,
his soul liberated from all sins, shall attain the supreme goal.
"Since the Dānavas were slain here by means of this trident with its many blades, this sacred ford (tīrtha) shall become renowned by the name Śūlakuṇḍa. || 171.124 ||
Having drunk the water from the Śūla here and having bowed to Bahumāṃsa, that best of men shall become invincible to all predatory creatures. || 171.125 ||
The delightful river Mandākinī, renowned for its pleasant currents, shall here become for you a torrent of blood. (171.126)
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and the sages whose wealth is asceticism [have taught] the divine Mātṛtantras and the supreme ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the Mothers.
We shall perform meritorious sacrifices by which you will attain the Brahma,
the Svāyambhuva, the Kaumāra, and likewise the Yāmala [tantras].
The Sārasvata, Gāndhāra, Aiśāna, and Nandiyāmala—
these are your tantras, as well as thousands of others.
There will be men who shall worship you with devotion;
to those men performing the sacrifice, you shall grant boons.
"You shall become goddesses who bestow divine perfections and possess divine yogas; and those women who shall always worship you with all the secret rites. (171.131)
The women shall become mistresses of yoga, possessing divine prowess;
and Chagala and Kumbhakarṇa shall be my two leaders of the gaṇas.
By my command, those two shall remain as your gatekeepers;
this place Koṭivarṣa is the most excellent and beloved abode of the Mothers.
"Having thus obtained those boons, the Mothers, who are the mothers of the world, declared: 'The cremation ground shall become a supreme, divine place that bestows happiness.'"
Having prostrated with devotion before the Lord of Gods, those who had been tormented rejoiced greatly;
from that time forth, they all remained together with the Moon-crested One.
They dwelt in Koṭivarṣa, bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds. Thus, O Vyāsa, that blessed Lord Śaṅkara became the leader of the hosts of Mothers, concerning whom you questioned me.

The man who constantly recites or hears this account of the origin of these sovereigns of the earth, who are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Śakra, and Anila, shall attain the heavenly world upon his death.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa. || 171.171 ||
The one hundred and seventy-second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"In former times, how were the mountains made wingless by Śakra?"
I shall declare that to you, O Vyāsa; listen to it all in its entirety.
Long ago, when Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas, had been slain by Viṣṇu of supreme vigor after he had assumed the body of a lion.
His son was the Daitya Prahlāda, who indeed became enraged toward Viṣṇu;
for when his father had been slain, that illustrious lord of the great Daityas [was filled with wrath].
For many thousands of years he performed fierce and great penance;
then the four-faced god was pleased with that lord of the asuras.
The granter of boons himself arrived and respectfully said, "I am here to grant a boon. Having bowed down to the boon-granting Brahmā who had come there, he spoke as follows: || 172.5 ||
Prahlāda, his limbs burning with indignation as he remembered the slaughter of his father, said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased and have come here as the granter of boons," (172.6)
"Viṣṇu killed my father, the king, through his illusory power (māyā) in battle;
act in such a way that I may likewise slay that Viṣṇu."
Then Brahmā spoke to Prahlāda, the best of the Asuras:
"Viṣṇu is invincible in battle and cannot be slain by gods or Asuras. (172.8)
"O great asura, by the grace of the God of gods, the creator of the world and husband of Umā, this boon cannot be granted to you by me."
"Choose another boon as you desire, for I shall grant it to you.
Then, having reflected further, that great Asura of vast intellect [spoke].
He spoke these words to the god seated upon the lotus-throne:
"If that Viṣṇu, the best of gods, is unconquerable and cannot be slain..."
"O Lord, by your command, may I become incapable of being slain or conquered by that Viṣṇu, or by Śakra, or by any other enemy. (172.12)
Having said "So be it" to that best of Dānavas, the god Brahmā,
seated upon his divine lotus-throne, vanished right there.
Having received that most wonderful boon from Brahmā,
Prahlāda also stood on the shore of the western ocean, his senses overwhelmed with anxiety.
"How may I slay Viṣṇu and Śakra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices?"—
while Prahlāda, the enemy of the gods, was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
The illustrious Himavat, the lord of all mountains,
having taken flight with his two wings, moved through the air and arrived.
For in ancient times, O Vyāsa, the mountains possessed wings;
they were all divine, capable of traveling through the sky, and ranged over all the worlds.
Then, seeing that he had arrived at the Himavat mountain, Prahrāda,
having first offered a welcome, spoke these words with joy.
"O Lord of the foremost of mountains, we Daityas are the grandsons of Kaśyapa;
you gods as well, O great mountain, are his sons. (172.19)
The origin of both us and you is from the same mountain;
for we are indeed gods, and you are our brothers among the gods.
"Disregarding us asuras, they rule their kingdom with arrogance.
O Great Mountain, let us join together and, having utterly defeated the gods, seize the entire three worlds and establish our sovereignty."
O Lord of Mountains, those regions where the sacrifice to the gods is performed, where the fires are offered,
and where the deities are gratified— [those you should visit].
Accompanied by all the mountain-dwellers, attack and slay him swiftly;
then, having deprived the gods of their sacrifices, we shall kill them at our ease and be set at rest.
Thus addressed by the king of the Daityas, Himavat, the best of mountains, spoke with apprehension to the lord of the Dānavas: "This is not proper. (172.24)
Then the great asura spoke once more to Himavat:
"O Lord of Mountains, if you know anything that is superior and more fitting than me."
Together with these mountains, I shall bring you to death at once;
therefore, O mountain, remain vigilant until I have slain you.
Then, seeing the king of the Daityas enraged, that best of mountains said,
"I shall do so," and thereupon the Daitya was pleased with him.
Then Himavat, the best of mountains, together with those other mountains,
having heard the words of Prahlāda, carried out the destruction of the country.
They ascended those mountains in which all rituals, such as sacrifices and oblations, are performed for the sake of the ancestors and the gods.
Then, when those regions had become desolate, Nārada, the best of sages,
reported everything regarding the transgression of the mountains to Śakra.
Having heard that, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, consumed by anger, approached the mountains and spoke in his indignation, "What is this? (172.31)
Then, O Vyāsa, the mountains said to the enraged lord of the hosts of gods:
"O God, out of fear of Prahlāda, the great lord of the Daityas, we [have fled]. (172.32)
"We have incurred this transgression, yet there is no fault in us whatsoever.
But if you consider it a fault on our part, O Lord of the Immortals," (172.33)
"Come to Prahlāda; let us go together quickly.
All this destruction of the sacrificial ground has been caused by him—the powerful king of the Daityas—in his desire to do you harm. (172.34)
"O Lord of the Gods, know that this is not our fault.
To those who spoke thus, Śakra became even more enraged at the mountains. (172.35)
Then, repeatedly hurling his thunderbolt, he rendered them wingless;
thus, all those lords of the mountains were deprived of their wings.
They fell upon the surface of the earth, O Vyāsa, like birds with severed wings;
then Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas and the foremost among the Asuras, heard this.
Afflicted by the severing of the wings of the lords of mountains, the leader of the hosts of Daityas became violently enraged; he reflected for a long time, "What shall I do? (172.38).
Having arrived at Badaryāśrama, he beheld Viṣṇu seated there;
a truly great and wonderful battle took place between him and Viṣṇu.
And Viṣṇu was not able to conquer that Prahlāda by his might;
a terrible, divine battle took place between them for a hundred years in ancient times.
Viṣṇu knew himself to be inferior to the Dānava Prahlāda;
then Viṣṇu, the knower of the highest dharma, was assailed in battle.
Unable to conquer the Dānava, the Lord became filled with wrath;
then, having meditated upon Mahādeva and having bowed down to him again and again, [he acted].
He remembered the wielder of the Pināka bow. 172.43.
Recalling that grace of Śiva— his invincibility and his being unconquerable by all the inhabitants of the world— Viṣṇu, the best of gods, [acted].
Having become possessed of the strength of a great being, the powerful one rushed toward the Daitya;
meanwhile, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu perceived himself to be failing.
And having realized that Viṣṇu was powerful, he retreated from the field of battle;
deluded by the splendor of Śiva, he perceived himself as unconquered by Viṣṇu.
Prahrāda, the lord of the Dānavas, realized that he had conquered himself,
even though he had obtained from Brahmā the boon of invincibility for himself.
The great asura considered himself already victorious in that terrible battle with the asura Prahlāda, which struck fear into the gods.
For a hundred divine years, there was a wondrous [conflict] with Viṣṇu;
[he was] not [superior] in sacred learning, nor in heroism, nor in valor, nor in splendor.
Neither in wisdom nor in righteousness was there an asura equal to Prahlāda;
nor was there a great king like Hiraṇyakaśipu who was his equal.
Neither Andhaka nor Hiraṇyākṣa was equal to Prahlāda in strength;
he who came to the state of a Daitya due to the curse of Bhṛgu was indeed Viṣṇu himself.
Even the perfected denizens of heaven envied the high-souled Prahrāda for his heroism, his sacred learning, and his humility.
In his kingdom, the subjects were no longer afflicted by suffering and grief;
thus did that best of Dānavas wage war against Viṣṇu.
With his body tormented by remorse and his desire for sense-objects gone,
he realized that the granting of boons and the fruit of asceticism are impermanent.
Free from desire for all undertakings and devoid of longing for sense objects,
he has renounced all actions and is devoted solely to the practice of meditation.
The great Daitya went forth into the religious life, desiring peace for the sake of attaining liberation,
having realized that birth leads to rebirth and understanding the supreme impermanence of all things.
Realizing that sovereignty is a source of suffering, Prahrāda, the knower of the supreme truth,
consecrated his son Virocana upon the throne of the sons of Diti.
Having made that lord of the Asuras the king of the Daityas and Dānavas,
and desiring the supreme attainment of liberation, he resolved to go forth into the homeless life.
Then, in order to seek the supreme reality— the unborn, auspicious state beyond the qualities—
he approached the sage Āsuri, the direct disciple of the Blessed Lord Kapila.
Having approached him as a disciple, he attained the knowledge of liberation—
the supreme reality of the primary elements (prakṛtis) as well as that of the transformations (vikāras).
Having known the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Puruṣa, the enjoyer who is himself devoid of being an enjoyer,
he was one who knew the supreme purpose of the science of liberation and had reached the further shore of the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
He became a perfected one (siddha) known by the name Pañcaśikha, the best of sages.
Having attained supreme yoga, that great sage, a teacher of Sāṃkhya,
was liberated from the threefold suffering and reached the imperishable state.
Thus the illustrious and high-souled Daitya king, the enemy of the three worlds, having maintained enmity for a long time with Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the gods,
later became a perfected being who grants fearlessness to the world and attained yoga.
Released thereafter, he indeed attained the immortal state, the primordial Brahman.
The knower of the field, awakened, detached from the qualities (guṇas), and freed from sufferings and the bonds of the fetters of existence—
this lord of yogis, liberated from the obstructions of darkness and delusion, became the sovereign of the Daityas.
Thus, O best of sages, Purandara rendered all those mountains wingless, as I was previously asked by you.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Severing of Parvata’s Wings," in the *Prahrādacarita* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and seventy-third chapter.
Vyāsa said:
When Guha had gratified the Lord of Mountains and restored Krauñca to life, and when he was honored by the gods;
Hara, accompanied by Pārvatī, went to the peak of the Himavat.
What else did the Lord do, and what did Pārvatī say to him?
Tell me this, O best of Brahmins, for I am not yet satiated with hearing it.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the lord of sages, the imperishable son of Brahmā, the seer and supreme master of yoga, related [it] according to the truth. 173.3.
When the God of gods had set out for the peak of the Himalayas together with Umā,
the Daughter of the Mountain bowed to the Supreme Lord and addressed the God.
For one who subsists on gleaned grains, a dweller of the Naimiṣa forest,
endowed with purity, austerity, devotion, and indeed tranquility— (5) 173.5.
I myself went forth to receive the honor due to the twice-born,
having witnessed that greatness of the ascetic brahmin.
"O Lord, I have reached a state of wonder that the twice-born are most excellent;
it is my conviction that Brāhmaṇas are even weightier than the gods.
Now, I desire to hear from you the supreme majesty of the twice-born. (173.7)
The God of gods said:
"It is even so, O Mother of the World, you who are saluted by gods and asuras;
the excellent ascetic brahmins are even weightier than the gods."
Those progeny of mine who were created first are indeed my source;
the Rudras and the twice-born of great power were previously created by me. (173.9)
Having beheld my own creation, even Brahmā, desiring to create, first created from his head the Brāhmaṇas of great splendor. (173.10)
For at that time, O best of the twice-born, I became the foremost among them;
consequently, all those excellent brahmins became my friends.
This is the supreme and highest creation of Parameṣṭhin—the Brāhmaṇas;
the fourfold aims of life, beginning with dharma, are all established in them. (173.12)
The deities are satisfied by the oblation which the learned Brahmins offer;
indeed, the entire world is established through the spiritual power of the Brahmins.
That which removes both death and birth is my Pāśupata vow;
no others can accomplish it, except for the most excellent of Brahmins.
I shall fully declare the characteristics of the twice-born; listen to this:
the rules for purity and uprightness, as well as their power and their duties.
One is a Brāhmaṇa by birth, but is called a Dvija (twice-born) through sacramental rites; one attains the state of a Vipra through knowledge. Thus, Brāhmaṇahood is traditionally held to be threefold.
Whether one be a Brahmin by birth or one who has mastered the Vedas,
it is recorded that the merit and demerit of protecting or killing them are equal.
He who is a Brahmin by birth, proficient in all the scriptures, endowed with austerity and purity, and is thrice-cleansed—he is called such. (173.18)
Whoever feeds such a person at a śrāddha or even in a rite for the gods,
that [offering] becomes inexhaustible for him through the satisfaction of those three pure ones.
A Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and constantly devoted to the fire-oblation, O Goddess, is considered the most excellent; when honored, he delivers his lineage.
O Goddess, even if someone were a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone in any respect, he too, as a teacher of the world, would be worthy of worship and a bestower of heaven.
The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, austerity, sacrifice, purity, straightforwardness,
truthfulness, and devotion to the Vedas are recorded as the supreme duties of the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa does not speak untruth; a twice-born man does not kill a living being;
a Vipra does not perform service [for others]; and a twice-born man shall not be a doer of evil. 173.23.
One who is both a brahmin and an ascetic does not undergo birth again;
having attained the state of a learned brahmin, what indeed has not been gained by that embodied being?
Indeed, those eight forms of mine known as the Sun, the Moon, and the rest—
all of them dwell within the Brāhmaṇa whose ascetic power has been augmented.
For, O Goddess, by sustaining themselves upon the splendor of the twice-born and the nectar of the cows, the Brahmins always prevail; therefore, they are the most excellent of all.
Nothing is impossible for those twice-born ones of supreme luster;
when enraged or when pleased, they bestow both good and evil.
But those twice-born ones who are ascetics and proficient in Vedic knowledge shall be givers of liberation; they are indeed the deities even of the gods.
Both I and the Grandfather are known as their two sources;
they were first produced from me, O Goddess, and thereafter from the Grandfather.
"We two are the causes for the twice-born because of our nature, and you alone are that very nature;
you are declared to be Prakṛti, while I am indeed the Supreme Puruṣa."
Those two who are remembered as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, whose natures consist of the qualities of rajas and sattva,
are born from us both as the Lords of Creatures at the time of creation.
For I am Agni, who is Tamas; Viṣṇu is Sattva, established in Brahman; know that you are Rajas, pervading the actions of all beings composed of the Guṇas.
These two, namely tamas and rajas, are known to be of the nature of delusion;
they indeed destroy sattva, and that [sattva] arises from fire.
For these high-souled twice-born ones are known to possess the brilliance of fire;
they prevail everywhere, and there is no means to restrain them.
Know that straightforwardness and equanimity are indeed the splendor within the twice-born;
yet, among those endowed with austerity and knowledge, straightforwardness is superior.
Absence of deceit destroys evils, and equanimity destroys the bond of delusion;
both of these are destroyed by straightforwardness practiced by the twice-born.
Formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, there was a twice-born man named Dānaruci, who was a knower of the highest dharma and lived by the practice of gleaning.
Having disciplined himself through all branches of knowledge, he grants fearlessness to all beings;
together with his wife, he is my devotee and is devoted to the fire-oblation.
O Goddess, having first fed the guest who has arrived, he then eats at the sixth meal-time; this is his supreme vow.
As he continued living in this manner, a great deal of time passed;
yet, whenever a guest arrived, no hesitation arose in him.
Endowed with austerity and purity, and devoted solely to uprightness, that twice-born man became exceedingly radiant with splendor, like the sun and fire.
The fire-god, pleased by his such asceticism, attained supreme satisfaction;
desiring to bestow auspiciousness upon him, he became the granter of his desired fruit.
Then, after some time, when the sixth mealtime had arrived,
the twice-born one was wandering about during a cold, foul day made harsh by snow and clouds.
Exhausted by hunger and fatigue, he did not see any guest;
when no guest was found by him anywhere even at the end of the day, [he entered his own house]. (173.44)
Then, having eaten nothing at all, that foremost of brahmins became devoted to fasting; he did not even consider his own exhaustion.
His highly fortunate wife also, devoted to the vow of fidelity to her husband,
then acted exactly as her husband had done.
O Queen, with his limbs tormented by cold and hunger, and beset by many pairs of opposites, that twice-born man became exceedingly exhausted by great suffering.
When the second [period] had arrived—the sixth mealtime—that twice-born man, due to the affliction caused by the cold and the storm, did not look toward the guest at all. (173.48)
Then Agni, having understood that supreme and great resolve of his,
[assumed] a deformed, loathsome form resembling that of a dog-cooker (śvapāka).
Having done so, he stood at the foot of the tree and granted him his sight;
meanwhile, that best of brahmins, afflicted by hunger, was wandering about in search of a guest.
He saw a dog-cooker (outcaste) standing at the foot of a tree— terrible, of deformed appearance, shivering with cold, and marked by hundreds of various wounds.
That best of the twice-born beheld one who was difficult to look upon, aged and afflicted, with worms and blood flowing forth, crying out, "O father!"
Then, seeing that wretched dog-cooker, the best of the twice-born spoke these sweet words: "Take heart, blessed one. (173.53)
And for the purpose of removing the cold, the twice-born one brought fire to him;
then, once he had been comforted by contact with that fire, the sage spoke to him.
"Come, eat; be my guest, O blessed one," he said respectfully.
Then the outcaste spoke to that wretched man, who was a treasure-house of asceticism.
"I am an outcaste, O best of the twice-born; give me food right here, for I am as despicable as the beasts and birds. (173.56)
"I am not fit to consume this cooked food," he said;
and knowing through meditation that Agni was present before him as he spoke thus, [the sage remained silent]. (173.57)
O tiger among the twice-born, he who was skilled in speech spoke these words:
"O sinless one, I do not despise birth, nor do I honor it. (173.58)
For this Self is all-pervading and resides within all living beings;
with devotion, I worship that Self, who is the supreme Śiva.
Considering the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa, to be present everywhere,
I have no contempt for animals, and especially not for those such as yourself.
"Everything is indeed that very same [Brahman]; devoted to austerity and purity, I worship it with an undistracted mind. Be free from doubt in this matter."
Since the Self is indeed omnipresent—in worms, insects, mice, and snakes; in dog-cookers, gods, and the twice-born—how can there be any contempt for us? (173.62)
"O noble one, I am not contemptible; come to me, you who are beyond reproach. Eat this prepared food and grant us your favor. (173.63)
Thus addressed by the lord of the twice-born, the outcaste then went to the house of that brahmin with a joyful heart, desiring to obtain his favor.
Then, with a mind pure in its disposition, he who delighted in giving performed for him a hospitable reception according to the rules, as if for a guest.
Having been fed, the bearer of oblations became manifest in bodily form and, being pleased,
bestowed upon him his desired and unsurpassed power of yoga.
Having attained supreme yoga, that best of the twice-born, subsisting on gleaned grains,
was liberated along with his wife and reached the immortal state.
Just as the perfected sage Kapila, the supreme knower of reality,
so too a Brahmin endowed with uprightness and possessing the marks of his station shall obtain nothing that he does not attain— O Goddess, from an auspicious state, an even more auspicious station.
This supreme and highest majesty has been told to you, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
By constantly hearing this and reciting it according to the rules, a wise and pure man [attains his goal].
This majesty has been described exactly as it is, O daughter of the Great Mountain King, for the sake of the twice-born.
O best of the twice-born, because they were the source of my creation, they thus attained supreme greatness.
Sanatkumāra said: Having described the greatness of the twice-born, there arose this meritorious dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, which destroys all sins. (173.71)
"O son of Parāśara, rich in asceticism!
Since you believe there is something to be heard from me, then ask with a concentrated mind. (173.72)
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Twice-born," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, that which was spoken by you at the time of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice—
Having attained the Pāśupata yoga, the dwellers of heaven, beginning with Brahmā, [attained their state]. || 174.1 ||
"O great sage, they indeed attained the supreme reality through knowledge;
tell that to me, your devoted disciple who asks you. (174.2)
"What is that supreme Yoga, the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge, by knowing which perfected Brahmins attain the highest liberation? Thus questioned by his disciple, the best of sages replied. (174.3)
Sanatkumāra said:
"Well done, O Vyāsa of great intelligence! You are a seeker of liberation, my son, since you ask me about that supreme knowledge and yoga pertaining to Maheśvara. (174.4)
That which is proclaimed as the reality of all yogic sciences is [taught] by those endowed with the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Āgama, who are experts in all matters of the inner self.
Even after attaining mastery through yoga, they did not perceive the ultimate reality,
O illustrious one, because they had not understood the knowledge spoken by Śaṅkara.
Just as it was told by Tryambaka to those celestial dwellers,
that very determination of reality I shall proclaim to you in brief.
It is not possible to describe that in detail even in hundreds of years;
however, I shall explain its established side, which brings about the arising and destruction of saṃsāra.
Having paid homage to Maheśāna, the Supreme Person who brings all beings into existence, I shall briefly declare this supreme doctrine which bestows both liberation and spiritual perfection.
The supreme secret of primordial nature, the individual soul who is the highest lord—
whom the followers of Sāṃkhya call the twenty-fifth principle, the unborn and all-pervading Puruṣa.

Moreover, the Yogas [declare that] he who at the time of creation brought forth the twenty-sixth principle—the pervasive one composed of the three qualities—is the god who creates the entire world. (174.11)
Having meditated upon the two high-souled Lords of Creatures, Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha,
and having bowed down to that Mahādeva, the three-eyed Lord and giver of boons, [he spoke].
I shall proclaim his doctrine, the definitive conclusion of the system of Yoga;
know this definition of Yoga as it is being declared by me. 174.13.
O great sage, through the practice of that conviction, the bonds of the individual soul are severed;
there is an external withdrawal of the mind once it is established within the Self. (174.14)
O Vyāsa, this intention regarding both the Supreme and the individual self—
that "this is experience"— was proclaimed of old by Śambhu.
Subtle and the remover of existence and rebirth for the gods who have sought refuge,
it abides within the self of the person whose mind is established in the Self.

Free from discursive thought, both externally and internally, it is subtle and joined with practice; it is characterized by subtle mental impressions (pratyaya) consisting of the notions of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
It has been stated that for the practitioner who is engaged in yoga, there is the complete cessation [of all things];
yet the supreme Lord Maheśvara is the deity who, as the uniter, is the underlying intention.
For then there is the intention of both the Lord and the self;
indeed, the taking up of bliss occurs through a single [act] by means of unification with contemplation. || 174.19 ||
For the practitioner who remains steadfast in this way,
this perfected fruit shall indeed be eternally his, like a mountain.
Now, the stages therein are proclaimed in due order:
withdrawal of the senses, and likewise breath control, meditation, and concentration—this is declared to be the practice of yoga. (174.21)
Having transcended the three [stages], the fourfold activities indeed proceed;
and death, O Sage, does not prevail over them.
For the elements become subject to him; of this there is no doubt.
Consequently, he becomes a practitioner who has conquered death. || 174.23 ||
O Vyāsa, these operations of reasoning are indeed proclaimed to exist upon the head, in the heart, and throughout the entire intermediate space; of this there is no doubt.
But these rites, bound to the three locations and established with four characteristics, cannot be accomplished anywhere by one who is negligent.
These three are always engaged in death and are characterized by delusion;
there can be no separation from them, yet ritual actions are performed as one.
Ignorance trembles within those activities that move both externally and internally; likewise, the practitioner who is disciplined trembles even during those activities situated in the middle.
The cessation of the elements, the senses, the mind, time, and the directions occurs through its power;
for there are only ten: the three times, the elements, and the expansion of the senses.
"Accompanied by the cessation of the movement of the mind and characterized by the absence of sense objects— this was declared of old by the Blessed One himself as 'pratyāhāra' (withdrawal)."
When there is no movement toward the various directions and the mind remains unshakably steady,
the arising of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) occurs simultaneously with the arising of yoga.
Knowledge pertaining to the three periods of time and the arising of sovereign power do not exist when the mind is wavering; they come into being only when it is established in equanimity.
Since the mind is the means for all this practice of yoga,
one should therefore exert effort toward the stabilization of the mind alone.
Meditation on the restraint of the vital breath is known as *prāṇāyāma*;
for the vital breath alone always acts as the charioteer of the winds.
The yogi should constantly practice the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for the sake of attaining progressively higher success within the range of the wind. (174.34)
One should know that the setting in motion of the light is a constant practice joined with repeated application;
twice in the apāna, once in the prāṇa, and likewise in the samāna. || 174.35 ||
By these, the subtle course of meditation, which effects the restraint of the vital breaths, proceeds;
by means of it, the yogin attains the supreme Person.
Through the single act of drawing [the breath] in and the repeated release,
this is designated as *kumbhaka* (retention), following the practice of *prāṇāyāma*.
The vital breath is indeed Vāyu, and that is the Self (ātman) within the body—the individual soul (jīva). One should know its two forms, both gross and subtle, in every respect. (174.40)
The unmanifest is of subtle form, whereas that which possesses characteristics of shape is gross;
beginning from the gross, one should discern the subtle through the practice of meditation.
O Sage, from planting [the mind] subtly, the light of illumination arises.
But when the mind of one meditating on a gross object has strayed in all directions,
as soon as it becomes radiant, one should immediately stabilize it once again.
One should practice the concentration of the mind on a mountain, a tree, the back of a wind-god, a chasm, rows of palaces, the ocean, or upon the earth.
That mind, having been established there, should again undergo withdrawal;
through delusion, it may bestow unconsciousness upon the wind, and for this reason, the observed result is otherwise.
Having withdrawn [the mind] from there, one should again practice the course of meditation that pervades all;
through constant practice while meditating, the mind and the vital breath [become unified].
For one engaged in the yoga of knowledge, when attachment to sense objects has been destroyed,
various obstacles born of the qualities such as *sattva* indeed arise;
for these obstacles to yoga manifest themselves for one who is practicing it.
Knowing these, one who is free from desire for sense objects and has conquered [the senses] through effort should stand upon the path to liberation, devoid of the three qualities.
Divine travel through the sky, union with hosts of celestial nymphs,
consecration by the gods, and the composition of wonderful poetry.
Attachment to the pleasures of sovereignty and the acquisition of abundant gold and jewels—these are obstacles arising from one's own being; however, one should recognize them as intuitive insights.

One should recognize that those [visions] characterized by pride regarding one's origin, which follow a sequence of divergent conduct and are obstructed by passion, are intuitive insights (*prātibha*); of this there is no doubt. (174.50)
One should designate consumption, colic, fever, insanity, leprosy, serpents, and planetary seizures— preceded by the emergence of agonizing pain— as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
The sage, constantly practicing yoga, should quickly discern and immediately treat those intuitive insights arising from the three qualities (guṇas).
Having focused on the vital breaths beginning with prāṇa and having withdrawn the mind,
one should indeed destroy all obstacles on every side by means of the kumbhaka breath-control.
Rajas, sattva, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of Pradhāna;
they are indeed the causes for the Great Lord's association with created beings.
These [faults] arise from the delusion of yoga for one who practices with self-conceit;
but when the yogi, free from effort and at peace, exerts himself with a conscious mind, [these faults cease]. 174.55.
Then intuitive insights arise and obstacles indeed go to their simultaneous destruction;
thereafter, the manifestation of those qualities becomes the cause of delusion.
One should know that Tamas is Raudra (belonging to Rudra), Sattva is established in Brahman, and one should know that Rajas belongs to Viṣṇu; Maheśvara is the destroyer of these.
Having known Mahādeva as the supreme, the twice-born man devoted to the practice of yoga,
liberated from the three qualities (guṇas), shall attain absorption into Śaṅkara.
First, one should purify one's own body through restraints (yama) and observances (niyama);
thereafter, free from both dharma and adharma, one should act according to that which is prescribed by the scriptures.
One should practice meditation gradually according to the instruction,
having conquered the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, which fall within the range of the ears and other faculties.
He is equal toward gods and animals, free from the sense of "mine" regarding all things,
liberated from all undertakings, and devoid of both merit and sin.
Free from dualities, one should practice yoga in a secluded place,
