having abandoned pride along with restrictive observances, and relying on the certainty of Sāṃkhya.
One should constantly practice the supreme yoga of Maheśvara;
there are eight eternal primary natures (prakṛtis) and sixteen transformations (vikāras). || 174.63 ||
The twenty-fifth principle is the Puruṣa, which is the domain of the Sāṃkhya school's established doctrine.
This alone is the supreme secret in the Sāṃkhyas' determination of reality:
having known the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, one is liberated. (174.64)
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fierce Pāśupata [Rite]," within the section on the rules for meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: Yoga and Sāṃkhya—these two are everywhere declared to be the two-fold knowledge.
Among them, some were devoted to Sāṃkhya, while others relied upon the path of Yoga.

The unmanifest (avyakta), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)—these eight are indeed the primary natures (prakṛtis), together with the five subtle elements (tanmātras). || 175.2 ||
They say there are five sense organs and five organs of action;
together with the mind and the five elements, these are known as the sixteen modifications.
The Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth principle, devoid of all undertakings;
he is eternal, omnipresent, subtle, conscious, and free from the three guṇas.
Pure, stainless, the enjoyer, and a non-doer, he stands like a witness;
having known him, they do not enter again the cage of saṃsāra.
These twenty-five principles were proclaimed by the Sāṃkhya practitioners and yogis, for by knowing them, one is indeed liberated from birth.
Subtle, unmanifest, the object of enjoyment, delighting in all things, and fickle; it is to be known as eternal, insentient, and the fulfiller of all desires.
Tamas, sattva, and rajas—these three qualities reside within objects;
for it is through their unvarying presence that all this is established.
Sattva produces illumination; rajas incites attachment;
and tamas causes delusion—thus is the expansion of the qualities described.
The functioning of these [elements], which are designated as *guṇas* and whose activities and effects are distinct,
is said to be governed by a cause, namely the purpose of the *puruṣa*. (175.10) Divine [existence] is of eight varieties, while that of the animals is recorded as being of seven kinds.
And this human state is beyond conceptualization; all of it consists of these very qualities.
Whether it be deluded or unconscious, gross or subtle, formless or even possessing form—everything is said to consist of the three qualities (guṇas). || 175.12 ||
For these qualities of the yogin are proclaimed to be obstacles to liberation;
indeed, bondage occurs only for one who is attached, while the unattached is said to be liberated.
Through their differentiation, the three qualities remain eternally present in one who abides in primordial nature (prakṛti).
The creation of the elements, which exists in a state of transformation and is based upon dharma according to its divisions, is recited by those who know Sāṃkhya as being threefold.
It is said to be of three kinds: the perfected (saṃsiddha), the natural (prākṛta), and the modified (vaikṛta).
Among these, those who are perfected through dharma abide in the yoga of Maheśvara.

O Vyāsa, those who are experts in the analogies of the Sāṃkhya school do not accept origination; for them, dharma is traditionally held to consist of five aspects, arising again through the connection with substance.
For those who rely on causes do not indeed maintain that the effect exists [prior to its production];
from Pradhāna, the intellect (buddhi) arose repeatedly, characterized by a predominance of the quality of sattva, and from that, the person (puruṣa). 175.17.
Through the transformation of the primal qualities (guṇas), like water and other elements,
it is designated as volition, form, and determination.

For the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is indeed the intellect (buddhi), since no other [distinct] cognition arises; some, however, maintain that it is the mind (manas), produced by action and consisting of a collection of qualities. || 175.19 ||

"I alone am the doer"—this is declared to be egoism (ahaṃkāra). It is also considered to be the mental construction regarding the sphere of the senses. From the luminous egoism, which has become the intellect (buddhi) and arisen from the quality of goodness (sattva), [the sense organs arise]. || 175.20 ||
The five sense organs have arisen from the emergence of *sattva*;
for by means of these organs, the seeker of liberation is either awakened or awakens [to reality]. (175.21)
Therefore, they are proclaimed as the "organs of cognition" by those who contemplate the principles of reality.
Therefore, they say that the organs of action are born from the rājasa quality;
furthermore, from the tāmasa ego, the subtle elements (tanmātras) came into being.
Some say that [the elements] are all-pervading;
and that [bondage], which arises from merit and demerit, is of various kinds.
It goes everywhere for the accomplishment of its purpose, pervading all beings and deluding them;
it is powerful, the refuge of all, subtle, and its path through the quarters is unobstructed.
That which is the cause for embodied beings has been declared as the *liṅga*;
and that creation which was described as threefold is further said to be ninefold.

The thousands of different bodies resulting from the modification of primordial matter (prakṛti) are known as the prior creation of the principles (tattvasarga); after that follows the subsequent creation of the physical aggregates (piṇḍasarga).
From that, the third creation, consisting of the causal conditions (pratyayas), is proclaimed;
it comprises four states: non-attachment (asakti), dissolution (vilaya), contentment (tuṣṭi), and perfection (siddhi). || 175.28 ||
But in the creation of consciousness (pratyayasarga), other divisions are recorded due to their diversity;
there are fifty divisions in total, and their qualities are ten.
Indeed, these sixty categories are proclaimed by Kapila and others;
that contentment is divided into nine kinds, and accomplishment (siddhi) is likewise eightfold.
Their opposites are likewise remembered as being fivefold;
they consist of eight divisions, distinguished by three types, and are bound by ten types of karmic effects.
These sixty categories constitute the knowledge of number; such is the sacred teaching.
Some recognize them as being one less than sixty, while others know them to be one more. (175.32)
For indeed, my dear child, it was by me alone in the past that the inner reality between Prakṛti and Puruṣa was sought within the five stages born of the qualities. || 175.33 ||

Having understood and realized the great Sāṃkhya system— that which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)— one knows the twenty-fifth principle, the unborn, the enjoyer, and the one possessed of self-conceit.
My doubt was not dispelled until I had understood the Supreme Lord himself, who, as the God of gods and the creator of the world, [spoke to me]. (175.35)
O child, having been initiated into your own yoga by Śambhu, you were freed from doubt;
then, having known the twenty-sixth principle, the all-pervading Lord.
"O twice-born one, I am liberated through the perfection of yoga and have become free from delusion;
yet, if the Puruṣa is the enjoyer of Prakṛti, he himself experiences [the fruits].
He who is beyond these two, eternal, the twenty-sixth, the Lord, the all-pervading—
by knowing Him as the supreme reality, one is released from the bondage of birth.
Even after having mastered the entirety of Sāṃkhya through the investigation of the distinctions between the guṇas,
liberation does not arise from the mere awakening to the twenty-fifth principle;
for he remains bound by the guṇas born of Prakṛti, which are the fetters of the enjoyer.
The enjoyer consists of egoism; because of its nature as the Puruṣa, it is not the liberator. Even by knowing that, liberation devoid of mental constructs would not occur. (175.40)
This detailed exposition of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has been stated in brief;
now I shall proclaim the true nature of Yoga, which brings about the destruction of suffering and rebirth.
The origin of embodied beings and that by which dispassion arises,
as well as the abandonment of dharma and adharma, free from truth and falsehood.
The practice of yoga, free from attachment to others, subtle knowledge beyond reproach,
liberated from all clinging, is the cause for attaining the Lord.
The union with the state beyond duality that brings about perfection, which destroys the arising of the inauspicious,
which is the consciousness of supreme attainment, and the certainty regarding the stages of the meaning of reality.
This entire system of Pashupati, which removes existence and rebirth, is free from the objects of the senses; it is the attainment of the abode of immortality.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 175.175 ||
The one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said: How a living being is born, and how it attains dispassion—[this shall now be told].
And how he awakens—O Vyāsa, I shall tell that to you.
Space, wind, fire, earth, and likewise water—
from the aggregation of these together, that which is called a body is born.
All tastes are of the nature of Soma, as is the fourfold food;
for embodied beings, the production of rasa results from the consumption of food.
From the essence (rasa) arises blood; from blood, flesh is said to be produced;
fat is produced from flesh, and from that, bones come into being. 176.4.
Marrow is to be known as arising from the bones; from that, semen is produced.
Through the union of blood and semen, the embryo is formed in the woman. (176.5)
Through the union of the seasons and by the power of destiny and karma, both the woman and the man attain oneness at the conclusion of their sexual union. (176.6)
Then, having attained oneness and impelled by the wind,
they became a *kalala* in one night and an *arbuda* in five nights.
In seven nights it becomes flesh, and in a month there is the emergence of sprouts;
from that point onward, O twice-born one, the differentiation of the embryo occurs.
Endowed with a head, hands, face, shoulders, neck, back, and so forth,
the emergence of the eyes, ears, and other features occurred after five months.
But with all its limbs fully developed and endowed with the nine apertures,
that embryo becomes manifest after exactly eight months.
When the ninth month had arrived, he remained there, endowed with all necessary materials,
like a conscious being within that [womb] which consists of the five elements.
With limbs drenched by the moisture of the womb and beset by every suffering,
the creature dwelling there should remember its birth from all origins.
"Having died, I was born again; and having been born, I have died again.
Now, as soon as I am born, I shall practice yoga alone."
"No longer shall I enter again into this saṃsāra of impure origin.
While he was reflecting thus, the ninth month arrived. (176.14)
For the embodied being who is bound by his own karma, as soon as he is born,
the tamasic wind enters his body, depriving him of memory.
By which the deluded one becomes joyless and finds no delight within himself;
[he perceives] the entire fourfold collection of beings as consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma. 176.16
O observer of noble vows, it is from such a conjunction that this has arisen and will continue to arise;
therein, those who, through association with the virtuous and by the dawning of auspicious karma, [attain liberation].
Devoted to the search for the scriptures and avoiding sinful conduct,
they consider the affliction born of worldly existence to be tormented by the fear of birth and death.
Having cultivated detachment from birth onwards by bringing all undertakings to an end, he remains covered only by desire, anger, passion, longing, greed, and delusion.
For they seek the auspicious goal, the secret vision of the inner self;
having attained supreme yoga, they find that Brahman which is the highest.
I shall fully declare to you that cause of awakening to Brahman,
which is the secret of all yogins and the manifestation of all yoga.
Thereafter, I shall declare to you that supreme Māheśvara yoga:
the fire of splendor, the fire born of desire, the fire of wrath, and the fire of the glance.
The digestive fire and the elemental self—these five are the fires of the body:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
These five winds are eternal, arising within the body of the embodied being;
for they originate from space, and the body abides within them.
It is strewn with flesh and blood, a collection of sinews, fat, and bones;
it is enveloped in skin, foul-smelling, and filled with excrement and urine.
It is as impermanent as the appearance of lightning in the clouds, resembling the sudden shattering of an earthen vessel;
joined with every kind of misfortune, it goes to destruction before long.
It has a single form, nine gates, three pillars, and five deities; it is crowded with sense objects and senses, and afflicted by manifold diseases. (176.27)
The body, held together like a machine by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other winds,
repeatedly falls apart when it is released from those winds that sustain life.
Like an unbaked clay vessel that shatters from a fall due to the passage of time,
the five elements depart entirely from the body.
In the same way, they enter the self, and the self swiftly enters them;
for among all beings, the wind is supreme, and the individual soul (jīva) is bound to it. 176.30
The vital breath (jīva) is not separate from the living beings as wind and fire joined together;
there is no other form of the jīva that is seen when the embodied being dies. || 176.31 ||
The God who is beyond the five forms is considered subtler than the subtlest;
he neither sees, nor smells, nor hears, nor speaks.
Enveloped by the vital breath (prāṇa), the individual soul (jīva) neither knows nor touches;
O twice-born one, that which is called the vital breath is the great wind that sustains the soul.
For it indeed speaks and breathes within all embodied beings;
that vital breath sustains the internal fire, and it is remembered as the *jīva*.
For fire, sustained by the vital air, circulates through the bodily functions;
that which is the fire within the body is designated as the "living soul" (jīva).
For it is indeed contained within all beings as the bond for the undertaking of action;
thus this body consists of the qualities of the five elements.
When that transformation has perished, one is said to be "dead.
The elements, the senses, the mind, the living soul, and the objects of the senses are bound by the fetters of passion. (176.37)
In the heart, within the pericarp, resides the eternal treasure of splendors,
the all-pervading Self, which is forever free from sense objects and the like.
The All-pervading Lord abides there, by knowing whom one is liberated;
He is reached through the perfection of yoga by one who knows the practice of meditation and ritual action.
Through the mastery of the practice of the channels and by means of constant application of yoga,
he was seen illuminated by rays of light, liberated from all transformations.
O best of Brahmins, liberation is indeed seen [to follow] from that,
for by means of the thorough knowledge of the twenty-sixth principle, one attains dissolution therein.
Subtle, pervading all living beings, and residing within one's own body— that which perfected yogis, freed from all bonds, clearly perceive.
O best of the twice-born, I shall explain to you that supreme practice of yoga, which is the highest means for attaining knowledge of the Lord.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Third [Section] on the Rules for Meditation," within the Description of Pāśupata Yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
The inner self is endowed with consciousness, and the mind is known to be born of volition.
And because of the agitation caused by the movement of the great elements, the individual soul (jīva) is said to be fire.
The mind does not exist apart from the body; if that [body] does not exist, from where could it come?
Nor does the mind exist without the living soul (jīva), and that [soul] also does not exist without the mind. 177.2
The vital breath (prāṇa) is called the individual soul (jīva); it proceeds from touch.
The mind binds everything; such is the Vedic revelation regarding the undertaking of action. || 177.3 ||
For all these, coming together, sustain the embodied being;
he among them whose mind is predominant is proclaimed as "the one possessed of mind. (177.4)
But with the mind one discerns the basis of the auspicious and the inauspicious;
having fixed that mind within the consciousness, one should become constantly delighted in the inner self.
Having restrained the senses and transcended objects such as sound,
the embodied soul intent on the commencement of meditation shall become free from karma.
The senses do not bind the mind that is situated within the body;
the individual soul (jīva) should be known as being of the nature of bondage, due to its attachment to the auspicious and the inauspicious.
From the excess of the two qualities of rajas and tamas, which are of an inauspicious nature, suffering is born; happiness is produced from sattva.
For embodied beings, suffering arises from the transformation of pleasure;
and pleasure, O Brahmin, arises again from the reversal of suffering. (177.9)
Thus, mutually interconnected, born from the transformation of the three qualities,
and consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it remains pervading all beings.
The destruction of that [mind] is declared to result from the concentration of the mind, from aversion toward sense objects, and from the complete avoidance of attachment. || 177.11 ||
Those who are intent on restraining desire, who have abandoned anger and the like,
and who are free from the sense of "mine" and egoism, are not bound by actions at all.
For this self is all-pervading, subtle, and devoid of enjoyment;
yogins perceive it through meditation by means of the cessation of the vital breaths.
A living being wanders through the cycle of existence among creatures of the four wombs for as long as it does not seek the Self, nor is it weary of birth. (177.14)
Although one perishes by failing to realize Brahman due to attachment to meditative absorption,
nevertheless, through union with Brahman, one shall not undergo birth again.
Then the sage attains supreme sovereignty born of meditation and yoga;
having realized the Supreme Self, he shall not return again from that state.
Even unwholesome actions, even those committed through great evil,
a living being who is devoted to meditation brings swiftly to exhaustion after having performed them.
Having attained the complete destruction of karma through the method of meditation, O great sage,
the yogi remains fearless, endowed with supreme sovereignty.
Sensual desire, anger, attachment, hatred, and the fixation on passion—these are the most base states; one who is freed from these is truly liberated.
Pride, hypocrisy, egoism, sophistry, arrogance, envy,
harshness, and cruelty— these are the dispositions bound to the kṣatriya.
Those in whom these delusions do not exist find the Self as the Lord;
they have transcended the state of delusion and are always equal in pain and pleasure.
Endowed with freedom from possessiveness and other such qualities, he is recited as a "Yogin," having completely abandoned the sacrificial rite— the bond of delusion belonging to Viṣṇu.
Constantly devoted to the inner self and desiring liberation, a Brahmin should completely renounce the three aims of life and find delight in the pursuit of yoga.
He is worthy of worship by the dwellers of heaven and is called a Brahmin;
through meditation, his karma—whether evil or auspicious—is exhausted.
Then, with his karma exhausted, the yogi attains that supreme Brahman;
having attained yoga, the meditative sage can accomplish whatever he desires to do.
Whatever is intended by the mind of that person quickly comes to pass;
upon seeing the yogin, people are liberated from their sins at that very moment,
and even he who merely converses with him attains a good rebirth.
O Brahmin, having understood yoga alone to be the supreme means of liberation from all that is inauspicious,
the wise twice-born indeed became seekers of release.
Those who know meditation, the object of meditation, the Supreme, and the Sustainer,
are liberated from the bondage of suffering— through burning, scorching, and being scorched.

Through the renunciation of all undertakings and the avoidance of the sense of "mine" and so forth, the Sāṃkhya and Yoga traditions are one in their singular aim: liberation through the realization of reality.

Among the foremost followers of Sāṃkhya, the Puruṣa is taught to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Their departure at the dissolution of the body is recorded as being like the extinguishing of a lamp.
The Lord, liberated from everything, is regarded by yogis as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
for yogis, endowed with supreme sovereignty, indeed enter into Him.
He who unites the self with those dhāraṇās, as well as with the prāṇāyāmas, attains supreme yoga.
The yogi who is endowed with non-violence and other virtues, who is free from envy,
and who practices meditation— he shall conquer both death and birth.
Free from qualities, free from egoism, having conquered the pairs of opposites, unrestrained, subsisting on food obtained by begging for alms— one who desires liberation is thus designated.
One who is equanimous toward all undertakings, who has abandoned all supports,
and who has transcended the path of action, is proclaimed a meditator (dhyānin).
O Great Sage, he whose mind is not agitated when encountering suffering,
and who does not rejoice in happiness, is designated as one who possesses meditative concentration.
The path that bestows the attainment of liberation is proclaimed to be threefold:
the first is said to be based on convention (saṃketana), and the latter is remembered as being based on discourse (saṃkathana).
And the third is the "attached" (saṃsakta); hear this distinction among them:
having fashioned an image of the Lord and being endowed with the ten observances (niyamas), [he is the attached]. || 177.38 ||
The sage who worships while meditating is called a *saṃketana*;
he is unattached to the pleasures derived from the Vedas, his actions are characterized by purity, and he has no kinsmen.
Having abandoned [all else], one should meditate on the Lord; that is called "discourse upon Him" (saṃkathana), which, through the renunciation of all undertakings, is practiced by Kapila and others.
The path of conversation is remembered as that which illuminates the fire of yoga;
but he who is free from conceptual construction sees everything as Brahman alone.
One whose conduct and ritual actions have been entirely abandoned, yet who remains attached to meditation, is said to be "attached.
This applies to the threefold path, including both its rules and its lack of rules.
These very various types of conduct are proclaimed;
O Sage, all three of these are paths of meditation that serve as causes for liberation.
Having correctly understood these, the sage, free from the sense of "mine," takes refuge in one or another;
he then attains that supreme meditation by which he finds the Ultimate.
O Vyāsa of great intelligence, listen to all these methods of meditation as they are being described by me, which bestow the fruit of mastery over yoga.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 177.177 ||
The one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Brahman is declared to be of two kinds: indeed, the perishable and the imperishable.
For by knowing both of these, one is indeed released from all bonds.
The twenty-fifth principle is perishable, yet it is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
the imperishable Supreme Brahman is known as the twenty-sixth. || 178.2 ||
Having made the mind one-pointed through repeated applications of concentration (dhāraṇā),
preceded by withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), one should perform the restraint of the vital breath (vāyu).
One should practice withdrawal (pratyāhāra) for even half a muhūrta or a single moment;
from that, the binding of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) lasts for three thousand moments.
Having assumed that which is proclaimed as the svastika and other postures, in which the mind has been practiced, one should perform the practice of meditation in a solitary place. 178.5.
Whether afflicted by hunger, or having overeaten, or even if beset by the pain of illness, a wise man who desires meditation for himself should not meditate. 178.6.
Then, having formed the yoga-hand gesture with the right hand over the left, he should remain with his face slightly downward, gazing at the tip of his own nose. || 178.7 ||
Without touching his teeth with his lips, recollecting the Brahman as the syllable Om,
the wise man, free from the sense of "mine," should meditate, preceded by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having joined the self with the Self, one should withdraw all the limbs;
motionless and with eyes closed, one should fix the concentration (dhāraṇā) within the heart.
Like a stone, motionless, the sage should practice meditation; the steady concentration of the mind upon a single point is known as *dhāraṇā*. 178.10.
Thus, for that sage, the yogin who meditates day by day,
all transformations born of the qualities (guṇas) which cause obstacles perish.
And he seeks the Supreme Brahman residing within his own body,
having achieved unification of the vital breaths and the mind through the restraint of the senses.
By renouncing all things, one attains liberation without doubt,
having brought all the spheres of the senses under control through withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Then, free from the pairs of opposites and practicing the concentration of the mind,
one should unify everything within the mind and discern the supreme reality.
When, meditating upon the eightfold perfection that has reached mastery,
he beholds it through the complete accomplishment of yoga, then he is proclaimed a yogi.
When one who is disciplined beholds the gods, such as Brahmā, Soma, and others,
this is indeed called by yogis the perfection born from the transformations of yoga.
The perfection of yogins comes through the mind, and that of the Sāṃkhyas from the ascertainment of the principles;
there is no distinction among yogins except for the method of Maheśvara.

The perfection of meditation for the yogins and the ascertainment of the principles for the Sāṃkhyas—both these, the concentration on meditation and the determination of the meaning of the principles, are non-different. || 178.18 ||
Freed from all bonds, devoid of the faults of attachment, and having completely abandoned passion, delusion, and the like, he is designated as "liberated."
When one who is disciplined, no longer perceiving the objects of the senses such as sound through repeated perfection in yoga, then he beholds that Supreme.
Agitated by the fear of birth and death, and free from the defects of association,
one should take up silence in the forest and meditate upon the imperishable syllable Om.

That which is proclaimed as the first vowel at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas—He who is beyond that [vowel] when it has dissolved into its source is remembered as the Great One (Mahat). || 178.22 ||
He who knows the threefold configuration, the three measures, the three Brahmas, and likewise the three syllables— both that which is devoid of measure and that which possesses measure— is liberated.
Neither fire, nor wind, nor moon, nor sun has power there over the Great Goddess, the Sovereign who is free from the threefold conceptualization.
The syllable *oṃ* is proclaimed as the supreme reality, both the self (*ātman*) and Brahman;
it is perceived by the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through self-awakening and by yogis through subtle vision.
In this very way, always meditating, one should yoke the mind to the Self;
the yogi attains the Lord, having reached whom he is liberated.
But by restraining all the senses from sound, form, and the rest,
the yogi, having understood that they are born of karma, destroys the defects without remainder.
Then, purified by the power of meditation, he attains the liberation of all the Victors;
practicing daily, O Vyāsa, he attains yoga within six months.
And he beholds the Supreme Brahman, by which one may be liberated from bondage;
having known that Self as supreme through the power of yoga, the great sage, endowed with supreme sovereignty, shall attain the immortal state. 178.29
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, the fifth in the section on the rules for meditation within the description of the Pāśupata Yoga, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"That which is called the Great (Mahat) by me is perfected within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)."
Therein are the five organs of action and the five organs of cognition.
The five elements and the mind are here; these are known as the sixteen transformations:
namely, the Great Principle (mahat), the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi). || 179.2 ||

O Vyāsa, these eight primary constituents (prakṛtis) reside within the body; furthermore, these twenty-four principles have been declared by the yogis. The body stands supported by these [principles], which pervade the three worlds. (179.3)
In the center of the navel, however, one hundred channels are established;
as for the others throughout all the limbs, they carry water, food, and the essence of nutrients.
Thirty thousand of those are situated in the stream of the vyāna;
other channels of the udāna are established at the crown of the head of Brahmā.
Resting upon the nave of the wheel and supported by the aggregate of the elements,
situated in its center is the soul of action, touched by the qualities (guṇas) and the deluder of beings.
Resembling the radiance of the stars, his splendor was like a mass of moonlight;
standing there, he appeared like ten thousand suns, causing distress to others.
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, is the source of all beings; established in the qualities (guṇas), he is like a fire that has arisen, resembling a mountain mist.
Beyond that as well, there arises the pure one, like a great fire that has blazed up;
it is radiant, blazing on all sides, free from conceptual construction, and stainless.
Resembling smokeless embers, his coming and going are not perceived;
he is the twenty-sixth principle, the subtle Puruṣa, the supreme and all-pervading Lord.
O Vyāsa, this very one has been described as standing beyond the beyond of others;
by knowing this Mahādeva, the sage is liberated at that very moment. || 179.11 ||
Abiding in the transformations of the three qualities, the twenty-fifth principle is said to transmigrate further, being deluded by ignorance alone. (179.12)
Deluded by passion, he wanders among gods, humans, and animals;
through the concentration on the Twenty-sixth, his perfection arises from transformation.
Freed from action and its effects, the omniscient creator of all, the Lord, filled with supreme sovereignty, the Great Lord who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 179.14 ||
The Unborn, the Self-existent, the Twenty-sixth, is indeed the immutable, immovable, and eternal;
from him the principles (tattvas) are born, as well as the Puruṣa together with the qualities (guṇas). 179.15.
And in that very twenty-sixth Maheśvara they dissolve;
having known this Great Lord, the perfection of liberation is attained.
Having known this, one would not be smeared by actions that are bonds of delusion,
just as fire at the end [of time] would consume the entire multitude of beings without exception.
One who knows the twenty-six categories likewise burns away all karmas;
just as the all-pervading ether, being subtle, is not defiled at all.
The yogin who delights in the Twenty-sixth is not smeared by sins in that way;
there is nothing beyond the Twenty-sixth, therefore one should be devoted to that as the supreme.
Having abandoned oneness with that very [body], he attains the body [of the Self], along with the entire multitude of beings without exception, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu. || 179.20 ||
O Vyāsa, it is born from Īśvara and dissolves into that very same one;
there is indeed nothing else superior to him, for he should be known as abiding everywhere.
He whom the perfected ones who know the inner self worship as the Supreme Self—
he is this all-pervading God, the twenty-sixth, the Supreme Lord.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these are the five winds in the body; one should strive for their restraint.
Having attentively unified the apāna and the samāna breaths,
one should settle the prāṇa, together with the vyāna, into the udāna.
Then, by the power of yoga, one should bring the vital breath to the tip of the nose once;
having established an auspicious gaze, one should thereafter contemplate the Twenty-sixth.
Fifteen measures are declared for the first joint-binding;
twenty measures are to be known for the fifth, which is the joint-disjunction.
In a silent and solitary place, free from worldly desire and with senses conquered,
one should assume the svastika, padmaka, bhadra, or siṃha-kacchapa postures.
Occupying a single seat and recollecting the Twenty-sixth [Tattva], having withdrawn all his limbs, he should practice meditation, motionless.
One should slowly circulate the breath through the channels situated within the currents;
one should remain thus with a disciplined mind, free from longing, through the yoga of meditation.
As long as one perceives that which resembles the orb of the moon situated in the heart,
once the light-body (jyotirdeha) has been beheld, the sovereign power of yoga proceeds.
Therefore, through such constant practice and the resulting engagement in the perfection of yoga,
the yogin’s knowledge regarding the objects of the three times becomes direct perception.
Diseases do not enter him, nor does he become possessed by suffering;
moreover, a fragrance arises from his own body and his form becomes divine. (179.32)
His word shall be unfailing in bestowing both curses and favors,
and there shall be for him no adverse consequence resulting from his actions.
O Vyāsa, among all those who possess knowledge, among ascetics, those who observe vows, and among Brahmins who practice austerities, the yogi is declared to be the most excellent. (179.34)

A living being is not liberated from this worldly existence, which is beyond darkness, in any other way than by abandoning the bonds of yoga and attaining full knowledge of the Twenty-sixth Principle.
Having conquered the eightfold binding of postures by means of the sixfold yoga as well as the fivefold [yoga], || 179.36 ||
Having conquered the fourfold prāṇāyāma by means of the excellence of the *mātrās*, and having conquered the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) with the senses, and the senses with their objects; 179.37.
Free from egoism, fear, fatigue, anger, and greed;
moreover, devoid of envy, unattached, without affection, and likewise without longing.

Having established the seat of yoga, which is devoid of qualities as previously described, one should meditate in the heart upon that God—the all-pervading Lord of the universe and the universe itself. (179.39)
Without beginning or end, peaceful, and devoid of the three qualities;
placing the tongue against the palate, he did not let his teeth touch one another. (179.40)
One should unite the senses and the mind within the Supreme Self,
having gathered all that into the mind and restrained both the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Meditating repeatedly on the syllable Oṃ, having withdrawn his limbs like a tortoise,
he should fill his entire body with it and then dissolve everything into the Self.

Having withdrawn that [expansion] once more, the sage should again initiate it repeatedly through the movement of the channels and the vital breaths, so that the all-pervading being becomes further extended.

During the first and last watches of the night, his mind is said to be characterized by *sattva*; at midday and in the afternoon, he should meditate on the dark [form], which is characterized by *tamas*.
One should constantly practice the rājasa meditation during both twilights;
furthermore, by meditating on the Taijasa deity everywhere, one shall conquer the guṇas.

O Vyāsa, for one who meditates thus at all times, that sovereignty proceeds by which, having realized the twenty-sixth principle, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) dwelling within the heart, [one attains liberation]. 179.46.
Having voluntarily cast off its own body, it dissolves into that very [Supreme Self];
the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Cause, the Great Puruṣa.
The Lord, devoid of qualities, the enjoyer, is proclaimed as the twenty-sixth;
he is the pervasive, supreme one, who is both the non-existent and the existent, and who has become the source of all manifestations.
He is awake while [others] sleep; he eats, remains seated, and gives.
He is the creator and the destroyer, the Great Lord who transcends the qualities (guṇas). 179.49.
Thus has all this been told to you— the exposition of all yogas,
the primordial Pāśupata yoga that bestows the state of liberation.
O sinless one, I shall proclaim to you that subtle and supreme knowledge, free from all conceptual proliferation, which has issued forth from the mouth of Hara;
through the perfect realization of which, there remains nothing further to be known. (179.51)
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and eightieth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, in ancient times, at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the deities beginning with Brahmā [acted].
Afflicted by the fear of Vīrabhadra, they went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
When they were assailed by the Lord of the Gaṇas, they entered heaps of ashes;
once they had entered the ashes, they attained the supreme splendor of Śaṅkara.
At that time, those fierce beings became like initiated sacrificers,
their limbs smeared with ashes as they observed the vows of Śaṅkara.
Then the God, the Lord of Umā, bestowed his own yoga upon them—
that reality which excels all the sciences of liberation.
O Vyāsa, that yoga which was initiated by the foremost of yogis, headed by Hiraṇyagarbha, is complete and accomplished through arduous means.
O great sage,
by practicing this supreme yoga of Maheśvara which has been directly revealed by the Blessed One, they attain either the supreme light or the sovereignty of yoga after thousands of other births.
In truth, for those celestial beings who have taken refuge in him,
this has been ordained through his very thorough understanding [of reality] in this very birth.
Having undertaken the Pāśupata vow, one attains knowledge within six months;
having attained that great mastery of yoga, O Vyāsa, one is liberated. (180.8)
Having cast all phenomena outside through the power of the partless [Self],
and having received the Pāśupata initiation, they enter that Maheśvara.
Endowed with all-knowledge yet excluded from the dharma of asceticism,
this vow taught by Śiva consists merely of the practice of using ashes.
Whether they be most wicked or righteous, those who are devoted solely to the Lord are liberated by serving him; learn of that great vow.
There is no dharma without adharma, nor is there any inauspiciousness without dharma; these two are bound to one another. Therefore, having abandoned both of them— || 180.12 ||
Having abandoned both dharma and adharma, one should practice the Pāśupata vow;
then, having attained this yoga, one obtains great sovereignty.
Merely by taking up the ashes, there is liberation from all bonds;
one is liberated simply by being touched with the ashes purified by Brahman.
Fire burns what is produced by Soma; they know the Lord to be Anala (Fire).
Having come together with Soma, Agni burns again both the done and the undone.
By means of the sacred ash, all those who possessed pride, beginning with Brahmā, were liberated;
for the ash is the splendor and the power [of Śiva], the purifying Lord himself.
O Vyāsa, he who performs the bath with ashes uplifts himself;
through the yoga of Śiva and by means of ashes, he is liberated from the bondage of the fetters. 180.17.
The gods originate from Soma, and the ancestors are born from Agni;
therefore, the entire world is established as being composed of the essence of both Agni and Soma.
Īśvara, Agni, and Soma—these are said to be his fiery splendor.
Touched by that splendor, the twice-born is liberated from birth. 180.19.
Having abandoned Sāṃkhya, as well as austerity and Vedic duties,
one who is purified solely by bathing in ashes goes to that supreme state.
Even if one indulges in sense objects and remains devoted to great unrighteousness,
by later becoming intent on devotion to Śambhu, one is indeed purified by the sacred ash alone.
He who, having consecrated himself with the sacred ashes of Brahman, makes himself the sacrificial animal and offers it into the fire of Mahādeva, becomes a sage performing the sacrifice of Śiva.
Having swiftly attained the supreme yoga, he shall be liberated from bondage;
thus, having undertaken this vow and become a Pāśupata ascetic, [he attains liberation].
One should practice this supreme secret knowledge of Maheśvara, [understanding] how the three—the object of knowledge, the knowledge itself, and the knower—exist within the body. 180.24
The self, who he is and how he is situated in the three places,
and how indeed the self abides within the channels and within the self itself.
O Vyāsa, it abides hidden everywhere within all beings, like clarified butter within milk; by knowing which, one is liberated.
That Self cannot be known in any way without knowledge;
who can know Maheśvara, who transcends form, sound, and taste? || 180.27 ||
For thus, O illustrious and sinless one, from the temple of Tryambaka, I shall tell you the means for cultivating self-knowledge.
In the beginning, this entire world was indeed nothing but darkness;
there were no gods, no wind, no sky, no sun, and no moon.
Nothing whatsoever exists as real in any way within the world;
it appears as pure, stainless, imperishable, and supreme sovereignty.

Listen now as that imperishable Brahman is being described: it transcends all states of existence and qualities, is free from conceptual construction, and is stainless; it moves both outside and within, is radiant, indestructible, supreme, and eternal. (180.31)
The syllable "Om" is the single imperishable (aksara) from which all that is perishable has emerged;
consisting of three letters and three measures, the syllable Om is designated as Brahman.
In the syllable *a* is Viṣṇu, in the syllable *u* is the Grandfather (Brahmā),
in the syllable *m* is the Lord (Īśa), and in the measure (*mātrā*) Prakṛti is remembered.
Those two gods, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who are known to have emerged from the Lord, constantly remain at the side of the Lord, having assumed the state of Prakṛti as women. 180.34.
In the form of his consort, that Prakṛti always worships Śambhu;
Prakṛti is known as the perishable (kṣara), while the Lord himself is the imperishable (akṣara). || 180.35 ||
For that Prakṛti, bound by the qualities (guṇas), emerged from Īśvara;
Mahādeva is her creator, from whom Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha [Brahmā] arose.
The two Prajāpatis were born bound by the three qualities; Maheśa, however, having stepped over them, stands beyond Prakṛti, which consists of those qualities.
Having become the all-pervading Lord residing in the letter *ma*, he indeed enjoys and moves about.
Having known this supreme secret, I have spoken this imperishable truth.
O Vyāsa, by that very meditative absorption through which this Lord was conceptualized,
the sage— having entered Him and being liberated in soul— becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Those who stand on the wrong path, devoted to logic and reasoning, do not know him—the enjoyer, the Lord of nature, the Supreme known as the Twenty-sixth. (180.40)
The syllable Oṃ is eternal primordial nature (prakṛti), and within it the Lord (Īśvara) resides, just as clarified butter exists within milk, O Vyāsa. (180.41)
O Sage, he who, meditating upon the syllable Oṃ, has transcended primordial nature (prakṛti), is that great Lord; he is liberated from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu). || 180.42 ||
Nature (prakṛti) is known as the sovereign (īśvarī), who deludes through the bondage of the qualities (guṇas).

Indeed, she is the nourisher (bṛṃhaṇī) because of her nature as Brahman, and she rests in manifestation (vibhava) because of her nature as Viṣṇu. By the grace of the Lord, this Nature consists of the three qualities.
Possessing self-conceit, she is the creator of existence; Maheśvara is her enjoyer.
She has eight arms and three feet, as well as five bodies and faces;
she has two eyes, is established in the five activities, and is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses.
For she is remembered as the Mother of the World, born from the transformations of the three qualities (guṇas);
both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as both knowledge and ignorance, belong to her. 180.46.
Arising, as well as destruction, the performance of action,
the causal sign, and the womb— these, in brief, are the states of existence.
The syllable Oṃ was born from Īśvara, and it is established in him;
from Oṃ arose the entire world, up to the abode of Brahmā.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, the yogis such as Kapila and others, having realized this, worship the syllable Om as the supreme Brahman, free from conceptual construction.
For that very Self is all-pervading, and it alone is the cause;
thus those two, having become the primordial nature (prakṛti), abide as originating from the syllable Om.

Having understood that Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha are the Lord and the object of enjoyment, whose natures consist of the qualities (guṇas), and having abandoned those two—named the Veda and the sacrifice—which were created by them and bound by dharma; || 180.51 ||
The two great delusions are rooted in darkness (tamas) and joined with attachment to sense-objects;
they are preceded by goodness (sattva), have passion (rajas) as their middle state, and are always accompanied by pleasure and pain.
The two fools wandering in saṃsāra are joined with all that is impermanent;
the wise man, desiring the Lord, should be devoted to the yoga of meditation.

Therefore, primordial nature (prakṛti), having arisen, perishes within that very [Self] by which the Lord is known; established in the Self through yoga, nature does not bind him, and he is liberated from the ocean of existence.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 180.180 ||
The one hundred and eighty-first chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
The self (ātman), the subtle [body], the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and likewise the qualities (guṇas).
The elements, the aggregate of the senses, the subtle essences, and the ten vital airs.
O observer of noble vows, they are sequentially divided within the body according to their respective locations,
in the three states of dreaming, waking, and deep sleep.
But that lotus which faces all directions in the heart, within the pericarp,
is surrounded by subtle threads above [the head] of all embodied beings.
Therein the self, together with the vital breath and the mind, is established;
the perfected Śiva-yogins call that state "deep sleep. (181.4)
Jvālinī, Stimitā, Dhūmrā, Vidyunmeghā, Viśālinī, Mālinī, Śaṅkarī, Sumaitrī, and likewise Bodhanī. || 181.5 ||
These ten great channels are established in that living being;
whether he is lying down or awake, they sustain the embodied soul.
Furthermore, that self which is all-pervading, when joined with fire and wind, is called the *jīva* in relation to objects such as sound and the rest. (181.7)
Egoism is considered to be the intellect (buddhi), and the dispositions and the mind are born of the body;
together with the individual soul (jīva), they abide, supporting the embodied being.
All these together, with the individual soul (jīva) as the fifth,
constitute the pericarp situated in the void by means of the threads, facing in all directions.
Abiding subtly within the mind is that which is named Śītāṃśu, the thread;
it is declared to be the consciousness itself, and it is remembered as the Puruṣa.
Egoism is the Jīva, while the thread is born from Bhāskara;
the mind is Soma, and likewise pleasure is Brahmā, as are knowledge, dharma, and delight.
Taste, the self, the great herbs, the expansion of states born of the mind, ego, fire, death, suffering, and likewise disease; || 181.12 ||
Lust, anger, old age, thirst, and unrighteousness are the qualities of darkness (tāmasa).
Viṣṇu, intellect, as well as the effect, the cause, and the earth itself [are the qualities of goodness]. 181.13.
Knowledge, dispassion, and space constitute the expansion of the rājasa state;
situated within the individual soul (jīva) is the subtle, smokeless flame of fire.
It is indeed the nectar of all beings and their supreme goal;
situated in its center is the gentle nectar, the lunar orb.
In its center, the Lord Jīva is seen, resembling fire;
he is full of essence, red, preeminent, joyful, and likewise possessed of flavor.
Vidhūmā, Amṛtā, Nikuṇṭhā, and Bahuvistarā—
these exceedingly subtle channels, having pierced through the ten fires,
constantly satisfy Soma, the support of all beings, with milk that is like nectar. 181.17.
Soma, being satiated by those [waters] with all essences, juices, and potencies,
grows and envelops that flame situated within the living being.
That very thing is declared to be the nectar, the supreme abode of the Lord;
for when the essence of the soma is drawn up further by the crest [of fire], || 181.19 ||
At that time, this living being born from all wombs remains awake;
the other channel, called Amṛtā, is established in sleep.
When he drinks the Soma, he is said to be asleep;
having conquered both these states which are the bases of sleep and waking, he is called a sage. (181.21)
Neither waking nor sleeping, one should contemplate through the yoga of meditation those states such as the sense of "mine" and whatever aversion belongs to the mind.
The detachment that belongs to the intellect is not by means of that which yogins awaken;
for whatever the mind conceives and whatever the intellect discriminates, [that is not the awakening]. (181.23)
Or rather, whatever the ego may do, one should abandon it all through knowledge of that [Self].
For one who is free from activity, how can there be action? Without that, how can there be bondage? (181.24)
How can one who is purified and free from the bonds of karma be bound?
For some do not know that these sense-objects originate from the moon.
Fire is said to be the enjoyer of those [elements]; by what can its knower be bound?
Knowing this, one should abandon anxiety and always remain devoted to yoga.
The heat of fire is its sin; this is declared to be the quality of its brilliance (tejas).
That which is its nature (prakṛti) is the individual soul (jīva), while the flame itself is Maheśvara.
He who can burn the fire with his own brilliance yet is not himself consumed by it—by him Prakṛti has been transcended; by him Maheśvara has been attained.
For this world is bound by the bonds of karma; how could one who is free from action be bound?
Those who possess the knowledge of yoga, who are free from the sense of "mine," abide in the vow of Śaṅkara.
They go to the supreme state, having abandoned their own bodies and cast off illusion;
yet there is another, further knowledge, even more subtle than this. (181.30)
I shall declare it to you, O Vyāsa, for you are a devotee of Śaṅkara;
other yogis do not know this most wonderful secret. (181.31)
Except for the perfected Pāśupatas, there exists nothing among all beings that is not [composed of] mind, intellect, ego, the senses, and the three qualities. (181.32)
Modifications do not touch its essence; they remain external to it.
It is seen everywhere, yet it is not seen by everyone.
It is perceived in this way through meditation; by no other means can it ever be seen.
Those yogins who perceive through knowledge the Supreme Lord— who transcends all states of being and qualities, and who is well-conceived— are remembered as the highest.
This shadow which is seen resting within the range of the eye is called the *jīva*, O Vyāsa; it is the cause of stability for embodied beings. (181.35)
There dwells that supreme Self, subtle, situated in the midst, and imperishable;
he is known by the name Mahānāga, the wind whose domain is space.
She is established in space, in the pericarp, in the channel, and in the individual soul (jīva);
she is Gāndhārī, Vijayā, Saṃjayā, and Talavartinī.
O Naga, within these channels the vital air circulates;
those two, Jayā and Vijayā, are known as the carriers of the prāṇa.
In the *apāna* [vāyu], the two channels, Talagā and Gāndhārī, are conjoined with Nāga;
through yoga, they are impelled by Nāga along with the *apāna* and the mind.
That vital breath, satisfying the fire that carries the oblation both externally and internally,
sustains the body with longevity and with strength.
But there is another channel called Suṣumṇā, situated within the moon, fire, and mind;
it resides in this body composed of the elements, as well as in the tortoise and the vital air.
Fixed at the ankle and the palm, the nikunthā and prasāriṇī, joined with the samāna and vyāna breaths, indeed nourish the blood and flesh. 181.42.
The udāna is that other wind which is called kūrmāra;
both are established upon the balance-beam fixed at the navel within the channels.
Now, one wind moves through the nāḍī, while the other moves upward;
the one situated below is connected to the feet, and the one moving upward is located in the head. (181.44)
The wind known as Devadatta, which is created, and that other wind, Anila—
these two, bound by fire and moon, are the causes of life and possess great power.
One increases the fire, while another satisfies the Soma;
these are Devadatta, Mahānāga, Kṛtakūrma, and Dhanañjaya.
Those five vital breaths are renowned as the sacrificial fires;
whatever is offered or sacrificed into them reaches the Soma.
Sacrificers enter the Soma; for them there is no characteristic of liberation.
That which is known as the radiance of fire and the essence derived from plants—[these are their lot]. (181.48)
That which is the libation of Soma, situated within the karṇikā, is seen in the eyes as this light that illuminates the shadow. || 181.49 ||
That living soul is the self of all beings, established therein;
subtle and contained within the light, it is remembered as the supreme dharma.
That is declared to be the immortal; it is said to be attainable through knowledge. There is no goal higher than that, which consists of knowledge and realized wisdom.
Having understood this, one should utterly abandon delusion born from the transformation of the three qualities (guṇas) regarding that non-dual Self, the twenty-sixth principle, the Lord.
Who else, being skilled in yoga, would create a division in the Blessed One?
One should not conceptualize that Lord, who is stainless and free from conceptual construction.
Free from delusion, having abandoned all worldly associations, and devoid of ritual actions and duties,
those who observe the vows of the Lord enter that Great Lord.
Thus, O Vyāsa, this yoga of Maheśvara has been declared to you;
it is the perfect union with the Lord, which is not found elsewhere. (181.55)
"O Brahmin, whatever doubt you have and whatever you deem worthy of inquiry, ask that immediately, O Brahmin; there is nothing that I should not tell you. (181.56)
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 181.181 ||
The one hundred and eighty-second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, Lord of all yogins, saluted by all the immortals!
Oh, what knowledge you have proclaimed, which brings about the cessation of ignorance!
Today I have become free from doubt regarding the supreme Mahādeva;
from Śaṅkara, Prakṛti was born, and Brahmā and Viṣṇu are of his very essence.
"Having known the Lord as the Twenty-sixth, one is released from bondage"—having thus spoken the entire compendium prior to the path of all yoga. (182.3)
"Who else could speak such knowledge, both partless and with parts?
O best of Brahmins, by hearing this, I have realized that my body is liberated."
"O Father, through your grace I have attained auspicious knowledge;
being free from doubt and at peace, there is something I wish to ask you. (182.5)
Therefore, I inform you of this; you ought to explain the final goal.
Thus, O Sage, one who is endowed with such knowledge and has attained yoga becomes a sage. 182.6.
Having abandoned the body without affliction, how does the yogi, endowed with the power of yoga, attain that Brahman, the partless Supreme Lord? || 182.7 ||
"O best of sages, tell me the means for attaining the support of the Lord, which is the attainment of liberation; there is nothing else remaining for me to ask. (182.8)
Thus addressed by his disciple Vyāsa, the great-souled one,
that best of Brahmins, related the definitive conclusion of the Śiva-siddhānta.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the supreme knowledge which has the Lord as its foundational cause, by means of which yogins devoted to wisdom are liberated according to their own will. 182.10
Having understood this triple departure and having practiced it repeatedly,
one should abandon one's own body like an enemy and attain dissolution in the Twenty-sixth.
Those channels, held by the vital air, sustain the embodied being;
of those hundreds, there are indeed one hundred that are situated in the center of the pericarp.

The channels (nāḍīs) are situated depending upon that [central channel], extending from the navel down to the feet; they are further recorded as being fixed at the head and likewise established in the hands. (182.13)
O Sage, having relied upon that [central] channel, those seventy-two thousand other channels once again take refuge in the pericarp. 182.14
The subdivisions of each of these are said to be increasingly subtle;
within them moves the vital breath (prāṇa), which originates from the space of the pericarp.
Therein, O twice-born one, the Self previously described remains, subtle and difficult to perceive;
the sage skilled in yoga should resort to that radiance of his which is hard to behold.
That fire is distributed throughout all the channels of all embodied beings;
by means of it, the channels make the mind perceive external touches as expanded.
Having withdrawn that fire through the eyes and brought it to rest within all the channels, one should make the mind one-pointed and fix it upon the Self. 182.18.
The wind named Dhanañjaya, who always throbs within the heart—
its three openings, they say, are the head, the navel, and the heart itself.
Those other vital breaths which have not been mentioned, and the winds that I have described—
all of them are under the control of Dhanañjaya and are dependent upon him.
By its power, these [vital breaths] ascend; when it remains steady, they remain established.
Having reached the binding of the navel, they abide at the opening of the channels.
The second is in the pericarp, while the third is situated in the palate;
the razor, the axe, and the trident—this is called the threefold departure.
The spear is fixed in the heart, the razor at the navel, and the axe resides in the palate;
the three are bound to the palate or the heart and established at the navel.
When the two palates are separated, all vital breath is released;
when the triad is drawn back and separated from the navel, it is released into the pericarp.
Having joined [the breath] within the self, one should cast the mind upward;
by this practice, O best of Brahmins, the sage is liberated at that very moment. (182.25)
This voluntary abandonment of the body has been proclaimed to you;
[it is distinct] from those actions previously performed that are bound by merit and demerit.
Listen to this by which the life-force of the yogi is not bound:
death is said to be of two kinds, namely external and that born of the body.
Death by means of poison, weapons, fire, serpents, fanged beasts, wind, and water is known as external; now learn from me concerning the body.
Death may be either internal, arising from disease or arising from time;
that which arises from time is said to be due to old age, while that which arises from disease results from the exhaustion of the vital humors.

O Sage, death resulting from mutual conflict born of the application of yoga is difficult to encounter; so too is that which is brought about by the means of yoga, and that which arrives through the exhaustion of time. (182.30)
But listen, Vyāsa, to the distinction between their two types of transformation in brief:
one arises from the exhaustion of time, while the second is desired by the mind. (182.31)
This sound produced by resonance which is heard through the connection of the ears first dissolves into the tortoise; by that means, the fire should abandon its radiance.
Then that fire becomes lusterless and is deprived of its connection with sound;
transcending the qualities of sound and touch, it relinquishes its connection with form.
When the fire has thus been extinguished, all the vital airs (anila) then,
seeking union as one, cut through the vital points (marmāṇi).
Kūrmāra, Devadatta, Kṛkara,
and Nāga indeed quickly unite with Udāna and enter into the pericarp.
Then the breath rises upward as the mind and life-force depart;
thereafter, the light from the eyes quickly enters the moon.
The senses follow the mind, and the mind follows the departure of the vital breath;
when all of these have dissolved, the wind [of the breath] should suppress the vital breaths.
Then, being oppressed, they all become unified as the wind, having abandoned their respective places and whatever actions were inherent to them. (182.38)
All the vital breaths (vāyu) gathered in one place fill Dhanañjaya;
for there Śeṣa remains, having abandoned his life-force.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the consciousness, and likewise the individual soul—
driven by the vital wind, these quickly depart from the body.
Then another subtle body, previously acquired, arises for him;
joined to that, the living soul remains there once more, deluded. (182.41)
Thus, indeed, this condition of all classes of beings is brought about by Time;
without Yoga, the subtle state of Maheśvara cannot be attained.

Whether sitting or asleep, O Vyāsa, one who has practiced the restraint of the upward departure (utkrānti) is liberated by his own will, provided he has known that Great Lord (Maheśvara). || 182.43 ||
The sage should then hold a razor, an axe, or a trident;
thereby all his transformations, along with the sense organs, dissolve away.
And he beholds the Lord Brahman, the twenty-sixth principle, abiding within his own body;
for the mind of a living being who is perishing becomes intensely agitated and inert.
Overcome by that pain, he fell into delusion and could not perceive the object of his knowledge;
yet, O Brahmin, by this very act, he was entirely freed from all suffering.
Having understood the five categories of objects, one who is firmly established in the end of suffering ascends easily to the summit of the palace of Brahman, as if from its floor.
Purified by the five Brahmans and initiated with sacred ash, the twice-born yogi whose mind is single-pointedly fixed on Śaṅkara attains this knowledge. || 182.48 ||
Even with great effort, they do not find this Maheśvara yoga, which is partless and the cause of liberation, unless they have attained the vow of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, practicing the Pāśupata vow and becoming devoted to Mahādeva, may you attain this knowledge.
It is not so; other yogins do not find this supreme Brahman, except for those Śiva-yogins who have taken refuge in Mahādeva.
This entire method for liberation, free from all causal conditions, has been declared by you, O Vyāsa, to be partless, for there exists nothing higher than it. (182.52)
In this way, the Pāśupata brahmins, having entered that Maheśvara who is without parts through yoga, are liberated and freed from rebirth.
I shall describe that divine abode of Mahādeva, which stands beyond the world of Brahmā and where his devotees go. 182.54.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, the ninth in the section on the rules of yoga within the description of the Pāśupata yoga, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The one hundred and eighty-third chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Of truth, of the great people, and likewise of austerity...
And he stands above the seven realms of the past, present, and future.
The world wherein the Blessed Śambhu dwells is entirely auspicious;
it cannot be defined by logic, for all worlds are established within it.
Above, across, and below, the worlds are bound to that;
the entire cosmic egg is established within that world of Śiva.
He does not perish at the time of universal dissolution; he is eternal, immovable, and the abode of the gods, where I, Sanaka and the others, and Brahmā, the Grandfather himself, reside.
And the Siddhas, headed by the Bālakhilyas, as well as Kapila and others,
having attained the yoga of Śiva, were freed from the qualities of sattva and the rest.
We remain at peace, O Vyāsa, serving that Lord;
for this Lord is as subtle as an atom, perceivable by the hearts of the wise.
There resides Vigraheśvara, endowed with supreme sovereignty;
likewise, forbearance, truth, fortitude, austerity, and even detachment [are present there]. (183.7)
The state of being a creator, knowledge, dispassion, self-awakening, and supreme lordship—
these qualities abide eternally in that divine Maheśvara.
This self, the fire of yoga, the supreme lord who emits Brahman, assumes a complete form and effects the maintenance of the world. || 183.9 ||
The eighth is the eternal syllable to be meditated upon, the cause of liberation;
it is the abode of Māyā belonging to that Lord, and the cause for the dissolution of the world.
Above the world of Brahmā, at a distance of twenty million yojanas from that great-souled one, stands the city of Sthāṇu.
This much is known as the upward movement and the end of the journey;
in that city, there dwell beings who are innumerable, eternal, subtle, and likewise imperishable.
The primordial natures (prakṛtis) of Śiva, characterized by the authority of knowledge, abide;
from them were born the two Great Lords, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the progenitors of creatures. 183.13.
To those two who had become his primordial natures (prakṛti), he granted supreme creatorship—
[creatorship] that is imperishable, stainless, subtle, partless, and yet also possessed of parts.
Established in the firm, embodied, supreme, and divine state at the level of the ultimate atom,
there occurs first the manifestation of that light within the primordial darkness of the mind.
When that golden mundane egg, which leads to liberation, was present,
it then became the Great One (Mahat), eternal and omnipresent, arising from the Lord.

Therefore, that which is without differentiation from the seed is known as the all-pervading Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); Prakṛti is declared to belong to Viṣṇu, and she has emerged from him. || 183.17 ||
For the purpose of creating the gods, asuras, and others, she again assumed the state of Brahmā,
following the division of the cosmic egg from the lotus-born Brahmā, whose essence is Śaṅkara.
O Vyāsa, that abode of the Lord of Form, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign, known by the name Śivapura, is the destination of the yogins who have attained mastery over the Lord.
A hundred times one hundred thousand yojanas is said to be the extent of the terrestrial sphere; it is recorded as being spread out in the center of that [world-system].
It was well-encircled by a great wall made of gold, possessing a brilliance exceeding that of fire and shining with the form of the sun.
Adorned with four golden gates embellished with jewels and pearls,
that beautiful city, frequented by the Siddhas, shone resplendently.
O Sage, in that City of Śiva, inauspicious states such as old age, death, fatigue, disease, anger, delusion, and intoxication do not prevail.
Extending for a hundred times a hundred thousand yojanas in every direction,
that city of the bull-bannered god is all-pervading and magnificent.
The divine emerald ground brings pleasure by its mere touch;
it is like lapis lazuli gems and resembles the rising sun.
In some places red lotuses and in others white ones shone forth,
as large as great lakes, with stalks resembling lapis lazuli.
Fragrant and highly precious, they were laid upon the surface of the earth,
resembling sapphire and possessing the luster of great jewels.
In some places there were blue lotuses, half-red in hue, wafting divine fragrances, extending everywhere throughout that place.
O son of Parāśara, learn now of those great rivers that flow with the water of nectar within that city of the blessed Lord Śambhu. 183.29.
Varadā, Vareṇyā, Vareśā, Varavarṇinī, Vārāhī, Vāribhadrā, and Varā—these indeed are the great rivers. || 183.30 ||
They carry that nectar-like water mixed with various flowers;
neither gods, nor lords of sages, nor asuras, nor ancestors [can do so]. (183.31)
Nor indeed would others be capable of knowing that wondrous city—
those who have awakened within their inner minds, who are permeated by devotion on all sides,
and whose minds are fixed solely on Śiva; those men, O Vyāsa, rejoice therein.
In the center of that city of the Lord of Gods, who possesses the splendor of the blazing sun,
stands the palace Digbhadra, resembling a peak of Mount Meru and radiant as the sun.
The palace was a hundred thousand feet high, moving at will and made of gold;
it was adorned on all sides with great jewels that could not be gazed upon.
With lapis lazuli that resembles the sky, with crystal possessing the luster of the moon, with coral resembling the sun, and with others made of sapphire; 183.35.
Adorned with banners that in some places had the brilliance of moonbeams and in others took the form of sunrays, that place shone forth, cooled by pleasant breezes.
That city shone, strewn with trees resembling mountains, which bore variegated blossoms of every season as well as wish-fulfilling jewel-fruits.
Just as Meru is the greatest and most excellent among all mountains that support the earth,
even so did that city shine, situated above all the worlds.
There, Viśveśvara himself, Hara, the lord of the great elements,
the twenty-sixth Supreme Lord, dwells eternally together with his consort.
Lakṣmī, Meghā, Dhṛti, Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, and Sarasvatī—
these mothers of the world rejoice there together with Umā.
O child, those men who have dedicated their souls to the state of Śiva and are devoted to Rudra— wherever they may die, that very place is remembered as their abode.
And those Maheśvaras, O Vyāsa, who dwell in the abode of Śaṅkara—those sages devoted to Śaṅkara, listen to them with a concentrated mind. (183.42)
I, as well as Sanandana, Sanaka, and Sanātana;
Ṛbhu, Brahmā, the eldest of the gods, and also Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
— — — — — — the disciple Siddha Pañcaśikha, as well as the sage Hayaśiras, Yājñavalkya, and others. 183.44.
Three-eyed, possessing bodies like Śaṅkara and endowed with supreme sovereignty,
they stand at the base of the Lord, beyond the qualities (guṇas), seeking liberation.
When the destruction of the world has arisen, known as the great dissolution (mahāpralaya),
they enter into the Lord and attain final liberation.
And those by whom the Śiva-liṅgas were seen, O best of Brahmins, namely Kedāra, Madhyama, and Girīśa in Mahālaya; || 183.47 ||
The god Catuḥśṛṅgeśvara, Maheśvara at Śrīgiri, the lord of gods Kārohaṇa, and Śaṃkara at Gaṅgādvāra; likewise Mahādeva Bhadreśa and Śaṅkukarṇeśvara. || 183.48 ||
Both Mahākāleśvara and Gokarṇa,
as well as Avimukteśvara and whatever other [shrines] exist upon the earth.
They too, O Vyāsa, go after death to that city of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
and as for the Pāśupata yoga which has been described by me to you—
Having undertaken the Pāśupata vow, he too practices it there;
those best of men who possess constant devotion to Bhava have already achieved their purpose.
O Vyāsa, those who have died [there] go to the city of Śiva, three-eyed and with spears (paṭṭiśa) in their hands;
resembling Nandīśa and Skanda, they are endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty.
O Vyāsa, they always become Rudras standing by the side of Śaṅkara.
Thus has this entire supreme Māheśvara Yoga been described to you.
Having thus known the Supreme Lord as both with parts and without parts,
you shall be liberated from all bonds and attain supreme liberation.
And by the power of this knowledge, you shall become a yogi whose very self is yoga,
a sustainer of the world, and a promoter of the Smārta dharma.
By the power of your knowledge, you shall create the Purāṇa for the sake of understanding the principles of cosmic stability within the cause of the universe's origin,
and you shall compose the Veda remembered by Svāyambhuva for the purpose of propagating the dharma of sacrifice.
But by recollecting from consciousness, you will transform it into fourfold.
This entire irreproachable Vaivasvata Manvantara consists of those dharmas that maintain the stability of the world, with the Vedas and Smṛtis as their foremost authority.
Your teachings shall circulate, and you will become a Tīrthaṃkara;
having attained the vow of the ashes, which brings liberation from the bonds of the Paśus.
"Endowed with the knowledge of Śaṅkara, you shall attain dissolution in the Lord.
Thus addressed, that best of brahmins, with the hair on his entire body bristling with joy, [spoke].
Having approached that Lord of Sages, he received the consecration by ashes;
and at that very moment, this yoga manifested within that great sage.
Having saluted his preceptor, the son of Brahmā, who was possessed of great luster,
Vyāsa wandered over the earth for the purpose of visiting the shrines of Śarva.
Vāyu said:
Thus questioned by the wise Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra,
the lord of sages, narrated the Purāṇa concerning the birth of Skanda.
This great ocean of all knowledge is a meditation arising from the yoga of Śiva, which is endowed with all the scriptures and describes the stability of the world throughout the various Manvantaras.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having understood this, practice the Pāśupata vow and, through the yoga of Śaṅkara, attain absorption into the Lord. 183.65.
Having investigated this tradition, that great sage Vyāsa, the bull among ascetics,
composed the sciences connected with the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
From this [source] emerged the Dharmas as well as the Yogavidyās;
O twice-born ones, Nandīśvara declared that the Purāṇa is the first and the primordial.
He who knows this in its true essence is renowned;
by him the three goals of life are attained, and through this, liberation is born.
By this, life is increased; by this, everything is obtained, O Brahmins, just as Hara is the primordial creator of the entire world. 183.69.
Likewise, this supreme Purāṇa is remembered as the most ancient of all Purāṇas; those Brahmins by whom it has been studied—[their sins are destroyed]. (183.70)
— one who hears [this] shall attain union with the All-pervading Lord. 183.71.
By its service, one attains perfection in yoga and the supreme liberation;
O best of the twice-born, this is the first meritorious and supreme hymn of praise concerning the birth and heroic exploits of Skanda, the Lord of Umā.
All those lords of the *nāgas*, lords of the asuras, yakṣas, and gods, along with the *siddhas* and the foremost of the twice-born,
possessed bodies like the blazing sun and fire, were three-eyed, and shone with the luster of the moon.
You shall attain the city that is undecaying and infinite, the abode of the Lord.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Ārṣa Skandapurāṇa, together with the rules for yoga practice, is completed. —
It was completed on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra in the year 234 Ālaṣka.
This scripture, the Skanda Purāṇa, has been written for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings. 183.1.
May it be auspicious.
(2043 Mārga) The eighty-eighth chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Aryaman struck Prahlāda, the foremost of the Daityas, with many arrows;
he shattered his formidable chariot and cut down his banner.
The valiant Prahlāda, having indeed abandoned his excellent chariot,
fled away just as Rāhu at the appointed time flees from the sun that dispels the darkness.
And as his enemy rushed forward with speed, bewildered, Aryaman struck him with many arrows, just as a cloud strikes a mountain with rain.
Without even counting the arrows, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu rushed forward with speed,
driven by anger, pride, and arrogance.
Seizing the pole of his gold-adorned chariot along with the charioteer,
he then roared out of joy.
Anuhrāda, having reached Dhara, was pierced by him in the middle of the chest;
drawing his sword with speed, he approached Dhara’s chariot. (188.6)
Having severed his banner, his horses, his charioteer, and even his bow, as well as his standard,
he returned once more to his own chariot.
By that deed, Dharā was severely afflicted by the Daitya;
and in this manner, other mighty gods were likewise [afflicted] by other lords of the Daityas.
Some were conquered, some were threatened, and yet others stood ready for battle once more;
then there arose a tumultuous conflict between the gods and the dānavas.
For those desiring to conquer one another, the battle brought fear to the timid;
then there arose kettledrums, conchs, and paṭahas, along with āsekya and puṣkala drums.
Jharjharyas, pepukas, ḍiḍṇimas, and goviṣāṇakas were sounded by the thousands in the armies of both sides, O Vyāsa.
Then [the river] flowed with currents of blood, with banners and flags for its trees,
abounding in elephants and horses for its crocodiles, and with excellent chariots for its turtles.
Abounding with hair as its moss, having bowstrings for its cords, with hissing weapons for its frogs, and foam-like silken garments and parasols; (188.13)
The excellent *uṣṇīṣa* was the swan, and the hands, feet, and head were the pebbles;
the necklaces and armlets were the sand, and the crown was the full-blown lotus. 188.14.
A terrible river, flowing with the mud of fat, blood, and phlegm, and carrying away elephants, horses, and chariots, began to flow, destroying life and vitality.
In that place, the rākṣasas bathe, drink, and take their pleasure;
they also dance in various ways, inspiring fear in those who are timid.
Vultures, jackals, dogs, cats,
and crows took their delight, devouring eyes, hands, feet, and entrails.
"This elephant's foot is mine; this bandage of fat is mine;
and this bright trunk is mine, as is this arm that sheds blood. (188.18)
"This is mine, this is not yours; take it, look!"—thus did those cruel flesh-eaters quarrel there.
And other great chariot-warriors there, having abandoned their slain bodies,
departed for the assembly hall of Brahmā in celestial chariots crowded with women.
Others, performers of evil deeds, being struck by those blinded by rage,
fall into a terrible hell, crying out again and again.
Some, uttering piteous cries,
tormented by arrows, die in battle by the hundreds and even by the thousands.
Others were chewing on grass, while others cried out, "O brother! O son!
Wailing and terrified, the people gave up their lives with great difficulty.
Some great chariot-warriors among the gods and asuras,
their lips bitten together and their vital organs pierced by arrows, fell to the earth like trees.
Inauspicious jackals howled, and the Rākṣasas let out loud bursts of laughter;
likewise, men, elephants, and horses uttered cries of distress.
There were the lion-roars of the heroes and the abundant sounds of their arms,
as well as the noises of being drawn bows and the sounds of musical instruments.
Then Indra, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Yama, the powerful Kāla,
Varuṇa, the Maruts, and all the Viśvedevas [arrived].
Mitra, Jayanta, Bhaga, Pūṣan,
and Aryaman, as well as Rudra who bears the skull and the Vasus of great strength.
Nāsatya, Dasra, and the Pṛśnis, the best of gods—
these and other preeminent deities, mighty of arm.
The powerful ones displayed their force against the army of the Dānavas,
roaring like oceans or like fires at the end of an eon.
Like tempests out of season, like great mountains immovable, like bulls bellowing, and like elephants trumpeting in rut. || 188.31 ||
Seizing like crocodiles and tearing like sea-monsters,
raining down like clouds and roaring like lions,
they all with great force checked the army of the Dānavas.
That army of the Danus and Dānavas, its momentum shattered by Devavega and though exerting itself,
becomes supportless and utterly overwhelmed, like a blade of grass caught in the mouth of a fire.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the Battle.
